en: Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa Pastime.
Śrī Śuka said:
The Blessed One also, beholding those nights when the jasmine flowers were in full bloom during autumn, set his mind on sporting, relying upon his yogic power.
Śrīdhara:

In the twenty-ninth [chapter], however, there are the dialogues between Hari and the gopīs for the sake of the rāsa dance, as well as the wonder of his disappearance during the intensity of that rāsa. (a)
Victorious is the Lord of Śrī, the ornament of the circle of the gopīs' rāsa dance, who destroys the pride of Kāmadeva— the pride that had grown so great as to conquer even Brahmā and the other gods.
Is this not, rather, the opposite? For from his diversion with the wives of others, there is the perception that he was conquered by Kandarpa.
Not so; for it is said: "Resorting to *yoga-māyā*," "Though delighting in the Self, he took pleasure," and "The direct churner of Manmatha himself. [All these refer to] within the Self.
Because independence is proclaimed in such passages as "His amorous play was restrained" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.17) and so forth;

therefore, the truth is simply this: the imitation of the *rāsa*-pastime is for the purpose of demonstrating the conquest of desire. Furthermore, under the guise of erotic narratives, these five chapters are specifically intended for renunciation (*nivṛtti*).

We shall make this clear: the meaning is that those nights were promised by me when I said, "O cowherd women, having gone to Vraja, you shall enjoy these nights with me once they have been accomplished" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.27). ||1||

Vaṃśīdhara: The speech of Hari with the gopīs constitutes the prima facie argument (pūrva-pakṣa); the reply constitutes the counter-argument (uttara-pakṣa). "In the excitement" means at the commencement of the rāsa—a specific kind of dance—or, as the sense implies, during a festival. "Of him," that is, of Hari; "of the disappearance" means of his vanishing from sight; "the curiosity" [is the subject].
And curiosity. ||a||

He is one who destroys the pride and arrogance of Kandarpa—that is, Kāma—who has become so arrogant as to have attained victory over Brahmā and the other gods; he is thus "the destroyer of that pride. He is Maṇḍana because he adorns and beautifies.
He raises a doubt regarding the impropriety of the *rāsa* dance with the words "But surely... (*nanu*). This refers to the *rāsa*-pastime. He refutes this with "Not so" (*maivam*).
For the Lord’s diversion is not like that of an ordinary person, because of His independence and lack of subservience to anything else.
"Mimicry" (*viḍambana*) means imitation; "pretext" (*apadeśa*) means a disguise. "Intent on renunciation" (*nivṛtti-parāḥ*) means those whose purpose is renunciation.

Because of such statements as, "The self becomes detached from desire through the excessive indulgence in desires," the supreme state (*parāvasthatva*) will become manifest upon the cessation of the supreme love for the Lord previously performed by the women of Vraja toward all objects pertaining to this world and the next. Who are they? Those who... thus [it is said].

"Pratiśrutāḥ" means "promised"; such is the meaning. However, it should be understood that in this context the word *tat* does not refer to common renown (*prasiddhi*). Alternatively, [the phrase] "having seen those ignorant creatures"—of what nature were they? "Rātrīḥ," meaning pervaded by darkness like the night.
Likewise, "śaradā" refers to those who cut or shatter like arrows—namely, sons and others who cause suffering;

toward them, there are notions of pleasure, as if they were blossoming jasmine flowers and the like. Not seeing a means of rescue for them apart from their own beloveds and so forth, [the poet] employs that illusion (*māyā*) regarding non-unions, or rather, for the sake of non-union with the impure and so forth.

"Resorting to that *māyā* for the sake of yoga within himself"—according to the *Śāśvata* lexicon, *māyā* means compassion (*kṛpā*), saliva (*lālā*), primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), and likewise deceit (*chala*).
Alternatively, [it refers to] those subjects in the form of seekers of knowledge (*jijñāsu*). Of what nature are they? [They are so called] from the root *rā*, meaning "to give."

Or [he refers to] those noble women who have practiced renunciation for three nights and offer themselves; likewise, those who are detached from sense-pleasures— which pierce like arrows when characterized by blooming jasmine flowers— having resorted to compassion for their sake, so that there may be a non-union with them and the sublation of the superimposition of the adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Alternatively, *yogāya* means for the sake of yoga, which is non-difference from Brahman; *mā* means valid cognition, and [the word *upāśrita*] refers to those [cognitions] by which [He] was resorted to for that purpose.

Or else, those nights (*rātrīḥ*) were the cowherd women (*gopī*) who offered themselves to Him; they are called *śaradā* because they "cut" (*dyati*) like an arrow (*śara*) during separation from Him.
They are those whose *mallikā* jasmine flowers are in full bloom (*utphulla*), and for them, it was for the sake of non-union with Him due to family shame and other such constraints.
Or, having taken refuge in compassion for his own yoga;
or else, with his mind fixed upon that beauty of her limbs— which, being unfit for others and unsuitable for anyone else, is fit for him alone.

Alternatively, she whom the Blessed One has taken as his refuge is Rādhā. Of what nature is she? She whose limbs possess eternal beauty (*mā*). He too has fixed his mind upon her, in whom that very union (*yoga*) is the beauty (*mā*). The rest is the same.

Alternatively, *yoga-māyā* refers to the flute, whose sound (*māyā*) leads to union (*yoga*) with the beauties of Vraja; this is the form derived from the root *māṅ* (to measure/sound) with the suffix *ghañ*. Having resorted to that [flute], he drew it forth from between his belly and his garment and placed it in his mouth.

Alternatively, *yogamāyā* refers to Śrī Rādhā, who attains—that is, reaches—the splendor of *yoga* (union) and *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment), for she is the cause of the *rāsa*-dance; one who has taken refuge in her with the mind [is called *yogamāyāśrita*].
Or else, *yogamā* refers to Rādhā, because she is measured or known (*mīyate*) by *yogas*, that is, by yogins such as Brahmā and others. And since... [yac]... [the rest of the sentence follows].

"She is to be contemplated by the lords of all"—this is the statement of Nārada in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. The meaning is: she is that splendor toward which even the Blessed Lord set his mind to sport, having taken refuge in her. Having done what? Having beheld the blossoming jasmine flowers. Of what nature were they? Star-like.

Those nights are called *trapanti* because the stars (*nakṣatrāṇi*) are ashamed (*trapante*) or feel embarrassed (*lajjante*) by them. The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to the root *trap* preceded by the prefix *tārā* according to the *uṇādi* rules. By what means? It is by the autumn (*śarad*), so called because it protects (*dayate*, i.e., *rakṣati*) from the arrows (*śarebhyaḥ*), namely the arrows of Kāma; thus it is *śarad*. The elision of the vowel *ā* after the suffix *kvip* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. [It means] "by the multitude of gopīs."
The meaning is as follows:

Or rather, that Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is "āpita," meaning devoid of any other protector, and thus independent—even He set His mind upon going to Himālaya to conquer desire and for the sake of sport. Ahead, on the Himālaya...

It is called *āgama* because one is measured—that is, harmed—by Śiva; the dative case is used here according to the rule "the word following a verb meaning 'to act' takes the dative when it denotes the object of the action. This conduct is clear in the Śaiva tradition. Having done what? Having [avoided] those who protect from the enemy—the science of desire (*kāma-śāstra*)—thus they are *artātryas*. The meaning is "rows of women. Whom? Her.

This is because of the statement beginning with, "having taken refuge [against] the enemies that are the senses, which are difficult to conquer. Of what nature are they? They are those in whom *utphulla-mallikās*—that is, *mallikā* flowers—are present; the meaning is that they have performed their adornment (*kṛta-śṛṅgārāḥ*). Having seen them.
Alternatively, because of the state of being as piercing as an arrow (*śara*), he protects (*dayate*) from *saṃsāra*; thus, he is *śaradaḥ*.
By that [knowledge], his intellect became pure. "Ām" refers to wandering in this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*);

"āmupa" is knowledge because it protects one from that [wandering]; he was dependent upon that. The meaning is that he engaged in dalliance after reflecting with the thought, "I must conquer this desire through women under the pretext of play. Enough of this elaboration.

From this point forward, following this asterisk, we shall present the entire commentary on the *Rāsapañcādhyāyī* composed by Viśvanātha Cakravartin, titled *Savaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī*. This is because we were not fully satisfied with the few alternative readings provided here.

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "The Lord also," and so forth. Although the Lord is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise, in that *rāsa*-pastime He resorted to *yogamāyā*, which is expert at bringing about what is difficult to accomplish. Here, that which was difficult for the Blessed One [to achieve] must be justified.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: having been thus instructed, he set his mind on sporting. As for the activity of *yogamāyā*, all of this occurs according to the principle stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.1.25: "But the work of *yogamāyā* will come to pass for the sake of the task.
For instance, when the gopīs departed from their homes, they were beyond the sight of their husbands, sons, and others, who remained unaware.

Their knowledge was such that they thought, "Our respective wives are staying by our own sides" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38), and so forth; likewise, during their return as they were, they thought, "We are eating, having set aside our meal" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.6), and so on, as well as regarding their various appropriate dress and ornaments at the time of the Rāsa dance.

[The term] *sampādana* [means]: in the state of identity (*tādātmya*), assuming forms such as hostile *pūtanā* demons; at the end of the *rāsa*-dance, after the water-play, the providing of different garments, ornaments, and so forth; and other similar instances should be inferred accordingly.
This is because, in the verse beginning with "those nights" (*tā rātrīḥ*), many nights are not perceived simultaneously. This...

The meaning is as follows: for indeed, since this rāsa-līlā was actually to be accomplished over many nights, He made the resolve that "may many nights be gathered together in one"; and having seen the nights appearing at that very moment in personified form with their hands joined in reverence, [He accepted them].
The object expressed by the plural number is the referent of the pronoun, and this is its limit:

either "the nights [spent] during the autumn or the year," or else, "in which the *mallikā* flowers are in full bloom"; or alternatively, the meaning is "the autumnal nights in which the *mallikā* swans are in full bloom (*utphulla*) and radiant. By that—
Or rather, it means "those nights which are the nights of the autumn season. ||1||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Obeisances to Kṛṣṇa, the relisher of the rasa of the rāsa dance! Thus spoke the illustrious Bādarāyaṇi. The venerable Śrī Vyāsa Bādarāyaṇa performed great austerities at Badarikāśrama;
he was the son who was the very fruit of his penance.
The fact that [this narrative] consists of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of love for the Blessed Lord, who is the glory of omniscience, and so forth, has been suggested.

Because it was spoken by Him, it is intended that this narration is in every respect both a means and an end, and is composed of the aesthetic flavor of love. Therefore, the implication is that this should be heard with devotion.

Now, demonstrating that His primary purpose for that incarnation is the expansion of a particular kind of divine love by means of fulfilling the desires of the illustrious gopīs, and revealing that sporting with them alone constitutes His supreme bliss— therein, through such acts as drinking the nectar of their lips and so forth.

Describing the Śrī Rāsa-krīḍā with those women who are truly His equals— due to their perfect accomplishment of the expansion of special love through the experience of the particular sweetness of the Śrī Bhagavān’s form and other qualities— the author, using the fifth chapter which is as dear to Him as His own life-breath, first shows the necessary ingredients for that pastime therein:

And while describing the attraction of the assembly of Śrī Gopikās, he speaks of the manifestation of a particular state of being (bhāva) on the part of the Blessed Lord as the cause thereof, saying: "The Blessed Lord... This pastime should be understood to have occurred during his youth (kaiśora), at a time appropriate for it. Thus it is stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Madhusūdana, whose nature is immeasurable and who has destroyed his enemies, took delight with them during the nights, honoring his youthful age. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.60).
And in the Śrī Hari-vaṃśa:
"Knowing the proper time for his resolve, he took pleasure with those young cowherd girls at night, honoring their youthful beauty. (Hari-vamśa 2.20.18).
And this is because, at the commencement of the *rāsa* dance, he is supremely enchanting due to the recollection of his particular excellence, such as his beauty.

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa was not able to state explicitly— as in the passage beginning, "And thereafter, having reached the age of paugaṇḍa in Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.15.1)— that "that play pervaded the entirety of His youth," and so forth; all of this shall be explained in its proper place later, for the sake of illustration here.

At the beginning of their youth, this is called the first night’s play. The term "Bhagavān" is used here with the intention of manifesting the essence of His entire divine majesty (*bhagavattā*) during the *rāsa*-dance. Nanda and the others became immersed in supreme bliss, and the Blessed Lord Himself was likewise immersed in supreme bliss.

The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is that he set his mind upon, or desired, becoming a jewel and performing a particular kind of sport. "Those nights" refers precisely to the meaning suggested by those [words]; or else, they are indefinable.

The meaning is that they are most excellent at all times, consisting of the essence of supreme bliss, and fit for his sport. By the use of the plural number, it is understood that his sport occurs over many nights;
and that will clearly manifest with particular distinction. By means of the autumn, the *mallikā* jasmine has blossomed fully and opened its flowers.

Regarding those [flowers]: although all kinds of flowers bloom eternally in Śrī Vṛndāvana, which is the abode of all seasons, and specifically in autumn, even the jasmine, white water-lily, red lotus, and others blossom, nevertheless, the term "full-blown jasmine" (utphulla-mallikā) is used with the intention of referring to its specific blossoming during the night. Thus...

"Even at the beginning, [he saw] the lotus-filled [lake]," and so on. Having observed these excitants (*uddīpana*) and having reflected that she was a fit object for his love, he—being a particular manifestation of the power of *saccidānanda* known by the name Yogamāyā—resorted to her as an instrument and manifested [the pastimes].
Thus, among all his divine sports (*līlā*), the Rāsa dance is especially distinguished.

The specific supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and so forth are intended here. Furthermore, the fact that every divine play (*līlā*) consists of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) has already been explained previously in the eighth chapter regarding the childhood pastimes.
Alternatively, *yoga* refers to sovereignty; *māyā* conjoined with that is compassion (*dayā*). For the word *māyā* is used in the senses of both deception and mercy.
The meaning is that Viśva, having resorted to her as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), expanded his own sovereignty and compassion through the *rāsa*-pastime.

Alternatively, the word "api" (even/also) may be construed right here [with "Viśva"], where "yoga" refers to delighting in the Self (*ātmārāmatā*) and "māyā" refers to that which is of the nature of concealment (*āvaraṇātmikā*).
Even though he was constantly resorting to deceit (*kāpaṭya*) or to illusion (*māyā*) joined with yoga, at that time neither yoga nor illusion remained; rather,
his true nature, which consists in the expansion of the wealth of love for his own lotus feet, became manifest.
The meaning is as follows:

Or rather, even though he resorted to that *māyā*—which, in the context of union (*yoga*), means deception, like that found among the wives of sacrificers—at that time his *māyā* had not yet ceased during their encounter. This applies to all [the women] indeed.
Because a specific form of direct union with the Gopīs was accomplished, and because even those who had attained perfection achieved that [union];
or else, she is *Yogā*, for she is *Mā* (Lakṣmī), who eternally joins [the Lord] and attains union upon His chest.

The meaning is: "even though he is constantly present in her, and even though she is always serving him. Thus, it is intended that the *rāsa*-pastime would not be accomplished with her, and that she would be difficult to attain.

Alternatively, *yogamāyā* refers to the flute, which has the word *māyā* for its purpose of union (*yoga*)—that is, for the sake of joining (*saṃyoga*). [The term] *mā* is used in the sense of measuring (*māna*).
The form "śabde" is derived from the suffix *ghañ*; she has taken refuge in that.

Alternatively, *yoga-māyā* refers to Śrī Rādhā, in whom there is the measure (*mā*) or sufficiency (*paryāpti*) of *yoga*, meaning union (*saṃyoga*). Or else, it refers to her who possesses the *mā*—that is, the *lakṣmī* or prosperity—of *yoga*, meaning union.

She who goes to, that is, attains [the goal], is Yogamāyā, who is Śrī Rādhā herself; he has taken refuge in her with his mind, because the rāsa-krīḍā is caused by her, as is well known in the Padma Purāṇa. ||1||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Salutations to the lovers of the rasa of the *rāsa* dance! Here, in this commentary, the phrase "the intensity of the *rāsa*" (*rāsa-saṃrambha*) means that one observes the pride associated with the commencement of the *rāsa* for that purpose. Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of being the conqueror," it refers specifically to the state of being a conqueror whose agent is Kandarpa (the God of Love).

The meaning is "by way of a condition" (*pratyayāt*). Now, by the force of this context concerning the great majesty that is about to be described—beginning with the words "Then, at the root [of the tree], Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said"—this very point is established:
that the blessed Śrī Bādarāyaṇa, Veda-Vyāsa, [attained that] through the performance of great austerity at Badarikāśrama.

And since that omniscient one’s austerity was characterized solely by the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it was appropriate for him to apply his resolve toward that most supreme goal; thus, although his son was the fruit of such austerity and possessed qualities such as omniscience and being composed of the nectar of love for the Blessed Lord to a greater degree than others, [he was not born].
Nevertheless, even as it vibrates [in the heart], the culmination of the greatness of its etymological derivation occurs right here;

therefore, it is implied that it should be heard with such devotion alone. In the reading "Śrī Śuka said," however, because of the nature of its supremely radiant rasa, the quality of its most tender speech is demonstrated; hence—
It is indicated that this [scripture] must be heard with precisely such a state of mind; for indeed,

the primary purpose of the Śrī Bhagavān— who performs everything for the sake of the happiness of His beloved alone— is simply to fulfill the heart's desires of the beautiful women of Vraja, who possess a love that surpasses all else.

Thus demonstrating that very state to be his bliss surpassing all others, and revealing it therein— as the direct destroyer of the God of Love, as possessing a body that is the sole abode of the Fortune of the three worlds, and as that for which the Gopīs performed penance— he [describes] those things difficult even for those who delight in the Self of all to obtain.
Because of the experience of the Lord’s unique form, taste, fragrance, touch, and sound—
and because His nectar-like flavor from His lower lip is absolutely impossible to find elsewhere—
He performs the *rāsa*-dance play together with those women who are worthy of Him, through the perfect accomplishment of the expansion of that particular love.

He describes [the seasons] in five chapters, which are as dear as the five senses themselves—beginning with "Where the bee-like eyes, having drunk the nectar from Mukunda’s mouth... and so forth; with "The gopīs experienced supreme bliss at the sight of Govinda... and so forth; with "Thus autumn, with its clear waters... and so forth; and [then] in Hemanta.
And by the verse beginning with "In the first month, you moved," he has specifically described their [the women's] and his own fresh passion;
and by the verse beginning with "O dear one, like a lotus well-born in an autumnal lake," he has expressed his laughter.

Recalling what was described by them through such passages as "beginning with," "at the end of the day," and "in secret, the arising of desire in the heart," and remembering their own future description of the new union as something to be characterized by its extreme excellence, the Blessed One says: "The Blessed One also... The word "also" (api) refers to those [women].
It causes one to forget the fresh passion previously described; indeed, by the preceding statement,
it makes known the very novelty of this union— that for all this time those women had been intent on making love with minds fickle due to their passion, whereas the Blessed One...
Although love had arisen within him, he waited for a specific time with fortitude and did not act now;

for these girls, having reached the middle of their youth, were unique among maidens due to their bestowing of all happiness, their auspiciousness, and their manifest excellence in flute-playing and other arts. And by me [this was observed] regarding these young women.

"Enjoy the nights," thus was it promised; yet, seeing that those very nights had arrived, and because his fortitude had dissolved due to the intensity of his passion at the onset of the full moon night, he perceived them as being that very circle [of the moon] through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), just as in the passage beginning "The sages delight in themselves," O Blessed One.
Although He was already fulfilled in all His purposes, by perceiving those nights as an intensifying factor (*uddīpana*),
the greatness of His love for them— whose very forms served as the objects of that perception— is shown through the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*). For this very reason,
even His youth, in which all His purposes were manifest, came to be honored, as stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*.
This has been shown:
"Honoring his youth, that Madhusūdana,
whose self is immeasurable and who has destroyed his enemies, took delight with them during the nights" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.60).
In the *Hari-vaṃśa*:
"Knowing the proper time for his resolve, he took pleasure with those young cowherd girls at night, honoring their youth. (HV 2.20.18) Thus it is said.

In this context, the phrase "one who knows the proper time" (*kālavit*) has been explained; and the statement "he gazed upon those nights and rejoiced with them" indicates the meaning of the expression "he set his mind on sporting. The use of the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) suffix here indicates that the action is for the agent's own benefit (*svārthakriyā*), according to the rule: "The [suffix] following a root marked with a svarita accent is used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent."

Thus, by resorting to this specific grammatical rule (*pā. 1.3.72*), the word *tāḥ* (those) itself reveals its own charming temporal distinction; and having manifested that, the author also displays the splendor of Śrī Vṛndāvana as kindled by it, saying "by autumn" (*śaradā*). By means of autumn, those [forests] are such that in them the jasmine (*mallikā*) has blossomed intensely.
Because the mutual conjunction [of these factors] is unprecedented, this indicates the extraordinary nature of both this autumn and the jasmine flowers;

by this, all flowers whatsoever are implied, thereby demonstrating that the objects of perception (ālambana), the time, and the place bestow supreme bliss consisting of love upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa. For this reason...

This desire for amorous play (*riraṃsā*) consists precisely of that specific love characterized by *hlādinī* potency and manifesting as divine play (*vilāsa*); it is not composed of material lust (*prākṛta-kāma*). Therefore, their explanation—that this [text] is a weapon against the pride of Cupid—is likewise entirely appropriate.
Furthermore, he himself will state that these five chapters are devoted to renunciation (*nivṛtti*).
In the thirty-second [chapter], Hari, his heart moistened by the pangs of separation from their conversation,
appeared there and consoled those gopīs, honoring them.
"The son of Nanda has arisen, ever delighting the gopīs whose hearts are overwhelmed by the surging waves of the nectar of His own love. Thus it was said;
and the illustrious Lord of Sages will also say this very thing: "And this is the sporting with the women of Vraja..."
In the passage beginning with "viṣṇoḥ" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.40), explaining how He accomplishes what is difficult to achieve,
he says: "Resorting to *yogamāyā*— the supreme, inconceivable power— in its proximity, wherever He sports,
there He is always reached by her, just as the sun is always reached by its own rays."

The state of possessing such power by His very nature (*svābhāvika*) has been indicated; by that, the performance of those seemingly difficult pastimes (*durghaṭa-tallīlā*) will be established—this is the intended meaning. Through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), "union" (*yoga*) means conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For that purpose, there is *māyā*; according to the *Viśvakośa*, *māyā* [is used] in the sense of deception and in the sense of grace (*kṛpā*). He has resorted to that [grace] preeminently (*upa*). Furthermore, those...

Having observed [the moon] in succession up to the full moon (rākā), his desire increased more and more; thus, when the general meaning has been established, this specific detail should also be understood: having returned home in the evening on that full-moon night, and having performed his meal and other duties, he went from his mother’s quarters to the door of the moon-chamber (candra-śālikā) in the bedchamber.
The meaning is that he determined it to be something that could be accomplished immediately. ||1||
The sequence of the composition: By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the Lord also," it is implied that his beloveds are also included.

They captivate our minds by their own sweetness; for even the autumn season consists of the time of pastimes filled with such rasa, characterized by the blossoming of jasmine flowers. [He employs] *yogamāyā*.
"Resorting to" means being near;
that is to say, by virtue of the opportunity for such service, one is situated in proximity to such power. ||1||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, having quelled the pride of Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others,

the Blessed One— desiring to commence the dance called *rāsa*, which involves being simultaneously joined by a multitude of many beautiful women in order to quell the pride of Kandarpa— once manifested the majesty of His own yogic power.
In that regard, the definition of *rāsa* is as follows:
"Where a single dancer dances in a circle with many dancing girls moving about, the wise know that indeed as *hallīśaka*."

This very same [dance], through its various movements and rhythmic bindings (*tāla-bandha*), becomes primarily the *rāsa* dance; it does not exist even in heaven, much less on earth. Because of its difficulty, its supreme loveliness, and because it must be maintained with equal timing for a long duration, one must perform many nights in this manner in a single place.

Because his resolve had been made, at that very moment he beheld before him many deities presiding over the night who had appeared; seeing them, he desired to sport, as the Lord said in the passage beginning with "The Blessed One" (*bhagavān api*).
Although the Blessed One possesses inconceivable majesty, having resorted to his *yoga-māyā*, he set his mind on sporting.
The meaning is this: in this play (*vilāsa*), many difficult combinations of events are conceivable;
however, those can only be accomplished through the power of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*), being capable of being performed by mere will alone.
Nevertheless, the manifestation of such power within the sweetness and tenderness of the subsequent aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not particularly pleasing.

The meaning is that he, having relied upon her as one who is to be commanded—having previously relied upon her as his own embodied power of yoga (*yoga-śakti*) which had descended [to earth] long ago with the words, "She will manifest for the sake of accomplishing each respective task" (*bhā.pu. 10.1.25*)—commanded her, saying, "In this pastime, everything must be accomplished by you. Thus.

This is another meaning: having done what? Having observed those nights—that is, having kept in mind that those many nights previously calculated should be gathered together—this is the meaning of the word "tāḥ" (those).
The plural form "rātrīḥ" (nights) is used because it is impossible for many nights that arrive in succession to be perceived simultaneously.

The phrase "the presiding deities of the night" expresses a plural sense; for within the glorious form (vigraha) which is a mass of bliss, since there is an absence of internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), only the power of will (icchā-śakti) is possible,
even though [the form] is the object of an action to be accomplished by extraordinary effort (alaukika-kṛti).

The meaning of the word *manas* is that he made his mind the object of an action to be accomplished through worldly effort, and thus he took possession of his mind. Through the taking of possession of the mind, there is also the taking of possession of the mind-born [passion]. Of what kind were the nights?
They were those in which the *mallikā* jasmine flowers bloomed in autumn; "autumnal" (*śāradya*) means belonging to the autumn, and "blooming *mallikā*" refers to the blossoming jasmine.

*unmallikāḥ* means blossoming jasmine; *phulla-mallikāḥ* also means blossoming jasmine. In spring, they are *unmukha-mallikāḥ* (upward-facing jasmine); in summer, they are *phulla-mallikāḥ*. Subsequently, by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound, the masculine form is established through the rule of *puṃvadbhāva*.
By this, the nights associated with autumn, spring, and summer, having come together in one place—

The meaning is that deities conceiving themselves as one hundred and eighty nights arrived all at once. It was not only out of timidity; "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) signifies supreme sovereignty. This being so, he remained as if having slept for a single night, as before, in the presence of his mother and father. For this indeed—
His sovereignty. ||1||
Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (Śrī-Rasikāhlādinī): I bow to the Guru, the ocean of mercy, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss,
by whose grace many have attained the knowledge of the Bhāgavata.
Having churned all the Vedas like nectar from the ocean of milk,
that knowledge of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata was proclaimed by the Blessed One himself; now,
let its entirety, which constitutes its very essence, be declared in five chapters.

In that regard, the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*) has first been determined according to the tenth *skandha*. Therefore, here in these five chapters, the mutual cessation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His beloved circle is described.

That [cessation], however, consists of a state of playful love (*preman*) characterized by pastimes, preceded by the suppression of other mellows (*rasa*), and abiding within the body, senses, and mind.
Regarding "cessation" (nirodha): the definition of love (*prema*) is given in the *Rasārṇava*: "That love is the bond of feeling between the two youths, devoid of duality" (*Raṣū* 2.112).
In this love, there is an embrace between the circle of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds like milk and water, due to their state of aesthetic unity (*sāmarasya*).
It cannot be distinguished by way of deficiency or excess. As it has been said:
"Between the two selves, and likewise between the served and the server, there is an embrace like that of milk and water, as well as the state of being the locus of objects."
Such a state even in women is designated as *preman* (love);
here, the wise should understand that there are twenty-two kinds of *śleṣa* (cohesion).
For instance, the complete union between the minds of the beloved circle and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is like that of milk and water;
everything else has already been explained in the *Bhakti-rasa-taraṅgiṇī*,
wherein there is a unification of the heart, senses, and mind with the body, senses, and mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The queens of Vraja sang of their own hearts with the following verse:
"Our minds, though they find happiness in our homes, have been stolen away by You; even our hands, though they remain for household duties, have been carried off."
"Your feet do not move even a step from the soles of Your feet; how then shall we go to Vraja, or what indeed shall we do?
This is the union with their own hearts, performed by the queens of Vraja [and] performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

He said: This has been described in passages such as *bāhu-prasāra-parirambha* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.46) and elsewhere in *gaty-anurāga* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.2). However, this particular form of union occurs only through *nirodha* (suppression), and there is an illustration of that therein.
"The two pigeons, their hearts multiplied by affection, being householders,
bound eye to eye, limb to limb, and mind to mind.
Regarding this, some say the creation was for the sake of enjoyment, while others say it was for the sake of sport.
"This is simply the very nature of the Lord; what desire can there be for one whose desires are already fulfilled"?

Furthermore, from the sūtra *lokavat tu līlā-kaivalyam* (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.33), it is seen that in some instances it is called *līlā*, in others *krīḍā*, and in others *karman*. Among these, an action performed through *yogamāyā* is *līlā*.

Action manifested together with a circle of loved ones is *krīḍā* (play); however, because it shares the commonality of play, the bodily exertion involved is termed *karman* (action). All three of these do not deviate from the nature of *vilāsa* (graceful charm).
An example of *līlā* (sportive dalliance) is the definition: "Action manifested through the sweet sentiment (*madhura-rasa*) is *vilāsa*."

It is said that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, entered into two of them at a time [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.3]. His effortless entry into their midst was due to his power of lightness (*lāghava-śakti*); that is indeed a playful pastime (*līlā-vilāsa*), a noble activity performed together with them [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.43].

It is indeed play (*krīḍā*) and pastime (*vilāsa*). Consequently, even the general bodily activity described as "in the grove of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇopavana*) is nothing but pastime. Elsewhere, however, that [activity] belongs to different subjects within the *vatsalya* (parental affection), *sakhya* (friendship), and other rasas; here, however, there is a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatva*). Thus...
Having described cessation (*nirodha*) from objects of different natures, cessation from those of the same nature is stated here:
"They came together, their efforts unobserved" (*bhā.pu.* 10.29.4), because of their sovereignty over bodies;
thus, the cessation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is described by the Lord of Sages: "The Blessed One also... (*bhā.pu.* 10.29.1).
He declares the excellence of the work by means of its specific relationship, subject matter, and purpose:

the relationship is that of the expounder and the expounded. Therein, the subject matter (*pratipādya*) is the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His beloved circle; the expounder (*pratipādaka*) is Śrī Śuka. Of that [work]...
The inclination toward the manifestation of divine pastimes occurs precisely through restraint. As it has been said:

"O royal sage, although he was firmly established in the state beyond the modes of nature (nirguṇya), his heart was captivated by the pastimes of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttama-śloka), such that he studied this narrative" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.1.9).

"Even though he delights in the Self, he took delight [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.42]; even though he is the Blessed Lord,"—thus there is a cessation due to his divine sovereignty. Just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa engages in pastimes precisely through the manifestation of his divine sovereignty, so too does the Lord of Sages engage in the exposition of these pastimes. Therefore:

He speaks of the excellence of the relationship between the object of instruction and the instructor: Śrī Kṛṣṇa is both the object and the substratum for His beloved circle, just as the moon is to its moonlight; likewise, the beloved circle is both the object and the substratum for Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Otherwise, in the absence of either one, it would be a mere semblance, [as would be the case] with the heart of the beloved circle.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa is both the object and the substratum, like the moon and its moonlight. The beloved circle is both the object and the substratum of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s heart. Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body is both the object and the substratum of the beloved circle. Śrī Kṛṣṇa is both the object and the substratum of the beloved circle’s heart.

The beloved circle is both the object and the locus for Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s heart; Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body is both the object and the locus for the beloved circle; Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s consciousness residing within the beloved circle is both the object and the locus; and Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body residing within the beloved circle is both the object and the locus.
The mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has the minds of His beloved circle as its object and support;

the eyes of the beloved circle have Śrī Kṛṣṇa as their object, and so too do the eyes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thus, the state of mutual subject and object is described, and it is this alone that is stated to be the subject matter of the book, and nothing else.
Thus [it is said].

By this, the excellence of the subject matter has been stated; now he speaks of the excellence of the purpose: "by means of the manifestation of the eternal youthful play, through the pacification of the disease of the heart, which is worldly desire."

This very purpose— that those who possess mundane desire may witness the mutual pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His beloved circle, and thus experience longing and become favorable toward them— will be explained further ahead with the words: "The sporting with the women of Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.42).

The Lord of Sages, possessing this very inquiry and intending to describe his own intended pastimes, first elucidates the mental play (*mānasī-līlā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, beginning with the arising of *bhāva*. Regarding that, it is said in the *Rasārṇava*: "The first modification of the mind, which is otherwise changeless, is *bhāva*."

In the *Sāhitya-darpaṇa*: "Bhāva is the first modification in a mind that is otherwise devoid of change" (*Sāḍa* 3.93). Regarding the definition of love (*prema*): "That love is the bond of feeling between a young couple that is free from differentiation" (*Raṣū* 2.112). Thus, love is indeed a specific kind of *bhāva*.
The two are not synonymous. Although love is indeed indivisible and eternally established,

and its means of accomplishment are likewise eternally established, nevertheless, the sequential arising of the relationship between the limb and the possessor of the limb is figuratively attributed to the related entity, just as in the case of the relationship with a kingdom.
Now, the state that serves as the limit [of love] is described. As it is said therein:
"The first stage of love is designated as *bhāva*.
Here, the *sāttvika* emotions, such as tears and horripilation, appear in only slight measure."
But through transformations of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth, it incites one toward sexual union;
*bhāva* itself, when its transformations are only slightly perceptible, is desired as *hāva*.
When *hāva* itself attains fullness,
it is indeed designated as *helā*, having reached the highest state preceded by love.
In that regard, through the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary states (sāttvikas), the transitory emotions (vyabhicārins),
the objects of perception, and the attendants, Kṛṣṇa indeed attains delight.
In this context, the determinants (*ālambana-vibhāva*) are Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the circle of beloveds;

the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) are the moon, moonlight, sandalwood paste, the autumn season, jasmine, and so forth; the consequents (*anubhāva*) are the mutual transformations of the eyebrows, eyes, and other features of the young couple; and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) are the thirty-three [emotions] when they are not within the range of sight.

The transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) are lassitude, delusion, fainting, dejection, and so forth. The objects (*viṣaya*) are the mutual limbs and other parts of both [the hero and the heroine], while the attendants (*paricāra*) are the female friends and so on. Through these, the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is brought forth.
Emotion (*bhāva*), however, is a mental state that arises as a transformation in the mind when it is affected by the excitant factors (*uddīpanavibhāva*).
The awakening of the internal state (*bhāva*). When that occurs, the radiant permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is established.
When that is established, Śrī Kṛṣṇa considers Himself to be full of bliss; therefore, this work has been undertaken for His sake.
In this regard, the verse cited by the teachers as the introductory benediction (*upoddhāta*) is now explained:

Victorious is the Lord of Śrī, the destroyer of the pride of Kandarpa— who was himself deeply rooted in the pride of having conquered Brahmā and the other gods— and the ornament of the circle of the Gopīs' rāsa dance;
he has become such as this.

Alternatively, He for whom the circle of the gopīs' rāsa dance is an ornament—this mutual relationship of the decorator and the decorated being common [to all beings]—is the divine manifestation of that which was previously described as ordinary desire; for this divine desire, by the discharge of its final element, overcomes even Brahmā and the other gods. Thus is desire.

He was overcome by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. This will be explained further on. From the indicative mark in the passage, "Having restrained his amorous passion within himself" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.26), it is clear that he was indeed conquered by the extraordinary desire characterized as *nirodha* (spiritual restraint); for, disregarding his status as the Lord of Lakṣmī, he became the ornament of the circle of the Gopīs' rāsa dance. And He will say:

Even though he delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*), he nonetheless took delight [in the gopīs]. Furthermore, his state of delighting in the Self appears to have been made secondary, because the intended meaning is the attainment of his true nature through the manifestation of sweet rasa (*madhura-rasa*) by means of sporting with the gopīs. Moreover, by the phrase "he is directly Manmatha," it is indicated that even Manmatha lacks the power to delude him here within the Self.
The statement "his sexual passion was restrained" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.26) is indeed wonderful;

for when the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa was obstructed by the amorous charms of the beauties of Vraja, even the activity born of the mind was restrained— thereby implying the restraint of even the final element (*carama-dhātu*), which is the specific activity of the mind.

"Extinction has arisen"—this is how the meaning should be understood. Otherwise, there would be no reconciliation for the cowherd women of Vraja who possess many herds; therefore, another distinct characteristic of their extinction will be described.
With their senses overwhelmed by the joy of contact with his limbs, the women of Vraja were not even able to straighten their hair, their silken garments, or the ribbons on their breasts.
"O best of the Kurus, their garlands and ornaments were disarrayed. Thus it is said.
He states the subject at hand: "In this context, play (līlā) is declared to be threefold: mental, as well as vocal," and so forth.
And by means of the body, there are three types, each of which has its own distinct divisions.
Mental pastimes, such as: "When they have arrived, I shall offer them a beautiful welcome;
I shall display the great fear that exists both here and in the hereafter."
Afterwards, I shall proclaim the Dharma through an examination of their hearts;
I shall listen to their reasoning and their supreme loss of fortitude.
I shall perform a wonderful rāsa-dance with all of them,
including embraces, scratching with the fingernails, and excellent conversation and jesting.
Together with them, I shall perform the granting of boons just as it was done before;
for thus is the mental sport itself, consisting of the bliss of meditation.
Furthermore:
"Welcome to you, O fortunate ones; what pleasing service may I do for you?
This and similar speech is known as *vācikī* (verbal) [courtesy], intended for the purpose of testing their disposition.
"The body is considered to be manifold, beginning with the 'outstretched arms' [mudrā]," so it is said.
Now, if the eternality of the *līlā* (divine play) is heard in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* as being authoritative according to the Vedas and Purāṇas—[as it says]:
"That Madhusūdana, honoring his youthful age... always intoxicated by the rasa of the *rāsa* dance"—then that...
Standing among the multitude of Vraja goddesses, He indeed sports like a horse; how then can it be called the *rāsa*-pastime?

To this he says: as it has been stated—"Madhuvana is meritorious, where there is the eternal presence of Hari"; and furthermore, "Mathurā is [meritorious], where the Blessed Lord Hari is eternally present. Thus, in Mathurā...
Just as the eternal presence [of the Lord] in Devakī is described as if it were a beginning due to His manifestation therein,

so too here, this rāsa-sport of the maidens, occasioned by the granting of boons, is depicted as if it had a beginning. Yet, in this Vṛndāvana forest, the seasons indeed revolve according to the divisions of space, and likewise—

In this region, the dwelling place of the autumn season, having seen the splendor produced by autumn, those promised nights entered the path of my memory; seeing those promised nights and seeing the *mallikā* flowers in full bloom because of the autumn, [I thought: "You shall enjoy these nights. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.27)
This is a qualification of the night. Although the Blessed Lord is fully endowed with all sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*), he disregarded them and set his mind—
meaning, he directed his heart— toward sporting with the beauties of Vraja solely through the play of the nature of cessation (*nirodhātmaka-vilāsa*).
Go! The gopīs are of five kinds: the eternally perfected (nitya-siddhās), those perfected through worship (upāsanā-siddhās), the Śrutis, the Ṛṣis, and the goddesses.
The eternally perfected ones have been seen. A desire to sport arose in the Śrutis.
That is stated in the Bṛhad-vāmana Purāṇa: "He who stands in the midst of that cluster [of trees], Acyuta, in the form of a youth"—thus [they saw] him.

Upon seeing them, a desire to sport with them arose in him. The Blessed One granted them a boon: "In the former Sārasvata Kalpa, you shall become the cowherd girls (*gopīs*) in Vraja. As for these maidens who are now the *Śrutis*, having seen their former passion and being purified by the merit arising from the worship of Kātyāyanī, I have granted this boon under a pretext: 'You shall take delight with me.'"

Regarding the word "nights": those maidens remained waiting for that time out of a desire for dalliance born of fresh passion, thinking, "When will he call us and give us pleasure? Therefore, as each promised time arrived and seeing those promised nights pass, he set his mind on sporting with them. Now—

The sense is that it was precisely the nights of the autumn season that became the awakeners of emotion (*bhāva*). He will state later the signs for the awakening of emotion: "She sang sweetly, enchanting the minds of the fair-eyed ones. Although there were twelve residents of Vraja qualified for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and everyone heard the resonance, nevertheless—
"Only those who are already possessed of a sweet longing are attracted by the sound of the flute, not others.

[An objection: "But why was this not done at the very time of granting the boon? [The reply: "They were not delighted then; the intention here is that, because they were of tender age previously, it would have been inappropriate to summon them for the sake of amorous play. Now,"

She was seen to be suitable because her age was conducive to amorous play, and she was brought [to him]. Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s age has always remained that of youth (kaiśoraka), and therefore his fitness for amorous play arose. This was stated by Parāśara: "And Madhusūdana, honoring that age of youth..."
"The one of immeasurable self, having destroyed his enemies, took delight with them during the nights" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.60).
And in the Harivaṃśa:
"Knowing the proper time for union, he [approached] the young women and the cowherd girls at night."
"Respecting his youth, he rejoiced with them" (Hari-vamśa 2.20.18).

By the phrase "with full-blown mallikā flowers," the quality of the creepers of Vṛndāvana as an excitant (*uddīpana*) is indicated; by the phrase "autumn arrives," the similarity between the autumn season and [the state of the youth] is also indicated.

Now, one might ask: how can there be amorous dalliance with so many of them by Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone? And how is it that they are all present together at one and the same time? If it is argued that this will be explained later—that He entered "into each pair among them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.3)—to that he replies: "having resorted to Yogamāyā. Regarding this, some say:

*Bāhu* is a certain inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*) employed for the play of *yogamāyā*; as will be stated later, it is "possessed of inconceivable power by the Lord of Yoga" (*yogeśvareṇa... acintya-śaktimatā*). He has taken refuge in its vicinity (*upa*), that is, near it. And she [the *māyā*] is restrained in each of her respective functions within the natural domain of Kṛṣṇa; as will be stated later, she considers herself thus.

"His own respective wives, who were staying by his side, [were the inhabitants of Vraja]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.37). Alternatively, it means he has resorted to that *māyā* which, in the context of *yoga* or union, is *kṛpā*—that is to say, affection (*sneha*).
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, *māyā* can denote both compassion (*kṛpā*) and deceit (*dambha*).

Or rather, "yoga" refers to union with the beauties of Vraja; "mā" means the splendor or beauty therein; "āya" means the attainment of that [splendor]. He never at any time abandons that flute (*muralī*) which has resorted to its vicinity (*upa*), just as another hero, having resorted to the pleasure of pursuing a heroine, never leaves her side.

In that same way, Śrī Kṛṣṇa also, regarding the flute as His companion, remains ever dependent upon it; this is indicated by the word "He sang sweetly" (*jagau kalam*). Alternatively, even though He possesses the perfection of yoga, such as mystic power and so forth, He set His mind on sporting there, having taken refuge in the flute.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "even though there was the attainment of the powers (*aiśvarya*) and so forth of yoga, she disregarded them. The grammatical construction is: "having perceived [the nights] as conducive to amorous play, she took refuge in those very nights which had been promised."

Alternatively, the locative case in *yogamāyām*—meaning "in yoga," "in the union," or "on account of the chest-union"—indicates that although *Mā*, that is, Lakṣmī, was present there, He disregarded her; this is the sense. The meaning is that He resorted only to those [gopīs] with whom He had dalliance and whose thoughts were fixed on Him. This is either an implied meaning (*ārthika*) or expressed through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanāvṛtti*).

Or rather, she is some elderly ascetic woman who has resorted to a yoga-māyā that is favorable for amorous play; or else, the masters of spiritual knowledge (abhijña) say this: in the context of *yoga* characterized by sexual union (*saṃbhoga*), she has resorted to—that is, she possesses in an eminent degree—that *māyā*, which is the skill in accomplishing the impossible. [The word *upāśritaḥ* is used] in the sense of "possessing" (*upādhike*) as its object.

The state of being "capable of being spoken" (pravacanīyatva) refers to the proximity of many [energies] through a single essential nature; for it will be stated [in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.3] that "among them, two by two," and thus it means the measure of being near to oneself alone.

Or rather, in this yoga, *māyā* is simply the inherent power of lightness; thus, the nights are women, autumn is a woman, and even the jasmine flowers are of the female species. Therefore, in such a region of Vṛndāvana, devoid of any male entry, [she saw] that which is fit for dalliance.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having seen the eternally perfected assembly, He set His mind upon sporting with the gopīs of Vraja;
that is to say, He fulfilled His desire. This is because His desires are true and His resolves are true, according to the Śruti: "His desires are true, His resolves are true."

Or rather, although the Blessed One is *bhaga*— meaning one who possesses all auspicious attributes— and although He is full of every happiness because He is the son of Nanda, because He is the object of the essence of parental affection (*vātsalya-rasa*), and because He was cherished by Nanda and Yaśodā, yet for the duration of a year He maintained His composure toward them.
Seeing the nights well-known for awakening the sweet sentiment (*madhura-rasa*), she set her mind on sporting.

This indicates that the loss of her fortitude occurred through the sight of the night. Furthermore, he explains the specific quality [of those nights] with the words "autumn" and "full-blown jasmine"; the sense is that autumn provided assistance.

Alternatively, "māyā" refers to deceitful conduct—that is, hypocrisy—and he resorted to this by manifesting such artifice in the presence of the inhabitants of Vraja. The meaning is this: even though he was always in the company of the beauties of Vraja, he did not display his amorous play as perceived by others, because aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is manifested only when it is concealed from view.

It may be found in the *Śruti*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "māyā" refers to both compassion (*kṛpā*) and guile (*dambha*). Without a support or locus for sweet flavor (*madhura-rasa*), he does not consider himself complete; for this very reason, he set his mind on sporting.
Or rather, even the Blessed One, setting aside both yoga and sovereignty, set his mind on sporting.
Having taken refuge in that very same compassion (*māyā*) which exists in the immobile trees among the limbs of the *āgama*,
he took recourse in affection for the trees of Vṛndāvana; reflecting, "I shall act so as not to cause them contraction [of their nature],
thinking, 'These are useful for my pastimes and are witnesses to my play,'" he remained in their midst.

"He set his mind on sporting" means that he formed a resolve favorable to delighting the hearts of the beauties of Vraja; for indeed, these trees are worshipped by the best of gods and immortals, as the affection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for them is well known. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
Having bowed to my gurus, Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa and the feet of Gaṅgā, who possess great love,
I offer salutations to Śrīla Narottamanātha and the Lord Gaurāṅga.
Having bowed again to the venerable guru, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion,
and to that Śrī Śuka— the lord of the world and the eye of the universe— I take refuge in him.
To Him who is dearer than life to the cowherd women, the exceedingly powerful Lord,
for the sake of His beloved service, I offer myself and my own.
Then, with five chapters equal to the five vital breaths,
the sage described the *rāsa* dance of Hari, the crest-jewel of all the perfections of His divine sports.
Victorious is Rāsa, by which the cowherd women, granted supreme fortune,
while remaining on the earth, surpassed even the nectar (rasa) situated at the highest point of all.
In the twenty-ninth [chapter], the harshness of the sound of the flute and the raining down of poison are described,
as well as the disappearance of the pastimes through the longing of the cowherd girls, who are like *cātaka* birds.

Indeed, here, while the Blessed One was seven years of age, on the new moon day of the month of Kārttika, he brought about the destruction of Indra’s sacrifice by raising the doctrine of *karma*. On the first lunar day of that bright fortnight, there was the festival of the sacrifice of Govardhana; on the second, [he performed the same] on the bank of the Yamunā.

The festival of the feast on the second day of the brother (Bhrātṛ-dvitīyā), though not described by the illustrious Lord of Munis (Śrī Munīndra), is to be understood from that very source. Therein are also described Indra’s words of anger; the lifting of Govardhana from the third day until the ninth; on the tenth day, the abundance of the cowherds’ astonished stories; and on the eleventh day—

The consecration of Govinda; on the twelfth day, the journey to the world of Varuṇa; and on the full moon, the journey to the world of Brahmā. Then, because autumn has concluded, in the following year, when He is eight years of age, the Rāsa festival takes place on the full moon of Āśvina.

The jewel upon the crown of all pastimes and festivals begins to speak of Him: although the Blessed Lord was already full of the six divine opulences, He set His mind on sporting, [finding] the time, place, and persons that serve as the excitants (*uddīpana*) and the objects of perception (*ālambana*) for that pleasure— the autumnal nights, Vṛndāvana, and the women of Vraja.

The meaning is that [he] is attracted by his all-surpassing sweetness. [He possesses] the vocal quality, beauty, delicacy, fragrance, sweetness, cleverness, and the triple arts (tauryatrika) of hundreds of millions of playful women who are wish-fulfilling gems of radiant aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Desiring to perceive with his own ears and other senses various most beautiful things,
and wishing to cause her to perceive his own beauty and other qualities with her ears and other senses,
he acted whenever it was during that very same night, being under the sway of love and without interruption.

Impelled by the power of His resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), through the power of Yogamāyā— which is capable of accomplishing the impossible— He brought forth and displayed more than a hundred billion nights within the span of that very single night of four watches, completing so many displays of sport. Therefore:

The plural form "those nights" (*tā rātrīḥ*) is used because of the expression "having observed those nights. It will be stated later as well: "the night of Brahmā has returned. Due to the employment of the well-known word *tat* (that), there is an excellence of the nights characterized by various qualities.
They are "those in which jasmine flowers bloom even in autumn," for the [word] ending in *ṭap* [indicates] that the jasmine is in full bloom during the autumn season as well.
"Even in autumn there are jasmine flowers; here, the fragrance of the Kula-pati (the Lord of the clan) surpasses even the scent of *kunda* garlands"—thus even the *kunda* flowers [are present].

"He took delight in the breeze fragrant with the lotuses that gladden his heart"—thus even the lotuses bloom at night. This is the excellence of Vṛndāvana. In the reading "jasmine flowers blooming in autumn," the term refers to the autumnal [season].

And those [flowers], as well as the blossoming jasmine—having said "He began to sport; he took delight," someone might explain that for the Blessed One, who delights in the Self and whose desires are naturally fulfilled, his dalliance with the women of Vraja is merely an external, novel pretense; therefore, [the author] says, "He set his mind on sporting."

It has been made known that this delight is internal alone and not external. One might argue: "While it is true that this delight is indeed internal, it occurs only in accordance with the request of the beautiful women of Vraja because they are His devotees. It is for this reason that the *ātmanepada* ending is employed in the word "ramate" (He delights). Regarding the delight:

It makes known His intent for their own happiness; and thus, because the beautiful women of Vraja possess such love, the Lord—even though He is Himself naturally full of all happiness—set His mind upon sporting with them, just as it is said, "The sages delight in the Self," and "Lord Hari possesses such qualities. Therefore, [this is the nature] of the beautiful women of Vraja.

Moreover, there is the supreme excellence: likewise—"Madhusūdana, honoring his youthful age, that one of immeasurable self who has destroyed his enemies, took delight with them during the nights" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.60). Thus it is said.
Knowing the proper time for his resolve, he took pleasure with those young cowherd girls at night, honoring their youth; [Harivaṃśa 2.20.18].
In the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* and the *Hari Vaṃśa*, the phrase "mānayan" means "honoring" or "showing respect."

In the absence of sporting with them, even His own youth would be rendered desolate; therefore, it has been said by the great authorities: "Hari makes His youth fruitful by sporting in the grove. Thus, the excellence of the women of Vraja is proclaimed in every respect. Therein—

In order to resolve all the duties mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, he says: "He has resorted to (upa-āśrita) his own yogamāyā, which is a function of his inconceivable spiritual power (cic-chakti-vṛtti)," because of the usage that one who has resorted to her also resorts to her on behalf of those who have resorted to him; thus, her excellence in fortune is also emphasized here. ||1||
Then the king of stars (the moon), anointing the face of the eastern quarter with his most auspicious reddish rays, [arose].
He has risen up for the people, cleansing away their sorrows,
like a far-sighted lover for his beloved.

Śrīdhara: At that very moment, for the sake of making that known, the moon, the king of stars, rose up. What was it doing? It was as if its beloved, whose sight had been long withheld, were anointing the face of its own beloved—the face of the eastern quarter—with red saffron.

With his most peaceful and most blissful rays— meaning, by anointing and turning them ruddy with the dawn-red glow— he, the well-known king of stars (the moon), likewise wipes away— that is, removes— the sorrows, the exhaustion from heat, and the afflictions of the people (carṣaṇīnām). ||2||

Vaṃśīdhara: At that time, during the occasion of the Lord’s desire for amorous play; the meaning is: with the intention that there might be a clear vision of the cowherd women in the darkness for the pleasure of that Hari. He shines with the *uḍus*, i.e., the stars;
just as I [shine] among the stars when the moon is king, so too does the Blessed One shine among the women of Vraja.

The word "udurāja" (king of stars) is used with the intention of signifying "being a king. He is one whose appearance or form (*darśana*) is long and vast; this means that because the full moon possesses all its digits (*kalā*), it is so described. "Priya" means husband. [He is the husband] of his own beloved. "Aruṇa" refers to saffron, redness, the twilight glow, or the charioteer of the sun.
Dharaṇī: "The eastern quarter" refers to the wife of Indra; that is, the wife of another. By this, according to the maxim "Whatever a superior person practices...
(Gītā 3.21), since Candra, the founder of our lineage, has smeared the face of the eastern quarter—the wife of Indra—[with his rays],...

Then, reflecting that "since this has come down through our family lineage, there is no fault in such an action for us," he said, "May the Blessed One be pleased," which was stated by the venerable teacher [Śrīdhara Svāmī] as "for his pleasure" (*tat-prītaye*).
This is the meaning. Here, the act of applying the ointment (*vilimpana*) is precisely what brings about the state of being reddened (*aruṇatāpādana*). [This applies to] the *carṣaṇīs*.
"Whether among humans or among crops, Aryaman’s wife Mātṛkā and their offspring are the *carṣaṇis*.
For it is there that the human race was fashioned by Brahmā," as it is said in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.6.42.

*Carṣaṇayaḥ* means humans. According to the *Nirukti-kośa*, *carṣaṇi* refers to a human being, a crop, one exhausted on a journey, or a draft animal. In the sense of "crop," it should be understood that the *śucis* (rays) have withered in appearance due to the heat of the harsh sunbeams. ||2||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "At that time," and so forth. "At that very moment" means at the precise instant when he set his mind on sporting; it implies that he approached him like a servant who has perceived the time for service. ||2||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, manifesting the state of mind of the Blessed Lord— who, out of His own desire for amorous play, perceived even the moon as if it were His beloved, ready to sport with Him as the eastern direction was with Her beloved—
the [appearance] on this night, which is the very crown of those nights, indicates all auspiciousness.
He says something else as well, beginning with "tadā" (then). By the phrase "the king of the stars," it is suggested that they too rose up as his attendants.

The two instrumental phrases "with rays" and "with the reddish [light]" function as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for both; the meaning is "by means of the color sustained by the rays. [The sense is] "smearing [them] especially."

This lunar day (tithi) is indeed the full moon night (rākā) with the specific intention of the full moon; and its fullness [on this particular day] is due to the will of the Blessed Lord, as is evident from the natural propriety of the statement "at that time" (*tadā*) in relation to other lunar days. Alternatively, it is because it serves as an excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for Him, just like nights when jasmine flowers are in full bloom.

Because of the propriety of its spontaneous emergence; and because, according to what will be said later—"colored by the rays of the full moon"—the intended meaning refers specifically to that lunar day (*tithi*), just as in the expressions *saḥ* (he) or *tāḥ* (they). Not only is the heat thus removed from the eastern direction alone, but from all people as well; hence he says "of the subjects" (*carṣaṇīnām*). [The word is] *śucaḥ*.
The sufferings caused by the heat of the autumn sun, or rather, the mental sorrows [of the Lord],
arise spontaneously from their own nature through the non-manifestation or manifestation of those who are the supreme power and the locus of all powers;
thus, just as the day of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s birth and other such occasions are dear to Him, so too are they dear to His beloved.

The specific differences in their respective inclinations have been shown through such qualities as being possessed of passion, goodness, and non-difference from one another. For this very reason, by the phrase "one who sees afar" (*dīrgha-darśana*), it is suggested that he wipes away the tears of grief of his attendants and, in that manner, anoints them with supreme bliss; thus, his extreme longing is indicated.
In this way, all of this manifestation of the desire for amorous play by the illustrious Blessed One is to be inferred. ||2||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, as if manifesting the internal state of the Supreme Lord— who, out of His own desire for amorous play, perceived even the moon as His beloved and was intent on sporting with it— the [moon], possessing a particular emotion aroused by the recollection of that desire for play, together with the eastern direction as His heroine...

He describes the moon’s rising by demonstrating its status as the leader, saying "then" (*tadā*): at the very moment the mind was placed upon the discus, it was implied that the stars—the kings of the constellations (*uḍu*)—also rose up as its retinue.
Furthermore, regarding those [stars], there is an intention to suggest their limited radiance on a night of the full moon.

The description of the moon as "secondary" (gauṇa) is made in consideration of its retinue. The expression "smearing [the world] with excellence" refers specifically to the full moon; its fullness may be due to the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī), or even without that, on another lunar day, in view of the Lord’s desire for dalliance. [The rays are described as] "most peaceful and consisting of nectar."
The meaning is as follows: Because he removes all suffering, he is celebrated as the one who increases the ocean of water;

not only has the heat of the eastern direction been removed by him in this way, but the heat of all people as well, as he says with the word "carṣaṇīnām"—meaning the sorrows, that is, the sufferings of the heat produced by the autumnal sun—and this moreover...

This was primarily intended by the Blessed Lord to dispel the long-standing anguish of separation felt by the group of cowherd girls by means of kindling their desire for amorous play; for by removing the sorrow of those who are worshiped by the world, the removal of the world's own sorrow is accomplished spontaneously. Thus, the Beloved [acted] toward his beloved.
Thus, by means of [his] passion, excellence, non-otherness, and so forth, the particularity of their mutual affection has been shown.
For this very reason, as he wipes away the tears of grief from his attendants, he seems to anoint them with a hand consisting of supreme bliss.
By the phrase "far-sighted," his extreme longing is indicated. Thus, everything [is explained].
This manifestation of the desire for amorous play by the illustrious Blessed One is to be inferred. ||2||
The sequence of composition: with hands [touched] by that dawn-red glow. ||2||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, he states—in the verse beginning with "tadoḍurāja" and so forth—that during all those nights described in that manner, the moon alone was the sole hero (nāyaka) in his full splendor.
"At that time" (*tadā*) means at that very moment when the Blessed Lord set His mind upon sporting; at that very same instant, this [moon] became the servant's...

This is the manner [of his appearance]: that his approach occurs simultaneously with the will of the Lord; he who is thus renowned for his perfection has risen, the king of stars. What was he doing? With his rays (karaiḥ), he was anointing—that is, coloring—the face of the eastern quarter with a redness (aruṇena); this word "aruṇa" denotes a quality. He was thus beautifying it.

The meaning is as follows: although he is the lord of many nights, nevertheless the eastern direction alone is his beloved; thus, at the outset, he entreats her with respect. Furthermore, what is he doing? He is purifying—that is, bringing about the state of stainlessness—of the *carṣaṇīs*, that is, the people. In this regard, there is an illustration: "the beloved."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, although the beloved of all the goddesses of Vraja, wipes away the grief of the cowherds and their friends; with his reddish saffron and through the specific movements of his hands, he smears the face of his beloved Rādhā—this constitutes a sentence-based simile (vākyārthopamā). Of what nature is he? He is like the moon, the king of stars, who is dear to her.

"Far-sighted": because he will continue to exist for many nights in a state of complete uniformity, his vision is long and undivided; alternatively, his vision is long—that is, eternal—along with his beloved, since she is under his own control.
Alternatively, "dīrgha-darśana" means one who has long eyes. ||2||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, although Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s mind was already filled with the desire to sport (*riraṃsā*), when it underwent its first transformation in the form of *bhāva*, the moon also arose from that mind—

according to the Vedic revelation that the moon is born from the mind because it is both an effect thereof and an excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*)— since [the mind] was now oriented toward producing an effect.

The effect arises of its own accord. Just as the night, autumn, and jasmine possess the quality of being excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), so too does the moon. Therefore, he describes its rising with the word "then" (*tadā*):
causing a slackening of passion for them, just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa caused a slackening of passion for Ramā.

In that same manner, the Moon also, having obtained his own full and radiant essence within his own [beloved], rose up to experience the full essence in another’s, namely the eastern direction; for according to the sacred tradition (*śruti*), the eastern quarter belongs to Indra alone among the guardians of the directions. What was he doing? He was kissing the face of the eastern quarter.

The eastern quarter, possessing a former passion, was anointed with a reddish unguent by the most peaceful rays [of the sun]. Therefore, as if perceiving that her connection was merely with the Sun (Sūrya) and not with Aruṇa, he rose up manifesting his own redness as if out of anger;
yet, reflecting upon her former passion through the blossoming of the night-lotuses, jasmine, and other flowers, which served as the expansion of her face, he departed.

Following her with his most peaceful rays, which were like his own hands, the sun, manifesting a lover’s feigned anger by smearing the face of that quarter of the sky with the glow of his rising radiance,
appeared as if he had perceived her state of passion and, finding it elsewhere, had departed; yet in reality, it was otherwise.

It was previously stated that the very affection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s mind is the moon; and because it is an effect of the mind, the author will state in the subsequent verse that it is "reddened like fresh saffron," according to the maxim that the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect. Furthermore, what was he doing while [shining] for the *carṣaṇīs*—those who possess knowledge of what has been done and what remains to be done?
O twice-born one, cleansing the sorrows of people— those subsequent torments born of the rays of the autumnal sun— as he provides rest; or rather,
as he cleanses and removes the sorrows and later regrets of those wandering everywhere, who, in the absence of the worship of the Blessed One, have encountered fear from the demons.

The sense is that because the bliss of the Blessed One was manifested by means of the full moon, at that very moment the removal of the distress of all the inhabitants of Vraja occurred; for they might otherwise have become agitated for another reason. And he will say: "thinking [them] to be standing by their own side. When that [moon] had risen...

For all beings, supreme bliss indeed arises. The removal of heat is the intermediate operation, as is the cessation of darkness; furthermore, just as the delighting of the minds of the cowherd women of Vraja is the primary aim of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, so too it is for the moon.
The primary objective is the removal of previously accumulated sins, while the incidental benefit is the removal of the sins of all people.
To illustrate that two tasks have been accomplished by the moon, he provides a corresponding example: "like a lover to his beloved.
A "lover" (*priya*) is one who has not seen [his beloved] for a long time and is thus an object of affection.

Just as one who has been long filled with longing, having his distress dispelled by the sight of his beloved, might smear his face with fresh saffron intending to remove the heat of separation from her, so too by this [verse], two effects are indicated: the removal of the torment of separation and the bestowing of supreme bliss. ||2||

Viśvanātha: He says that immediately after that, another excitant (uddīpana) appeared—"then the moon, the king of stars, rose. Furthermore, he says "the *kakubha* [tree]" to show that this was not merely an excitant, but rather served as a witness (*pramāṇībhūta*) to that lover of the cowherd women over a long period of time.

He whose sight is dear— that beloved lover— just as he anoints the face of his own beloved wife with red saffron held in his own hand, so too does he anoint the face of the eastern quarter with the rising glow of dawn,
which is red and held by his most peaceful and most pleasant rays.

"Smearing" means making red; he is indeed well-known as the one who [removes] the sorrows—that is, the distresses—of the *carṣaṇīs*. According to the statement in the Sixth Canto, "Aryaman’s mother is Mātṛkā, and their sons are the *carṣaṇīs*, wherein the human race was fashioned by Brahmā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.6.42), this refers to the sorrows of the human races.

*Mṛjan* means removing. This is the meaning: although he is an ancient personage belonging to Kṛṣṇa’s own lineage, and although he is the king of the twice-born (the moon), and although he possesses many wives worthy of his dalliance, he touches with his own hands the face of another’s wife—the wife of Indra—from the eastern direction; and while touching it, he himself...
If he, being attached to her, makes her likewise full of love for him, then— considering that Kṛṣṇa belongs to that lineage, is of youthful age, is of the cowherd class, has not yet married,
and is devoid of his own wife— he delights the species of human women by means of his own beauty.
"What indeed is the fault in sporting with a cowherd woman? ||2||
Having seen the full-orbed moon, which possesses a bed of night-lotuses, resembles the face of Lakṣmī, and is reddened like fresh saffron;
And that forest, anointed by those tender rays,
sang sweetly and charmingly to the hearts of the fair-eyed women.

Śrīdhara: [He saw] the moon—*kumudvat*, meaning that which possesses blossoming *kumudas* (lilies); whose orb (*maṇḍala*) is not fragmented; whose luster is like the splendor of the face of Ramā; and who is as red as fresh saffron. Having seen such a moon, and likewise its forest...
