Seeing it colored by soft rays of light, he sang—that is, he chanted—sweetly and melodiously.
How? In a manner that was captivating to those women whose glances were lovely and enchanting. (3)
Vaṃśīdhara: *Kumuda* is a lotus that blooms at night. It is that which is to be made to bloom, or to be manifested.

Alternatively, it refers to that which possesses *mud* (joy) on the earth (*ku*), namely its radiance; [the phrase refers to] that of the moon. By "rays" (*gobhiḥ*) is meant its beams. According to Keśava’s statement: "The word *nṛ* [is used for] women, heaven, thunderbolt, water, ray, eye, arrow, and hair."

*Rañjitam* means adorned. Regarding *kalam*: according to the *Medinīkośa*, "the word *kala* [is used] in three genders for a toll (*śulka*), and in the terminology of drama for a sweet sound; it is also [used] for indigestion.
However, the hidden meaning is as follows: *vāmadṛk* refers to the letter *ī*; that which is joined with it is *kalam*, the seed-syllable *klīm*. *Aṃ*.
"He honors and addresses Vāsudeva"—thus [is the meaning of] *aṃ*; this *manas* has the suffix *-am*, and the absence of the elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

Having heard that, it is understood that Vāsudeva causes [the drum] to be sounded. Furthermore, *aharam* means "he takes away" or "abandons" the vowels *au* and *a*; in the word *kalam*, this occurs through the abandonment of the two *a*-vowels followed by the connection with the vowel *ī*.

It becomes "klīm. And so it is said: he uttered the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja). Through the opening of the joint of the bamboo, he caused desire to sprout as if by sowing it in the field of her heart, which was moist with the essence of love parched by separation; this is the truth. ||3||
* Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "The forest," and so forth. *Tat komala-gobhir añjitam* (anointed by those soft rays) may be taken as a compound word (*samasta-pada*). He sang melodiously;
therefore, it should be understood that the flute is the instrument of the singing. [He] cooed on the flute (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.21.2).

Thus, because of what was stated previously. The meaning of the word *kala* is this: when a sound is sweet yet indistinct, it is called *kala*. Because of its indistinctness, there arose for everyone the perception that the song was sung by my name;
this [song] was pleasing to the Vaiṣṇavas. And then, having seen him, through the manifestation of a particular state of being (*bhāva*), he came to the forest.
And seeing that place on the bank of the Yamunā colored by those rays—
now famous as Rāsaulī— and having come to the village square established by Śrī Vajra, He sang some song with His enchanting flute, just as before, during that night.
He also speaks of his manifested excellence in the training of the flute, beginning with the words "Having seen... He saw her who delights those called *ramāṇas*—
that is, those whose forms are the supreme *ramā*s— or rather, among those beloved women,
she who is the most beloved, Rādhā, for the sake of attaining whom alone he had mastered the special training of the flute.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: surely, for so long a time she had been indifferent even toward union with them [the other women] in order to reveal [her own beauty]; yet, seeing a face resembling hers, having reflected upon that, or having remembered it through him, she sang in a sweet voice (*kala*) to make herself known.
For the purpose of providing a specific illustration through a general category, [the word] *kumu* means *kumuda*.
Thus, Viśva states: "The word *kumu* is also said to mean a white water-lily (*kumuda*). Alternatively, it may mean "possessing that" (i.e., possessing fragrance).

The suggested meaning (*dhvani*) is that the white water-lilies were blooming at that time in order to manifest their own splendor. In this case, [the intended sense] is conveyed by the adjectives alone.

The moon is obtained as the substantive (viśeṣya), as in the example: "This one rises, the breaker of the seal for the lotuses. In the case of the face, it should be understood that the gender is changed according to the substantive, [interpreting it] as "that which exists by virtue of being the object of the earth's (kuḥ) joy (mut). This is because she is the very form of supreme bliss (parama-ramā).

The unbroken orb consists of sixteen digits. Alternatively, it refers to a circle—a collection of parts—possessing its full measure, which is reddened by the hue of fresh saffron. Having thus demonstrated the suitability of the time for amorous dalliance, he now demonstrates the suitability of the place as well, with the words "and the forest. Of that...

It was colored on all sides by cowherds who, due to their first awakening [of love], possessed only a slight measure of radiance; or rather, using the past passive participle in a sense denoting the agent (*bhāve niṣṭhā*), it means "colored by them"—that is, where there was the coloring of Kṛṣṇa.
The absence of the long vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Thus, the kindling of emotion has been shown. *Kalam*...

It should be understood that he played the flute in such a way that it was both sweet and indistinct. This is known from what will be said later, beginning with: "O dear one, who is this woman [whose ears are filled] by your flute-song of nectar-like, melodious words" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.40).
In that context, its sweetness is for the purpose of enchanting, while its indistinctness is for all of them.
This flute-playing is intended to cause others to mistake it for being composed of their own respective names, and to prevent them from discerning its specific nature as "this is a flute.
Now, one might ask: why did its sweetness not attract everyone? To that, he says: "of those with lovely eyes" (vāmadṛśām).

The meaning is that he proclaimed a specific passion (*rāga-viśeṣa*) which serves as an excitant (*uddīpana*) for the primary aesthetic flavor (*ādi-rasa*) alone, in such a way that it would be captivating for those women who possess such a disposition. And it will be stated [later] that "it increases the god of love" (*anaṅga-vardhana*). Indeed, it is surely named *madhyama* and so forth, since it was said regarding the varieties of *maudava-rāga*: [text follows].

"Beginning with *madhyama* and ending with *ma* (the note *niṣāda*), born from the *madhyama*-scale (*grāma*) and its melodies (*rāga*), this [song] should be sung in the evening during the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, excluding *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata*. Here, *ma* refers to the note *madhyama*, and *ṛdha* refers to the two notes *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata*; that which is called "seizing" (*graha*) is the initial note.

Regarding the statement "offered at the beginning of the song" and so forth, previously it was said, "O King, the sound of the flute is enchanting to all beings"; because that referred to a general subject, according to their own nature, there occurred merely a state of infatuation for them. But now, because it serves as a specific stimulant (*uddīpana*) to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), there occurs an attraction. Thus it is there.

In that regard, there is indeed a specific distinction concerning the bamboo tubes (*vaṃśya*), as it has been said: "The eight openings, beginning with the *tārā*, have a measurement of one and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) apart;
then, where the mouth-opening is at one and a half finger-breadths, so too is the [subsequent] finger-breadth."
The head of that flute is four finger-breadths long and the tail is three finger-breadths;
it is known by the wise as having nine holes and measuring seventeen finger-breadths.
If the distance between the aperture of the *tāra* and the mouth [of the *nāda*] should be ten finger-breadths,
it is explained as "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*) and likewise as "Deluding" (*saṃmohinī*).
If that [note] were between Sūrya, it would be considered Ākarṣiṇī;
if it were between Indra, the flute would then be Ānandinī.
This very flute, beloved by the cowherds, is renowned as the *vaṃśulī*;
it is of three kinds: made of jewels, made of gold, and made of bamboo. [Bharata-śāstra 2.1.368–72].
Therefore, this golden one should be known to have the opening of the mouth (*tāra-mukha*) at a distance of twelve finger-breadths. Thus...

"The excellence of the song of those fair-eyed women should also be understood"—by this pun (*śleṣa*), the meaning is that as they looked at him with crooked glances, their entire collection of senses, beginning with sight, was as if drawn away by the very root of their minds being pulled toward his form. Herein lies the secret: by means of the pun, he sang the "seed-syllable of desire" (*kāma-bīja*), for—

That which is connected with the left eye, together with "kala"—these three initial syllables are manifested. Of what nature is it? It is "manohara. By the word *manas*, its presiding deity, the Moon, is expressed. And because he takes the form of that [left eye], he is a "taker" (*lavaka*); since he "takes away" or attracts (*harati*) it, it is "conjoined with that" (*tat-saṃvalitam*).
The meaning is as follows: the point is that its possession of sound is due solely to the inherent nature of the flute's resonance. Thus it has been said:
"Kalā is Māyā, and Lavakā is the Form; He is delightful with the resonant sound of the flute playing in rhythmic measure (kala). ||3||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, with the manifestation of a particular internal emotion (*bhāva*), He sang something on His flute like a "bewitching mantra" (*mohana-mantra*) for the purpose of attracting the Śrī Gopīs; thus he says:
"Having seen," etc. *Kumut* means a water-lily (*kumuda*). Accordingly, Viśva states: "The word *kumut* is also said to mean a water-lily."

"Endowed with that" means that at that time the night-lotuses (*kumuda*) were in full bloom. For this very reason, it will be said by the illustrious gopīs: "In Vṛndāvana, which is delightful with night-lotuses, jasmine, and the moon" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.43).
Alternatively, *ku* refers to the earth (*pṛthivī*), and *mud* is joy; thus, "endowed with that" means endowed with the joy of all beings arising from its appearance.
The meaning is that Ānanda was indeed thus. The reasons for this are given by the words beginning with "akhaṇḍa.

Regarding the phrase "because of its unbroken orb, it resembles the face of Ramā": it should be understood that by the recollection of Lakṣmī’s face, the desire for amorous play (riraṃsā) is manifested.

[Objection: But the face of Ramā is always smeared with excellent saffron (*sat-kuṅkuma*), whereas the moon is white; how then can there be a similarity between them? To this he says: "fresh" (*nava*). This is intended to refer to the very moment of its first rising. Fresh saffron is employed precisely because it intensifies the emotional mood (*bhāva*). Thus, [the word] "of time" (*kālasya*) indicates its suitability.

Having thus shown the location, he further indicates it with the words "and the forest": [the forest] is colored, reddened, or made the object of passion on all sides by the soft rays (*gobhiḥ*) of that moon, which possess only a slight amount of light due to its recent rise.
Alternatively, the word *gobhiḥ* ends in the instrumental case; *añjitam* means "smeared," and here too the meaning is the same.

In this way, the intensification of the emotion (*bhāva*) has been shown. *Kalam* means sweetly; or rather, it should be understood that she sang on the flute in such a way as to be melodious (*kalam*). O dear one, what woman [is there] for you?
This is because it will be stated later, beginning with "the nectar of the flute-song of the Lord of Time" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.40).
The meaning is that those most beautiful women possess *vāmāḥ*—that is, charming eyes—or alternatively, that those most clever women possess *vāmā*—that is, a sidelong glance. This...

And it is merely a description of His own nature; for since all the women of Vraja are by their very nature such [beings], He captivates or attracts their minds— whether by a particular appointment, or by specific modes of passion, rhythm,
and so forth— so that it may be "mind-captivating" (*manoharam*), as compared to other days at that time.
A specific type of song is intended [here], because on other days such a state occurs through the singing of the flute. ||3||

The sequential arrangement [of the text] is as follows: [She is established] by virtue of being the form of Mahālakṣmī; or else, because she is the cause for the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, "Ramā" here refers to Śrī Rādhā, according to the previously cited statement: "O King, the sound of the flute is enchanting to the hearts of all beings" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.6). This constitutes her distinction.
He said: "Captivating to those with beautiful eyes. The intended meaning is that this is due to the specific singing which intensifies the primary aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Regarding the composition of the extensive sequence: the Blessed Lord, having seen that [moon] risen, did not delay for even a moment for the sake of his pastimes; thus he says, beginning with "Having seen," etc. [The moon] is called *kumudvant* because it illuminates the night-lotus (*kumuda*).

It exists [there], thus it is "kumudvān"; the *a* is elided due to its inclusion in the *naḍādi* group. Upon seeing him, the moon sang melodiously—that is, he played the flute; for it is said, "he cooed upon the flute. What did he sing?
To this he says: the meaning is "that very thing which is captivating to those with beautiful eyes. This refers to the phrase "of those with beautiful eyes" (*vāmadṛśām*).

The meaning is this: that which she sang was heard only by the lovely-eyed woman, but not as it was previously described—charming to the minds of all beings. For if that were the case, everyone would have heard it.

Therefore, if they had not come specifically for the sake of the lovely-eyed woman and not merely as friends, then [the song] would have been heard even by the friends while they remained at their parents' house.

He continues in this manner; even toward his parents, he remains performing acts such as lying down at the proper place and time, just as on each preceding day, and he is seen doing so by them. Thus, his inconceivable power of yoga is perceived in this very way. Following this same direction, [it is understood that] he who resides in Vṛndāvana...
That which is considered "eternal" must also be established. Of what nature is the moon?

It has an unbroken orb; that is, it is full. Again, of what nature is it? It resembles the face of Ramā; having abandoned Ramā, during his play with the gopīs, her face was always reddened with anger, and he is like that. That...
He reveals this very point: "reddened with fresh saffron. Not only is He seen thus, but what is the forest like?
It is "anointed by His tender rays"—that is, smeared or colored by His soft cow-like beams. Alternatively, *abhirañjitam* may be read as a single compound word. For this very reason:
The phrase "red as fresh saffron" is to be understood as a qualifier of the forest. ||3||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described the emergence of the excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), he speaks of the excellence of the locus of playful charm (*vilāsādhikaraṇa*) as well: "Having seen the excitant, she manifested her play consisting of sound";
that is, having seen the moon which possesses white lotuses (*kumudvant*), she sang upon her flute so as to produce a sweet melody.

"He has played" [the lute]. Although situated in the sky (*ākāśa*), he is "Kumudvān"—one in whom joy (*ānanda*) exists—meaning he is on the earth (*pṛthivī*). Thus, it is indicated that he bestows joy upon those people who dwell on the earth. Alternatively, *kumut* means a blooming white lotus (*kumuda*); in this sense, it is an indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others, such as other flowers that bloom at night.

"Even the flowers have blossomed"—this is the meaning. Since Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s heart is full of rasa and remains unbroken, even the moon has attained its state of being "unbroken" (akhaṇḍa), because it is His effect; thus he says: "whose orb is not broken. By this, his quality of bestowing complete bliss upon all people is indicated. Furthermore, what [more]?

The radiance of his face is truly like that of Ramā (Lakṣmī), because he is her brother; for this very reason, it is suggested that upon seeing the moon, there arises a state of laughter through the recollection of Ramā’s face. Furthermore, even the Lord of Sages (the Buddha) speaks of this similarity through his knowledge of the mind. Alternatively, "Ramā" is so called because she delights (ramayati).
A certain queen of Vraja [beheld] his face, which was equal to that [of Kṛṣṇa]; furthermore, how was it? It was reddened by fresh saffron (*navakuṅkumāruṇam*).
By this, it is indicated that at the time of his marriage, the face of Ramā (Lakṣmī) was likewise colored with fresh saffron;
for this very reason, it is red. Just as the moon possesses a redness at its rising, the redness of the man’s face is also inferred.
Furthermore, since even saffron is counted among the excitants (*uddīpakas*), having seen that the forest too was an excitant of sweet passion,
he [the deer] approached it without hesitation, as it were, by means of the moon's rays— beams characterized by a soft and pleasant touch and imbued with fresh affection.

Although the greenness of the leaves and the whiteness of the flowers were already colored, they were nevertheless made crimson by the rays obstructed by [the sun's] redness; thus, its nourishing quality is expressed. Or rather, it is said that a particular luster was cast upon them by his rays—tender, pleasant to the touch, and tinged with the rosy glow of sunrise.
The verbal root *rañj* is used in the senses of straightness, manifestation, beauty, splendor, and gait. Not only was the forest colored [delighted],
but the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa was also colored [delighted], since He sang so softly, indistinctly, and sweetly while playing the flute.

The meaning is this: it is indeed a marvel that even Kṛṣṇa’s mind was colored by that moon with its own rising glow; or rather, *kala* means the face (*mukha*) which takes (*lāti*) or grasps the mouth, thus signifying a full face; and that [face] is singing, how charmingly—that is, captivating—to the eyes of beautiful women (*vāmadṛśām*). *Vāmā* refers to those with lovely eyes.

"Of those whose glances are captivating," or alternatively, "of those whose side-long glances (apāṅga) are lovely (vāmā) and curved"; or again, "of those whose glances—meaning their beautiful sights or, by extension, their insights—are lovely. The meaning is that [this state] is enchanting even to the sages. The intention is as follows: in Vraja, there are twelve who are qualified to experience the aesthetic flavor (rasa).

Nevertheless, the cessation of those who are devoted to sweet flavors is described; the cessation of those whose limit was set by that [experience] is described during the experience of specific pleasures, for they remained right there, having arrived by way of the sound of the flute. ||3||
Viśvanātha: And then, upon seeing him, he experienced the transformations of wondrous love;

and remembering the traditional teaching that "whatever a superior person does, that very thing other people do" (Gītā 3.21), perceiving that same dharma of that man—who was the ancestor of his own lineage—within himself as well, he acted entirely without hesitation.
He says that he made a certain unfailing effort to bring another's wife [to him]: "Having seen... (*dṛṣṭvā*).
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "kumu" means a night-lotus (*kumuda*), as it is stated: "The word 'kumu' is also applied to the night-lotus.
It may also be explained as: "having seen himself as one who exists for the sake of causing that [lotus] to blossom," since neither the subject nor the attribute has been explicitly stated. Not so.
The meaning is "full" (pūrṇam), referring to Him whose essential nature is the entire universe as an unbroken circle.

Because He is the brother of Ramā (Lakṣmī), His face resembles hers. Alternatively, according to the Smṛti: "She who consists of all Lakṣmīs, who is all-beauty, the enchanting, the supreme," Ramā refers to Śrī Rādhā. They take delight (ramante) [in Him].

Alternatively, *ramā* refers to those who delight [others], namely the gopīs; he whose luster (*ābhā*) is like that of their faces—this implies that by seeing him, they have ascended the path of memory. In the other sense, it means that from him comes a perfect radiance (*ābhā*) upon the faces of those *ramās*, which manifests the internal transformation caused by love (*kandarpa*). [He beheld] himself as such.

It is reddish because it is pervaded by the glow of sunrise, like a lump of fresh saffron; alternatively, it is reddened by the application of fresh saffron. Likewise, the forest is colored—that is, smeared or beautifully tinted—by its soft rays (gobhiḥ);
or, in the alternative sense, [it is colored] by those well-known [rays].
"Adorned with cows"—meaning beautified by the luster of their own bodies or by the cows being protected by him; the absence of the suffix *ṭac* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

Having seen these excitants (*uddīpana*) and objective determinants (*ālambana*), he sang sweetly (*kalaṃ*) on the flute—the word "on the flute" (*veṇunā*) being understood from the context. Who? [Kṛṣṇa].
"...your three-limbed flute-song of nectar-like sweet words" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.40), as stated in the subsequent verse.

How so? Because they sing in a way that is captivating even to young women whose glances are themselves charming—according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that "women desire him who sings"—and by means of *śleṣa* (double entendre), [the word] *kala* [is understood].

The phrase "ka-kāra-la-kāraṃ vāma-dṛśām" is a word with its case-ending elided; "vāma-dṛk" refers to the fourth vowel (the letter *i*), and together with that, he recited the fifteen-vowel Kāma-bīja—this is the secret.
It is "manohara" because it attracts the mind, being the mantra of the Great Manmatha who constitutes one's own essential nature.
The meaning. ||3||
Having heard that song which increases the god of love,
the women of Vraja had their minds captivated by Kṛṣṇa.
With their earrings swaying from the speed [of their movement], they approached one another unobserved at the place where their beloved was.
Śrīdhara: Those women whose efforts were unobserved and undisclosed to one another so that there would be no rivalry;
they came by way of the path of the sound of singing wherever their beloved was. They were those whose earrings were trembling and flickering with speed and velocity. (4)

Vaṃśīdhara: [He said this] for the sake of non-rivalry—that is, for the cessation of rivalry; the meaning is that there might otherwise be jealousy regarding the act of following him in death (*sahagamana*). That Kṛṣṇa, at whatever place [he might go], there the earrings shall become chariots, wings, and goads; or else, the earth itself, which is now contracted, will expand before them.

This is what is suggested by the phrase "with earrings swaying as they move" (java-lola-kuṇḍalā). (Viśvanātha, *Toṣaṇī*) *Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "Increasing the bodiless one"—the meaning is that my bodiless desire (*anaṅga*), having become embodied (*aṅgī*), increases within the body through love. "With efforts unobserved by one another" is due to the absence of conversation. As for... [text fragment]...
Or rather, their efforts unnoticed by their husbands and others, they came together and approached one another;

"with earrings swinging with speed"—here, even the swaying of the earrings is due to speed, which indicates an excess of slowness [on their part], and thereby a gait like that of a *kalahaṃsa* (swan); and as for the earrings—
The state of having earrings of a different kind from those of Westerners; or else, "those with earrings that are not restless due to speed"—meaning those whose earrings are slightly swaying. ||4||

The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: Others, however, did not hear that song of his, yet they were nonetheless attracted by it; thus, indicating his particular power, [the author] says: "Having heard" (niśamya). That aforementioned manner—the Cupid directed toward the Blessed Lord, which issued from the flute of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

It is so because it now causes that which previously existed only as a present state to increase; for although the capacity to increase the god of love (anaṅga) was already implied by the phrase "charming to the eyes of beautiful women," nevertheless, this is a *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific assertion) intended to express its excellence, and the use of the word *anaṅga* is because [love] previously existed only in the form of a seed and a sprout.

The word *sthitaḥ* (situated) now conveys the sense that he has "put forth new shoots" (*pallavita*). By this, his singing is also metaphorically imagined as a sprinkling of nectar. Because of its immediate effect, the women of Vraja are specifically intended here by the force of the context. For this very reason, [he is described] by Kṛṣṇa, the supreme attractor.

Those whose minds—or their entire mental faculties—had already been previously seized and drawn away; specifically, having now heard the song, they arrived. The reason for their not being noticed by one another has been explained by them.

Or rather, even though they were friends with one another within their own group, the reason for this was "Kṛṣṇa"— that is to say, because at that time their hearts were so captivated by Kṛṣṇa that no room remained for reflection. For this very reason, [the text says] "with speed" and "they came," since for Śrī Bādarāyaṇa, their own state of being is always manifest in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Or rather, because of the news of their going there, a particular state of emotion arose in her; through the dawning of the thought of going there herself—just as they did—the proximity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa manifested as if it were before her very eyes. As for the phrase "then they went," the word *saḥ* (he) refers specifically to the lover (*ramaṇaḥ*), and *yatra* (where) refers to that very place.

The meaning is that it is a place consisting of supreme bliss. The intention is that because that flute-playing is of the nature of the supreme art of attraction (*paramākarṣaṇa-vidyā*), there was not even wandering or the like elsewhere. [From] the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: that aforementioned form of Cupid (*anaṅga*) arising from the flute of Śrī Kṛṣṇa...
It is so called because it increases even now the desire for the Blessed Lord that already existed previously.

Although the quality of increasing the god of love (*anaṅga*) was already implied by the phrase "charming to those with beautiful eyes," nevertheless, this is a specific figure of speech (*viśeṣokti*) intended to express its excellence; furthermore, the use of the word *anaṅga* refers to those women themselves.
This is because, through the excellence of desire in the form of love (*prema*), there is an intention to exclude the vulgar elements of desire caused by worldly sexual practices;

or else, it is because even though the god of love (*anaṅga*) lacks limbs, he becomes possessed of limbs by virtue of having the Blessed Lord as his object—such is the general direction of the argument.
"Those women" refers to the young maidens of Vraja, or those women who were in Vraja. By Kṛṣṇa, the supreme attractor.
Those whose minds—or their entire mental faculties—had already been previously captured, drawn in, and possessed;
and especially now, having heard such a song, they arrived.
Or rather, even among those who were friends with one another within their own group, [they looked] at each other...
The reason for the effort being unobserved is given as "Kṛṣṇa. The sense is that at that time, because her mind was drawn away by Kṛṣṇa, there was no opportunity for reflection.
Alternatively, it is because of that very [distraction] which consists of the natural rivalry arising from a particular intensity of love (*prema*).

Because they appeared from within another herd; or else, because they were unable to signal that [fact] due to extreme haste in their journey, for that very reason their earrings—ear-ornaments—were dangling with the speed of their swift movement. Thus they arrived.

This is because Śrī Bādarāyaṇa was always vividly present in the proximity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; or rather, through the arising of a particular state of emotion upon hearing news of their departure, he experienced a vivid manifestation of being in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as if it were his own direct experience.
Alternatively, "ājagmuḥ" means they ran toward [Him]; or alternatively, "ā... jagmuḥ" means they went forth completely by means of total renunciation, as will be stated many times hereafter.
He is the singer of the flute-song that causes supreme delusion; or alternatively, He is desired through long-term vows and the like, because—
Or, "Kānta" means one's own charming master; or else, it is that from which there is the end (anta), that is, the ultimate limit (niṣṭhā) of some happiness (ka). ||4||
The sequence of composition: *ājagmuḥ* means "they arrived" or "they reached. ||4||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Regarding what was said—that [the flute-song] is enchanting to those with leftward glances—it is precisely this uniqueness that is expressed in the verse beginning with *niśamya*. Having heard (*niśamya*) that sweet (*kala*) song of the flute, the women of Vraja came; no one else did so, because they lacked the opportunity to hear it. Where did they come from?
Thus he says: "When he... and so forth. Of what nature is he? He is *kānta*, meaning desirable. Of what nature is the song?

It is *anaṅga-vardhana*. *Aṅga* refers to the arts of love (*kāma-kalā*), while *aṅgin* refers to love itself (*prema*). Therefore, *anaṅga-vardhana* means that which increases the possessor of the limbs—that is to say, it increases love. Of what nature are they [the women]? They are those who have been seized by Kṛṣṇa.
Their minds were such that there was no occasion for the God of Love (Anaṅga) there. Their efforts toward one another were unobserved;
because of their spontaneity, there was no prior agreement, and not out of jealousy. Even so, they all went forth at once, bound by a single thread like wooden dolls, and not otherwise.

In the sequence of what precedes and follows: even by their movement, which possessed such speed and velocity that the earrings themselves were swinging, it is implied that the movement itself was naturally profound and steady. ||4||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Then, in response to the inquiry as to what was done after hearing the call marked by His flute-song and their own respective names, he says: "Having heard" (*niśamya*). Having heard that song, the women of Vraja came. Although all of them had indeed come, those to whom Śrī Kṛṣṇa had granted a boon were the ones specifically summoned. Nevertheless...
All those who had previously experienced the bliss of Kṛṣṇa have indeed assembled. What kind of song?
It is one that increases *anaṅga*—that is, it increases a transcendental longing directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
what was already established now attains further growth. Regarding this increase of *anaṅga*:

The flute-song itself, combined with its specific mode of expression, is the unique cause [of the arousal of love]. However, the "bodiless one" (Anaṅga) is a mental state, existing as the mind; it cannot be perceived by any other means. Previously, when Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s mind first became inclined toward amorous play, that very "bodiless one" manifested through the medium of the sound of the flute.

The meaning is that He has been set in motion by the beautiful women of Vraja; since their pre-established beauty already exists, the sense is that by uniting with Him, they have attained great increase. By His very desire, Śrī Kṛṣṇa has embraced their desire within Himself, and through that means, it has been taken up by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself.
The meaning is that those whose minds were drawn [to Him]— once the mind is drawn, it follows the nature of the mind by its own very essence—
or rather, that which increases His bodilessness (anaṅga), namely, the bodilessness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself from before.

It is so called because it causes [desire] to increase; or rather, that song employed for the purpose of enchantment increases—that is, makes surge forth—that Kāma who is eternally established as Anaṅga (the bodiless one) and exists as something transcendent. Likewise, it is that which was taken up by Kṛṣṇa through his own form and sweetness for the purpose of enchantment.
Those whose minds [were captivated] were not [won over] by mere enchanting song alone;

or rather, it refers to that which increases the god of love (anaṅga) among one another. This is an expression of the personal experience of the narrator, Śrī Śuka, stating how they proceeded. Although they had set out with their respective groups, nevertheless—

"Mutually indicative, with unobserved efforts": the meaning is that their efforts were not perceived or made known to one another because their minds were drawn toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa; since He drew away even the body and senses from among the group of senses, even the organ of speech did not utter what they desired.

Since they were not following their own bodies, they returned by the very same path through which the flute-song had come; and when there was the expectation of "Where [is he]?", at that moment, the beloved seen before—
whose form is as enchanting as ten million Cupids— appeared there, accompanied by passion and granting his boon.

In a secluded place, refined by the excitant conditions (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), young maidens who have not yet tasted the bliss of sexual union arrive first; they [gaze upon] his phallus while their earrings sway with their rapid movements.
The distinction here is that it is only maidens who wear earrings (*kuṇḍala*), whereas other women who have already experienced intercourse wear ear-rings (*tāṭaṅka*).

Alternatively, it is that in which "kānta" (the beloved) is the end (*anta*), meaning the supreme limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*) of that which consists of delight (*ramaṇātmaka*), namely, the highest bliss (*parama-sukha*). Or rather, it is an adjective qualifying the locus itself. ||4||
Viśvanātha says: Those [gopīs], like dolls strung upon the thread of melodious song, approached the presence of Kṛṣṇa;

thus he speaks: "That song, though enchanting, increased the longing of the mind. Moreover, Kṛṣṇa had sent into Vraja a great thief known as the Flute-song, and by that [thief]... [the women of Vraja were captivated].

Having entered the treasury of the inner organ through the door of the ear—which is without a bolt—and having stolen the great treasures such as fortitude, modesty, fear, and discernment along with the mind, he brought them back immediately and gave them to Kṛṣṇa; thus it is said: "The minds were taken by Kṛṣṇa," for the minds are indeed mental (mānasa).
The sense is that those qualities belonging to the mind— fortitude, memory, discrimination, modesty, fearfulness,
and so forth— came to Kṛṣṇa, the great emperor of thieves, as if to request back their respective properties.
At that very moment, I think, they were so preoccupied with seizing that great thief that they had no regard for one another.
Those whose efforts were observed followed right after the thief. Where?
To where that beloved was, with speed and velocity; they whose earrings were swaying, and who also possessed bracelets, small bells, and so forth, accompanied him.
The sense is that those treasures situated outside the house were not stolen by that thief because he perceived them as being of little value. ||4||
Some, full of longing, went forth abandoning their milking;
others, having placed the milk on the fire, departed without removing the *saṃyāva* from the oven.
Some, setting aside their own food, served it to others while nursing their infants with milk;
some attended to their husbands, foregoing their own meals.
Some anointed themselves, others wiped away their tears, while some applied collyrium to their eyes;
with their garments and ornaments disarrayed, some went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa.

Śrīdhara: By hearing words indicative of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, those whose minds were inclined toward Him departed as if illuminating the immediate cessation of activities pertaining to the three goals of life (traivargika). Abandoning their work half-finished, they went away. Thus it is said: "milking," [referring to] milk situated in a vessel upon the hearth.
Having placed this on the fire, some women departed without waiting, leaving the wheat-cakes and the cooked grain-meal uncovered and not yet removed from the heat. 5–6.
Others were wiping [the ground] and performing tasks such as massaging the limbs.

To show that any action performed with a mind intent on the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa bears fruit even if done otherwise than prescribed, he says: "vyatyasta" (reversed). This refers to holding [the objects] upside down, both in terms of their position and their essential form.
Those whose garments and ornaments had been exchanged for their opposites. ||7||

Vaṃśīdhara: The sound of the flute is a word indicative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Those whose minds are *pravaṇa*—meaning inclined toward or attached to—that Śrī Kṛṣṇa; for the *Dharaṇidhara* lexicon states that *pravaṇa* means "inclined" or "attached. "At that moment" refers to the moment of hearing the sound associated with the Blessed Lord.

The meaning is as follows: He uses the word "iva" (as if) to suggest that even for those whose minds are fixed on Hari, actions pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika*) must be performed for the sake of maintaining the world order (*loka-saṃgraha*). Thus he says, "as if illuminating. "Half-completed" means half-finished. The term *avasita* may denote prosperity, being known, or having reached its conclusion; it functions here as an adjective modifying the object.

Thus says the *Medinī* [lexicon]. That is "half-finished. "In the oven" (*cullyām*) means in the apparatus for confining fire, that is, in the hearth; "oven" (*cullī*) means a funeral pyre or a hearth—thus says the *Medinī*. "Having placed upon it" (*adhiśritya*) means having set it on to cook.
"This decoction" (*etat kvātham*) refers to the boiling of milk. "Waiting" (*pratīkṣamāṇāḥ*) means unable to endure any delay of time.
Without having caused [them] to descend, and without having caused [them] to be planted. ||5||

Serving those who were eating by placing food into their bowls; nursing their sons with milk—that is, causing them to suckle at the breast; serving them by massaging their feet and so forth; and eating themselves—having set aside [the food] and abandoned [their own hunger]. ||6||

For those whose minds are attached to Him and whose hearts are fixed on Kṛṣṇa, there is a reversal of position: the ornament of the feet is on the arms, and the ornament of the arms is on the feet; that which covers the upper body is on the lower body, and that which covers the lower body is on the upper body. There is also a reversal of form: the lower garment is held by its upper portion.
By the lower part of an upper garment; in this same way, it should be understood regarding ornaments as well. ||7||
* Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

* Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus described the attainment of that [state], yet due to the agitation caused by the song of the Supreme Enchanter, one disregards one's own body and its physical functions, and abandons self, karma, the world, dharma, and so forth.
In order to provide a specific understanding of the three verses concerning those who have set out, he again describes their very exertion in setting forth;

therein, at the outset, he speaks of the abandonment of their own caste-duties by some of them in this pair of verses beginning with "duhantyaḥ. The word *duhantyaḥ* means "milking cows," the sense of the causative (*ṇy-artha*) being inherent, thus meaning "causing [others] to milk."

"They approached" means they went toward the sound of the flute-song. The phrase beginning with "some" (*kāścit*) refers to the fact that among many groups (*yūtha*), some were joined together in a single purpose, as will be stated later: "The leader of hundreds of groups of women" (*vanitā-śata-yūthapaḥ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.44). "Doha" means milking or milk. This is the reason for their approaching in such a manner.

"Anxious" means unable to endure any delay of time; this reason is to be followed throughout the subsequent [sections] as well. The word "others" (aparāḥ) connects both with what precedes and with what follows; likewise in the following cases.
"The rest" refers to those [other matters].
Or alternatively, having placed milk on the hearth and not yet removed it from the fire even though it is cooked, and having likewise placed *saṃyāva* on the hearth and not yet removed it;
thus, having stated the omission of three primary evening rites for some [women], in that very context—

Declaring the renunciation of worldly duties through three verses, he first speaks of the abandonment by some of their common relatives, servants, and so forth, with the verse beginning "pari" (10.42). The word "pariveṣayantyaḥ" implies [food] for their relatives, servants, and others; having abandoned that serving, they departed.

The connection is with what precedes. He speaks of the abandonment of some who were exceedingly affectionate by means of the verse beginning with "pāyayantyaḥ. The word "hitvā" (having abandoned) is understood from the context. According to what follows, they have abandoned their brothers, sons, and so forth;
otherwise, there would be the fault of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*). Having thus described the abandonment of the world, he describes the abandonment of dharma.
He said: "Desiring to serve, serving, and attending upon Him by providing warm water for bathing and other such services, they will establish [Him].
He also speaks of some abandoning even the concern for their own bodies: "Eating" means consuming food;
by this it is shown that among those possessed by love for Him, there is no consideration for bodily purity or impurity.
It is understood. ||5-6||

And for some, even in separation, they repeatedly apply ornaments to their limbs out of hope for a reunion day by day; thus, following the style of the *Gītagovinda*, he describes the abandonment of even their own bodily attire through intense longing, which is itself a manifestation of love for the Blessed Lord, beginning with the words "limpantyaḥ" (smearing).

"Smearing" means applying body-unguents; it should be understood that they even cast aside such things as ointments. The word "others" (anyāḥ) is to be construed with the two words beginning with "smearing" (limpantyaḥ). Showing the reason for that very point, [the text asks] what must be done:
the concern for the physical body and so forth has been abandoned. Of some... [of these women].
He also indicates that a lack of coordination among the specific parts of the body has arisen by saying "disordered" (*vyatyasta*).
This is the emotional response (*anubhāva*) called "bewilderment" (*vibhrama*), which follows from the eagerness (*autsukya*) characterized by the previously mentioned abandonment of everything.
As it has been said:
"At the moment of attaining the beloved, due to the agitation of the onset of passion,
there is *vibhrama*— the displacement of ornaments such as necklaces and garlands from their proper places" (Uṇādivṛtti 11.39).
By this it is shown that for those of such a nature, the manifestation of love toward the Blessed Lord occurs through emotional intensity (*āveśa*) rather than according to formal expectation.

It is understood that later on, she herself dressed him in the very same way he had been dressed by her; thus, one should infer that among these acts, such as milking and so forth, there is a progressive excellence due to their being indispensable requirements. In this manner, all of them set out and went toward Kṛṣṇa.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Describing through three verses how [the gopīs] departed by disregarding their own bodies and bodily functions, and by abandoning their selves, actions, worlds, and duties— due to that most enchanting song of His— [the author first describes] the abandonment of their own caste and duties by some of them.
He said: "They are milking. They are milking the cows, meaning they are performing the act of milking (*doha*) or [obtaining] the milk (*dugdha*).

For at that time, even the cowherd women were engaged in milking the cows for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. Alternatively, the term *dohayantyaḥ* contains an implied causative sense, meaning "they are causing [others] to milk."

They approached; they went toward the flute-song. The passage beginning with "Some... and so forth refers to the various divisions of the large multitude, as will be stated later: "the leader of hundreds of groups of women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.44). Their individual names are not mentioned out of respect for their great number. Or rather, of them...

Because of the particularity of their remembrance, they fear a deficiency in their love; this has indeed been explained in the first section of the *Śrībhāgavatāmṛta*. Likewise, the reason for their departure is that they are "eager," meaning they are incapable of enduring any delay of time. This is the reason.

The word "also" (*api*) is to be understood as following everywhere. The word "others" (*apare*) connects both with what precedes and with what follows; so too in the subsequent cases. The rest has been explained by them.
Alternatively, [the meaning is]: having placed the milk on the hearth and not removed from it even when cooked, and likewise having placed the *saṃyāva* on the hearth and not removed from it. ||5||

Having thus stated the abandonment of the three primary evening rites by some, and having described the abandonment of worldly duties by others in that same context through three verses, he first speaks of the abandonment of common relatives, servants, and so forth by some, beginning with the verse starting with "pari. [The women] were serving food.

They remained distributing and offering food and other provisions to their kinsmen, servants, and others; having set aside the serving of that [food], they departed—this is the connection with what precedes. Although even this is included within the other evening duties, nevertheless, for women, [the service] to the husband...
The general direction is this: by disregarding relatives, dependents, and so forth, one should attain happiness within the very abandonment of worldly dharmas.
Regarding some of those who should not be disregarded, she speaks of their abandonment with the words beginning "pāyayantyaḥ" (nursing) and ending with "pādābhyām" (with her feet).
The word "hitvā" (having abandoned) is understood to carry over. She has abandoned her children, such as the sons of her sisters, and thus [describes] the abandonment of the world.

Having stated the abandonment of dharma, he says: "serving" (*śuśrūṣantyaḥ*) means "those who serve" (*śuśrūṣamāṇāḥ*), serving by providing warm water for bathing and other such needs. "Eating" (*aśnantyaḥ*) and "feeding" (*āśayantyaḥ*) contain an implied causative sense (*antar-bhūta-ṇic*); thus, "feeding their husbands" refers to the act of causing them to eat, that is, the state of being a feeder.
Or rather, thus has the renunciation of worldly conventions been stated previously even for those supreme women who were devoted to dharma and other virtues.
Having thus stated the abandonment of the three primary evening rites by some,
in that very context, the renunciation of worldly conventions was stated for others, and the abandonment of concern for the body for yet others.

He says [the answer] with three quarters [of a verse]: "eating" means consuming. Thus, by the renunciation of food, the disregard for the body—which is the means of pleasing the Blessed One—is expressed.
By this it is understood that among those permeated by love for Him, there is no consideration regarding the purity or impurity of the physical body.

"Smearing" refers to those who apply sandalwood paste and the like as anointment to their own bodies; it should be understood that they have set aside such acts of anointing and so forth. Thus, by the renunciation of even the refinement of enjoyment, the neglect of the body is established.
And for some, due to supreme longing, it is for the sake of pleasing the Blessed Lord.
He also speaks of the abandonment of their vessels, implements, and ornaments for their own bodies with the words beginning "limpantyaḥ" (smearing).

It should be understood that by saying "limpantyaḥ" (smearing), which means "applying body-unguents," they have cast aside even the act of smearing and so forth. The word "anyāḥ" (others) is to be construed with each of the three phrases ending in "limpantyaḥ. Showing the reason for this very point, he asks: "What..."?

What is to be said? It is that the dependence on the body and so forth has been abandoned. [The author] says "confused" (*vyatyasta*) because even the non-forgetting of the body has arisen in some [of them]. This is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) called "delusion" (*vibhrama*) of the longing (*autsukya*) characterized by the aforementioned state of renouncing everything. As it has been said:

"At the moment of attaining the beloved, due to the agitation of the onset of passion, there is *vibhrama*—the displacement of ornaments such as necklaces and garlands from their proper places" (Uṇī. 11.39).

By this, it is shown that for those of such a nature, the manifestation of love for the Blessed Lord occurs through intense emotional absorption (*āveśa*) rather than according to deliberate expectation.

It is understood; however, it should be known that subsequently he himself properly caused him to wear what had been worn by that very person. In this way, because these acts such as milking and so forth are necessarily required, their relative superiority should be inferred in ascending order.
Alternatively, the sole intention here is simply the abandonment of one's own respective *prārabdha* karma.
In that regard, the wearing of disarrayed garments and ornaments signifies merely the abandonment of the customary manner of wearing clothes and so forth;
and the reason for this in every instance is stated as "those whose minds have been seized by Kṛṣṇa" and "those who are intensely longing."

Thus it is said: in this way, all of them went indeed into the presence of Kṛṣṇa—the supreme attractor, the beautiful dark one, the son of Śrī Yaśodā. The meaning is that they did not remain at a distance due to shame or other obstacles, because they were utterly infatuated. Even though he was where their beloved was...

By the phrase "they came there," only the act of going into his presence is expressed; nevertheless, because of supreme delusion and extreme impetuosity, there is a further specific description with the intention of expressing that they went exceedingly close—this is the general direction [of the interpretation]. ||7||
Thus, in this manner, all of them set out and went toward the presence of Kṛṣṇa. ||7||

The sequence of events: Milking and causing others to milk, they approached and moved forward (5). [They approached] the children, sisters, brothers, sons, and so forth. Because of the statement "milk, cow's milk, and the breast for the sons," there is a diversity of focal objects (*ālambana*). All of them are the substrata for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the autumnal poetic narrative [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*].

This is because there would be a contradiction with the fact that [the women] will be the locus of the rasa to be described in [10.33.25]. Furthermore, those referred to as "serving" (śuśrūṣayantyaḥ) should be understood as only certain maidservants within the inner apartments; for other women are excluded by such statements as, "of their husbands, children, and friends" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.32], and so forth. //6//

*Prīti-sandarbha* 344: "Āvega" (agitation) occurs when the mind is in a state of flurry, as in the verse beginning with *duhantyaḥ*. This is clear from the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, in order to manifest the intensity of their longing, [the author] first establishes the past time by stating that they had previously arrived, and then describes the manner of their return from the very beginning.
He demonstrates the emotional state (bhāva) called agitation (*āvega*) with the words beginning "milking, they approached" (*duhantyo 'bhiyayuḥ*), and so forth, [using] many [expressions].

The word *duhantyaḥ* contains a causative suffix (*ṇij*); the meaning is that they were having [the cows] milked through their brothers and others. Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the milking" (*dohaṃ hitvā*), the meaning is that they did not return home from the place of milking, but rather came directly from there.
Some, having placed milk on the fire— not merely having it nearby— and others, having not removed the *saṃyāva* (sweetmeat) from the oven nor taken it down,
were serving it while their elders were eating;
and others were feeding cow's milk to infants and children whose offspring they were protecting.
Some were smearing [their bodies] with unguents, others were applying ointments, while others were performing a thorough cleansing of their limbs;
some were anointing their eyes, coloring them with collyrium;
some were serving their husbands—those who take pride in their spouses—delighting them with attentions such as ritual service; and others were eating.
While she was eating, he cast that [food] away. ||5-7||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described their departure in general through the state of their minds being attracted to Kṛṣṇa, [the author] now says that they went by abandoning their homes and so forth in the form of non-return, like yogīs, showing no regard for their bodies or bodily needs and having no attachment to worldly or otherworldly activities.
Regarding the phrase "milking": in that context, some have set out, abandoning their attachment to what has already been milked—that is, the milk which constitutes their very livelihood.
Thus he says, "milking," which describes the arrival of those who have attained perfection through spiritual practice (*upāsanā*). Here, the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) is indeed inherent.
The meaning is "milking. They departed without even considering how things would fare once the milk—the object of the milking—or the vessel had been left right there;
that is to say, they went with *abhiniśaṅkam*, meaning they went without having any fear toward their husbands and others.

Some, being eager and unable to endure any delay of time, placed the milk they had brought upon the hearth and departed even before it had boiled; others went away leaving the *saṃyāva*—a wheat-flour cake—even though it was uncooked, because of their eagerness. "Eager" (*samutsukāḥ*) is an adjective qualifying all of them. (5)
Thus, it has been stated that some women, possessing worldly means of livelihood, departed after abandoning their homes.

Now, he describes the abandonment of dharma characterized by service to husbands and others—with the words "serving them. Some, while serving prepared food to their kinsmen, were concerned with what was required for them.

"Having gone without giving [them food], they attended upon [the Lord]"—thus the arrival of those in the form of sages was described. Some, while nursing at their breasts infants who were the objects of their maternal affection, departed, abandoning their love without waiting for the children's satisfaction; thus it is said, "while nursing."

Regarding those in the form of forest-dwellers in the Daṇḍaka forest, it is said that some, while serving their husbands, departed after abandoning the dharma characterized by such service. It is stated that they served and attained perfection through the arrival of those in the form of sages who had achieved success through worship; for even though dharma is accomplished through service to one's husband, [this was not the case here].

And there is the pacification of the torment of desire. Thus, it is said that by means of a worldly thing, a worldly thing is the essence. Even for those causes that remove worldly torments, the non-worldly torment of desire is extinguished, as indicated by the absence of capacity. Some, while eating—that is, consuming food—[do so].
Having cast it aside and abandoned it, they departed, without waiting for their bellies to be filled. ||6||

Having thus described how their minds, drawn by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, reached as far as their bodies, and how they abandoned all attachments, [the author] says "limpantyaḥ" (anointing), describing how they departed without even regarding the ornaments of their own limbs, not even considering whether these limbs would be fit for his dalliance.

Some, while applying ointments such as sandalwood paste to their own bodies, departed after casting aside that which was only half-applied. Others, while massaging their limbs with unguents and the like, departed without waiting for the application to be completed on all parts of the body. Some were applying collyrium to their eyes.

They departed, some with their garments and ornaments disarrayed. Thus, when there is a lack of concern for the body and its belongings, a confusion is described regarding even the garments and ornaments, as well as the hands, feet, and so forth, through such reversals as wearing them upside down or half-worn; and that [confusion] is indeed nothing but longing (autsukya).

Those who had been engaged in play likewise all went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa. The young maidens, however, remained waiting and vigilant. But they had already abandoned their homes; those who were previously married had gone forth, having cast off all concern for their bodies and their houses. ||7||

Viśvanātha: At the time of their approaching His side, because the delay was unbearable due to their supreme longing, He speaks through three verses of the absence of regard for actions that are the locus of "mine-ness" and "I-ness," and states that some of them abandoned the duties of their own class: "Milking the cows, causing them to be milked, [performing] that milking..."

Abandoning the task of milking, they rushed forward and ran toward [the kitchen]. Having placed the milk that had been drawn into a vessel upon the stove and set it over the fire, some, without waiting for the boiling to finish, [prepared] *saṃyāva*—a mixture of wheat flour and sugar—even though the wheat-grain food was still cooking, they did not remove it from the heat nor take it down. ||5-6||

He speaks of the abandonment of the duties common to all women: while serving food—that is, attending to their husbands by providing warm water and so forth—they abandon certain necessary physical acts and dress;
"anointing" means applying ointments such as sandalwood paste to the body, and "rubbing" means wiping it clean.

Regarding some women who are performing tasks such as massaging with fragrant unguents (*udvartana*), he states that due to the force of their agitation (*āvega*), there is even an absence of familiarity with the specific parts of the body—this is expressed by the word "crossed" (*vyatyasta*).
This is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) known as "confusion" (*vibhrama*). As it has been said:

"At the moment of attaining the beloved, due to the agitation caused by the onset of passion, there is confusion (vibhrama), which is the displacement of ornaments such as necklaces and garlands from their proper places. [Uṇī. 11.39] Thus ends [verse] 7.
Though they were being restrained by their husbands, fathers, brothers, and kinsmen, those women,
their hearts stolen by Govinda and deluded, did not turn back.
Śrīdhara: And he says—"tā vāryamāṇā" (verse 8)—to show that obstacles do not prevail over those whose minds are drawn by Kṛṣṇa.
Vaṃśīdhara says: "For those who are devoted to Hari, there is the destruction of all obstacles"—thus he says, "Not so" (*na ceti*).

They "prevail," meaning they become capable. Even when restrained by their husbands—either through instruction in dharma or by physical means such as seizing the hand—because women share in the auspicious and inauspicious karma of their husbands; or by their fathers out of affection; or for fear of ill-repute.

Out of affection she is protected by her brothers, and out of fear of family disgrace by her kinsmen. According to the Smṛti, "The father should protect the maiden; the husband, when she is grown up; and the son, in old age; and in the absence of these, the agnates"—thus there are four protectors. The implication is that sons are generally not mentioned here because they have not yet been born.

The meaning is that their very selves, known as the individual souls (*jīva*), were carried away by Govinda; thus, the sense is that they went for the sake of life, lest there be a severance from life upon His departure. Furthermore, the meaning is that they became deluded, being devoid of the knowledge of His departure due to the influence of an overwhelming infatuation. ||8||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: “Being restrained,” and so forth. This means they were restrained by verses and other means;
the negative particle (*na*) connects with the distant [verb]. Therefore, they did not turn back, because they were inferred—that is, conjectured:
“Are you staying at home? Or have you gone somewhere for another task?”—thus they were speculated upon.
Their minds were carried away by the sound of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s flute, so they did not realize they were departing for that place; thus,
thinking each his own wife was by his side, the inhabitants of Vraja— this is the connection with what will be said in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38.

Alternatively, there is a word-break as *tā vā*. They were not being sought after or approached by their husbands and others; here the particle *vā* implies a rhetorical question (*kāku*). The meaning is that their husbands and others did not follow after them. Why?
Because they were deluded (*mohitāḥ*). They were not considered (*mā ūhitāḥ*) or reflected upon [by others], since their very selves had been carried away by Govinda.

Their own bodies had been carried away by Govinda; therefore, they were not noticed by them. Alternatively, though being restrained by their husbands and others, they did not turn back, because they were deluded—that is, they were driven on. ||8||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, [the author] speaks of the abandonment—even by those women who were forced by their own [relatives] to attend to external affairs—of even such things as shame (*lajjā*), which are so natural to noble wives that they are extremely difficult to cast off; he says, "They... All of them, though questioned by their husbands and others as to where they had gone outside during the night, [responded:]...
The meaning is that although they were repeatedly restrained with persistent insistence, they did not turn back, but indeed went on.

Why? Because they were deluded, their discrimination destroyed. Why was that? Because their very selves—their minds—had been carried away by Govinda. This should be understood as the reason for the laxity of even their husbands and other relatives.

Because the mere devotion to Him possesses the power to remove all obstacles, some women who reside there— such as those with husbands living nearby, or with fathers and other relatives, or even those unmarried to their fathers and others— [are protected].

"A father should protect a maiden; her husband, when she has reached maturity; and her son in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen [should do so]; thus, a woman never possesses independence. Such is the traditional law (smṛti). (8)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, [the author] describes the disappearance of all their deliberations, even as they were being exhorted by their own kin, because their hearts had been stolen by the Blessed Lord—beginning with the words "tāḥ" (they).
All of them were being restrained by their husbands and others through the demonstration of dharma and other means.
Even though they were being restrained from going by means of taking them by the hand and so forth, they did not turn back, but rather went on;

this is the meaning. Why? Because they were deluded, their discrimination destroyed. Why was that? Because [they were led] by Govinda, the Lord of Gokula. Or alternatively, he is so called because he perceives (vindati) the senses (gāḥ) as his own master (īśvara).
Those whose very selves and minds have been carried away by Him—by the Greatest One. For when property has been stolen by the greatest [thief], those who are small [cannot recover it];

and in the other sense, when that which is most dear to millions of lives has been stolen from within by the Great Deluder (Mahāmohana), who is the Inner Lord, others—that is, external beings—lack the capacity to restore it. In this regard:

An illustration should be seen as follows: just as a boat being carried away by the force of a current would not stop even when those standing on the bank cry out "Stop! Stop! or by those already on board attempting to hold it back;
likewise, in the case of *nivṛtti*, there is a separation from the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is called the "self" (*ātman*), which has been carried away—that is, drawn off—by Govinda.
The word *syāt* (it might be) implies that they have gone solely for the sake of their livelihood; this is the meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*).

In that context, first, it is said "by the husbands," because they are primary due to being the recipients of the wife's good and bad fortune; and then, because the blemish touches them merely through the daughter's deficiency, it is said "by the fathers" out of affection. And then...

Out of fear of ill-repute and out of special affection, she should be protected by her brothers; furthermore, out of apprehension regarding a stain upon the family, she should be protected by her kinsmen.
A father should protect a maiden, a husband when she has reached maturity, and a son in her old age.
In the absence [of these], the kinsmen [shall act] in this manner; women never possess independence in any circumstance.

Since it is stated thus in the Smṛti, four protectors are mentioned here. Among them, sons are generally not included because they are not born in this [state]. Furthermore, it should be inferred that among these—beginning with the husband—there is a progressive decrease [in authority], because there is a progressive decrease in both subjection to and connection with each respective [protector]. Nevertheless...
Even when each preceding generation has desisted from activity, each succeeding generation continues therein,
out of regard for the continuity of the family collective;
or else, because each preceding generation has abandoned [the world], each succeeding one acts out of fear that they might seek refuge elsewhere.

The prevention occurs gradually. Alternatively, it should be discerned that some [daughters] are [prevented] by husbands residing near them, while others are [prevented] by fathers and so forth; and among those, it should be distinguished that some wives are indeed unmarried daughters living in their own homes, along with their husbands and fathers and so forth. The rest is the same.
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, one might ask, "How was it that they were not prevented by their husbands, fathers, or brothers? To this he says: "tā vāryamāṇāḥ" (being restrained), and so forth. By their husbands, fathers, and brothers...

The meaning is that they were not restrained by their kinsmen. Those who were already married were stopped by their husbands, and those who were unmarried by their fathers and others; for this very reason, they did not turn back, as there was no obstacle [to their departure]. How was it that they were not prevented by each of those [relatives]? To this he says:
"Mā ūhitāḥ"—they were not suspected or conjectured [to be leaving] due to the power of her *yogamāyā* (illusory potency). Each and every one of them [was thus deceived].
Only those standing nearby knew [this]. Or rather, why did they not turn back through reflection?
To this he says: "Their souls were stolen by Govinda. When the self (ātman) exists, qualities such as the intellect (buddhi) arise;
when these exist, reflections proceed. The meaning is that by the abduction of the self, everything has been abducted.
The negative particle *na* is to be applied to both [terms] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye. ||8||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: When it was seen that even those preoccupied with duties such as their bodies and homes, and those occupied with serving their husbands and others, came having abandoned their sense of possessiveness (*mamatā*), then some were forbidden by their husbands and others, and this memory arose:
A father should protect a maiden; her husband, when she has reached maturity; and her son, in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen shall protect her.
"A woman has no independence anywhere" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.85).

Thus, having previously abandoned both worldly and otherworldly duties, even though they were possessed of shame as noble ladies of the family, they departed after perceiving that shame was an obstacle; regarding this, he says: "Those women"—those who...
At the time of their arrival from the mountain, they came within the range of vision of their relatives, but they were stopped by them;
nevertheless, they did not turn back, for they had already gone, being infatuated. The meaning is this:
these women had been summoned by Kṛṣṇa. Having observed their agitation upon hearing the song of His flute, [the relatives] attempted to stop them.
[The flute-song] proceeded. Immediately after hearing the flute-song, they too became indifferent to restraining those [women].

For this very reason, they were not restrained despite firm effort. Therefore, if they had remained devoted to nothing else, they would not have become so immersed in the pleasure of the flute-song; otherwise, how could they have disregarded their husbands and others?

There must have been a reason for their arrival, since they were thus deluded; it was already stated that "they resorted to yogic illusion," and he will say later—"thinking [the Lord] was standing by their side. He states the cause for this: those whose self (ātman), mind (citta), and bodies were carried away by Govinda. Furthermore, just as the Gaṅgā...

Just as a river flowing toward the ocean disregards obstacles such as mountains and enters the ocean alone due to its excessive love for it, so too these women, though seen by their husbands and others and restrained by the display of threats, did not turn back; rather, they were utterly infatuated.
"Those whose discrimination has been destroyed" means those who lack discrimination regarding anything other than attaining Kṛṣṇa. ||8||

Viśvanātha: Now, it is indeed appropriate that they abandoned all other expectations due to the intensity of their love; however, how was it that their husbands and others abandoned their expectations for them? To this he says: although those noble wives were being restrained by their husbands, and those noble daughters-in-law by their fathers and others, they did not turn back from there.

The cause is that Govinda has taken away even fear, shame, and the like—what need is there to mention them? For he has snatched away those very selves [of these emotions] as well; thus the meaning is that they are deluded and fainted, like puppets moved by the strings of the Sūtra. Even for the bodies of wives and others whose life-breaths have departed, there is fear of instability [caused] by their husbands and so forth.

If it is argued that such movement elsewhere is not possible, this is true; however, this apparent contradiction should be understood as a manifestation of *yogamāyā* (divine illusory power), conceived precisely for the sake of providing a resolution for those various gopīs who, at each respective moment, were led away by their own husbands and others as imagined [by that power].
The method by which they were turned back toward their respective homes by their husbands and others will be explained further ahead:
"Some gopīs who had entered the inner apartments were unable to find a way out."
Endowed with the contemplation of Him, they should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa with their eyes closed.

Śrīdhara: Those by whom no exit was obtained; the meaning is that even before, they were already engaged in the cultivation of that [thought], and at that time they meditated upon it all the more intensely. ||9||
Vaṃśīdhara: "Into the interior of the house"—that is, into the middle of the house; there they went and were restrained. Some among them were portions of Mahālakṣmī. "Exit" means going outside.
Alternatively, it means that like other gopīs, they did not obtain an extremely swift departure like that of birds (*vīna*). Or else:
The sense is that even the exit of a bird from a hole was not found by them;

having made this their primary concern, they were as if possessed by thieves seeking an escape. They were endowed with the contemplation—that is, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—of devotion toward that Kṛṣṇa, even prior to hearing the sound of his flute.
"At that moment of hearing the sound of the flute"—this is the meaning. That is to say, because hearing that [sound] makes known His manifestation, it serves as a cause for meditation. ||9||

* Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "Those who have gone into the inner apartments," and so forth. It should be understood that the gurus were seated at the door of the inner apartment. Alternatively, the word "some" (*kāścit*) refers to those who lack the authority to go [outside]; otherwise, the phrase "some... desiring to serve their husbands" would be inappropriate here.

And in the passages "leaving that while serving [the meal]" and "not eating, having set aside the food," there is indeed their presence within the house and their proximity to their husbands and others. How then did they go there? For these are precisely the gopīs who were previously described as having young children. Regarding them—
Or rather, the sense is that there is no fitness for contact with his limbs. ||9||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And if they had been obstructed by such an obstacle, they would have immediately fallen into a state as if they were in their tenth stage [of life]. Thus, demonstrating the particular nature of the internal state (*bhāva*) of all of them through an illustration, [the author speaks] while they were still in the midst of setting out.

He describes a specific state of some [of them] with three verses beginning with "antar. This is the meaning: the beloveds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Vraja are indeed of two kinds—those who are eternally perfect (nitya-siddhāḥ) and those who have attained perfection through spiritual practice (sādhana-siddhāḥ).
Among them, the status of being eternally perfect for one group is established by their very distinction [from others] in the *Aṣṭādaśākṣara* and other scriptures.

Because the methods for worshipping Him are clearly manifested, and because both His Vedic scriptures and the modes of worshipping Him have existed without beginning or end, it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*:
"In palaces made of clusters of wish-fulfilling gems and surrounded by desire-trees..."
"Surabhi protects those surrounded by hundreds of thousands of crores;
he is served with the agitation of hundreds of thousands of millions of Lakṣmīs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.29),
thus [described] by those permeated by the essence of bliss and pure consciousness.
"By those very arts (kalās) which are His own essential nature,
He dwells in Goloka itself" (Brahma-saṃhitā 5.37);
"The beloved of Śrī is the Supreme Person" (Brahma-saṃhitā 5.56)— these indeed are they.
They are described as being His [Kṛṣṇa’s] Lakṣmīs. Regarding the preeminence of Śrī Rādhikā among them, it is stated in the Bṛhad-gautamīya:
"The goddess Rādhikā, who consists of Kṛṣṇa, is declared to be the supreme deity."
"She consists of all prosperity, she is all-beauty, the supreme enchantress.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa* regarding their mutual inseparability: "The divine Mādhava shines among the people with Rādhā, and Rādhikā likewise with Mādhava. Therefore, in the *Matsya-purāṇa* and other texts, [it is said of] Rukmiṇī...

Although Rādhā is in Dvāravatī and [the other] in the forest of Vṛndāvana, their inclusion here should be understood as being due to their commonality as Śaktis; nevertheless, their specific distinction must be recognized. Now, regarding the attainment of the lower goddesses through spiritual practice, it is stated in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
In former times, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
upon seeing Rāma, who was Hari himself in a beautiful form, desired to eat him there.
"All of them attained womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. [Bhṛṅgariṣi 1.2.301-2] Thus it is said.

Because of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the phrase "having reached Hari" within the context of *Gokula*, and according to the principle stated in *Bhagavad-gītā* 4.11, "In whatever way they approach Me," the meaning is that the great sages were previously worshippers of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with such a disposition.
Therefore, the phrase "having seen Rāma" refers to those whose impressions of worship had arisen through the attainment of similarity of form (*sārūpya*). Hari...
Out of modesty, they desired to enjoy only their own chosen Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, yet they did not choose Him directly;
consequently, by the grace of Śrī Rāma—who, like a wish-fulfilling tree, grants desires even without speaking—their cherished goal was accomplished.
This is stated in the words "All of them... [referring to the verse beginning with *te sarve*], meaning that having attained femininity from the womb in Gokula, they remained in Gokula itself.

Having become like oceans and having attained Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, within Gokula itself according to their own desires and latent impressions (vāsanā), and finding Him manifested right there within the inner chamber,
they were liberated from the ocean of worldly existence immediately thereafter; and it should not be said that this applies only to those born in Gokula.

Since it is impossible for the descent and pastimes (*avatāra-līlā*) to possess mundane characteristics, and because they are indeed mixed with the mundane, it is heard in scripture that even the venerable Queen Devakī gave birth to those known as the six embryos;
thus, there is the well-known tradition in the *Bṛhad-vāmana* that at times the Vedic seers (*śrutayaḥ*) became cowherd women (*gopyaḥ*). For this very reason, it is so.
It will be explained:

"We women have fixed our minds upon the arms of the Lord of the Wide Earth, which are like the coils of a serpent; we too are equal to them, for those who see with equanimity find nectar in His lotus feet. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.23)
