Thus, Gāyatrī was born among them; as it is stated in the *Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa* of the *Padma Purāṇa*, regarding the marriage of Gāyatrī—who had assumed the form of a cowherd girl—to Brahmā, Lord Viṣṇu spoke to the cowherds:
"Since she has been recognized [as his wife], this girl is therefore given to Viriñci."
"And in your family, I shall take an incarnation for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods; my beloved wife shall also come into being.
Therefore, regarding the statement [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.1.13], "For the sake of pleasing Him, let the celestial women be born," this is also [to be understood in this way].
It has been explained in that manner. For this very reason, their fourfold nature is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"The gopīs should be known as the Śrutis; those born of sages are the daughters of cowherds;
and they are daughters of gods, O King of Kings, and by no means human."

In this context, only the cowherd girls (gopikās) are eternal and never human; for their ordinary human nature has been negated. Furthermore, these girls are identical with those mentioned in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* as being within the inner chambers, who have attained a state of similarity to liberation (*muktatva*).
It is obtained because they are described as "some who desire to serve their husbands"; thus they are to be understood.

Since no separate duties such as milking are mentioned for them, and since their status as being within the household has its primary purpose (*tātparya*) in the service of the husband, their role as means to the goal is established by the scriptural account of their renunciation of the body in the *Pādma-Uttara-khaṇḍa*.
And it is thus conceived; and that being so, whatever women have arisen in Gokula who, by the power of their spiritual practice,
have attained perfected and complete *bhāva*, yet are not possessed of perfected bodies like other eternally perfected beings,
they remain within the inner apartments solely for the purpose of serving their husbands and so forth.
Because the gates of the city and so forth were blocked, they could not emerge by any particular means;

thus, since their very existence in such bodies was considered a hindrance to their direct union with Govinda, they did not engage in activities such as the slackening of devotion to their husbands as they had done previously.

This is to be understood: because they could not find an exit [from their hearts], those women who were engaged in the meditation upon Him and whose minds were filled with longing for Śrī Kṛṣṇa meditated upon that very Kṛṣṇa, who was the captor of their own hearts, as long as they remained there.
Regarding His majesty in that state, it is said: "By means of a particular kind of sorrow and through the intensity of their absorption in meditation."
With eyes sealed; or rather, those whose vision—meaning all other forms of knowledge—is closed or withdrawn. ||9||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "If they had been obstructed by such obstacles, they would have immediately reached the tenth stage [of death]. Thus, illustrating the particular state of mind of all of them through an analogy, he describes the specific condition of some of them with three verses beginning with *antar*.

Some, being portions of Mahālakṣmī or perfected through spiritual practice (*sādhana*), remained at home; for this very reason, they were confined to their doors and so forth by husbands and others who were merely nominal. Alternatively, because their fathers and other elders sat at the doorway, they did not obtain the special opportunity suitable for approaching the Blessed Lord. As it is said:

Or, like other gopīs, they were such that their exit—the going out, departure, or path—was for the sake of moving with extreme speed, like birds (*vīn*); or rather, those [paths] through which even the exit of a bird (*vi*) occurs from a crevice; and for this very reason, Kṛṣṇa, who attracts one's own heart.

They meditated—specifically, they intensely contemplated—the form that is a mass of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-ghana-mūrti*). This is according to the principle stated in such passages as *The object of meditation [should be resorted to] in times of distress* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.13), for the sake of deliverance from great calamity; or else, because the specific contemplation of Him arises spontaneously through the failure to obtain one's desired object. How did they meditate?

Of that aforementioned dalliance with Śrī Kṛṣṇa—or rather, of that most secret sexual union—endowed with or joined by the contemplation thereof, or being possessed of yoga; moreover, they were those whose eyes were closed, meaning their eyes were half-shut. Or else:

The women are those whose eyes are closed either due to a particular kind of suffering or due to a particular state of meditative absorption (dhyāna). Alternatively, they are those whose "locana"—meaning both the eye and all other forms of knowledge—is "mīlita," that is, hidden or vanished. Thus they are so described. ||9||
The sequence of composition: the group of eight beginning with "within" (antar). ||9||

(Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha 145): Thus, in this very way, the association of those whose forms consist of bliss with Śrī Kṛṣṇa by means of those very forms has been described. And the majesty of their forms has been stated there: "The Lord, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa].

[10.33.6] and so forth. And by Śrī Uddhava, while offering salutations to them, first demonstrating that they alone are the supreme bearers of the body with the words, "First these are the supreme bearers of the body" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58], he then asks in the middle: "Where are these women? [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.59].

Having thus restated the opponent's view, the author refutes it with the verse, "This is not a limb of Śrī" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.60), demonstrating that they are distinct even from Lakṣmī by showing their nature as her beloveds, and thereby establishing their supreme eternity; and therein, the grace that arose...
By this, having indicated that their devotion remains eternally internalized, he further demonstrates— through the verse beginning with "O, the dust of their feet" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.61)—
that the dust of their feet constitutes his own supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*). In which [dust] they took refuge...

By the verse, "The state of Mukunda, which is sought by the Vedas" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.47.61), that very state has been established as the supreme human goal; and by the passage beginning with "In that Vṛndāvana," the same quality has been established for Vṛndāvana. To further strengthen this through contrast, [the author speaks] of other [places].
For those who are newcomers whose bodies have not yet been perfected, the attainment of union with Him occurs precisely through the abandonment of the physical form;
this he states with the passage beginning "Having entered within the house" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.9) and ending with "And thus one should not feel astonishment" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.16).
[The verse says: "Having entered within the house, they served their husbands..."
"Some" here means those mentioned previously; in this context, "within" is quite explicit. ||9||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Showing that those who possessed offspring, due to a lack of qualification, abandoned that body and immediately went there in another form, he says with three verses beginning with "Those who had gone inside the house. Some women who possessed offspring, being disqualified, by fate happened to have gone inside the house.

Although they were ineligible and thus unfit for physical contact with the limbs [of Kṛṣṇa], yet desiring merely to see Him, they wished to go outside; however, finding no way out, they remained absorbed in meditation upon Him. To indicate the sign of such meditation, it says: "with eyes closed" (9).

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Furthermore, while all those who reached the presence of Kṛṣṇa did so through the weakening of obstacles, he now describes how those who were blocked by the intensity of obstacles immediately fell from their bodies; prior to that, he explains the manner in which they reached the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—*antar*.

Thus: some who were perfected in spiritual practice (upāsanā-siddhāḥ), having gone to the house with the desire to perform certain household duties, were blocked by their husbands and others upon seeing the agitation caused by the arrival of others immediately after hearing the flute-song; therefore, they did not obtain an exit—meaning those by whom no exit was obtained.
Thus it has been said:
"The gopīs should be known as the Śrutis; the daughters of the cowherds born of the sages were actually daughters of the gods, O King of kings, and by no means human."
Furthermore:
"Know that Mathurā is eternally mine, as well as the forest of Vṛndāvana, the Yamunā, the cowherd girls, and likewise the cowherd boys. Thus it is said.
These gopīs, however, being ever devoted to Kṛṣṇa, meditated upon Him alone in order to dispel their obstruction.
As they looked at the faces of their husbands and others with eyes full of anger, unable to find the door of exit, their eyes became closed. How were they? Before their movement was checked...

They were also engaged in the secret practice of that meditation. It is heard that when they were thus absorbed in meditation, if an obstacle arose, the intensity of their flood of love would increase;
just as when the flow of a river is obstructed by mountains and the like, its velocity becomes even greater.

Thus it is said. Therefore, just as they were previously delighted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa through kissing, embracing, and so forth, they should meditate while endowed with that very same contemplation (*bhāvanā*). For that which has not been experienced is not remembered.
Alternatively, "endowed" means being joined with those who are contemplating His previous amorous pastimes (*pūrva-ramaṇa*) through that same contemplation.
They attained union with the true form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; or rather, they were "yoked" like yogīs—the sense of "like" (iva) should be understood here.

Having first forgotten their own bodies and then visualizing His various limbs, they meditated with focused mindfulness. Of what nature were they? Their eyes were closed; their vision was not directed toward external objects.
Alternatively, they are those whose eyes—their capacity for deliberation—have been closed or slackened;
even though they were devoid of other knowledge, they meditated upon Him alone to attain Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The sense is that, because there was no other means [of attainment], a slackening occurred regarding the investigation of any alternative methods. ||9||

Viśvanātha: Here, the matter is analyzed according to the method set forth in the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*. To begin with, the gopīs are of two kinds: those who are eternally perfected (*nitya-siddhāḥ*) and those who have attained perfection through spiritual practice (*sādhana-siddhāḥ*). Those who have attained perfection through practice are further divided into two types:
those belonging to the group (*yauthikyaḥ*) and those not belonging to the group (*ayauthikyaḥ*). And those belonging to the group are themselves of two kinds.
Because they belong to the group of the Śrutis, they are the "conduct of the Śrutis" (śruti-caryā), and because they belong to the group of the Ṛṣis, they are the "conduct of the Ṛṣis" (ṛṣi-caryā).
Consequently, their fourfold nature is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The Gopīs should be known as the Śrutis; those born of the Ṛṣis are the cowherd girls."

"And the daughters of the gods, O king of kings, are by no means human. Thus, although their humanity is established by their very nature as cowherd girls (*gopī*), this prohibition—"not human"—indicates the absence of their being ordinary humans. In this context, they are indeed eternally perfected (*nitya-siddha*) cowherd maidens.

Because there is no mention of their means of attainment (*sādhana*). Even though they possess the state of being cowherd girls (*gopī*), the fact that the worship of Kātyāyanī is a means of attainment indicates nothing other than her human playfulness (*nara-līlatva*), precisely because her state as a cowherd girl is already established; this has been explained in detail in that very context. As for their state of being eternally perfected (*nitya-siddhatva*), however—

This is because their nature as the *hlādinī* potency is established by the statement in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, "Those who are permeated by the essence of bliss consisting of consciousness," and also by the *Bṛhad-gautamīya*, "She who is the great *hlādinī* potency," as well as because Kṛṣṇa’s dalliance with them is beginningless.

Because they are specified among the mantras consisting of ten, eighteen, and other numbers of syllables; because the meditations on those mantras and the Vedic injunctions prescribing them have existed throughout time without beginning or end; and because of the celestial maidens known from the authority of the scripture: "May the women of the immortals appear" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.1.23).
The fact that [the gopīs] are portions of eternally perfected gopīs is explained in the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*.
As for those who have attained perfection through the practice of the Vedic path:
"O You whose beauty exceeds that of ten million Cupids, when You are seen, our minds..."
Having attained the state of a passionate woman, they were undoubtedly agitated by love.
Just as the cowherd women dwelling in your world worship the Lover, considering him to be the essence of desire, so too do those born of human beings act out of their own desires.

This is understood from such extensive statements of Vāmana and from the conduct of the sages (*ṛṣi-carīṇām*). Furthermore, the fact that those described in the *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi* as "worshippers of Gopāla who previously had not attained their desired perfections" (*gopālopāsakāḥ pūrvam aprāptābhīṣṭasiddhayaḥ*, *Uṇī.* 3.44) were indeed in such a state is established.
In the past, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
having seen Rāma, who is Hari, there with his beautiful form, desired to eat him.

"They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula; having obtained Hari through desire, they were then liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. Thus it is stated in the *Pādma-Uttara-Khaṇḍa*.
Here, the phrase "having seen Rāma, they desired to enjoy Hari" indicates that [this occurred] by means of beholding the beauty of Rāma.

The meaning is that by remembering their own worshipful Lord Hari Gopāla, they desired to enjoy Him alone; however, out of modesty, they did not choose Him directly. Then, he says "all of them" to show that through the grace of Śrī Rāma—who, like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpa-vṛkṣa), grants desires even without speaking—their desired goal was accomplished. [They chose] Hari.

The fruit that was intended was "attaining through desire"; therefore, the unintended fruit is that they are liberated from the ocean of existence—that is, from *saṃsāra*—precisely because of that desire. In this regard, [it is said]: "Mothers, fathers, sons... (BhāgP 10.29.20), and: "O dear one, the service of husband, children, and friends... (BhāgP).

Thus, from the observation of the subsequent text beginning with "husband, sons, lineage, brothers, and kinsmen" [10.29.32], it is seen in the commentary on the Tenth Canto composed by Śrī Kavi-Karṇapūra Gosvāmī that the gopīs who had offspring were indeed confined within their inner apartments. Therefore...
In accordance with that, the universal [explanation] (having first grasped the root meaning,

it is then commented upon) is as follows: the truth here is this— the sages who were devotees of Gopāla, through the sight of the sweetness of Śrī Rāma’s form, ascended to the stage of the sprout (*aṅkura*) characterized by the firm inclination, taste, and attachment of *rāgamaya-bhakti*.

Even though their impurities were not yet fully ripened, they were brought to Gokula by the goddess Śrī Yogamāyā and born from the wombs of the gopīs as girls; among them, some— due to the abundance of association with eternally perfected gopīs— began even from the stage of the transition between childhood and youth.

Having attained their former passion and achieved the manifestation of contact with Kṛṣṇa’s limbs, their impurities were completely burnt away as they ascended to the stages of love, affection, and so forth. Although married by the cowherds, they remained free from the blemish of contact with those limbs through Yogamāyā alone; having become embodiments of pure consciousness, they were enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa within that state.

At night, during the time of the flute-playing, although they were being restrained by their husbands, they nonetheless went to meet their Beloved, accompanied by the eternally perfected gopīs, by virtue of the grace of Yogamāyā’s assistance. However, some [gopīs],
due to the lack of fortune to associate with the eternally perfected gopīs and others, had not attained love and thus their impurities (kaṣāya) remained undestroyed.

Led by the cowherds and enjoyed by the cows and cowherds, they became possessed of offspring. Indeed, immediately thereafter, through the abundance of their association with eternally perfected gopīs and others,
and due to the intensity of their longing for contact with Kṛṣṇa’s body, they became filled with *pūrva-rāga* (pre-attachment) and even became objects of His compassion.
Because their bodies were unfit for union with the limbs of Kṛṣṇa due to the lack of assistance from Yoga-māyā, they were forbidden by their husbands;
unable to go to meet Kṛṣṇa and seized by great distress, they viewed their husbands, brothers, fathers, and others as enemies to their own lives, as death approached. As was the case for others...

They remembered their mothers and other kinsmen; likewise, they remembered Kṛṣṇa, the sole kinsman of their very lives. He says "within" (antar) to express this: the meaning is that they were unable to escape because they were being restrained by their husbands—who were sitting there with threats and sticks—and thus remained ever confined.

Even though they were absorbed in meditation upon Him, at that moment they thought: "Alas, alas! O sole kinsman of my life, O treasure-house of the arts of Vṛndāvana! Even in another birth may I become Your beloved;
yet at this time of death, I did not behold the moon of Your face with my eyes. Be it so; let me see it even with my mind."
Saying to themselves, "I see," each of the women, with eyes closed, meditated intensely. ||9||
Their inauspicious karma was shaken off by the intense heat of their unbearable separation from their beloved;
their merit was exhausted by the bliss of attaining the embrace of Acyuta through meditation.
Even by uniting with that very Supreme Self through the notion of him being their lover,
they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the material modes, their bonds utterly destroyed.
Then the gopīs, whose desire was for Kṛṣṇa, abandoned their bodies and went to heaven;
having fully realized Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Brahman, they departed beyond time.
And previously they were endowed with knowledge, and for the most part it was so even then;
therefore, their departure to the Supreme Brahman was not due to desire.
For the Śruti declares: "There is no liberation without knowledge; there is no other path."
At that time, devotion is conjoined with desire, and from that, knowledge leads to liberation;
therefore, even in liberation, desire follows after their devotion.
Because they are always hostile toward those who possess water (the devotees), the lowest darkness belongs to the haters;
and even those such as the King of Cedi who share in the sentiment of hatred are designated by the word "liberation."
One following the path of devotion attained liberation separately by the grace of Viṣṇu;
even Kāma, though a doer of evil, became a bestower of grace through devotion to Viṣṇu.
Moreover, Viṣṇu would liberate even a devotee who is joined with a soul that was once hostile.
"Oh, how exceedingly compassionate is Viṣṇu, because of his liberation of Śiśupāla! Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa.

It is not appropriate to conceive of the Great-Grandfather of the world as a lover; nevertheless, Śrīdhara does not [fully] explain this in terms of his being Brahman. Furthermore, at that very moment, having attained that Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa, through meditation, they abandoned their bodies composed of the *guṇas*; this he states in two verses beginning with "duḥsaha. Now, how is this so?
Fearing that they might have departed because of a lack of knowledge [of Him as] the Supreme Self, he says: "even with the notion of a lover.
For the power of an object does not depend upon the mind; the sense is that even by perceiving Him otherwise, they were like those who have drunk nectar.
Now, one might ask: even if that were so, how could they depart while still bound by the karma of *prārabdha*? To this he replies: "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*).

"Those whose bonds are destroyed. Now, one might ask: how can *prārabdha* karma be destroyed without experience (*bhoga*), since it is said to be destroyed only through experience? To this he says: "By the unbearable...
Those whose inauspicious karmas have been shaken off—that is, gone—by the intense heat of the suffering caused by that unbearable separation from their beloved.

The meaning is that their sin is exhausted by the experience of the supreme suffering of not attaining Him. Likewise, those whose auspicious bonds of merit (puṇya-bandhana) are exhausted by that bliss which consists in the enjoyment of supreme happiness through the embrace of Acyuta attained by means of meditation (dhyāna); therefore, [this occurs] through the attainment of the Supreme Self by means of meditation.

Vaṃśīdhara says that through the complete destruction of all karma by means of the pleasure and pain experienced at that time, they abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*. He states "and what more" (*kiṃ ca*) to show that they did not merely contemplate [the Lord], but actually attained Him; "at that very moment" (*tadānīm eva*) means simultaneously with the time of meditation. "Composed of the *guṇas*" (*guṇa-mayam*) means the product of the three *guṇas*. Now, one might object:

One might suspect that while the abandonment of the body may occur in any manner whatsoever, association with it in its distinct form is extremely difficult for the ignorant; thus he says, "But surely" (*nanu*). The power (*śakti*) of a substance such as fire consists of its capacity to burn and so forth.
It burns only one who possesses the cognition (*buddhi*) in the form of the knowledge that "this fire is a burner"; [for] knowledge...

It does not depend [on anything else] and it does not desire [anything]. This should be understood as being like one who, even while thinking otherwise and even knowing "this is water," becomes free from old age and death by drinking that which is perceived through the cognition of water; such is the meaning, such is the intended sense. Otherwise, even one who has drunk the nectar would die; this is certainly so.

Following the Smṛti which states, "The performed action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must be experienced," he raises a doubt again with the word "nanu" (surely). Even so, although knowledge exists, let it be granted that the attainment [of results] occurs through the power of the object;
however, it should be understood how they abandon the body. To that question: "sadyaḥ" means at that very moment. What?

Furthermore, the destruction of bondage is seen to occur only through the exhaustion of commenced merit and demerit (*prārabdha-puṇya-pāpa*); how does this apply here? Thus he raises the doubt with "But surely" (*nanu*). The answer to this is "unbearable" (*duḥsaha*).
That which is unbearable—that is, impossible to endure—is the separation from the Beloved Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa; it is a worldly disjunction (*sāṃsārika-viyoga*).

By that—meaning by that intense, most extreme heat, which is the experience of fever—the impurities, the non-virtuous sins, are shaken off and cast away. "By the experience" means by the undergoing of that supreme suffering which consists in not attaining [the desired object]. The intended meaning is that sin is exhausted precisely through the experience of suffering. How so?

In response to this expectation, he says: "Thus" (*tathā*). Since the attainment of the Supreme Self alone is the cause for the abandonment of the body composed of the *guṇas*, for that reason [he speaks]. If someone should raise the doubt, "How can there be the destruction of those [karmas] whose fruits have not yet begun?
he says in reply: "The lover" (*jāra*). A lover, or paramour, becomes even more dear than the husband; him...
They have fully realized—that is, they have correctly known—Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa himself;
for it is well established that roots meaning "to go" (gati) also carry the sense of "to know.
By this, it is indicated that even those karmas already set in motion are destroyed through the knowledge of Hari, who is the original archetype (bimba).

The realization of that [state] consists in the non-connection with and the destruction of both subsequent and prior [actions], according to the Sūtra. This is supported by the Śruti: "His friends [take over] his good deeds, and his enemies [his] evil deeds. The meaning is "of that knower.
Furthermore, even for those who have cast off their bodies like a snake sheds its skin, disappearance is effected through the power of Yoga-māyā.

Just as the body of the demon Aghāsura was made to disappear for a year, so too was the forgetfulness of the besiegers produced; otherwise, the public scandal caused by the siege and other such acts would have been difficult to avert. (10–11)

The Chest of the Caitanya Doctrine: Those whose inauspiciousness has been shaken off by the intense heat of unbearable separation from their beloved, yet whose auspiciousness has also been shaken off—this state of having both auspicious and inauspicious qualities constitutes the nature of *prārabdha* (fructifying karma) that initiates that body. Therefore, these are indeed human bodies.

In accordance with the explanation of the previous verse, however, there is no destruction of the pleasure and pain arising from the sight or non-sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa within that body when they are established by their very nature; for those two are not perishable but indeed eternal, since both consist of bliss alone. ||10||

Therefore, they abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*, but they did not attain *kaivalya* by merely casting off the body; rather, the meaning is that they attained a body devoid of *guṇas*, contracted within the limbs of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. As for the phrase "with the notion of a lover" (*jāra-buddhyā*), the word *jāra* refers solely to their perception. Alternatively, it means that [Kṛṣṇa] causes the body composed of *guṇas* to decay (*jarayati*).
"Jāra" means a lover; thus, "jārā-cāsau buddhiś-ca" refers to that intelligence by which they abandoned the body composed of the modes (*guṇa*).

Having attained the body that is beyond the modes (*nirguṇa*), what did they become? To this he says: the meaning is that they became united [with Him]. Of what nature was He? The Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Of what nature were they? The *gopīs* alone.
They were indeed the wives of cowherds. Furthermore, they had attained an exit within their inner hearts (*antaḥkaraṇe*);

that is, they had attained an exit in the form of despair, realizing that union with Kṛṣṇa would not be possible with this body. Having returned home, they remained right there in the house. Alternatively, "home" refers to the human body.

Because they remained solely as the wives of cowherds, their bonds were immediately destroyed; "bond" refers here to home and so forth, due to the attainment of a body devoid of [worldly] qualities—this is the connection with the three [verses]. Alternatively, they abandoned the body composed of qualities with the thought that it was merely a paramour. By this, it is shown that the gopīs were of various kinds, as was previously stated. ||11||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And then they say that they immediately attained union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, using the two verses beginning with "duḥsaha. Therein, they describe the result of longing with the half-verse beginning with "duḥsaha," and the result of meditation with the half-verse beginning with "dhyāna": through longing, they attained a union that was difficult to endure.
Thus they say: there is the state known as *vipralambha* (separation), characterized by the unbearable absence of the Beloved; by that [state] comes intense torment;

by that, their impurities are shaken off. By the cause of meditation, they attain the bliss of embracing Acyuta—the one renowned among his own devotees for being never-separate (*acyuta*); by that, their auspicious merits are exhausted. In this regard:
By the words "unbearable" (*duḥsaha*) and "intense" (*tīvra*), the ultimate limit of suffering is shown;

by the words "infallible" (*acyuta*) and "blissful cessation" (*nirvṛti*), the ultimate limit of happiness is shown. O Blessed One, impurity (*aśubha*) is that which produces suffering during its prior state when it has attained constant conjunction [with the self].
The manifestation of separation from Him and the auspicious manifestation of union with Him— which brings about happiness precisely during that state of separation—
are both present simultaneously now, even though they are to be experienced gradually through those two very mental modes (*vṛtti*) by which the practitioner attains mature love.
Thus, it is said that enjoyment has arisen, and thereby its state of being shaken off and its exhaustion are expressed. ||10||
Therefore, they gathered and met with Śrī Kṛṣṇa at that very place; likewise, there is the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya cited in the Vāsanā-bhāṣya:
"At that very moment, they reached the glorious Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees."
"Through meditation, [the Gopīs attained] supreme bliss and Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Gokula.
Because those two words do not have the same meaning as "sin" and "merit," and because they each bestow their own specific results, it is all the more so for sin.

Because it lacks the power to manifest the love born of separation from the Blessed Lord, there is no birth as a bondage of karma for Vaiṣṇavas; according to the *Pādma Purāṇa*, Uttara-khaṇḍa, Kārtika-māhātmya, they certainly lack such a birth resulting from their own *prārabdha* karma. Rather, the teacher’s son has been brought here.

According to this principle, since both the protection and non-protection of *prārabdha* karma consist solely of the will of the Śrī Bhagavān— who is expert in increasing one's own love— it has not been explained otherwise.
Now, one might ask: "Are they united with him as lovers? He says: "No;

rather, through such passion and longing, by which [the Lord] has been made accessible, even with the notion of him being a lover—and because he is the Supreme Self, the supreme essential nature of all, and because his status as a husband is established by his very nature as the protector of all, just as the term 'lover' (upapati) and others imply—he is attained."

The meaning is that for those women who bear specific dispositions, he is indeed the form of a husband (*pati-rūpa*) even by virtue of being their lover (*ramaṇa*). Even when he is approached with the notion of a paramour (*jāra*) due to the non-attainment of his status as a lover,
because of the boldness of the desire to obtain that very status of a lover, the state of being a paramour is impossible in him who possesses all [the qualities of a husband].

The sense is that, as in the expression "even with the intent to kill, [he is called] *hari*," and so forth, she refers to him as something to be abandoned even with the thought that he is a lover (*jāra*), because she has discarded both her former husband and his body. For instance, according to the *Viśva-kośa*: "In the root of the *paṭola* there may be pleasure (*ramaṇa*); likewise, *ramaṇa* means a lover (*priya*)," and "husband (*dhava*) means a lover (*priya*) or a master (*pati*)."

Furthermore, according to the *Amara-kośa*, which states that "husband (*bhartṛ*), lover (*jāra*), and paramour (*upapati*) are synonyms," one should not consider the terms denoted by "lover" and so forth to be identical to those denoted by "husband" and so forth;
rather, because the former implies ownership while the latter implies theft, they are indeed contradictory entities.

Even there, by not employing another word that is *sabhyam* (refined/proper) and instead using the *asabhyam* (unrefined/improper) word "jāra" (paramour), one perceives only the intention of censure (*nindā-tātparya*), just as in the case of the word "jighāṃsā" (desire to kill). This is because, according to lexicons such as the *Trikāṇḍa-śeṣa* and common usage, "jāra" means "sinful husband" (*pāpa-pati*). However, [the situation differs] when, through a certain passion (*rāga*), the state of being a paramour (*jāra-bhāva*)...

Although they committed acts censurable by the world that transgressed the boundaries of social custom, having indicated those very acts as praiseworthy, and although they were designated as "lustful" due to the similarity of their specific gestures, they nonetheless possessed the singular nature of pure love because their intent was solely to be favorable toward their beloved. And so it is said:
It will be said: "That lotus-foot of yours, O well-born one, [was placed] upon their breasts" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.19), and so forth.

For this very reason it was stated in such passages as: "Oh, even by those who enjoy the dust of their feet... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58), and "Those who, having abandoned the noble path which is so difficult to leave... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.61), and "These women are supreme... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.62).
"Even the sages, fearing worldly existence, desire that which we [also] desire" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58).
Thus, preceded by the renunciation of all that is to be abandoned,
there is the attainment of the crest-jewel of the supreme human goal, characterized by Kṛṣṇa, who is relishable through the nectar of great love (mahā-prema).
Having shown this, he states the incidental result: "and they abandoned their bodies composed of the modes" (*guṇamayaṃ ca dehaṃ jahuḥ*).

Since, by the manner previously described, their bonds were instantly destroyed, the attainment of a body consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) is also indicated. This is what is meant: the word "also" (*api*) here [is used].

The state of being abandoned by the notion of [the Lord as] a lover: in the passage, "Even by giving her breast to Hari with the intent to kill, she attained the goal of the righteous" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.35), the [notion of] intent to kill is shown to be something to be abandoned, because of its connection with those respective words through the expression of censure. The reason for this is that [it was directed toward] the Supreme Self; for the Supreme Self is not...
Even one who is designated by such censurable words may be worthy [of respect]. And the reason for this is: "unto Hari" (haraye).

Here, the word *hari* refers primarily to the state of captivating all hearts through great qualities such as compassion; for one who is thus constituted cannot be an object of malice (*jighāṃsya*). Even though he is unworthy of this or that [specific action], each such [quality] remains.

If she has somehow been born, then because she is the Supreme Self and the Sustainer, she is unfit to be abandoned due to her performing all that is beneficial; one should regard the hatred toward her— which is merely a semblance of devotion— as being like the act of suckling at her breast, and thus perceive her as having the nature of a nurse characterized by such [devotion].
Indeed, he did grant them internal union through that specific form of great devotion described in the verse beginning with "O, unbearable separation from the Beloved" (duḥsaha-preṣṭha-viraha);
for how could He not grant the state of His own beloved consort appropriate to that? This is the logical connection with what was stated previously.

It should be understood that this refers specifically to Gokula, which is a particular manifestation of the realm known as Goloka. For this very reason, the Blessed Lord sent a message through Uddhava:
"Those who remained in Vraja while I was sporting in this forest during the night..."
"Those auspicious women who had not attained the essence of the *rāsa* attained it by contemplating my prowess.
(Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.37) This *rāsa* should be understood as having occurred on that very day, because that alone is intended here;
for even though such a manifestation could have occurred on another day as a pastime of the cowherds (*gopālīlā*), they did not feel any resentment in this instance.

According to what will be stated in the passage beginning with "khalu kṛṣṇāya" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38), it is understood that for the sake of preventing the arising of suffering and other afflictions in His consorts and others, He caused the bodies abandoned through His own *māyā* to vanish and manifested others who were identical to them. Thus, for that duration of time...

Even the beloveds of the Śrī Bhagavān, who had attained the secret of the rāsa dance, did not know the true extent of His power as a manifestor of experience until they heard the message beginning with "That which was by Me" delivered through Uddhava.
Alternatively, what is surprising about their approaching His presence by following the sound of the flute? For:
Some, even while being restrained, reached him within the inner apartments; thus he says "within" (antar).

They are those whose inauspiciousness in the form of separation has been shaken off—that is, destroyed—by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa due to such intense longing; or alternatively, they are those by whom the inauspiciousness of the worlds itself was shaken off.

As it is said: "One endowed with devotion to Me purifies the world" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.40.24). Likewise, they are those whose auspiciousness—which is nourished, inexhaustible by such bliss, and opposed to decay—is their own union with Him in that same manner; and likewise, their auspiciousness is nourished for the worlds as well.

Or, as before, "those from whom auspiciousness [proceeds]" refers to the body consisting of qualities (*guṇa-maya*) and the state of separation (*viraha-bhāva-maya*), meaning their entrance [into the heart]. This was likewise shown in the third [chapter] in the context of creation regarding Brahmā.
The rest is the same. The connection [is established] because she became manifest within that very inner chamber; thus, she is "one who has gone into the inner chamber" (*antar-gṛha-gatā*).

Thus, by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For this very reason, they are those whose bonds have been instantly destroyed and who possess opposition to all attachment to those [objects]. Likewise, they are those who have not yet obtained the *rāsa*. This is to be understood as occurring on that very night, for the reasons previously stated. ||11||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And then, she says that they immediately attained union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa through two verses beginning with "duḥsaha": due to meditation—and especially because of the vivid manifestation of His form, qualities, and so forth—the separation from their dearest one became unbearable; therefore, by that...

They possess intense fervor; by that, their impurities are shaken off. Even toward that Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa, they are united with Him solely through the thought of Him as a lover (*jāra*). Because He constantly consumes them with the particular fire of love, He is called a *jāra* or *upapati*;
it is with that perception and that very disposition that they are joined, and not with the perception of Him as the Supreme Soul. Thus they are "well-joined" (*saṃgatāḥ*).
The meaning is that they have attained [Him] and have united with Him;
thus, eternal union through supreme love is intended.
How did they abandon the body composed of the modes? Rather, [they abandoned] that which is beyond the modes.
The meaning is that they have attained bodies fit for eternal association with the Lord;

the underlying sentiment is that they are united through the attainment of a form consisting of the solid mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*). Furthermore, this "association" is characterized by eternal union, like Śrī who eternally resides on His chest, or like the Great Potency (*mahā-śakti*) and others.
This is to be understood. Even there, some distinction should be inferred because they associated with Him while perceiving Him as a lover (*jāra*).
Thus, it was said by the Blessed Lord through Uddhava:
"Those who remained in Vraja while I was sporting in this forest during the night..."
"Let the auspicious women who have not yet attained the essence attain it by reflecting upon my prowess.

(Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.37) In this verse, by the words "the auspicious ones" (*kalyāṇyaḥ*) and "by reflecting upon my prowess" (*mad-vīrya-cintayā*), a specific kind of attainment is intended. This will become clear later in that very same section; it has already been indicated elsewhere as well.

In this context, by the words *duḥsaha* ("unbearable") and *tīvra* ("intense"), it is indicated that the suffering experienced through the enjoyments of the great hells and other realms for infinite millions of kalpas is exceeded by a suffering ten million times greater than that.
Likewise, by the words *acyuta* ("imperishable") and *nirvṛti* ("liberation"), [it is indicated] regarding infinite millions of kalpas...

The bliss derived from enjoyments such as universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) and self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), as well as even the bliss of liberation (*mokṣa*), which is superior to those, is implied here; for all of that is merely like a drop compared to the great ocean of the bliss of embracing the glorious Lord. And in that regard, by virtue of its connection with the glorious Lord—
The destruction of each respective latent impression (vāsanā) should also be understood [as implied]. For this very reason, the prefix *pra-* is used in the word *prakṣīṇa* (completely destroyed).

Likewise, that which is called "inauspicious" (*aśubha*) is specifically a type of karma that acts as an obstacle to eternal union with the Blessed Lord. And "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) is that which is the cause of a specific pleasure arising from the Blessed Lord’s conciliation and so forth toward those who possess honor and other such qualities.

There is a distinction in their meritorious deeds (*sat-karma*), as well as in the specific destruction of their respective [karmas], due to the establishment of their eternal union (*nitya-saṃyoga*). For this very reason,

because they lack the particular bliss of love that arises through separation (*viraheṇa*) and through honor (*māna*) and so forth, their good fortune (*saubhāgya*) must be understood as inferior to that of the other women who remain here.

Alternatively, they immediately abandoned even their bodies composed of all excellent qualities because that [body] was confined within the house by their husbands and others, thereby obstructing the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, the meaning is that they united with that very Śrī Nanda-kiśora through another body suitable for Him. Why? Because He is the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
The meaning is "most dear. The reason for this is: "with the thought of [him as] a lover. The rest is the same.

Or rather, by the power of meditation, their bonds—the door-obstructions created by their husbands and others—were instantly and completely destroyed; even though they were in such a state, [they perceived Him who is] composed of the qualities (*guṇa-maya*).

They abandoned their bodies, though composed of all excellent qualities, for the sake of that separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the most beloved of their dear ones— which was unbearable; therefore, they were shaken— that is, destroyed— by the intense heat of that great internal fever, or rather, by that [fever] which caused their fresh splendor to quickly fade away.
Furthermore,

"acyuta" refers to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who— by the authority of His own words such as "While I was worshiping Him behind my back" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.21)— is free from separation even during periods of absence, having attained union through meditation or by means of meditation; or else, it means "uninterrupted" (acyuta).

That is to say, they abandoned even that bliss characterized by the supreme happiness (*nirvṛti*) arising from the embrace of their Beloved alone; or rather, they abandoned it even though it was distinguished by that very bliss consisting of the embrace itself, which is perceived as being essentially the joy of union through a particular form of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Why? Because their auspicious signs have perished within the house due to confinement by their husbands and others;

or because their auspicious marks, such as forehead tilakas, have been destroyed during efforts to escape outside through contact with walls, door-panels, and the like; and because their radiance has vanished due to being worn out by great feverish heat.
The meaning is that, due to the disappearance of the *tilaka* and other marks, one considers oneself unfit for service to the Blessed Lord because one's body has become similarly soiled and decayed.

Alternatively, by resolving the compound (*praśleṣeṇa*), it refers to the non-destruction (*akṣīṇa*)— that is, the absence of decay— brought about by the embrace of Acyuta attained through meditation.

They abandoned even that auspiciousness characterized by the *rāsa*-dance and other pastimes, because through that very [abandonment], the perfection of all pleasure and delight was achieved; yet, being thus situated, they still gave it up. Why?
Because they were shaken by the intense heat of unbearable separation from their beloved. "Shaken" (*dhuta*) means shaking off or being tormented.
That is to say: those for whom that very same impurity, inauspiciousness, or great misfortune [remains], meaning again, out of fear of separation;
or else, those whose radiance (*bhā*), which is swift and unhesitating, has been shaken, agitated, and removed.

The meaning is that this is because their discernment has departed due to the heat of the intense separation. For this very reason, they have "immediately had their bonds completely destroyed. "Immediately" (sadyaḥ) means at once; "completely destroyed" (prakṣīṇa) refers to the bond, which is the bond of hope.
That bond of hope—such as "we shall obtain the pastimes of the rāsa dance and so forth by protecting our bodies"—has also perished.

This is the essential point. Otherwise, like other gopīs, there would be the impossibility of abandoning their direct residence within Vraja and their presence in Śrī Vṛndāvana. Therefore, the good fortune of the Śrī Gopīs who dwell here is indeed superior to theirs, solely by virtue of their eternal union [with the Lord].
Because there is an absence of the suffering of separation, they are praised by some as being unsatiated by any particular state of being (*bhāva*).
It is indeed explained in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta* that even in separation, a particular bliss may arise through the emergence of a particular intensity of love (*prema*).
Or rather, they caused [their sins] to disappear; or else, although they attained union with and attachment to that Supreme Self through the very notion of Him being their lover,
their inauspicious karmas were shaken off— that is, destroyed— by the intense heat of the unbearable separation from their beloved.

Those by which the threefold affliction—the impurity of the worlds—is [removed], possess the power to destroy the threefold affliction of the world because such specific affliction consists of the intense overflow of profound love for the Blessed Lord. Likewise, they have inexhaustible auspiciousness through the bliss of embracing Acyuta attained in meditation; "inexhaustible" (akṣīṇa) means nourished.
To those [goddesses] who have entered into the very intellect that is the auspiciousness of the worlds— since such meditation brings about the worldly prosperity of the worlds,
it brings about an increase in auspiciousness— those true ones abandoned their bodies composed of the *guṇas*. Here, the *guṇas* are the internal states (*bhāvas*).
Straightforwardness, steadiness, gentleness, the lack of knowledge regarding the means of exit, and timidity toward elders and others are internal [fetters];

while being scorched, staying within the house, and being bound are external. They abandoned the body which consisted of—that is, was dominated by—these. Here, the abandonment of those respective states is what is called the "abandonment of the body. As it is said:

In the context of creation, it is stated in the Third Canto that for Brahman, the relinquishing of various states is itself the relinquishing of the body. Therefore, those whose bonds have been destroyed— meaning those internal and external obstacles that constitute the fetters which hinder the attainment of the pastimes of the Blessed Lord on the following day— have their bonds completely eradicated.

"O auspicious ones, those of you who were tormented by your straightforwardness and other virtues, and who—because the time was spent that night in the bliss of embracing Acyuta—did not obtain the Rāsa dance. Thus, through knowledge liberation is attained; through affectionate devotion (prīti-bhakti) the world of Vaikuṇṭha is reached; and through pure love (prema), one becomes a subduer of the Blessed Lord, and therein [one acts] as His mistress.
The established conclusion is that union [with the Lord] occurs in Vraja through a specific intensity of love characterized by eternal dearness;
therefore, the essential meaning is that the *rāsa*-dance play must be cultivated in every way by everyone for the sake of generating such a state of being—
this is the sequence of the context, which has not been explained [in detail].

(From the *Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, 145): "Inauspicious" (*aśubham*) refers to fear of the guru and the like, which act as obstacles to attaining Śrī Kṛṣṇa. "Auspicious" (*maṅgalam*) refers to the means for attaining Śrī Kṛṣṇa, such as reflecting on the assistance provided by friendship and other such qualities. Furthermore, there is no bondage of karma or rebirth for Vaiṣṇavas.

For it has indeed been stated: "It exists" (vidyate) [Pañcapurāṇa 6.229.58]. Furthermore, the use of that word is observed in other instances as well, even in places where its literal occurrence is impossible—as in "Prosperity shall dwell upon my breast, its sins struck down by your feet" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.89.11), and so forth. In that case, just as...
Just as in that case, one must investigate another meaning for the sake of establishing the true import of the words of the Blessed Lord; so too here,
according to the established doctrine indicated from the Supreme Self down to a blade of grass [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.11], Śrī Kṛṣṇa is by His very nature...

The state of being the object of supreme love has been shown. Even by that cognition [of her] as a "lover" (jāra), she is joined with Him by that alone; it is not a direct attainment in the actual form of a lover. By placing that state at the forefront, the intensity of her worship is manifested, since she is designated by the word "lover."
Having demonstrated the transgression of worldly norms and conventions, it is shown that such a state of being is utterly unrestrained.
"Bondage" consists of dwelling among elders and other factors that oppose the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||11||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: By the intense heat of the unbearable separation from their beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their inauspicious karmas were shaken off and thus destroyed; by the bliss derived from the embrace of Acyuta attained during meditation, their auspicious karmas were exhausted.

"Those who possess auspicious deeds" refers to those [women] for whom there are such [deeds]. By this, it is shown that the exhaustion of auspicious karma occurs through the single suffering of separation from Kṛṣṇa; thus, because of that separation, the intensity of suffering is emphasized. Likewise, up until the exhaustion of happiness, it occurs through the single bliss of meditating upon Kṛṣṇa.
By the word "born," it is implied that the bliss of that meditative absorption (dhyāna) transcends all other forms of happiness. ||10||

Thus, when the exhaustion of their auspicious and inauspicious karma had occurred and the fall of the body initiated by that karma was imminent, he describes what happened at that time with the words "tam eva" (that very [body]). With the notion that it was a paramour, they abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*. While this body existed, he became a paramour; therefore, thinking "this body must be discarded," they abandoned it with the notion that it was a paramour.

The cause is this: they abandoned that which consists of the *guṇas* and attained a body free from the *guṇas*; such is the objection. However, [the author] shows that they ultimately attained a form worthy of contact with His limbs; for at that very moment (*sadyas*), they became united with Him alone—Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

This is the meaning. By this it follows that the mundane body alone is commenced by auspicious and inauspicious karma, whereas the extraordinary body of a devotee is commenced by the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, these [women] were perfected at that very moment, like the wives of the sacrificers mentioned previously. Consequently, their bonds have been destroyed.
They are eternally liberated. ||11||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, since their minds and senses were so captivated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their husbands and others lacked the power to restrain them;
thus, when only their physical bodies remained as a hindrance, what occurred? In anticipation of this question, one who is well-acquainted with that account [proceeds].

The Lord of Sages, as if seeing that which is distant and concealed as if present before his eyes, has already stated: "Yogis perceive correctly. Therefore, having caused the disappearance of the body—which is perceived by ordinary people as consisting of the material qualities (guṇas) due to its human appearance—and which was not entered by the Lord and others;

"Having left there only His shadow, they reached Śrī Kṛṣṇa immediately"—this and other points are expressed in the pair of verses beginning with *duḥsaha*. *Duḥsaha* means unbearable; *viraha* is separation from the most beloved one, and the *tīvra-tāpa* (intense heat) caused by that separation has shaken off all inauspiciousness and misfortunes.
"Of whom" refers to those [women]. By the word "unbearable" (*duḥsaha*), their lack of any remedy is expressed.

Elsewhere, when one is deceived, even friends protect their lives through various beneficial counsels and by means of bonds and the like; but here, due to the absence of companionship with friends and others, they [must act] by themselves alone.

They have experienced the heat of separation; or rather, by that intense and unavoidable torment arising from the unbearable separation from their beloved, they have shaken off— that is, cast away— the inauspicious [impurity],
whether it be known as the lack of auspiciousness consisting of an obstacle to union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, or that which is called the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Those [actions] which, having been performed, result in the attainment of divinity and are produced by such acts as *kṛt* (the first of the four classes of karma).

Now, one might ask: how can that which is produced by *kṛt* and other such acts be called "unwholesome" (*aśubha*)? It is because it produces the happiness of heaven upon its maturation; however, it is not the case that the wholesome is produced by the unwholesome. This is stated therein.
It is now established as being auspicious (*śubha*), because it is perceived as such despite its appearance of causing suffering, just like asceticism (*tapas*).
Just as asceticism appears to be inauspicious because it produces bodily affliction,

yet it actually generates the auspicious happiness of heaven and so forth, so too here, through the initial unseen potency (*apūrva*) produced by the inauspicious [action], the auspicious [result] is produced.

Even the bliss of heaven, which is of the nature of auspiciousness, is indeed destroyed. Just as in Yoga both of these are to be abandoned because they are obstacles to the attainment of Brahman, so too it is said that for those dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, both are indeed obstacles.
Having shaken off impurity, he speaks of the rejection of even auspiciousness by one who has become inauspicious: "By meditation...

etc. That cessation which is bliss, attained through meditation, belonging to this infallible Kṛṣṇa—who is devoid of even a moment’s lapse from His playful charm—and which arises from the contact of all limbs through the embrace of a close hug; or else:

Having attained in meditation the cessation of union with the imperishable, their auspiciousness—the primary fruit consisting of the bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the removal of inauspiciousness such as heavenly happiness—has been diminished and cast far away; for when the cause is destroyed, the destruction of the effect is inevitable. Therefore, they are perceived as being of an auspicious nature [only in appearance].

They abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*. This is because the abandonment of the body composed of the *guṇas* is figuratively described as the abandonment of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Now, one might ask: how can the bodies of those dear to Kṛṣṇa be said to be composed of the *guṇas*, given that they are not material (*aprākṛta*)?

And because it is extraordinary (*alaukikatvāt*)? True; it is like the expression, "those who have accumulated a mass of merit departed together. For those perfected through spiritual practice (*upāsanā*) who have previously accumulated a mass of merit, the body is distinguished by that merit; thus, through extraordinary spiritual practice, they have attained a body fit for the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

That primordial form which brings about divinity remained as it was; for this very reason, they abandoned the body composed of those qualities. Thus, when the qualities are abandoned, the abandonment of that which is composed of the qualities is also stated—just as the abandonment of the kingdom is figuratively attributed to the king immediately upon the abandonment of the connection.

It is stated separately that "they abandoned their nature consisting of qualities" (*guṇamayaṃ jahur*) for the purpose of clearly demonstrating this manifestation. Furthermore, by means of the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*), it is implied: if there had not existed for these [women] an *apūrva*—produced by the performance of rituals and so forth—which brings about divinity and the like, then they would not have been bound by their husbands and others.

It is known and inferred: having performed these [actions], they were distinguished by their unprecedented nature because they were restrained by their husbands and others, like ordinary women; for this very reason, because the cause—the unprecedented merit—has perished, they have departed.
[This was done] by one who is devoid of ordinary qualities, whose essence is a mass of sweetness characterized primarily by amorous charm.
They attained Him with bodies identical to those of the eternally perfected Vraja-gopīs.
Now, what is the cause for attaining such a transcendental body? It is said:
[the body] was nourished once its [previous] exhaustion was removed by the embrace resulting from the union with Acyuta attained through meditation.
Those for whom the cause is entry into the maṇḍala.

Now, one might object: if it is attained through consciousness or by means of another body upon the abandonment of the current body, then the description "consisting of the qualities" (guṇamayī) would be redundant; it would have been more appropriate simply to say that they abandoned their bodies. To this, [the author replies]: In that regard—

He provides the resolution: because they are divine beings (*deva*), the celestial maidens (*devāṅganā*) possess eternity as a matter of course; however, it is said that their attainment [of that state] occurs through a body that is eternal and a mass of consciousness (*caitanya-ghana*). It is not, however, through a body resembling that of a celestial maiden.
He states the reason for this: "their bonds have been instantly destroyed. By the prefix *pra-*, there is an expression of excellence (*atiśayokti*).

Because their bondage— consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the conditioned tendencies (*saṃskāra*) toward divinity and the like— has been exhausted, they have indeed attained those [realms] in a manner consistent with the eternally perfected and beginningless [beings]. For these beloveds of Kṛṣṇa do not, like the gods, ever again possess that which brings about divinity through a partial divine form.
It has already begun; nor is it denied by anyone that the embrace of one distinguished by every beauty by a bodiless consciousness produces aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Or rather, it is shaken off by the intense heat born from the unbearable separation from the beloved.

Those [women] for whom the impurity characterized by the cessation of the husband and so forth has been cast aside—this is because the sweet flavor consists of both *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and *sambhoga* (union). Although *vipralambha* is perceived as being like suffering, the expression "those who have shaken off impurity" (*dhutāśubhā*) is merely a verbal convention; in reality, however, even *vipralambha* culminates in [the same state].

Because it is stated that [the state] has the nature of bliss (*sukha-rūpa*), the uninterrupted experience of the suffering of the heat of separation must be understood as being characterized by bondage;

thus they say, "they abandoned what was distinguished by bondage. However, the notion of a lover (*jāra-buddhi*) is not abandoned, because it generates a specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); such a cognition is produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
For the establishment of the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), one requires the *anuyogin* (the subordinate partner) and not the *pratiyogin* (the opposing partner).

Now, if it is argued: "But surely, the notion of a paramour (*jāra*) is indeed censured; since the possibility of entering the eternal circle (*nityamaṇḍala*) does not arise as long as that notion exists, how can it be said that they are united with him alone? [The response follows:]...

To this he says: "If the perception of these women as mere paramours were censurable, then how could Uddhava—the great devotee and knower of the supreme truth—have requested the dust of their feet? [The Lord replies: "These are indeed supreme embodied beings. On this very point, it was later said by the Blessed One's own mouth to Uddhava:

"Those auspicious women who remained in Vraja while I was sporting in this forest during the night, having failed to attain the *rāsa* dance, attained Me by reflecting upon My prowess. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.37).
The truth here is this: those who were turned back by their husbands and others, He gave them shadow-forms (*chāyāmaya*) from Himself.

Like Chāyāśuka, by the power of meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they made their own bodies invisible and reached Him with worldly bodies resembling His; for this very reason, He will say later: "The residents of Vraja, thinking each her own wife was standing by her side... regarding them.

Nor should her husband and others be made to suffer; they too, being agitated by their own respective sentiments, must be protected. This was accomplished through the power of *yoga-māyā* alone. Or rather, having rendered that very body extraordinary like Dhruva’s and established one similar to it in its place, he—
They attained that state; by that intention, it is said that they "consisted of qualities" (*guṇamaya*), meaning they offered themselves to their husbands and others.
Now, one might object: even though the body of one confined within a house closed by doors and so forth becomes extraordinary (*alaukika*), [how can this be compared?].

How is it possible to go into the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa? The answer to this is as follows: just as Arjuna described seeing the son of the brāhmaṇa surrounded by a cage of arrows and his journey to the city of Mahākāla, this is not an excessive burden for Yoga-māyā, because her power is inconceivable. Or else:

Those who were engaged in the contemplation of him—meaning those engaged in the contemplation of sexual pleasure directed toward him—took on bodies suitable for such pleasure with him; whereas they had abandoned the contemplation of pleasure directed toward their husbands and others by casting off their [previous] bodies. For in this context, the abandonment of contemplation is intended to be expressed through the abandonment of the body.

However, the abandonment of the body is not intended here in any literal sense; rather, because it is intended that the body be made to disappear and because the shadow-form has been established right there, the abandonment of mental conception (*bhāvanā*) on the part of Brahmā is what is described as the "abandonment of the body. For this very reason:

Since the attainment of the Supreme Self, preceded by the relinquishment of the body composed of the *guṇas*, is designated as the state of liberation (*mukti*) through the common consensus of all people, there is nothing at all inconsistent [in this]. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Here, concealing from the external world the most secret object to be attained by the gopīs, and while making known to them the external meaning for those [outside] but the internal meaning desired by Himself regarding the principles of devotion and realized knowledge for His intimate circle, He speaks by means of a double entendre (tantra): "Duḥsaha... and so forth. In that regard:

He says that Kṛṣṇa granted liberation to those who were outwardly directed: they were those whose impurities had been shaken off by the intense heat of the suffering caused by separation from their beloved;
and by the blissful joy (*nirvṛti*) resulting from the embrace of Acyuta attained through meditation, their [remaining] auspiciousness was exhausted.
Those who possess such merit have, therefore, exhausted the bondage of their *prārabdha* karma.

Even with the thought that he was merely a lover (*jāra*), they attained that very Supreme Self and abandoned their bodies; yet for those turned inward, there then arose immeasurable sorrows and joys born from both separation from and union with their own Beloved.
He says that they gradually became those who had attained their heart's desire:
those by whom the inauspicious [karmas] were shaken—that is, caused to tremble—by the intense heat of unbearable separation from their Beloved;
and having observed the intensity of the heat of separation from their Beloved for those [women].

The meaning is that even more than a thousand inauspicious forms— such as the Vāḍava fire residing in millions of universes, Mahākāla, and Kuṭādika— trembled with the thought of their own defeat, having abandoned their own intense pride.
By Acyuta, who was attained through meditation and arrived through his own manifestation, at that very moment, of the wonderful...

By that embrace— the embrace of His body, which is full of love, composed of consciousness, and characterized by such a nature, self-conception, and so forth— the auspiciousness of those [gopīs], both material and spiritual, was diminished and made lean; for them, there arose the bliss born from the embrace of their beloved, who had become manifest.

The meaning is that, upon beholding thousands of experiences of the bliss of Brahman— which is free from the objects of the millions of universes and is denoted by the word "auspiciousness"— all other pleasures became inferior and exhausted in comparison to it.

The interpretation that the accumulated sins and merits are destroyed by the suffering and happiness arising from separation from and union with the Blessed Lord— on the grounds that these must be exhausted solely through the experience of their own fruits— is not tenable in the Vaiṣṇava tradition;
for such [states of] separation from and union with the Blessed Lord are not themselves the fruits of sin and merit.

They say that the destruction of *prārabdha-karma* occurs only during the stage of *bhajana* for those who have ascended to the level of cessation from misfortune (*anartha-nivṛtti*). Consequently, they have united with that very Supreme Self— the object of supreme love— even through the most base perception of Him as a "lover" (*jāra*), compared to [the gopīs] such as Rukmiṇī and others who possessed the perception of Him as their most exalted husband.

They have attained this even from the presence of their husbands in the form of the Buddha; and even from the perspective of the husband, they do so while perceiving him as a lover—from that unsurpassed excellence of love determined by Uddhava’s words beginning with, "She who, abandoning her own kin and the noble path, which are difficult to forsake... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.61).
Likewise, in this incarnation, His pastimes are seen as elevating even the most humble objects;

for instance, even compared to His pastime as the Great Emperor of emperors, Bhīṣma said: "He who has taken up the whip for the chariot of victory, who holds the reins of the horses, and whose splendor is worthy of being beheld" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.9.39).

The excellence of the sport of being Pārtha’s charioteer; likewise, the inferiority of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) even compared to the superior sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*), and within that, the inferiority of the illicit love (*aupapatya-bhāva*) even compared to the conjugal love (*dāmpatya-bhāva*);
and similarly, the inferiority of ornaments made of guñjā seeds, red ochre, or peacock feathers even compared to the superior ornament of jewels.

The excellence [of this] is indeed evident. Some, having come together and spoken of cessation due to the favorable influence of yogic illusion (yogamāyā), approached Him who was sporting in the rāsa dance that very night; others did so on another night as well.

Now, one might object: "It is not fitting for the Lord's pastimes to be with those women whose bodies were enjoyed by other men. To this he says: "They abandoned [their bodies]. The singular number is used with respect to the genus (jāti). According to some, the disappearance of that body was made unperceived by his own *yogamāyā*; others, however, say as follows:

They say: here, the body to be abandoned consists of the *guṇas* alone; therefore, because of the addition of the qualifier "consisting of the *guṇas*," it is understood that their bodies were of two kinds prior to the blowing of the flutes—both consisting of the *guṇas* and consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Among those, the bodies consisting of the *guṇas* are the ones enjoyed by their own offspring.
They indeed abandoned those very [objects]. This is the discernment taught by the Guru:

from the very moment of beginning devotional practice through devotion, when pure devotion consisting of hearing, chanting, remembering, prostrating like a staff, and serving has entered the ears and other senses of the devotees—[one realizes] "I am devoid of material qualities and have taken refuge in Him."

According to this statement of the Blessed One, a devotee, while making the qualities and other attributes of the Lord objects of his own ears and other senses, becomes *nirguṇa* (devoid of material qualities). Yet, even while making worldly objects such as sound and so forth objects of his senses, he remains *guṇamaya* (composed of qualities). Thus, the body of the devotee possesses a partial *nirguṇatva* (freedom from material qualities).

And there would be a state of being composed of the *guṇas*. Consequently, according to the maxim— "Devotion, experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment [are satisfaction, nourishment, and the removal of hunger through eating]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.42)— there would be a corresponding gradation in the increase of portions of the *nirguṇa* body in accordance with the degree of the growth of devotion.

Furthermore, there would be a gradual diminution of the portions of the body composed of the modes of nature; however, when complete love arises, those portions of the body composed of the modes having perished, the body becomes perfectly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Even so, the fall of the gross body occurs for the sake of the realization of the true state of being, which uproots all outward-facing tendencies through the yoga of devotion.

And for the sake of preserving its secrecy, it is shown by the Lord himself through His illusory power (*māyā*), as in the case of the Yādavas during the *mauṣala-līlā* (the pastime of the clubs); yet at other times, it is not shown, as in the case of Dhruva and others, for the purpose of making known the excellence of their yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*). The authority for this is found in the Eleventh [Canto].
In the twenty-fifth chapter, while demonstrating that faith and the other qualities are composed of the modes of nature, [the Lord says]:
"O gentle one, he by whom these qualities born of the mind have been conquered through the yoga of devotion, being established in Me, attains My own state of being. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.32]

By this, the Blessed One has stated that the conquest and indeed the destruction of things composed of the material qualities (guṇas) occurs through devotion alone. Therefore, those [goddesses] whose inauspicious bodies composed of the qualities have been shaken off, discarded, and burnt away; yet, through the bliss of embrace, their auspicious bodies consisting of pure consciousness (cinmaya) have not been digested but have increased.

The intended meaning is also that "those [women] of whom [these qualities exist]. Therefore, the sense is that they have fallen away from their state after having attained conformity with *yogamāyā* by being freed from the bonds of ignorance and by warding off [the cycle of] husbands and so forth;
however, it should not be explained as meaning that for them, the falling of the body occurs solely due to the power of death.
"Those auspicious women who, while I was sporting in this forest at night, remained in Vraja without attaining the *rāsa*, have attained Me by reflecting upon My prowess"— thus,
in the words of the Blessed Lord, the use of the term "auspicious" (*kalyāṇyaḥ*) indicates that they were protected from their husbands.

Furthermore, although they desired to abandon their own bodies due to the torment of separation from Me, at the commencement of the supremely auspicious rāsa festival, death—which is inauspicious and not desired by Me—did not befall them;
for it was the Lord’s intention that they remain possessed of all auspiciousness. Thus, they spoke to Uddhava:

And from the words of Śuka, "Delighted, their memories were awakened by His message" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.40.38), it is understood that those who had previously not attained the rāsa-dance and were confined within their inner apartments spoke thus; by that means, they abandoned their bodies composed of the material modes without even death. Their bodies were tormented by the intense heat of separation.

Having abandoned their state of being composed of the *guṇas*, those whose bodies were made of *guṇas* attained a state of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), just as Dhruva and others did; this is understood to be the true meaning of "leaving the body. Likewise, here [it is said] they "did not obtain an exit," there they "remained in Vraja," and here they "attained the embrace of Acyuta through meditation"; there they "attained" it.

The phrase "by thinking of my prowess" (*mad-vīrya-cintayā*) signifies the same meaning as before. However, here the expression "assembled together" (*saṃgatāḥ*) indicates a difference in meaning—namely, that they had not yet attained the *rāsa* dance—which explains the twofold nature of the gopīs confined within the inner apartments. This is just as when one understands that seven or eight fruits have fully ripened.

Knowing that this is a true mango tree and that its fruit is ripe, one plucks all the fruits from the tree and brings them home. Having brought them, those which, at the appropriate time and through the sun's rays and other factors, possess beauty, fragrance, sweetness, and delicacy for the king—

Those fruits that have become fit for enjoyment and pleasing are prepared by skilled attendants and offered to the king for his use at the proper time; however, those which are ripened on the inside but unripe on the outside—
being devoid of qualities such as beauty and thus unpalatable— are known to be unfit for the king.

Just as [fruits] are ripened through the application of specific heat and then offered to the king on the second or third day and so forth, in that same way, among the cowherd women born in Gokula who follow the conduct of sages,
those who first abandon their bodies composed of material qualities—

Their bodies became composed of pure consciousness; untouched by other men, they were brought together with the eternally perfected gopīs and others by Śrī Yogamāyā. Some were brought there that very night after all the others, while others had only a slight trace of worldly attachment remaining.
Seeing this, out of the very heat of separation, they set out during the nights themselves in order to bring him back.

Then, having attained the pastimes of the *rāsa* dance and other delights, they returned to their husbands' homes at the end of the night along with the eternally perfected (*nityasiddha*) gopīs; from that time on, Yogamāyā herself protected them while they were united with their husbands.

"Those who were devoid of possessiveness toward husband, children, and so forth, and were overwhelmed by an excess of love for Kṛṣṇa, were perceived by their own relatives as if they were possessed by demons because they did not nourish their own offspring, their milk having dried up; thus everything is faultless. But others say:

Even those confined within the inner apartments who do not have children of their own are referred to by terms such as "offspring" and so forth in the preceding texts; they state that the son of a co-wife, the son of a foster-mother, or the son of a brother is to be understood [by these terms]. (10–11)
The King said:
"O Sage, they know Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved, but not as Brahman."
How can there be a cessation of the flow of those notions of the qualities, [given that they are themselves] qualities?
