Śrīdhara: [An objection is raised: "Just as liberation does not result from worshipping one's husband, sons, and so forth—even though they are in reality Brahman—because of the absence of that realization, so too, in the case of Kṛṣṇa, how can association with Him be a cause of liberation due to the absence of the realization that He is Brahman? Thus he raises the doubt with the words, "They know Kṛṣṇa," etc., [and answers it by saying] "the Supreme."
Simply lovely and desirable. ||12||

Vaṃśīdhara: Since the knowledge of Brahman is the cause of liberation according to the scriptures, and since he observes that they lack such knowledge, he raises an objection as if not knowing how their liberation could occur: "But surely...
[He says] this because of their devotion to him—that is, by serving their husband and son—and because they likewise lack [philosophical] understanding.

Due to the absence of the realization that he is Brahman, there is association with that Kṛṣṇa. O Sage, you whose nature is to contemplate His various pastimes; [He is] the supreme lover, the paramour, and the husband. Those whose intellects (dhī) are fixed on the modes (guṇas), that is, on sense objects—there is the cessation (uparama), the turning away from the flow of the modes, which is the flow of worldly existence (saṃsāra).

How can there be cessation from saṃsāra through the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti-mārga*), which is [usually] attainable only through the path of renunciation (*nivṛtti-mārga*)? [This is known] from the Vedic scripture: "Arise! Wake up! Alternatively, it refers to those devotees whose intellect (*dhī*) is fixed upon the *guṇas*—namely, the Lord’s beauty and other such qualities. It is that in which there is a flow (*pravāha*) of *guṇa*, consisting of service to the Lord.

How did his body meet its end? Through such statements as "May I, even as an insect, become devoted to You," there is an intensity regarding devotion; the underlying sentiment is that liberation is not for the sake of increasing devotion. As stated in the *Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "They know Kṛṣṇa to be the supreme beloved. Kṛṣṇa is the supreme...
They know [the objects] only as desirable, and not as Brahman; therefore, how can there be a cessation of the flow of qualities for those worldly beings who perceive them as qualities? (12)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He is called *Parīkṣit* because he perceives (*īkṣate*) with a comprehensive disposition (*pari*), meaning he knows the inner intent (*bhāva*) of all. Although he himself already knows the respective greatness of each [deity], nevertheless, for the sake of dispelling the doubts of those who are inwardly perplexed, he speaks by means of specific meanings.

A specific doubt has been elaborated; and for those who doubt while being outwardly directed, a doubt consisting of discourse on the knowledge of Brahman was elaborated in order to dispel other doubts—the reading "the King said" (rājovāca) occurs in some places. Here too, it concerns only the discernment of all states of being.

Because of the intended meaning of the word *rāja*, the venerable Lord of Sages (Śrī Munīndra) will likewise provide a corresponding reply; thus, while the outward-turned (bahir-mukha) interpretation of the meaning is well known, this is the meaning according to the inward-turned (antar-mukha) method.

Now, it was stated that they "abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*. In that context, if by the word *guṇa* the triad of *sattva* and so forth is meant, and if by the suffix *mayaṭ* a transformation (*vikāra*) is intended, then since the body to be abandoned would already possess the nature of being composed of those [qualities] by its very own nature, what is the purpose of that specific mention? Therefore, [it must be understood] according to the previous [explanation].
The succession of the mental virtues has been described in detail above; regarding this, we now ask:

if it is said that "they knew Kṛṣṇa," was this for the purpose of indicating that other women who had attained the Rāsa dance were already free from the three modes of nature (*nistraiguṇya-dehatā*), or that these very women were to obtain such a body?

To indicate that, it is specified here as "consisting of the modes" (*guṇamaya*); yet, since that [specification] serves as an illustration for such a body, one might also obtain the notion that the flow of mental qualities is likewise [of the same nature].
To address that as well, he asks: "They know Kṛṣṇa."

And this is the meaning: they know that Kṛṣṇa alone as the Supreme, the Absolute, the Beloved, who is most dear to them because of His enchanting qualities of all-surpassing wonder; they do not know Him as Brahman, nor as a specific manifestation of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.
Therefore, for those whose consciousness is fixed on His qualities, there is no fixation on Brahman.
The meaning is as follows: their internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa) is an intellect directed toward those qualities of His which are renowned for being non-relinquishable;
and because they are solely devoted to Him, their qualities—consisting of the flow of love attached exclusively to His qualities—are of a non-material (aprākṛta) nature.

Therefore, since those [qualities] are not established in the body, let there indeed be their cessation; however, how could there be the cessation of such an uninterrupted succession of qualities? This is the meaning. As is the case with those who meditate upon Brahman, there is not merely the manifestation of His essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather the manifestation of Him together with His qualities (*guṇa*). Therefore...

The meaning of the statement is this: those qualities found in the worshippers of Brahmā consist solely of the material modes (*prakṛti-sattva*); therefore, the cessation of the flow of those very qualities is possible for them alone, but not for those like him (Śukadeva) in whom the qualities of the Lord have manifested. Furthermore, by means of a pun (*śleṣa*), he asks Kṛṣṇa: "They know You as the Supreme, the Absolute, the Beloved."

But there is no cessation of the flow of qualities consisting of worldly existence for those whose minds are fixed on the gunas, perceiving only "this one is beautiful" or "this one is clever," O Sage, O Omniscient One! 12.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Śrī-yuktaḥ Parīkṣit spoke as if for the purpose of testing others, and not out of ignorance or doubt; this is the sense. *Param* means solely beloved, the goal, or beautiful; or alternatively, *param kāntam* means the lover, the paramour—this is the meaning. Therefore...

For those whose intellect (*dhī*) is fixed only upon his qualities—such as beauty, sweetness, compassion, and so forth—and not upon his true nature (*tattva*), how can there be the cessation (*uparama*) of the flow of qualities, which is *saṃsāra*?
How can liberation (*mokṣa*), the crest-jewel of all human goals, be achieved? For it is only by knowing him [in his true nature] that one transcends death.

This is because, according to the authority of such scriptural passages as "He comes" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8), the cessation of saṃsāra is established solely through the knowledge of the true nature of the Lord; and with the intent that liberation is difficult to attain, considering its preeminence over all things. Or rather, it refers to the state of that which has been declared in the scripture to be the means for liberation.
This question is to be considered:
or rather, [it concerns] one who is supremely beloved, enchanting like ten million Kandarapas, or most dear to ten million selves;
for this very reason, [the focus is] on his qualities alone—such as beauty, sweetness, cleverness, and affection—and not otherwise.

How could liberation— which is utterly insignificant— be possible for those beloved consorts of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose feet are served even by true devotees who regard liberation as a blade of grass because their own wisdom consists in realizing His very nature?
This question arises from reflecting on the extreme insignificance of liberation.

"O Sage! O Omniscient One!"—the sense is that since you already know that account, you alone are capable of providing its resolution. However, in reality, O Lord, [it is said]: "May I, even as a worm, become one devoted to you in birth after birth throughout thousands of wombs."
Because the Lord prays for birth and so forth— through words such as "and so on"— with the sole intent of increasing the devotion of His devotees,
the cessation of saṃsāra characterized by birth and so forth is inappropriate. Therefore, through detachment and other means,
there is even the assumption of a body beyond the modes (guṇātīta-deha) by abandoning the body composed of the modes (guṇa-maya-deha), which is the cause for the nourishment of devotion.

"It is indeed improper"—this refers to the position that [the body] is composed of the six qualities (*sad-guṇa-mayatā*). For those who possess the qualities, meaning those who possess knowledge of the qualities;

how could there be the cessation of that body in which flows the stream of qualities such as the beauty and charm that please the Blessed Lord? This is because one considers the body to be unfit for the service of the Blessed Lord.
This is because there is no abandonment of such bodies by them due to an unbearable burden of suffering, nor from any higher realm;
or rather, because even for those whose minds are fixed on the qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— such as His beauty, fragrance, and so forth— or on the rāsa-dance and other pastimes,
their spiritual quality remains in Śrī Vṛndāvana, unlike that of other gopīs.

How could there be an end to the flow— or, by repetition, the succession— of His extraordinary excellence, characterized by such things as His actual residence within the cowherd settlement and His pastimes such as the rāsa dance? For that [excellence] cannot cease even through the abandonment of a body composed of all auspicious qualities.

Furthermore, since [the body] is devoid of deliberation and so forth, how could there be a falling away of such a body—though being abandoned by those [faculties]—by virtue of its own inherent nature? This is the meaning. ||12||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, in this context, Parīkṣit asks with wonder—"They know Kṛṣṇa," and so forth. O Sage! They know Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved, as their dearest one; not...

But [if they were] by virtue of being Brahman or the Lord, how then could there be a cessation of the flow of the *guṇas* for them? For their intellects regarding the *guṇas* consist of the thought, "This is my beloved," directed toward the *guṇas*. (12)

*(Kṛṣṇa-sandarbhaḥ 145)*: Here, regarding the statement "they abandoned their bodies composed of the modes" (*guṇa-mayaṃ dehaṃ jahur*), there arises a doubt on the part of the King: "They knew Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ vidur*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.12). O Sage, they knew Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the supreme, absolute beloved, their hidden lover, but not as Brahman. If that is so, how...?

Is the cessation of the flow of their qualities possible? For one who possesses the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Brahman, there would be a cessation of the prior flow of illusory (*māyika*) qualities due to the arising of that very qualityless [Brahman].
But in the case of those who contemplate Him solely as the Beloved (*kāntatayā*), there is the arising of His quality which transcends the material (*prākṛta*) qualities.

The meaning is: even in the absence of the qualities of Prakṛti, since those qualities which follow after the Supreme Person possess the quality of being connected to those [divine] qualities, how can there be a cessation of them? Or rather, how can the flow of those qualities ever come to a final end in a transcendental sense, such that you speak of liberation from them?

The state [of being]. This establishes the distinction from the perception [of Brahman] as Brahman; for those whose minds possess the intellect regarding His supreme beauty and other qualities—even while they have abandoned the intellect fixed on Brahman—therein lies "subsequent liberation. Because it is difficult to grasp, like the legend of Purañjana and others, it is stated by Himself.

This is the explanation. For it is thus obtained by the force of the illustration: just as here the word *caidya* includes the *kāruṣa* as well, so too [it applies] to those two, Jaya and Vijaya, and to their [sons].
"You ought to explain this connection with a body for those inhabitants of the city of Vaikuṇṭha who are devoid of bodies, senses, and life-force. Thus,
by way of Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira’s question, [it concerns] those two whose forms are imperishable because they possess non-material (aprākṛta) bodies.
While they were thus situated, the Blessed One said to the two cowherds: "Go; do not fear; may there be peace!
Although I am capable of destroying the splendor of Brahmā, I do not wish to do so; this is my resolve. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.29)

Thus, in accordance with the words of the Blessed One, and according to the prose section of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, Jaya and Vijaya descended into the cycle of worldly existence solely for the sake of the Lord’s divine play (*līlā*), under the pretext of the curse of Sanaka and the others, in order to amuse Himself by attracting the hearts of His devotees.

For the purpose of playing at war and the like, or by his own will which brings about the impossible, he three times entered another earthly body composed of the *guṇas* into his own supreme body of light consisting of the *siddhis* such as *aṇimā*.

For this very reason, regarding the verse in the Seventh Canto, *kṛṣṇa-cakra-hatāṃhasau* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.45), the commentary states: "Those two whose sin (*aṃhaḥ*) was destroyed by Kṛṣṇa’s discus; of those two, only the sin was destroyed, but not they."
Likewise, for that very purpose and by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, even at this time when their non-material forms were obstructed from meeting Him,
they did not feel resentment toward Kṛṣṇa, being enchanted by His illusory power (māyā).
"Just as the inhabitants of Vraja thought, 'Our own respective wives are standing by our sides' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.37),
so too is there entry into that body composed of the *guṇas* which was fashioned at that time; it is with reference to this very [body] that [the following is said]."
In the case of the illustrative example as well, it is said: "They abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.11).

The meaning is that because the qualification would otherwise be redundant, it does not mean "their own" [body]. And in that regard, just as there was an appearance of hatred toward those two together, by the power of that very recollection—even of that which was accompanied by hatred—[the result followed].
By abandoning such limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), one vanishes from that state and attains the Blessed One;
likewise, by the power of His intense love, there is the attainment of Him. And in this regard, the attraction of the devotee’s heart occurs in this way:
"Oh, such is the sweetness in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by which they [the gopīs] [desire] His direct manifestation!"
"They were even prepared to give up their lives," so it is said. ||12||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, since it has been stated that they "abandoned the body composed of the *guṇas*," there arises the perception among all people that those who were bound have become liberated through meditation; for according to the scripture (*śruti*), liberation (*kaivalya*) results from knowledge alone. And that knowledge has as its object liberation itself, not the *guṇas*.

Even though these [devotees] have virtues as their object, when their object is a lover (*jāra*), how much less could there even be a possibility of liberation for them? Since it has been stated that liberation is to be rejected by all Vaiṣṇavas, how much more so for those who are dear to Kṛṣṇa; thus, she was free from doubt in her own mind regarding them.
Although he knew that they were all entering the eternal maṇḍala, Parīkṣit questioned them, his mind wavering with doubt because the faces of everyone appeared displeased.
This questioning arose from his desire to examine Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to test the inner disposition of everyone present, and to discern the true essence of their devotion.
The question was not asked out of ignorance or for the sake of mere debate, but rather out of consideration for everyone;

however, [he spoke of] Kṛṣṇa alone as the beloved, unmixed with [other qualities like] sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth—or else, "beloved" means "charming," that is, a lover (*jāra*). It is heard thus from those who possess knowledge (*viduḥ*), meaning from the wise.

Liberation is possible. And in that regard, Śrī Kṛṣṇa says that liberation occurs through such knowledge, but it is not as if that [liberation] exists [independently]; He says this because liberation is not possible for one who possesses knowledge of Brahman, nor for one intent on its means. Nor does that exist; He says: "In the case of those whose intellect is fixed on the modes, within the mode..."

[The phrase] "of those whose intellects [are fixed] upon the beauty and other qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," or alternatively, "of those whose intellects are fixed upon the quality of sporting with Śrī Kṛṣṇa in secret," or again, "of those whose intellects are fixed upon the quality of dancing, singing, and so forth conducive to the rāsa-dance"—

how can there be a cessation of the flow of such qualities? That is to say, how could there be the cessation or termination of that "quality" consisting of the playful pastimes of the rāsa and so forth?

Question: Since the flow of the qualities (*guṇa-pravāha*)—the flow of the *rāsa*-pastimes and so forth—is possible even by its own nature upon the abandonment of the body, how is it that these [gopīs] have tasted [it] with a particular savor of Kṛṣṇa’s bliss, whereas the eternally perfected ones (*nitya-siddhāḥ*) have not? [Answer: Of the eternally perfected ones...

Due to the absence of such suffering from separation, there arises an intensity of passion through the state of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). Since the radiant love consists of both *sambhoga* (union) and *vipralambha*, by comparison with that, those who are eternally perfected are considered inferior; for even by abandoning their bodies, they do not attain the playful pastimes of the *rāsa*-dance, which is the flow of transcendental qualities.
And how was its deficiency described? It was said:
"The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) does not attain fullness without separation (*vipralambha*);
for when cloth and such are dyed with *kāṣāya*, a much greater redness arises."

When they abandoned their bodies composed of the modes of nature, they united with that very Supreme Self; by this statement, the conviction arose in everyone that they had attained liberation characterized by *sāyujya* (union). Since that [attainment] seemed improbable, the King asked: "For those distinguished by the mood of the *rāsa*-pastime, attainment of the *rāsa*-pastime itself is what is appropriate."

For those endowed with the contemplation of Brahman as *sāyujya* (union), *sāyujya* is appropriate, but not the attainment of the *rāsa*-pastimes; for it is well known that "the thought at the end determines the destination.
Alternatively, since it is logical [to interpret] it as secondary (*gauṇa*), it refers to those whose intellect is fixed upon that cause of the flow of qualities (*guṇa*).
The cessation—that is, the destruction—of the flow of qualities, which is saṃsāra, is what is meant by liberation (mokṣa). How could this be possible?

For these goddesses, who were perfected through worship in a previous birth and remain so even now, how has liberation occurred without the contemplation of the great Mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" and the like, which are the means to that [liberation]? By these [goddesses]...

However, since they abandoned their bodies created through the power of playful imagination (*vilāsa-bhāvanā*), it would not be possible for them to attain the *rāsa*-pastimes without a body. Otherwise, by performing sinful acts that lead to divinity, one might attain the state of a god; or by committing an offense against Brahman that leads to non-divinity, one might attain the state of a demon. This would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).

For it has been stated by the Śrutis that liberation is difficult to understand for one who desires its departure [from the world], as in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.87.21: "for the sake of realizing the truth of the Self. Furthermore, it is heard here and there that other Vaiṣṇavas have no longing even for the various forms of liberation, such as the phrase "not even the vault of heaven" (*na nāka-pṛṣṭham*) [in Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
And because this has been stated in such passages as [10.16.37], the question "how much more so for these beloveds of Kṛṣṇa? follows.
O Sage! because of the fact that this contemplation has been practiced many times. (12)

Viśvanātha: Having observed the doubts residing in the hearts of some of those outsiders merely by looking at their faces, the King— though he himself already knew the intended meaning of the parrot's words through their favor— pretended to doubt for the sole purpose of dispelling their uncertainty.

Thus he says: "Kṛṣṇa. O Sage, O Omniscient One! They know Kṛṣṇa—the Supreme Self—to be the Supreme Person, the Beloved, their own Consort; yet they do not know Him as Brahman. Therefore, for those whose intellects are fixed on His qualities, thinking "Let us sport with Kṛṣṇa," there arises [the desire] for those [qualities].
How can there be a cessation of the flow of qualities? [The answer is: "Only by knowing Him does one transcend death.

This is because scriptural and traditional (smṛti) passages such as "They perceive the Self as the very nature of the Self" state that the knowledge of the Supreme Self alone is the means to attaining liberation. ||12||
Śrī Śuka said:
This has been told to you before, how the King of Cedi attained perfection.
Even an enemy [would honor] Hṛṣīkeśa; how much more so those who are dear to Adhokṣaja?

Śrīdhara: He refutes [the objection] with the words "it has been said. This is the intended meaning: Brahmanhood is veiled in the case of individual souls (jīvas), but for Kṛṣṇa, because he is Hṛṣīkeśa, it is unveiled. Therefore, there is no dependence on the intellect (buddhi) in that case. ||13||

Vaṃśīdhara: Through devotion, by means of the consciousness arising from the constant remembrance of Hari’s majesty, there is liberation fit for cessation (nivṛtti), but not through desire and the like; for by that [latter], one merely attains heaven and so forth. This is because Vijayadhvaja stated: "Then the gopīs, desiring Kṛṣṇa, abandoned their bodies and went to heaven."
This does not appear appropriate here; rather, the solution stated by the venerable teacher himself is excellent.

Thus he says: "He avoids" means he speaks an answer, though with indistinct speech due to some degree of indignation or the like. As if angry, thinking, "Alas, this man is doubting the greatness of the Blessed One," he says: "It has been said."

For the Blessed One does not possess an ordinary form like that of ourselves; thus he says, "This is the state of being. The nature of Brahman (*brahmatva*), which is the state of being Brahman (*brahmabhāva*), is veiled by ignorance that has transformed into the form of the senses and so forth, just as fire is covered by ashes. Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded. (Gītā)

As stated in [5.15] and other passages: because He is Hṛṣīkeśa (the Lord of the senses), because He is the Supreme Lord, and because He has brought Māyā under His control through omniscience, there is no obscuration caused by her. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no need for intellectual deliberation regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa; there is no requirement for the knowledge that "this one is directly the Supreme Brahman. Thus is the sense.

Just as fire, when unobstructed, performs its functions such as illuminating and burning, but not when obstructed, so too is it with the individual souls (*jīvas*), because their nature as Brahman is obscured. In that regard, liberation occurs only by making the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the self the door; however, for the Blessed Lord, since His nature as Brahman is unobscured, [liberation occurs] even without such knowledge.
The intended meaning is that [the Lord] bestows liberation.
Furthermore, the implication is that due to the extreme agitation born from separation from their beloved, they accepted the destruction of their bodies.
This shall be the answer to your question later on in the Seventh Skandha. Even one who is hostile...

Even while acting with hatred, he attained perfection—union (sāyujya)—by constantly fixing his mind upon Him with a sense of enmity. Those for whom Adhokṣaja—the Supreme Brahman Himself, who is not an object of sensory perception—is the beloved, the object of their deep affection; whether that flow of consciousness is conditioned or unconditioned.
The reality is that it is the cause for attaining that. ||13||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "The cessation of the flow of their qualities never occurs"—this very prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). And it will be said:
"Those who served with love by massaging His feet and so forth..."
"What can be said of the austerity of those women who worship the Teacher of the World with the thought that He is their husband? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.90.27).

Thus, Sarasvatī established the underlying tenet that worship performed solely out of the perception of Him as the Supreme Beloved brings about the cessation of the flow of the material qualities (*guṇa*) and effects the pacification of that flow.

Nevertheless, Śrī Śuka establishes the conclusion: "It was said before," and so forth. Even though it has been stated repeatedly with words of challenge, you still do not understand. How did the King of Cedi attain perfection? For he attained it even as an enemy, a hater; how much more so then those who are dear to Adhokṣaja! [He destroyed] sin.
The beloveds [attained] the perfection that was their own desired form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||13||

The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: "Śuka is endowed with Śrī. Having understood that Parīkṣit’s speech was intended to dispel the doubts of those seeking to deceive the outward-turned (bahirmukha), [the author], though aware of its purpose, says something as if censuring the outward-turned under that very pretext.

Because he spoke indistinctly out of indignation, he said exactly as follows: "It was said previously. Having attained their desired goal—the state of being attendants once more—and through meditation intensified by the persistence of enmity, having reached the nature of Acyuta, those two attendants of Viṣṇu went again to the side of Hari.

Thus, from the seventh [chapter]; then, even when aversion toward Him arose, they attained Him once again through their own very qualities, which remained latent within them. Therefore, for those who have taken refuge as objects of Adhokṣaja’s affection, by virtue of their ever-increasing love, those [qualities] become manifest.
The meaning is that its attainment occurs simultaneously with that [attainment of the Self]. However, by me [it was said] "the body composed of the qualities" (guṇamaya-deha) in the sense that,

even though it is joined with the internal and external bodies— which are manifestations of the functions of the essential power (svarūpa-śakti)— and with the true qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti) and its evolutes (prākṛta), such as beauty and so forth, along with the root-nature itself.
The meaning is that what is intended [is the body] alone, because it serves as the qualifier.

If the question is based on a pun (*śleṣa*), then this is the meaning of the answer in its second sense: regarding the statement [in Gītā 4.11], "In whatever way they [approach me]," I do not manifest other qualities toward them; rather, [I manifest those qualities] of my own accord.

The intended meaning is that all [these qualities] indeed exist. Therefore, due to such an immersion in devotion, even in the absence of one's own conscious contemplation of them, those respective potencies manifest them at their own appropriate time;
otherwise, for those who worship from afar and are solely intent upon His sweetness, there would be no attainment of Him at all.

It may be so. To this he says—"even one who hates"—intending that one should hear the illustration by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument; for otherwise, even in that case, his sovereignty would manifest as the bestower of liberation and other such fruits.
He states the reason for the manifestation of each of these through the two names: "Hṛṣīkeśa" and "Adhokṣaja."

By means of the etymological derivation of both names, it has been shown that for their establishment, independent of any knowledge of them, their specific excellence as qualities shines forth. ||13||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Śuka endowed with Śrī. Because of his speech being indistinct due to some degree of indignation and so forth, he is likened to Śuka; this should be understood further in what follows. However, although knowing that the King was aware of his own intention, [he spoke] under that pretext as a cause for the King's question.
Addressing certain people who are motivated by such causes, he replies as if in anger: "It has been said.

Regarding that, in the first case, even though the devotees have brought about the cessation of saṃsāra, because of their suspicion toward the king, a lack of conviction regarding the majesty of the Blessed Lord arises; thus, he speaks as if in anger.

He replies: "It has been said. [He is called] *hṛṣīkeśa* because he is the supreme benefactor, as he provides the functioning of all the senses (*indriya*). Alternatively, *hṛṣī* refers to a particular kind of grass; like that, [his hairs] are fine, long, and sparse. Or else, *hṛṣya* refers to rays; like those, they are radiant and abundant.

The meaning is that he whose hair is [black] is supremely beautiful. Even Śiśupāla, the King of Cedi, though hating such a Kṛṣṇa, attained perfection—characterized by the attainment of the form of eternal existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda) which transcends the material qualities (guṇātīta); or rather, he attained his own desired goal.
Furthermore, you have attained and reached liberation characterized by being an attendant of the Blessed One; this has indeed been explained to you previously in the seventh chapter, as follows:
"Like one who was lying beneath a cart and, upon the falling of the cart, was freed from the axle and born anew."
Adhokṣaja is the son of Śrī Yaśodā; the meaning is that those who are dear to Him, or His own beloveds, attain perfection—what more need be said? This very intention has been revealed by them.
Therefore, out of fear of separation from their Beloved, they do not desire even the destruction of birth and so forth, though it is desired by other devotees.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the second case, even the King of Cedi attains his own desired goal; however, the beloveds of Adhokṣaja, out of fear of separation, will attain the fulfillment of their desire for eternal union with Him.

What more need be said? Thus, the resolution is that even such a body was abandoned solely out of fear of the unbearable pain of separation. Oh! What more need be said regarding how the King of Cedi attained perfection at the end of the sage’s curse—which had granted him lordship over the three worlds—by becoming dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and how the gopīs attained perfection through their love for Him?

He has attained the state characterized by the realization of the form of Saccidānanda which transcends all qualities (*guṇātīta*), but not the state of disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*). What need is there to mention that the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa attain such perfection? Therefore, fearing the excess of agitation born from separation from their Beloved due to the overflowing intensity of their particular love, they— [proceeded].

The destruction of birth and so forth has been accepted. As for the statement that even for devotees, the assumption of a body beyond the modes (*guṇātīta-deha*) is improper— therein, a specific state of being cultivated with humility through the perception of [the Lord] as the Supreme is [granted] as a body beyond the modes to the most eminent among the great devotees.

Because there is generally no excellence in the transformation of their love, it does not please them; however, for the beloveds of the Blessed Lord, whose minds are elevated by their affection, there is no great aversion toward that [devotion].
In the third case, even the King of Cedi, though hating Hṛṣīkeśa, attained success—the fulfillment of his own desire.
Furthermore, he attained the characteristics of an attendant of the Blessed One.

In this context, the name *Hṛṣīkeśa* denotes the general nature of the illustrious Blessed One, whereas the name *Adhokṣaja*, according to its etymological derivation as previously stated, denotes His specific nature. Therefore—
Manifesting a certain extraordinary sweetness in both their incarnations and the one who descends through them,

the beloveds of the illustrious Prince of Vraja, who are endowed with supremely sweet love, always remain in Vraja— just like the other queens of Vraja— in accordance with the desires of Him who resides in Vraja.

What need is there to say that they will attain the perfection of the playful manifestations of love and so forth? However, this abandonment—which I indicated by characterizing it as invisibility, or rather, which I manifested as the very renunciation of worldly existence through the renunciation of the body—has not been perceived by those such as yourself; thus, everything is beyond reproach. 13.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Following the question, Śrī Śukācārya, as if slightly provoked to anger yet maintaining his composure, will provide this reply; his intention is as follows: "O King!"

For doubt arises regarding a matter that is yet to be accomplished, but not regarding one that is already established. As for what was said—that having abandoned the body composed of the modes of nature (guṇas), they attained a body free from those modes—that was merely a restatement of an established fact; it was not spoken by me as a mere fabrication. Therefore, what doubt can there be in this matter?
In the case of Kṛṣṇa, it is love alone that effects such a transformation, and not knowledge of Brahman. What need is there for more?
For these women, it was indeed love; even for those who harbored hatred toward Him, there occurred a cessation of the flow of the material modes.
This is the greatness of love: that it brings about a body that is favorable to itself and devoid of the material qualities (nirguṇa).

But since all of this is rooted solely in the fact that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the ultimate substratum, he speaks while manifesting an outburst of anger, beginning with the words "It has been said," and so forth.
The meaning is: although this has already been stated many times previously, you are still deluded. What is that? He says: "Even the King of Cedi, though hostile, attained perfection... and so on.
He attained the status of an eternally established attendant (*pārṣada*), but not liberation (*kaivalya*). As he proceeded exactly as it was, what more need be said?

For those who worship the beloved of Adhokṣaja as their own lover will surely become His favorites; what then can be said of this? Therefore, for them, the cessation of the flow of material qualities (*guṇa-pravāha*) occurs precisely through the knowledge of Him as the Beloved.
Furthermore, there is knowledge through the state of Brahmā. ||13||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, having thoroughly understood the king’s question and having discerned the mental disposition of certain proponents of logical reasoning (*hetuvādins*), [the author], as if manifesting his own view with agitation toward the king— who had asked the question and knew his own intention— proceeds to provide an answer through skillful statements of reason.

Demonstrating the impropriety of such a question from those dear to Kṛṣṇa, and revealing that the presence of doubt and contrary conceptions regarding their attainment of Kṛṣṇa brings about misfortune, He answers them while accepting a delay of two or three moments or more.
To answer the question, "How can there be a cessation of the flow of qualities and a withdrawal from the playful pastimes of the *rāsa*? he says,

beginning with the words "It was stated previously," indicating that even after a mere two or three moments of cessation, there occurred a resurgence of those pastimes even more intense than before— within the context of the Lord’s majesty (*bhagavan-māhātmya*).

Addressing those endowed with the cultivation of aesthetic sentiment (*rasa-bhāvanā*), he says: even though you have seen the Rājasūya sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira and the entry of the hostile Caidya into it by Śrī Kṛṣṇa behind his back, you remain doubtful.
This was already told to you by me previously in the seventh canto; why then do you [doubt]?
"Forgotten?"—this is a statement made with regret.
"Even Hṛṣīkeśa"—meaning even the one who sets the senses in motion; the word "even" (api) is connected to both parts.
Even Caidya, though he hated Him while ignorant of His nature as the Lord, was nonetheless an eternal attendant.

Due to a delay in time, he again attained the status of an attendant (pārṣada), but did not attain liberation in the form of absorption (sāyujya) into Brahman. If the liberation of the queens of Vraja were intended [by the author], then he would not have used the King of Cedi as an example.

"Beloved of Adhokṣaja"—how much more so, then, for those who are "adhokṣaja-born," meaning they are born from or manifest within the internal senses (akṣa) that are turned inward toward Adhokṣaja. Alternatively, when Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was lying beneath the cart, was released from it, the gopīs said to the Queen of Vraja: "By good fortune, your son has been born again!"

Thus it was said by Yaśodā: "He was not born from me, but was born from Adhokṣaja; he is Adhokṣaja. The meaning is: what more need be said regarding those who have attained the perfection of His own beloveds—that is, they have entered into His very nature? For others, there is only the attainment of His form devoid of attributes (nirguṇa-svarūpa).

"It is improper for devotees," [he says], because I have indicated that the very abandonment of mental constructs (*bhāvanā*) is what constitutes the abandonment of the body; therefore, you must not pose such a question—thus he provides the restriction. ||13||

Viśvanātha: The venerable Lord of Sages (Śrī Munīndra), knowing in his mind that this was not actually a question from the King, yet wishing to rebuke them under the pretext of ignorance—thinking, "You who ask thus are truly devoid of intelligence"—said: "It has been said," etc. Previously, in the seventh book itself, even one who is an enemy...

The meaning is this: if union (*sāyujya*) is obtained even through a state of opposition characterized by hatred, then what need is there to mention the case of a state of conformity characterized by desire? Regarding the term "Hṛṣīkeśa":
although He is ungraspable even by the senses (*hṛṣīka*) of Brahmā and others, He descends of His own accord through His unconditional compassion.

The sense is that even among those who are not the most base in the mortal world, she becomes an object of perception for their senses by His own inconceivable power in order to uplift them; thus, this too is one aspect of His compassionate sovereignty. These [gopīs], however, are dear to Him, the Transcendent One (Adhokṣaja), who is beyond the reach of the senses.

They are indeed the very objects and substrata of affection. And here, by citing the King of Cedi as one who attained perfection—thereby setting aside the proximate Aghāsura and using the distant King of Cedi as an illustration—he speaks this with a hidden meaning to the king; for even in the case of the King of Cedi, [perfection was attained] due to the intensity of his resolute attachment to hatred.
The cessation of the body composed of the qualities (guṇas) resulting from the sage’s curse is indeed its end;
however, his internal body composed of consciousness (cinmaya), consisting of the personal attendants (pārṣadas), remains eternally indestructible.
As it is said: "The sins destroyed by Viṣṇu’s discus" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.45); that is, the sin (aṃhas) was destroyed by Viṣṇu’s discus.
"Thus, but not those two"—the meaning is that he has attained accomplishment, having reached his desired goal, the state of being an attendant [of the Lord]. As it is said:
"Through meditation characterized by intense persistence in enmity, one attains the nature of Acyuta."
Then, according to policy, the two attendants of Viṣṇu went back to the side of Hari. Thus [ends the verse]. 13.
O King, for the sake of the ultimate liberation of those who possess knowledge, there is the manifestation of the Blessed One—
who is imperishable, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, yet whose very self consists of the qualities.

Śrīdhara: [An objection: But how can the embodied soul (dehī) be unobstructed? To this he says: "Of men" (nṛṇām). [The Lord is] the self of the qualities (guṇātman), the controller of the qualities. Since the manifestation of the Blessed One is of such a nature, it is not appropriate to speak of similarity with the body here; this is the intended meaning. ||14||

Vaṃśīdhara: He raises the objection—"But surely..."—on the grounds that there is a contradiction for one who asserts that [the Lord] is covered by connection with a body, since even a fool knows that the body itself is a covering. In reality, the Blessed One has no body at all, as is explicitly stated in the very passage: "He appears as if possessing a body through Māyā" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.55).

Intending to cite the Vedic scripture, "Or [the Self] dwells bodiless," he says: "Of men. An incarnation (*avatāra*) is a manifestation of this nature—that is, a manifestation in a form distinct from the material (*prākṛta*), which is to say, a divine manifestation (*prākaṭya*). Since he possesses a body that is a mass of consciousness (*cid-ghana-mūrti*) with worldly power, for that reason there is no similarity to an embodied being (*dehin*).
"Resemblance to an ordinary person. Regarding this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it is "appropriate," meaning it is fitting; such is the sense.
How could the Son of Nanda—the sovereign of many millions of universes who manifested a pastime-form for the purpose of pacifying the suffering of His devotees—[act otherwise]?
The intended meaning is that the state of being equal to another would be possible. ||14||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, the power of that meditation has been described. In that regard, at the time of the manifestation of the Lord, [there is the case] of a follower of the Lord who possesses the power of an adventitious demon.
Since there is even the Lord’s assistance in accomplishing this for them—who possess such love for the Blessed Lord as did the King of Cedi—it is a matter of course that He would do so for others;
thus he says: "Of these" (nèṇām). This means: for the sake of the supreme welfare of all living beings, which is the fruit of all spiritual practices.

[The phrase] "for the sake of attaining the bliss of His own pastimes, preceded by the perfection of various corresponding capacities"—the meaning is: "solely for the purpose of accomplishing that. "Manifestation" (*vyakti*) means becoming visible. To determine that it is for that specific purpose, he says:
"of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*). Otherwise, [He could have done so] merely by the movement of His eyebrows.

The meaning is that for one capable of destroying millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), an incarnation is not possible for the mere purpose of removing the burden of the earth. "O King"— the sense is that, just as kings like you travel here and there solely for the welfare of living beings.

He speaks of the very nature of the Blessed One through four qualifying attributes beginning with "of the unmanifest" (avyaktasya). He is "immutable" (avyaya), meaning that he does not diminish even by constantly bestowing himself upon various devotees in manifold ways.
Why is this? Because he is "immeasurable" (aprameya), which means he is unlimited. And why is that? Because he is "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa).

Of Him who has transcended the qualities of *māyā*. And why is that? Because the qualities of *māyā* are the motivators of the Self. Or rather, His manifestation as birth is solely for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); otherwise, it could not possibly occur in any way. Thus he says: "of the Imperishable," meaning devoid of modifications such as birth and so forth. Furthermore:

The reason why He is the object of the immeasurable is stated as "consisting of qualities" (*guṇātmanaḥ*); this means He is intent on manifesting all His own infinite qualities—such as compassion and so forth—which were like those in a state of sleep, acting as their awakener. The rest is the same.
This is the underlying meaning (*bhāva*) of these two verses, as explained in the *Bhāvārtha-dīpikā* (on 10.29.13) and elsewhere.

In the commentary, this is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt of those who look outward. Their intention is as follows: "Now, if even desire and so forth are effective in Brahman, then since the individual souls (jīvas) also possess oneness through their commonality of consciousness (cit), they too must have the nature of Brahman; consequently, such [powers] would also exist in the Lords (patis) and others? To that, he says: "In the individual souls... and so on.
The reason for being veiled should be understood as the state of having knowledge dependent upon the senses (*hṛṣīka*), according to the method of the opposite of what will be stated hereafter.

In that regard, his own state of being veiled is due to outward distraction, while [the veiling] of others is due to grasping only their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); because he is the Lord of the Senses (*hṛṣīkeśa*), he is not under the control of the senses, as previously explained.
That is its arising. Therefore, since it consists solely of self-luminosity, and since Brahmanhood is thus established as being entirely unobscured,
the meaning is that whatever activity may occur therein through desire or other factors, the experience of the reality (vastu) nonetheless certainly takes place.
"Is it not the case that 'possessing a body' (dehin) means being perceived as having a body, like a husband and so forth? To this he states the established conclusion:

"Of the Blessed One alone. The meaning is: because of the distinctness [of the Lord] from each of those particular [conditions]. Being of such a nature—that is, having the nature of the unconditioned Brahman—how could there be similarity to one who possesses a body? Therefore, there is no state of possessing a body.
Because that very body has the singular nature of the supreme reality, which is characterized by a manifold variety established through the power of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*);
and this is known from the authority of those various scriptures practiced by the experience of the wise. And as follows:
This has been explained in passages such as: "There is nothing higher than this, which is Your supreme essential nature" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.3). ||14||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By means of even some slight connection, everyone attains their own desired goal, whether it be a particular state of being (*bhāva-viśeṣa*) or the Lord Śrī Bhagavān Himself, through the power of the Blessed Lord; thus he says in two verses beginning with "nèṇām."

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). That itself is the object (*artha*), the fruit; [the phrase *tadartham*] means "for that. Alternatively, the supreme good is liberation (*mukti*), and devotion is its object. Or again, the supreme good is devotion itself, and its object is love (*prema*); [the phrase *tadartham*] means "for the sake of bestowing that. Manifestation (*vyakti*) is becoming visible. Thus.

The intended meaning is precisely the state of being the Lord (Bhagavān) in person. For this very reason, [it refers] to the Supreme Lord who has descended as the Bhagavān. Alternatively, it means "for the sake of their ultimate liberation" alone.
The reason for this is stated as "of the Bhagavān. Otherwise, [he could have accomplished it] by a mere movement of his eyebrows.

The meaning is that for one capable of destroying millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), an incarnation would be inappropriate for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa and others who were merely a burden to the earth. "O King"— the sense is that just as [Viṣṇu] descends for the welfare of the worlds, so too does the arrival of a king such as you [occur].
He speaks of the very state of being the Blessed One (Bhagavat) through four qualifiers beginning with "of the unmanifest" (avyaktasya).

It is "indestructible" (avyaya), meaning that it does not perish even through the giving away of the self and so forth. Why? Because it is "immeasurable" (aprameya), which means it is unlimited. Why is that? Because it is "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa), meaning it transcends the qualities of Māyā. That...
And why? Because the self is the initiator of the qualities of *māyā*.

Or rather, their manifestation—that is, birth—is solely for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); otherwise, it could not possibly occur in any way. Thus he says: "of the imperishable," meaning devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth. Furthermore:
The cause for the manifestation of even such an immeasurable [Being] is "the one whose nature is excellence" (guṇātmanaḥ).
This means: he is intent upon manifesting all his own qualities, such as compassion and so forth, as their conscious source. The rest is the same.

Alternatively, one might ask: "In that case, how can there be the act of attracting another's wife? To this he says: the meaning is that for the Imperishable One, nothing is lost even by the diversion of another's wife.
Again, one might ask: "Even so, what indeed could be His purpose in that? To this he says: it is the sport (*līlā*) of Him who is immeasurable and beyond the reach of thought.
The meaning is: by whom can it be conceptualized? Why? Because He is "devoid of qualities yet the self of the qualities" (*nirguṇasya guṇātmanaḥ*).
Although He is devoid of qualities, He is the self—the substratum—of the qualities. By virtue of being devoid of qualities, He is untainted by their defects;
and by virtue of being the self of the qualities, His union with the illustrious gopīs is established as the final conclusion (*siddhāntaḥ*).

Or rather, if it is argued: "Even so, for the sake of our pleasure, please investigate this yourself and speak," he replies to that: [He does so] because, although He is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), by means of His own qualities which impel the Self, and through the *rāsa*-pastime which establishes supreme love for the worlds, He is the perfection of all excellent qualities.
The manifestation of this will indeed occur later in the dialogue between Śrī Parīkṣit and Śuka through a series of questions and answers. ||14||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.

(*Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* 145): By the word "of them" (*eṣām*), it follows generally that [the manifestation] is for the ultimate liberation of the individual souls (*jīva*) themselves, and when manifested, it is all the more so for the devotees (*bhakta*). Otherwise, its manifestation would be...

He says "of the immutable" (avyayasya) to show that [such a thing] could not possibly occur. "Of the one devoid of qualities" (nirguṇasya) means of one who is free from the material qualities (prākṛta-guṇa).

"Of the one whose nature consists of qualities" (guṇātmanaḥ) refers to him for whom those qualities such as sovereignty (aiśvarya) and so forth are indeed the very forms of his own self (ātman-svarūpa). ||14||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: In this very way, the greatness of Kṛṣṇa is such that He has appeared for the sake of the ultimate liberation of human beings; therefore, He performs such pastimes. This is stated in the verse beginning with "nṛṇām" and so forth.
[He is] "nirguṇasya," meaning devoid of material qualities, yet "guṇātmanaḥ," whose nature consists of the [transcendental] modes.
Of the effort toward qualities such as affection for devotees; here, the word *ātman* signifies "effort. ||14||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, it may be argued that for the King of Cedi—who, having received a demon body due to a curse from Brahmā, had obtained the prospect of regaining his status as an attendant (*pārṣada*) at the end of three births—it would be appropriate for him to obtain a body as an attendant immediately after the fall of that [demon] body. This is the case for these [women].

Immediately after casting off the body composed of the modes of nature (guṇa-maya-deha), there is entry into the eternal realm (nitya-maṇḍala). If one asks how this is so, he says: by whatever means—even through a connection with any other rasa beyond the sweet rasa (madhura-rasa)—one prays to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and because this has been seen many times before, he says "of men" (nṛṇām).

The manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the incarnate Lord whose essential nature is inconceivable sovereignty and who is capable of removing the burden of the earth by His mere will; His purpose is generally for the ultimate good and liberation of all beings who wander upon this earth— the supreme goal of human life.
Devotional yoga (bhakti-yoga) is for the sake of attaining Him.

Alternatively, "niḥśreyasam" refers to the state [of liberation]; its "artha" is supreme love; thus, "for the sake of attaining that" means for the sake of attaining that [supreme love]. The primary purpose of the incarnate Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the removal of the earth's burden.

It does not exist [in them], yet there is a manifestation intended to spread everywhere that same state of being which exists in the beauties of Vraja. The mention of "men" is illustrative; it should be understood to apply even to animals, birds, trees, and so forth. Thus it is said: "Then the cows, having quickly returned to the cow-pen... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.13.24).

Thus: "O Mother, it seems that the sages in this forest are indeed birds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.14), and "Oh, these [trees], worshipped by the best of gods and immortals" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.15.5). This is because the internal state (*bhāva*) is manifested even toward those [objects], even though the Blessed One is capable of subduing even Brahmā and the other gods by His own sovereignty.
The manifestation of the Incarnate One has appeared for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of His various incarnations, portions, and opulences—

O King, this is the address. Just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa gladdened those who were merely human by bestowing the nectar of divine love, so too have You [gladdened] those among the inhabitants here who were merely human.

"Men are to be protected by promoting devotion (*bhakti*). The dative case in *niḥśreyasārthāya* is used in the sense of purpose. In this regard, the fourfold objects of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) serve as the cause; for one who is "undecaying" (*avyayasya*)—meaning devoid of decay even when giving his own limbs to devotees—for what purpose does he give himself? In that regard:

The reason is as follows: for one whose nature consists of qualities (*guṇātman*), the qualities are compassion and so forth; having attained identity with these, He therefore gives Himself to His devotees out of compassion alone, because it is His very nature.
[Objection: But how can there be imperishability (*avyayatva*) even when giving away the Self?

To this he says: "Immeasurable" means that which is beyond logic and is unlimited. In the giving of that which is limited, there is depletion. Furthermore, it is said: "Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be subjected to logical reasoning.
Why is that? Because [Brahman] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), having transcended the qualities of *māyā*. The reason for this is: "[It is] of the nature of the qualities (*guṇātmanaḥ*)."
Of Him who sets in motion the qualities of Māyā;

or rather, of Him who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), Himself free from attributes, yet whose very nature consists of qualities (guṇātman); and of that Self who, being like a mirror for the qualities, the very selves, and the essential forms of the beauties of Vraja, serves as their locus of reflection.
The sense is that because qualities such as skill in the arts of dance, song, and so forth are reflected [in Him], He has come to possess a nature consisting of those qualities (*guṇātmakatva*).
Alternatively, it means one whose own mind (*ātmani citte*) possesses the qualities— such as beauty and the like— of the queens of Vraja, who are themselves composed of qualities (*guṇātmaka*).
Although He Himself is devoid of qualities and delights only in the Self, He nevertheless disregarded His own qualitylessness;
being attracted by their qualities, He caused them to enter the divine circle situated upon the pivot by causing them to vanish within His own body composed of those very qualities.

[Objection: But if He is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), how could He have acted in this way? To that he says: "Of the immeasurable one, reasoning is untenable" (*aprameyasya tarko'pratiṣṭhānāt*). Or rather, even for one like me who is devoid of qualities, there are qualities such as chanting and so forth which consist of qualities; [He acts] for the sake of those who set such [qualities] in motion, even though He Himself is devoid of qualities like us.

The intention is that His manifestation is for the purpose of engaging them in qualities such as the description of Rāma’s pastimes. For this very reason, at the conclusion [of the tenth canto], the departure from the rāsa-dance will become clear so that He may make everyone—both Himself and others—His own through the sport with the women of Vraja (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.40). Therefore...
In whatever way possible, even a mere connection [with them] is the cause for all to transcend saṃsāra; how much more so for those dear to Kṛṣṇa! ||14||

Viśvanātha: Since the Blessed One has descended with the thought in his mind, "I shall uplift even those people who lack the means for ultimate liberation, provided they have some slight connection with me," he says in two verses beginning with "Of men" (*nṛṇām*): [liberation] exists in some.
In some cases the goal is *sāyujya* (union), in others *sālokya* and so forth, and in others it is love; yet for Him—
who is capable of dissolving millions of universes by the mere movement of His eyebrows—
the manifestation [of the Lord] is solely for the purpose of slaying Kaṃsa and others who have become a burden to the earth, and cannot be justified otherwise.

The meaning is that for the Immutable One, there is no passing away even by the surrender of His own self for the sake of each devotee; how so? To this he says: "of the Immeasurable," meaning one who cannot be measured.
The sense is: who knows the reality in that matter? For He is "devoid of qualities," meaning free from the material *guṇas*.

Furthermore, the sense is that the ocean of non-material, conscious-blissful qualities— which constitutes the very nature of the Self whose essence is composed of auspicious attributes— can indeed not be measured.
Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, a sense of oneness, and even friendship toward Hari indeed attain identity with Him.
For those who possess desire, their state of desiring, and for those who possess anger, their state of anger, always persists as identification with that;
even in liberation, the women of Vraja remained desirous of Viṣṇu.
"And those who are constantly hostile toward Hari remain in darkness due to that hatred. Thus it is said.
"For through devotion there is indeed the state of eternal longing, but not without liberation;
therefore, for those possessed of devotion toward Hari, liberation occurs even by way of such longing."
"The gods are always devoted through affection; the celestial nymphs are devoted by virtue of being desired;
some [others] are devoted without desire, but solely through devotion alone.
One attains liberation through no other means than appropriate devotion. Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Liberation is attained through devotion or through devotion born of desire, and not by any other means;
through devotion born of desire one attains the celestial nymphs, but for others, it is certainly not through mere lust.
Janārdana is to be worshipped as a father-in-law by the wives of the gods, and as a lover by certain celestial nymphs; such is their fitness.
"Without worship by one who is qualified, liberation will not be attained by anyone;
for the performer of unqualified worship, there will be hell.
Therefore, having ascertained one's qualification, the worship of Hari should be performed. Thus it is said in the *Bhadrikā*.
And Janārdana is to be worshipped by Brahmā as his father through his sovereignty and glory;
likewise, he is the grandfather of the other thirty-three gods.
"To all people, the Blessed One is my great-grandfather;
Viṣṇu is the teacher of Śrī Brahmā and the teacher of the teacher of the gods."
"The Guru is the root of all people, the Supreme Person;
the Guru is Brahmā, and the eternal Viṣṇu is the deity of this world. Thus alone should worship be performed, and never otherwise. So it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa. (15)
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "kāmam" (at will) to show that attachment to Him in any way whatsoever is the cause of liberation. "Aikyam" means a connection; "sauhṛdam" means devotion. ||15||

Vaṃśīdhara: Because Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed the unconditioned Brahman, for that reason—*yathā kathañcit*, by whatever means or in whatever manner—there is *tatrāsaktiḥ*, an intense attachment to Him. *Kāmam* refers to love for the beloved; *krodham* refers to that which is of the nature of fire, meaning hatred; and *bhayam* means "this one is mine."

Because of death, there is constant reflection on the means for its cessation. *Sneha* is affection (*anurāga*). *Aikya-sauhṛda* (unity and friendship) have already been explained by the venerable teacher’s feet. Those who perform (*vidadhate*) these [practices] attain identity with Him (*tan-mayatā*), which is union (*sāyujya*); this has been clearly demonstrated in the Seventh Skandha. Therefore, by you—

First, let this general conclusion be understood; thus he says: "Granted that the cowherd women and others [direct] desire toward Him, the Caidyas and others anger and hatred, Kaṃsa and others fear, Nanda and others affection and parental love, those who delight in the Self unity, and the Vṛṣṇis, Pāṇḍavas, and others friendship—they constantly offer these."
Even now, by assuming various states, they attain identification with those [states];

this makes known the eternality of those various divine pastimes (*līlā*). "Attaining identification with them" means that the *gopīs* and others become absorbed in them, as in the expression "a lustful man is possessed by women. Others [attain] union (*sāyujya*). ||15||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Let alone the matter of those belonging to the specific time of that manifestation; however, this same principle applies even to those who are eternal. Thus he says, "Kāmam" (at will).

In that regard, *kāma* is of two kinds: consisting of love (*premamaya*), as in the case of the *gopīs* and others; and consisting of the desire for amorous play (*riraṃsāmaya*), as in the case of Sairandhrī and others.

Anger and hatred, as in the case of the Caidyas and others; fear, as in the case of Kaṃsa and others; affection, as in the case of Vṛṣṭi and the Pāṇḍavas, or as among the illustrious residents of Vraja; unity, as among those who delight in the Self (ātmārāmas);
and friendship, as among the Krathakaiśikas and others. Among these, however, fear and hatred are not approved.

Indeed, one who considers himself to possess auspicious qualities yet acts terrifyingly—even if he is hidden—will lead to the welfare of both the one who fears him and the one who is openly hostile due to envy and the like; for what common person could stand before him? One should perform various deeds, but only with affection or genuine friendship.

The intended meaning is indeed that everyone should do so; this has been stated by the venerable Nārada in this very way: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.31). Here, the phrase "by whatever means" means "by whatever suitable means. For this reason, it is said in that very same place:
"It is my firm conviction that a mortal does not attain such absorption through the yoga of devotion as he does through the persistence of enmity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.26).
And in that regard, having transcended the yoga of devotion consisting of reverence for the commands of the scriptures, one proceeds on the path of ecstatic emotion (*bhāva*).

Since even that [enemy] is seen to possess a power that causes him to become absorbed in that [Lord], affection (*sneha*) and friendship (*sauhṛda*) are indeed acknowledged; thus it is said, "even one who hates [Him]," for in that case, oneness is not acknowledged because such qualities of His do not manifest. The word *eva* (indeed) [applies] to each [term] individually.

Those who, for the sake of attaining their purpose, perform [the practice] according to the alternative reading— whether it be "tanmayatām" or "tat-tad-bhāva-samucitāvirbhāvam tad-eka-sphūrtim"— the readings are indeed of the same meaning. However, the Blessed Lord is indeed to be grasped through exclusive devotion (*ekayā bhaktyā*).
For it is said in the words of the Blessed Lord: "The self is dear to the virtuous through faith" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.14.21).
It is seen by yogis through devotion;
it is never seen without devotion.
"Janārdana cannot be seen through anger or through envy," according to the statement in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa,
and also from the Śrī Gītā: "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by yoga-māyā" (Gītā 7.25).

Although its truthfulness is not experienced as such by those who hate it and others, but rather quite otherwise, nevertheless, through its power, truthfulness manifests even indirectly at a later time; thus, anger and fear are also included here, let alone those dear to Adhokṣaja. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa]
[10.29.13] By this [verse], it should be understood that *kāma* (desire) is exalted because of its extreme dearness.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, even by some slight connection with Hari—who attracts all minds and removes all defects—the word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of "only" (*eva*). [This refers to] desire and so forth.

Or rather, people who constantly perform [evil deeds] while indulging in desire and so forth; or else, the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest who were well-known for their desire and so forth, as well as Keśin, Kaṃsa, and others.
Or else, the construction is: "those [who dwell] in that Hari of yours. In some readings, the word *vidadhate* (they perform) appears.
This is indeed certain. Through meditation, they attain absorption (*tanmayatā*) consisting of exclusive devotion to Hari;

or else, by attaining states such as *sārūpya* (similarity in form), they reach His very nature. By the word "eternally" (*nityam*), it is indicated that through repeated practice and steadfastness in each respective stage, there is no delay in reaching that state of absorption. Otherwise...

Because [the state] is occasional, due to the absence of constant absorption in that [divine nature], rapid identification with it is not established. Furthermore, even if there were similarity of form,

there would be differences such as being a devotee or a non-devotee, resulting in the attainment of specific pleasures, the mere destruction of suffering, and so forth, as well as distinctions such as being an attendant of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha or residing in the world of the perfected beings (siddhas).
According to the Vaiṣṇava doctrine, there must indeed be a distinction.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "for the sake of the supreme good of men," he states the reason: for (hi) because even while performing [actions] such as desire and so forth, they attain absorption in That (tanmayatām). The rest is the same. "Friendship" (sauhṛdam) is the illustrative example.
In some versions, the reading is "vā. Consequently, the word "vā" here has the sense of comparison (*upamā*). Thus it was said by the venerable Nārada in the Seventh Canto:
"Just as the mind [is fixed] upon the Lord through desire, hatred, fear, or affection, so too [should it be fixed] through devotion."
"Having entered into Him and abandoned that sin, many have attained His state" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.29).
Furthermore:
"The cowherd women out of desire, Kaṃsa out of fear, and King Śiśupāla and others out of hatred..."

"O Lord, you are the Vṛṣṇis because of kinship, they are out of affection, and we are out of devotion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.30). In this context, the term "gopīs" is used from an external perspective, referring merely to their desire for a paramour;
or rather, all factors such as desire and so forth are grouped together here simply with the aim of attaining absorption in Him (*tanmayatā*).

In terms of the result, however, there is indeed a great distinction; this is the general direction. All of this has already been explained in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*, and it has been further elaborated by the great souls in the *Rasāmṛtārṇava* through the manifestation of various specific details.
This too shall be explained in its proper place further on. (15)

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. (*Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* 145): "In that case, how does such play lead to the ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) of the senses? It is said: it occurs through the awakening of this [knowledge]. Thus he says, "At will" (*kāmam*), and so forth. Here...

By the term *tan-mayatā* (being composed of that), an abundance of that [quality] is expressed. In this context, regarding desire (*kāma*), affection (*sneha*), and so forth, the final meaning is "having a self colored by that," as in the expression "the fool is full of women" (*strīmayo jālmaḥ*).
Regarding anger (*krodha*), fear (*bhaya*), and unity (*aikya*), it means those [states] have for the most part dissolved into that, as in "water is full of milk" (*dugdhamayaṃ jalam*).

It is logical that even a single word may have different meanings depending on its qualifiers, according to the maxim: "And there may be a difference in meaning for a single word due to its qualifiers, as in the case of the word 'Brahman' [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.3.4]. The mention of anger and fear here is solely for the purpose of establishing the point by way of contrast with other cases, and not with the intention of prescribing them. Nor is it...

It is wonderful that others become fulfilled by following the states of being, such as desire, of the illustrious gopīs and others; thus he says, "Not [only this]. What need is there to mention that liberation is possible for some, even from the world? He says, "Because," referring to those who, through the ripening of their worship during the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*), [attain it].
They explain that these [attributes] belong only to the adventitious self and not to the eternally established one who has attained the body of existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda);
therefore, there is no fault. ||15||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therefore, even those who direct desire and so forth toward Him attain identity with Him; how much more so, then, those who possess love? Thus He says: "Desire, anger," and so on.
Desire [is seen] in Kubjā; anger in Śiśupāla and others; fear in Kaṃsa and others; and affection in His parents.

One should understand that the unity of the Vraja boys consists of friendship, while that of the cowherd women consists of love; these lead to absorption (*tanmayatā*) according to their respective capacities. In some cases, there is absorption into His very form, and in others, total dissolution (*laya*). ||15||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: To those among the goddesses of Vraja who were doubting regarding their attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the author], strengthening this point by means of another illustration, declares their supreme excellence over all other beloveds of Kṛṣṁa through the logic of *kaimutya* (a fortiori). In that regard, first, those means for attaining the Lord in this world have been stated.

In that context, it was stated that even hatred serves as a cause for attaining Him, and that its purpose is evident through the example of the King of Cedi. Thus, while explaining how the other [emotions] also serve as means for attaining Him,
he states that the first triad is merely restated (anūdyatva) and the final triad is what is prescribed (vidheyatva).
Because we observe the simultaneous employment of words distinguished by the relation between the subject of reference (*anūdyam*) and the predicate to be enjoined (*vidheyam*):

"desire" (*kāma*) is the subject of reference, and "affection" (*sneha*) is the predicate to be enjoined; for a specific kind of affection is seen to be characterized by the locus of desire. Likewise, having referred to "anger" (*krodha*) as the subject of reference, "unity" (*aikyam*) is the predicate to be enjoined; if there is unity together with the locus of anger, then...
Because one observes the cessation of anger. Thus, having referred to fear (*bhaya*), friendliness (*sauhārda*) is what is enjoined;

since fear is the material cause (*upādāna*), if friendliness occurs together with that [fear], then because one observes the cessation of fear, it is possible for there to be a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), just as in the case of the statement "he cleanses the house."

For it is a logical principle that "splitting the sentence" (*vākya-bheda*) is a flaw. Regarding the word *kāmam*: when one offers desire and so forth to Hari—who by His own majesty has the nature of removing all defects—those who perform such acts attain identity with Him; this is indeed certain, as indicated by the particle *hi*. By the example of the King of Cedi (*caidya*), [it is shown] that in that regard, [desire is offered].

The sages of the Daṇḍaka forest, who directed their longing toward Him in the form of women, obtained birth in their desired Vraja and enjoyed amorous pastimes with Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Those such as the King of Cedi, who manifested anger through enmity, attained their desired state once more as His personal associates (pārṣadas). Those who manifested fear...

Kaṃsa and others attained liberation characterized by *sārūpya* (identity of form) through their state of being, like insects and bees. Yudhiṣṭhira and others, who were portions of Dharma, performed affection and thus attained Kṛṣṇa himself, who is eternally worthy of service and who fulfills all desires. The Yādavas, who were portions of the gods, established a relationship of oneness (*aikya*) [with Him].

They attained residence in the world of Siddhas, which is their own desired goal, and other such things. It is everywhere proclaimed that those Vaiṣṇavas who perform friendship and devotion characterized by love attain Kṛṣṇa himself, who is the very form of their refuge, as their own desired object— constantly, until death, and without interruption.

The meaning is "devoid of any intervention. Although the cessation of saṃsāra certainly occurs when the group of six beginning with desire is practiced due to the power of the objects, nevertheless, there is a difference in the result according to the difference in the means. When this entire collection of means is attained at some point, [the state of] being absorbed in that does not [occur].
"It shall be accomplished," because it was asked, "What is that which is not a hindrance? This has been stated in the Seventh Skandha:
"By fixing the mind upon the Lord through desire, hatred, fear, affection, or even devotion, many have abandoned their sins and attained His state. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.29)

By virtue of the authority of Nārada’s words, others who act in this same way also attain the Blessed Lord alone; for it is well known that "intention (bhāva) is the cause of one's state," and thus intention alone is established as the unerring means. Furthermore:
"The cowherd women out of desire, Kaṃsa out of fear, and King Caidya and others out of hatred [attained Him]."
"O Lord, you Vṛṣṇis are [related to us] by kinship, you by affection, and we by devotion.
Although desire and the other [motivations] are thus mentioned in general within the list [of motivations], it is nevertheless stated again in that very same place:
"It is my settled conviction that a mortal does not attain such absorption through the yoga of devotion as he does through the persistence of enmity. Thus,
the excellence of the persistence of enmity is stated when it is to be practiced.

"Because attachment characterized by aversion is seen to be accompanied by longing. This is because, in other contexts concerning desire (*kāma*), attachment is observed to be more prevalent. When there is reverence for the commands of the scriptures and reverence for the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*), desire and the like necessarily fall into a state of inferiority. Nevertheless, it is not so [in this case].

By the phrase "by means of bhakti-yoga," it is stated that through intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*) in narration, there arises a preeminence of the continuity of enmity (*vairānubandha*). Even more so than that, when the continuity of desire (*kāmānubandha*) is to be practiced, there is indeed an excess of attachment toward worldly activities; however, in this case, the continuity of desire to be practiced pertains to the extraordinary (*alaukika*).
Because of their attachment to the extraordinary [path] through yoga and other means, when the path of rasa (rasa-mārga) is investigated,
it is found that among the six sādhanas, desire alone is preeminent due to the preeminence of its object; otherwise,
how could these women— who are exalted by those who know the supreme reality— be made to pray for the dust of his feet?
Furthermore, they would not have been designated on earth as "the cowherd women who bear slender bodies.
Now, if there is indeed an excellence in the persistence of desire, then how is it that Bhīṣma said: "The cowherd women truly returned to their natural state" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.9.40)?

It is true that attachment to sense-objects is base; however, Bhīṣma’s qualification was solely for the knowledge of the Lord’s majesty, as he lacked abidance in the Lord’s essential nature.
