Otherwise, it would be inconceivable to strike with weapons at the divine form, which is a mass of sweetness and possesses a delicacy exceeding even that of the śirīṣa flower.
Therefore, this was stated because there is an absence of the production of [other] aesthetic flavors (rasas) such as the path of passion; hence, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, when the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas) such as desire and so forth are examined, since the state of being inseparable from contact with the reality known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa is present, it is precisely that *rati* which attains its highest excellence.
Thus it has been said:
"The desire for a specific connection with a body may indeed be twofold, arising through the distinction between proximity and non-proximity."
The state of being fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa within the mind during the exhilaration produced by that [love] constitutes their *rati*,
known as *sambhoga* and *viprayoga*, which they experience in succession.
For the blazing up of the mind caused by anger and envy is what occurs;
when that [blazing] is in a state of melting, it is designated by the term "hatred."
Fear is a state of mental agitation arising from the perception of one's own impending calamity;
it is of two kinds: for the purpose of destroying that calamity, and indeed, for the purpose of pleasing [the one who can remove it].
Among these, the first is indeed hatred; the second bears the name of attachment (*rati*).
Affection (*sneha*) has as its object one's children and so forth, and is characterized by the relationship between the protected and the protector.
The relationship between the served and the server is distinct; that too has been described by the wise as being of three kinds.
Others have declared it to be mixed with either service to the Lord (dāsya) or friendship (sakhya).
That state of blackness in the mind, characterized by a melting born thereof,
becomes the affectionate love (*vatsala-rati*) through the relationship of the protected and the protector.
The delight and affection that proceeds from the relationship of served and server,
as well as the affection born of kinship— both of these attain the state of rasa as previously described.
One is called affectionate devotion (*vatsala-bhakti*), while the other is the beloved devotion (*preyo-bhakti*);
their union is seen among the Bhojas and Vṛṣṇis through the enjoyment of love.
Friendliness (*sauhṛdam*) and benevolence (*sauhārdam*) are indeed devotion itself. This was stated in the Third [Canto]:
"Merely by hearing of My qualities, the movement of the mind toward Me, who dwell in the cave of all hearts, becomes uninterrupted, just as the waters of the Gaṅgā flow toward the ocean."
The characteristic of *bhakti-yoga* that is indeed beyond the material modes (*nirguṇa*) has been thus illustrated [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.29.11–12].
Among these six means of accomplishment, due to the excellence of the object of focus, there is an excellence of the passion born of desire (*kāma-jā rati*).
Devotion mixed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is considered to be the passion born of desire, just as in the case of the passion resulting from a continuous bond of enmity.

And in the case of pleasure born of fear, the attainment of the Blessed Lord occurs preceded by the abandonment of fear and the persistence of enmity. Regarding the imitation of the Blessed Lord’s state as a Yādava, the relationship [with Him] is the cause,
because it is stated that the relationship is "preceded by such imitation."

Attainment occurs precisely by first abandoning worldly attachment, just as in the case of Kāma. The affection directed toward the Pāṇḍavas was premised upon the relationship of protector and protected;

however, that very affection, having caused them to abandon worldly sentiment, became the cause for attaining the Blessed Lord through a supermundane disposition. This is the majesty of devotion (*bhakti*).
And it has indeed been observed in the case of Nārada and others; this is the general direction [of the argument]. ||15||
Viśvanātha: Therefore, you should first grasp this general conclusion, as he says:
"Let the cowherd women and others [attain] desire; the Caidyas and others, anger and hatred; Kaṃsa and others, fear;
Nanda and others, affection and parental love; the self-delighting ones, unity; and [others], friendship."

Regarding the examples of Vṛṣṭi, Pāṇḍava, and others: the phrase "constantly performing" indicates that even now, by manifesting various states, they attain identification with them; thus, it makes known the eternality of those respective pastimes.
Others explain that the gopīs and others attain identification with Him—that is, absorption in Him—just as a lustful man is said to be "consisting of women."
Union [with the Divine]. ||15||
O unborn Blessed One, you should not feel astonishment at this regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of yoga, for by him all this is liberated.
Śrīdhara says: Nor is this an excessive burden for the Blessed One; thus he says, "And not so. For even these things beginning with the stationary world are liberated through Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (16)
Vaṃśīdhara says: "That is not surprising there," and thus he says, "Not so" (*na ca*). An "excessive burden" (*atibhāra*) is something difficult to accomplish.

Likewise, "wonder" (*vismaya*) consists of such doubts as: "How can there be a cessation of the flow of qualities for those whose intellects are fixed on the qualities [of the Lord]? Regarding the word "by you" (*bhavatā*): by you, a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the time of your very birth... [it has not been so].

He says, "Let it be performed by another; let it indeed be done," because from Śrī Kṛṣṇa this world becomes liberated, and by whose grace one is released from this saṃsāra which consists of supreme suffering; for the Śruti says, "Not by another. "Immobile" refers to trees and so forth. Therefore it was said by Brahmā: "In Vṛndāvana, something..."
"Of shrubs, creepers, and herbs" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.61), and so forth; by the word "and so forth," stones and other such things are included.

This is well known from the *Ahalyopākhyāna* in the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Furthermore, because the incarnator is non-different from the incarnations, Cirañjīva Bhaṭṭa has stated: "He who is Rāma is indeed Kṛṣṇa. ||16||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: It is appropriate to feel wonder at an incarnation elsewhere, but not here;

thus he says, "And not so. One should not feel such wonder regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Lords of Yogins. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "again"; the meaning is that [wonder] should not be felt again. For, having beheld Him...

Even these trees, shrubs, and so forth are liberated. What need has he for the knowledge of Brahmanhood? Therefore, just as the perception of Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved is both delightful and conducive to the highest good, so too is the cognition of Brahman in this [Kṛṣṇa]; thus, one should not be surprised by this—this is the meaning of the great sentence. ||16||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Not so" means that while it may indeed be done by another, it must certainly not be done by you—who, having known His majesty from the time of [His] birth—should not act thus. For this very reason, the word "by you" (*bhavatā*) is used out of respect; it is not the word "by thee" (*tvayā*), which is the specific reason for not causing astonishment regarding the Blessed Lord.

Endowed with all sovereignty without exception. [Objection: If that is so, then how is there birth from the womb of Devakī? To this he says: "O Unborn One"—meaning that unlike an ordinary living being (jīva), You are not born, but rather You manifest Yourself by Your own will out of affection for Your devotees and other such motives. Precisely because of Your divine nature, You are the Lord of the lords of yoga; and even therein, You are Kṛṣṇa.
The meaning is: a manifestation that is completely full in every respect. ||16||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is that such wonder, doubt, or a sense of astonishment should not be entertained again. Regarding the word "bhavatā" (by you): let others indeed do so; but by you—who have been cognizant of His majesty since birth—it should never, under any circumstances, be done.

The meaning is "indeed" (*eva*). For this very reason, it was said [by Nārada] out of reverence, "May it be so for you," and not "It is so by you. The reason for not expressing astonishment is that the Blessed One is endowed with all-encompassing sovereignty (*aśeṣaiśvarya*). [An objection: "In that case, how is there birth from the womb of Devakī? To this he replies: "O Unborn One (*aja*)," meaning one who, unlike an ordinary living being (*jīva*), is not born, but [appears] solely by His own will.

The meaning is that He manifests Himself spontaneously through His affection for His devotees and other such qualities. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can there be the perception of Him as the son of Devakī and others? To this he replies: *Yoga* is a specific power for accomplishing what is difficult to accomplish; the masters (*īśvara*) of that [power] are Śrī Śiva, Sanaka, and others, and He is the master even of them. Therefore...

The meaning is that even when manifesting by His own will and Himself, He may also become the son of Śrī Devakī and others through a particular power, because of Her inconceivable sovereignty. For this very reason, [it is said] "since [He appeared] in Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman in human form."

Or rather, the meaning is that for this very reason, Kṛṣṇa is well-known as an ocean of the nectar of His inconceivable and infinite majesty. Alternatively, [it refers to] the Blessed Supreme Lord; "from Him" means from the Unborn (aja), who—unlike the individual soul—is devoid of material birth, because He manifests Himself by His own grace. For this very reason, [He is the source] of the masters of yoga.

Because it manifests a special form of devotion toward the Lord— who is to be served through the devotion of those such as Śrī Nārada who are steadfast in *bhakti-yoga*— or rather, because it manifests His own entire wondrous sovereignty toward the Lord by those masters of yoga who possess great and marvelous powers; and even therein, [it does so] in Kṛṣṇa, the festival of Śrī Gokula.
This is the meaning: because from Kṛṣṇa this entire world, consisting of both the moving and the non-moving,
even though devoid of all other means, is itself specifically liberated by His mere will, or even by the mere appearance of some slight connection with Him.

The meaning is that one attains the realm of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha. And this is with the intention of attaining Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha through the future [manifestations] of Indraprastha and so forth, as well as the trees and creepers; thus it is said in the first book, in the hymn of praise by Śrī-Kuntī:
"These inhabited regions are prosperous, with their herbs and creepers fully ripened;
indeed, the forests, mountains, rivers, and oceans flourish by your glances" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.8.40).
Thus, by the words "prosperous" (*svṛddhāḥ*) and again "they flourish" (*edhante*), [the meaning is established].
What is intended here is precisely the fitness for attaining Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha; the rest has been explained by them.

Alternatively, one might ask: "How could that state of being absorbed in Him—which is difficult to achieve even through great means such as numerous sacrifices and yogic practices—be accomplished in some way or other through a connection with desires and the like? To this, he says: "Not so" (na ca).

The meaning is the same. Therefore, upon hearing of this *rāsa*-pastime and so forth, even those who are intent on liberation and other goals should not remain indifferent by perceiving it merely as a worldly play of desire; rather, for the sake of attaining their own desired ends—and especially for devotees—for the sake of attaining that which transcends them, this [pastime] should always be regarded as the supreme fruit.
Thus, it has been firmly established that "She alone is to be served" is the intended meaning for introducing this section; such is the direction.

Alternatively, by virtue of their extraordinary fortune as the daughters of the King of Vraja and the cowherds of Vraja, they too—having had their obstacles destroyed—were immediately united with Śrī Kṛṣṇa in that very same body, and at that very moment engaged in the rāsa-dance pastimes.

"It obtained" (alabhanta) is how it should be explained. For instance: having gone inside the house, they were bound by the animals and placed within the home by their husbands and others; therefore, finding no way out despite their efforts, they became absorbed in that contemplation—that is, they became absorbed in the contemplation of her *rāsa*-play with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Then, their bonds having been destroyed and their fetters rendered utterly loosened by the power of meditation alone, they abandoned through that very meditation the body—which, because it was bound in many ways by the husband and others, was composed of qualities (*guṇamaya*) and thus abounding in snares (*pāśapracura*), being made of snares (*pāśamaya*). [They realized: "I am not bound by anyone."
However, the meaning is that each [of them] considered themselves to be already liberated.

Thus, the abandonment of the body is said to occur precisely through the abandonment of such mental conceptions (*bhāvanā*). Just as at the beginning of creation, the abandonment of various specific conceptions by the venerable Brahmā was itself the abandonment of those respective bodies, so too is it described in the Third Canto.
And then, by the power of meditation, their bonds were instantly destroyed; that is,
the restraint imposed by their husbands and others through fetters, or rather, being such that they were free from obstacles such as the closing of doors— thus qualified [they remained].

The intended meaning is: they abandoned the state of being bound by the body. Consequently, they united with that Supreme Soul, who is indeed in the form of Śrī Nanda-kiśora. The reason for this is: "distinguished by the perception of Him as their lover."

Alternatively, the meaning is that the Supreme Self is her supreme beloved; this is the reason for the perception of Him as a lover, for otherwise such supreme dearness could not be established. He describes the power of meditation: by meditation alone, that intense heat of separation from her beloved which was difficult to endure was shaken off, cast away, and rendered insignificant.

The world is impure because of the excess of all its suffering; the rest is the same. And thus, the meaning of the verse beginning with "While I was sporting at night" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.37) is this:
although they remained in Vraja bound by their husbands and others, they subsequently [became free] through contemplation of my prowess.
They did not fail to attain the essence (rasa), nor was the essence unattained; rather, they were filled with rasa itself.

And this is the meaning of Śrī Parīkṣit’s question: it refers to those whose meditation (dhyāna) is directed toward the qualities (guṇas)—such as the compassion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—perceiving Him with the thought "He is my beloved," and not toward His form that transcends the qualities (guṇātīta). This pertains to their meditation.

Although a deficiency has been indicated, [one might ask]: "How can there be the cessation—that is, the withdrawal—of the succession of snares employed by husbands and others for the purpose of binding? To this, Śrī Śukadeva says: liberation from the bondage of saṃsāra may somehow occur through meditation.

It goes without saying that for those who are most beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, liberation from the bondage of the noose occurred through the particularity of their meditation upon Him; this is established by the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutika-nyāya). By the words beginning with "it has been said," he states that even through meditation performed with hatred and the like, one's desired goal is accomplished. The rest is easily understood. ||16||
*Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, having abandoned the state of being possessed by anger, he instructs out of affection for his disciple, beginning with "And not thus," and so forth. Furthermore, one should not feel such astonishment; indeed, it is not thus.
The meaning is "it must be done. By you, the grandson of those who know the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Where?

In Kṛṣṇa; let doubt be cast elsewhere. Of what nature is He? Unborn, self-luminous, the Blessed Lord of inconceivable supreme sovereignty, the Lord even of the masters of yoga, capable of acting or not acting.
"Capable of acting otherwise": by this it is meant that even through the knowledge of Brahman nothing happens to Him;
yet, even through the mere knowledge of His beloved, there occurs the auspiciousness of union with His limbs.
This power to act otherwise constitutes His status as the Lord of the lords of yoga (Yogeśvareśvaratā), because by it even these trees, shrubs, and so forth are liberated.

In being the agent of liberation, there is the state of being the Lord of the Lords of Yoga; in not being the agent when bringing about the fulfillment of the purpose of non-devotees, there is the state of being the Lord of the Lords of Yoga. ||16||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Nevertheless, observing that the king’s face was filled with astonishment, she dispels his wonder with these reproachful words: "And it is not thus.
Therefore, let those who are possessed by the misconceptions of impossibility and contrary notions feel astonishment due to their lack of devotion.
"O sir, this is unbecoming of you. Since you have heard of the greatness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa many times before and have even seen it with your own eyes, you should not feel such astonishment toward Kṛṣṇa.
Toward what kind of Lord? Toward one whose opulence is inconceivable, and who, by His own sovereignty, is also the cause of worldly existence."
It is capable of establishing the cessation of the flow of qualities such as desire and anger; as it was said by the Blessed One’s own mouth:
"For those whose intellects are absorbed in Me, desire does not lead to further desire."
"Roasted and boiled grains are generally not fit for seed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.26).
If you feel astonishment at the non-experience of an experience, then anyone else will likewise do so,
precisely because of the non-experience of an experience.

Furthermore, of what nature is He? [He is] "unborn" (aja). If the birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa were like that of an ordinary soul through the connection of semen and blood, then there would be a question preceded by doubt;
however, since that is not the case, he says: because He is unborn, devoid of material birth, even though born of Devakī.

Birth is indeed accepted in that which has become the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the sentiment of parental affection (*vatsala-rasa*), established as His eternal motherhood. He manifests by His own will out of affection for His devotees. "The son of Yaśodā" and "the son of Devakī" are His essential form (*svarūpa*); His true nature (*dharma*) is birthlessness (*ajatva*). Even though He is situated externally, He remains so.

This was said for the purpose of describing the event of the entrance: just as He exists externally as fullness of bliss (*ānanda-pūrṇatva*), so too He desires to enter the womb of Devakī, which is of the nature of bliss. Therefore, one should not feel astonishment toward the Unborn (*aja*).

If it be asked, "How can there be the state of being unborn (ajatva) in the case of the celebrated son of Devakī?", he says in response: "In the Lord of the Lords of Yoga. Yoga, however, is the power to accomplish the impossible. By that power of yoga, having assumed numerous bodies for the sake of enjoyment, [He remains unborn].

Having obtained power through the grace of the Blessed One, yogins, by means of a manifold array of bodies, enjoy their pleasures and attain the destiny they desire. Their yoga, however, is an adventitious quality, whereas in the Blessed One it is non-adventitious; this alone is the distinction. As for the Blessed One, he—

Even though he is distinguished by those qualities, he bestows the fruits of yoga upon others; since he brings about the transcendental nature of their bodies as they attain yoga, one should not feel astonishment at their entry into the eternal maṇḍala.
Furthermore, of what kind is he? He is Kṛṣṇa. As for the etymological meaning that "kṛṣ" denotes the earth and so forth, that is merely derivative.

But [the word "Vraja"] is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to Yaśodā’s suckling child, according to the maxim that "conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) supersedes etymological derivation (*yoga*).

By means of its connection with Yaśodā alone, the excess of affection among the inhabitants of Vraja is indicated; for it is a well-known fact that all people feel affection toward those who are their own kin. This is the *līlā*.

This [grace] has been bestowed upon those whose forms possess faultless and perfect qualities, even though they are unfit for such experience; thus, although wonder exists, you should not feel wonder.
He speaks of the majesty of this connection: "Because of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," this world, beginning with the immobile, [has come to be].

He is indeed liberated. This is the point: who is it that possesses the senses? When one possesses the senses and has the authority [to act], if the act of worship is not seen, and if by that [omission] there were a cessation of evil, then there would be no contradiction with the established doctrine. For, in that case, [the doctrine] would have a visible purpose.

One should not feel astonishment, for the connection with Śrī Kṛṣṇa in cases such as the twin Arjuna trees has been observed repeatedly and is established beyond doubt; moreover, it was spoken by His own mouth:
"O, these [trees worship] the one adored by the best of gods and immortals" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.15.5), as has been heard many times.

And Śrī Śuka, having related his own experience, caused the King’s astonishment to vanish—so says Viśvanātha: "Not so. Let another indeed be made to feel astonishment; but in this matter, you, who have known His majesty since the time of His birth, should not feel it, even though the Lord was merely a cowherd.
"Even though He is the son of Devakī, even though He is the Lord of the masters of yoga (yogeśvaras) despite His passion for the cowherd women, and even though He is Kṛṣṇa,
an incarnation of Śarva— in Him, even this entire world beginning with the immobile is liberated," so says the venerable Svāmīcaraṇa.
Or rather, even now, the world remains distinct from the retinue of His pastimes.
By recollecting each respective state of desire, affection, and so forth, one is liberated from the flow of the gunas and becomes free. ||16||
The Blessed Lord said: Having seen those women of Vraja approaching His presence, the Blessed Lord [spoke].
The best among speakers spoke, bewildering them with the artistry of his words.
Śrīdhara: He states the subject at hand with the words "Having seen them," etc. "With the charms of speech" means with the playful graces of her voice. ||17||

Vaṃśīdhara continues with the subject at hand—"the matter in question. "The best among speakers" refers to those superior to the four-faced Brahmā, the hundred-faced Śeṣa, the thousand-faced Viṣṇu, Vyāsa, and others. "Those" refers to the gopīs.
According to Mādhava, the word *peśas* denotes a limb, radiance, playfulness (*helā*), and powder; it is masculine.
He spoke, deluding [them] with words that signified indifference, entreaty, awakening, and duality;

therein, he especially deluded them with those indicating indifference, making them as if bewildered, while with those conveying entreaty, he especially made them affectionate—this is the distinction. Thus it was said.
"Out of shame at their own emaciation, they say nothing"—the meaning is that this is due to their exquisite beauty. ||17||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, in this context of the *rāsa-līlā* consisting of the supreme nectar, although such an interruption is inappropriate, this question was asked solely for the purpose of bringing about single-mindedness among all.

"Was composed by you. Indicating that "I too have merely manifested this system of established doctrine solely out of deference to you," he, though unasked, suddenly speaks what was already present in his own eagerness: "They were drawn by the flute-song and became utterly overwhelmed"—he demonstrates that very point.

The meaning is that the women of Vraja were fit to remain only within Vraja itself, and not to come into the forest outside; even there, they came into his very presence, not remaining at a distance out of shyness or the like. Having seen him, they spoke words with "peśas"—that is, with the playful charms of speech. And these [words] are of two kinds: verbal...

And there are also those based on meaning (*ārthika*). The former [consist of] specific qualities such as the arrangement of very graceful syllables, easy and charming pronunciation, and the movement of the eyelashes of the beautiful face and eyes accompanied by a smile.
The latter consist of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotional state (*bhāva*), ornament (*alaṃkāra*), and subject matter (*vastu*). These too are of four kinds.
They consist of modes of indifference, modes of solicitation, modes of establishing the meaning of those two together, and modes of the actual reality.
And this being so, the meaning is: "deluding" means making them lose their minds and lose their discrimination; "acting" is the sense [of the verb].

This should be inferred according to the specific context. In that regard, "priority" belongs to those [meanings] consisting of verbal expression, prayer, and the actual reality; "subsequentness" belongs to the other two.
Furthermore, among these, the verbal meanings are by nature characterized by indifference toward the objective meanings, especially with respect to the state of being (*bhāva*).

These were indeed composed for the purpose of increasing longing within oneself, and not for the sake of indifference, because it is stated: "He set his mind on sporting" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.1) and "He sang sweetly, enchanting the hearts of the fair-eyed women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.3). Therefore, in this context, it is merely by the artistry of words, and not otherwise.
The meaning is "in terms of the underlying intention.

Thus, by means of dissimulation—where there is one thing in the mind and another in speech—their despondency is produced through longing; and by that, their discernment is taken away. Even in that regard, it consists of supplication.
These [words] have as their sole cause his own eagerness; however, the mediation regarding the purpose of that pair is for the sake of playful curiosity.
Thus, he states the speaker’s fitness through the method of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"): "the best among speakers."
He is the most eminent among those who possess mastery over all speech, because the Blessed One surpasses all others through such innate knowledge and other qualities;
or rather, the word "all" (nikhila) should be understood as being included everywhere. For instance, [it applies to] the women of Vraja.

Although they were renowned for being devoted solely to innate, natural love; although they had experienced such transformations of that love; although they had at that time come into His very presence; and although the Lord Himself, being all-knowing, was directly aware of their inner state—even upon seeing them face-to-face—He [remained silent] regarding their words.
Deceiving with charming and deceptive words and bringing him to a state of extreme distress, he spoke.
For what purpose? The meaning is: for the sake of a particular jest, as he was the best among those skilled in humorous speech. ||17||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Drawn by the song of the flute, all those women of Vraja—exceedingly agitated and entirely youthful—[approached]. Or rather, the meaning is that they were fit to remain only in Vraja and were not meant to come into the interior of the forest; nevertheless, they arrived at his very presence. Not [elsewhere].

[The gopīs], standing at a distance out of shame and other such feelings, saw him and spoke what is about to be described, beginning with "Welcome" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.18). For what purpose? The meaning is: by means of the "peśas"—that is, the playful charms—of his speech, he especially deluded them and captivated their hearts, in order to greatly increase the desire directed toward himself.
And that will become manifest before you.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be such delusion through mere play of words? To this he replies:
"Among the eloquent speakers, such as the illustrious Four-faced One (Brahmā) with his thousand mouths, and among the poets, such as the illustrious Vyāsa and others..."

"Supreme. Why? Because the Blessed One is directly endowed with all sovereignty. Or rather, "by the artistry of words"—that is, by specific turns of expression; for a single utterance, being simultaneously characterized by indifference and by prayer, touches two mutually contradictory poles precisely through the skill of this deceptive method. This is the meaning.

Even though its primary purpose is to directly instruct on dharma and other such matters, it serves to strengthen the specific bhāva directed toward Him by means of His own intense desire for amorous play. The reason for this is that He is "the best among speakers," or else, as it is said:
"He set His mind on sporting" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.1), and "He sang sweetly to the fair-eyed women."
By the verse beginning with *manoharam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.3), His desire for amorous play (*riraṃsā*) with them is clearly expressed.

Thus, while one thing was in His mind and quite another in His speech— deceiving them through such dissimulation (*avahitthā*) by means of the playful display of superior speech regarding dharma and other matters, they were rendered unable to determine the true meaning of His words.

In reality, however, that [statement] is merely a conventional mode of expression using the "beauty of the artistry of speech," and it makes it clear that such a state of being does not actually exist;
or rather, the meaning of the words should be understood as being inherent everywhere. For instance:
Although the women of Vraja were devoted to their innate, natural love for Him, and although they were in such a state,

and although at that time they had come into His very presence, and although the Blessed Lord Himself, being omniscient, was fully aware of their inner feelings— nevertheless, by means of His words, that is, through deceptive speech...

Causing him to be utterly bewildered and bringing him to a state of extreme distress, he spoke. For what purpose? The meaning is: for the sake of a particular jest, as he was the best among those skilled in humorous speech.
Or rather, by means of the "ornaments" of his words—that is, through the playful charms of his speech—for the purpose of making him listen to them.

The meaning is as follows: Alternatively, he spoke while deluding them with his own beauty (*peśaiḥ*). Why? Because of the elision of the letter *a* (*akāra-praśleṣeṇa*), the sense is that they were "speechless" (*avācaḥ*), not saying anything out of shame. Therefore, the meaning is that he spoke for the sake of the joy of hearing their replies. Why? Because he is the best among speakers (*vadatām śreṣṭhaḥ*).
The meaning is that those who are skilled in the art of expression naturally take pleasure in hearing the eloquence of others' speech;
the rest is the same. Thus, in every respect, this should be understood as being solely for the purpose of increasing mutual affection in reality. ||17||

The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained. The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now he states the subject at hand, beginning with "Having seen them," and so forth. The Blessed One spoke—he who is the best among eloquent speakers. What was he doing? [He was speaking] with the ornaments of speech (*vācaḥ-peśaiḥ*). Of speeches...
"Deluding by means of *avayas*"; *avayas* refers to various types of states (*bhāva*). [The term is derived] from the root *piś*, meaning "to divide.

These [states] consist of distinctions such as acceptance, neutrality, avoidance, and so forth. In negation there is affirmation; in affirmation there is negation—this is the sense of the aforementioned contradictory definitions. ||17||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, he states the subject at hand with the words "tā" (they).
Those who were summoned by the sweetness of the flute's sound and by its name; who, abandoning household duties such as milking [the cows] and so forth;
who, abandoning their religious obligations (*dharma*) by desiring to hear [him]; and who, abandoning bodily refinements (*saṃskāra*) by anointing themselves [with fragrant pastes].

By the statement "the women of Vraja have come together solely out of love," the arrival of the five types [of gopīs] is indicated; those who are unaware of specific clevernesses (cāturī) come near, whereas those who possess specific cleverness would remain at a distance through dissimulation (avahitthā), but that is not the case here.

It arises from coming with agitation. Furthermore, when they are deluded, a particular cleverness does not take hold. Having seen them, he spoke. If one asks what he said, in response to that expectation, [the answer is] that which was previously thought regarding the "mind-wheel" (*manaścakra*), namely, in the context of the play of the mind (*mānasalīlā*).

Now he spoke. Doing what? "Bewildering with the charms of his speech"—causing them to reach a state of particular delusion through the play of his words. Previously they had been enchanted by the sound of his flute; now, in order to test their inner disposition, he intended to strengthen that very same feeling according to the maxim of "driving in a post" (sthūṇā-nikhanana-nyāya).
By those very words, having created a sense of deception right before him, she spoke "Welcome" and so forth with a harsh demeanor in order to teach him the sequence of sweet sentiments.
Indeed, having summoned us with the sound of the flute, he now speaks thus with literal meaning solely for the purpose of testing our inner disposition.

How could it not occur to their minds that he turns them back by his speech? To this he replies: he is the best among eloquent speakers such as Śeṣa and others. He states a qualifying epithet containing a reason for this:
"the Blessed One" (Bhagavān). [He does so] because, having produced deception through his speech, he intends to nourish it with the sovereignty of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
He is capable of displaying his own playful charm through a single body alone amidst many [women];
or rather, by means of the artful refinements of speech— which outwardly indicate righteousness, aim at turning others back through the display of fear, and conceal his desire for dalliance— within.

The meaning is: by means of those things which demonstrate the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*)— which, preceded by my indifference toward dharma and so forth, nourish the substratum of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and are smeared with the skill of deceit— he brings [the listener] to a state of comprehension through his power of perception, while intending to delude them such that there is one thing in the mind and another in the speech.
Or rather, [he was] "bewildering" her with the loveliness of his own limbs— that is, acting while devoid of the sense of what ought to be done—

and for that very reason, because his eyes were struck by the mass of splendor of that body, he was unable to grasp the beauty of the entire face simultaneously; thus, first of all, his eyes were fixed upon the lotus-feet.
Their speech was downward-turned;
or rather, having assumed a rigid seal upon their mouths, they were unable to say anything at all;
or else, due to being possessed by another spirit, or because of their arrival, or due to excessive breathing, there occurred such behavior as the bending down of their voices and so forth.
Or rather, she replied to them while maintaining a wordless silence, unable either to act or even to speak, wondering what he would say once he had recognized her gaze. ||17||

Viśvanātha: Having resolved the incidental contradiction, he states the subject at hand: "They were drawn by the sound of the flute"—[he who is] the best among those eloquent in speech, possessing skill in expression, [and who knows] the time, place, and occasion. The word *piśa* means a limb; it is a form ending in the suffix *ghañ*. Thus, *peśaiḥ* refers to the limbs of speech.

By deluding them with the sound of his flute— using those harsh and tender elements that convey the expressed, the indicated, and the suggested meanings— he seeks to further enchant them who were already enchanted; herein, by means of harsh speech directed toward them,
the three heart’s desires of the Lord, the beloved object of their affection, will be fulfilled.

"Even when my indifference is observed, not even a trace of affection diminishes in them; thus, I shall demonstrate the purity of affection in the world. Likewise, in our union, I shall adopt a feigned hostility consisting of affectation—a quality belonging to the heroine of today's drama—as if it were its opposite."
[She thought: "I shall cause these women to accept this courtesy which consists in manifesting a longing for the hero's virtues;

and even upon meeting, I shall create an appearance of the opposite. Thus, she [perceived] the internal words of those most modest young women, even though they were concealed by their natural dissimulation (*avahitthā*).

Thinking, "I shall listen by means of bringing about a reversal of their natural state," [he observes: although the collection of limbs such as the breasts of amorous women is concealed by clothing and thus hidden, it acts as a source of wonder;
likewise, the internal longing of those women, though covered externally by bashfulness, acts as a source of wonder.
Connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*) consider this; however, even when it is revealed, a certain hero does not wish to see the unobstructed limbs of his beloved heroine as she might desire,
nor does he wish to hear her inner words of longing which are unrestrained by bashfulness, as if they belonged to another man.
Just as he does not wish to see or even listen when in the presence of his own peers and others,

so too Kṛṣṇa— who previously had never seen them— now desires to hear the multitude of internal words of those gopīs, whose every limb was once concealed [by him], yet are now unrestrained in their aversion toward him. For this very reason, even though he is their dear playmate...
It should be understood that he did not, at that time, make [the world] his own companion. ||17||
"—o)0(o— Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! What pleasing service may I do for you? Is all well with Vraja? Tell me the reason for your arrival."

Śrīdhara: Seeing that they had all arrived in a state of agitation, he spoke as if with fear: "O flute-player, [is it well] with Vraja? Vaṃśīdhara replied: "O illustrious ones, has your arrival in the forest been auspicious? Or rather, no; therefore, what pleasing service may I do for you? There is nothing that can be done by me."

All the cowherd women, with agitation, trepidation, and as if with fear, spoke as follows: "Of the Vraja, is there perhaps no affliction—that is, is there an absence of distress? Thus, in response to the expectation and request that they state the reason for their hurried arrival, she said: "But for me..."

"Mahābhā-rūpā" means those whose form consists of my great fortune, or "mahābhā" refers to Rādhā, she who possesses great luster (ābhā) and beauty; they go to her with the disposition of friends—thus [it is said]. Alternatively, "mahā" refers to Rādhā, who is honored (māhyate) by me; those in whom her radiance (bhā) has arrived are "mahābhāgāḥ. Thus, your beautiful arrival has occurred.

Perceiving the fear regarding their husbands and others who had gone to Vraja, He said: "May there be well-being—that is, freedom from fear—for you and for Vraja, those belonging to Vraja. You are weary, deluded by Māyā, and asleep; tell Me the cause of your arrival, which has been suspected. Or rather, [tell it to] Me, whose very nature is that which wards off (araṇa) whatever brings suffering (kaṃ) upon arrival."
The hidden meaning is: "Engage in some conversation. ||18||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: First, He expresses acceptance: "Welcome" (*svāgatam*) signifies acceptance with great joy, as if saying, "You have come well. "O fortunate ones! What dear service may I perform for you?"—what should I do that is worthy of your affection? "In this matter, I am like one in debt"—this is the expression of acceptance.
Thus [he speaks]. He states their indifference with the words "of Vraja," etc., [saying]: "Tell the reason for your coming. (18)
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Initially assuming a state of indifference, he speaks with respect:
"Welcome. The meaning is that your arrival has been auspicious; or alternatively, in the question "Has your arrival been well? [he says] "Great is the portion," meaning good fortune.
This is an address to those women whose characteristics are devotion to their husbands and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is: "What can I do that is pleasing for you?
Indeed, I am unable to do anything. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Tell me what I should do. By serving the beloved feet of these highly fortunate ladies, even my own [life]—
"Things are called *bhāvas* because they are destined to become specific states (*dharma-viśeṣa*). Previously, this was said even regarding the wives of the sacrificers;

however, there, having shown respect by saying 'Please be seated,' one could only say 'What can I do? and thus there was merely indifference. But here, through the double entendre (*śleṣa*) 'What is dear [to you]?', there is also a state of longing."

This is the distinction. In reality, however, having seen their arrival in such a manner, he spoke with supreme affection, saying "Welcome," and so forth. He addressed them as "highly fortunate ones" (*mahābhāgāḥ*) because they had come to him alone, having abandoned everything else, and because he himself was surrounded by various beloved people.

By reflecting on the absence of such [self-centeredness], and with the intention of expressing the greatness of His love even toward Himself, it is said that "partaking" (*bhāga*) here means "devotion" (*bhajana*). Therefore, being completely under the sway of their love, He says, "the Beloved" (*priyam*).
And this is entirely natural for one who is the crest-jewel of the clever, being adept at captivating those dear to Him; such is the direction of the argument.

Thus, in this very manner, as well as in other instances, the actual meaning—beginning with "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) and ending with the word "iti"—is to be understood. Immediately following that, however, [the meaning] consisting of jest and so forth is to be understood. For instance, by means of a jest such as "Welcome," one speaks to those who have arrived, relying as it were upon the conventions of good conduct.

Having spoken what was appropriate, she saw that they had all arrived simultaneously in a state of agitation; then, she herself also, as if with feigned fear and agitation, asked regarding Vraja: "Is there well-being? Is there auspiciousness?"

"O Caturasiṃha! If that is so, then would not the cowherds and others also have arrived? "True. "In that case, surely some trouble regarding women must have occurred for someone," he said with great pomp, as if suspecting such deceit, "Speak! [Tell me] the cause, the reason, or the purpose of your own arrival."

Alternatively, not having determined the intended meaning of those words, and out of shame upon seeing them [the gopīs] remaining silent, he asks with a sense of agitation—as if suggesting that they say nothing because of the force of their grief, or because inauspicious things should not be heard—and as if raising some other topic entirely: "Of Vraja... and so forth. Thus.

One should understand that even the initial apprehension and so forth were all merely a pretense; nevertheless, observing them with serene faces while they remained silent, he acted as if ill at ease and spoke with feigned modesty: "Speak!
The meaning is: "Let my own improper conjectures be; you yourselves must speak."
In this context, it has been stated that each individual speech consists of both equanimity (*samupekṣā*) and earnest entreaty (*samprārthanā*);

therein, its nature as equanimity has been elaborated upon, and now its nature as earnest entreaty is being described. This very point, by way of double entendre (*śleṣa*), is to be applied to every subsequent verse. For instance: "O you of great fortune! Great... [and so on].

"Fortune is the lot of those for whom there is such a moonlit night, and even in that place, such a forest; and even there, such youth and so forth of yours; and even in that regard, this person who follows you is so favorable—this is indeed great fortune.
Thus, he speaks the "stairway of prayer" in the form of a question regarding what is desired: "Kaccit vo," meaning "Is it well with you? etc.
He utters a request for their welcome: "What dear thing may I do for you? The meaning is that whatever dear wish is in your hearts, that alone is what I must pray for.
Seeing them speechless there, he speaks again from another perspective to offer a prayer: "Of Vraja... and so forth.
He expresses a request: "Speak! The sense is: "Do not be ashamed. ||18||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: First, assuming a posture of indifference, he says respectfully, "Welcome. The meaning is that your arrival has been auspicious; or rather, have you come well? It is a great fortune and good luck for me.

This is an address to those women whose characteristics include devotion to their husbands (*pātivratya*) and so forth. Therefore, "what dear service may I do for you?"—the meaning is that I am unable to do anything at all; or else, the meaning is: "Please command what I should do. By performing what is pleasing to those of great fortune, my own [merit] also [increases].
The term "bhāvas" refers to those things that are destined to possess specific qualities (*dharma-viśeṣa*). All of this leads to a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*) by its very nature.

In the world, such questions generally proceed out of respect; for this very reason, it was said in the same manner previously even regarding the wives of the sacrificers (*yajñapatnī*), solely because of their status as Brāhmaṇīs.

"Please be seated out of great respect"—this is the specific distinction, for these women are by their very nature dear as the inhabitants of the cow-pen (*vrajāṅganā*). Alternatively, by the direct verbal expression "What is pleasing to you?
he indicates even greater indifference toward them than toward those [other women]. In reality, however, it is these [cowherd women]...
Seeing their arrival in such a manner, He spoke with supreme affection, saying, "Welcome," and so forth.

He addresses them as "O highly fortunate ones" (*mahā-bhāgāḥ*) with the intention of highlighting their extraordinary good fortune, which surpasses even that of Mahālakṣmī due to the *rāsa*-pastime; or rather, because they have come to Him alone, having renounced everything else out of exclusive dependence on Him.
Because they lack such [greatness], he spoke with the intention of expressing his own superiority even over them. Therefore, being under the sway of their love, he said: "The Beloved.
And this is natural for one who is the crest-jewel of the clever, being skillful in winning over those dear to him.

This is the general direction. For this very reason, there is a distinction regarding these [wives] because they are mentioned as "the wives of the sacrificer" (*yajñapatnī*); thus, it is indeed appropriate that [the mantra] says "what is dear to you" (*priyaṃ vaḥ*).
In this context, it has been stated that each individual *vāk* consists of both a sense of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and a sense of prayerful entreaty (*samprārthanā*); therein—
The state of being composed of equanimity has been elaborated; now the state of being composed of longing is expressed by means of paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
For instance: "O highly fortunate ones! Welcome to you, for whom there is great fortune (*mahābhāga*).
Since you are so highly fortunate, here is such a moonlit night (*jyotsnī*), here too such a forest, and here too such a companion."
"This person is favorable toward you, and even in that regard, such [qualities] as your fresh youth and so forth—this is indeed great good fortune!

Therefore, I shall do something pleasing for you. Or rather, the word "vaḥ" (for you) connects with the final word [of the verse]: "What desired thing of yours shall I do? I will accomplish whatever [you wish]," even though...

In the expression of a double meaning (*artha-śleṣa*), consistency with the literal sense of the syllables is not strictly required; nevertheless, we shall strive in some way to please the wise and the virtuous. Having thus spoken what was appropriate to those assembled according to the custom of the conduct of the good, they all arrived together in a state of great excitement.
Having observed this, he himself also asks with feigned fear and agitation: "Of Vraja... [meaning] well-being or auspiciousness. "Kaccit" is used for inquiry.
[The interlocutor objects: "But, O Lion among the Wise! If that were so, the cowherds and others would also have arrived. [He replies: "True."

Then, as if suspecting out of craftiness that some demons or others might surely cause trouble regarding women, she spoke with haughtiness: "Speak!"—referring to the reason, cause, or purpose of her own arrival. Alternatively, they remained silent due to shame, because the intention behind her speech had not been determined.

Having observed them, and thinking they were either unable to speak due to the force of their grief or that it was improper to hear such inauspicious news, he—as if conceiving some other thought and appearing somewhat distracted—asks: "Of Vraja?
Thus, it should be understood that all subsequent doubts and so forth are merely feigned; nevertheless, they remained silent.
Beholding them with serene faces and manifesting his own consolation, he said as if with modesty: "Speak.

The meaning is: "Since the cause for all of you coming here to my side during these nights is likely due to the ill-timed rain caused by Śakra and the like, and because it is difficult for me to conjecture, you yourselves must speak."

In reality, this is merely a playful jest. And this is the underlying meaning of the pun: moreover, by your very arrival, the welfare of Vraja is manifest. Therefore, tell me something—what shall I say to you, who have made my coming (*āgamanakam*) itself your refuge (*araṇam*, i.e., *śaraṇam*)? By me...
The meaning is: "What will you do with this conversation? Alternatively, since indeclinables have multiple meanings, it means: "Tell me something. ||18||
The sequence of composition consists of the successive exchange of greetings and responses, beginning with "Welcome" and so forth. ||18||

Prīti-sandarbha 332: A dialogue consisting of a statement and a reply is known as *saṃlāpa* (Uṇādi-sūtra 11.85). An example of this is: "Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones," and so forth, up to: "It is evident that you are born to remove the fear and suffering of Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.41). Here...

Among the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the first meaning consists of His request for their company, even though they were acting with resistance while enchanted by the flute and other instruments. The second, however, consists of His refusal of their company and the inquiry into the reason for His arrival, intended as a jest and to test their true disposition.

In the same way, even in their words, there is the form of rejecting that request; for this very reason, because they consist of mutual and equal cleverness, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is nourished to an extreme degree. "Welcome" is exactly the same in both cases. (18)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therein, first, having expressed his acceptance, He says "Welcome," and so forth. O highly fortunate ones! O you who possess supreme good fortune! "Welcome" means you have arrived with ease; "what dear service may I do for you? means what pleasing act, appropriate to your affection, may I perform for you?

"Even though I am the Lord, I am indeed unable to act [independently]; therefore, I accept that I am like a debtor to you. He speaks from a position of neutrality: "Is all well with Vraja? Tell me the reason for your coming;
for what purpose have you arrived? Speak of that. (18)
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Then, for the purpose of examining their inner disposition (*bhāva*), He spoke such words as "Welcome" and so forth.

In Vraja, there are five kinds of gopīs: those who are eternally perfected (*nitya-siddhāḥ*), those perfected through spiritual practice (*upāsanā-siddhāḥ*), those in the form of sages from the Daṇḍaka forest, those in the form of the Vedas (*śruti-rūpāḥ*), and celestial nymphs (*devāṅganāḥ*). [This is] in order.
With two verses each, the Leader of the separate groups replied: to the *nitya-siddhas* with the two verses beginning "svāgatam"; to the *upāsanā-siddhas* with the two verses beginning "mātara";
to those in the form of sages (*muni-rūpa*) with the two verses beginning "tad yāta"; and to those in the form of the Vedas (*śruti-rūpa*).
"Service to the husband" [is taught] by two verses; "not leading to heaven" regarding the celestial nymphs [is taught] by two verses.
Thus, there are ten statements. However, indifference, lack of desire, having expectations, and having desire have their purport within a single statement.
Indeed, the first two [types of union] constitute the fourfold [union]; however, separation causes affliction and consists of the latter two.
Enjoyment brings about the cessation of affliction—"O noble ones, welcome to you who possess supreme good fortune;
what is dear has indeed arrived for yourselves. Beyond this, what more [could there be]?

"I shall do what is pleasing to you. The meaning is that there is no need for anything further once [your wishes] are fulfilled. If there is still something lacking, then please command me. Through this special mark of respect, indifference is expressed; we have no particular desire of our own—it is simply the performance of what is dear to you.

The phrase "attainment of a specific quality" (*dharma-viśeṣa-prāpti*) indicates a state of desirelessness. Alternatively, the actual meaning is as follows: "O fortunate ones" (*mahābhāgāḥ*); those who possess great *bhāga*, that is, good fortune (*bhāgya*). Or, those who possess great *bhāga*, that is, devotion (*bhajana*). Or, she who is both great and [fortunate]... [the text continues].

"Joy has come upon them": because a special brilliance has arisen in the faces of those who have arrived by abandoning their husbands and others, since they have come disregarding all obstacles. "Welcome to you"—welcome to you who have come to your own place, your place of delight. "What dear thing may I do for you?"—what pleasing service may I perform for you?
They arrived immediately after hearing the sound of the flute; thus it is indicated that "this was well done.
It is further suggested that from now on there will be enjoyment according to their desire. Therefore, their state of expectancy and their possession of longing are indicated.

Having thus rejoiced in their arrival and perceiving their agitation, He said: "Of Vraja" means of your own dwelling place; "well-being" (anāmaya) means free from calamity, which is to say, auspiciousness. The word "anything" (kiñcit) is used as a gentle inquiry; for if there had been any calamity for everyone, then all the elders and youths... [would have returned].
Observing that the children felt shame at having come to him in such a state of illness, he spoke to dispel it:

"Tell me, speak the reason for your coming; if it is something within my power, then I shall provide a remedy. If not, then understand this and depart. In this matter, I have no self-interest, nor is there any desire on my part."

By means of indirect indication (*vyañjanā*), he expresses the actual meaning: "Is there some well-being, health, and absence of affliction for everyone in Vraja, including you, your husbands, sons, and so forth? Having raised such a doubt through a previous question, I employed a particular cleverness (*cāturya*) in such a way that it was as if someone had said: "There is no one."
Regarding the phrase "he will not come here": if there is doubt, speak; to those who do not speak due to hesitation, he says:

"Tell the reason for coming—the specific desired object that is the cause for your arrival. Speak all of that with your own mouths, by which longing for pleasure you have come; I shall [fulfill] all of that."
"I shall accomplish it.

Or rather, having ascertained the absence of distress through inquiries after his health, through his affection, through his remaining silent, and through the serenity of his countenance, he said: "Regarding the purpose of your coming, and likewise whatever happiness [you may have found] in coming..."

Tell me that which is your non-conflict (*araṇa*), your refuge (*śaraṇa*), and your support (*āśraya*). Or else, tell me what happiness you find there through your arrival and your staying—that non-conflict, that refuge, that place—so that I may provide for it accordingly. Tell me whether you will sport in the forest, on the sandbank, or in the water; I shall arrange it just so.
The meaning is that, by way of figurative expression (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*), it is like an echo fulfilling one's desire;
thus, its state of being dependent and its state of having desire are demonstrated. ||18||

Viśvanātha: Now, regarding the meeting of men and women who are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), this is the manner of that flavor: men manifest their eagerness for sexual union, while women are intolerant of it and become angry.
Therefore, first adopting that very manner of flavor, Kṛṣṇa says: "Welcome to you all."

"Has your journey been pleasant? The sense is: since you are so highly fortunate that from birth onwards you have never once beheld the face of suffering. Or rather, this is not a question, but a response; therefore, your auspicious arrival has occurred today."

"What has come here has been well done; for, O highly fortunate one, all actions of those possessed of good fortune indeed bear fruit and become sources of happiness for both oneself and others—this is the sense.
Therefore, what pleasing service may I do for you? Now, in this lonely forest at night, by a youth alone..."
"Tell me what hospitality pleasing to you young women I might be able to perform;
since I desire to do what is pleasing to you, you should kindly and candidly express your own wishes, so that I may proceed with them without any doubt. This is the intended meaning.

And then, [she says]: "O you great reckless libertine! Since you dare to speak thus even to us, who are devoted wives, do you not fear both dharma and the king? When he, failing to receive a fitting reply, implies the meaning of bodily union by saying, "What can I do for your pleasure?"—[she speaks].

Having observed that silence alone is characterized by social convention and rooted in shame, the Blessed One reflected: "If these women do not today accept their own appropriate bashfulness, then I too must not manifest my own appropriate eagerness; rather, it must be mingled with bashfulness."
And just as in the variety of sexual union (*sambhoga-bheda*), even the reversal [of roles] is beautiful during the act of union (*samprayoga*),
so too in the variety of sexual union, let even the reversal be beautiful during the meeting (*sammilana*). However,
this is due solely to their extreme helplessness arising from drinking the intoxicating wine of the sound of the Great Enchanter’s flute.

Considering that there is a reversal of one's natural disposition, and therefore, out of courtesy, I must outwardly manifest a feigned aversion simply to comply with him— since I lack any actual helplessness— whereas inwardly there remains a natural longing, and so forth; and thus, in order to ascend the path of feigned aversion...

He asks with fear and agitation: "Of Vraja? The sense is: "I do not know if all is well and auspicious in Vraja; is there currently some calamity caused by Indra or others in Vraja, such that all of you have come to me in fear, having been driven away for the sake of your own protection?"
And then, while they were speculating among themselves with smiles and looks of wonder, "What is this wave of his roguery today?", [the speaker said]:
"Ah, it is understood by your very silence; if there is no trouble, then tell me, for what purpose have you come? As for me—"
The sense is that [he] is not capable of inferring [it]. ||18||
"— O slender-waisted ones, this night is of terrible form and frequented by fierce creatures; return to Vraja, for women must not remain here."
Śrīdhara, observing a gentle smile born of modesty, said: "This is the night. (19)

Vaṃśīdhara: The "gentle laughter" (*mandahasita*) refers to the smiles of the cowherd women. This night, though it delights those who are licentious, is the very form of that which causes fear to the terrible;
thus he says: it is frequented by "terrible creatures," such as tigers and the like. Or else:

Or perhaps they are *rākṣasīs*, fierce beings because they roam at night; or they are women of timid nature; or else, this place is frequented by us, who are fierce beings carrying staffs and blankets. "Sumadhyamāḥ" means those with slender waist-regions. The intention of the Buddha's address is that they are not fit for cowherds.
This is primarily a prayer; the intention is: "Abandoning them, serve me.

The second meaning is as follows: She is like the risen full moon, enchanting to people, yet of terrible form. Yogis, whose nature is non-terrible (aghorasattva), have resorted to her because they are free from the crowding of common folk. Therefore, do not go toward Vraja.
One should remain here; let others indeed stay elsewhere. Women must not remain by my side, because, having observed celibacy from childhood, I have avoided association with women. ||19||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Regarding prohibition, he states an injunction: "This night is of terrible form," and so forth.

This night is frequented by fierce creatures; therefore, this night is fearsome, and for that reason one should not remain here. "Go to Vraja"—this is the prohibition against staying. In that very place...

And the meaning is injunctive; for instance: "This night is of a non-terrible nature, frequented only by non-terrible creatures such as deer and the like, but not by tigers and the like. Return [to] Vraja, do not stay here, O slender-waisted ones! By you women—who are like the very personifications of beauty (lakṣmī)—[this place is to be avoided]."

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Anticipating their argument—that this [act] is directly perceived—he confirms it: the sense is that, therefore, it is not proper for noble women to go outside to the forest and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If many [women] go together, it does not entail fault; and even if it were to entail fault," [then...]

"Is there no such night even in Vraja? To this he replies: "Terrible," etc. Here, in this forest alone, her form is terrible, which means there is the manifestation of a nature characterized by *tamas*; it is not so in Vraja because here she is without assistance, whereas there she has great assistance. Likewise, here she is intensely frequented by terrible creatures.
And [the place] is pervaded. Therefore, saying "go back toward Vraja," he says "no" with the intention that you should turn back and go, for delay here is not appropriate.
But then, how is it that you remain here? To that he replies: "by women. But not...
The implication is that men of little strength are like women. Furthermore, O slender-waisted ones!
By the maxim that "where there is beauty, there virtues dwell," it is not fitting for you—who are both beautiful and virtuous—to remain here; this is the sense. The rest has been stated by them.

Or rather, suspecting their presence through a pretext—thinking, "O crest-jewel of connoisseurs! Surely we too have come here to sport or to gather flowers and such, just as you have"—he says: "The night," etc.
This is indeed the night, and not the day.
"Surely, O night-dwellers! What fault could there possibly be in that? To this he replies: "Terrible...
O lotus-eyed one! This night is full of moonlight. To this he replies: "Abounding in terrible creatures... By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), [the meaning is]:
you, being many and moving in groups, go toward your own husbands who are staying there in Vraja; abandon them and [unite] with the solitary one.
"Because I am unable to act kindly toward so many [creatures], I cannot remain here"—this is a particular kind of jest.
"But, O best of timid ones! We have no fear of these fierce creatures."
To this, he says: "O you of beautiful waists!"—that is, O you with slender waists!

The implication is that for these delicate women with thin bodies, there would indeed be fear of those who are more powerful. In reality, however, this is intended to manifest their own state of emotion (*bhāva*) toward him, and to increase their longing through playful jesting.

And this has a double meaning (*śleṣārtha*); he says [the following] in the first half-verse so that she does not turn back from her own desire due to the apprehension of danger: "This night, which delights people because the full moon has risen, is of terrible form," and so forth; the sense is that therefore no one will come here. Therefore, in this place...
You should remain in the very presence of me, the Hero;

or else, with a non-terrible form due to the departure of darkness, through the attainment of mutual friendship by virtue of the inherent nature of Vṛndāvana, you should dwell among all living beings who are themselves non-terrible and incapable of causing fear.
Because this moonlit night is nearly at its end, it is frequented only by non-terrible beings such as bees, cuckoos, and the like;

or else, "Aghora" refers to one whose *sattva*—meaning strength—is not terrible (*ghora*), that is, not producing fear for the wicked when the letter 'a' is separated [from *ghora*], or rather, not causing fear to anyone at all. By me, who possess such a nature.

The phrase "niṣevitā" (frequented) is said for the purpose of consoling the young women; having heard this, she looks back with a smile at her friends standing behind her and replies with the second half [of the verse]: "Therefore, by all means, do not go toward Vraja;
you must remain right here. Why? Because of women—for those of the female gender...
The meaning is that it is appropriate to remain in such a place. Furthermore, O slender-waisted ones!

because of your supreme beauty, it is indeed fitting to remain right here in my presence; this is the meaning according to the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*. This [place] is perceptible. He states its very perceptibility: "terrible" (*ghoram*).

She whose very nature is such, because she is characterized by *tamas*. Furthermore, she is intensely frequented and pervaded by terrible beings—that is, living creatures. Therefore, with the intention that "you must turn back and depart; delay here is not appropriate," he says: "No"—meaning, not in this forest. Moreover, O women of beautiful waists! [O] beautiful ones!
The sense is that it is simply not fitting to remain in this terrifying time and place of fear.
The rest has been clearly suggested by them.
Or rather: "O crest-jewel of connoisseurs! Just as you, so too we [desire] to sport here with flowers and the like."
If it is argued, "We have come to perform [the ritual]," he says in response: "The night. This is indeed the night, not the day.
[Objection: But are we not those who revel by night? What fault, then, is there in that? To this he replies: "Terrible," and so forth.

By its very nature it produces fear, and even there it is frequented by terrible creatures; or rather, O lotus-eyed one! this is a moonlit night. Regarding that, he says: "by terrible creatures. Therefore, women should not remain here in the forest; it is not fit to stay. Thus, return toward Vraja.

Through a pun (*śleṣa*), she says: "You many women, go back to your respective groups—that is, to the multitude of men in Vraja, namely your own husbands. Since it is impossible for me alone to perform the service dear to you all, I cannot remain here. This is a particular form of playful jest (*narma-viśeṣa*).

"O best among the timid! We have no fear of fierce creatures. To this she replied: "O slender-waisted ones!"—meaning, O women with thin waists! The implication is that for delicate-limbed and weak women, there is indeed cause for fear of those who are most powerful.
In reality, however, this was [an expression] of their own internal emotional state.
It is for the purpose of strengthening [her resolve]. Or rather, it is for the purpose of increasing her longing through jesting.
And in the sense of a pun (*śleṣa*), the meaning is that no one will come here because of its terrible creatures and so forth.
Furthermore, this night is called *rajanī* because she delights people, as the full moon has risen.

By the elision of the vowel *a*, she is of a non-terrible (*aghora*) form due to the departure of darkness (*tamas*). Alternatively, she is peaceful (*śāntā*) because of her connection with the month of Kārttika, which is pure, sattvic, and auspicious.
This is the meaning: her fitness for the auspiciousness of the *rāsa* dance.
Furthermore,

it has been inhabited day after day by beings such as your husbands and others who, by performing terrible rites, are fear-inducing; or else, by beings who— due to the very nature of Vṛndāvana— are not fear-inducing at all, having attained mutual friendship.

[By] all living beings; or rather, by non-terrible creatures such as deer, peacocks, and the like, which produce delight; or else, [by one whose] nature or power is terrible, causing fear to the wicked; or rather, [by one whose] nature or power is non-terrible, not causing fear to any people whatsoever—[such is] my [nature].

This is for the sake of comforting the ignorant. Or rather, it is by me—whose very nature is non-terrible, peaceful, and bestowing happiness—that [the path] has been practiced; thus, this is a declaration of one's own cleverness. Therefore, do not return to Vraja under any circumstances.
You must remain right here. Why? Because even there, [you will find] women. He said: "O..."
"O you of beautiful waists! means "by those who are most beautiful. Therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed appropriate for you to remain right here in my presence. ||19||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: This is the night. Even if she has somehow arrived, you must not now go toward Vraja because of the night’s terrible nature and so forth; you ought not to go. However—
"You women must remain right here in my presence; it is fitting for you to stay. By addressing them as "O slender-waisted ones," he further revealed his weariness regarding their departure. (19)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Regarding the injunction [to depart] preceded by a prohibition in the form of a jest, he says: "This night," and so forth. This night is of a terrible nature because it is frequented by fierce beings (sattvas), that is, living creatures;
therefore, return to your homes. Women must not remain here. As for women remaining...

They are not fit [to stay]. Or rather, it is a prohibition regarding staying there, stating: "One must not remain with women; if you do not go, then I myself shall go. The injunction is: "Return home.
Thus, both the prohibition and the injunction, as well as the injunction and the prohibition, are contained right here. This is the night.
She is of non-terrible form because of her clarity like moonlight, and is frequented by non-terrible, peaceful beings such as deer;
therefore, there is indeed an absence of fear here. For that reason, do not return home;
you ladies must remain here in Vṛndāvana. From now on, you must stay in Vṛndāvana alone.

The meaning is that you must not go home. O women of slender waists! Or rather, [you who are] with "strībhyaḥ," meaning by means of these fortunes (ībhyaḥ) among women, or by the fortunes of women. ||19||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: She whose form is *ghora*—that is, whose form is terrible and fearsome due to her *tāmasa* nature; [or] by those beings, that is, creatures, who are *ghora*, meaning fearsome and predatory. She is attended by such powerful beings. Therefore, return toward Vraja; go!

He himself provides the resolution: "O timid ones, women in general should not remain in this forest, let alone young women like you. Addressing them with intentional meaning, he says: "O slender-waisted ones, it is not even appropriate to stay here during the day."

"How much more so for you all at night? Furthermore, seeing that you have arrived, even this night has become terrible to me; if someone were to see me in your company, who knows what might happen? Such a state is appropriate only for one who is desireless and indifferent in a lonely forest."

But seeing your bold arrival while you, who possess slender limbs, were full of desire, even this night— which is by nature a source of delight— has become terrible to me. Because there was no peace for me in consoling you as you gathered in groups, therefore, I, being free from desire and indifferent, [sought] privacy with you.

Staying [there] is not appropriate; desirelessness and indifference are indicated by the word *sumadhyamā*. That which is frequented by fierce beings (*ghora-sattva*) yet also frequented by beautiful women is a marvel—a contradiction characterized by paradox—which indicates the night’s state of being full of longing while still being dependent [on others].

Thus he states its nature as an excitant (uddīpana-vibhāva): "This night, being perceived, causes passion; it is a 'rajanī' [night] suited for those with desire. Of what kind is it? By the elision of the vowel 'a' (*akāra-praśleṣa*), it is "not terrible" (*aghorarūpā*), because it is illuminated by the rays of the moon as if it were day.
Or rather, even though she possesses a non-terrible form (*aghorarūpā*), she is perceived as having a terrible form (*ghorarūpā*) by those such as your husband who are like me;

this indicates that one should roam about without fear, thinking, "No one will come here. Furthermore, [she is surrounded] by beings—living creatures—who are terrible in their essential nature, fearsome in their disposition, yet peaceful.
It is frequented; as it is said in this very context: "Where even men, deer, and other animals dwell together despite their natural enmity.

By this, the absence of creatures that would obstruct one's pleasure is indicated. Alternatively, it means it is frequented by non-terrible beings, such as pigeons, cuckoos, cranes, parrots, and mynas.

This is the demonstration of the excitant factors (*uddīpana-vibhāva*). Alternatively, she was resorted to by one like me who desires another—by one whose strength is truth, which bestows peace upon non-terrible beings and dispels the heat of passion.
Or rather, she was resorted to by terrible, passionate beings (*rājasa-sattva*) such as yourselves, who are great adventurers.
[She] has been served [by you]. Therefore, do not return to Vraja.

If it is asked, "Where should we stay? he says: "Stay here in secret with women. Furthermore, what more need be said? By such indirect suggestion (*vyañjanā*), you—who are supremely clever—have revealed the act of dalliance.
When it is indicated that [the self] is dependent upon its own state of being subject to desire. ||19||

Viśvanātha: Alas, alas! While they were conversing among themselves with sidelong glances, saying, "Having destroyed our shame and other virtues rooted in family dharma, this man who enjoys us every day now draws us near with the sound of his flute and asks for the reason," it is indeed true that—
"Why do you speak with side-long glances cast at the creepers, saying, 'We have come for the purpose of gathering flowers that bloom at night and are suitable for the worship of the gods'?
This is improper, because it is inconsistent with the time, the place, and the person—the word 'night' [being used here].
For this [night], though abundant with moonlight, is of a terrible nature precisely because it is night; thus [it is dangerous] among the roots and tender shoots of the creepers."

The sense is that because subtle snakes, scorpions, and the like are difficult to perceive, this time for gathering flowers is inappropriate. Furthermore, the sense is that because this region of Vṛndāvana is frequented by fierce creatures such as tigers and the like, it too is inappropriate due to its connection with such a time. [Fierce creatures such as tigers... by them...
The sense is that even this region of Vṛndāvana has become unsuitable due to its association with time, as it has been frequented [by others].
Therefore, return to Vraja.
[Objection: "We shall go after resting for a moment"; to that he says: "Women must not remain here."

The sense is that, due to the connection of time and place, although you possess the characteristics of being suitable recipients (*pātra*), such things are nonetheless improper. Furthermore, O slender-waisted ones, you are beautiful young women; and I too am here as a handsome youth. Even though you are most virtuous and I am Kṛṣṇa, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).

Thus, by the authority of the *Gopālatāpanī* Śruti, even if he remains with me as a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), there is no fault whatsoever; the sense is that even so, your mind and my own are indeed untrustworthy.
In this way, the inner longing thus hinted at becomes further clarified by the double meaning (*śliṣṭārtha*). For example:

"If you do not speak the reason for your arrival out of shame, do not say it; I already know it, so listen to the truth. To this he says: "It is *rajani* because it causes passion (*rañjayati*); because it consists of moonlight, it is of a terrible form (*ghora-rūpā*), and therefore [it is frequented] only by non-terrible beings (*aghorasattvaiḥ*) such as deer and the like."
The meaning is that because Vṛndāvana is non-violent by its very nature, it is frequented even by tigers and other such beasts; therefore, one should not fear them here.
Alternatively, one need not fear one's own husband or others here, because this place is frequented by fierce creatures.

The implication is that they will not come here. Therefore, do not go toward Vraja; you should remain here in my presence. Why? [Because] you ask, "What is the use of women?"—meaning, why do you keep only women by your side?
To this he says: "O slender-waisted ones," referring to those women who possess both beauty and youth.
