The meaning is that the central regions become beautiful only by you ladies and not by others;
thus, the meanings of Kṛṣṇa’s words should be understood as consisting of indifference (upekṣā) and expectation (apekṣā). ||19||
Your mothers, fathers, sons, brothers,
and husbands are searching for you, not seeing you; do not feel anxiety for your kinsmen.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "O mothers," they search for and seek out. The meaning is: "Do not cause fear or distress to your kinsmen; do not do so. (20)
Vaṃśīdhara says: He speaks of another point as well—namely, that if they were to remain here, their kinsmen would suffer distress.

To this he says, "And what more? Mothers [would worry] out of affection; fathers out of fear of censure; sons, being children, for the sake of breast milk and the like; even brothers out of fear of censure alone; and husbands out of suspicion of infidelity.

"Bhītiḥ, bhīḥ, sādhvasam, bhayam" [are synonyms for fear], according to Amara. "Do not fail to show the full extent of your goodness (*sādhutva*) among your kinsmen"—the sense is that it is not appropriate for virtuous women to go outside at night. This is the meaning, because [the situation] leads to a state of apprehension (*sādhvasa*).
The intended meaning is that the sense [of the verb] should be expressed through the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending. However, regarding the request, [the Lord says]:
"Do not feel fear or agitation caused by the dread of your kinsmen, thinking, 'They will see us and search for us'; for they are deluded. Moreover, having come here, they might see you by my side."
Then there would surely be shame and fear for both you and me. Not seeing me, they will search for me;
therefore, do not fear your kinsmen. The particle *māṅ* follows both [verbs]. (20)
The Chest of Caitanya’s Teachings: [The devotees] call out, "Mothers! Fathers! to the unmarried girls; "Husbands!

to those who are married; and "Sons! to those whose sons have grown up. Because those with children have departed to other bodies, they search for them in vain, not seeing them; yet they know that those very persons remain right there.

It should be understood that this is solely by my power, because it will be stated later: "The inhabitants of Vraja [returned] to their respective wives" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38). Therefore, the word *mā* ("do not")—meaning "do not feel fear toward your kinsmen"—should be applied to both [parts of the sentence] according to the maxim of the crow's eye or the eyeball. Alternatively, [it may mean] "fear regarding kinsmen."
"You have played, having cut [them down]"; for it is established that the root *kṛñ* means "to injure. The meaning is that there is no fear at all regarding their kin. ||20||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, O lion among men! Anticipating the objection—"What fear can there be for us who stand in the presence of you, the supremely powerful one?"—he speaks with apprehension, beginning with "O mothers. Here, the mention of "mothers, fathers, brothers" was spoken by the young girls upon seeing [the Lord], and is understood as a sign of their maturity.

As for what was said regarding "having seen [them], they are indeed my sons," that shall be established as being merely a figurative expression intended for jest. The word *ca* (and) serves to include what has been stated. The particle *hi* indicates certainty.
Therefore, if at any time even one among them should come here and see you by my side—
The meaning is that both [parties] would then experience shame and fear. Therefore, by remaining here, do not cause me any trepidation or fear regarding my own people or myself;
or rather, O knower of great mantras! they will not come into the midst of this most difficult forest.

Even if they have arrived, they will certainly not see [you]; regarding this, he says: "Do not give rise to fear from the apprehension of some misfortune to your kinsmen due to your failure to reach them, according to the maxim that 'the virtuous are affectionate toward their kin.
Therefore, return out of love for them"—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, in these two verses:

This should be explained by turning back [to the previous context]: "O lady of good conduct, we do not fear anything while staying by your side. Anticipating this, [the sage] says "No" with a gesture, preceded by the closing of his eyes, thinking:
"Women must not stay by my side, for I am one who has observed celibacy since childhood."

The meaning is: "due to the avoidance of association with women. Oh, alas! Indeed, even if there were some fault in the occasional cohabitation of young girls or old women, that might not occur; but you have ascended to the peak of fresh youth—thus he says, "O slender-waisted ones."
"O you who are clothed in great deceit! It is indeed true that our association with you occurs many times over in Vraja;

to this he replies: 'here' (iha). By the specific expression on his venerable face, he indicates the particular fault of being in this secluded forest at the time of dusk (pradoṣe). Therefore, here now, because of your company, my..."

Or, if the reading is *duṣkīrtiḥ* (ill-repute), it means that indeed there will surely be fame; in every respect, [the news] has already spread. Now, [one might object]: "O Supratiṣṭha, do not fear ill-repute, for no one will know of it. To this he replies: "The mothers.
The sense is that they have certainly come here and will surely see [it]. Therefore, [regarding] my kinsmen...

"Do not cause me fear regarding my ill-repute. This is the literal meaning; however, the underlying intention (śleṣārtha) is that she spoke thus in order to lead them to a well-concealed place far from the spot where she was playing the flute, by instilling in them a sense of dread. Furthermore, there is no need to suspect the arrival of their respective kinsmen here, because:
The word "mātaraḥ" (mothers) and so forth; the particle *hi* has the sense of emphasis (*eva*). In this dense forest, they search about while remaining truly sightless, like the blind;
therefore, the meaning is that they will not see [the goal] even by way of many paths. And for this reason, do not fear your kinsmen. ||20||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, O lion among men! Anticipating the objection—"What fear can there be for us who stand in the presence of you, the supremely powerful one?"—he speaks with apprehension, beginning with the word "mothers. First, they are "mothers" due to a particular affection; then, because of that affection and their inability to wander much further in the forest...

And because of the fear of scandal, fathers—due to a lack of special concern regarding their married daughters—become lax; consequently, sons become like non-sons. This is because a particular sense of shame arises due to the mother's fault, whether for the sake of concealing her paramour or to avoid being seen as audacious.

Whether due to childhood or an inability to endure much wandering, when their respective [duties] have become lax, O brothers— because of their natural extreme affection— and even when those [wives] have somehow fallen into laxity due to shame and the like,
the husbands certainly seek them out, since they share in the merits and faults of their wives. While they are thus searching for them...
Since there is a progressive superiority [of the deities], by that [succession] the arrival of the lords is necessarily intended.

Alternatively, they remain as they are, some as mothers and some as fathers. Or rather, by the very reasoning already stated, due to affection and so forth, some are mothers and some are fathers; thus, all of them are present in various places.
Not seeing them thus, they search for them in houses or in forests; not looking [directly], they seek them here and there.
"Hi" is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*).
Therefore, if at any time they should come here and see you by my side, then—of you...

The sense is that there would surely be shame and fear for me as well. Therefore, by staying here, do not cause me anxiety or fear regarding my own self and my kinsmen; or rather, O master of great mantras! they will not come here into the midst of this most inaccessible forest.

"Even if they have arrived, they will certainly not see [you]. To this he says: "Because you have not reached [them], do not cause fear or apprehension among your kinsmen through the suspicion that some misfortune may have befallen you;
for it is a rule of conduct that the virtuous are affectionate toward their kin. Therefore, turn back out of love for them"—this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, suspecting that [the sages might think], "O observer of noble vows, we who stand by your side do not fear anything from anyone," he speaks with dramatic gesture while first closing his eyes—the meaning being: "Women must not remain here by my side, because I have avoided association with women through lifelong celibacy (ābāla-brahmacārin). Oh, alas!
"O Śiva, Śiva! It is said that for children or even for the elderly, no fault whatsoever can possibly arise from association;
yet you have ascended to the peak of fresh youth," thus she says, "O lady of slender waist.
[To this he replies: "Indeed, O master of great deceit! Your association with us occurs many times within our homes."
Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this place. Here, by the specific phrasing of her venerable face, she indicates the particularity of the time as being at nightfall in this desolate forest.
Therefore, thinking, "Now, through association with you here, my ill-repute will surely be widespread," she has departed altogether.
"O Supratiṣṭha, do not fear ill repute on the grounds that no one will know [of it]"; to this he replies with the word "mothers.
The implication is that they have surely come here and will certainly see it. Therefore, do not cause my kinsmen to fear for my ill repute; or rather, your mothers and others [will see it].

Fearing that you might come to my side by departing from your homes and so forth, they will search for me everywhere, not seeing me there; the meaning is that, being in my vicinity, they will certainly find me. Then, when they have arrived here and see me accompanied by you, they will [speak] ill of me on account of you because of the ill-repute caused by you.

The meaning is: "Have fear of my kinsmen who are angry with you. The rest is the same. In reality, however, he confirms for them the absence of fear from those [kinsmen]; this is the general direction. And this is the sense of the *śleṣa* (punning) construction; for the word *hi* is used here in the sense of *eva* (indeed). They search while truly not seeing, like the blind.
Therefore, the meaning is that even by searching many paths, they will certainly not see [you]. Alternatively, the word *hi* is used in the sense of *api* (even).
"Searching like the blind, though not seeing—what [can they do]? By way of a rhetorical question (*kāku*), the meaning is "certainly nothing.
Since you have provided them with assistance, do not fear those relatives. ||20||

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. Regarding the *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): He says "O mothers" to indicate that one need not fear one's kinsmen while remaining in my presence. Do not feel any trepidation toward your kinsmen, for those [relatives], such as your mother and others, are...

The kinsmen search for him at night without even seeing him; therefore, the sense is that there is no possibility of their coming here. "Sons" refers to the sons of a brother-in-law and so forth, or the sons of co-wives and so forth. (20)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He states the reasoning for [Kṛṣṇa] having said, "Return home again," beginning with the words "O mothers" and so forth. [The terms] "mothers," "fathers," and "daughters" are addressed to the young girls; "sons" and "well-nourished sons" are addressed to those who are deluded in their respective ways, as well as "brothers" and "fathers. Alternatively, [the terms refer to:]...
Since "fathers" and "sons" are mutually dependent, it should be understood that [the term] "sons" refers specifically to the sons of the fathers.

Just as when it is said, "the father and son have arrived," it is the son of the father who is understood, so too by the word "son" which is in close proximity to the word "father," the half-brother (vaimātreya-bhrātṛ) is to be understood.

By the word "brother" (bhrātṛ), "uterine brother" (sahodara) is also meant. Since they do not see you, they search for you; therefore, do not feel fear toward your kinsmen (*bandhu*). "Do not do so" is the meaning. The argument against returning home is as follows: your mother and others, not seeing you, will not search for you.

"By the power of my *yoga-māyā*, they remain as if they were actually seeing me; the meaning is: 'How will they act? For it will be stated later: 'Thinking [of us] as standing by their side' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38). Therefore, do not feel fear for your kinsmen (*bandhu-sādhvasam*); do not do so—the negative particle *a-* is to be elided."
In the absence [of other words], the negative particle *na* (or *naḥ*, *naḥ*)—that is, the vowel *a* alone—is the expresser of negation. ||20||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: The leaders of the groups who have attained perfection through worship reply with the word "mothers. Although they were married and staying at their mothers' homes, being completely overwhelmed by their affection, they were drawn back by the sweetness of the flute's sound; thus they respond, searching for you out of their particular love, not seeing you in their houses.

They will also come to the forest; then there will be a disruption of the aesthetic flavor (rasa-bhaṅga). Observing their inability to wander through the forests, and fearing a stain upon the family, their parents will also search here and there.
Even though she has been married, because she has not gone to her husband's house, they will search everywhere but find her nowhere.
"If they do not find you, even though they come to the forest, then a great calamity will occur. Considering their mother's disregard, the sons, now grown up, search for her;
perceiving the futility of their wandering, the brothers search, having returned from the houses of their siblings.

Having stayed in the houses of their husbands, they have returned from there and reply: "Your husbands are searching for you; out of fear of the stain upon their reputation, they will search everywhere for the sins of their wives.
The arrival of others is occasional, whereas the arrival of husbands is considered a certainty.
Therefore, if I were to come here, see you in my presence, and then go to the side of the King of Vraja and report it,
I would suffer great shame; furthermore, no one would place any trust in you,
as I am afraid of the ill repute that would result from you.

"There is fear for you because of the stain upon the family; therefore, for the sake of my own welfare and yours, it is altogether improper to remain in the forest. Thus, do not cause anxiety or fear for your kinsmen by wondering where you have gone; do not harbor such fear, disregarding your own well-being."

"What purpose do you have for me, who am indifferent and without desire, by remaining here?"—this is the meaning arising from the literal words. In the case where there is dependence and desire, the meaning arising from the context states:
"Your mother and others are searching for you; they are seeking you. By means of a verbal artifice, he expresses the intended pun: "Let them search! (or "Search [for me]!").
What is the use of searching for them? For I have made such a compact that even though your mother and others see you, they will wander about as if blind;
they will not come here, because passion accompanied by fear does not bestow happiness. Therefore, being free from fear, [come] with me.
It is indicated by the word "dwells" (*viharati*). Otherwise, if I were indifferent, my mother and others might have come here; therefore, this was said for a specific purpose. ||20||

Viśvanātha: Now, it is true that even at night, even in the forest, and even for young women, there is no fault in traveling in groups, nor is it noticed by people; nevertheless, your kinsmen will certainly search for you now out of fear for your safety, so do not cause them distress.

He said: "O mothers!"—[meaning] "They are searching for you," [referring to] the sons there who are only two or three months old, who are not intent on seeking [you], but who cry out while nursing their infants, saying, "The calves and the young ones!
This, too, was spoken by the Blessed One [to illustrate] his own lack of specific knowledge regarding them.

There is no fault here, for it was spoken by one who has already led [them] away. Therefore, do not cause, do not produce, the fear of your kinsmen arising from not seeing you. Alternatively, they will simply search without seeing you; however, they will not see you in this forest which is neither too far away nor too dense.
The meaning is: "Do not fear those relatives; sport here with me at your own will during the night. ||20||
The blossoming forest was seen,
illuminated by the rays of the full moon, beautified by the sprouts of trees swaying playfully in the breeze from the Yamunā.
Śrīdhara: Addressing those who were looking elsewhere with a slight touch of amorous anger, he says: "It has been seen.

It was colored by the rays of the lord of the night, the full moon; it was beautified by the trembling sprouts of the trees, which were shaken by the slow movement—the playful motion—of the breeze that touches the Yamunā. ||21||
Vaṃśīdhara: [Looking elsewhere] The forest! [In a tone of indifference: "The forest has been seen by you.
Of what nature? It is one in which flowers have come forth; thus, a smile is perceived from you.
The implication is that even the forest laughs upon seeing your improper conduct. Furthermore—
Noticing them turning their gaze toward the sky as if to reproach fate, he says: "O Rākā!

Even the Lord of the Full Moon (Rākeśa), having formed a union of singular flavor with the forest, laughs. Again, noticing them facing the Yamunā with great indignation, he says: "O Yamunā! And the Yamunā too...

The meaning is that [the wind] instructs her, under the pretext of shaking the water and the tree-sprouts, "Do not remain here. In another sense, it suggests: "This place is exceedingly beautiful and suitable for a lover; therefore, enjoy yourself there. ||21||
*Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: "The forest has been seen," and so forth.
Having further established the excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) through such qualities as being in bloom and being illuminated by the rays of the moon, [the speaker says:
"Therefore, go from there; do not delay for long. This is the injunction; this is the sense of a prohibition.
Therefore, do not go; you shall go to the cow-pen after a short time, with some delay.
"Serve your husbands"—this should be applied everywhere. Do not serve your husbands, the lords of the house; rather, serve me, your most beloved, for you are virtuous and true.

The accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative; for it is the virtuous who truly devote themselves to me alone. Or rather, [the phrase] "to us as husbands" uses the plural to express supreme excellence and great respect.
Alternatively, the forest was seen as the excitant condition (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), while I too was seen as the objective condition (*ālambana-vibhāva*); that...

"If you are able to go, then go"—this is a sarcastic statement. Up to the words "duhyatā" (let her milk) and "bālāś ca" (and the young girls), it should be understood that these refer to women belonging to another. Even though she has seen me, her attachment to home and so forth has not yet vanished;
thus, by manifesting a desire to depart that does not even exist, she taunts him out of curiosity.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, their looking elsewhere due to the anger of affection (*praṇaya-kopa*) is imagined otherwise; the connection with what follows is that "that which was seen has gone. Visibility is expressed by the qualifiers beginning with "in full bloom" (*kusumitam*). In that regard, when the forest is gazed upon due to a slight anger of affection, it was seen.
It is said that "the forest" refers to what is seen above; "stained by the rays of the lord of the night (the moon)" refers to what is seen below;

and "the Yamunā" refers to what is seen on the banks of the Kālindī—thus it should be discerned by them. Or rather, since they have been disregarded by us through the transgression of the words of Mahāmohana and others, how can there be any fear?

Then, having reflected for a moment with feigned deliberation as to what the purpose of coming here at night with such effort might be, he said: "Ah! I understand; by good fortune, you have come on this night of the full moon to behold the splendor of my Śrī Vṛndāvana. Let it be so."

Pointing with his finger and so forth to show that it was indeed accomplished, he said playfully: "It has been seen. The meaning is the same as before. In reality, however, by directly pointing out such things as the forest, he increases her very emotion (*bhāva*). And this has a double meaning (*śleṣa*): not only is there an absence of fear of him here, but moreover—
He himself demonstrates, for the purpose of illuminating this state, that it is also a treasury of supreme bliss: "It has been seen.
The syntactical connection is: "Such a forest, endowed with all virtues, has indeed been seen; therefore, do not go to the cowherd settlement. (21)

In the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*, perceptibility (*dṛśyatā*) is expressed through such qualifiers as "in full bloom" (*kusumitam*). Alternatively, it should be understood that by the Yamunā’s glancing at the forest due to a slight pique of love, she is personified as the river Yamunā herself. In that context, through her association, there is coolness (*śaitya*); through her playfulness (*līlā*), there is gentleness (*māndya*); and through the forest being in full bloom—
The three qualities of the wind—namely, that its fragrance is inherent—are to be inferred; the others have been manifested by them.

Or rather, if you should ask, "Why should we fear, since we have already disregarded those [objections] by transgressing the words of the Great Deluder (Kṛṣṇa) and so forth? then, by such an effort, at night...

"What could possibly be the purpose of his coming? he thought for a moment with feigned deliberation, and then said with a display of conciliation: "Ah! I understand; by good fortune, you have come on this night of the full moon to behold the splendor of my illustrious Vṛndāvana. Very well, that purpose is already accomplished."

Or rather, if you should ask: "Surely we have come here to experience the moon of Śrī Vṛndāvana and the pastimes of sporting on the banks of the Śrī Kālindī, having disregarded the bonds of home and so forth; so why should there be any fear?"—this is true. Nevertheless, [consider] that supremely beautiful Vṛndāvana, the moon risen therein, and likewise...

Thinking, "By good fortune, this vision of the graceful movement of the breeze sporting upon the beautiful Kālindī has indeed been attained," he spoke playfully while pointing with his finger and so forth, saying, "It is seen. The meaning is the same as before; however, in reality, by directly showing such a forest and so on, it was indeed [for the sake of] desire.
[The word] "vivardhayati" [means] "increases. And this is for the sake of a pun (*śleṣa*): according to this interpretation, it is seen by two [means].
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Such a forest, endowed with all virtues, has indeed been seen; therefore, do not go to the cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*).
Alternatively, even though such a forest has been directly seen, a delay during the night's dalliance is improper.
"So be it; let us go to the banks of the Yamunā, which are suitable for that. ||21||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Prīti-sandarbha 332: By showing her own pleasure-grove, she inflames their emotion, thinking, "The forest has been seen. (22)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Again, [the Lord] says "Go home" or "Do not go"—addressing these two alternatives alone—with the verse beginning "The forest has been seen," etc., consisting of one and a half verses. That which they had come to see out of a desire to behold the beauty of the forest has now been seen. Of what nature was the forest? It is described by the three qualifiers beginning with "in bloom" (*kusumita*).

Therefore, go to the sound; do not delay—this is the meaning. What is to be done upon arriving there? To this he says: "Serve your husbands. Regarding the word "husbands" (*patīn*), since the etymological derivation is "those who protect" (*pānti*), they should be understood as referring to anyone who protects in whatever manner. Furthermore, they cry out.

And let the calves drink [milk] while they are young; the meaning is that you should milk them afterwards. "Young" (*bālāḥ*) is an adjective qualifying the calves. O virtuous ones (*satīḥ*), O good women! In the alternative [poetic] interpretation, the excitant factor (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) is manifested by the phrase "the forest has been seen," and so forth. Therefore, do not go to the cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*); do not [abandon] your husbands.
"Listen! And let not the young calves cry; do not let them drink [milk], nor milk them—this is the meaning. Do not go away for long; stay right here always—this is the meaning.
The particle *mā* should be joined with each verb. (21–22)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: To those who, through the perception of a meaning derived from words, did not understand the actual reality; who were looking elsewhere by casting their glances upward and downward; and whose eyes were somewhat agitated with excitement, he said:
"It has been seen. Having perceived their excessive reserve, [he spoke] with a slight touch of affectionate anger here and there.
Looking about, and having set aside their initial conjectures upon seeing [him], they thought:

"Surely, having experienced distress at home due to being preoccupied with service to their husbands and others, they have come here out of a longing to behold Vṛndāvana; therefore, let our hearts be satisfied for a moment by the sight of the forest."

He says, "Let them extinguish [the fire],"—anticipating the sight of the forest by his sidelong glance, he speaks as if the matter were already determined. The forest has been seen, and it is in full bloom;
thus, an expression of its extraordinary beauty is indicated.
Looking upward, Manmatha (the god of love) said: "Anointed by the rays of the full moon.

Regarding those glances spreading toward the clusters of trees situated in the region of the Kālindī, he spoke with another imaginative supposition: "By the Yamunā. [The trees] were trembling due to the playful movement of the breeze dwelling upon the Yamunā.

It is adorned by those trembling tree-sprouts; even the trees, deeming your presence here improper, seem to ward you off with their sprout-like fingers, as if filled with longing to see the forest, saying: "Go home from this point onward."

"If I were to leave you here while I have come to look at the forest, it would be improper for me to remain indifferent"—this is the meaning under the view that he is concerned [for them]. However, his intention is actually quite different. If you have come here for the sake of pleasure, then look at this excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*); thus he says: "The forest has been seen. He has seen the forest.

This is a question posed with a suggestive intonation (*kāku*). He qualifies the forest: having seen your arrival, even the forest—as it were—has become thrilled with horripilation due to its own particular state of emotion; how much more so, then, for me?
By this, he indicates the preparation of the bed, the fan, and other such items that will be performed hereafter. The forest...

Of what sort? It is colored by the rays—the hands—of the lord of the night (the moon); even the moon has shown favor toward our beloved through its hands, for by its softness it is endowed with a particular luster.
By this, the brilliance of the forest and its quality of dispelling darkness are indicated.

Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? By the play of the breeze associated with the Yamunā, they cause the trembling of the trees; thus, their swaying leaves seem to teach the shaking of hands. Or rather, as if showing through the coming and going of the forest leaves that such happiness does not exist elsewhere.

The autumn season has been graced by this coolness and by your arrival; even the trees have manifested a state of *sāttvika* emotion through their connection with me. Therefore, since this forest is distinguished by every excellent quality, it is indeed desirable; thus, the intended meaning is that it is improper to go to Vraja. ||21||

Viśvanātha: Then, as they were looking all around out of shame, he said, "It has been seen. [Thinking,] "Ah, it is understood that they have come for the purpose of seeing the forest," and then, when they looked upward, he said, "O Rākā's Lord" (referring to the moon). When they looked toward the direction of the Yamunā, he spoke of the breeze touching the Yamunā.

With her slow, playful gait, she causes the sprouts of the trees to tremble; thus, even the sight of the forest and such—which was desired as being graced by those blossoming trees—is fulfilled for one whose mind is set on this. The sense is: "Do not delay! In the alternative sense (pakṣe), this Vṛndāvana is the most excellent of all, and therein [dwells] the Full Moon.
There too is night; there too is the Yamunā on all four sides;
and there too are breezes endowed with coolness, gentleness, and fragrance—these are the excitants (uddīpana-vibhāvas).
And as for the substratum (ālambana-vibhāva), I am indeed present here; thus today your state of being connoisseurs has been tested.
"It will come to pass," [he said]. ||21||
"—O virtuous women, go now to the cow-pen without delay; attend to your husbands. The calves and the young children are crying; give them milk and milk the cows."
Śrīdhara: O virtuous ones, O truthful ones! ||22||
Vaṃśīdhara: Since your kinsmen fall into fear upon not seeing you, for that reason, do not delay;
go quickly to the cow-pen. Let those calves drink, leave them by the side of the cows, and milk the young ones, filling their own bodies with the essence [of the milk]. This is your divine duty.
The Vedic form *duheḥ* [is used]. In this alternative case, the word *mā* is to be construed everywhere: "Do not go to the cow-pen.

Of what kind? "For a long time," meaning experienced for a long duration. "Do not serve your husbands, since they are asleep. "The calves do not cry; therefore, do not let them drink. And "the children do not cry."
By the phrase "do not harm them either," it is implied here: "Delight yourselves in this very place. ||22||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, because of the sight of the forest's beauty and the fulfillment of his own desire, he causes it to resound—that is, he makes it vocalize—by means of the sounds of high-pitched singing, churning curd, cows, and so forth.
Ghoṣaḥ. By way of pun (*śleṣa*), however, it means "go to that abode of cowherds (*gopāvāsa*) which proclaims (*ghoṣayati*) the conduct of all [the gods]";

in some places, the reading is *goṣṭham*. The sense is that all the necessary provisions for you are right there, so it is fitting to go to that very place. "Do not delay" (*mā ciram*) means "without delay" (*acirāt*). Or else, [the meaning is] "there... [as follows].

"Do not delay"—this is the meaning. For what purpose? "Serve [and] attend upon your husbands. Why? "O virtuous ones!"—O you who are true! Otherwise, there would be a violation of your status as chaste wives (*sādhvī*). Therefore, the implication is that your remaining in the presence of me, another man, is improper.

Now, one might object: "Are not those most wicked ones—who, unable to endure service to You, the Supreme Object of Service, were always full of envy—already abandoned by us? And has not even Your status as a devoted wife been cast far away, having made Your lotus feet the foot-scraper? Anticipating this, [the Lord] speaks another alternative with apparent compassion.

Relying upon [the children], he generates affection for the calves and so forth—as they cry out. Therefore, "make those calves drink" and for the sake of the infants, "milk the milk," meaning "cause it to be milked. And this is with reference to the cows and other animals dear to them, who have been inspired with confidence merely by the presence of each respective person. In this regard, this...
The reality [of this] is as follows: with reference to them, it is said in the *Gopālatāpanī*: "He indeed becomes your Lord";
in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "The beloved of Śrī is the Supreme Person";
there are also mantras such as the ten-syllable one; and likewise, in the Vedas, Āgamas, and so forth, they are called "the wives of Kṛṣṇa" in this very context.
It is understood that for those supreme goddesses of fortune, whose sole beloved is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, marriage elsewhere is impossible;
and it is by Yoga-māyā herself—whom he had previously employed for that very purpose—that he relied upon her to increase their longing, as is evident from that fact. Indeed, she who...

By imagining them to be like him, she considers them her husbands and deceives them; as it will be said: "She was indeed not envious of Kṛṣṇa," and so forth. Consequently, because there was no physical union with them, she remained childless;
yet, solely through a special affection, she nurtured those sons whom her brothers-in-law and others raised.

They are called "sons" because they are conventionally treated as sons in the world and, in particular, are protected as such; for this reason, even with reference to Śrī Baladeva and Sāmba, Śrī Śuka used the expression: "Accompanied by his sons and daughters-in-law, he departed, greeted by his friends" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.68.52).
Therefore, because they lack breast milk, one causes them to drink cow's milk alone; thus it is said, "cause them to drink" (pāyayata) and "milk [the cow]" (duhyata).
For this very reason, the Sage also stated: "causing their young ones to drink milk" (pāyayantyaḥ śiśūn payaḥ) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.6].
Here, he says simply "young ones" (śiśūn) and simply "milk" (payaḥ), but not "sons" (sutān) or "breast" (stanam). And if...

If they were born from their very wombs, then, due to the deformity of those who are the heroines of the *rāsa*-dance and the original heroines of the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*), there would be a corresponding deformity in that *rāsa*-dance and its aesthetic sentiment.
This is evident in the words of the Blessed Lord in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* (10.29.20): "Mothers, fathers, and sons... and so forth.
For some, even at night and in the forest, because they were searching for their mothers and others, a state of being half-old also came upon them; yet that would have been excessive,
and that was not approved by the venerable Vaiśampāyana, who, knowing the proper time, gathered the young cowherd girls together at night.

By this [verse from *Ha.vam.* 2.21.18], the illustrious Śrī Munīndra, while describing the excellence of the excitants (*uddīpana*) of those very forms that serve as the objects of focus (*ālambana*), did not consider [the Lord’s own perception of them]; for in passages such as *bhagavān api tā rātrīḥ* [Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.29.1], he describes the objects of focus through the excellence of their excitants.

Having recollected their exquisite beauty, he set his mind on sporting with them; this is also implied. Furthermore, their exquisite beauty and their relative immaturity in comparison to the Blessed Lord will be described by the verse beginning, "Just as a great emerald in the midst of golden gems" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.7), and by the phrase, "He shone like the moon... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.8).

By the statement, "surrounded by stars" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.43), and by the statement, "like lightning, they shone within that circle of clouds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.8), it is clear that the Lord’s description of them as His daughters is intended solely as a jest, and not as an expression of any fault. Thus, the words [of the Lord] are to be understood.

"Deluding them with His forms" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.17). Therefore, in the verse "Laughing, He spoke to the gopīs with compassion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.18), the nature of His jesting is seen to be even more evident; for otherwise, such talk as "Mothers, fathers, sons" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.20) and so forth would be merely a fabrication.
Furthermore, by the maxim "I both revile and drink [it]," their acceptance would result only in supreme distaste. Let alone their own expression of faults;
even the mere existence of such a defect in the objective support (ālambana) would cause a total destruction of the supreme aesthetic flavor (rasa).

And that [attainment] is possible even in the case of another virtuous leader whom poets have accepted as a subject for description, let alone in the case of Him, the Supreme Person (parama-puruṣottama), who is the object of description for the class of great poets and has descended for the purpose of describing His specific nectar of divine play (līlā-rasa). And it will be said: "He partakes..."

"Having heard of such pastimes, one becomes intent upon them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.36), and "He, having internalized within himself the essence of all the poetic narratives of autumn, enjoyed them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.26). Therefore, even their husbands and sons are perceived as mere illusion.

"Having a secondary meaning"—this is the sense of the pun (*śleṣa*): therefore, because there is an absence of fear from kinsmen and because the complete collection of conditions for delighting in the beauty of the forest exists, do not go away for long, that is, quickly. If you should go...

The meaning is: "Then, because of the delay, you shall go only at the end of the night. Due to the particle *ca*, the word *mā* is connected everywhere even after [the subsequent items]. "Do not serve your husbands," and "do not serve virtuous and faithful wives (*satī-sādhvī*)," meaning that you shall not even attain their state.

"Because of the destruction of the happiness of independence and so forth"—this is merely a jest; "O child, let not the young ones cry," and "therefore, do not make them drink [milk], do not milk [the cow]," thus independence is indicated. ||22||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, because it fulfills one's own desires through the sight of the forest's beauty, it "proclaims" (ghoṣayati)—that is, it makes sound—by means of the loud songs and the lowing of cows used for churning curd and other activities. By way of double entendre (*śleṣa*), it proclaims the entire conduct of everyone.
"Go to that cowherd settlement, Ghoṣa; do not delay—meaning, go immediately—or rather, do not make any delay there. For what purpose? To serve—that is, to attend upon—your husbands.
Why? Because you are *satī*s—O virtuous women! Otherwise, there would be the risk of violating your status as chaste wives (*sādhvī*). Therefore..."
The sense is that your remaining by my side is improper.

Now, it may be argued that those who were extremely wicked and constantly envious, unable to endure your service to the Supreme Being, have indeed been abandoned by us; yet you have made me the *nirmañchanī* (the wiping cloth) for your lotus feet, having accepted me as your wife.

Fearing that [the milk] might be spilled from afar, he takes recourse in another compassionate alternative and generates affection for the calves and others—[expressed by the word] "they cry. Therefore, make those children drink the milk; and for the sake of the calves, milk the cows—the meaning is that [you should do so]. Because there is a particular degree of affection toward the children compared to the calves, for their sake...

The subsequent explanation is as follows: in this way, for the purpose of exclusion, one should infer in every case that each succeeding statement is more significant than each preceding one. The mention of "pāyayate" (he causes to drink) at the beginning is because it must necessarily be performed quickly.
Or rather, O crest-jewel of cowherds! [The cows] will surely cause the calves to drink by means of the cowherds milking the cows.
Therefore he says: "Milk the cows. The meaning is that during the milking, the calves and the young ones themselves will naturally come to drink that very milk.

The truth here is this: those blessed gopīs were exclusively beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; although some among them had somehow undergone marriage, they were "married" to husbands in name only, for under various pretexts they deceived their husbands and, having no sexual union with them, remained childless. Only...

Out of insistence on the part of their husbands and others, or due to their own particular eagerness, some among them nurture the sons of others as if they were their own children; thus, because of their own lack of breast milk, they feed them only cow's milk. In reality, however, all of this is merely in jest; for this very reason, they are called *satīs*.

And this is the sense of the pun (*śleṣa*): therefore (*tat*), because of the absence of fear regarding kinsmen and because of the presence of the complete collection of delights such as the beauty of the forest, do not go for long (*aciram*)—that is, quickly (*śīghram*). If you do go, then the meaning is that you shall depart only at the end of the night with delay.

Alternatively, "mā yāta" means: do not go toward that sound which has been repeatedly experienced for a long time as being ancient and as a source of suffering such as lack of independence; the meaning is that you shall not go there again. Because of the word "ca," the particle "mā" is to be connected with every subsequent clause. [Thus: "Do not serve your husbands, nor [be] chaste wives."
"O virtuous ones, do not serve [us]; do not follow even their path"—this is the meaning.

The phrase "because of the destruction of the happiness of independence and so forth" is merely a jest. Calves and others do not cry at all, since the drinking of milk by cows and so forth is accomplished through the milking performed by cowherds and others. Therefore, you shall not let them drink, nor...
The phrase "you shall not be deceived" indicates your independence due to the absence of any other duty;

or rather, the meaning is that from this point forward you shall no longer engage in duties such as service to a husband. By this also, he says that there is no obstruction to your dharma in any way—addressing them as "satīḥ," meaning "O virtuous women."
Because, in reality, they have no master, and because of their devotion to me. ||22||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.

The *Prīti-sandarbha* (332) concludes: "Therefore, go"—meaning, because this night is of a terrible nature and so forth, for that reason, do not go to the cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*) for a long duration.

"Do not let them go away just now; do not let them depart immediately. Then, having gone there, "do not serve even those whom you have designated as your husbands, thinking 'they are your husbands,' O virtuous ones (satīḥ), you who are truthful and most excellent.
And as for those such as Vatsa and the others, "do not let them cry out; therefore, do not give them milk, and for that purpose, do not milk [the cows]."
And so it is. ||22||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: The previous verse should be consulted.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, with two verses, [the Lord] speaks to the leaders of the group who are in the form of sages: "Therefore go," etc.
If the fulfillment of their desires has occurred through the sight of the forest, then [let them go to] the cow-station, Vraja.

"Go! Surely you have already come after abandoning Vraja; what is the purpose of going there again? To this he says: "In Vraja there will be the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma. Teaching this, he says:
"O virtuous ones (satīḥ), you have come having abandoned service to your husbands; therefore, a loss of dharma has occurred."
The attainment of desire is rooted in Dharma. When Dharma is lost, the loss of desire also occurs; when the milk is lost, the destruction of wealth also occurs;
and by the abandonment of the suckling infant, the loss of the happiness of nursing and so forth also occurs.
Go to Vraja for the sake of attaining these four goals; do not delay for long. Those who have come here having abandoned their husbands, you must serve those husbands.
As for those who have come having abandoned milking, their calves, being tied up, continue to cry out. And those whose infants are still unsated—
"They cry out" means "milk them, cause them to be milked. The children, being unsatisfied, cry out;

[the Lord says,] "give them their mother's breast to drink. This is His own secret instruction: that by staying near Me, who am indifferent to worldly affairs, there will be a loss of dharma and other virtues, whereas for those who have gone there, everything will be attained.
This is the state of being dependent.

Regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) in the verse: "O virtuous ones! O truthful ones!"—because of their affection for the primary husband and because they have come here having abandoned their nominal husbands, their status as chaste women was known previously.

The prohibition was stated as a jest; now he states the actual meaning: "Therefore (*tat*)," for that reason, "do not go to the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*) for long (*ciraṃ*)," that is, for a great length of time; rather, "rejoice right here with me.
Or else, "come to me (*mām āyāta*)," that is, reach me, for a long time; or else, "not for long (*aciraṃ*)."

Do not go quickly to the cow-pen or the settlement, for the faults of going there have been experienced many times, as you returned after suffering the hardships of the night and so forth. Otherwise, that suffering will certainly occur again. If there is hesitation on the part of your husbands and others, then, having first provided full amorous pleasure, [proceed].

"You shall go at the end of the night. The word "mā" (do not) applies to every clause: "Do not serve your husbands," because it has been established that they have repeatedly experienced opposition toward them in my form.
[Objection: But they have come here having abandoned their crying children and infants; therefore, for Rāmaṇa, there is the recollection of them.

If it is argued that [the effort] will be fruitless, he says in response: "The calves and the children do not cry, because their purpose is otherwise accomplished; since the milking of the cows has already been performed by the cowherds, and milk is required for them as well, no concern need be felt regarding the soothing of the children."
Since this has already been arranged by the senior nurse and others, one need not worry about it.

To make the meaning clear, he says: "Do not let those children drink milk; do not milk the calves"—that is, do not have them milked—because that matter is already accomplished of its own accord. Therefore, play with me without any hesitation.
The meaning [is as follows]. ||22||
Viśvanātha: Therefore, do not go slowly, but rather go very quickly; this is the meaning.

Even though they are *satīs* (chaste wives), you should serve them in order to grasp their dharma; the sense is that they too are indeed worthy of veneration. Having thus addressed the married women (*paroḍhā*), she spoke to the maidens (*kumāryaḥ*): "O calves, [of] cows..."
"They are crying out; milk them, cause them to be milked! The one who follows the way of sages said: "The children are crying; give them drink.
Alternatively: "Therefore, do not go away for long, even throughout the entire night, but stay with me."

The sense is: "Enjoy yourselves. The underlying thought is: "Do not neglect your husbands and virtuous wives, for it would be improper to render useless such beauty and youth as have been bestowed by the Creator. Likewise, "do not milk [them] nor cause them to drink"—what use have you, who are devoted to me, for those?
Such is the intended meaning. ||21-22||
or else, because of my great affection, your minds have been restrained;
for you have come here appropriately, as all living beings feel love for me.

Śrīdhara says, addressing those whose eyes are agitated by agitation: "Or rather," etc. "With restrained intent" means with their minds brought under control. "Appropriate" means logical. "They rejoice" means they become delighted. ||23||
Vaṃśīdhara: "Saṃrambha" refers to the onset of anger; by this, their eyes are agitated, meaning their vision is wandering.

Alternatively, the two particles "atha" and "vā" indicate either agitation or auspiciousness. Regarding me as the object, "jantavaḥ" means mere living beings. Therefore, the sense is: "rejoice! ||23||
The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā further states the view of neutrality (tāṭasthya), beginning with "Alternatively" (athavā) and so forth. ||23||

Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: Now, as if to turn back those whose eyes were agitated by fury, [the Lord] speaks, greatly provoking them by pointing out that [His nature] is common to all living beings, beginning with "Or rather" (athavā). This is an alternative view, intended to set aside the previous argument starting with "The forest was seen. "The affection (abhisneha) which [you have] for Me..."

The excellence of the commonality of affection—therefore [it is said]. The specific state of being male or female for the sake of sexual pleasure is not grasped here, because such specificity is absent. For this very reason, he speaks together with indifference: "For indeed, all living beings feel affection toward me. By the direct statement "out of love for me," he includes that as well.
He relaxes [the tension]. For this very reason, she acts out of reverence. As for the other [explanation] by them:

or rather, thinking, "Alas! They have indeed been abandoned; what then is the use of even mentioning their names? he states another alternative with praise, beginning with "Or else" (athavā). This is the meaning.
It is just so. In reality, however, such indifference is intended solely to increase the intensity of the emotion through a clever artifice.
And this is the meaning of the pun: even though they have come for another purpose, nevertheless...

"Rest here for a moment at my request. Having said this, he states another alternative with the word "or else" (*athavā*). By the prefix *abhi*, the perfection of affection is expressed, thereby indicating the very emotion (*bhāva*) known as *rati*. Consequently, if you have come out of deep affection for me, then this [resting] is entirely appropriate.
The meaning is that this is indeed appropriate. The reason for this is as follows: "creatures" refers to all living beings;

"in relation to me" means they take delight in me—that is, they become affectionate toward me. The implication is: what then can be said of those who possess such a state? For this very reason, you [should act] with love and respect.
Thus, the meaning is: "Therefore, now enjoy yourselves with me as you please. (23)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "From that specific affection (*abhisneha*), which is a particular kind of love (*prīti*) toward Me"—by this, the specific state of man-woman relationship known as sweet love (*madhura-prema*) is excluded. For this very reason, he speaks of servitude (*saudāsya*): "Because all living beings indeed feel love for Me. This is because of "affection toward Me" (*mad-abhisnehāt*).
By speaking directly, she also softens him; for this very reason, she addresses him with respect as "bhavatyāḥ" (your ladyship).
Alternatively: "O best of the sweet-spoken! Then let our desire be fulfilled.
To this she replies: "They bring about only joy," because joy is a particular form of devotion (*bhakti*).
The sense is: "Enough with the act of physical contact. Something else has been suggested by them.

Or rather, thinking, "Alas! They have all indeed been abandoned; so what is the use of even mentioning their names? he states another alternative with praise, beginning with "Or else" (*athavā*). This is the meaning.
It is exactly so. Or rather, the meaning is: "by that [love] which you have for me.

By the elision of the vowel *a*, it means "those whose intentions are unrestrained" because of their supreme saintliness (*paramasādhvītva*). Or else, it means "those whose intentions are unrestrained by affection directed toward me," due to their devotion to their husbands (*pātivratya*) regarding other men.
Because of the impossibility of [the object] being the domain of the password. Thus, the distinction of existence has been refuted in both ways; nevertheless, that which has arrived remains.
The rest is the same. In reality, however, such indifference is for the very purpose of increasing existence through the method of the fourth stage.

And this is the intended meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): "Aha! Even though you are so deeply devoted, why do you offer prayers filled with such incitement? To this he says, "Or rather" (*athavā*). By the word *abhi*, which expresses the perfection of affection (*sneha*), only sweet love (*madhura-prema*) is indicated. Generally speaking, all living beings are dear to me.

Therefore, you Gopīs are the most excellent of all, for your intentions are restrained and your minds are brought under control by your intense love for Me. Or rather, even though you were not of your own free will due to fear of your husbands and others, that you have come here because of the cause of your intense love for Me is entirely appropriate; indeed, it is so from every perspective.
Because you possess a distinguished love directed toward me; for this very reason, you are acting with such reverence.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Now, enjoy yourselves with me as you please. ||23||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: "If you have come here of your own accord solely out of love for me, such that there was not even a need for my request, then what you have done is most appropriate," he says—*athavā*.
Thus: "In me, by me. The sense is: if even mere living beings feel affection for me, then that affection of yours, O passionate women, would consist solely of the state of being a lover. ||23||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, [the Lord] speaks in favor of the command "Go back to Vraja" with the words "Or rather," and so forth. "We have not come out of a desire to see the forest and such; we have come solely for the purpose of seeing Him"—if this is said, it is indeed appropriate, for [our presence] is constrained by my affection (*abhisneha*).

[This applies] only to the virtuous, because living beings take pleasure in me; indeed, even mere living creatures take pleasure in me, how much more so you ladies? Therefore, my appearance before you was entirely appropriate. The meaning is: "Go now to Ghoṣa. In the alternative sense: "Your intentions are restrained by your deep affection for me."

We know that they have come from him; therefore, whatever is appropriate from this point forward will surely be fitting. Since living beings take pleasure in me and become truly joyful, how is it that you shall also be joyful? The meaning is: "Do not go forth with a cry. (23)
*Rasikāhlādinī*: "Indeed, having abandoned affection for husbands and others, you have come to serve You because of Your attraction; why then do You turn us away?
Thus they speak, assuming the literal meaning of the words and adopting a harsh tone out of agitation.
He replies: by pointing out that [the situation] is common to all living beings, he reveals his own indifference.
As for the phrase "or else" (*athavā*): if it is asked, "But why, having summoned us here, do you mock us? he says this in response.
"Or else" indicates an alternative position; "you have come here because of your affection for me" is a statement made out of respect.

Because the affection they have for me has drawn away from the affection they previously had for their husbands and others, and because it has been offered to me; therefore, their intentions are restrained and their minds are brought under control. Consequently, due to their supreme chastity, they have not come for the sake of pleasure. Or rather, such is your opinion.
On account of me, they have come here without hesitation, out of affection in whatever manner it may be.

Since their intentions are unrestrained and their minds are not under their own control, for that very reason He teaches the discipline of the mind; for when the mind is disciplined, a special state of devotion toward Me, the Supreme Person, arises.

The sense is that there shall be no violation of their chastity (*satītva*). Previously, when their minds were unrestrained, whatever occurred is now appropriate and fitting for you—those whose intentions and hearts are constrained and bound by affection toward me, in my very presence. For this reason, by anyone...

They are not bound [to him]. Or rather, it is indeed appropriate for you as well; for it is not improper for someone to go into the presence of that person toward whom they have a special affection. Thus, he reveals his own lack of desire [for her].

"Since all living beings, every creature, feel affection for me—that is, they bestow their love upon me—is it not the case that physical contact with them would be improper due to the absence of any purpose?
My state of celibacy has surely been heard by you before; therefore, understand this and depart"—this is the meaning arising from the word *iti*. Now...
He states a meaning that arises from the literal sense: "Or rather, let her go.

Not understanding the prohibition against going to the cowherd settlement (vraja) mentioned in the previous verse, she—appeasing him with restless glances and manifesting her longing—confirms his pleasure in the forest. The meaning of the verse remains the same.

The meaning of the term *bhāva* is indeed distinct from mine; it is free from fear and is called "born of affection. The fourth *bhāva* is named *rati* (love). Therefore, the meaning is: "having attained that. "With their intentions restrained" means those whose *āśaya*—that is, their minds (*citta*)—have been restrained or controlled by me alone. When the mind is restrained, they come of their own accord.

"My mind has embraced your minds like milk and water; only our bodies have not yet embraced one another. Therefore, the thought that 'now all this enjoyment will be accomplished' is appropriate, since you have come; thus it was fitting that you did what was right. Thus he resolved in his mind.

Thus, by my merely awaiting his arrival while previously contemplating this very thought, it has come to pass accordingly; the sense is that there will be enjoyment for as long as I desire. Regarding the appropriateness of the meaning, he says by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori): since even mere living beings (*jantu*), all creatures whatsoever, are dear to me and are the objects of my affection...
They feel affection; how much more so, then, does she, who is a jewel-casket of love for Me? As it has been said:
"O King, who indeed is not possessed of senses? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.2). Thus, the mere possession of senses is the specific qualification for one who desires to attain such affection. ||23||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— For women, service to the husband with sincerity is indeed the highest duty.
That is the failure to provide for one's kinsmen and offspring, O auspicious ladies.
Śrīdhara: He turns [the disciple] away by demonstrating the fear of both seen and unseen [consequences], with the three verses beginning with "Of the master" (bhartuḥ). ||24 ||25||

Vaṃśīdhara states the established conclusion of the scriptures: visible fear consists of things such as royal censure, while invisible fear consists of hell and the like. Without guile—that is, without deception—one’s supreme duty is the protection of one's kinsmen, the kinsmen of one's husband (such as fathers-in-law and others), and one's progeny.

Because it is prescribed by the scriptures; otherwise, one’s welfare would perish—thus the Fully Awakened One said, "O auspicious lady. To serve me, the protector of all, without guile—that is, with sincerity—is the highest, most supreme dharma, because it is the cause of my grace. Indeed, through service performed without guile...

For it is said: "Hari is pleased by one who gives himself [in service]," and so forth. Therefore, one should serve his kinsmen—the gods beginning with Brahmā—through sacrifices and other rites; and one should provide for all beings, both stationary and moving, according to their needs through repeated protection, which for stationary beings consists of the constant sprinkling of water and the like, and for moving beings... [of food and shelter].
The meaning is: "by the giving of food, clothing, and so forth. ||24||
The *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā* states the refutation: "Of the husband," and so forth. "Go! Go!
Let the husbands be served"—this is the injunction. Therein lies the prohibition:
by the singular form "of the husband" (*bhartuḥ*), his own status as a husband alone is indicated; [it refers to] my husband, the Lord of the Three Worlds.

Let service be rendered; for me, service alone is the supreme duty. As it was before, so it remains for you women who are like Lakṣmī herself. Your kinsmen are indeed my own kinsmen—such as yourselves.
[The suffix] *uṅ* is applied after the word *bandhu* to form the feminine. Among those various offspring...

The meaning is: "of those born of noble lineage who have descended together with me. Another meaning is: "mutual nourishment and protection is the supreme duty; that is to say, devotion and the friendship spoken of by Me is the supreme duty. ||24||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might object: "If our love for you is certain, then service to you is also appropriate. Anticipating this, he establishes [the position] through the *Dharma-śāstra* with three verses beginning with "Of the husband" (*bhartuḥ*). Service and so forth are the duty specifically toward the husband and others, but not toward anyone other than them.

And for us, that [devotion] is supreme when compared to other dharmas. But surely even that must be performed by us according to what is appropriate; to this he says: "with no guile" (*amāyayā*). The sense is: in the worship of me, the Supreme Person, there would be nothing but hypocrisy; therefore, even that [worship] would be tainted. O auspicious ones, O virtuous ladies, it is exactly thus.
The sense is that this is what is appropriate for you; and this is an encouragement through deception. In reality, however, it is merely a mockery, because he lacks the highest dharma.
"In this world, only this much is recorded as the supreme dharma for men."
"Bhakti-yoga toward the Blessed One is [attained] by means of chanting His names and so forth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.3.22).
This is because of the words of Śrī Dharmarāja. Furthermore, this has a double meaning: it is not only appropriate on account of my affection, but also—

He says "even for the sake of dharma" and explains it with the word "of the husband. [She serves] with sincerity (*amāyayā*), meaning solely through her own virtuous disposition and conduct, and not by means of being coerced. For that husband alone, service is the supreme dharma, as well as for his kinsmen, and so forth. This is stated elsewhere.

"Since the illustrious Bhīṣma, who knows the supreme dharma, abandoned you, he cannot be established as your husband according to dharma. Therefore, because they are covered by a lack of true devotion, those men are merely husbands through illusion and deceit;
however, since I am characterized by true devotion, I alone am the true husband whom you should serve."
The meaning is as follows: here, the sense is that from childhood onwards, your very hearts are my witnesses;
in reality, however, this very point will be established [later]. ||24||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Service is dharma. And if it is performed with sincerity, with a pure disposition, or with exclusive regard for dharma alone, then it is "supreme," meaning most excellent; this is certain (*hi*).
Likewise, there is service to one's kinsmen, such as mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law, as well as to one's subjects.

For sons, servants, and others, providing for them through service such as following after them and nourishing them is indeed *dharma*. If it is done without guile (*amāyayā*), it is even more so. By the two uses of the word "and" (*ca*), the primary equality of both [types of service] is also indicated.
The sense is: "O auspicious ones! O virtuous ladies! That alone is appropriate for you. Or else, O... [the rest of the address].

O you who possess auspicious fortune! Therefore, the sense is that this will succeed for you alone; and this is merely an encouragement through artifice. Other [commentators] have explained it differently: "Or rather, living beings are indeed pleased; or perhaps it is even appropriate that they have come, but—"
"I would obtain [this] only through the supreme dharma, and not otherwise. Addressing him with the seal of instruction, he says: "Of the husband," and so forth.
The meaning is the same as before; however, in reality, it is merely a mockery born of jealousy, since that [other man] lacks the status of being the supreme dharma.
Even in the second position, it is merely a jest;

for that [state], which is attainable solely through the love accomplished by devotion such as hearing [the scriptures]—which renders the four goals of human life (catur-varga) insignificant—is not attainable through external duties such as service to one's husband. Therefore, the description of that duty as "supreme" is [ironic].
Moreover, it is indeed out of sport. For this very reason it was said in the *Gītā* and other texts: "Having abandoned all duties" (*Gītā* 18.66), and so forth.
And this has a double meaning: not only for the husband, but also for his kinsmen and for those like me.
Service is the supreme duty. Or rather, O auspicious ones! O supreme devotees of Viṣṇu!
This is indeed the duty of other ordinary women, but not yours—who are the best among all classes of women and who are engaged in devotion.

It has been stated thus because of a disregard for one's own duty (*svadharma*), as in the passage beginning: "Having abandoned one's own duty, [one should resort to] the lotus feet of Hari" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.17).
This point, moreover, has already been explained extensively in the *Haribhaktivilāsa* under the characteristics of the *ekāntin* and other sections.

Or rather, [it belongs] to my husband, the Lord of the World. Or again, since he is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), in reality I myself am his husband. Or else, because he protects the cow-pens and so forth from rain and other calamities, I myself am directly the protector of all those residing here; the word *ca* is used in the sense of "also. What more need be said?

"Service to my husband" means service to my kinsmen, such as Śrī Nanda, Baladeva, and others; likewise, service to my subjects, such as Śrīdāma and others, or the servants of Śrī Nanda’s household and so forth; or, in general, service to all Vaiṣṇavas.
Even non-sustenance is the supreme dharma; the rest is the same.

Therefore, let my service be performed with a pure disposition. Or rather, the sense is that since you have come here for this purpose, it is indeed appropriate. Furthermore, even regarding the matter employed for the enjoyment of the nectar of the Śrī Bhagavān—

Many meanings follow from a single word; among them, this meaning takes the form of lordship. Alternatively, he speaks of the ultimate truth itself in the guise of a joke, saying "of the husband" and so on in three verses, [intending]: "Listen to the very essence and the entire secret of Dharma."

For you women of Vraja, service to your husband is unrighteousness and sin; yet, for those devoted to Him, the abandonment of their own dharma— which consists of the acts of devotion such as hearing and so forth— through a lack of guile is a higher form of unrighteousness, indeed a great sin.
Because great calamity arises from engaging in the duties of others, such as service to a husband; thus it is said in the *Gītā*:

"Death in one's own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear" (*Gītā* 3.35). Alternatively, the syllable *a* is Viṣṇu, who am I myself; in me, through illusion (*māyā*), by means of deception consisting in the abandonment of devotion and so forth—
"That which is service to the husband"—the rest is the same.
For those devoid of devotion to the Blessed Lord, all actions result in either futility or the opposite [of their intended fruit]. Thus it is said in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya*:
Of what use are the Vedas, or the scriptures, or the frequenting of sacred pilgrimage sites?
Of what use are austerities or sacrifices to those who are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu?
And in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Revākhaṇḍa*:

"O Acyuta, even that which is unrighteousness becomes righteousness when performed by Your devotees; O Hari, even that which is righteousness becomes sin when performed by those who are not Your devotees."
And this is clearly evident in the *Bhaktivilāsa*, the *Śrīvaiṣṇavamāhātmya*, and other such works. ||24||

The sequence of the argument: Or, regarding the sense of "petition," the phrase "of the husband" (*bhartuḥ*) is used with the intention that he is indeed a false husband; the meaning is that from childhood onwards, [your love] has been directed toward me alone, and not toward him who is your actual husband—thus, "of the husband" is used in a purely figurative sense.
The sense is that because there was no possibility of her falling [into sin] through force due to the maiden's own refusal, Ambā was abandoned by Śrī Bhīṣma, who knew the supreme dharma. ||24||

Prīti-sandarbha 332: Now, as for the objection that there is fault for women in abandoning service to their husband, he says in response: "Service to the husband... Service to that very husband who is free from deceit is the supreme duty, as is service to his kinsmen. But for you, because you have not been enjoyed [by him],...

Since no marital conduct is observed among those being perceived, it is inferred that this has been fashioned by someone through mere illusion (māyā); therefore, there is no fault—this is the intended meaning. ||24||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, that which was said—"Go back to the cowherd settlement, do not delay" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.22)—is stated in accordance with that: "Of her husband," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
In the alternative sense, the meaning is "of me," my husband, because of the use of the singular number. "Without guile" means without deceit.
Indeed, this is certain. O auspicious ladies! For me, my kinsmen, my friends, and my subjects of noble birth, the supreme duty (*dharma*) is mutual nourishment—that is, mutual protection.
Or rather, the meaning of the sentence is that the two—service to me and mutual affection—are the supreme duty.
Therefore, the essential meaning is: "Perform service unto Me alone, preceded by mutual affection.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, for the purpose of inquiring into the inner sentiment (*bhāva*), [the Lord] describes the religious duty (*dharma*) addressed to the leaders of the group who are personified as the Vedas. This is the statement of Brahmā to Bhṛgu in the *Bṛhad-vāmana-purāṇa*:
"The women of Vraja, O son, are indeed the Śrutis;
I am not Ananta because of that, nor is Lakṣmī equal to them anywhere.
[Regarding the word] *bhartuḥ*: service to the worldly husband who provides nourishment for his progeny.
Following that, it is the duty of sons, daughters, male servants, and female servants to perform service as is appropriate.

O auspicious ones! O you who are the very form of blessing! I am not merely a worldly husband; rather, compared to the duties prescribed for women—such as the worship of deities and so forth—service to the husband is paramount.

This refers to the excellence of dharma in general, but not to its superiority over the dharma of the Blessed One; for that [superiority] is not established by my worshiping Him while I am independent and indifferent. He states the actual meaning: "Service to the husband is the supreme [duty] only for ordinary women."

The highest dharma is not for you who are fond of worldly intellect. O auspicious ones! O ladies of beautiful form! For you, the worship of Me alone is the supreme dharma. As for that extraordinary husband who nourishes the essence of rasa, it is I myself; [the service] of worldly husbands and the like—
Because service does not constitute the supreme dharma,

and because they lack the capacity to ward off misfortune from them, the status of "husband" for those [sons] and the status of "kinsman" for their wives are merely conventional; as it has been stated in this very same work:
He would not be a guru; he would not be one's own kinsman;
he would not be a father; she would not be a mother;
it would not be destiny; and he would not be a husband.
"One who does not release one seized by death... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.5.8). Therefore, service to Me is the supreme duty toward My wives;
they are My kinsmen and My companions. Or else, My kinsmen are the Vaiṣṇavas, and [the same applies] to service toward them as well.
It culminates in this: as it has been said, "The virtuous are my heart, and I am the heart of the virtuous;
they know nothing other than me, nor do I [know anything] even slightly other than them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64).

Or rather, if the service of my husband— the protector— which consists of acting for his pleasure, that is to say, delighting him, is performed by you, my beloved wives, without guile and without deception,
then that is the supreme dharma; [otherwise] it is merely the service of an ordinary husband performed by you women without guile.

If it occurs through lack of compassion—that is, through an absence of affection—it would then be a different kind of dharma. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "māyā" refers to both deceit and affection. This is because affection involves an intense attachment to oneself. As it has been said:
"For those whose minds are possessed by sense objects, immersion in Kṛṣṇa is very far away."
"Can one who is traveling toward the western direction (the quarter of Varuṇa) ever reach the eastern direction (the quarter of Indra)?
Furthermore: "Having abandoned one's own duty, [one should resort to] the lotus feet of Hari" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.17).
When service to Me is accepted as one's own duty by abandoning one's own duty, then...
Who indeed would accept that the worship of Me constitutes *dharma* by the mere renunciation of *adharma*?
For it cannot be maintained by anyone that *dharma* arises simply through the renunciation of *adharma*.
[Objection: But is it not heard in worldly tradition that the service of one's husband and others is *dharma*? [Reply: True.

Nevertheless, because it is well known that worshiping Me preceded by the renunciation of one's own duty (*sva-dharma*) is the supreme duty (*parama-dharma*), it is stated in the *Gītā*: "Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone" (*Gītā* 18.66), since this was spoken by Me myself. This is because [the path of devotion] involves the relinquishing of affection for the husband and others.
Therefore, by the evidence of my renunciation, service to me alone is your primary duty;
or else, it is the service of my kinsmen— those who are my companions and friends— which consists of pleasing them through compliance, and thereafter, that of the devoted maidservants as well.

"To bring delight to your minds is the supreme duty. Furthermore, because it is nowhere heard that the practice of any other duty is possible through the abandonment of service to Me, therefore—even though [the Lord] is dependent on others—you must act in a manner conducive to His pleasure; this is an "implied meaning" (arthotthārtha) [derived from the literal sense]. ||24||

Viśvanātha: Or rather—"Alas! These reasons for their coming were imagined by me in vain; now I have understood the true reason," he says: "Their intentions were restrained—that is, their minds were captivated—by that affection toward me which is all-encompassing; therefore they have come. That is appropriate."

The sense is that this success is achieved through the mere gain of my sight; for living beings, even those who are merely creatures, feel affection toward me—this is my innate good fortune, not something acquired through effort. By this, it is implied that you ladies possess only a general affection for me, and do not possess a specific affection characterized by the condition of desire (*kāma*).

In this context, "affection for me" (mad-abhisneha) refers to love consisting of the state of being a lover; for that reason, those whose hearts have been made into a machine— meaning, "I exist as one drawn by the very machine of your minds"—
their coming is appropriate and fitting, not devoid of justification.
The meaning is this: even ordinary creatures feel affection for me, how much more so then you ladies who possess such noble dispositions!

Now, if you think, "We indeed possess deep affection for you," then why do you repeatedly say, "Therefore, go to the cow-pen"? For a person whose heart is full of love does not [drive away] the person who is the object of that love.

One would be able to renounce [worldly ties]. "That alone by which dharma is accomplished must be performed even by those who possess affection for their kin"—this is the doctrine of the scriptures, and thus he says: "Of the husband," etc.
"Supreme" means excellent; "without guile" means not while being unchaste. [This applies] to his kinsmen.
[This refers] to mothers-in-law and others.
Alternatively, since women are the subject under discussion, the meaning is "of you ladies," who are specific women—the beauties of Vraja.
Service to the husband is the supreme duty, not [service to] one's own self; therefore, he...
The sense is that it is not to be practiced. As it has been said:

"One who knows the Dharma should abandon these five branches of non-dharma—pseudo-dharma, the dharma of others, semblance, analogy, and deception—just as one abandons unrighteousness" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.15.12).
Thus:

because I am Viṣṇu and because you are Vaiṣṇavīs, the worship of Me alone is your own duty (svadharma), while any other is merely the duty of another (paradharma). He who, having abandoned all duties, [worships] Me...

The meaning is that the injunction for devoting oneself to Me—preceded by the renunciation of other duties—is expressed in the verse: "But he is the best of beings" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.32). ||24||
Even if he is ill-behaved, unfortunate, aged, dull-witted, diseased, or even destitute,
a husband who is not an outcast must not be abandoned by women who desire their own welfare in this world.
Śrīdhara: *Phalgu* means trivial or insignificant. *Kṛcchram* means difficult to accomplish. *Aupapattyaṃ* refers to the pleasure of a paramour. ||26||
