Vaṃśīdhara: He states that even when a husband possesses such qualities as bad character, it is not proper for women to abandon him—beginning with the words "duḥśīla" (of bad character). "Duḥśīla" means one who is full of quarrels and the like. "Durbhaga" means lacking virility or devoid of charm. "Vṛddha" means advanced in age. "Jaḍa" means one who lacks the knowledge of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

A sick man is one whose limbs are broken or deficient; or alternatively, one afflicted by diseases such as leprosy. Even if he possesses wickedness and other such traits, if he is free from the five great sins (mahāpātaka) such as the killing of a Brahmin, then he is indeed pure. For it is said: "A husband defiled by a sin must be awaited until his purification."

This is according to the statement of Yājñavalkya. "By those desiring the world" means by those who desire fruits such as heaven. Alternatively, if even one such as this [me] exists, then I should not be abandoned; for he is a *pati* (protector) because he possesses that quality. Or else, the *pati* is the resident of Vraja, and you must not abandon him—that is, you must not depart from him. [The root] *ohāṅ* means "to go."
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "One who is ill-behaved," and so forth. This applies only to those who desire worldly things, and not to those who desire Me;
for those who desire Me worship Me alone and attain Me—just as it is said: "Even those who worship other deities go to Me" (*Gītā* 9.25). ||25||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O you who are clever only at instructing others! Since the husbands have now been abandoned in every respect, what is the use of instructing them on service and so forth? To this they reply: "He is ill-behaved (*duḥśīla*)," meaning addicted to theft and the like; "unfortunate" (*durbhaga*), meaning devoid of fortune and the like, that is to say, one whose efforts are fruitless.

"An elder" means one overcome by old age. "An idiot" means one lacking capacity for ritual actions and so forth. "A sick person" means one seized by a major disease. "Indigent" means extremely poor, in the sense of being unable even to fill his own belly;
the word "api" (even) is to be construed with each term. Even if he is possessed of bad character and other such faults, he is not to be abandoned.
But since the resident of Vraja is endowed with every excellent quality, how could he be abandoned?

This is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also). [She says: "By those desiring the world," meaning by those who have expectations for both worlds; otherwise, there would be nothing but suffering in this world and the next—this is the sense. And in that regard, only the sinner is to be abandoned.

He said: "One who has not fallen" (*apātakī*). A "fall" (*pātaka*) is a specific type of sin that causes one to fall [from one's status]. Thus, the *Smṛti* states: "One should attend upon a husband who has not fallen.

Therefore, the sense is that since none of those present here possess even a mere trace of sin, he is certainly not fit to be abandoned. However, in reality, even though their firm devotion was certain...
It was said in that manner precisely for the purpose of increasing longing.

And this is the meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): since it is established that, in reality, I alone am the husband; and since it is established that, according to such statements as "you are ill-behaved," a husband must not be abandoned even if he is possessed of various faults; [the following ensues].

"How can I, a husband endowed with every auspicious quality, be abandoned? But how is it that they, who are possessed of various defects and are not husbands, should not be abandoned? To this he says: "One of bad character," and so forth. (25)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O you who are clever at instructing others! Since the husbands have been abandoned in every respect, what is the use now of instruction regarding service to them and so forth? To this they reply: "He is ill-behaved (*duḥśīla*)," meaning addicted to theft and the like; "unfortunate" (*durbhaga*), meaning devoid of good fortune and the like, and thus one whose efforts are fruitless.

The meaning is as follows: "old" means overcome by decrepitude; "dull-witted" means lacking capacity for ritual actions and the like; "sick" means afflicted by a major disease; "poor" means extremely destitute, in the sense of being unable even to fill one's own belly—the word "api" (even) is to be construed with each term. Thus, even if one is possessed of immorality and other such faults, they are not to be abandoned.
But since the resident of Vraja is endowed with all excellent qualities, how could he be abandoned?
This is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also).

Among the terms beginning with "duḥśīla" (of bad character), one should observe that each subsequent term denotes a lower degree of worthiness. In that regard, compared to one who is of bad character—

From one who is weak comes one who is unfortunate and base, because misfortune being ordained by fate is unavoidable. Even more so than that is the old man; due to the decline of all capacities inherent in old age, and because he is generally disliked by women and fails in domestic duties and the like, his status is indeed base. Even more so than that is the fool.

Because all defects arise from ignorance of dharma and adharma and from the inability to accomplish virtuous deeds; furthermore, because he is always disregarded by all people due to his being afflicted with disease and the like, accompanied by compassion [for him]; and furthermore, because he is base due to the loss of the boundaries of all virtues through the deficiency of hunger—this is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "by women," it refers to them...
Because each [of these] leads to a separate destiny, it is indicated that one might even be held by attendants at times.

"By those desiring the world" means by those who have expectations regarding both worlds; otherwise, there would be ill-repute and so forth in this world, and rebirth in hell and so forth in the next—this is the meaning. And in that regard, only those devoted to great sin should be abandoned.
Thus he says: "one who is not fallen" (*apātakī*). And so the *Smṛti* states: "One should attend upon a husband who has not fallen [from dharma].
Therefore, the sense is that since all those present here are likewise not fallen, he is certainly not fit to be abandoned.
However, in reality, if at some later time a consideration of dharma and so forth should arise from any cause...
It may be that a weakening of their specific devotion toward Him occurs;
therefore, by first personally causing them to hear the Dharma, He has strengthened their devotion by dispelling that [weakening].
Alternatively, this too is merely a jest, as before, in comparison with their actual worship of Him.
Because even a husband endowed with the six qualities beginning with good character must be abandoned, that [abandonment] has indeed been described.

And this is for the sake of wordplay (*śleṣa*): "I am a *pati* because I protect (*pāti*) from calamities; thus, even though I am possessed of bad character and the like, and even though I am an *apātakī*, meaning one who has not fallen away from dharma—even so, by those desiring both worlds..."
Even by you women, the ladies of Vraja, who desire husbands, sons, and the like, He is certainly not to be abandoned;

rather, the meaning is that He is always to be united with through embraces and other such acts. But I am certainly not like that, for I possess all excellent qualities and am the sole beloved of yours.
Because it is the opposite of that. And since you, out of regard for me, are indeed indifferent to the world, the sense is: why then would you not embrace me even now?
Or rather, an ordinary husband, even if possessed of such six defects, is not to be abandoned; but I—
"In reality, you are indeed my Lord, directly endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers; how could you be one to be abandoned?

That you have come here having renounced everything is entirely appropriate. Or rather, He is not to be forsaken even by those who desire worldly things, but especially by those who seek the supreme goal."

The meaning is this: even one endowed with good character and the like, and even one who is not a fallen sinner (*apātakin*), must be abandoned; for she, being drawn by her supreme passion for me, has indeed transcended the boundaries of both worlds. In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has already been set forth.

Alternatively, being envious of the cowherds, he says: "Even if a husband is of bad character and so forth, he must not be abandoned—that is, he must not be left by the women, the women of Vraja; for the root *ohāṅ* means 'to go' [and thus 'to leave']—even if he is ill-behaved, wrathful, unfortunate, ugly, old and decrepit, dull-witted and foolish, or diseased."
Always diseased, poor, and lacking much wealth in cattle; for those who desire the world and crave impure worldly things, there is this sequence of events:
"In this very way, he is of bad character," and so forth, should be applied. ||25||

Prīti-sandarbha 332: Even while accepting his status as a husband, [the speaker] rejects service to him by another means, even through the medium of scriptural statements, saying "he is ill-behaved. The sentiment is one of indignation: "He is not to be abandoned only because he is not an outcaste; they, however, are indeed outcastes. (25)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, by that same sequence, he illuminates two meanings—beginning with "one of bad character" (*duḥśīla*). In the context at hand, this is easy to understand; therefore, the sense is: "Having gone to Ghoṣa, you must serve your husbands alone. In the alternative sense—this is as if [said] by those desiring the world, but not...

"By those desiring me": even by those desiring me, having abandoned their husbands, I alone am to be worshipped, because I alone am the true husband. Therefore, "do not go to Ghoṣa"; the meaning is: "abandoning [your homes] right here, worship me. (25)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: [The opponent] argues that by causing one to abandon service to oneself and instead instructing service to the husband and others, the scripture—regarded as a matter of verbal cognition—is like a person afflicted by bile who abandons sugar from the tongue and uses salt instead; thus, why does it cause us pain, as if offering us something alkaline?
Observing this, in order to strengthen his own desire to listen, he speaks again of that very same Dharma:

[he is] an elder who has seen no results, one whose physical vigor has declined with the passage of age, one weakened by the performance of rituals, one who is deluded, one afflicted by royal diseases, and one who was a committer of great sins in a previous birth.

According to the Smṛti, "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa [suffers] from consumption"; thus, he is "without wealth," meaning impoverished, because he is incapable even of filling his own belly. Even if a husband is possessed of the six defects, if he is a protector, then he must not be abandoned by other women—meaning by worldly women—even if they have been abandoned by him of their own accord.
The word "api" (even) is used because those who desire the world—that is, those desiring both worlds—hear of censure in this world and hear of the suffering of hell in the next world.
He says that if there is a connection with a great sin (mahāpātaka), then she must indeed be abandoned; however, if she is not a sinner (apātakī), she is not to be abandoned.

An outcaste is to be abandoned; however, your husbands are not of such a nature. Rather, they are well-behaved, fortunate, young, skillful in performing their duties, free from disease, possessed of abundant cattle, wealth, and grain, full of desire for you, and free from sin. How [could they be otherwise]?

Should they be abandoned? [The answer is: Only when even a single fault exists is such a course entirely appropriate, and not otherwise. Furthermore, the sense is that even toward one who is always indifferent and characterized by neutrality, affection is not appropriate.
Now he states the actual meaning: "Even a husband," and so forth, "though possessed of six faults."

He must not be abandoned by you women who act rightly; how much less so by me, who am endowed with virtues such as excellent character? Because I am possessed of the other six qualities, I alone am the primary husband, for I am capable of warding off fears such as excessive rain. One like me [should not be forsaken] by those like you.
A husband must not be abandoned. The intended meaning of the term "one who has committed a sin" (pātakī) is this:

there is no possibility even of the mere presence of a minor fault in Vraja, much less the occurrence of a mortal sin (mahā-pātaka); for a prohibition is only applicable when such a thing is possible. As it has been said:
Those who offer salutations to non-Vaiṣṇavas while feeling compassion for Janārdana, and likewise those who engage in quarrels with Vaiṣṇavas, fall here [into hell]; of this there is no doubt.

Having said, "Let them be restrained," when an attempt at restraint through quarreling occurred, the transference of sin arose from that quarrel. Because of my efforts to restrain those who were being led astray by me, and because of my agitation with envy, the transference of a great sin has also accrued to me; therefore, those who desire worldly well-being must certainly abandon them in every way.

The hidden intention is as follows: "The world" (*loka*) is that which is perceived or manifested—that is, the mode of the bliss of amorous play. Therefore, you who desire it must not abandon me, your husband, who bestows your own desired objects; rather, you should enjoy yourselves with me, who am compassionate. ||25||
Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: "How can we, who are full of affection for you, serve those husbands of ours who are unsuitable, contrary-natured, and disagreeable?

To this he replies with the word "duḥśīla" (of bad character). He says "apātakī" (one who has not fallen from grace), because of the traditional law (smṛti) which states: "A husband should attend upon one who has not fallen [from virtue]."
The meaning is that a husband who possesses the cause for falling—that is, one who has committed a sin—is to be abandoned by those desiring the world;
that is, by those longing for the happiness of the husband’s world. In the alternative sense, "by those desiring the world" means by those [desiring] this world and the next world.

It is not that he should not be abandoned by those who are concerned with such things as very trivial fame and pleasure; rather, you, having cast away both worlds with a handful of water and sporting in the ocean of the pleasure of my sweetness, have abandoned your husband from the very beginning. ||25||
Adultery by a woman of noble family leads everywhere to a lack of heaven, brings ill repute, yields meager results, involves hardship, causes fear, and is universally despised.
Śrīdhara: "Phalgu" means trivial or worthless. "Kṛcchram" means difficult to accomplish. "Aupapattyam" refers to the pleasure of a paramour. ||26||

Vaṃśīdhara: If it is asked, "Since desire is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and since that [desire] is not attained due to the fault of having [only] a husband, why should one not effect the fulfillment of birth through some other means in order to remove the fruitlessness of birth?"—to that, he states the refutation. The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). An *upapati* is a substitute for a husband (*patyuḥ pratinidhiḥ*).

"Jāraḥ, jāras tūpapatiḥ samau" (A paramour, a lover, and a gallant are synonyms), according to Amara. The connection with that [paramour] constitutes an act characterized by vulgarity; for a woman of that [noble] family, such an act is everywhere despised and censurable, whether the man be superior, inferior, or middling—this is the syntactical connection. How so? It is said: "it does not lead to heaven."

It is indeed contrary to heaven; on the contrary, it bestows torments such as the seven iron spikes and the like. Moreover, it is disgraceful, causing ill repute both in this world and the next. Nevertheless, it is not abundant—that is, its fruit is meager and insignificant—because its scope is limited to a short duration, occurring only occasionally. It is a hardship.
Thus it was explained by the venerable teacher (Svāmīpāda): "Difficult to accomplish" means because it must be achieved through great exertion on the part of the agent;
"fear-inducing" means causing fear of death and so forth; [it is difficult] during sexual union because of the arrival of her husband and others—this is the meaning.

In this sense: *upapati* is one whose husband (*pati*) is near (*upa*); the state of being that is *upapatitva*. This refers to the proximity to a husband for eight watches (*yāma*). As for *kulā*, it means she who takes (*lāti*) or accepts (*ādadāti*) what is contemptible (*ku*); and she is a woman (*strī*), and [this state] belongs to her alone, and not to you who reside with me. Even in the case of Tārā, Ahalyā, and others, [this is so] because of their transgression.
Rebirth was not considered contemptible, because husbands would accept [their wives] again. ||26||

The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: Anticipating the objection that "abandoning one's husband is a great fault," he says, "It does not lead to heaven," and so forth. The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) here refers to the entire universe (*viśva*).
Even throughout the whole range of existence, from Brahmā downwards, having a paramour leads to the exclusion from heaven.
The second meaning is that while [others] suffer infamy and the like, such is not the case for me, who have transcended all;

my intention is that I have no husband other than myself, for I am the Lord. And thus says Lakṣmī: "O Hṛṣīkeśvara, women indeed worship you by their own vows" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.18.19); he alone shall be the husband.
"Free from fear from any quarter, he himself," and so forth. ||26||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might object: "O Prince of Śrī-Vraja, by Your command, their status as wives must certainly not be abandoned; rather, let them always possess that status in name alone, while the actual practice of being Your wife should remain with You. Anticipating this, [the Lord] spoke what was most displeasing to them by censuring their long-held desire.
With feigned indifference (*avahitthā*), she spoke as if with indignation: "It leads away from heaven" (*asvargyam*).

This means it is unfavorable for attaining the world of *svarga*. "O passionate women! Since heaven has never been seen, let there be no longing for it; however, there is certainly a longing for fame in this world, and that [practice] is an obstacle to it."
He said: "It is disgraceful. It is a destroyer even of previously accumulated fame.

[The opponent objects: "But surely this is well-guarded; who indeed would know of it? To that he replies: "Even so, it is insignificant and trivial because of its instability. [The opponent objects: "But, O Acyuta! That [fame] of ours with you is indeed perfectly stable."

To this he replies: "Even so, it is difficult and hard to accomplish. [The opponent objects: "But O free-roaming lion! Since you wander at will in Vraja and in Śrī Vṛndāvana, it is indeed easily accomplished. To this he replies: "Even so, there is fear from the next world and sometimes from the Master (Svāmī) and others; that [fear] 'vahati'—meaning it brings or causes [distress]."

That [is true]. But, O you whose sweet lips are to be sipped like nectar! Since everything has been disregarded by us in comparison to you, there is no fear from any quarter; to this he replies: "Nevertheless, everywhere..."
It is loathsome and censured both in one's own country and in foreign lands, and in the conventional and the ultimate senses; for "hi" indicates certainty.
But surely, O Lord of the Knowers of Reality! even loathsomeness is quite bearable through the attainment of one's own desired goal.

To this he replies: "by a woman of good family" (*kula-strī*). The singular number is used for the genus. The sense is that even a stain upon the family is utterly improper for women of good family and must therefore be avoided by all means; however, in reality, it is merely for the purpose of increasing longing as before.
And this is the meaning based on word-play (*śleṣa*): as before, a husband is one who has acquired [his status] through dharma, whereas a paramour (*upapati*) is the opposite of that.

Furthermore, observing that in common worldly usage the term is established in another sense, this statement from the *Smṛti* suggests a joke by means of equivocation (*chala*). She whose husband (*pati*) is near (*upa*) her is a "near-husband" (*upapati*), and she belongs to him.

The state of being a wife (*bhāva-aupatya*) means proximity to the husband. That [state] is in every respect associated with defects such as the failure to attain heaven. Thus, in the context of "service to the husband," it should be explained that the highest degree of unrighteousness (*adharma*) resides precisely in the other [i.e., the husband]. ||26||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O Śrī Vraja-yuvarāja! By Your command, their status as husbands must certainly not be abandoned; however, let their husbandhood exist in name only, while the actual practice of being husbands remains with You alone. Anticipating this thought, [the Lord] spoke what was most displeasing to them by censuring their long-held desire.
With feigned indifference (*avahitthā*), she spoke as if with indignation: "It is not conducive to heaven" (*asvargyam*).

This means it is unfavorable for attaining heaven, or rather, that it destroys the heaven previously acquired through merit. "O passionate women! Since heaven has never been seen, let there be no concern for it; however, there is certainly a desire for fame in this world, and this [act] is its obstructer."
He said: "It is disgraceful. The meaning is that it is even a destroyer of previously accumulated fame.

[The opponent objects: "O you who transcend the world! Who indeed would know this so well-kept secret? To that he replies: "It is trivial (phalgu) and insignificant (tuccha) because of its instability. [The opponent objects: "But, O Acyuta! That which is with you is certainly very stable for us."

To this he replies: "Kṛcchram" means difficult to accomplish. [An objection: But O free-roaming lion! Since you wander at will in Vraja and Śrī Vṛndāvana, it should indeed be easy to accomplish; to this he replies: "Bhayam"—fear from masters and others, as well as from hell and so forth—"tad-ā" means that which brings or leads to that [fear].

Or rather, it is something despised and censured even in the world and in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because it causes shame or evokes disgust; "hi" indicates certainty. [Objection: O Lord of the Knowers of Reality! Even such disgust is easily endured for the sake of accomplishing one's own desired goal. To this he replies: "by a woman of good family" (*kula-strī*). The singular number is used to denote the class (*jāti*).

The sense is that, because it brings disgrace upon the family, such conduct is utterly improper for their wives and must therefore be avoided by all means. In reality, however, this is intended precisely to strengthen his own affection for them, as before. Furthermore, there is a pun here: the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "even" (*api*). Even illicit love (*aupapatya*), which takes the form of being non-heavenly and so forth—

This indeed applies even to a woman of noble family (*kula-strī*), for we hear of such [transgressions] even in the cases of Tārā, Ahalyā, and others. Therefore, the sense is that because she is common [to both], there is no specific fault [in her case]. Furthermore, a *kulā* is a woman who takes (*lāti*) or gives (*ādi-dāti*) what is contemptible; for her alone does [the act] lead to the loss of heaven and so forth. But for you—
For those who accept my state of being—the essence of the entirety of all things—it should be understood that this is not so; this is the intended meaning, and it should be known as a jest (*narma*).
Alternatively, *narma* says: "near" (*upa*) means in proximity. She whose husband is near is an *upapati*;
her state is *aupapatyam*, which means proximity to the husband. That is in every respect.
"It is fraught with defects such as not leading to heaven," he said, referring to Rādhā by the term "family woman. (26)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): Anticipating the objection that [the act] might be accepted as not being a sin, he rejects its practice by means of a deceptive device, suggesting another meaning for a different Smṛti passage with the words "it does not lead to heaven" (*asvargyam*). Upa...
She whose husband is nearby is an *upapati*; her state is *aupapatyam*, which means proximity to the husband. That indeed leads away from heaven. ||26||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Again, he speaks in that same sequence, beginning with "not leading to heaven" (*asvargyam*).
For a woman of good family (*kula-strī*), having a paramour—that is, the act of taking a lover—is in every respect not conducive to heaven, and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is:
"Go to the cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*) and serve your husbands. In the alternative interpretation: for a woman of good family, having a paramour...
"Everywhere [the practice] leads away from heaven," and so forth; however, this does not apply to me, who transcend all things, because there is no possibility of rebirth for me.
I alone am the true Lord. Therefore, the meaning is: "Abiding here without hesitation, worship me. ||26||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: [The opponent] thinks that by verbal cognition, [the scripture] instructs service to the husband and others while causing one to abandon service to the Self, just as one overcome by bile abandons sugar on the tongue and applies pungent grain-powder; thus, [the opponent asks]: "Why does this cause us pain, like salt?"—is it making us suffer?

Observing this, in order to strengthen his own desire to listen, he speaks again of that very same Dharma because of the visible results: "The old man" refers to one whose age has undergone transformation;
"lax in performing actions" due to delusion; and "the sick man" refers to one afflicted by a king's disease because of having committed great sins (*mahāpātaka*) in a previous birth.

According to the Smṛti, "The killer of a Brāhmaṇa [suffers] from consumption"; thus, he is "without wealth," meaning poor, because he is incapable even of maintaining himself. Even if the husband is possessed of the six defects, if he is a protector, then he must not be abandoned by other women—meaning worldly women—even by those who have been abandoned by him of their own accord. The word "api" (even) [indicates this].

Therefore, for those who desire the world—that is, those desiring both worlds—since one hears of censure in this world and hears of the suffering of hell in the next world, it follows that if there is a connection with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), then [the person] must certainly be abandoned.
He says: "If he is not a sinner (*apātakī*), he should not be abandoned; if he is a sinner (*pātakī*), he should be abandoned. It is thus for you as well.

But husbands are not like this; rather, they are virtuous, fortunate, young, skilled in performing their duties, free from disease, and possessed of abundant cattle, wealth, and grain. Since they desire you and are free from sin, how could they be abandoned? Only if even a single fault were present would it be entirely appropriate [to leave them].
"Not otherwise" means that furthermore, even toward one who is always indifferent and characterized by neutrality, passion is not appropriate; this is the sense.
Now he states the actual meaning, beginning with "duḥśīla": [even] a husband, though possessed of the six faults...

He must not be abandoned by you ladies who act rightly; how much less so by me, who am endowed with virtues such as excellent character? Because he is possessed of the other six qualities, and because he alone is capable of warding off fears such as those arising from transgression during separation from his primary husband, one like me should [be supported] by women like you.

A husband must not be abandoned. Regarding the term "one who has committed a sin" (pātakī), the intended meaning is this: in Vraja, there is not even the possibility of merely minor sins, much less the occurrence of a major sin (mahā-pātaka). Only when such a thing exists can a prohibition apply. Thus it has been said:
Those who bow to non-Vaiṣṇavas while being addressed as Janārdana, and those who engage in quarrels with Vaiṣṇavas, fall [to hell] here; of this there is no doubt.

Having said, "They are being restrained," when a quarrel arose during the act of warding them off, a transgression leading to a downfall occurred because of that quarrel. Because of warding off those who were inclined toward me, and because of being agitated by jealousy for me, a great transgression leading to a downfall has also occurred for me. Therefore, they must be abandoned in every way by those who desire worldly well-being.
That which is perceived and illuminated is the "world" (loka)—the mode of the bliss of amorous play.
Is it not so that I, your husband who grants your own desires, must not be abandoned by you who long for that? The hidden intention is: "Rejoice with me, who am compassionate. ||25||

Viśvanātha: You ladies naturally possess a general affection for me; however, a specific affection that is contrary to dharma must be abandoned by all means. Thus he says: "It does not lead to heaven" (*asvargyam*). If you say, "Let there be no heaven," [he replies: "If it is disgraceful, let there be no fame either" (*ayaśasyam*). If you say, "Let there be no fame," [he replies: "Then let there be no happiness either" (*asukham*). If you say, "Let there be no happiness," [he replies: "Then let there be no life either" (*anīpsitam*). If you say, "Let there be no life," [he replies: "Then let there be no union with you either" (*asaṅgatam*). If you say, "Let there be no union," [he replies: "Then let there be no death either" (*aniṣṭam*). If you say, "Let there be no death," [he replies: "Then let there be no separation from me either" (*aviyogam*). If you say, "Let there be no separation," [he replies: "Then let there be no sorrow either" (*aduḥkham*). If you say, "Let there be no sorrow," [he replies: "Then let there be no joy either" (*anandam*). If you say, "Let there be no joy," [he replies: "Then let there be no existence either" (*avastum*). If you say, "Let there be no existence," [he replies: "Then let there be no non-existence either" (*anāśvam*). If you say, "Let there be no non-existence," [he replies: "Then let there be no liberation either" (*amokṣam*). If you say, "Let there be no liberation," [he replies: "Then let there be no bondage either" (*abandham*). If you say, "Let there be no bondage," [he replies: "Then let there be no merit either" (*apuṇyam*). If you say, "Let there be no merit," [he replies: "Then let there be no demerit either" (*apāpam*). If you say, "Let there be no demerit," [he replies: "Then let there be no virtue either" (*adharmam*). If you say, "Let there be no virtue," [he replies: "Then let there be no vice either" (*adharmaḥ*). If you say, "Let there be no vice," [he replies: "Then let there be no dharma either" (*adharmam*). If you say, "Let there be no dharma," [he replies: "Then let there be no adharma either" (*adharmam*). If you say, "Let there be no adharma," [he replies: "Then let there be no worldly activity either" (*akarma*). If you say, "Let there be no worldly activity," [he replies: "Then let there be no renunciation either" (*akarma*). If you say, "Let there be no renunciation," [he replies: "Then let there be no action either" (*akarma*). If you say, "Let there be no action," [he replies: "Then let there be no inaction either" (*akarma*). If you say, "Let there be no inaction," [he replies: "Then let there be no effort either" (*akarma*). If you say, "Let there be no effort," [he replies: "Then let there be no fruit either" (*aphalam*). If you say, "Let there be no fruit," [he replies: "Then let there be no seed either" (*abījam*). If you say, "Let there be no seed," [he replies: "Then let there be no field either" (*akṣetram*). If you say, "Let there be no field," [he replies: "Then let there be no rain either" (*avarṣam*). If you say, "Let there be no rain," [he replies: "Then let there be no harvest either" (*anāśam*). If you say, "Let there be no harvest," [he replies: "Then let there be no sustenance either" (*ajīvitam*). If you say, "Let there be no sustenance," [he replies: "Then let there be no death either" (*amṛtyum*). If you say, "Let there be no death," [he replies: "Then let there be no birth either" (*ajanma*). If you say, "Let there be no birth," [he replies: "Then let there

"You speak falsely that it is trivial; if you say, 'This is not trivial because it is experienced as the most excellent,' then [the objection is] that it consists of the hardship of warding off the suffering of the husband and so forth.
Indeed, [this is true].
"The fickleness, the rarity, and the very obstacles encountered by women—I consider these alone to be the supreme weapons of the five-arrowed god [Kāma]. (Uṇī.
3.20) And: "Even though it is suffering, the mind is attached to it as if it were pleasure. (Uṇī. 14.126)

If it is argued that, according to the treatises on aesthetics (*rasa-śāstra*), on the contrary, that hardship is actually a cause of supreme pleasure for us who possess passion— [we reply that] it is terrifying because, being forbidden by worldly custom and sacred scripture,
it brings about fear both in this life and the next.
But is it not said:
"Indeed, it is precisely where there is a specific prohibition and where deer-eyed women are exceedingly difficult to obtain that the hearts of city-dwellers become intensely attached"? [Uṇī. 3.21]

This is because it is stated in the science of aesthetics (*rasa-śāstra*) that, on the contrary, this very [act] is what produces aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). To this, he says: "it is loathsome. In every place and at all times, the act of adultery—the action performed by a paramour with a woman of good family—is loathsome.
The meaning is that a woman of good family who behaves in such a manner is censured everywhere.

In this regard, although you may well endure even self-reproach for the sake of achieving your own desired ends, how could I bring about the censure of you, who are the objects of my affection? Therefore, the intention is: "Go back to your own assembly."

As for the objection that "this [practice] is censured everywhere," this is indeed a universal rule; however, in the present case, you have already heard from the lineage of Garga’s own mouth that I am equal to Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, even in my taking a wife, there is no fault whatsoever, because as the Supreme Lord, I transcend all auspicious and inauspicious karma.
The state of being. ||26||
"Devotion toward me arises from hearing, seeing, meditating, and chanting my glories;
it does not arise in the same way through mere physical proximity. Therefore, return home."
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [it is said] "from hearing," etc. (27).

Vaṃśīdhara says: He states the means for attaining his own pleasure with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*). Others say: Since you are the primary husband, serving you is not like serving a paramour—which leads to the loss of heaven and so forth—but rather, even more than serving a husband, it is the primary means for attaining heaven and other such rewards. Even if this is so...
Devotion (bhakti) toward me arises through hearing my name and so forth; it does not arise in the same way through physical proximity.
For those who possess splendor, extreme closeness is as terrifying as fire—this is the intended meaning. Therefore, having returned home, one should practice devotion to me.

He said: "Go back. In this sense, it means: "Since [the goal] is not attained through hearing and so forth in the same way as it is through direct proximity, therefore go to those who have not yet taken wives; or rather, enter my own bower-houses," is the meaning.
Now, how else could you conceive of this? We have not come for the sake of contact with your limbs;

rather, because of the authority of Garga’s words that "there is no other equal to Nārāyaṇa," we have come desiring devotion to you, knowing you yourself to be Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, [spend] this very night...
If you should say, "Please, out of compassion, place us right near You and cause us to serve Your lotus feet," to that He says:

"From hearing [and chanting]," and so forth. It is well known among you that pure devotees do not desire even proximity, such as *sālokya* and the rest, just as they do not desire hearing, chanting, and so on.

The sense is that [the emotion] arises merely by hearing of the Vaiṣṇavīs. In the alternative interpretation (pakṣe): the emotion of love (kandarpa) does not arise from hearing and so forth in the same way as it does from close proximity; therefore, "do not go toward the houses"—thus there is a connection through repetition (*āvṛtti*). Or else, by eliding the letter *a* as a synonym for the negative particle *na*, [it means] "not-houses" (*agṛhān*), i.e., "not the houses."
The meaning is "departed" or "gone. ||27||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "By hearing," and so forth. The external meaning is: "If you are attached [to me], then remain here by means of hearing [the teachings] and other such practices. The internal meaning, however, is: "My affection for you is not as great through hearing and so on as it would be through close proximity and union; therefore, return home."
The meaning is external; however, the internal sense should be understood as "us who are houseless and have not taken wives.

The plural form in "pratiyāta" (go back) is as before. Or, it may mean "those who are houseless," having abandoned their homes and gone to the forest specifically for the sake of association with those like you. ||27||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, fearing that [the devotee] might not desist even after being refused in many ways, He prescribes indifference by means of the denial of [any] emotion—starting with "from hearing" (*śravaṇāt*). Just as emotion arises through hearing and so forth, it would not arise through proximity or physical contact; rather, it arises through longing during separation.

There is an instantaneous increase in that [intensity]; however, the sense is that in the case of union (*saṃyoga*), there is a slackening of longing. Thus, even though their state has reached the highest pitch, it is merely concealed by the artifice of describing it as "unaccomplished" (*asiddhatā*). In that regard, in the stage of prior passion (*pūrva-rāga*), there is generally first hearing, then seeing, and then the attainment of union.
The continuous manifestation of that [state], and consequently how that occurs, has been described in this sequential manner; however,
in reality, it belongs to those whose right-natures are rendered exceedingly tender by the weight of incessant love due to their supreme curiosity.
This is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the agitation of her love.

Furthermore, this has a double meaning (śleṣa): "Indeed, that very state of being through which your own status as their husband was established—and by the absence of which their lack of a husband was established—is no longer possible for you, because of your distance."

Regarding the statement "because of their proximity," he says here: "from hearing" (*śravaṇāt*). Just as devotion toward me arises through the specific manner of tasting [the nectar] from hearing and so forth, it does not arise even through physical proximity. Nor would it exist even toward others who are close by and consider themselves masters (*pati*).

The meaning is as follows: Just as a bond of affection arises through proximity between two people worthy of mutual love, it does not arise through hearing and so forth; since this is well-known in the world, the word "other" (anya) is dependent on the context (artha).
Furthermore, because the matter was introduced in that very manner from the outset, it is established by the context (prakaraṇa). Therefore, [the reference is] toward the home.

The negative particle *na* is connected with both [words], as in "do not go" (*na yāta*). Alternatively, the prefix *prati-* is observed to be used in senses such as negation, rejection, or opposition, even when there is a contradiction with the literal meaning of the root; therefore, the meaning here is "go against," that is, "make them objects of opposition to going. Thus...
Their conversation, as before, is of two kinds: in some cases it is strictly according to the facts, and in others it is to be understood as being renewed through the manifestation of passion. ||27||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, O You who are attainable through love alone! If it is argued that since love is the goal of all, one's own duty consists indeed in both external and internal [practices] performed with that love, then one should simply practice hearing about Me (*mac-chravaṇa*) and so forth. Or rather, O Śrī Puruṣottama! Only Your grace is required.

If you say that nothing else, such as family and so forth, is required, then my grace is accomplished only through love directed toward me; and that [love] is achieved solely through hearing [the scriptures] and other such means, not by physical contact with my limbs. Or rather: O friend who accomplishes all goals! Even when love for you has been perfected, is there nothing further?

If it is argued that [detachment from] loathing and so forth is for the sake of accomplishing the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then one should simply practice the means for that; thus, following the method of the scriptures and with a particular kind of unbearable indifference, he speaks to his most beloved and discerning friend: "From hearing," and so on.
There is either a combination or an option regarding hearing and the other [means]. The realization of the reality is accomplished by even one of these alone.

This has indeed been explained in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*, in its *Uttara-khaṇḍa* and elsewhere. Among those, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) refers to the stories of the Lord and so forth; "seeing" (*darśana*) refers to the sacred form (*śrī-mūrti*) and so forth, or even seeing Me from afar.

"Constant chanting" (*anukīrtanam*) means the continuous chanting of my name as the primary focus. This is because, in passages such as *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.2.40—"One who observes such a vow becomes filled with love through the chanting of his own beloved Name"—it is stated that this alone is the internal means for the arising of that very devotion (*bhāva*). Thus, proximity is indeed required for the purpose of direct vision.

To avoid that [misunderstanding], the vision of Him is first mentioned with the intention of indicating its secondary (gauṇa) nature. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect among these [stages] should be inferred in successive order. Among them, hearing (śravaṇa) comes first; without it, all [subsequent stages] do not arise from knowledge. For this very reason, it is said at the outset: "He is to be heard and glorified" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.14].

First, there is the instruction on that very [practice], such as its performance and so forth. Following hearing, one sees the divine form and other manifestations out of a desire to behold the Blessed Lord; from that, meditation becomes exceedingly easy.
From that, chanting arises spontaneously due to the attainment of deep mental absorption. Therefore—

The reason why my affection arises [toward her] is not due to proximity, presence, or physical contact with her limbs; for according to the maxim that "proximity is a cause for disregard among mortals," and so forth,
or because of the contraction of the mind through its non-contradiction with the scriptures— by the word "thus" (tathā), it is meant that it is not of such a nature.

But rather, it is even less than that. Or rather, it does not occur in that manner; instead, it occurs by transcending worldly norms, through total indifference, and only by means of supreme effort. Therefore, the sense is that one should perform hearing and so forth while abandoning close association. For that purpose:
"Go home indeed, for that very happiness is accomplished right there through the absence of all contraction and the like.
In reality, however, all of this is due to supreme curiosity; or rather, it is because of those women whose simple natures have been made exceedingly tender by the weight of incessant love.
This is merely for the purpose of demonstrating the intensity of their love; such is the general direction.

Furthermore, this has a double meaning (*śleṣārtha*): according to the logic already stated, you must always maintain an unrestricted disposition toward Me in every way, and it should not be said that the state called "love" is accomplished merely through hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.
Since [the goal] is accomplished most effectively by the mere touch of the limbs, and not through hearing and so forth, he says:

"It does not happen in the same way from causes such as hearing as it happens through close contact"—this is how the words should be construed. Therefore, for that reason, with the elision of the letter *a* (i.e., *agṛheṇa*), go toward us who are "without houses" (*agṛhān*), meaning those who have not taken wives.

The meaning is "worship. The plural number [of "houses"] is used out of a desire to express His own greatness for the purpose of enchanting them, while the non-use of the word "Self" (ātman) directly is due to His cleverness and other such qualities.
Alternatively, "agṛhān" refers to places other than houses, such as the banks of the Yamunā and so forth. Or else, it refers to "houses."

The meaning is: "Enter my bower-forms. By the word "houses" (gṛhān), he intends that since these bowers and so forth are indeed pleasure-houses or his own home, one should always dwell within them alone.
With the fuel of ten verses, he playfully kindled the fire of indifference within all directions for those whose souls were softened by love.

In this regard, these verses should be viewed in reverse order. The verse beginning with "From hearing [the sound] in the downward direction" refers to the fact that due to a particular intensity of heat, the fire itself blazes upward from its crest. The verse beginning with "Not leading to heaven" refers to the upward direction; because of the censure of what is desired there, there is a burden of suffering like a headache. Thus...

In the eight directions beginning with the east, those such as Duḥśīla and the others are to be discerned respectively and in their proper order. Otherwise, among those eleven types of [energies] that arrive in groups through the eleven bases such as burning, abandoning, and so forth,
ten verses would apply there [to each of them] individually.

Some should be understood according to their respective contexts— some by way of reverse order, some later by way of direct order, and so on as appropriate. Among these, first, regarding the first half-verse, it refers to all [the gopīs] facing [Kṛṣṇa] at the very beginning, with their garments and ornaments disarrayed due to their state of extreme agitation as they beheld Him.

Likewise, there are two other [verses], beginning with "asvargyam" (not leading to heaven), and so forth. Of these, the first is [applicable] to all [the wives] because they alone are intended by that [statement]; the second, however, is [applicable] generally because it teaches the manner in which the state arises. [The phrase] "this is the night for those who anoint [their eyes]" is intended to refer to the vision of beings of terrible nature and the like, by means of the collyrium for the eyes.

"Waiting upon those who wipe [the feet]," refers to the mothers; for it is logical that even relatives connected to the body are expected in relation to the body itself. "Waiting upon those who anoint," refers to what is seen; for in relation to fragrance, the expectation of flowers is also appropriate. "That goes to those who eat" is the quarter-verse. This is a summary of women's eating.

Because it is expressed through gestures alone, the initial brief statement—"Serve [your husbands]"—is made as a mere injunction directed toward those already serving their husbands, with the intention of expressing its obligatory nature; its expansion will follow later. Similarly, "Make [the children] drink" is said to those who are already nursing their infants, for the sake of urgency.

Regarding the passage beginning with "they cry out" (*krandanti*): since service to the husband (*bhartṛ-śuśrūṣā*) is precisely what is required, there would otherwise be a lack of regard for the household and bodily tasks—such as milking—which have that [service] as their sole cause.
Therefore, because its virtues and so forth will be described in detail later as the root of everything, it is treated first here.

According to the maxim of the needle and the frying pan (*sūcīkaṭāha-nyāya*): "Milk for each of those who are milking. Now, for the sake of strengthening the service to the husband, there are three [verses] addressed generally to all [wives], beginning with "Or else" (*athavā*).
Among these, the phrase "Or else" implies that, in comparison with the affection directed toward one's own [child], the service to the husband should not be abandoned.
In order to dispel doubts, according to the maxim of "extracting thorns," the arousal of one's own affection is like placing milk on the fire; the three types of women— those who cook the *saṃyāva*,
those who serve it, and the mistress— are so designated because their respective actions serve the purpose of attending to the husband and his kinsmen.
Service to the husband and so forth, as well as [service] to their kinsmen, has been enjoined; this is because there is no distinction between them one another.

Otherwise, such various statements would be made merely for the sake of jest or out of an abundance of curiosity. Likewise, because they possess mutual consensus, what is said to one applies to the others as well; thus it pertains to all of them indeed.

Because all words ultimately converge with one another in every respect, all words should be understood as generally directed toward all [objects]. The manner of that has already been written above; this is the general direction. ||27||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: Now, fearing that even in me this [devotional] state (*bhāva*) might lead only to suffering, he says "by hearing" (*śravaṇāt*) so that she does not turn her face away. Just as by hearing and so forth...
The state of being separated from Me is full of suffering due to the failure to attain Me; however, through proximity—that is, the attainment of Me—it does not exist.
Therefore, for that reason, go toward the *kuñjas* (groves), which here function as substitutes for the home; enter them.
Here, the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a paryudāsa (an exclusion implying a similar substitute). Thus, the meaning of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s words is in the form of a prayer.

This has been explained. However, another meaning is well-known. In that context, the term "sons" serves as a rejection [of the objection], even by way of an outburst of fault-finding accompanied by irony. ||27||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Again, he concludes with two points by means of that same sequence, beginning with "From hearing" (*śravaṇāt*). This state of being Mine (*mad-bhāva*) becomes full of rasa, and not merely through proximity. By the word "yathā" (just as), the word "tathā" (so) is implied.
The affection [felt] through hearing and so forth is not as it is through proximity; therefore, return to your homes.
(In the alternative sense: The affection for me is not as it is through proximity as it is through hearing and so forth.
Since the fruit of hearing and so forth is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), one does not return to one's home; for in its absence, there is indeed none for us.
"No," because the simple vowel *ā* expresses negation. ||27||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, in order to recall the pleasure of amorous dalliance previously experienced, [the author] states "from hearing and so forth" (*śravaṇād*) to show the superiority of the pleasure derived from hearing and other such acts over the pleasure of physical union, by means of a state of detached indifference. "Hearing" refers to the excellent qualities of the crest-jewel of heroes; "seeing" refers to the essence of their loveliness.

Regarding the Śrī-vigraha (the divine form), it is described in passages such as *barhāpīḍam* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.5] and so forth. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of its various limbs. Chanting (*kīrtana*) is the narration of My births, deeds, and qualities;
whether performed collectively or individually, this is the cause for the arising of ecstatic emotion (*bhāva*). In some cases, it occurs through hearing alone.
The arising of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), such as that of Rukmiṇī and others, as in the verse beginning, "Having heard of his qualities... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.52.37).
In some cases, it arises from seeing him, as in the house of Bhauma: "Seeing that best of men enter, the women were utterly infatuated."
"With their minds they chose as their desired husband the one bestowed by destiny" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.59.34). In some cases it is through meditation, as in the case of Devahūti:
"She meditated upon that very god, her offspring Kapila Hari."
"O child, she soon became free from desire for such a home" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.33.22).

This is because of the recitation [of the Lord's names] in certain instances, as in the case of Nārada: "While he was singing of his own heroic deeds, the Lord whose feet are the source of all holy places and whose glories are dear..."
"As if summoned, he quickly comes before my mind's eye" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.6.34).

Whether these [means] are taken as a combination (*samuccaya*) or as alternatives (*vikalpa*), they are the cause for the arising of *bhāva*. If it is argued that even the presence of just one of them results in the manifestation of *bhāva*, then, although these have equal fruit, regarding *śravaṇa*...

Its primacy consists precisely in its being pursued everywhere. Although proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is also heard of as a cause, nevertheless, just as hearing and the other [means] are established as not otherwise possible (*ananyathāsiddha*), so too this [proximity] is not said to be so; for here, proximity is the cause of disregard for mortals.
Because there is an absence of causality for the arising of a more intense state of being (*bhāva*); whereas here, there is contact with a limb (*aṅga-saṅga*).

And because, when that [contact] exists, a slackening of the state of being is observed. Therefore, by the meaning arising from the words "he went back toward his home," his own indifference and lack of desire are suggested.

Now he states the meaning arising from the sense: "Is it not the case that here something must be enjoined? Is it the state (*bhāva*) that is to be enjoined, or is it the proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) that is to be enjoined? To this it is replied: the state alone is what is to be enjoined.
For it is only in that [state] that the fourfold [means] beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*) are established as not otherwise possible, whereas this is not the case for proximity.

Because it has been stated that the sweet sentiment (*madhura-rasa*) consists of both separation (*vipralambha*) and union (*sambhoga*). In the case of separation, the capacity of hearing and other senses to bring about the manifestation of emotion (*bhāva*) has indeed already been established. However, where even physical proximity is heard to be a cause for the arising of emotion—as in the verse beginning "O female osprey, you lament... (*kurari vilapasi tvam*... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa])—[the same principle applies].
[10.90.15] That was not stated with the intention of asserting its occasional occurrence. Therefore, it is the existence of the entity itself that is to be predicated;
proximity is not the cause for the existence of the entity, nor is it to be predicated separately.

Now, if this were the case, then in the total absence of bodily contact at all times, there would be a deficiency in the sweet flavor (*madhura-rasa*), because that [flavor] consists of both [components]. Therefore, even when in close proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), it must be enjoined;
and if that were so, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Consequently, it must be the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) due to its proximity.

The state of being an object to be brought about belongs to the *bhāva* (the action). Proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the result here; for nowhere is the state of being an object to be brought about heard of in relation to a result. Just as in the case of "one should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice," where the sacrifice is the object to be brought about with reference to heaven, and the offering of the *māka-puroḍāśa* and other materials is the object to be brought about with reference to the sacrifice.
Likewise here too, there is a state of being the object of an injunction (*vidheyatva*): with reference to proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), the entity is the object of an injunction;

and with reference to the entity, the fourfold practice beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the object of an injunction. Therefore, it has been rightly stated that "it is not so by way of proximity," for nowhere is it accepted that something is the object of an injunction merely by being referred to by another.
Thus, through the prior arising of the internal state (*bhāva*) produced by hearing and so forth, the result of proximity has indeed already occurred.
Therefore, do not return home, setting aside the fruit; the negative particle (*na*) is to be construed with both [clauses].
Or else, even though proximity has failed to arise despite the fourfold causes such as hearing and so forth, nevertheless—
Existence does not occur. Since hearing and the other [means] are inconclusive, existence is unestablished;

when that is unestablished, how can there be happiness? Or rather, from the cause consisting of hearing and so forth, it has indeed arisen in me in such a manner that, through this proximity, my own home—the abodes of delight—is near at hand.
The forests, riverbanks, the waters of the Yamunā, and so forth—do not return [to them], but rather return constantly;

the intended meaning is that in this way the fulfillment of your desires may come to pass. Thus, having removed his own apparent indifference, by means of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*), he [speaks] preceded by a prohibition against returning home.
Indeed, for the sake of enjoyment, having made one's stay in the middle firm, this [state] arises from that purpose. ||27||

Viśvanātha: But how can you think otherwise? We have not come for the sake of union with your limbs; rather, because of the authority of Garga’s words that "there is no other equal to Nārāyaṇa," we have come desiring devotion to you, knowing you yourself to be Nārāyaṇa. Therefore...
Thinking, "Please have us remain right near you this very night and graciously allow us to serve your lotus feet," he says:
"From hearing [of You]" (śravaṇāt). Indeed, pure devotees do not desire even proximity, residence in the same world, and so forth, as much as they desire hearing, chanting, and other such services.

The sense is that this reputation has indeed been heard by you Vaiṣṇavas. In the alternative sense, passion (*bhāva*)—in the form of Kandarpa—does not arise from hearing and so forth in the same way as it does through close proximity;
therefore, do not go toward their houses. The connection is made by repeating the negative particle (*nañ*). Or else, it refers to the letter *a*, which is a synonym for the negative particle.
The meaning is that by way of close contact, one should not go toward houses [that are] not one's own. ||27||
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus heard these unpleasant words spoken by Govinda, the gopīs—
Dejected and with their resolutions shattered, they fell into a thought that was difficult to overcome.

Śrīdhara: Not explained. Vaṃśīdhara: Having heard this, Śrī Śuka said to Parīkṣit—who was asking what was said by them again—the word "iti," meaning "thus. [The words of the gopīs were: "Return; you must not remain here."
"Of slender waists" is the manner [of their description]. "Unpleasant" means that which turns back the longing of the mind.

"Despondent" means unable to either remain or go. "Whose resolve was broken" refers to those whose desire—namely, the mental wish, "We shall sport with the Delighter of Nandana"—has been shattered. "Anxiety" (cintā) is the unease of the mind caused by sorrow.

"Difficult to overcome" means unavoidable without the grace of the Blessed One. Alternatively, it means "especially dear. Those whose dejection (*sanna*) has departed are "depressed" (*viṣaṇṇā*); and those who are such and whose resolutions are unbroken—that is, whose desires have been fulfilled—form a single compound.

[He performed] reflection, deliberation, or investigation—which is difficult to transcend and which removes the suffering caused by the mind; for Yādava states: "The words *cintā*, *carvā*, and *vicāra* [are synonyms]. (28)

"Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā": thus [beginning with] "this is disagreeable" and so forth. Having heard this with its hidden meaning as if it were disagreeable, they fell into reflection. The sense is that, not having understood the underlying intention, they became anxious. ||28||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, this statement regarding Govinda as the Lord of Gokula was spoken clearly and explicitly only concerning Gokula in general—how much more so concerning His own [people]—and yet it was a disagreeable word.
This is because its intention remains uncertain due to its touching upon two possible meanings, given the nature of their longing. Regarding those [gopīs]:
They were despondent because only equanimity remained manifest; therefore, they were tormented.
Since their resolve—the long-cherished desire for union with his limbs—was shattered, they fell into an insurmountable anxiety, a brooding born of failing to attain the desired object. This...
Though his nature was once tender and softened by love, he has now become utterly hard due to our misfortune.
Therefore, what should we do now—should we entreat him with piteous words and falling at his feet? Or should we respond with a retort?
Or perhaps, exerting ourselves for a moment to maintain our composure, should we turn back toward Vraja out of feigned indifference?

The meaning is that they reflected: "Could we possibly determine the intent of this one whose depth is so difficult to fathom? Or rather, could we immediately cast off our lives—either directly before him or indirectly by such means as entering the Yamunā? ||28||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: this is the title. It refers to that which was spoken by Govinda—the Lord of Gokula, the object of his own innate abundance of love—or that which was said [by others] as something disagreeable due to the force of supreme love, either because of an immediate failure to grasp the intended meaning or because of perceiving the literal sense as unpleasant.

The meaning is: having heard something undesirable, or rather, the opposite of what is dear, or something hateful; or else, because her intention was uncertain due to its touching upon two possible meanings, they understood it as being precisely unpleasant to them because of the weight of their longing.
Therefore, they were dejected and tormented;

for their resolve—that is, the mental aspiration directed toward the specific service of Him—had been shattered. Consequently, they fell into an endless and insurmountable anxiety, a brooding born of the failure to attain their desired object. This...
Though his nature was once tender and moist with love, through our misfortune he has become utterly hard-hearted.

Therefore, should we now entreat him with prostrations and piteous pleas? Or should we go to Vraja with a reply, or perhaps by exerting ourselves for a moment to maintain our composure out of sheer necessity?

The meaning is that they reflected as follows: "Either by returning, we might determine the intent of this one whose depth is so difficult to fathom; or else, we might immediately abandon our lives—either directly before him or indirectly through such means as entering the Yamunā."

Or rather, they experienced a thought characterized by despondency, such as "Alas! What indeed shall we do? Where shall we go? and so forth; or, being dejected, they fell into reflection. There are two causes for their dejection: first, hearing something unpleasant; second, [the loss] of the most beloved person.

Because supreme suffering arises of its own accord merely by hearing unpleasant words; furthermore, "broken" refers to another [cause]: the meaning is that one's own long-desired object is shattered through total indifference toward sense objects. ||28||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.

Regarding the *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): next, following the hearing of such words from Kṛṣṇa, there is the description of their state through the three verses beginning with "vipriyam ākarṇya" (having heard the unpleasant [words]).
Since, due to reasoning, there is no certainty regarding his intention because of the two possible meanings,
and since the rejection [of him] alone is clearly manifested through its compatibility with her longing,
his words are disagreeable to them and cause their despondency and so forth; for in both cases, anxiety is appropriate.

Even in gestures such as averting the face, there is no disruption of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Furthermore, it is stated here that even when the heroine herself makes an advance, she may draw a line on the ground with her foot. (28–30)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, due to the profundity of the Lord’s words and the intensity of their own longing, even those who are exceptionally learned understood the meaning exactly as they heard it;
thus, according to the maxim that "the hearts of kinsmen are apprehensive of what is undesirable," there was a perceived harshness in those words.
Knowing that they had reached such a state, he says "iti" and so forth. Having heard Govinda’s speech, the gopīs fell into anxiety. Of what kind? "Iti vipriyam"—disagreeable in this manner;
or, in another sense—even though it was agreeable (*priya*) in its various (*vividha*) and specific (*viśiṣṭa*) ways. Thus.
The word "api" (even/also) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. ||28||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, having perceived the state of mind of the gopīs—who were tormented by the heat of separation and were unaware of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s intention—Śuka speaks, making it heard to all, describing the matter in the manner previously stated: "When he spoke with insistence, 'Go back,' [the thought arose: 'He is abandoning us...'"
When the meaning "he does" was thus determined, they regarded returning home again as being like vomiting;
yet, because he was the son of the Lord of Vraja, they considered his word to be inviolable, and thus,
fearing the stain upon their beloved, they were devoid of any desire to abandon their bodies.

Slightly comforted by the remembrance of the call of the nectar-like sound of the flutes marked with their own respective names, they thought: "We shall enjoy these nights together"; yet, failing to obtain that promised object and becoming distressed regarding their beloved, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s departure elsewhere was forcibly halted by our presence in the midst of the forest.
Suspecting that he was calling them there only to mock them, thinking such a response would be improper,
and seeing themselves as if fallen into a fire reaching the clouds, the gopīs were devoid of any sense of what ought to be done;
they were ignorant of his particular cleverness, or rather, they did not speak of their mutual passion to one another.
Or rather, concealing the loss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhaṅga*) in harsh speech; or rather, exhausting their own aesthetic flavor along with that [of the speaker];
they fell into an insurmountable and endless anxiety. The cause for the onset of this anxiety—

He said: Govinda is he who has taken a vow to protect Gokula; for it was said, "By my own yogic power I shall protect [them]; this is the vow I have undertaken. Alternatively, he is Govinda because he finds (vindati) the senses (gāḥ) as objects of enjoyment. Or else, he is Govinda because he finds the cows that are the Vedas in the form of the Upaniṣads.

He is Govinda because he finds [the world] as his own possession. His speech—his word—is "vipriya," which means that from which the pleasant has departed due to its harsh expression; yet in reality, it is "viśiṣṭapriya" (distinctly dear), because through the function of its underlying intent (*tātparya-vṛtti*), it establishes [the truth], having not been rendered unstable. This is now evident upon examining the underlying intent.
This knowledge was indeed unpleasant because it was followed by such a powerful undesirable consequence;
hearing as if a marvel this unpleasant news regarding their beloved object of affection, they became despondent, having fallen into despair,
and being unable to provide a fitting reply, the functions of their speech and other senses [were suspended].

Because of that very contradiction, when dullness has arisen in the mind, they reach a state resembling a wall or similar objects, due to being devoid of any sense of duty and because of the certainty of death. As it is said in the Rasārṇava:
"Due to the failure to complete an undertaking, the non-attainment of what is desired, or through calamity..."
But that remorse which arises from the full recognition of one's transgression—
That despondency is threefold, based on being superior, middling, or inferior;
seeking companions, means, and reflection are considered [the primary factors] in the superior type.
Lack of enthusiasm, despondency, and so forth are considered the intermediate [mental states].
The consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*) of the lowest [state] would be despondency, staring, weeping, sighing, brooding, parched mouth, and the like. (Rasārṇavasudhākara 2.10–13)

Regarding that, he states the qualifying reason: "with their resolves shattered. Those whose resolve—that is, their desire—is shattered. He specifies that very desire: "Having gone to the region of Vṛndāvana, we shall indeed behold Kṛṣṇa."
Conversation with the beloved and glancing from the corner of the eye.
Embracing, scratching with the nails, and likewise touching; the drinking of the nectar of the lips, and the arousal of the hair—these constitute enjoyment.
Then, one should speak of one's own desired object, smell it from all sides,
constantly go into its presence, and always maintain meditation upon it.

Because such a desire had been frustrated, they fell into anxiety: "At the time of granting the boon, he was not known to be like this; now, due to the adversity of our own fate, he has become clever at speaking unpleasant words.
Now that we have set out for Vraja, who knows what might happen? At this moment—
They were not even able to remain still; due to the overwhelming force of the prohibitive words, they fell into a desperate state of anxiety, wondering, "Where shall we go? What shall we do? ||28||

Viśvanātha: He who finds (*vindate*) or obtains (*labhante*) various kinds of speech-plays (*vāg-vilāsān*) is Govinda; his speech (*bhāṣitam*). From the root *bhāṣ* meaning "to speak clearly," it follows that [he utters] clear sentences.
Having heard that very [speech] which is unpleasant, yet endowed with the puns of sound (*dhvani-śleṣa*), it becomes unmanifest (*avyaktam*) in its pleasantness for him.

The meaning is: "even though [the truth] has been correctly understood by their intellect. Not perceiving any cause for the unpleasantness of his clear speech, yet doubting whether even his indistinct speech might be pleasing, they—due to the arising of dejection born from the underlying emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love—think: "Truly, he disregards us because we are unworthy."
Having decided, "It is indeed so," they became despondent.

"For whose sake we came here, disregarding our husband's family, our father's family, dharma, fortitude, fear, shame, and the like—he indeed disregards us. With their resolutions shattered, they fell into anxiety: "What..."

Should we entreat him with words faltering with sobs? Or, exerting ourselves with feigned resolve and artificial guile, should we turn back toward Vraja to ascertain the disposition of this one whose depth is unfathomable? Or rather, should we abandon our very lives?

And in that regard, would He do so directly or indirectly, perhaps by entering the Yamunā? Alas, having abandoned our lives, how could we behold His glorious face? Therefore, having abandoned [our lives], how shall we remain here, or how shall we perform the "eating of vomit" consisting of the worship of the husband and others as ordained by Him?
"How shall we prevail? Where shall we go? What shall we do?"—the meaning is that they became thus bewildered as to what ought to be done.
[The Lord], having summoned the flocks of *cātaka* birds that were the multitude of *gopīs*...
When Kṛṣṇa rained down poison by the sound of his own flute, they drank it immediately, utterly amazed;
for who among them would abandon their own vow? 28.
Having covered their faces with their hands, they sighed, their bimba-like lips drying from the breath; scratching the ground with their feet, they lamented.
Wiping the saffron from their breasts with the swords they had seized,
they stood silent, burdened by a weight of immense sorrow.

Śrīdhara: He describes the state of those who have fallen into anxiety with the words "having done so" (*kṛtvā*). Having cast their faces downward (*ava*), their lips—which resemble *bimba* fruits—are drying up due to the breath rising from grief (*śucaḥ*);
likewise, they are scratching the earth with their thumbs, and [their eyes] are filled with tears stained by collyrium (*kajjala*).
They stood silent, washing the saffron from their breasts, for they were those who bore the burden of immense suffering. (29)
Vaṃśīdhara says: if one asks what they became when filled with anxiety, he replies with the words "having made," etc.
By the "upward-moving" (udgata) breath—that is, the vital air (prāṇavāyu)—the bimba-fruit [lips] become exceedingly soft and red. Regarding the word *adhara*: it refers to the lips (*oṣṭha*).
According to the Medinī lexicon: "The word *adhara* is masculine when referring to the lip; otherwise, when not referring to the upper lip, it is used as a common noun."

The sense is that her lips have become parched by the heat of the fire of internal grief. In this regard: "A beautiful woman, pierced in her limbs by the arrows of Love, with her vulva perspiring, bends her face downward and scratches the ground with the nail of her big toe."

Thus, it should be understood that she has displayed a state of being well-known from the *kāma-śāstra*. By the word "tears" (*asraiḥ*), it is indicated that they have manifested the internal torment of love through their eyes.
Because harsh speech is inappropriate for tender faces, the mirror is implied by the phrase "having cast down their faces."
Remaining silent, they reflect: "Though his nature is moist with affection and tender, he has become utterly hard due to our misfortune;
let him be entreated by grasping his feet, touching his chin, and so forth. Or rather, what is the use of a reply?"

Perhaps, by exerting effort for a moment through the support of fortitude, we might ascertain the intent of this one whose depth is unfathomable and difficult to fathom; or else, we might immediately give up our lives there,
whether in his presence or out of his sight, by entering the Yamunā or some other means.

These are mere conjectures. Furthermore, is it perhaps due to our own delusion that others have arrived who are actually different from those we know, and he is speaking thus out of ignorance to test us? Or is it for his own inquiry as to what should now be done? Or else, having heard such an exceedingly cruel collection of words, do we still live even now?
Thus, for her own observation: what is the use of looking at the face?

For the lotus-faces of their lower-lip bimbas are withered by the smoke of sighs from the fire of grief; they are almost closed because of its oblique nature. Or rather, is it because of their perception of [her] own moon-like state upon seeing that [face]?
"His non-appearance is due to the closing of his lotus-eyes for the purpose of warding off delusion"—thus there are many other [explanations] as well; enough of this elaboration. ||29||

The *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā* states regarding "having done" (*kṛtvā*) and so forth: "They say it is indeed thought. All these [heroines] are threefold according to the aforementioned classification of *dhīrā*, *adhīrā*, and so on. And thus:
"A *madhyā-dhīrā* [heroine] would burn [her lover] with anger through a dear, sarcastic, and indirect speech."
The *dhīrā* (composed) woman expresses herself through weeping, while the *adhīrā* (uncomposed) woman does so through harsh words.
(*Sāhityadarpaṇa* 3.72). When all three types speak together simultaneously, there is a threefold mode of speech for each.
As in the examples: "by those who have taken up swords" (*asrer upātta-masibhiḥ*) and "having wiped their eyes" (*netre pramṛjya*), etc. (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.30).

Those who are both steadfast and unsteady, whose voices falter due to agitation—these are the *adhīra* (unsteady). As for those described in the upcoming verse, "The feet do not move even a step" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.34), they are the *madhyā-dhīra* (moderately steadfast). ||29||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: For this very reason, they remained silent. For a moment, due to being overcome by supreme anxiety, the functioning of their faculty of speech did not manifest. By the words "śucaḥ" (sighing) and "śuṣyat" (drying up), the heat and length of their breath are implied; the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) indicates the uninterrupted nature of that drying.

The word *bimba* implies a ruddy hue and tenderness; therefore, the extreme parching and withered state of the lips are already indicated. Scratching the earth with the foot—that is, with the big toe of the left foot—is an indicative mood (*anubhāva*) of anxiety. Its meaning is: "O Earth!
May you split open; we shall enter. Thus, she remains standing upright.
It is understood that the phrase "by those who have taken up the *masī* [cosmetics]" indicates the streams of tears as they wipe away the saffron from their breasts;

the plural number is used here to express the abundance of those streams. In all these cases, the cause is that they are "burdened with the weight of great sorrow," meaning they are overwhelmed by immense grief.
