The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, having described the manner of their external state, he also speaks of their internal state with the word "on the ground" (*urvī*). By this, a condition equivalent to fainting is indicated; it is not mentioned directly because such a state is difficult to hear about.
The particle *smā* indicates what is well-known. Even by way of a jestful remark, one should not entertain the notion that such grief on their part is impossible.
This is the state of being. Or rather, it expresses astonishment: "Oh, the greatness of love! For even she experienced such suffering.
Or else, since indeclinables have multiple meanings, it signifies distress itself. ||29||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: For this very reason, they remained silent. For a moment, due to being overcome by supreme anxiety, there was no manifestation of the functions of the vocal and other senses. By the words "śucaḥ" (with grief) and "śuṣyat" (withering), the heat and length of their sighs are implied. "Bimba... [and so on].

The redness and tenderness [of her lips] are like those of a ripe bimba fruit; therefore, the extreme parching and withered state of her lower lips are indicated. Scratching the ground with her foot—that is, her left foot—is a sign of a particular state of anxiety. "O Earth! Be rent asunder; we shall enter," so she says to it.

This is the state of being. Thus, it is understood that they are standing upright. By the phrase "with their hands holding mirrors," the streams of tears are indicated as they wipe away the saffron from their breasts.
The plural number is used for those [streams] as well, with the intention of expressing their abundance. The cause for all of this is the despondency of great suffering.

"Bharas" means those [women] for whom there is a burden; by this, even though not explicitly stated, suffering, distress, and so forth are included. The meaning is that through that, pallor, paralysis, and other such symptoms have also arisen. "Sma" indicates well-known renown. The sense is that you should entertain the possibility that they possess such grief even through playful speech. Alternatively, it is used in the sense of wonder.

"Even for her, such suffering arose; oh, the greatness of love! These expressions of anxiety do not undermine the specific meaning of the forthcoming reply in the form of a refusal, because such [anxiety] is possible for women of noble family when there is a request made by a lover. Regarding them:
And because it has as its nature the emergence of the emotional states (bhāva) that are not incompatible with the aesthetic flavor (rasa). ||29||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
[Prīti-sandarbha 355]: Meditation (*dhyāna*) is called reflection (*cintā*)—as in the verse beginning, "Having made faces full of tears," and so forth. (29)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He describes the manner of her anxiety with the words beginning "having... (*kṛtvā*). Having cast her faces downward; of what sort? Those in which the lips are parched by the sighing (*śvasana*) that arises from the cause of grief (*śucaḥ*);
by this, the long and hot nature of the sighs is suggested. With her foot...

They did not write anything upon the ground intentionally; rather, having taken up their brushes with tears mixed with collyrium, they stood silent, wiping away the saffron from their breasts with those very tears. They said nothing at all. Why did they not speak? To this he replies: it was because of the burden of great sorrows.
In these [states], because they are permeated by a heavy burden of suffering, there is a choking of the throat; thus, from this, the engagement of passion occurs.
"Sma" indicates certainty. ||29||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Regarding the phrase "having done so" (*kṛtvā*), it describes the external and internal state of those overwhelmed by anxiety due to grasping the meaning as they heard it. They remained silent for a mere moment because, when there is a stupor born of anxiety, a response does not manifest. Having done what? Having cast their faces downward (*avāñci*).

Having cast a harshness upon the face of Śrī Kṛṣṇa because they could not bear what was seen there, she describes them with a qualifying term containing a reason: those for whom the burden (*bhara*) of great (*uru*) suffering was heavy; for even another person, overcome by a load, turns his face downward, and thus [they did so] due to the grief (*śucaḥ*) arising from sorrow.

Their lips, resembling bimba fruits, wither from an exceedingly hot breath; for when their minds are scorched by a heavy burden of sorrow, even the breath becomes heated, thereby drying up the ruddiness and tenderness of the lips. This very state is the nature of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*); thus, there is dejection (*dainya*).

It is indicated [as follows]: scratching the earth with their feet—that is, with the marks of their big toe nails—as if longing to enter a chasm; or rather, even the Earth reproaches you for being fit only for the enjoyment of the Boar, for you do not feel that same sorrow which arises from her husband’s indifference.

The scratching of the ground is done with the intention of asking, "Do you know why you do not give us a place to enter? Or else, for Queen Sītā, who is overwhelmed by a heavy burden of sorrow due to her husband's indifference:
"Just as you gave a place [to the earth], so too should you grant us a place."

Of what sort are they? They are those who, with their hands stained by soot—those hands which have taken up or grasped the *maṣi*, that is, the collyrium—are wiping or washing away the saffron from their breasts. The underlying sentiment is: "Enough of this collyrium and saffron on the breasts for those who have been neglected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. By this, the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as loss of color (*vaivarṇya*) and paralysis (*stambha*) are indicated.
"States are to be known"—and furthermore, "heavy with the burden of suffering" means that internal fainting and so forth are to be understood.
By the phrase "they stood silent," lack of enthusiasm and agitation are shown. (29)

Viśvanātha says: He describes the outward manifestations (*anubhāva*) of anxiety with the words "having made... and so forth. By saying "having cast their faces downward," shame (*lajjā*) is implied. Out of deference to love, we have now attained shame precisely through the abandonment of our natural modesty;
for even though we are women of noble family whose shame is concentrated in abundance, [we have now become ashamed].

The abandonment of shame is indeed caused solely by love (*prema*). And in the opinion of those who know the essence of love, that [abandonment] occurs only in what is praised (*saṃgīta*), not in what is censured (*vigīta*). Moreover, this is the very definition of love: that which excessively subjugates even the Supreme Lord, its own object, is called love. Therefore, if...

When this Kṛṣṇa, the object of our love, did not come under our control, we realized that our love itself was non-existent. What was the cause for this abandonment of shame? It was remorse, shame, and anxiety. In explaining the remorse, he describes their faces: what were the faces like? From *śucaḥ*, meaning from grief.

The sense is that those [lips] whose bimba-like lower lips were drying through the hot breath of a rising wind— just as when ripe bimba fruits wither in the heat of the sun, their bulk diminishes and they become clearly darkened— so it was with the lips due to shame and anxiety.

He explains: by scratching the earth with their feet—that is, with the big toes of their left feet—their intention is: "O Earth! Split open; we shall enter into you. He explains their grief and torment:
they are wiping the saffron from their breasts with tears that have taken on the quality of ink (kajjala).

By this, the poetic suggestion (*dhvani*) is implied that the carpenter of separation, with the saw of great remorse, has applied two lines of dark thread to split [the heart] in two. By the use of the plural "with tears" (*asraiḥ*) and the present tense "wiping away" (*mṛjantyaḥ*), the continuous flow of the tears like a stream is indicated.
It is not even stated that they moisten their inner garments with so many tears;

rather, it is merely imagined thus: in the dispute between the two Yamunās arising from her eyes—intent on extinguishing—and the fire of anguish arising from her heart—intent on drying them up—it was seen that neither achieved victory nor defeat.

The sense is that those who bore the burden of immense suffering remained silent, as if their consciousness had departed due to an inability to endure that weight; consequently, the phrase "they stood" implies that they remained upright like lifeless dolls whose consciousness had vanished. ||29||
To Kṛṣṇa, who was speaking as if he were someone other than their beloved, they, having renounced all desires for the sake of that purpose, [said]:
Wiping their eyes, which were impaired by weeping,
those who were deeply devoted spoke with voices somewhat faltering due to agitation.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "dearest" (*preṣṭham*): they spoke with voices faltering due to a certain intensity of agitation and the onset of anger. The cause of this agitation is expressed by the words "dearest," and so forth.
They were addressing one who was replying as if he were someone other than their beloved, as if rejecting him. (30)

Vaṃśīdhara: Not only did they remain observing silence, but he says "and moreover" (kiṃ ca) to indicate that they were also saying something. He says "dearest" (preṣṭham) because speaking of one's suffering is appropriate only for a most beloved person. "Gadgada" means faltering syllables. By the word "saṃrambha," the biting of the lower lip is implied.

It has been indicated: [he was] "repudiating"—that is, rejecting—the enemy who was otherwise dear to him; the meaning is that even at that time he was saying such things as, "Abandon your anxiety, do not weep, be composed, go home," and so forth. For his sake—that is, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—he was "turned back," meaning abandoned. All [of them].

Because he is the lord (*pati*) of all desires (*kāma*), those [women] by whom he is desired as their object are thus described. "Afflicted" (*upahate*) means distressed by weeping (*ruditena*). "Devoted" (*anuraktāḥ*) means unable to abandon him.
*Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: [She saw him] rejecting even her most beloved, dearest one, as if he were someone other than her dear one, or as if he were merely someone other than her lover. Now, why did she not turn her mind away from him? To that, it is said: for his sake—that is, for the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—by means of the object [of her desire].

The sense is that they were turned back in such a way that not even a trace of connection with them remained, for those [women] by whom all other desires distinct from Him had been cast aside. Therefore, the meaning is that they were unable to turn Him back.
Why? Because Kṛṣṇa, by virtue of being a mass of supreme bliss and by His power to attract all hearts...
And [they saw] the son of the illustrious King of Vraja, renowned by that very name.
Now, how could those overcome by great sorrow even be able to speak? To this he says: "With agitation," etc.
The sense is that because of indignation—which is the effect of despondency—it serves as a veil over that despondency. In that state, there was the wiping of the eyes.
And that [state] arises from the conjunction of two emotions by its very nature as a mixture of affection and anger;

it consists of words preceded by a glance at her venerable face. Thus, in the ultimate sense, "shame" is understood to be somewhat relaxed, because the element of despondency is included therein; the resulting effect of those two is a faltering voice (*gadgada*).
"Being devoted" is the cause in every instance, such as despondency and so forth. ||30||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: [One should approach Him] who, though most beloved and dearest, acts as if He were someone else's beloved, rejecting [the devotee] like an unpleasant person. Now, one might ask: "In that case, should the mind be withdrawn from Him? To this he replies: "For His sake"—that is, for the sake of attaining Śrī Kṛṣṇa—or rather, for Him.
They have been specifically turned away from that ineffable and most secret object, as well as from the particular sports with Him;

though naturally attached, they have been forcibly cast off. They are those by whom all desires—whether the enjoyment of sense objects or every other remaining longing—have been abandoned. Therefore, without Him...
The sense is that nothing else whatsoever is pleasing in any way at all. Why? Because [he is] Kṛṣṇa, whose form is a mass of supreme bliss, who attracts the mind, the delight of Śrī Yaśodā.
For this very reason, the word "sva" (one's own) has been used here even with the particle "ayi," which is said in view of common usage and so forth. Or alternatively:
Regarding the meaning of "afterwards": because an immediate response does not arise due to the weight of her great sorrow, she did not speak immediately;
one might indeed suspect that she might have felt some contempt for him due to excessive persistence. To this he says:
"She is devoted," because through her devotion she dispels that suspicion. Or rather, even if there were contempt...
The meaning is: because of the inability to abandon it, or because of the cessation of inquiry.

Now, one might ask: how can those overwhelmed by great suffering even be capable of speaking? To this he says: having especially wiped his eyes, which were afflicted—that is, pervaded—by weeping due to great suffering, with tears flowing of their own accord.
Having wiped away [the tears] and removed the tears; in an alternative reading, even in the reading *pramṛjya*, the meaning is the same.

"With supreme effort" means having resorted to a momentary support. Or rather, even though there is the power of speech over a vast region, it appears that passion alone is the cause, because love possesses manifold playful manifestations (*vilāsa*). And therefore—

She rubs her eyes to produce moisture, either by her very nature of overflowing love or for the purpose of speaking after first beholding the Blessed One’s face; thus, in the ultimate sense, the disappearance of her bashfulness is understood. The word "slightly" (*kiñcit*) indicates the smallness of her agitation due to [the Lord] being naturally most dear to her.

Or perhaps because of their tender nature due to their own love; or rather, they spoke with indistinct voices through an ineffable and great agitation, since they were deeply enamored. Something else was also suggested by them; or rather, they did not say anything at all, such as "it is thus" or "it is so," and so forth. Why?

"Of voices faltering with agitation" means that their throats were choked with tears due to the onset of affectionate anger. Why is that? "They are devoted. This means they were naturally devoted even before; now, upon hearing such words, their passion has become especially intensified by a further surge of longing.
Alternatively, the meaning is that she has developed a particular passion [for him], and is not even indifferent (*upekṣā*).

Or else, because something indescribable is expressed through various words of affection, which are themselves charming, such speech serves as the cause [of her state]. "The most beloved," and so forth; [referring to him] who speaks unpleasant things at every step.

Just as before; or rather, by means of the present tense indication, the meaning is that he speaks every moment unpleasant words such as, "Abandon your anxiety even now! Do not weep! Be at ease! Go home!"—the word *iva* (as if) is used here because, when one investigates the actual intent, it pertains to a jest or the like.
Because of the conclusion. And that has already been written before:
"I bow to those Śrī-Nāgareśvarīs, by whose very grace that [truth] regarding Śrī-Nāgareśvara is understood from the spoken word. (30)
The *krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, regarding the fact that the words of the Blessed One possess two meanings, due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of various recollections, there arises a reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*) as to whether "this" or "that" [is the meaning], and not even for the subsequent one.

Anticipating that they might be struggling, [the author] reveals their intention to speak by showing that they have gained the power to speak due to the slight easing of the burden of their sorrow, beginning with the words "preṣṭham" (dearest): "This dearest one, our beloved, would never speak such an unpleasant thing; reflecting on how he could have said it then... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "as if something other than dear": the word *iva* connects with "spoke to Kṛṣṇa. Of what nature were they? They were such that all desires had been turned away—that is, brought to a complete cessation—for the sake of Him.
Having done what? Having wiped their eyes, for the purpose of beholding His face; [the implication being] that there was nothing else present here.

Having reached a decision, agitation arose; by that, their voices became faltering and half-articulate. As for their eyes, how were they? "Afflicted by weeping" means swollen and red; "anuraktāḥ" is a statement of their actual nature. "Sma" indicates wonder.
The plural number here implies that all of them spoke in succession, and it should not be understood as occurring all at once.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Regarding the emergence of the transitory moods (*vyabhicāri-bhāva*), it was stated that the cause was precisely the description of what is disagreeable.

Now, because the permanent mood (*sthāyi-bhāva*) has become firm, they have gained some confidence; with their lips quivering from the onset of anger, they began to speak. Thus he says: "The Beloved."

Thus: "O dearest one (*preṣṭha*)"; though most beloved, He appeared as if other than beloved, as if unpleasant—but not actually unpleasant—due to their examination of His state (*bhāva*), yet not by way of their own mental fluctuations (*hṛd-vṛtti*). By the maxim of "driving in a pillar," they [perceived] that very state as the True Self (*sadātman*), and not as a mere quality (*guṇa*). This is the meaning of what was said: that the conventional (*rūḍhi*) [meaning] has its scope in the etymological (*yoga*) [derivation].
According to the maxim "it carries away [the mind]," the word *kṛṣṇa* is conventionally established as referring to the son of Yaśodā and Nanda.

Because the Queen of Vraja has departed, He is capable of fulfilling the desires of all, and is endowed with the qualities of intense sweetness (*ghora-lālitya*). The definition is given in the *Rasārṇava*:
Completely free from anxiety regarding his parents, beloved by his mistress,
clever, in the bloom of youth, and possessing the qualities of steadfastness and grace.
This is declared to be its essential nature; all qualities are considered to be qualities [of that].
Now, having rejected [all things], why did they not go home?
To this he says: "All desires have been turned away from that object"; that alone is the object, the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*).
For the sake of attaining that [state], all desires—objects pertaining to this world and the next—have been turned away from and abandoned by them;

for, due to the manifestation of the bliss of pleasure previously experienced, those [desires] appear as if newly covered over. As the Śruti says: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss."

Because they had no other recourse, they remained right there; having somehow taken hold of their wretched state, their speech was initially paralyzed due to being overwhelmed by a burden of grief. Now, however, perceiving her glance slightly softened by compassion, they spoke and gave their reply, for they were deeply devoted.
The meaning is that, due to her exceedingly firm affection, the faults of the hero do not manifest [to her]. Having done what?
Having wiped her eyes, which were obscured by weeping; for the wiping away of tears was performed because, out of eagerness, they were an obstacle to perceiving his complete beauty.

And there, because they were proud with the weight of their passion, yet remembering his rejection, they spoke with slightly agitated, faltering voices; that is, their voices were somewhat faltering and indistinct due to a slight anger born of love. The sense is not that they became despondent. ||30||

Viśvanātha: Then, why do you weep like those in a forest? Why do you not quickly go to your respective homes while Satya, with a gracious countenance, is present? By these words of the Lord, uttered loudly and entering through the path of their ears, they were awakened from their swoon.

They made a certain request, as he says: "He who was previously most dear to you because his body had been joined with yours many times, and who now speaks words exceedingly harsh, saying, 'Serve each your own husband—who is like a stranger to you and hostile toward you—without any cause whatsoever. And this is not at all [to be wondered at]."

It might occur; therefore, for that purpose, they have been brought about in such a way that even a trace of connection with anything else does not exist for them. Because the word "other" (*anya*) is not used here and the word "all" (*sarva*) is employed, it signifies the bliss of the Blessed One.

The intention of Śrī Śuka is that [the Lord] is not described by the word "kāma" (desire). The sense is: having wiped away the eyes that were blinded and impaired by weeping, [they thought], "This end of ours has arrived; let us die even once more after beholding this lotus-face," out of such longing. Alas, alas!

"How can such a life-ending punishment be inflicted even upon one who has been a lover, and for no offense at all?"—from such a thought arises agitation (*saṃrambha*). Furthermore, because we lack the corresponding beauty, qualities, and so forth, we are unfit for physical union; therefore, thinking "we shall abandon [him]," there is an absence of agitation (*saṃrambhābhāva*).

And so: "those whose voices are faltering due to some degree of agitation. Now, one might object: since they are devoid of love in either case, it would be more appropriate to simply desist from them; to this he replies: "they are enamored.
The sense is that those blinded by passion cannot endure rational deliberation. (30)
The gopīs said:
"O Lord, you ought not to speak such a cruel thing."
Having completely renounced all sense-objects, take refuge at the base of Your feet; O Lord difficult to restrain, favor us as devotees,
just as the Original Person favors those seeking liberation.

Śrīdhara: "Nṛśaṃsam" means cruel. O you who are difficult to restrain and act according to your own will, favor us—us who have served at the base of your feet as devotees—and do not abandon us. ||31||

Vaṃśīdhara: O Lord, O Master of my life! [This is] cruel, like the essence of a thunderbolt, tearing the heart with its hardness. The use of "mā" (do not) is due to the inequality of suffering or because of the nature of women. We are your devotees; do not abandon us. Otherwise, as it is said: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way I reward them."

The statement in Gītā 4.11, "I favor those who favor Me," would otherwise be rendered meaningless. O you who are obstinate and stubborn toward your own [interests]! Or rather: O friend, abandon completely (ā) this stubbornness (duravagraha) which is so difficult to restrain. The illustration is as follows: just as the Primeval Person, Mahā-Viṣṇu, [acts] toward those seeking liberation through their desire for liberation...
"He does not abandon those who worship Him," as stated in such passages as "In whatever way men approach Me... (Gītā 4.11).

In reality, however, *avagraha* means the obstruction of rain; thus, *duravagraha* means being free from that obstruction. The meaning is: one whose nature is to shower down the desired objects of His devotees.
Alternatively, he is "Bhavān" (the Lord) because he possesses *bhāni*—either the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) or rays (*gabhastis*)—and thus he is the Moon;

or he is "Bhavān" because he possesses *bhā-bhayadāḥ*—messengers who cause fear—and thus he is King Yama. Even by the Moon, Rohiṇī was cherished while other wives were abandoned; and Yama, indeed, is the one who inflicts suffering upon the worlds. And he...
And he ought not to speak cruelly, because you are different from those two; therefore, do not speak thus—this is the meaning. ||31||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "Not so," and so forth. For in these [devotees], during the state of experiencing suffering, there is the perception of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as possessing complete sovereignty; whereas in the state of experiencing pure bliss, there is the manifestation of His supreme loveliness (*parama-priyatva*). Indeed, the manifestation of the Lord through love is never sublated.

For the ignorance of His lordship is born of delusion, whereas love is the destroyer of delusive knowledge. Indeed, love is the instrument for valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus, when the experience of suffering remains uncontradicted and His lordship manifests as it truly is, they speak according to reality: "O All-pervading Lord! We have no dependence on anything whatsoever, only..."

"You alone are our sole refuge," they say: "Having abandoned all sense objects through total renunciation, we are Your devotees; do not forsake us at Your feet. We are not women driven by lust. To indicate the reason for their abandonment, they say: "Since You speak so cruelly and harshly, therefore You ought not to speak such harsh words to us."
Thus is the objection based on his knowledge of dharma: "For so long you have taught nothing but dharma;
now we shall teach you dharma. Devote yourself to us, for the abandonment of devotees is indeed unrighteousness."
"What use have I, who am independent, for dharma and adharma? To this he replies: "O you of difficult restraint, O self-willed one!
Just as the Primeval Person (Ādi-puruṣa) favors those seeking liberation, so too do you favor us.
The Primeval Person is Nārāyaṇa; he does not abandon those seeking liberation. [In the other sense,] he is not independent.
[The word] "bhavati" [is used]. Thus, the meaning is: "How does one worship? If that is so, this acceptance of devotees is indeed a religious duty (*dharma*).
[The objection follows: "He does not abandon even those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), yet you abandon even your devotees; oh, what hardness there is in you!"—this is the censure. ||31||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "The Śrī-gopīs said... Here, it should be analyzed as follows: although it is possible for a simultaneous manifestation of identical speech to occur due to having attained an identical state of emotion (*bhāva*), nevertheless, because speaking all at once would result in excessive clamor and thus fail to produce the highest aesthetic relish (*rasa*), [the Lord spoke] to certain principal gopīs.

This statement should be understood as follows: it refers either to the simultaneous conclusion of those respective great sentences, such as "Therefore, be gracious to us, O Giver of Boons" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.33), "Sprinkle me,
my dear" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.35), "Be gracious, O Destroyer of Suffering" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.38), and "Place that [within us], O Lord" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa...).

Thus, each [goddess] has presented her own intended statement ending with the fourfold formula, either sequentially or by first establishing the statements of those preceding her. And their fourfold nature arises from their being situated in groups according to the four directions. Nevertheless, of all of them...
And their being present before Kṛṣṇa is like [the description] "surrounded on all sides by circles of many rows of people" (*puru-rāji-maṇḍalaiḥ abhyānanāḥ*).
I bow to those Śrī-Nāgareśvarīs, by whose very grace the true nature of speech is known regarding those [other goddesses], the Śrī-Nāgareśvarīs.

Obeisances to the Blessed Lord, the beloved of the lives of the assembly of Śrī Gopīs. Now, [the Gopīs say: "Whether our devotion to You by abandoning husbands and so forth constitutes dharma or adharma shall be considered later. Alas!
For Your part, however, the fault of unrighteousness in abandoning us is difficult to avoid. Thus they say: "Not so" (maivam). "Not so" (mā).

The negation is placed at the beginning because of extreme distress and agitation. "In this way" means something like this, even though it resembles her words; what more need be said? This is the meaning. Why?
Because it is cruel (*nṛśaṃsa*), meaning it pierces the heart with hardness like the core of a thunderbolt (*vajrasāra*). Or else:

"Directly murderous," "cruel," "a killer," "fierce"—thus says Amara. To speak clearly means to say; or rather, what need is there to mention speaking, let alone acting? And in that regard, Your Honor is renowned for having a nature tender with love—this is the meaning. Furthermore, O Lord! He [addresses him].
"O Lord of our lives! Therefore, it is simply not fitting for you [to speak thus] toward us"—this is the intended meaning.

Here, because it is stated that [his voice] was "stammering with agitation," even in cases of wretchedness and the like, *praṇaya-kopa* (loving anger) is to be manifested through either word or tone. Thus: "Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.18).

The sense is that such words as these, though spoken by you with respect, according to logic, and even gently, are intended solely for the purpose of turning [him away]; thus, because they obstruct the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), they are in fact the opposite in meaning. By this, the response to the first quarter-verse beginning with "svāgatam" [is to be inferred].

"Now then, O sweet-spoken ladies! What should I do?"—in anticipation of this inquiry, they say: "Devote yourself to us; follow us by fulfilling our desires. Why? Because they call themselves "devotees at the very base of your feet"—this is an expression of wretchedness. The omission of metaphors such as "lotuses" [for their feet] is due to their statement of their own cruelty.
This is said with the intention of [refuting] hardness and so forth. By this, the answer is given to the verse [beginning with] "What is dear? (18b):
"Indeed, I truly honor the wives of the illustrious cowherds; however, it is only proper that my conduct be for the benefit of your husbands and others, and not of such a kind as this."

Regarding this, they say: "having completely renounced" (*santyajya*). Having thoroughly abandoned all objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), such as husbands and so forth—with the firm resolve never to take them up again—because these things are contrary to your worship.
By this, the entire passage beginning with "the health of Vraja" [18c] and ending with "is being milked" [22d] is explained.
The answer is: because all of them are included within the sphere of sense objects (*viṣaya*), and by abandoning those, affection for the body also dissolves;
for without that affection, even such statements as "this night...
[19a] would be unworthy of acceptance.
They speak by way of contrast: "O you who are difficult to restrain, O you of stubborn persistence! Do not abandon us, for we have no other resort"—this is the meaning;

the implication is that otherwise there would indeed be a fault. How so? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] shows that even for the Lord, who transcends both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), there is a necessity to observe those very duties. Thus...

They say: "O Lord. In that regard, [He is the refuge] even for those seeking liberation, let alone for those desiring something other than that; or rather, for those not seeking liberation, who do not even desire mokṣa, but are solely devoted to bhakti—this is the meaning.
Or else, for those seeking liberation who do not wish to renounce anything other than Him, just as He...
"Out of regard for the vessel alone, You accept and take possession of everyone; likewise, please accept us.

In some readings, the word "bhajataḥ" appears with the accusative ending. In that case, however, the qualifying term "mumukṣūn" (those seeking liberation) is used, because [the Lord] makes them his own in both states—both as the means and as the goal.

He turns away those who have worldly desires—the meaning is that he does not abandon them even as they pursue him; thus, by the force of the sense, one should explain the word *bhajasva* by changing its grammatical case. Here, even for those who have attained firm devotion to Kṛṣṇa solely through His being the son of the illustrious Gopendra, [it is said]: "For whomsoever there is unalloyed devotion to the Blessed Lord... with all [other qualities].

For it is said: "The gods dwell there by virtue of their qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.18.12). All perfections such as liberation and all wondrous enjoyments are the servants of the great goddess that is devotion to Hari, following her like maidservants.

Thus, in accordance with what is stated in the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*, she serves all things—even those that are not directly perceived—such as knowledge and the rest. Therefore, although this subject matter consists purely of love (*prema*), it is also expressed in words as consisting of supreme sovereignty and knowledge; this is for the purpose of indicating the very greatness of her [the Goddess].

Impelled by powers such as knowledge, it manifests for the wonder of particular devotees. Alternatively, such a statement may arise from a sense of humility, wherein one’s divinity is contemplated through the manifestation of one's own greatness.
For instance: "O All-pervasive One! O Thou who pervades both the external and the internal!"—thus You [perceive] our entire state of being.
He already knows this. Therefore, we, being devoted, have taken refuge at the soles of Your feet; please accept us.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of rendering void such statements as: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).

"O venerable feet of the Knower of Reality! Why do you desire the pleasure of sense-objects? To this they reply: "Having abandoned... The implication is that, therefore, we desire only the bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-sukha*).
[This refers to] that particular sport with you.
Because it consists of the very essence and totality of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), being the manifestation of the playful ripening of love;
and because of the truth of Your own word, "In whatever way they approach Me" (*Gītā* 4.11), you too ought to worship us by renouncing everything else, just as we do.
This is a statement of hidden intent (*gūḍhābhiprāya*): "O you who are difficult to restrain! O you who act according to your own will! Do not abandon us who have sought refuge in you;

because you are the Supreme Lord, unrighteousness (*adharma*) cannot touch you at all, for that would contradict the scriptural teaching of your 'truthful resolve' (*satya-saṃkalpatva*). Furthermore, the loss of your promise would be utterly improper."

The meaning is as follows: even having abandoned all objects of sense, from sovereign empire up to the station of Vaikuṇṭha, you should still accept and embrace other people who are unable to abandon you—that is, those who do not desire liberation (*amumukṣūn*). In the second interpretation, "te" is taken as the dative case, meaning "to you" (*tubhyam*); thus, it does not mean "those desiring liberation" (*mumukṣūn*).
Or rather, it is the fourth [case], because you, O Lord, are worshipful by the entire world; otherwise, your status as a deity would not be established.

Even there, it is in the sense that the Blessed One is the Original Person (*ādi-puruṣa*) exactly as he is, in his fullness. And in this regard, even Abhīrī’s repetition of the first quarter of the verse spoken by the wife of the sacrificer [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.23.29] is due to a portion of her shared distress.

It should be understood that even when the cowherd women were in distress, the very nature of those whose souls were infused with cleverness was such that their requests were seen as having the purpose of refusal.

For indeed, it is not fitting for him to speak such cruel words as, "Let me do some such pleasing thing for you; tell me something with me," and so forth. The reason for this is that those very women who, having abandoned all sense objects, are devoted to the soles of your feet—how could he [speak thus] to them, who are otherwise so difficult to restrain and act according to their own will?

"Be thus; devote yourself to us with your whole being. To the point that "the powerful ones devote themselves only to their devotees and not to non-devotees," they provide an illustration by saying "O God.
In this matter, the underlying sentiment—that in reality all of this is merely a jest—is clearly expressed. ||31||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Since the Blessed Lord has here correctly spoken the first quarter of the verse beginning with "yajñapatnī," the blessed Śrī-gopīs likewise spoke the first quarter of the verse beginning with "yajñapatnī" in that very same way. In reality, however—
This is not so; for since his deceptive speech and their cries of distress would result in a correspondence through similarity, [the objection] is refuted.

The word "ma" (do not) is used at the beginning as a negation. The meaning is: "By reason of extreme distress and agitation, even such a statement—though somehow similar to this [deceptive] speech—is impossible; what more need be said? Why?
The meaning is that it is cruel, like the essence of a thunderbolt, in its hardness, and thus heart-rending;
or rather, it is a direct destroyer of life. According to Amara, *nṛśaṃsa* means a killer, a murderer, or one who is cruel.
To "gaditum" means to speak clearly, or even to utter at all; how much less, then, could he possibly engage in worldly discourse? In that regard:

And you are one whose very nature is moist with love; therefore, let someone else speak—this is the meaning. By addressing him as "Your Honor" (*bhavān*), there is respect due to prior praise intended as conciliation. Through wordplay (*śleṣa*), he is the Moon (*candra*), for it possesses the stars (*bhāni*) by presiding over them;
the meaning is that he who is the Moon, because he increases the ocean of desire, is certainly not worthy [of speaking].

Even in that regard—O All-pervading Lord! O Master of our very life-breaths! Or rather, since You are all-pervasive both externally and internally, You surely know every state of ours; therefore, it is not at all fitting for You to act thus toward us. This is the underlying sense. Thus, [the Lord spoke] with great respect: "Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.18), and so forth.
The sense is that even though it was spoken softly and in accordance with logic, because it obstructs the essence of love (*prema-rasa*) and was uttered merely for the sake of turning [her away],
it is in fact the opposite in meaning. By this, the response to the first quarter-verse beginning with "svāgatam" is to be inferred.

"O dear ones who speak so sweetly! If you ask what I ought to do, they say: 'Devote yourself to us; do not follow [others] merely by fulfilling their desires. Or rather, 'Serve us constantly'—the meaning is, 'enjoy us with love.
Why? Because the dust at the soles of your feet is our sandal."

This is the meaning. The reason for not mentioning metaphors such as "born from a lotus" (abja) is due to the intention of expressing harshness and hardness through the use of the term "cruel" (nṛśaṃsa).
Alternatively, the "foot" itself is the root—the cause or support—of all things. Those who are devoted to it are those who have begun the act of devotion;

here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the initial action (*ādi-karman*) and also in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.71. Thus, they are those who have commenced the practice of worshipping it.

"Even now," because of the lack of complete devotion; this expression of wretchedness and humility is made with the desire for the status of a maidservant. Alternatively, "has served" means "has taken refuge. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of rendering void such statements as: "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly" (Gītā 4.11).
By this, the answer to the question "What is pleasing? regarding the feet [of the Lord] is given:

"Indeed, O wives of the cowherds! Since you are always attached to household life through attachment to sense objects, your company is difficult to attain; why then should you be worshiped by me? For you who are not dispassionate, from where..."

What is meant by "being My devotee"? To this they say: "Having completely renounced... Having thoroughly renounced all sense objects—the goals of the senses—which are accomplished through [the mediation of] a husband and so forth, with a firm resolve never to accept them again;
for, since the attainment of Your lotus feet alone, which are the root of all things, brings about the fulfillment of all goals.

Or [it may be] due to opposition to your worship. By the renunciation of sense objects, the renunciation of the feet [of the Lord] and so forth is indeed indicated, since the husband and others are rooted in those [objects].
Or rather: O venerable feet of the knower of reality! How can you desire the pleasure of sense objects?
Regarding this, they say: "having abandoned [all else]. The sense is that, therefore, we desire only the ultimate bliss (paramārtha-sukha).
This is because the specific play with you is the very essence and the entirety of the core of all human goals (puruṣārtha), being the manifestation of the ripening of love.

The hidden intention is this: based on the truth of his own word, "In whatever way they approach Me" (Gītā 4.11), you too ought to worship us by abandoning everything else, just as we have done. By this, the answer to the statement "the well-being of Vraja" (18c) should be inferred.
The intended meaning is that, by abandoning all objects of the senses, even that [desire] falls into indifference; therefore, enough with speaking of its auspiciousness.
Now, O fickle ones! I fear unrighteousness (*adharma*). Regarding that, they say what should be practiced: "O you who are difficult to restrain! O... [he says].
O crest-jewel of those who act according to their own will! Or rather, O you of stubborn persistence! Do not abandon us, who have sought refuge in you and have no other resort.

For by abandoning those who have sought refuge due to being difficult to restrain, only unrighteousness (*adharma*) arises; and especially because it would result in the violation of your vows, such as being one of excellent conduct (*suvrata*). Furthermore, because you are the Supreme Lord, unrighteousness cannot touch you.
Such is the sense: the abandonment of one's own thesis (*pratijñā-hāni*) is indeed utterly improper. Alternatively, *duravagraham* means a stubborn persistence; abandon it completely.
If you say, "O talkative ones! You women are not suitable for me," then that is true.

Nevertheless, they state by way of an illustration that accepting all people who worship Him through total renunciation is the duty of a Great Person (mahā-puruṣa)—namely, "the Lord" (deva). The intended meaning is that as a deity, He must necessarily fulfill the desires of His own devotees; and in this regard, He is the Original Person (ādi-puruṣa).

He is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), because He has the necessary duty of fulfilling the desires of His devotees. In that regard, this applies even to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), let alone those who desire Him alone. Or rather, by eliding the letter *a* (reading *amumukṣūn*), the meaning is: those who do not seek [liberation] but are solely devoted to devotion (*bhakti*). Just as He worships them, so does He accept them.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "serve" (*bhajasva*). Alternatively, regarding the word "properly" (*yathāvat*), even so, by implication it results in a mere illustration. The sense is: "Just as he serves and accepts all of them merely out of regard for service, so too do you serve us."

Or rather, if it is argued, "O virtuous ladies! That action is indeed improper for me," they reply to that: even though the Lord is the Primordial Person (*ādi-puruṣa*) and expects worship from those who serve Him, He nevertheless serves those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), fulfilling their desires even by granting them liberation. Therefore, [His conduct] is not [inappropriate] because His dealings follow the will of the devotee.
The sense is that a fault would otherwise result. The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].

Alternatively, it refers to the supreme sovereignty accompanying the wonderful variety of the internal *mahābhāva* of the beauties of Vraja, who have attained firm devotion to Kṛṣṇa precisely because He is the son of Śrī Gopendra.

He describes it even though it is not useful for his own purpose; otherwise, the beauties of Vraja might think that they were ignorant of the true nature of the Lord. And that description of His majesty occurs only at a time of supreme distress, for at a time of bliss, they do not possess even the knowledge of His majesty.

Since it culminates in nothing but the experience of bliss, even there the sweetness of one's own essential nature (*nijabhāvamādhurya*) never undergoes any change. This is because, even in descriptions of His sovereignty—as in the verse beginning "O friend, when He appeared" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.31.4)—friendship remains unswerving. Thus it is said: "O All-pervading One, O Lord who extends both outside and within! (*vibho*)!

Thus, you surely know our entire disposition. Therefore, since we have taken refuge in you, the root of all, please accept us. Otherwise, there would be the contingency of rendering void such statements as: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that very same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).
Or rather, they say with a lingering affection: "O *bhaktābhaja*! [The term] *bhaja* means 'one who worships';

*abhaja* means 'one who does not worship. O *bhaktānām-abhaja*! [That is,] O you who do not even worship those who are devoted! O you who are difficult to restrain even toward your own kin!"—thus [addressing him] regarding all objects of sense.

Or rather, even having abandoned everything from imperial sovereignty up to the station of Vaikuṇṭha, those people who do not desire liberation and yet are unable to enjoy Your foot-base— because of the particular sweetness of Your foot-base that excels all else, please favor them; accept them, for otherwise the Lord's status as worshipful by the world would be otherwise.
The perfection of divinity; even therein, the Blessed One is the primordial Person (*ādi-puruṣa*) in his true and complete nature.

Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment in manifesting His own blessedness (*bhagavattā*). The general statement is for the purpose of strengthening one's own conviction by demonstrating the underlying logic. Therefore, they are yours; do not [abandon] us.
"Leave it. The rest is the same.
Although the words of the gopīs were spoken out of distress, Bhāratī, their friend, sang [the response] among the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, protecting their dignity through the use of double entendre.

For indeed, [He] ought not to say such things as, "I shall perform such a disagreeable and cruel act," or "Speak something with me. The reason for this is as follows: the meaning is that for us who have surrendered by renouncing all objects of sense, it would be a fault to engage once again in the enjoyment of those very objects. Why?

And [abandon] that which is difficult to restrain and difficult to grasp. Therefore, abandon it! Just as the Primal Person (Ādi-puruṣa) favors those seeking liberation, so too do You favor us; grant us the supreme state, and not the pleasure of sense objects—this is the meaning. Only then will there be for us a true welcome and great fortune, and the well-being of Vraja.

Or rather: those devotees who have abandoned all sense-objects and taken refuge at the base of your feet—serve them alone, however you wish, according to your own unrestrained will. Abandon us completely;
for the powerful ones serve only those who are devoted, not those who are undevoted.
Regarding this, they state an illustration: "O King. (31)
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. Regarding the *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): now follows their corresponding statement, beginning with "Not so" (*mā evam*).
The word "not" (*mā*) serves to reject their request; [it refers to those] who, having abandoned all objects of sense—including husband, sons, and so forth—[have attained this state].

Worship those very women at the base of Your feet in such a way that they become difficult to restrain and unrestrained; by using the term "base of Your feet," You proclaim Your own superiority over them. But as for us, who are not like them, abandon us even in matters such as the pursuit of right vision (*samyag-darśana*). For in that regard, there is the worship of others.

And regarding the renunciation of one's own [interests], he provides the example of the Lord (*deva*) as the conduct of the virtuous. For He, having abandoned sense objects, ritual actions, and so forth, favors only those seekers of liberation who worship Him, and no others;
thus says the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Not so," and so on. These are the middling [devotees].

The wise ones say: "Therefore, O Lord"—this is an address using an indirect expression. You are one whose vow is true, having declared: "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).
Thus, you ought not to speak such a cruel and harsh thing. Then, what should be done? They say: "Us..."

"Devote yourself; do not abandon me"—the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here because the fruit of the action is intended for the agent. In my devotion, the sole fruit is the fulfillment of my own promise. In what manner shall I devote myself?
To this they reply: "In the same way that the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Primordial Person, devotes himself to those seeking liberation. This is the meaning.

But he gives himself alone to them. [The King asks: "Does he not, in fact, grant them liberation itself? [The Sage replies: "If you ladies desire that, then I shall certainly give it. Go home. They said, "No; we have taken refuge at the soles of your feet as your devotees."
But we devotees do not care for liberation at all. Therefore, since this very example shows that there is no returning again in liberation, may there likewise be no returning again to our home;
rather, let us remain together. Having done what, then, should [the Lord] be worshipped?
Regarding this, they say: "Having completely abandoned all objects of sense, [one remains] just as they are," and so forth;
for we too are likewise. O you who are difficult to restrain! O you who are hard to attain! ||31||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, unable to endure even a moment without attaining the bliss of union due to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s state of stern reserve, they spoke in the manner of reproach; yet, not knowing how to manifest their pride, they, being truly overwhelmed, gave this reply: "Not so! O [Lord].
"O Lord! Because you are the son of the King of Vraja, it is improper for us to neglect you"—this is the meaning.

The word *bhavat* signifies one who is worthy of honor; thus, that which was spoken with such respect—"Welcome to you"—is not appropriate, for this greeting is fitting only for certain guests, not for us.

If it is argued that "I have indeed shown respect by asking a welcome," to that he says: [it was] cruel and harsh, because it produces suffering in its ultimate result, like food mixed with honey and poison. Regarding the word *gaditam*, this is the intended meaning: the verbal root *gad* means "in distinct speech"; how could it even be considered in the mind?

Furthermore, you, who are a supreme connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), are not at all unworthy to speak; indeed, O Lord, you are capable of specifically instructing us in the sequence of sweet flavors. Yet, you speak not to disrupt that very flavor by which we were drawn and have come here.
The meaning is that speech directed with respect toward objects characterized by sweet flavor destroys the stable emotional state (sthāyibhāva).
If it is asked, "In my inquiry after your welcome, what offense have I committed? Why is such a reproach being made even for that?
they reply to this: "What dear service may I do for you, as was promised by you? [18b]

If [he] has entered the path of your memory, then serve us; if beautiful vessels are poison, what of it? The meaning is that service alone is compliance with the mind. "Delight yourself by complying with our mind"—the implication is that otherwise there would be a breach of your promise. Furthermore:

They said: "Your question, 'Is all well with Vraja?', is not fitting," for [the residents of Vraja] have abandoned all sense-objects and come to serve at the base of Your feet— meaning to become Your maidservants— having renounced all objects of the senses in the form of non-returning to them.
The enjoyment of sense objects, however, is rooted in a husband and so forth; since that is accompanied by causes [of bondage], it has indeed been renounced.
If it is asked, "Why is servitude accepted, abandoning the master of the household? they say in response:
"The fragrance of even that happiness which comes from being the master of the household does not exist in the happiness found in worshiping You," as was already stated previously.

Having understood this gradation, husbands and other worldly ties were renounced. Devotion to you is the ultimate limit of happiness, while the pursuit of sense objects is the ultimate limit of suffering. Therefore, due to their opposition to devotion to you, they abandoned sense objects along with their causes; having realized them to be of the nature of suffering, they attained [liberation] through indifference toward them.

Furthermore, the implication is that it is not fitting for you to cause us to recall our suffering by asking about our health, when that suffering has been removed through your worship, which is of the nature of bliss. As it was said—"Tell the reason for your coming" [18d], they respond to that: "Do not [ask us]..."
The meaning is: "Abandon [this] acceptance of us; rather, grant us your acceptance. Know that we have come to cause you to accept us.
Of what sort are you? You are a god, and we are worthy of serving as your maidservants. This is the extreme humility we have declared.
Alternatively, [the meaning is]: "O Lord, Your nature is play (*krīḍā*), yet play depends upon one's own [possessions]. Who, then, is Your own possession?

Is it that the thought arises in someone's mind, 'Play is an activity manifested together with a circle of loved ones; therefore, this circle of loved ones should be immersed in suffering'? This is a rhetorical question (*kāku-praśna*). O You who are difficult to restrain!
"Again and again you sing, 'Return to your homes.

Or rather, even toward the wicked such as Pūtanā and others, there is protection (ava-avana) and subsequent care; thus, by the planets, there is a settling [of the mind] in Hari, as it is said: 'Even though she intended to kill Him, she gave her breast to Hari and attained His state' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.6.35)."
Because it has been so stated;

or rather, it means the protection (*ava-rakṣaṇa*) against suffering (*duḥkha*). One whose grasping (*graha*)—that is, obsession (*āgraha*)—is of that nature has had its secret essence (*sva-rahasya*) expelled by the inquiry into freedom from illness (*anāmaya-praśna*). Some wicked ones are to be killed, while other wicked ones [are to be subdued].
The sense is that it is not fitting for you to show partiality by thinking, "They must be protected.
Now, if one should ask, "What fruit will there be for me, who am indifferent and detached, in worshipping you?
they reply to that: even though He is the Original Person, the Supreme Person, and remains untainted, just as [He bestows grace] upon those who worship Him...

He honors those who worship Him with full devotion by bestowing the nectar of His own lotus feet; furthermore, He honors those seeking liberation by granting them liberation. You, however, O Lord, are primarily characterized by divine play (*līlā*), and since such play is dependent upon Your own will, it follows that no fault attaches to You in fulfilling our heart's desire—this is the meaning.
Or rather, O All-pervading One! O Inner Controller of all! Your own internal mental modification (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) certainly knows [our state];

therefore, if devotees were not to worship You, it would result in the abandonment of their devotional practice. Consequently, as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.25.18, "My refuge is the cowherd settlement," the transgression of this vow would give rise to unrighteousness (adharma).

If it is asked, "But what is this unrighteousness (*adharma*) of mine, who am the Lord? they reply: "O you of evil persistence! He whose resolve is wicked. For indeed, there is the abandonment of dharma in the form of devotion to the devotees, and the acceptance of unrighteousness in the form of the loss of one's own promise and the desertion of the people of one's own *vraja*."
Thus, having abandoned that stubborn persistence, serve us with the resolve expressed in the words "My devotee never perishes" (Gītā 9.31); the meaning is: fulfill our desire. ||31||

Viśvanātha says: "It is improper that you teach us dharma while yourself desiring to create a heap of sin," they say; [the Lord replies] "Do not speak thus. You have spoken to each person in such a way as to be cruel, murderous, and directly lethal.

The sense is this: as the son of Nanda, who is renowned for his righteousness, he does not deserve [this]; rather, let some other man, whose livelihood consists in killing humans, deserve it. According to Amara, *nṛśaṃsa* means "cruel," "murderous," or "fierce. By you, even if they were numbered in the millions, such word-arrows have been discharged at us all at once.
"Cast off as you have just now, let us all depart for the city of Yama after abandoning our bodies, and not for the village of Goṣṭhapura as you have instructed. As for you,
take upon yourself the sins of killing hundreds of millions of women and go to Goṣṭha yourself!"

"If you do not wish to kill us women, then, having abandoned all other objects of sense, devote yourself to us who have served at the soles of your feet with devotion. By using the expression "other objects" (*anya-viṣayān*) here,
it is implied that contact with the limbs of the Blessed Lord is not truly an object of sense.
"O passionate women! Is your desire not appeased by your own respective husbands, such that you abandon them and devote yourselves to me alone? To this they replied: "O Duravagraha!
According to the rule of Pāṇini (3.3.52), 'ave graho varṣa-pratibandhe,' *avagraha* means a cessation of rain; thus, *duravagraha* refers to one whose obstruction [of rain] is difficult."

In the phrase "one for whom there is non-rain due to the obstruction of rain," since it is the cloud itself that is relevant as the referent of the external object (*anyapadārtha*), and because of the application of the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*), the meaning is: "O you who rain only poison! O cloud!
And therefore, even though you are far away, you alone, the dark cloud (*kṛṣṇamegha*), are our kinsman, we *cātaka* birds.

"Due to the fault of fate, you are raining poison today because of drought. If you do not rain water, then do not rain at all; for having drunk that which is rained as nothing but poison, we shall die—we do not even drink the water of the nearby lakes and such—know this to be our intention."
This is the meaning:

therefore, do not abandon us; the sense is that you should maintain your commitment to yourself. Now, it may be true that female cātaka birds depend upon the cloud, but the cloud does not depend upon the female cātaka birds.
If it is argued that whether the *cātaka* birds die or live makes no loss whatsoever to the cloud, that is true;
however, you are not merely an insentient cloud, but rather the crest-jewel of the wise, equal to Nārāyaṇa. Thus he says, "O God" (*deva*), so that those seeking liberation may worship You.

The meaning is this: although You favor even those who desire to renounce all sense objects by granting their cherished goals—because You are subject to Your devotees—why do You not favor us, who have renounced the entire range of sense objects for Your sake? ||31||
O dear one, you who know the Dharma have said that for women, devotion to husband, children, and friends is their own inherent duty.
Let it be so; yet, O Lord, you who stand at the very step of instruction, you are indeed the dearest friend and the very self of all embodied beings.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, as for what you said—"O knower of dharma" regarding "husband, offspring," and so forth—that was said with derision. Let this [derision] apply precisely to you, who occupy the position of being a locus for such instructions. The reason for your being a locus for instruction is that you are the Lord (Īśa). For, by the statement concerning the desire to know (vividiṣā), all instructions [are centered upon Him].
The intention is that [this is known] from the realization of Your supremacy as the Lord (*īśvara*). The reason for Your lordship is stated: "Indeed, You are the Self.

For the Self alone is the Lord and the enjoyer of everything that is to be enjoyed; therefore, since You alone are the dearest kinsman among all kinsmen, the duty to be performed toward all kinsmen should reside in You alone—this is the meaning. Alternatively:

Since you, the teacher of dharma, are present at this place and occasion for the instruction of dharma, and since we are here desiring to know dharma, let it be exactly as you, the knower of dharma, have said. However, you are not merely a teacher of dharma; rather, you are the Self (ātman). Or else, that which was said—this...

Let it be so for a person within the scope of the *Upadeśa-pada* (the path of instruction); but since you are the Lord, the Master, and the very Self (*ātman*) of embodied beings in the form of the fruit [of their actions], how could it not be so for you? Or rather, as it has been said, "Service to the husband and others is *dharma*"; let this be so for you alone.

Why? Because [the word] "pada" refers to the station or basis of those such as the husband who are taught in the *Upadeśapada* as being worthy of service. Why [is it not the Lord]? For no one—such as a husband, son, or the like—is designated by these names without the Lord as their underlying basis. The rest is the same. Enough with excessive detail. ||32||
Vaṃśīdhara: Regarding what was said—"O virtuous women, you must serve your husbands"—they reply with the words "Even though... and so on.

"One who knows dharma" means one who knows the treatises on the duties of women. "With derision"—because of the traditional law (smṛti) stating that "the highest duty is the protection of the distressed," since he abandons us who are distressed, his instruction on dharma is a source of ridicule.
The meaning is "thus. This refers to what has been stated here. The sense is that it concerns the subject matter of instruction, that is, within the scope of the teaching.

"Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting"—by this [scriptural statement], all instructions regarding the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, and so forth, are established.
The intended meaning is that the Supreme Lord alone is the means of attainment (*āpti*). The Lord is indeed the enjoyer;

for without an enjoyer, objects of enjoyment would be purposeless, like the house of one who is not its master. Since he is the Self, he is therefore the dearest kinsman, because he is the object of unsurpassed love. And thus says the Śruti: "This [Self] is dearer than a son..."
"Dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, is this Self which is more internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8). The sense is that it is the Self of all.
Furthermore, they say that while instruction is appropriate when there is a distinction between the teacher and the taught, it is not so when there is identity; and thus: "Now..."

Or rather: as for what was stated in the *Dharmaśāstra*, let that teaching indeed apply to an ordinary person (*prākṛtajana*) who falls within its scope; but does such a state of being within the scope of that teaching exist for you, the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign? The meaning is: it does not. This is a refutation of what was previously stated.
"Kāku" is a feminine noun denoting a modification of sound caused by grief, fear, and so forth; thus says Amara.
To the question, "Why is the Lord not an object of instruction? he replies with the words "yataḥ" (because):
since only the seeker (*sādhaka*) is an object of instruction, it is stated that the goal (*sādhya*) is to be attained through instruction.

Regarding the phrase "in the form of the fruit": although you have stated that service to one's offspring and so forth constitutes dharma, they say that even this is so because, according to the manner previously described—such as "by watering the root of a tree"—when the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is worshipped, those who reside within it (adhiṣṭheya) are themselves worshipped. They state this with the words "Or rather" (yad vā). He raises a doubt concerning the reason for this with the word "Why? (kutaḥ).

He raises a doubt regarding the cause even in that case of a presiding substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—asking "from where?"—because in the absence of a presiding substratum, there would be an absence of those things to be presided over. The rest remains as before. Alternatively, it means that for those women whose passion (*raṅga-rāga*) follows after [their husbands] such as the Lord (*pati*), that alone is their own duty (*sva-dharma*).
The sense is: "but not for us, your devotees. The sense is: "because they [the devotees] are beyond the reach of ritual injunctions.

In the Lord Vṛndāvana, which is praised even by Brahmā, Indra, and others; or else, it is so called because its very selves—the individual souls—are "bandhurāḥ," meaning bound by the fetters of love. Or else, [it is so called because...]

For embodied beings, the Supreme Self alone is the kinsman, and not others such as children and so forth; for it will be said to Uddhava, "I am the kinsman, the teacher, and the friend," and because of such statements as, "The self alone is indeed the kinsman of the self. (32)
*The Chest of the Caitanya Doctrine*: Furthermore, you are a knower of dharma; we are women, and even among them, we are cowherd girls (*gopīs*).

Nevertheless, some mature women said: "Whatever the sequence [of events], do you consider that to be dharma or adharma?"—beginning with the words "husband, children," and so forth. The term "of women" (*strīṇām*) refers to women in general, and not [to us alone].
"Self and others. [The phrase] "O dear one! by you, a knower of Dharma," is an ironic censure (*ākṣepa*), based on the impossibility of [you] having offspring of your own.
The meaning of the word "spoken" (*uktam*) is this: according to the maxim "who is poor in speech?", what is the use of what has been said?
Only when it is possible to cause [the truth] to be experienced does it attain the status of instruction (*upadeśa*). Therefore, this...

Instruction does not lead to direct experience. How so? To this he says: "Let it be thus," and so forth. The meaning is that this word of instruction may apply to you, O Lord; for only then does instruction become purposeful.
Alternatively, "me" is a singular expression; "me" means for me—that word of instruction from you should remain with you alone.
The particle *eva* is to be applied everywhere. The meaning is: "O Lord, let it remain with you alone; let it not falter.
For a cowherd, lightness alone is desired for each of the husband and the others.

It would result in the burden of following [you] everywhere; however, since your compliance extends to all places, the sense is that for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that alone should be done. For you are indeed—the word "kila" signifying certainty—the beloved friend and the very Self (*ātman*) of all embodied beings. Through connection with you alone, all dear ones, kinsmen, and even their own selves [become dear].

[The verses] proceed as follows: "Even the devotion to offspring rests in you alone; thus, one should not suspect a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa), because it is stated that [this devotion] is directed toward a common woman. Therefore, the same applies to friends and mothers who have conceived love for you.
What need is there to mention others, such as husbands and sons?"—such is the intended meaning. ||32||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might object: "Since her own duty has been stated in such passages as 'service to the husband' and so forth, how can she transgress it? Anticipating this objection from the perspective of the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*, [the author] refutes that view by resorting to the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, and through her intuitive insight, superimposes the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) upon him [the Lord].

They argue that by refuting his doctrine, we commit unrighteousness (*adharma*), as expressed in the words "husband and wife. This is said with derision, on the grounds that he is a knower of dharma (*dharmavit*) because he has mastered the meaning of all scriptural teachings according to the principles of the sūtras: "For therein all the Vedas find their source" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.13) and "But that [Brahman] is established through the harmony [of all texts]" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.14).
Regarding the object of that purport: therefore, let this sentence of instruction be directed toward you alone, the Lord, in this very manner of service.

[The opponent asks: "But how can the status of being denoted by the word 'That' (tat-padatva) belong to me? To this, they reply with a subtle quibble (*sac-chala*), using the particle *kila* in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).

How is it that you are the self (*ātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and even possess such a nature? To this they reply: "The state of being the self (*ātmatva*) consists in being the object of unconditional love, for one is indeed the dearest to all embodied beings. Therefore, because of that, you are the *ātman*; and furthermore, because you are the dearest to all, you are the *paramātman*. Likewise, you are the kinsman (*bandhu*) of all."

The Supreme Self, who acts for the benefit of others without any limiting adjuncts, is likewise such by virtue of being the illuminator of all; therefore, since you alone are He, your oneness with Him is established. Thus, the sense is: "I wish to serve you alone."

Or rather, O you who are honored by the class of those of virtuous conduct! Granted that you may renounce sense-objects, your own duty must certainly be observed. To this they replied with malice: "As for 'patī'...
Thus, let this very status of being a fit recipient of instruction belong to you yourself, the one who gives such instruction; you alone are the source of that.
The meaning is "you exist.

Now, how is this so? To that they say: "the dearest," and so forth. He is the dearest to all embodied beings—that is, to all living creatures—the attractor of their hearts, the kinsman who brings about the welfare desired by all. For this very reason, he is the Self (ātman).

Whether [the Lord] is the presiding deity of the heart or its impeller, what fault of ours is there? Rather, the fault is yours alone; indeed, you yourself are the one who ought to be instructed so as to abandon such a fault.
This is the meaning.

Now, as before, the position of divine lordship (*aiśvarya*) is also tenable; and that has indeed been explained by them. In that regard, since both meanings are accepted by us without distinction based on the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*), nevertheless, in this context, "being an enjoyer" (*bhoktṛtva*) should be understood as nothing other than "being a ruler" (*īśitṛtva*), just like the state of being an enjoyer [implied] in the designation of a king. Otherwise—

Because the intended meaning is not established in the case of the falling away from life; however, the general reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) is made with a view toward its being an illustrative example and with a view toward establishing that [the Self] is the essential nature of all things. In the second [section], the phrase "but not... and so forth is to be understood through an interrogative intonation (*kāku*); thus, the Supreme alone is the teacher, for the Self is not [otherwise].

The phrase "the Self alone" implies the absence of being a teacher. Therefore, the intended meaning is that since we lack the status of a teacher and have directly realized the Self, we do not fall within the scope of injunctions such as service to the husband (*pati-śuśrūṣā*).
According to the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava school, there are two other meanings. Alternatively, as it has been said: [1]→

[2][Author: ALC] Thus, in that context, the meaning of the first case (prathamārtha) is that [the Lord] is chosen as the locus (*āśrayatvena*) within the Master (*svāmin*), as in the passages beginning with "of the gods, sages, beings, kinsmen, and ancestors. Therefore, having thus established *dharma* by means of the greatness of His worship, [the author now proceeds] also by means of an investigation into the nature of reality (*vastu-vicāra*).
It is rejected.

As for the phrase "or else," it refers to the state of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*), which is the state of being the non-dual ground for the manifestation of each respective [object], according to the Śruti: "By whose light all this shines. Here, in the context of the meanings of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the word "kila" indicates certainty. This is the section on the teaching (*upadeśa-pada*).

Thus, the meaning is "one whose lotus feet are to be taught by the scriptures. They also explain it here as follows: "May this [instruction] belong to you alone; you yourself, having become a woman by conquering [the senses] in the form of Mohinī, should practice the dharma of serving a husband and so forth. Why? Because [the word] *upadeśapade* refers to a guru.
The meaning is as follows: otherwise, there would be no engagement by the disciples in an action not authorized by the guru.
And they say, "O dearest one," implying that you alone are capable in this matter. "Bandhu" means the self, whose nature is captivating; and here it has a prohibitive sense.

"O dear Kṛṣṇa! As for what was said by you—even though you are a knower of dharma—that the obedience of women toward their husbands and others is their own duty (svadharma) and is truly not adharma; the meaning is that this was propounded through a deceptive interpretation, by means of a different application [of the words].
This is because of the underlying intention [of the verse] beginning with 'He who bears [the world] without guile' (amāyayā yo bharati). Thus, O Lord, this is indeed the truth."
The meaning is that the teacher is capable of speaking and acting upon everything. The sense is: "Let all that rest in You alone; therefore, You Yourself must become the one to be instructed.
How so? To this they say: "Of those who bear bodies"—meaning the four kinds of living beings situated in Śrī Vṛndāvana and other places.

Furthermore, the beloved one (*preṣṭha*) is the object of love; the kinsman (*bandhu*) is the agent of love. For this very reason, they are the self (*ātman*), as in the verse: "The saintly are my heart, but I am the heart of the saintly" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64).
The meaning is that they are mutual abodes of each other's hearts. Therefore, if you yourself [are present] among these infinite [saints]...

The meaning is: "If you should become dispassionate [toward them], then we too shall likewise become so toward our own [possessions], however small in measure, through the application of things as they are and through the attainment of Dharma. And therein lies the humorous intent: "Be dispassionate toward us first!"

Alternatively, regardless of how the construction is interpreted, the point is this: since it has been stated that "service to the husband" and so forth—meaning the compliance with husbands and others—is the duty (*dharma*) of women, may this very thing be so in Your case, O Lord, who are the giver of such instruction; the sense is that the *loṭ* suffix here is appropriate for expressing a command (*anujñā*). For:

"Preṣṭha," and so forth. The meaning is that the deliberations of the husband are known only to us; thus says the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*. Now, O you who are honored by the class of those following right conduct! While objects of the senses may indeed be abandoned by you, your own duty (*svadharma*) must certainly be observed. Regarding that, [the author speaks] with derision:

They say: "That which... The word *aṅga* is an affectionate address. It is said "in the Lord" (*īśe*) because Vṛndāvana is remembered as the supreme, being praised even by Brahmā, Indra, and others, since it has been seen and heard [by them].
Or else, since you are the Lord of the entire Vraja, the statement "in the Lord" (*īśe*) and so forth is made. Precisely for the sake of avoiding what was stated [above], it is not...

However, according to their own inner disposition, He always manifests to them specifically as the Śrī Nandana, whose form is the condensed sweetness of existence, consciousness, and bliss; thus He is their *preṣṭha*, their most beloved, and not merely dear in the same way as others. And in that regard—

Among all embodied beings, even among all living creatures, there is no other who is a kinsman, a benefactor, or a friend to more than two or three, because the Self is indeed the Supreme Self—this is certain. The implication is that service to You alone is the supreme dharma; in comparison to that, everything else must be abandoned. Thus:
It has been said—"One should perform one's duties for that long" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.20.9), and so forth; this has already been written above.
Something else has been suggested by them:
namely, that even though you are a knower of dharma—one who understands the true nature of dharma—you have spoken of "your own duty" (*svadharma*).

The meaning is this: "The passion (raṅga) or attachment (rāga) belongs only to those women who are favorable toward, or devoted to, the service and compliance with their husbands and so forth, but not to others like us, for whom you alone are the beloved. Therefore, the sense is that in comparison to her, everything else is indeed to be disregarded. The reason for this is as follows:

Demonstrating His supreme dearness in every way and speaking with sound reasoning, they pray: "May it be so!
