He is the most beloved of all embodied beings, indeed of all living creatures; how much more so of us? The reason for His being the most beloved is that He is our kinsman, our benefactor, and our very bliss by nature.

The meaning is "an object of affection. Or, [it means] "the one who causes [us] to will"; thus, His nature as an external and internal benefactor is stated. Alternatively, it refers to that in which the selves—the individual souls—are beautiful through devotion, bound by the fetters of love, or are dear. Therefore, this is our own duty, or rather, the duty of all embodied beings.

"Let it be with you alone," meaning "and in that regard, in the manner we desire. It is not stated directly because it must be kept strictly secret. The reason for this is as follows: the two words *upadeśya* and *upadeśa* refer to those who are to be instructed and the instruction itself, which are said by all scriptures or by gurus to be worthy of worship through the renunciation of everything else.

"In him whose [there are] the glorious feet" means: the sense is that it is indeed proper that even one's own duty (svadharma) should be abandoned in comparison to your lotus-feet; otherwise, one might ask: "Since you are a knower of the essence, then let what is required be made manifest. To this [it is said]:
They pray with great earnestness:

"In the manner thus described, or for this reason, may you yourself—O Ānanda—not merely through an incarnation or other means, but directly, be the most beloved, the dearest kinsman, and the benefactor of all embodied beings, including even the servants and followers; how much more so for us?"
By these two words, mutual affection is intended. For what purpose? With you as the object.

Of what nature are you? You are the locus—the objective sphere—of that specific instruction regarding our desired worship which has been given by teachers and others, or by friends and others, in order to avoid rashness.

The meaning is that its non-mention [here] is because it is established by that very [means]. In this regard, for women, that [attainment] is established by their own nature alone; for men, however, it is through mere disposition (*bhāva*). Alternatively, it should be understood as occurring in another birth for those whose passion for that [state] is intense, such as the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest. This is the general statement.
[This is said] out of extreme longing and love.
Or rather, let this [instruction] abide in You, the Lord, the Master of those like us, who occupy the position of a teacher;
for You are our kinsman, O Ānanda, of beautiful nature, and for that very reason, the most excellent among all embodied beings.

Or rather, "it is thus" is an admission made with a touch of resentment. Regarding all instructions—those concerning you, your worship, or the words of other gurus and so forth—it is because [the authority] rests in the Lord, the Supreme Lord, or the Absolutely Independent One; or else, even there, it rests in you, the Lord of our very life.
Is such cruelty even possible among embodied beings—among us women who possess bodies?

O giver of bliss, is it indeed the body, or the husband, or the beloved who is our kinsman? By no means; rather, you alone are the most dear. Or rather, because the self is that which sustains the body, the self alone is the kinsman.

But by the elision of the vowel *a* (*a-kāra-praśleṣeṇa*), you are "most beloved" (*apreṣṭhaḥ*). Or, the particle *kila* expresses a conjecture (*vitarke*); thus, by means of intonation (*kākvā*), the meaning remains the same. The sense is: "Do you perhaps conjecture that we are unable to abandon our bodies? Just as those who have already been liberated from their bodies, we too shall [abandon] our bodies this very moment for your sake.

The sense is: "We shall abandon [them]. This is the answer to the statement, "This is the night. Because there is no fear of the terrible [beings] and so forth when disregarding the body, and because there is no purpose for going toward Vraja since You alone are to be worshipped, these three matters [would not exist] without Your sovereignty. In this regard—

This is not right. The meaning is: let that [fault] rest upon you alone; you yourself, having become a woman, must perform the duty of serving your husband and others. Why? Because [the rule states], "in the case of a teacher who is the locus of instruction.
Otherwise, students would not engage in an action that has not been performed by their teacher. And in that regard, you yourself...

They say, "He is capable"—meaning He is the Supreme Lord, the most capable one. Furthermore, one should not think that because of Your artificial womanhood, no one would feel affection for You; they say, "The Dearest," because Your very nature is the most excellent of all.
And this is the underlying meaning: "Obedience to husband, son, and friend is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of women.

In this regard, I am your friend, as it has been said, "O auspicious ladies, [you are the friends] of his kinsmen. Therefore, regarding what was said by you, who know the law: "O Kṛṣṇa, let my desire be fulfilled," may it indeed be so.

"So be it," "so shall it be"—these are four words. May that very thing belong to me, my lord and husband, at the station of instruction; for at the station of the scriptures' sound teachings, such as "for women, the husband alone is the teacher (guru)," he is indeed the master. O virtuous ladies! Let it be so—the husband.

Let it be so followed; however, today in the beautiful Vṛndāvana during the autumnal moonlight, let them experience the bliss of fearlessly beholding the forest and other sights at my side, for I have been accepted as their friend by all the residents of Vraja and as the object of their love. To this they replied: "O Dearest One!"—referring to you.

The meaning is: although you are the most beloved kinsman of the embodied beings who belong to Vraja, O Ānanda, you are of a fickle nature; because of this fickle nature, there is no trust in you. Or else, regarding what was said by you, the knower of dharma—that following husbands and others is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of women, yet it is truly *adharma* (unrighteousness)—[that too is not to be trusted].

"Let it be so with you alone, because you are the Teacher; in what way? You are the Lord, capable of saying and doing everything. Furthermore, people will not speak ill of you as you teach in such a manner, for no one will find fault with you since you appear in the form of the most beloved among all embodied beings. (32)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: Now they refute that instruction by means of the meaning of the scriptures, beginning with the words "yat paty-apatya" ("that [which is said regarding] husband and offspring"). "Svadharmaḥ" (one's own duty) means "su-adharmaḥ" (a very great unrighteousness). The term "dharma-vid" (knower of dharma) is used ironically.

It has been stated that this was established through quibble (*chala*), because in the passage beginning with "service to the husband," there is an intention to apply the words otherwise. This is a statement of instruction for the removal of unrighteousness (*adharma*): "Let it rest upon you alone—the teacher, the master, and the one of independent conduct; you yourself must turn away from unrighteousness."

The meaning [of the verse] is as follows: To the question "What then happens to you?", they say, "O Dearest One. You, our kinsman, our very self, of beautiful nature, are indeed the dearest to all living beings; therefore, by that very fact, we shall all become auspicious—this is the meaning. (32) [This is stated] specifically because she herself acts as the messenger.
The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) in the form of a prayer is to be seen in the commentary on verse 41.

Regarding the composition of the *Bṛhat-krama*: immediately after [the statement], "Then they abandoned their bodies composed of the modes" (*bhā.pu. 10.29.11*), even those who had attained perfection at that time [did so] by abandoning their material bodies.

Out of a lack of fortitude, they say: "That which begins with 'husband, children,' etc. O dear one! As for what was said by you, a knower of dharma—that for women, service to husband, children, and friends is their duty—let that remain as mere instruction for you alone, who are the one who gives such instruction, and not for us. Furthermore, by us... (Note: The text provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

"It has been abandoned along with their bodies. This is a statement addressed to a person: "Let it be upon you," meaning, "May you become a partaker of such suffering. That suffering is fitting for you alone;
because you are the Lord (*īśa*), you are capable of enduring everything—thus he says, "O Lord" (*īśa*). Now, out of the power of anger...

Reflecting that what was said was indeed improper, she says: "Peace! Peace! May that never happen to you—that you, who are the dearest friend and the very self of all embodied beings, of every living creature! 'Kila' (it is certain) expresses the subsiding of the emotion of anger. By this [statement], for women who are devoted to you..."
The continued pursuit of a husband, children, and so forth is nothing but great torment; the meaning is that this may never happen to anyone at any time. ||32||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: [Objection: "But surely sense objects are abandoned because they are tasteless in their ultimate transformation; that was well done.

However, dharma—characterized by service to husband, children, and so forth—is abandoned; that was not well done, because dharma produces happiness in its ultimate transformation. [Your] acceptance of an illicit lover is not good, for it is tasteless in its ultimate transformation."

If it is argued that [serving the husband] causes suffering, they respond with derision to his instruction on dharma—which disregards the sequence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own words—by saying "yat patyā" (that which is called 'husband'), being unable to endure such a teaching. They address him with the term "aṅga," meaning "O friend! as a form of address.
It is evident that you have rendered great service by instructing me in the Dharma; for it is said that obedience to husband, children, and friends is the inherent duty of women.
May all that has been spoken by you, who are a knower of such dharma, remain with you alone. Why? Because you are the Lord (Īśa).

He is the controller of Brahmā and others, capable of restraining even them—how much more so us? Or rather, according to the words of Garga: "Equal to Nārāyaṇa in qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.19).
Since His power has been manifested through such acts as the lifting of Govardhana, He is therefore the Lord of the entire Vraja.
The meaning is that the Lord is the refuge, being situated in the position of a teacher because He is the son of Vraja’s king.

For whoever is a master bestows instruction in dharma upon all; therefore, by virtue of His lordship, let all that which is to be performed for husbands and others—such as service and so forth—rest in You alone. Thus it has been said:
"Just as by watering the root of a tree [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.31.14]," so do the maidens,

who are personifications of the Vedas (*śruti*), state this established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "When you are worshipped, everything becomes worshipped," because you alone are both the kinsman and the very Self (*ātman*) of all embodied beings, of all living creatures.

By propitiating you, the propitiation of all living beings will surely be accomplished; how much more so that of our husbands and others? Therefore, through the means of propitiating you, what need is there for the service of husbands and others as described by you? Thus, without the propitiation of you...
The service being performed toward the husband, children, and others would result in non-service,
like watering the branches [instead of the roots].
Or else, [it refers to] the women who are our relatives— wives, children, and friends— as well as ourselves and others.
"You yourself have stated that for embodied beings, devotion to the Lord is their own duty.
Moreover: 'Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.'"
"O son of Kuntī, declare this with certainty: 'My devotee perishes not.

[Gītā 9.30–31] Furthermore, as for what you have said—"Women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras, they too attain the supreme goal"—let that remain with you alone, since you are the dearest object of my affection.

Let that which is to be done toward objects of affection be directed toward you alone, based on the realization that in reality no one is an object of affection. Furthermore, a kinsman (*bandhu*) is so called because he binds (*badhnāti*) others through mutual love;
let that which is to be done toward such kinsmen other than yourself be directed toward you alone—why [should it be otherwise]?
And since you are the Self, let that which is to be done for the Self rest with you alone.

Or rather, as for what you—knower of dharma—have said, "O dear one, that women’s duty is obedience to husband, children, and friends," this was not intended as instruction for those like me who are dear to you. For them [it may be so].
Let it be so regarding the place or occasion for instructions; this is not an occasion for instruction, but rather an occasion for delight.
Moreover, while You, the Lord and Controller, exist, there is no room even for Your own command, because You—

The meaning is this: for us embodied beings who exist solely for your sake, you alone are our dearest kinsman and our very self; therefore, since you are the Self distinguished by all virtues, nothing at all appears to us except through affection for you.

Alternatively, the young maidens present their own view: for women, there is no duty other than devotion to you. But you have stated that by causing them to abandon devotion to you, service to the husband and others is their true duty. In our view, however, devotion to you consists precisely in following the will of the husband and others.

In between, there is even greater unrighteousness (*adharma*). There is one unrighteousness characterized by the abandonment of devotion to you, and a second unrighteousness characterized by following [others] such as a husband after having abandoned him.
These two forms of unrighteousness cannot be accepted by us; therefore, this [is the nature of] the instruction.
Let these two types of unrighteousness abide in You alone, who are the locus and the object; they do not belong to us, for we lack the capacity [for them].

In what kind of You? In You, the Lord (Īśa), since it is heard that both righteousness and unrighteousness, as well as knowledge and ignorance, reside in the Lord; this applies only to those in whom the manifestation of Your lordship [is perceived].
Let those incited by you proceed toward unrighteousness; as for us,
however, you appear through your own example to be the dearest kinsman and benefactor of all embodied beings.

Alternatively, you—who know the nature of dharma—have stated that for women and other embodied beings, service consists of compliance with, attendance upon, and acting in accordance with husbands, children, friends, and others; and that this is their own duty (*svadharma*), meaning "it is our duty just as it is yours. This has been said in the Gītā: "I am equal toward all beings; I have no [partiality]..."

"There is neither one who is hateful nor one who is dear" (Gītā 9.29)—let such equal vision toward all beings, which constitutes following and pleasing others within the sphere of instruction as taught in the *Upadeśapada*, reside in you alone. You are the agent who does not depend on instruments (*upakaraṇa*), and the Self is the impeller by way of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*); such is [the nature of] this.
The sense is that even for those who have come here having abandoned their own dharma, though impelled by you, there will be no further engagement in this dharma.
Alternatively, it means that having said "with lack of faith" because nothing at all was obtained through service to husbands and so forth;

"Now, considering that these women must be instructed in their duties, you—who know the dharma—have placed us under your discipleship and spoken as a guru, declaring 'this is the duty of women. Yet, though you claim to be a knower of dharma, you have taught this with a deceptive intent; thus, your words are sarcastic, for you are merely a 'knower of women's duties' in the guise of a deluder."

When you said, "Some were being led away by you, while others were made to drink the nectar," you should remember what was taught by that statement; even now, you must learn from your own example that one should merely speak such words, rather than performing service to a husband and so forth. Now, you teach that "instruction for others is the mark of wisdom" at every step.

"I abide in the form of a guru. Having abandoned that, you must rely on the duties of a woman and serve our husband and the others. As it has been said: "Whatever a superior person practices, others strive to do likewise" (Gītā 3.21). By this principle, may this very instruction find its place within you alone.
The meaning is that the Lord is capable of doing everything; indeed, nothing whatsoever is impossible for You.

Although You are most beloved, through this instruction You appear like one who is unkind; as the very kinsman of embodied beings, You Yourself bind them. Causing them to abandon service to Yourself, You impel them toward service to a husband and others.

The self is its kinsman; through ignorance, it has another self as its enemy. Therefore, for those who know the true nature of things in this way, and who possess firm impressions from the teaching "the Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," this instruction regarding service—preceded by the renunciation of such meditation—is of no consequence whatsoever.
Let [the fruit of my merit] rest in You alone as its locus;
let it not terminate with us, for You are the dearest to all embodied beings, the attractor of their hearts, the kinsman, the bestower of desired fruits, and the conscious Self. Therefore—

Only for those whose very life is centered on you and who are impelled by you would the dharma characterized by service to husbands and others be accomplished; otherwise, according to the logic of the method described in the *Śāstraphala-laya*, that same fruit might accrue even to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). This [instruction] is taught in order to demonstrate one's own faultlessness.
"Service to the husband and others is not our duty, but rather yours alone.

Since you have abandoned your husband and others, as well as your own duty, it is determined that we are not to be rejected; by that same logic, it is also determined that you lack the authority to be an instructor. Thus it is said in the Eleventh Canto:
O King, he who has with his whole being taken refuge in the Refuge-worthy is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, ancestors, or men.
"He has gone away, abandoning Mukunda, to perform service [for others]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.41).

For us, there is no state of being servants to ritual injunctions (*vidhi*). Therefore, the sense is that in the absence of one to be instructed, the act of instructing is as useless as crying out in the wilderness. Herein lies the essential truth:

Being impelled by you, who set the functions of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) in motion, the service rendered to you that we perform will bear fruit for us; whereas the service to a husband and so forth, as taught through external functions, will not take root within us.

Alternatively, the service of the husband and so forth is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of women. As for what you said— that by teaching the duty of the body as if it were the duty of the self, a living being does not properly understand its own duty— all of this is not before us.
May this instruction rest upon You alone, the substratum whose nature is the service of the Self;

for You are the kinsman and the very Self of all embodied beings. Therefore, being instructed by us, may You practice the dharma consisting of the service of the Lord and others, since You are the protector of dharma.

And because [the Lord] is the primary agent: even without Your instruction, we shall ourselves investigate through the inquiry into the Vedic texts and perform only Your worship; such is the sense that Your status as our true instructor is real. Furthermore, according to those who know the Dharma, it is the duty of women to follow their husband and others.
"This was explained with derision," and so forth, as by Śrīdharācārya; enough of this prolixity. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Then, certain sharp-witted women, desiring to defeat him by means of those very words, said—"As for that which you have stated, namely, that 'obedience to husbands and so forth is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of women,' let it be so;
let it remain in this manner, for we do not dispute this point. This very thing is what we [accept]..."
The sense is that it is performed at every moment.

Now, by what manner? To this they say: only when you—the one who imparts the teaching, the very locus and foundation of instruction—are followed, is there the following of husbands and the other [relatives].

The meaning is that it is appropriate. According to the principle that first the teacher who instructs in Dharma is served, and afterwards the Dharma instructed by him is to be practiced, the scripture states that Dharma is accomplished only through sincere devotion to the teacher. In this context as well, if [the teacher] is indeed the Supreme Lord...
If he were the Supreme Lord, then what more could be said? Furthermore, because you are the Lord, you are the very Self (*ātman*) of embodied beings;
because you are the Self, you are the most beloved; and because you are the most beloved, you are the kinsman. This is the meaning:
according to the scriptures, service is prescribed toward husbands and others only when they are accompanied by the Supreme Self.

But according to the Dharmaśāstra, when they are suddenly expelled from their homes due to the absence of a self (ātman), their faces are scorched on the banks of rivers and the like; therefore, it is only through the persistence of a corporeal self such as yours that the persistence of [the wife's] devotion to her husband and others is established. What is the use of others who, being devoid of a self, are indeed opposed to that?
"By their husbands and others whose faces were scorched.

Now, one might ask: since full-blown love (pūrṇa-prema) obscures the knowledge of divine sovereignty (aiśvarya-jñāna), and since these women possess such complete love, how could such knowledge of sovereignty be possible for them? It is said in reply:

This love (prema), characterized as described in the *Nārada-pañcarātra* and other scriptures, and explained in works such as the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta*, is indeed an experiencer through the essence of both separation and union, possessing a constant and natural warmth and coolness.
Even if this [love] were multiplied by the qualities of a hundred thousand billion-fold Brahmā’s bliss, it would still remain [incomparable].

"does not equal even a single atom of the ocean of bliss that is devotion. (Bharata-Ṛṣi 1.1.38). According to this statement from the *Rasāmṛta*, even the experience of the bliss of Brahman—exceeding a supreme *parārdha* in duration—causes a heat in separation that is greater than that of ten million suns; yet it does not compare to any of the qualities related to His sovereignty and sweetness.
In this way, it illuminates the qualities of the Blessed One alone and does not obscure anything;

for, like the sun, separation illuminates everything. But in union, bringing even more delight than ten million moons, it illuminates the qualities of the Blessed One as consisting solely of sweetness.
Since union is like nectar (*sudhā*), it obscures sovereignty through its intoxicating nature;
therefore, one must understand that where sovereignty shines forth even during union, there the love itself is incomplete.
In this case, however, for these women who possess the contemplation of future separation, this manifestation of majesty occurs precisely in separation.
Indeed, love itself brings about love; for love reveals even greatness that does not exist, let alone that which does.
Therefore, an excess of that [love] results in an excess of that very [greatness], as seen in the life of Bharata and others:
"O, what austerities must this ascetic woman have performed, that she should [be so dear] to the earth," and so forth. Thus it is said.
The feet of Śrī Jīva Gosvāmī. ||32||
For the wise find delight in their own self,
which is eternally dear; what use have they for husbands, sons, and the like, which bring only suffering?
Therefore, be gracious to us, O Lord of the Givers of Boons; do not cut short our hope, which has been nurtured in you for so long, O Lotus-eyed One.
Śrīdhara: Strengthening this point through the example of the conduct of the virtuous, they pray: "They perform...

Those who are "skilled" (kuśala) are those proficient in the scriptures. And thus says the scripture: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self and this world are already ours? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). ||33||

Vaṃśīdhara: This refers to what was stated previously—that for embodied beings, the self alone is their kinsman. "By the conduct of the virtuous" means by the activity of the good. "Experts in the scriptures" means those skilled in discerning the essential from the non-essential.
The word *ātman* here ends in the locative case (*ātmani*), and the elision of the *ṅi* ending occurs due to its being a Vedic form, as in the expression *parame vyoman*. [It means] "in one's own..."

In the Self, which is bound by no cause, the husband and other relations are merely temporary objects of affection; for this very reason, they are the givers of suffering. Regarding the fact that those things which are temporarily dear cause suffering, the Śruti says: "He will afflict you who are dear. Here, "the dear" refers to the temporarily dear, such as sons, wealth, and so forth. This is because there is no separation from the eternally dear Self.

The objection that "it is only natural for children and young ones to cry out" has already been answered by the fact that [the Self] is the proper object of delight. He cites scripture regarding the renunciation of offspring and so forth with the words, "What is the use of offspring? The meaning is this: for us, it is the vision of the Self within the light of the Self (*ātmāloka*)—which removes the cycle of transmigration—and not sons or other such things. Like a lotus...

Since her eyes do not shine in the night, it is appropriate that she should show indifference toward us, who are otherwise most beautiful; this is indicated by the term "O Awakened One" (sambuddhyā). The sense is: "Do not cut down with the axe of your words the creeper of hope, which is her very form and deserves to be watered with the water of love. Regarding the word "Parameśvarī": even the Lord [is such].

A king and such fulfill [their promises]; how much more so you, the Supreme Lord? Therefore, they say with an address of reproach: "This cutting off of hope is not the nature of the Supreme Lord. Regarding the reading *varadeśvara*: having granted the boon, "You shall enjoy these nights with me," he has now become a breaker of his promise—just as before.

This is the intention of the Fully Awakened One, based on such statements as: "One experiences sufferings in the next world due to the theft of hope for an eon," and so forth. It should be understood that for those who are capable, the fulfillment of others' hopes is itself the Dharma. //33//
The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: He says "this indeed possesses authority" with the words beginning "for they perform," and so on.
"The skilled ones"—meaning those expert in discerning the essential from the non-essential—perform their devotion toward you alone.
By saying "the skilled ones," he speaks with reference to the young maidens; for these girls, while performing devotion toward you alone, [turn away] from husbands and others.

They became free from desire; for there was no possibility of longing for another's offspring or even for their own sons, as that would be merely worldly. But regarding you as their husband, it is not so; they say, "What have we not obtained?"—of what use are husbands, sons, and the like, who only cause distress? They are merely givers of pain, but you are not. You...
They say: "He is dear alone"—meaning He is both eternally dear and eternally the beloved.
Therefore, through our skill in discernment, we have abandoned husbands and others and fixed our love upon You alone.
Then, in anticipation of what kind of grace You might bestow upon us, they say: "Do not cut off our hope."
"Ādi": O lotus-eyed one! The sense is: "Behold us with a gracious glance.

Why do you look with contracted eyes? Because the lotus closes at night, the term "lotus-eyed" refers primarily to its closing; yet, that [closing] is intended to indicate [the need for] looking [with grace]. Thus it is said by those who have been carried away [by this meaning].
The expression. ||33||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus rejected service to husbands and others by the authority of the scriptures, she now rejects it even by the force of traditional conduct (*sadācāra*), as elaborated in the passage beginning with "mothers, fathers, sons," and so forth.
She avoids the objects of sense that are fetters of affection for them; this is expressed by the half-verse beginning with "they indeed perform... (*kurvanti hi*).

Indeed, this is well known; for according to the words of Śrī Garga, "Those fortunate men who feel affection for Him are the wise" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.18), those who are expert in discerning the essential from the non-essential feel *rati*—that is, affection—for You, who are eternally dear and the very embodiment of the natural object of love. Thus it is said.

They state that for him [the Lord], there is an intended vibration of bliss both within himself and toward others, whereas for husbands and other relatives, it is the opposite; for they cause suffering to their own kin and to themselves by being intent on preventing such devotion to the Lord through their aversion to Him. Therefore, by them...

"What need have we for husbands and the like?"—for although *sva* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it optionally takes the forms *smāt* or *smi* because it belongs to the group beginning with *pūrva*. Thus, they conclude what was intended to be said in accordance with the opening statement, "O you who are situated in the first direction, O devotee, worship [me]": namely, that [worship] is in relation to us.
The meaning is "with regard to us.

Intending to show that faith must necessarily be practiced, they express this by way of negation: "mā sma" (let it not be). "For a long time" means until the arising of enlightenment; "held" means maintained with immovability, together with their husbands.

The connection to that [worldly desire] has been cast aside; the meaning is: "Do not cut it, but rather make it fruitful. Otherwise, by its severance, our lives—which depend solely upon it as their support—would be instantly destroyed; this is the underlying thought.
They express this very hope with particular clarity: "O Giver of Boons! May the resolve toward young maidens..."

"O Lord, who has granted specific boons as described in the passage beginning with *vidita* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.25), you are capable of accomplishing even that which is difficult for others to achieve, such as the formation of the mind and other faculties! The reason for the phrase "held for a long time" is given by the address "O lotus-eyed one. As stated in the passage beginning with *śarad-udāśaya* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.2).
"Ādi" refers to what will be stated hereafter. "Ara" means the rim of a wheel; like that, the tip of its petal is "ara.
It is so called because it finds (*vindati*) the heart by cutting it, due to the intensity of passion being situated within. There is also a pun (*śleṣa*):
one whose eyes do not shine at night, like a lotus (*aravinda*). Therefore, even among those who are supremely beautiful—

Furthermore, there is a playful indication that it is indeed appropriate for you to show indifference toward us at this time. Moreover, by means of the metaphor of the lotus (*aravinda*), it is suggested that even a mere glance removes the distress of all;
therefore, the implication is that such a reversal of behavior toward us is improper.

Indeed, those such as the venerable Nārada and others, who are experts in the established doctrines of the scriptures, desire *rati* (devotional attachment) rather than mere *śraddhā* (faith), and they state that this [attachment] is appropriate for the "eternally beloved" (*nitya-priya*). Why is there both eternality and dearness? To that, they reply: even regarding one's own self, which is the object, [He is dear] because He is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) within the self.

This is the meaning, as it is said: "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.55). By this, His nature as bliss is also implied; otherwise, He would not be the object of unconditional love. Therefore, what is the use of husbands and the like to us? Rather, [He alone is].
The meaning is: "there is some purpose.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "Are not even your husbands and so forth eternally dear to you, just like those such as ourselves? To this they reply: "No, because they cause distress. What is the use of those things which are hostile to our worship of the Lord—which is desired by such a multitude of virtuous people? O... [addressing them].
"O Lord of Boons!"—by this, the infallibility of the Giver of Boons is demonstrated. This principle is to be inferred likewise in subsequent passages as well.
And this [statement] has a prohibitive purpose: "Now, if I am indeed the dearest to those who possess bodies, then—"

Suspecting that they might think, "Just as those [husbands] act with the love appropriate to themselves, so too may you ladies manifest toward me the emotion of passion (rati) which is appropriate to yourselves," they say: "O auspicious ones"— meaning virtuous women—
"by means of causes such as husbands who bestow distress and shatter happiness, [you have acted] toward your own homes and yourselves."

If You are eternally beloved, why would they find delight in You? Indeed, it is not so, for that would lead to the destruction of their own relish (*svāda*). Therefore, O Giver of Boons, O Bestower of Desires, O Lord, O Master of Gokula, be gracious to us! They say that grace alone is this: "May we never cease to be here for a long time."

"Let us stay. The use of the *luṅ* (aorist) for the root *as* (to be) in place of the *laṅ* (imperfect) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). The meaning is: "Grant permission to go home quickly. Likewise, you should cut—cut off—the hope fixed upon you, which consists of the desire for contact with my body; [the root] *dhṛñ* is used here in the sense of "remaining" or "persisting."

In the phrase "O Varadeśvara," the reading "Parameśvara" should also be understood in the same manner as "Īśvara. However, in the reading "chindyāt" for "chindyā," the word "bhavān" (you) must be supplied as an ellipsis. ||33||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O Moon of the Ocean of Desires! This is not said by us out of desire alone; rather, it is also because of our consideration of the conduct of the virtuous. Thus they pray with tears and plaintive intonations, saying "for they do... (*kurvanti hi*). Indeed (*hi*); [they find] delight (*ratiṃ*) in You alone, and not elsewhere.

It is *prema* (love), and not mere *śraddhā* (faith). The reason for this is: [it is felt] toward one's own kinsman, toward the self within the self, and toward the conscious agent; therefore, it is eternally dear because of its capacity to benefit both externally and internally, and because of its quality of bestowing happiness.
Alternatively, "O Self! O Eternal One! is an address; by this, the insentience of the husband and others is indicated.

And there is impermanence as well. By describing her as "thus" (tathā), "she" (sā), and "dear" (priya) respectively—on account of her being beneficial and her being natural—her contrary nature is also implied.
Therefore, the meaning is: what use have we for husbands and the like? Indeed, they serve no purpose at all.

For the purpose of a husband and so forth—even that which exceeds them—is perfectly accomplished through you alone. Moreover, they are sources of suffering because they are the cause of *saṃsāra* and because, being perishable, they give rise to grief and other afflictions.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), mother, father, brother, and others are included. Or rather, even though they are sources of suffering... *do* [is understood].

Regarding "avakhaṇḍane": they are simply not capable of completely cutting away suffering. Even if they were somehow, at some time, or to some small degree to cut away a bit of suffering, what would be the point of that? The rest is the same.

Alternatively, the meaning is: since those who are skillful and wise always take delight in You, who are eternally dear and the perpetual object of love, what purpose is there in husbands and others who cause distress and bring suffering to one's own self? Therefore...

Since your delight alone is the task to be accomplished—both by its attainment of virtuous conduct for others and by its causing distress to them—O devotee of yours, be gracious toward us; grant us the favor of acceptance.
[Objection: Surely women are generally fond of ornaments; thus, who else besides me [could be so]?

"Let the gift of ornaments and such be accepted. To this they replied: "He is the Lord even of all, including Brahmā and the others who grant boons; therefore, it is an extraordinary favor that is appropriate for you"—this is the sense. They express that very point with the words "mā sma" (let there not be). The particle "smā" serves to reinforce the meaning through its well-known usage. [This has been] long [expected].

Because of the onset of illness, or until the taking up of a new body, the hope for pleasure—held with steadfastness—has been rendered impossible by the husbands, as their connection [to her] has been severed. "Do not cut it off, but rather make it fruitful" is the meaning.
Otherwise, by its severance, we, whose lives depend solely upon it, would immediately...

The sense is that there would be the offense of taking one's life. The reason for the word "dhṛtām" (held) is: "O lotus-eyed one," meaning "O supremely beautiful one. Therefore, it will be sung further on: "In the autumnal lake... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.2], and so forth.
Or else, by the very vision whose nature is the metaphor of the lotus, for all...
The quality of removing distress and so forth is implied [by the term *īśvara*]. Therefore, the sense is that its opposite is stated in our case.
Furthermore, by the term *varadeśvara*, the boon previously granted during the theft of the garment is also recalled. Through pun (*śleṣa*), it means:
"O Giver of Boons, you who cut off the boons given by yourself! And they say that this is indeed appropriate—*īśvara*.

"Supreme independence" (*parama-svatantrā*)—this is a statement made in feigned anger (*praṇaya-kopa*). Although the boon was granted specifically to the maidens who have chosen Kātyāyanī, nevertheless, according to the maxim "those with umbrellas are walking," others as well are included by virtue of their equality with her as friends. The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].

Or rather, they say: "O great city! Let those who are somehow deluded resort to you; how could we not resort to you?"—this is expressed by the word *kurvanti*. [The meaning is: "We are skillful and clever (*vidagdha*);
therefore, what can those [others] do to us, who are clever? And especially toward us, a boon has been granted by you.
With the intention that [the gift] has been given, they say "that" (*tat*); the rest is the same.

By this, the answer to the word "mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) is provided, because they are to be disregarded due to their causing distress. Alternatively, according to the final position mentioned previously, they are strengthening the very fact of death.
They pray—that is, they act—in this manner: O you whose mind (*ātman*) is fixed upon your own wealth characterized by cattle;

this is a compound ending in *aluk*. By this, a lack of discernment and similar traits are intended. Since there is no one dear to you, in you who are thus unloved (*apriya*), for that reason, you are a giver of distress.

Why, and for what reason, would virtuous and clever women like us take delight in being with husbands and others who only cut short our happiness? Rather, the meaning is that we ought not to do so in such an improper place.
Therefore, do not be gracious toward us, and cut off our hope; [do not grant it] quickly, as one who finds a cow is called Govinda.

It is called *aravinda* because it finds (*vindati*) its extremity as a part of something extremely sharp; thus, it refers to a discus (*cakra*). By means of wordplay (*śleṣa*), it is indicated that his eyes are likewise like a cutting discus. This is an angry utterance by one wishing to die. Furthermore, it means that his eyes do not shine at night, being like lotuses (*aravinda*); therefore—

The sense is that even toward us, who are most beautiful, neglect is now indeed appropriate. Therefore, the response to their concern—expressed by you with the words "toward your mother" and so forth—is to be inferred as follows: by way of accepting the reproach, it is shown that what they said is entirely justified.

And this is the intended meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): "The auspicious ones" means those who are virtuous; [the question is] whether they can maintain affection for You—the Self, their own essential nature, which is eternally dear—even by means of causes such as husbands and the like that bring them distress? Indeed, they cannot. Therefore, O Giver of Boons! O Lord! [grant this] to us.

"Be gracious! After a long time, we must not remain here; grant us quickly permission to go home"—this is the meaning. As for the phrase "tvayi tu api," there is a word-break (*ccheda*). O lotus-eyed one! Cut, cut away this hope that you yourself have held for the sake of contact with our bodies.
Or rather, do not sever the hope directed toward the path leading to Vraja; the meaning is: do not cause it to fall from its course.

Do not conceal it. [An objection: "Surely you yourselves should observe and grasp it. To this they reply: "Held by you"—from the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "to remain," the meaning is that it rests in you alone, or is supported by you. ||33||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* (332): Alternatively, they refute [the objection] beginning with "out of affection for me" (*mad-abhisnehāt*) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.33] by saying "they indeed perform" (*kurvanti hi*). [The word *ārtihābhiḥ* means] those who pierce (*dyanti*) or cut through (*chindanti*) suffering (*ārti*); by such [means].

Since one’s own self, the body, and so forth are eternally dear by virtue of being causes such as a husband and the like, do those things which are beneficial toward them produce delight or the state of being a lover for You? The meaning is: "By no means. Therefore, be gracious to us; that is to say, abandon this stubborn persistence. In that regard:
"O Lord of Boons"—this is an address accompanied by a specific request; it is intended to make [the deity] understand: "Let this very boon be granted to us.
They clarify that very point: having pervaded that hope or longing which has been held—that is, maintained—within you for a long time.

"May we not cease to exist"—the meaning is that while that thirst remains fixed in your mind, we shall indeed remain indifferent; therefore, you should cut it off. "O lotus-eyed one"—the sense is that even with eyes such as these, crookedness is not fitting. [The form] *mā sma* is used with the verb *as* (to be) in connection with *mā*.
The form [of the suffix] *laṅ* is [as follows]. ||33||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "Indeed, virtuous women find delight only in you, and not in other husbands nor in children and the like; therefore, this instruction should not be given. Nor should our hope be destroyed," they said with tearful faces. Some women, both steadfast and wavering, said: "They do indeed... and so forth.
The virtuous and auspicious women find their delight in you alone—in you, indeed. In what kind of you?

In the Self (ātman), in the very Self; or "ātman" may be used as a form of address. Furthermore, in what kind? In the eternally beloved, the eternal friend. What is the use of husbands, sons, and others who cause them distress? They [find delight] in another husband, in a son, and so forth.
And they indeed render [all else] a mere trifle. Therefore, young maidens alone are truly skillful;

for, finding constant delight in You who are eternally dear, they held their husbands, children, and so forth as insignificant, since they accepted none other than You. Therefore, be gracious to us and do not speak thus, O Lord, Bestower of Boons!

"Do not sever the hope long held by me in you! O lotus-eyed one, be gracious so that the creeper of hope may bear fruit"—this is the repetition. "O lotus-eyed one" is the vocative address. Because the lotus closes at night, its eyes are understood to be closed; therefore—
It is called "harsh speech" because, according to worldly convention, it is not spoken with a gracious look; it is understood that Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke in exactly this manner. ||33||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Furthermore, since even liberated sages who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*) are seen to worship [the Lord], why this insistence on discarding established conduct (*sad-ācāra*) and instead teaching the service of husbands and so forth? [The text continues: "Mothers, fathers, sons"—this refers to the apprehension of their arrival.
"But how can you, who have [already] generated [this devotion], now act to restrain us?

With the intention that, "Our hearts are always longing for you; having seen the example of your engagement in virtuous conduct, we are most firmly attached—how could we turn back at a mere word?", they say: "They perform... and so forth.

The virtuous ones, skilled in discernment—Nārada and others—direct their devotion and love toward you, honoring you as the Supreme Object of Worship. Toward what kind of You? Toward the Self (ātmani), where the locative case-ending is elided, meaning "in Your own universal form. Furthermore, You are eternally beloved, being the very cause of all affection.
Even though indifference (*audāsīnya*) exists at the outset, it must be abandoned because of its inherent nature of being undesirable and because it does not bestow internal happiness.
Or else, O Self! You who are the presiding witness even over the body, senses, and mind of those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*). Or else—

The virtuous wives of the sacrificers, who possess the quality of detachment, direct their radiant, stable emotion of love toward You. "Hi" indicates certainty. Toward what? Toward one's own self—that is, toward one's own inner controller (antaryāmin) as one's essential nature (svarūpa). As it has been said by the Blessed Lord’s own mouth: "The saintly are My heart" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.68).
Thus it is said. For this very reason, in the case of the Lord and others, when they are made the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the sweetness of rasa is superior by virtue of their power alone;

whereas in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is so by their very being. Therefore, in that essential nature which is eternally beloved and always the natural locus of supreme love, there are those who cause eternal distress and are hostile toward it.

What is the use of a husband, sons, and so forth? What kind of happiness will there be? The meaning is: none at all. The underlying sense is that entities which are causes of *dharma* cannot possibly be givers of suffering.
For if these were givers of suffering, then they would not be fit for renunciation. As for those...
Those who are virtuous and unrefined follow the will of their husbands and others;

for those who are ignorant of their own happiness, such behavior is appropriate. However, instruction regarding service to husbands and others before us—who are wise—is utterly useless, like sowing seed in barren soil.

Furthermore, according to the Vedic scripture, "Indeed, everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self," those who desire the Self have concluded that sense-objects are the means to that end. For those who bestow suffering, service is painful;
for those who bestow happiness, service is pleasant. Since You, however, are the bestower of happiness, service to You is [the source of] bliss.
It is established by experience that bliss is indeed its very nature.

Furthermore, according to the Smṛti: "For a person, especially for a man, the self alone is the teacher" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.7.20), the meaning is that for us—who possess the contemplation of the Self within ourselves—there is no need for a teacher.

Since the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) consist solely of happiness and the absence of suffering, the service of masters and the like is neither happiness nor the absence of suffering; therefore, because it is not a goal of human endeavor, it is not to be pursued. Furthermore: "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.55).

And furthermore: "Just as the beauty of the face [is reflected] in its own reflection," this has indeed been determined by us who are afflicted by suffering. What purpose is there in opposing you by means of those things which cause such distress?
None at all. Moreover, service toward them is certainly not appropriate; for this very reason, regarding them—

The meaning is that there is not even a trace of connection with a self [of one's own]. Therefore, "be gracious to us"—that is, abandon your indifference. By the two words "O Giver of Boons" and "O Lord," they express their wretchedness through a plaintive tone (*sakāku*). Otherwise, delay in dalliance does not even enter the path of memory; [it must be] right now.

"Since you are associated with maidens, why do you agitate us all with these jesting words? You promised even regarding the maidens, 'By me these nights shall be enjoyed' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.27). Be gracious by fulfilling that promise; abandon your crookedness. This is the meaning. Since you are a granter of boons...

If the Lord were capable [of fulfilling desires] but lacked sovereignty over those to be ruled (*īśitavya*), his lordship (*īśvaratva*) would not be established. Furthermore, if the granting of boons were impossible, it would ultimately result in the non-existence of people.
[Objection: "But once I am known as the Lord, let my contemplation be performed by anyone, wherever they may be."
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of staying here?", they reply: "O lotus-eyed one!
O you whose glance removes the distress of the eyes! The meaning is this: You appear as the very embodiment of the mass of all beauty;
for those who worship Your state of majesty (*vaibhavāvasthā*), You are the Lord (*īśvara*), whereas for those who worship Your essential nature (*svarūpa*), You are beauty itself.

The object is [the Lord], but His lordship is not [manifested], because He is overwhelmed by love; thus, any occasional expression of it arises merely from an outpouring—whether through Garga’s statement, "He is equal to Nārāyaṇa in qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.19), or through the observation of superhuman deeds such as quenching forest fires and drinking [poison]. However, that knowledge remains indirect.
It appears as if so. Thus it has been said:
"For the cowherd girls, constantly beholding His face with its ever-risen smile and glance, crossed over their various labors with joy."

Just as in the case of the moon being perceived directly, its divinity and its nature as nectar are [perceived], yet for the *cakora* bird, its object is the nature of nectar and not its divinity; so too it is with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for although He is always perceived as having eyes that remove all suffering, how can this be for the maidservants?

Are you perceived as one who causes heat by virtue of having eyes that produce heat? This alone is a marvel: we perceive that which is the cause of coolness in union is itself the cause of heat in separation.
Or rather, O Lord of Givers (Varadeśvara)—O Lord of us givers [of boons], because you are the son of the Lord of Vraja—at that time...

"A boon was granted to you when you were seated upon the *kadamba* tree: 'O Śyāmasundara, we shall become your maidservants and perform whatever you command' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.15). Immediately after our promise was made, you also promised: 'With me, you shall enjoy these nights' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.27). From that time forward..."

The hope firmly held was the desire for union with Your limbs; even before that, in a previous birth, we were prayed for by You in the form of the Vedas, and a boon was granted through the persistence born of Your desire to act: "In the past Sārasvata Kalpa, you shall become the cowherd girls in Vraja. From that time onwards...

The form *dhṛk* is derived from the root *dhṛñ* in the sense of "remaining" (*avasthāne*). The ellipsis is: "You are unable to cause [her] to hear that she has remained [there]. Do not cut [it]. The particle *smā* expresses doubt (*vitarka*). Do not cut even for a moment the body fallen here into this fire, which is as terrifying as the flames rising upon Mahākāla.

It would be reduced to ashes this very instant, were it not for the hope that it might serve as the cause of your life. Since you have made a promise, hope has arisen; and that hope is now firmly rooted. If you do not fulfill your promise now, that hope will be severed. When our bodies fall, where will your pleasure be?
This is the intention.

Furthermore, even upon the fall of the body, we shall certainly attain you; however, how will the dalliance of our formless selves with you, who possess form, be possible, given that your very nature is that of delight?
Such is the intended meaning. ||33||
Viśvanātha: Some women, being "skilled" (kuśalāḥ), confirm that very meaning already stated by means of virtuous conduct (sad-ācāra) as they act in accordance with it;
those fortunate men who take delight in this [conduct].

"Enemies do not overcome these people, just as the Asuras cannot overcome the followers of Viṣṇu"—this is based on the conviction arising from Garga’s words. Furthermore, it should be stated according to the actual fact that the clever do not take pleasure in anything other than You;
for they say that for the wise, delight in You is indeed innate. The word *sve* means "in one's own. Thus, You—

Thus, they say that for them, the sense of "mine" (mamatā) resides in the self, and therefore the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) resides in you alone; consequently, their love for you is eternal, whereas their love for husbands, sons, and others is conditional and therefore non-eternal. Furthermore, they say that even among us, such love for those [husbands and sons] does not exist, because [we] cause distress by preventing your secret trysts.

"Since that [death] brings us suffering, therefore be gracious to us so as to let us live; or else, if you have married others, do not let us live. 'Why do you make these unmarried women weep? they asked. 'O Giver of Boons!
Your resolve is known'—by such words as these, you [spoke] to them. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.25). Thus, you [acted] toward them.
The meaning is: "They are indeed the givers of boons.

Now, [one might ask]: "In the case of these [goddesses], the worship of Kātyāyanī is the cause for their grace; but in the case of you, what is the cause for my grace? To this, they offer a request with a plaintive intonation (*sakāku*), saying: "In that regard, please be gracious without any cause at all. O... [He addresses her: "O..."

O Lord, do not now cut down the wish-granting vine of hope that I have long cherished in you for what you intend to do—hope that has been held toward you since my childhood; for a fruitful vine ought not to be cut down by a virtuous person. This is illuminated by the two words *cirāt* (long ago) and *chindyāḥ* (should you cut).
For they say: "Indeed, this creeper of hope was planted by you alone in the field of our minds.
O lotus-eyed one! At the very beginning of our youth, at the time of our first sight, [we were touched] by your eyes, which are like lotuses and were sent forth by you.

It is suggested that the seed of the creeper of hope, designated as "feeling" (*bhāva*), has been sown within the field of the heart after entering through the apertures of our eyes; thus, according to the method taught in the treatises on aesthetics (*rasa-śāstra*)— namely, "first the passion of the eye, then attachment of the mind, and thereafter volition"— that very thing is the creeper of hope.

How can she—who has been nurtured by hearing of and beholding your virtues and form, and who now bears fruit both already enjoyed and yet to be enjoyed—be cut down today by the axe of your harsh words? You surely understand the maxim: "It is improper to cut down even a poisonous tree after one has nurtured it oneself"—this is the implied meaning. ||33||
My mind has been carried away by pleasure toward home affairs, even though it should be occupied with the duties of my station; indeed, my hands too have been seized for domestic tasks.
Your feet do not move even a single step from the soles of Your feet; how then shall we go to Vraja, or what indeed shall we do?

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, they say that what was said—"Go back"—is impossible, because you yourself have carried away our minds and so forth; thus they say: "The mind. That mind of ours which for so long a time has been enjoying itself at ease in our homes—that has been carried away by you. And as for the two hands...
Or rather, "by you, who enter into domestic duties with a joyful nature. (34)

Vaṃśīdhara: Regarding cessation (*nivṛtti*), they state that it involves the absence of means preceded by the absence of purpose—with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) and so forth. Residence in the home exists for the sake of accomplishing household duties and for the sake of pleasure;
all of that occurs through the mind. But that has been stolen away by you. What, then, shall we do there?

"Having gone"—this implies a lack of purpose. Or rather, it should be construed as: "that mind which was carried away by you through the afflictions of saṃsāra. "Domestic" (*gṛhya*) means that which pertains to the home; and that is the "task" (*kṛtya*).
Likewise, [it refers] to that [task] characterized by sweeping, smearing, and so forth. The plural form "tasks" (*kṛtyānām*) is used with respect to the mind.
There is distress; it is not happiness. To express this with aversion, he specifies: "it exists as the nature of happiness" (*sukhātmanā*), meaning in the form of happiness.

For each word, "by you" (*tvayā*) is the substantive. They say that stiffness has also arisen in the feet—"the two feet"—implying the thought: "In the absence of the means for movement, how could going take place?"
The intention here is this: "It is not even possible to remain here because of your hardness; yet it is impossible to depart. Alas, what a tragedy! What is to be done now? (34)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Certain mature and self-controlled women say:

"Because you have stolen [it] with such ease and without effort—as was previously stated in the verse beginning 'the beloved with sarcastic irony'—it does not enter into the houses. Indeed, one who knows the Dharma does not seize the property of another; and even in that case, [the property] of women..."

"Having stolen your heart, return then to your home"—thus the departure for home is enjoined. This is your deceit: not only has your heart been stolen, but your hands as well, since they no longer enter upon household duties from the root of your feet, remaining instead clinging to your feet to massage them.
The meaning is that she desires nothing else besides him. Her heart has been stolen, her hands have been taken away;

having seen that, even her feet do not move. Having witnessed this injustice of yours, a paralysis has arisen [within me]. How can we go to the cow-pen? Or, staying here, how many more of your indifferent and harsh words must be heard?
In that case, the sense is that death alone is the refuge. ||34||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, raising the objection that even for the sake of protecting the happiness of household life one should not abandon one’s husband and so forth, they nevertheless state [the following], beginning with the identification of the fault in that very [household life]: "The mind...
By "with ease," meaning by way of its nature as happiness, [it refers to] the self-revealer; at that time, [there is the attachment] to the home and so forth.

The manifestation of their very nature as suffering has been intimated by the phrase "together with happiness. Even those two feet which formerly took rest during household chores or while walking have now been snatched away.
Therefore, the meaning is that they cannot move even a single step from the soles of your feet; they are unable to go. [This applies] to both the hands and the feet.

The "stealing away" (cāpahāra) refers to the seizing of the various powers of the senses; therefore, the sense is that their arrival occurs merely by drawing them in through fear. Thus, for this reason, how can we go to Vraja?

"If they are indeed weak, then let us go along with him as he goes ahead. To this they replied: "Having gone there, what indeed shall we do? The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Although the seizure of all the senses follows from the seizure of the mind, nevertheless, the specific mention of the seizure of the hands and feet is made.

This is for the sake of avoiding her departure elsewhere and the neglect of household duties such as service to her husband; "by them" means by those [qualities]. Or rather, that mind which was previously fixed upon pleasure or sense objects has been snatched away by you.

Or even, she does not enter at all. Why? The meaning is that one should cause the hand and so forth to enter into that particular task. Now, one might object: "Even so, let her be made to enter by the power of deliberation regarding the mistress of the house. To this they reply: "Even the hands, having been taken away, do not engage in tasks related to the household. Now, one might object: [...]

Nevertheless, since it is improper to remain here, you must depart; regarding this, they say: "Your feet have been carried away by You toward Yourself and drawn back; not even a single step does he move. The rest is the same:
therefore, Your mind is fixed on You alone, Your hands are occupied with tasks for Your sake, and Your feet are stationed at Your very place.

It is indicated that they enter here and nowhere else. To this, [the thieves] say: "We have not come here for the purpose of seeing him, as we have no need for him in the forest; rather, we have come here with the intent of robbing you of the wealth of your mind, and though we have encountered you, a thief, we have come to seize it."

Furthermore, we are not even able to go anywhere to cry out for help; because you have stripped us of our hands and feet, how can we, robbed of our wealth, return to Vraja? Or what shall we do? O best of thieves, master of great mantras such as the *stambhana* [paralyzing] spells, this is due to the power of some particular stratagem of yours.
This is the state of affairs.

And this is for the purpose of negation: "Indeed, having been drawn from our homes by the flute-song and thoroughly pacified by me, how could we possibly go away? To that they reply: "By the happiness arising from you within our homes..."

The mind has been stolen away because it enters into household chores; or rather, the mind itself is simply happy, and it is not that it has been stolen by the Blessed One, since it indeed enters into the home. Fearing that the hands might also become weary while engaged in household tasks, they say: "How is it that even the feet do not take a single step?"
We are indeed moving, and moreover, we are moving even far away. Therefore, why should we not go? Indeed, we must go. And what can we do in this matter? ||34||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By the word "consisting of happiness" (*sukhātmakena*), the fact that houses and such things consist of suffering is implied; or rather, it means "accompanied by happiness. Those two feet which were engaged in household duties or wandering about have also been snatched away. Therefore, they do not move even a single step from the root of Your feet; they do not go [anywhere else].

The meaning is "they are able. The "seizure" of the hands and feet refers to the seizure of the respective powers of those sense organs. Alternatively, if it is asked, "Are they not indeed speakers of falsehood? Then how did they come here?"—that would be improper.

They were drawn by His song, but not by their own power; otherwise, they say, going would have been possible even now. Thus they say: "The step. The meaning is the same as before. Then, for this reason, how shall we go to Vraja? "Are we not weak ones? [He asks: "Should you be sent away by me somehow? To that they reply: "What can we do?"
The word *vā* is used either to include what has already been mentioned or as a glance toward something else; or rather, it is used to include what has not been mentioned, and thus the meaning is:

"What indeed shall we pursue, or where shall we go?"—because the mind and other faculties have been carried away by you, they lack the capacity for independent activity; or, even if some slight capacity were present...

The sense is that there is no purpose served by [other] actions. Although the seizure of all the senses follows from the seizure of the mind, the specific mention of the seizing of hands and feet is for the sake of avoiding her husband's service and other household duties, as well as her going elsewhere on her own initiative.
The rest has been explained by them.
Or rather, let the mistresses of the house perform their household duties without attachment.
To this they reply: "Even our hands, having been taken away, do not find satisfaction in tasks related to the home. Indeed!
"In that case, go there and remain merely as a presiding authority. To this they replied: "Your feet have been taken away by you, so you do not move; the rest is the same.
Therefore, your mind is fixed on you alone, your hands are occupied only with tasks for your sake, and your feet are directed toward your own station."

It is indicated that they enter [here] and nowhere else. Alternatively, *bhava* means *saṃsāra*; by that ascetic, even the minds of people, which have been seized—that is, destroyed—[are restored] with ease, meaning effortlessly and spontaneously. They indeed take pleasure (*nirviśati*) in their homes; even their hands take pleasure in household duties; therefore—
The sense is that your urging is sufficient for the sake of service to your husband and so forth. If it is objected, "O you speakers of truth! Then depart," they reply with the words, "Your feet.
However, because of your hardness, it is not even fitting to remain here, nor is it possible to go. Oh!

"Tell us now what must be done," they said with agitation and distress: "What shall we do? This is the answer to the question, "The forest has been seen by him. Since, due to the seizure of their minds and so forth, they are incapable of gathering flowers and the like, even seeing that [forest] is futile; therefore, what is the use of it? And in the second case:
"Even though there was a desire to see the forest and so forth, because we were unable to wander due to the removal of our feet, right vision (samyag-darśana) was not achieved;
what, then, was the use of seeing it? By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), she says mockingly: "Since we had no purpose in the forest, we did not come for the sake of seeing it."

However, because you have stolen the wealth of our minds, we have come here for that very purpose; yet, even though we have encountered you, the thief, we are unable to seize you or take you away, nor can we go anywhere to cry out— meaning, because you have robbed us of our hands and feet.
And this is the meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): the negative particle *na*, occurring after each word, is to be connected everywhere.
Even if you, who consist of happiness, have not stolen our hearts, therefore it surely enters [into] the house; and since you have not stolen even our hands and feet, therefore...

"Regarding household duties, they both indeed partake in them; therefore, they both proceed toward their own place, Vraja. Thus, how can we go elsewhere, or for what reason should we carry out your command?"—this was spoken by him in a punning manner regarding the departure to the banks of the Yamunā and so forth.
This is refuted.

Or rather, since your mind has been easily carried away by the pleasures arising within the household, it enters into domestic affairs; likewise, both your hands too have been easily carried away by you into the household.
As you enter into domestic affairs so that your position may become firmly established, how could we not depart from your feet—the very root of dharma—as you move away from them?
Or rather, what else can we do? ||34||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.

Regarding the *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): the status of "hope" (*āśā*) as an object of action is like the expression "there is cow-milking" (*go-doha asti*); this is indicated by such passages as "from hearing and from seeing" (*śravaṇād darśanād*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.27).
They conceal the birth of their own true state, saying, "It is the mind. [The lover says: "Our mind remains in happiness alone;

it has not been stolen by you, since it enters into the houses. Therein the sign is that even the hands enter into the houses for the sake of household duties. As it was said: "O slender-waisted one!"
Regarding this, they say: "How is it that Your feet do not move even a single step from the soles of Your feet?
Therefore, how is it that we do not go to Vraja? The meaning is: rather, we shall indeed go.
As for what was said—that one should not go toward Vraja but should remain right here—they reply: "What else could we do? (34)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "We are not violators of your command; therefore, it is possible for you to go. However, due to your own fault, that does not happen," say the extremely clever, mature, and self-composed women: "The mind [is] with ease," and so forth. By you, the mind...
"Taken with ease" means stolen without effort, not by another thief.

Since the mind enters the houses through your particular exertion, it does not exist there due to the absence of that [other] mind. What fault is ours? Then let the mind be given; those who possess the mind are truly possessed of it.

Fearing that Satya might go home, they said—"Uta" expresses wonder. "Even the two hands do not find rest in household duties. The meaning is: beyond this, the two hands find rest only in your service, not in household duties. Therefore, what is the purpose of going there? [Objection: But even so, [he would go] unknown to me.
Thinking, "Go; let me not perform my household duties," they said: "The feet.
"From the root of your feet—that is, from the vicinity of your feet—not even a single step do your feet move; a paralysis has come upon them.
How shall we go? they asked. "How indeed shall we go? What will you do by not going? they were told.

They said: "What indeed shall we do? We do not even know that; what shall we do? Or rather, that mind which used to find rest in our homes has been stolen away by you. Our minds, scorched by the heat of saṃsāra, have been stolen away by you. Therefore, it finds no rest in the pleasures of home, nor for the sake of pleasure."
Everything else is the same. ||34||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: [The opponent objects: "Indeed, by remaining here in defiance of my command, a great calamity will surely occur. Therefore, it is more appropriate for you ladies—who have come here for the sake of seeing me—to return home rather than face the fire. To this they reply: "Because it is impossible [to leave], our hearts are dependent upon you."

Before beholding you, my mind was settled upon homes and domestic duties; that mind has now been carried away by you in its true nature as happiness—or rather, it has been carried away together with the happiness of home, and thus that happiness has indeed been taken away. Therefore, because they are essentially composed of suffering, homes have been abandoned.

Furthermore, you ladies have come for the purpose of seeing the forest, and that too has been accomplished, since the activity of seeing depends upon the mind. Up until this point, even the hands were occupied with household chores; let alone those, their capacity for performing such work is also gone.

Because they have been carried away by you yourself, they no longer apply themselves to household duties. Up until now, even their feet were intent on wandering here and there; let alone those other tasks, even those two feet no longer apply themselves to walking, for even their movement has been carried away by you yourself. Their feet do not take a step toward their own proper place.

"O moving ones, how can we depart from the soles of your feet? Or rather, having gone by whatever means possible, what shall we do, since our hands and feet are empty? Or else, go there without delay; as virtuous wives, serve your husbands at the cow-pen. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa]

[10.29.22] Thus, they say that this too is impossible: "That mind of ours, which previously, through ease and effort, was absorbed in various household activities before you carried it away; that very mind has now been stolen by you, the thief of consciousness, and no longer finds delight in them. O Sundara, let us be your maidservants; let us do your bidding."

"Your word has been spoken" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.12)—we promised you, "We shall make your words true," yet even that intention has not been fulfilled, because your yoga is of no avail when the minds are vacant;
for even a little service toward husbands and others depends upon the hands. Of those two as well...

Because the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) has been taken away by You alone; for without the power of action, it is impossible to serve the Lord and others. Yet, it is not that nothing is enjoined. Regarding the command, "Go from here," they say: "Your feet [have gone]; and those two feet have not moved even a single step from the place at Your lotus-feet.

The meaning is that even walking is impossible, let alone performing work from afar. If walking were possible because feet exist [in one who is] without movement, then walking would also be possible for trees, since they too possess feet.

The meaning is this: this pastime consists of cessation. Having drawn the hearts of the queens of Vraja toward Himself and placed them within His own heart, He embraced them like milk and water; therefore, they cannot be extracted.
The word "heart" (citta) is an indicator for all the senses. Thus, having stolen their very essence, He departs.
"Only as a joke.

Having thought to themselves, "Why do you mock us by summoning us to the forest with this great deluding mantra consisting of the sound of the flute? they said: "The mind [is drawn] by pleasure—that is, by the pleasure of amorous dalliance—as the cause."

Her distress has been removed by you; for this very reason, she enters—meaning she goes to sport—in the bowers and other dwellings within your home, and her hands also engage in household tasks such as preparing flower-beds and the like, since she has abandoned the service of her husband and others. Her feet [rest] at the base of your feet.
They do not move toward another place or position, because they have resolved to remain right here. They will perform a dance together with your feet. Therefore, how can we go to Vraja?
For what purpose should we go? We have abandoned Vraja entirely; otherwise, we would be like those who eat their own vomit.
"May we become so; moreover, having understood our resolve, please employ us in tasks suitable for amorous play.
Furthermore, know that we have come to be your maidservants so that we may do whatever you desire.
Or rather, once we have stolen away your heart and the like, and you have set out for Vraja, what will be your desire?"
[It] will come to pass. Seeing our condition, what shall we say when questioned by our husbands and others?
Therefore, the sense is: "Since [you have said], 'What service may we perform?', please employ us.
Or rather, if permission is granted for going to Vraja with your whole being, saying "Let her go," [then we shall follow].

"In that case, restore to us our mind and so forth which were stolen. But that is impossible for you; just as water and milk cannot be separated once they have become one, so too our mind and so forth, having been stolen and merged with your own mind and so forth, cannot be separated again."
"Returning that [jewel] to him is impossible for you," said Viśvanātha; "likewise, our going to Vraja is also [impossible]. But others, manifesting their own passionate love, said:
"O Emperor of Thieves! We have not come for the sake of anything else, but rather for that which was stolen by you."

They say that you desired only to seize your own wealth; they say that your mind has been stolen by you, and that in this matter no effort greater than that of an ordinary thief was required of you—hence the word "easily. This means [it was taken] merely by blowing into the holes of the flute. And yet, that wealth of the mind—

They say, "Our [concern] is even less. Since the mind enters into all houses without exception, by its removal you have deprived us of our very minds; therefore, whether those houses burn or flourish, what is it to us? This is the implied meaning, expressed through hyperbole regarding the houses.

The sense is that it enters into the auditory and other senses for the sake of their respective efficacy, such that without it even all the senses become dysfunctional. Therefore, they say that by the very abduction of the mind, all the senses have also been abducted by you. As for the two hands, which [are employed] in household duties...
"Enter! The meaning is that even these eyes and ears have been snatched away; indeed, all of them have been taken.
Now, [the opponent might say]: "O sir, go for now; tomorrow or the day after, having deliberated, I shall give you my heart. To this they reply: "Our feet do not move even a single step without him."
The meaning is: "Therefore, give us your heart; from that very place we shall go"—this is the intended sense. ||34||
