O dear one, extinguish with the flood of nectar from your lips the fire of passion in my heart, born from your smiles, glances, and sweet songs.
O friend, if we do not, our bodies consumed by the fire born of separation, attain through meditation the state of your feet.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, O dear Kṛṣṇa, extinguish this fire of longing—the fire of desire born within our hearts—by means of Your glance accompanied by a smile, preceded by the nectar of Your lips, and by Your sweet song;
otherwise, we shall first become a single fire, and then another fire will arise from that separation.
With our bodies fully engaged and our forms consumed by fire, like yogins, may we attain—that is, reach—the proximity of that state through meditation. ||35||

Vaṃśīdhara: Expressing their own desire, they say, "Sprinkle [us]. Since you have rendered us incapable by depriving us of the means for all worldly activity, they say that you yourself must extinguish the fire of our longing. The phrase *kala-gīta-padam* has been explained previously. Or else:

With a sweet song, that is, with a melodious chant—[the word] *hṛcchayāgni* refers to the fire of love (*hṛcchaya*), which is so called because of its similarity in producing heat; sprinkle that [fire], extinguish it, with the flow of nectar from your lower lip. Otherwise, first by this [song] and then by the second [means], [you will reach] his path, that is, his proximity. *Padavī* means "near."

"Viṣṇu is the protector of the path," according to Śāśvata; and by the maxim "whatever is one's final thought, that is one's destination," we shall certainly attain you. The sense is: while you merely wring your hands, only your deceit and the murder of a woman will remain as your legacy. Here is an illustration:
The wife of one who has been initiated. ||35||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Having resolved that death alone is the refuge, those of middle capacity say:
"Sprinkle us, O... and so forth. O You whose glance is accompanied by a smile!
O You who are thus endowed! Sprinkle—that is, extinguish—the fire of the heart's desire produced by Your sweet song.

That which lies in the heart is a "heart-lying" desire; that very thing has now become fire because of its burning nature. By what means is it to be quenched? To this he says: by the filling of the nectar of your lower lip.
[An objection: But if it is quenched by that, will it not increase? For indeed, the quenching of a lightning fire is by rainwater.
If it is argued that there is a common understanding that [the moon] only causes growth and not the quenching of that [fire], let it indeed grow; however, they say:

"We are not burned by the fire of the heart's longing which is sprinkled with the nectar of the nectar of your lower lip, but we are burned by the fire of separation"—"if not," and so forth. "If not," meaning if it is not sprinkled, then...

The meaning is that they command: "O Satīs, whose bodies have been consumed by the fire born of separation from you, through meditation upon your feet, may we go to, that is, reach, your path. The significance of the word "meditation" (dhyāna) here is this: "Whatever thought one has at the time of death, that shall be one's destination. ||35||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, even those situated in the second direction clearly express their longing for hope itself; by boldly indicating the inevitable fulfillment of that hope, they show that the rejection of its arrival results in nothing but fault on your part.

They conclude what was intended by way of this verse: "Siñca" means "extinguish. Although the action is mentioned first, due to the extreme intensity of the suffering, the word "na" (do not) is connected specifically with the fire residing in the heart.
Because that compound is a *tatpuruṣa* where the latter member is predominant, the word related to "laughter" [is understood].

The word "tava" (of you) is indeed obtained by the force of the context; for even without the word "tvac," since the meaning is understood, that specific mention is intended with the desire to express: "It is fitting that the extinguishing of the fire produced by you should be performed by you alone.
Furthermore, by the suffix "-ka" in the word "pūra," the greatness of the fire is also suggested, [the suffix] being used in its own sense.

The state of being held by the wind [the breath] in the sequence of laughter, glances, and sweet songs is implied. "Hṛcchaya" (the one dwelling in the heart) refers to Kāma; therefore, even for the medicine that turns him back, drinking the flood of nectar from the lower lip is required rather than its mere entry into the interior, thus indicating that it cannot be remedied by any other means.
And this has been indicated:
this is the direct prayer for the enjoyment of those whose minds are intoxicated by the honey of the sweetness of His flute and slender body.

For those who are enveloped by intense longing, made to dance by the pain of a mature, transcendent passion, even aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) does not conflict [with this state]; indeed, it is all the more so because it is expressed through concealment for the sake of negation. They confirm this very point by way of contrast: "If not," meaning, if you do not sprinkle [it], then even so...

"By meditation" means that we shall attain [that state] right now, according to the principle that "whatever thought one has at the time of death, that is one's destiny," and so forth; the *loṭ* suffix is used here because the time for its fulfillment has arrived. And in that context, they address him as "Friend!
to awaken affection for their own kin. These intentions follow the order of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).

Anticipating the retort, "Is not my vessel of water here merely a means for sprinkling the fire of the heart's passion born of laughter and the like?", they say: "With nectar. It would be sprinkled with nectar alone, and not with water or the like; moreover, it would be with its full abundance, and not with just a mere drop. [The suffix -mat] is used in the sense of the base itself.
"By that very [means]" is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Even that is difficult to obtain; where shall I find it? Furthermore, the existence of such a city is utterly impossible. Anticipating this doubt, they ask, "How can you hide this? and say: "Upon your lower lip... (tvad-adhareti).
"Ah! The quenching of that [fire] could not be achieved by any other nectar, but only by that which is connected to your lower lip.

Even there, because that fire has increased so excessively that it cannot be extinguished even by ten million young women, it must be quenched by its very flooding"—thus, great thirst is indicated. This applies likewise to the nectar to be described hereafter.
This is a supreme distinction.

Now, it may be asked: since you are indicated by the word "dhyānena" (by meditation) as those who will suddenly abandon their bodies, the means for that [meditation] is also seen [in you]. To this they reply: "viraha... (regarding separation). O, are we like others? No, we are not.

They are devoid of passion (anurāga), which is why we must seek external means for it, such as fire and the like. However, the sense is that it will arise from within itself, spontaneously. [The rest is] by them. Or rather, concluding what was intended to be said: "Indeed, how [can this be] in this difficult matter?"
Fearing the objection, "Why are you in such great haste?", they say that due to extreme sorrow, the very impossibility [of union] is the truth:

"If not... Even in meditation we do not go, because these bodies are fit and appropriate only for the fire born of separation, and not for those who are capable of the nectar of union; for that [union] is not accomplished here now.
The sense is that separation is certain not only at another time but even in another birth. By addressing him as "friend," they indicate that he too will experience future suffering there;
or rather, by the absence of immediate reunion with her, they suggest his abandonment of the body.

They say: "Even in another birth, may we through meditation reach the vicinity of Your feet or even the path to them"—this is their prayer. And therein, with the intention that it should be solely as friends, they address Him as "O Friend.
By this, the answer to the term "slender-waisted" is given: "Even one whose body possesses such excellent qualities according to Your desire must be abandoned [by You]."
Even if that [wealth] is abandoned, you must not be abandoned—this pair of verses is for the most part the same even in its sense of bestowing sovereignty.
And this is for the purpose of prohibition: "Therefore, O dear one! O great libertine! [do not abandon] us."

"Sprinkle with the very nectar of your lower lip that fire of love born in your heart through your natural smiles, glances, and sweet songs. Among us, there is no one at all whose own fire of desire she will sprinkle with the nectar of her lower lip"—this is the meaning intended for her own companions. Thus [ends the address] to those of her own group.
In every respect, complete indifference has been indicated.
Furthermore, there is the suggested humor (*narma-bhaṅgī*) that, when one's own desired and supremely sweet object is difficult to obtain, the greedy lick their own lower lip; unless it be so.

If, out of stubborn persistence, you do not desist from blocking our path without having heard our words, then we shall become bodies consumed by the fire born of separation from our own lord; that is to say, we shall die.
Nevertheless, even in meditation or in thought, we shall not—indeed, we will not—attain even the path to your feet.
The word "friend" (*sakhe*) implies that, having attained friendship through childhood play, you surely know our devotion to our own duty;
or rather, the word "if" (*ced*) is used here in the sense of certainty: "If you, as our protector, place your foot upon the head of obstacles."
As it is said in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (11.4.10): "And therefore, since our bodies have been consumed by the fire born of separation, we shall not go even to meditate upon Him. ||35||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Sprinkle" means "extinguish. This should be understood through the metaphor of [extinguishing] fire with a stream of water. First is the mention of the action. [The word *paramārti* (supreme pain) is used] because of the distraction caused by that supreme pain. The word *na* (not) is also connected with the fire dwelling in the heart (*hṛcchayāgni*), even though it has entered into the compound. The word *tvat* (you)— (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a verse from the *Bhāgavatam*, specifically 10.29.38: *siñca na tvad-viyogāgni-taptasya mama cetasah*). The translation reflects the grammatical and interpretive analysis provided in the Sanskrit commentary.)

With the intention of expressing that the extinguishing of the fire produced by you can only be accomplished by you alone, the word *pūra* (filling) also suggests the vastness of that fire; otherwise, since extinguishing could be achieved with even a small amount of water, the term "filling" (*pūrakeṇa*) would be useless. The suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).

It is implied, in sequence, that laughter and the other [emotions] serve as fuel and wind [for the fire of passion]. "Hṛcchaya" (dweller-in-the-heart) refers to Kāma, who lies or dwells within the heart. Therefore, even for the medicine that turns him back, drinking the flood of nectar from the lower lip is required in order to cause it to enter within; likewise, this [remedy] is such that no other counteragent exists.
And this has been indicated:

although the heroines' solicitation for union with the hero is effective through suggestion (*vyaṅgya*) rather than through direct expression (*vyakta*), nevertheless, for those women whose passion is extraordinary and mature, [it is so].
Because it is devoid of discursive thought due to the intensity of supreme agony, that [statement] is not contradicted here.

Alternatively, "that which fills with the nectar of your lips" refers to speech that fills and satisfies the listeners as if it had itself attained the nature of color through the filling of the nectar of your lips; by means of that [speech].

The meaning is: "Sprinkle the fire dwelling in the heart—the anguish residing within the heart—with the nectar of your words; that is to say, destroy our torment. Otherwise, if you do not sprinkle it, then by means of meditation—according to the maxim, "Whatever thought one has at the time of death, that is one's destiny"—one employs a specific practice out of supreme longing for the attainment of one's own desired goal.

It has been said: *yām* is used in the sense of possibility, meaning "we shall perhaps obtain. And therein, with the intention that there is no impossibility due to the power of your friendship, they address her as "friend" (*sakhe*). The rest has been suggested by them.
Or rather, those whose bodies have been consumed by the fire of separation caused by the constant meditation upon and contemplation of Your very feet;

in this context, "by meditation" serves as the means for further inflaming that fire of separation. Or else, [it refers to] the proximity to Your feet through the meditation of those very gopīs whose bodies were consumed by the fire born of separation.
The meaning is "eternal and ultimate union. We shall indeed go; therefore, only deceit and the mere act of killing a woman will remain for you, whereas we shall certainly attain union with you.
Alternatively, the meaning is that even those whose bodies have been consumed by the fire born of separation [from You] attain the state of Your feet, which is liberation (*mokṣa*).
The word "yām" (which) expresses a prayer. Now, one might ask: "How can there be liberation for Your devotees?
To this they reply: "By meditation," meaning by the thought or longing for liberation itself. Now, even so...
"That [liberation] would not befit you," they say; regarding this, they address him as "friend" (*sakhe*). The meaning is: "By our friendship, let this very thing be done for our benefit.
Thus, there is a prayer for the absolute non-existence of great suffering; liberation is the absolute non-existence of that [suffering].
This has indeed been explained in the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*.

Or rather, just as devotees and others might at times pray for liberation or other goals due to some suffering, so too might those women— who find their sole delight in wandering in Vṛndāvana— pray for the realm of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha, thinking that through meditation they might reach that state known as the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.

Simply out of the weight of their suffering; or rather, the sense is: "Even those cowherd girls whose bodies have been consumed by the fire born of separation from you, having made meditation their sole object, do not go near your lotus feet—how much less, then, shall we [ourselves] reach them? (i.e., how much less shall we reach our own selves?).
This is an expression of intoxication born of love; or rather, it is a prayer made with the intimacy of a friend, "Shall we not go?

Alternatively, the meaning is: "We shall follow the path of those gopīs whose bodies have been consumed by the fire of separation through meditation on Your feet—we shall die. Consequently, You too will surely feel remorse.

With this intention, they say: "O friend. Furthermore, regarding the view that those gopīs attained the *rāsa*-pastime with that very same body, [the verse speaks of her as a friend] because she was bound by husbands and others, and because she meditated on the means for their liberation; and because, due to their not returning for a moment, she contemplated their final state.
This is the general direction of the argument.
Or rather, [the question] "Shall we go near your feet even by means of meditation? is asked with a tone of irony (*kāku*);

that is, "Even if entreated by you later, we shall certainly not go. Or else, because this birth is endowed with all necessary conditions, that [attainment] cannot be accomplished here; and since it is impossible in another [birth], [the question is asked].
This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, with the weight of the pain of love, she prays: "Even in another birth, though we might approach your feet through meditation, we shall not even reach the path near them. And in that regard, the intention is expressed solely through her status as a friend.
They address him: "Friend! This is the answer to the statement, "Enough with this excessive prolixity; go there by this [path].
"When the fire of the heart's passion has been extinguished, we shall be able to go even with effort; otherwise, we shall surely die. What is the use of going by carriage and such?"

The meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): O friend! O great libertine! With the natural laughter, glances, and sweet songs of ours, a fire of desire has arisen within you; quench that with the very vessel of the nectar of your own lips.
Among us, there is no one at all whose fire of passion could be quenched by the nectar of another's lips.
The meaning is "he will look. Thus, the complete indifference of those belonging to his own class is indicated.

Furthermore, there is an implied humorous turn of phrase: when that supremely sweet object desired by oneself is difficult to obtain, the greedy lick their own lower lips; otherwise, if it were not so...

If, having not heard [this], you do not cease from your wicked persistence, then we shall become such that our bodies are consumed by the fire born of separation from our own husband; the meaning is: "it would be better for us to die.
Nevertheless, O friend, even in meditation upon or contemplation of your feet along with the senses, we do not attain even a path toward them.
The meaning is: "we shall go" or "we will not go. ||35||

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. Regarding the *Prīti-sandarbha* (332): concerning that which was said with longing, "Go back to your own homes," they say in response—"Sprinkle [us]," etc. "O dear one" (*aṅga*), O lustful one, from our own nature...

Sprinkling with the nectar from your own lips that fire of love which has arisen in you from the sweet song accompanied by smiles and glances— since that [nectar] of ours is somehow unattainable. For even another person, greedy for flavor, when failing to obtain the desired object, [licks] his own lip.
Thus, the word "licks" (*leḍhi*) also suggests a jest.

He states the reason for this with the word "no": as in the verse, "If You, the Protector, place Your foot upon the head of obstacles" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.4.10), the particle *cet* here also signifies certainty. And therefore, because...

It is certain that we have not become such that our bodies are consumed by the fire born of separation from you; therefore, even when meditating upon the object of your two feet, we do not reach, nor do we touch, their path. By addressing him as "Friend" (*sakhe*), he reveals his own words through the manifestation of the affection arising from their mutual childhood play in the past.
They manifested their straightforwardness. ||35||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "O All-pervading Lord! There is that which must be done, and we shall do it.

If You indeed do that very thing, then we shall certainly do it. If one asks, "What must I do?", listen: thus the *madhya-adhīra* (moderately impatient) speak again, beginning with "Sprinkle us, O dear one," and so forth. O dear one (*aṅga*)...

O you who possess a smile and a glance! Quench the fire of desire dwelling in the heart—that fire in the form of words expressing neglect toward me—with the full stream of nectar from your lower lip. By what means? With the vessel of the nectar of your lips; "ka" is used here in the sense of excellence. Quench that fire of desire which lies within the heart. What is it? It is the fire consisting of those words that demonstrate your indifference. How? By the filling of the nectar of your lower lip. O you whose gaze is accompanied by a smile! Quench it.

He whose skill in gazing is accompanied by a smile and a sidelong glance—if you do not act thus, then with our bodies consumed by the fire born of separation, we shall follow the path of your feet through meditation;
yet we shall not simply go there. For this fire that exists here is merely a burner.
It is not a "killer" (*māraka*); rather, a "killer" arises only from separation (*viraha*). This one, however, because it is born of song, is born of speech (*vāgja*) alone.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "By this [song], we shall be dried up; by that very moment, we shall be reduced to ashes. (35)
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, perceiving the softness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s heart through this expression of wretchedness, yet burning within with the fire of separation and unable to endure it, they pray:
"Sprinkle! O dear Kṛṣṇa, sprinkle—that is, satisfy—us. How? [As follows:]

In the context of the performance, they announce what is presented: "of yours"—this is to be understood from the force of the context. The fire is that very passion (kāma), which is the "dweller in the heart" (hṛcchaya) born from those two: your glance accompanied by laughter and your sweet song; it is "burning."

In response to the inquiry, "By what means is he to be extinguished? they say: by the very flood—the continuous flow—of the nectar of Your own lips; that is the water, and by that [it is to be extinguished]. Furthermore, we know the cause of this heart-disease in the form of desire, as well as the medicine that removes it.
We know this; however, both the cause and the remedy are under your control.
Therefore, this fire has now arisen and begun to consume us. Before it consumes us entirely, let a remedy be applied, as was done during the subduing of Kāliya.
By drinking the forest fire, the protection of all the inhabitants of Vraja was accomplished; likewise, protect us from this fire within us.
However, this fire cannot be drunk, because it burns only within and not without. Therefore—

"If you were to drink, this burning would happen to you just as it has to us; therefore, drinking is not appropriate for you. Furthermore, we ourselves have experienced its internal burning power. That forest fire was produced by some asura, but this fire [is produced] by your very laughter, glances, and sweet songs."

Therefore, having perceived the greatness of this fire— even greater than the forest fire— extinguish it by means of the filling of the nectar of your own lower lip, which is the cause of coolness. While the forest fire is seen within the range of all eyes,
this fire is not within the range of anyone's eye.
The sense is that once the internal heat has ceased through drinking the nectar of the lower [tongue], the fire itself will naturally reach extinction.
This is the essential point here: for it is well known that when the primary cause is removed, the disease also ceases.

When the arising of bliss occurs for us through the drinking of the nectar of the lower lip performed in secret, and when your eyes are closed, even your smiles, glances, and sweet songs will cease for a mere moment. Therefore, upon the cessation of that very cause, even the fire of the heart’s desire will remain unobserved by anyone.

The sense is that there will be a cessation [of the flow]. Although for heroines themselves, a direct request for the nectar of the lips is contrary to the *kāma-śāstra* and does not generate aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), nevertheless,
for these women who are infatuated, possessed of supreme love, and devoid of the discrimination between what is proper and improper— [The original text ends here.]
This was said because [the heart] is being consumed by the rows of flames of the fire dwelling within the heart.

They say: "If this were otherwise, then this great fame would be yours, and for us there would be great and true renown"—that is, "if you do not extinguish the fire dwelling within the heart, then we [shall fall] at your feet."

"By means of meditation, we go to the vicinity"—the meaning is "we shall go. Or rather, by means of meditation, we seek the path of their two feet; we shall attain it this very moment, and not at some other time.
In that regard, for those such as husbands and others who are intent on death and are turned away from the Blessed One—
Fearing that the fault born of attachment cannot be removed by any other atonement,

they state— beginning with "born of separation"— that one may attain Śrī Kṛṣṇa through the purification produced by entering the fire, thereby becoming fit for Him. "Those whose bodies have been consumed by the fire born of separation" refers to the fire residing within the heart.

The internal burner, having burnt the mind, when ashes have arisen, [continues] due to some particular spark that remains undistinguished from it; thus, when the body has become dry and wood-like, once it has fallen, no other fire arises, for they say of that very [fire]: "Those who have not attained the nectar of the lower [world] suffer separation."

[He] will be born. Therefore, we are those whose bodies have been consumed—that is, burnt—by the fire [of separation]. Or rather, we are those whose bodies have been consumed by the very fire born of separation; they are unfit for enjoyment and no longer suitable for dalliance, because they have become defiled through association with those who are averse to the Blessed One. For this very reason, [the fire of one who is] impure...

"Having perceived our unfitness for dalliance, you have rejected us; therefore, depart. Now, having burned this unfit body, we shall go to that place worthy of us—a state attained through meditation upon your feet—by means of union with you, possessing purified bodies. "O friend! [Thus she spoke.]
By this address, it is understood: "Surely one who is a friend does not deceive friends;

have I perhaps committed some deception? To this they reply: "Even though the medicine that extinguishes the fire dwelling in the heart is present, you do not give it. Or rather, as in the case of a yogi, by means of meditation now—

We shall attain the proximity that is the path of Your feet. In another moment, our bodies consumed by the fire of separation, we shall attain the proximity of Your feet—an immediacy through pure consciousness—once this body has been burnt; for in You, there is no cruelty toward one whose body is consumed.
It results in ill repute.
This is the intended meaning: the glance accompanied by laughter is the kindling, and the sweet song is the wind;
thus, the fire of the heart's longing produced by both is extraordinary (*alaukika*).
It is pacified by the filling of the nectar of your lower lip. This nectar of the lower lip is also supramundane;

for this very reason, there is the quenching of the supramundane fire by supramundane nectar, and not by the nectar enjoyed by the gods, because that [latter] is a cause of the torments of saṃsāra. For it is that very same fire which dwells within the heart.
In the absence of drinking the nectar of her lips, he produces the fire of separation and reduces his body to ashes;
therefore, it is only when we are possessed by the fire dwelling in our hearts that we shall attain you. Then that ascetic will also transfer into you. ||35||
Viśvanātha: Oh! Even at times other than the occasion for union, the bodies of these beautiful women, which they had desired to see naked, were seen on the day their clothes were stolen;
and even at times other than the drinking of wine, the shameless speech of these passionate women was heard.

He remains there; even now his voice is not heard. Alas, alas! They have been intoxicated by the sound of the flute, which is full of passion, and once again they have been overwhelmed by the charms of his words. Even that mind, upon which they relied to remain steadfast through shame, discernment, virtue, and fortitude—that too has been stolen away. Therefore...

While Śrī Kṛṣṇa was reflecting in his mind that these women generally speak with modesty and do not yet fully reveal their inner feelings through speech, certain of the most prominent gopīs—their natural dispositions overturned by the intense onset of the transitory emotion of madness—said: "Sprinkle! (siñca).

In this context, the word "hāsa" (laughter) implies its correlative term, which is understood to be "tava" (your). Thus, O dear Kṛṣṇa! by Your glance accompanied by laughter and by Your sweet song, that fire of the heart's desire—which has arisen, awakened, and flared up—is [extinguished].
Sprinkle and extinguish [this fire] with the flood of the nectar of your lower lip; for the suffix *ka* is used in the reflexive sense (*svārthe*).

If that very fire by which it was kindled is extinguished once discernment has been attained, only then will its transgression be pacified. Otherwise, the one who provided the fire incurs the sin arising from the burning of the house and so forth.
This is the intended meaning.
Here, by employing the word *hṛcchaya* instead of using *kāma*, the following is suggested: our desire indeed lies within the heart, and no one except you is able to awaken it.
And you, by means of the sound of your flute, enter our hearts through the openings of our ears;

having awakened the fire of desire lying dormant there, and having fanned it into a blaze with the ghee and honey of your smiling glances and the wind of your sweet singing, you begin to consume the very life-breaths residing therein. Therefore, [I fear] the sin of that burning—

If you are afraid, then extinguish it; yet there will not be even the slightest effort on your part for either its kindling or its extinguishing, because your smile and glance are the kindlers of that fire, and the nectar of your lower lip is its extinguisher. Both of those things reside in your moon-like face alone.

Therefore, having repeatedly observed that for you, a prince of such playful nature, sport consists primarily of both kindling and extinguishing fire—not merely the kindling of fire alone—it is this very thing that is seen even now. But surely, these [laughter, glances, and sweet songs] are my natural expressions. If, by means of these, young women...
"If you ask, 'Where, how many times, or by what means shall I then perform cures with the nectar of my own lips?'—

the truth is this: through the extraordinary remorse arising from the slaughter of thousands of women, this obstinacy of yours will surely pass away," they say— "if not, [then] those whose bodies have been consumed by the fire of separation..."
With our bodies consumed by meditation upon your feet, like yoginīs, we shall attain your path; may we reach it this very moment.
This is the meaning: we recognize ourselves as those whose asceticism was performed in previous births. That...

Since you do not accept this in this very life, we shall therefore not now take up an external, worldly fire for the purpose of performing penance; for the fire dwelling in the heart and the fire of separation from you exist spontaneously [within us]. Moreover, by that fire of separation which will become exceedingly powerful, even the fire dwelling in the heart [will be overwhelmed].

Therefore, even as our lives are being offered as oblations into the very fire of separation from Him, this resolve shall indeed be strengthened: "O, Fire of Separation from Kṛṣṇa! Desiring the touch of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, we offer our own lives unto You. Therefore, let us follow in the footsteps of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, unlike other people."
Place us in such a way that we remain unobserved, so that his feet may fall only upon our breasts and not upon the ground; and then,
with the fire of the fever of love extinguished by the very weight of your feet, we shall have our desires fulfilled.
"We shall become [so]. And even though you do not desire it, and even though you obtain the pleasure of touching our breasts, you will experience only the great remorse for killing a woman.
"Friend"—it is precisely because of our friendship that we desire this; you yourself [should protect] us, who are your friends.
The implied meaning is: "If you cause us distress, how is it that we do not likewise cause distress to you, our friend?
However, we know that wretched Love will indeed multiply even that sorrow of your remorse ten-millionfold and bestow it upon us alone; what can we do? It is our fate.

The forehead was created by the Creator in this very manner, as if already burnt. Therefore, O ocean of compassion, O you who perceive no change! Why do you sow the seed of the creeper of your own remorse?
Or why do you make us the ones to experience its fruit? Abandon your obstinacy; accept us!
There are indeed many echoes. ||35||
O lotus-eyed one, whenever the sole of your foot was granted a moment’s rest upon the lap of Ramā, you who are beloved by the forest-dwellers.
Ever since we touched [you], alas, when delighted by you, we are no longer able to stand in the presence of other people.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But surely they should approach their own husbands; they could extinguish this fire. To this, they reply with the word "when" (yahi): when there is an occasion, a festival, or an opportunity granted by Ramā (Lakṣmī).
Even then, it occurs only at certain times, not always. [This applies] to you, for whom the forest-dwellers are dear.

Because we were fond of the forest, whenever we touched upon any part of the wilderness, we were delighted and gladdened by you there; from that time on, we are not even able to remain in the presence of others. The meaning is that those trivial things do not please us. ||36||

Vaṃśīdhara: "Indeed, your husbands alone are capable of quelling the fire of passion," he says with the word *nanu*. When it is said, "this fire born of passion," they give the reply: "Not only has it granted a festival to Ramā alone, but it has done so for us as well, her devotees. Therefore, he says: "it has granted an opportunity."
"Or [he] has been granted leave. That too refers to the granting of leave. "Forest-dwellers" refers to cowherds (*gopa*), as it is said they dwell in forests and mountains.
"When" means *yarhi*, which signifies "at that time" (*tatra*) and "in that forest" (*vane*). This is the meaning.
For indeed, one whose habit is to cross the ocean does not have the desire to cross a small ditch.

The meaning is as follows: Alternatively, he is one for whom forest-dwellers and renunciants are dear; thus, since we too have abandoned everything and come to the forest for the sake of what is dear to you, take us [as well].

Alternatively, *ramā* is Śrī Rādhā because she delights (*ramati*) and gladdens (*ānandayati*) you; her sole of the foot is "given the opportunity" by you, meaning it is exceedingly soft and auspicious. From the moment we first touched it, we ourselves are unable to remain in the presence of others, let alone she.
By this, it is suggested that immediately after the touch of your limbs, the apprehension regarding the touch of other limbs has been dispelled.
From the *Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: "But surely what has been enjoyed by me is not suitable for you; how can she be enjoyed by you?
Thus spoke certain women who had only recently been married. [The verse begins with] "When," etc. O... [he/she].

O lotus-eyed one! Since the very day of our marriage, whenever and wherever we have touched your lotus-feet—at any place or at any time—from that moment on, it is not fitting to accept them previously and then abandon them now.
This is clearly evident even to you. [The author] further qualifies the soles of the feet with the word "ramāyāḥ" (of Lakṣmī).
"Only at some place, on some occasion"—this means "only when an opportunity has been granted. Or, "only in some place where a festival has been granted," meaning where an occasion has been provided;
the reason for this is that because we, the forest-dwellers of Vṛndāvana, are dear to you, that [meeting] is indeed difficult for her to obtain from you. (36)
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might object: "How can an offense be imputed to me when I am without fault?

When the minds and hearts of lustful women are agitated by the sight of my natural beauty and so forth, what can I do about it? Furthermore, even if I were not capable regarding those things imagined within the home," [the author] says in response:
"It is fitting for you, noble ladies, to remain right there. To this they replied with the words beginning "When...

(yadā). O lotus-eyed one! When—at the time of the arising of our indescribable merit—in some place difficult to attain, we were delighted by You through the manifestation of Your own inner nature, [we rested] at the soles of Your feet.
"We have been touched by your suggestive words.
"The Pulinda women were filled with the beauty of the saffron-paste from the lotus feet of the Wide-strider (Viṣṇu), which had adorned the breasts of their beloveds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.17).

Thus, according to the previous commentary on this point, even though the touch of her foot was somehow obtained by someone through some means, and although that [touch] became famous in her circles precisely because it was accepted as a mere part of the ritual for those who have performed the vow of Kātyāyanī, yet even those who had attained union with her were [united] by those who had attained union with her.
It should be understood that, having assumed a single identity with them, they spoke together. Of what nature was this?
The meaning is that the soles of their feet were granted a moment to Ramā, and thus a great festival was surely offered to her as well.
"Is this not merely a dream for you? Otherwise, even though it is eternal, it would still be like that even now.

To this they replied: "Because He bestows His own teeth and so forth continuously only upon the forest folk—the Pulindīs, the deer, and others—and not upon the people of Vraja, therefore [this is real] for us."

The meaning is that it is *sutarām* (all the more) difficult to obtain. Thus, by the abandonment of both Ramā and ourselves—who are worthy—and [the mention] of such [others] by their own form, a reproach is indicated.
Therefore, from the moment we touched her onwards, we have not been able to stand even in the presence of others.
"We are unable to do so. The meaning is that no other philosophical system (darśana) is pleasing to us.
For this very reason, the implication is that this is some kind of touch characterized by the power of a spell for eradication (uccāṭana-vidyā).
Now, [if you say] we are speakers of falsehood, they reply: "We always dwell in the midst of the assembly (goṣṭha-jana), and therein [we speak] plainly (añjas)."

The sense is that we dwell there by force, with ease and without effort. In the context of another's sovereignty, the cause for contact is found in some instances; in certain manifestations, a moment was granted to Ramā, while [the Lord] himself is dear to the forest folk—the inhabitants of Vṛndāvana.
The love of Śrī Gopāla and the others for Him is unswerving; oh, what misfortune it is that we have only occasionally touched upon it! The rest is the same.
Here, their explanation by means of the word "araṇye" (in the forest) implies only through association with those people, which is indeed a state of wretchedness.

The phrase "or rather, by this" provides the answer: we have come through a specific, natural love, and not through ordinary love like other people; this is intended as a denial. [Kṛṣṇa says: "O friend, you have reminded me well! By this he means that because of your friendship from childhood play, even your touch has occurred.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When" (*yarhi*). The meaning is: when, even though you were as fond of monkeys and such [in your childhood], your sole soles became an opportunity granted to Ramā, the beautiful woman, as she was intent upon approaching you in secret (*abhisāra*). From that time forward, we have not even touched those [soles], much less any other limb; for what kind of state [are they]?

Moreover, we have been delighted by you even during childhood, and you have engaged us in play; for this very reason, we are able to stand even in the presence of others, such as our mothers-in-law and so forth. Otherwise, we would be hated by them as well—this is the intended meaning. ||36||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, O great amorous ladies! If that is so, then your devotion is also seen toward Śrī Baladeva. Therefore, go to Him alone, the protector of desires; for how can I accept you as belonging to another? Anticipating this objection, they speak with an oath, beginning with "When... (yarthi). O [Lord]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

"O lotus-eyed one!"—by this, supreme beauty and other qualities are indicated as before. *Talam* refers to the essential nature (svarūpa), just as in the case of "the surface of the earth" (*bhūtala*), or else it means the lower part; "we have touched that" means we have attained a slight connection with it. This is a humble expression of love. She is called *Ramā* because she delights forever. Of Lakṣmī...

Even for her, [the opportunity] was granted only at certain times; therefore, although we—being forest-dwellers—are not fit to be your lovers, the fact that she is dear to you indicates your supreme compassion.
"In the presence of others" means if we should ever somehow happen to stand near other people. Likewise...

"Only out of sight, and not directly in our presence. "Añja" means that if we were somehow to stand before you, then it would be with the utmost suffering; the meaning is: even to stand [would be so difficult], let alone to sit or lie down. And that was by you yourself, O crest-jewel of the refined (*nāgara*).
They said, "It has been accomplished"—meaning, "You have delighted us on all sides. The word *bata* expresses either lamentation or certainty. The rest was explained by them.
Or else, although the root of Your feet is to be served even by Ramā, because it is dear to the forest-dwellers...

[This was] granted as an opportunity for the forest-dwellers themselves; therefore, at some place or at some time, whenever or to whatever extent we might have encountered [them], or rather, "wherever" means in some indefinable location. From that point on, you were made to take your pleasure.
They were satisfied; or rather, they were made to experience a particular kind of pleasure in dreams and the like. The rest is the same.
Or else: "O Great Deluder! Out of a desire for union with your limbs at another time, having gone home..."

"Let us stay"—even that is not possible, because you, a great rogue, have plundered every bit of domestic happiness; thus they say, beginning with "When... There are two reasons for their touch: "having seized the opportunity for Ramā. Having seized the opportunity (*ādatta-kṣaṇam*) means having taken the occasion for the sake of *ramā*, that is, for amorous play (*ramaṇāya*), [taking advantage] of the forest folk.

By the words "of my beloved," she refutes the fault of her own lack of discernment, implying: "Perhaps we have touched [him] while he was being entertained by you. Therefore, from that moment on, nothing else pleases her;
the sense is: "How can we go home?"
Or rather: for you, who are dear to the forest-dwellers, there is the foot-sole of that Ramā, Śrī Rādhā;

the rest is the same. Even though she is present right there [in the forest], nevertheless, by making known his steadfast devotion to remaining in her company, all the other gopīs likewise perceive him within themselves as if he were in her presence.
It should be understood that they spoke thus in order to produce joy; this is the answer to the phrase "or else" (*athavā*). [The meaning is:

"We have come solely through a special natural affection, and not through ordinary affection like other people. The double meaning (*śleṣārtha*) is: "O forest-dweller! because you always roam in the forest..."

Or, [the word *araṇya* may mean] one whose attendants and people are the forest itself; when we touched the soles of the feet of our beloved husband—of what nature were they? In some part or other, they granted no opportunity for *Ramā* (Lakṣmī) to sport; from that time forward, we have been delighted by you. But... by you... delighted.
O infinite ones, you have been delighted by this auspicious method; we, however, are not able to stand even before others in our true nature. ||36||
[The objection: "Is this not merely a dream for you? Otherwise, even though it is eternal, why would it still be so [only now]?

To this they reply: "[Because He is one who bestows His own teeth and so forth continuously only upon the forest folk, such as the Pulindīs and the does, and not upon the people of Vraja; therefore, for us...]"

The meaning is that it is *all the more* difficult to obtain. Thus, by the abandonment of both Ramā and ourselves—who are worthy—and by [the mention of] those of such [a nature] due to her own disposition, a reproach is indicated.
Therefore, from the moment we touched her onwards, we have not been able to remain even in a standing position in the presence of others.
We are unable to do so; the meaning is that other philosophical systems do not please us.
Therefore, the implication is that this is some kind of "expulsion" (*uccāṭana*) spell consisting of the quality of touch.
[Objection: But you are speakers of falsehood! You always dwell in the midst of the assembly (*goṣṭha*). To this they reply: "Directly" (*añjas*).

The sense is that we dwell there by force, with ease and without effort. In the context of another's sovereignty, the cause for contact is found in some instances; in certain manifestations, a moment was granted to Ramā, but [the Lord] himself belongs to those dear to the forest folk—the inhabitants of Vṛndāvana.
The love of Śrī Gopāla and the others for Him is unswerving; alas, what great misfortune it is that we have touched upon this only on rare occasions! The rest is the same.
Here, their explanation is "by means of *araṇya*," which, by its very connection to those people, is nothing but a display of wretchedness.

The phrase "or rather by this" provides the answer: we have come by virtue of a specific, innate love, and not through the ordinary affection shared with other people; furthermore, this [question] serves to negate that [ordinary affection]. With the words, "O friend, you have reminded me well!", [Kṛṣṇa implies]: "Because, due to our friendship from childhood play, even a touch from you all has occurred."

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "yarhi" (when). The meaning is: when, even while you were still a child fond of monkeys and the like, the sole of your foot became an opportunity granted to Ramā, the beautiful woman, as she was intent on going to meet him;
from that time onwards, we have not even touched that [foot], much less any other limb. In what state [was it]?

Moreover, we have been delighted by you since childhood and have engaged in play with you; for this very reason, we are able to stand even in the presence of others, such as your mother-in-law and so forth. Otherwise, we would be hated by them as well—this is the sense. ||36||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: [Objection] Surely, even during childhood play, touching and so forth occurred through friendship; so why, alas, are you now indifferent? To this they reply: "When... O [friend].

O lotus-eyed one, when—on some occasion—the soles of Your feet, which are dear to the forest-dwellers such as beasts and birds because You were friendly toward them in Your childhood, found an opportunity through the mediation of the beautiful Ramā, they became intent on following You; that is the meaning. From that time forward...
Thus, we have not even touched that [limb], let alone any other part of the body. Therefore,
having been previously delighted by you through your own natural firmness— even while we were engaged in childhood play—
we are now able, with ease and without effort, to stand before others such as our elders.
The word *bateti* expresses a sense of apprehension; the underlying thought is that otherwise we too would be abandoned by them. ||36||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, [an objection is raised]: "The substance that has been enjoyed does not become useful for us; moreover, you are married women. Therefore, you are not suitable for us. Anticipating this doubt, [the Lord] says: "The wives said—" beginning with "When... and so forth. "O lotus-eyed one! If at any time, anywhere..."

In our childhood, during games of dust and the like, we touched the soles of your feet; since then, we have been unable to stand before others. Let there be your company! This state of ours being related to another is merely a worldly convention, not a reality; you alone are our beloved.
We—of what kind of you? Of one dear to the people of the forest, beloved by the folk of Vṛndāvana;

for this very reason, our touch has occurred. Of what kind is the sole of your foot? It is one that grants a moment to Ramā, or grants her a festival, or grants her an opportunity; for on such an occasion, she obtained that touch.

The people of Vṛndāvana, however, always touch [the Lord], which demonstrates His dearness to the forest folk. And this is not found elsewhere; what proof is there? They say it by way of their own qualification: "You are unable to stand before others. What are we like? We are those who have been delighted by You, by You...
"By [him who is] the crest-jewel of all. Otherwise, how could we accept it? Therefore, the implication is that it is entirely appropriate for us to be unable to stand before others. ||36||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: "Indeed, I am your friend and am supremely compassionate; malice toward me is not appropriate, for I am here to instruct you in dharma through such words as 'you are ill-behaved' and so forth. To remain here is followed by powerful misfortune; therefore, having awakened from this delusion, resort to those [sages] alone, and for that very reason, [approach] this fire."
If He will indeed extinguish it, they say in response: "When... O lotus-eyed one!

O You whose eyes soothe the heat of the fire of desire in the heart! It is implied: how much more so by the gift of the nectar of Your lips? Therefore, whenever we have touched—that is, made contact with—the sole of Your foot.

Of what nature is the sole of His foot? It is one that has always granted an opportunity—that is, bestowed bliss—to Ramā (Lakṣmī) in some place or time; for, being ever delighted in the regions of Vṛndāvana, She never found a foothold there. [The verse continues: Śrī, reclining upon a beautiful couch, [worships] the supreme state of glory... with her own splendor.
She attends only upon him while he is resplendent, but not during such tasks as tending the cows; for although Lakṣmī dwells eternally upon his chest,

nevertheless, perceiving the superior auspiciousness of his feet, she becomes full of longing specifically for the soles of his feet, yet she does not obtain them at all times— since her very status consists in this weightiness.

He acts [thus]. Therefore, you do not grant the opportunity to serve him constantly. Oh, how inconceivable is the majesty of the nectar of his soles! For he obstructs everyone from all sides. Just as even Śrī desires to become a forest-dweller out of longing for the dust of his feet, so too do we.
We wish to become forest-dwellers.

Of what kind? [We wish to become those] for whom the forest-dwellers of Vṛndāvana—the Pulindas and others—are dear, because they are blessed by their habit of offering roots, tubers, and other forest produce.

"Because it was previously stated, 'The Pūrṇas and Pulindas' (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.17)," this statement is made with a hint of resentment: "But we, the people of Vraja, are not dear [to him]. Therefore, O lotus-eyed one! Since that time—that is, from then on—we have not even been able to stand here in the presence of others.

"We are able [to endure it]. But how much more so when she has been seated even in a place appropriate for such enjoyment, with regard to her lover?"—the meaning is that, therefore, this does not please us. Especially since she was enjoyed by you;
for it is precisely because they have experienced and remembered that enjoyment that they have come, for what is not experienced is not remembered.

Therefore, for those who have come to dwell in Vṛndāvana, it is improper to abandon it; however, because you are dear to the forest-dwellers, know that we too have come so as to become like them. Or rather, "araṇya" refers to Vṛndāvana; the "janas" (people) born therein are the deer, birds, and other such creatures.
Even they are dear to Him; as it is said: "O Mother, alas! [we are wretched]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.14), and because it was stated:
"Blessed indeed are even these deer, though their minds be dull" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.11).
These residents of Vṛndāvana relish that object which is our own enjoyment through the mere sight of Him and other such means.
The sense is that you have come here out of indignation alone and ought not to abandon [the people];

or rather, because [you are] dear to the forest-dwellers. For this very reason, having abandoned Vraja and made your residence in Vṛndāvana to cultivate affection for them, the residents of Vraja, however, are seized by envy.

He does not tolerate that in his presence; therefore, knowing that the forest-dwellers are free from envy and the like, grant us pleasure as we have come. Since you have previously delighted us, and because there is no obstacle here, our engagement in amorous play will proceed without hesitation. Thus...

It has been said: "Where even men, deer, and other animals dwelt together despite their natural enmity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.13.60). By the address "O dear one," this is indicated: you, who have been so favorable and a helper to us until now, wish to cause us to associate with those who are hostile—this is truly strange!
"Bateti" expresses grief.
Regarding the reading "añja," it means: by day, the forest-dwellers—the cowherds—are his favorites;
whereas at night, you sported with him without hesitation, and at that time, we touched the soles of his feet.
From that time forth, we have been unable to stand before others by our very nature;

however, it is pleasing to us to remain only in your presence, and the sense is that you are able to alter our nature. Since the refinement for love was produced by you alone, [we cannot endure] without a lover.
The meaning is that we are not even able to lead [him] toward knowledge. ||36||
Viśvanātha: Now, if that is so, then go to your respective husbands; they themselves shall extinguish this fire.
To this they replied: "When"—O lotus-eyed one!—"from the very moment we beheld your eyes, we have remained here having become bees. Thus, the passion of the eyes came first.

For it is stated in the Rasa-śāstra: "From that arises attachment of the mind, and from that, conceptualization. The sense is that for us, the very first sight of the eyes of Locanā is what initiates this prior passion (*pūrva-rāga*).
Furthermore, at that very moment—when, at some place such as Govardhana, [you beheld] the sole of your foot...
In a grove, we touched her breasts; how so?

It was a moment granted to Ramā—even to Lakṣmī, the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha and beloved of Nārāyaṇa—bestowing a festival of longing for dalliance, for the sake of which desire Śrī performed penance as a woman.

Thus, from the words of the serpent’s wives heard through Garga and others, it follows that this bestows a festival of longing upon us—the cowherd women dwelling in the forest. The underlying sentiment is:
"What wonder is there in this longing?"
Now, one might ask: "How can there be fitness for even Lakṣmī to obtain such a desirable object? To this they reply:

For you, whose beloveds are exclusively those born of the forest—the cowherd tribes—from that moment onward, it has been impossible even to stand before others, namely the cowherd women who are each their own respective wives, in our very presence.

The sense is: "Upon seeing them, we are unable to endure it; truly, compassion arises in our minds. Furthermore, it is not merely that we have touched them; rather, they were enjoyed by you in every way—that is, they were fully enjoyed at your pleasure and even brought under your control as men. Therefore, they are those who have already been enjoyed [by others].
"Do not send us elsewhere; we shall fall at your feet"—this was the meaning intoned in a plaintive tone. ||36||

Śrī, though she has already secured a place upon His chest, still yearns for the dust of His lotus feet, which are cherished by His servants; even though she has attained her station, she desires that which is served by His devotees.
Just as other gods exert themselves for the sake of obtaining her glance, so too have we taken refuge in the dust of your feet.

Śrīdhara: They say that the good fortune of Your feet is exceedingly wonderful—thus he says, "Śrī. Although she has obtained a place upon Your chest free from rivalry, she still yearns for the dust of Your lotus feet along with her rival, Tulasī. By saying "served by all Your attendants," he expresses the excellence of its supreme good fortune. Of her—

"Śrī [Lakṣmī] should look upon herself for the sake of her own vision"—for this purpose, there is the exertion of others such as Brahmā through their austerities; she is his *rajas* (creative energy), and in that same way, we too have taken refuge—thus says Vaṃśīdhara.
*Saubhāgya* means good fortune; *saundarya* means beauty. She is most wonderful, being one who is propitiated by all the gods.

"Because she is the dust desired by Lakṣmī. She is called Śrī or Lakṣmī because she is resorted to and served by all. Her state of being without a rival (asāpatnya) is due to her having been obtained alone. By "servants" (bhṛtyaiḥ) is meant Nārada and others who possess exclusive devotion; this is said in view of the Blessed One’s role as the sustainer of the universe and his protection of all beings.

Intending that the state of servitude belongs to all without exception, the Master’s feet have qualified the term "servants" by its universal application as "by all servants. *Atireka* means excess or abundance.
*Yasyāḥ lakṣmyāḥ* refers to that Lakṣmī. *Sva-vīkṣaṇam* is the looking toward oneself; [looking] toward ourselves, who are the self.
"Prapannāḥ" means they have arrived for the purpose of serving the dust of your feet. ||37||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: [It is said that] Lakṣmī is granted an opportunity only at certain times, not always.
To elaborate on what was stated regarding others, [the author says] "Śrī" and so forth. O friend!
We have taken refuge in the dust of your feet; the meaning is that we seek shelter in the pollen of your feet. Only...
We indeed offer our obeisances even to that which is frequented by Your servants; for it is the glory of Śrī, as he elaborates upon the greatness of Śrī: "How then shall we attain that?
One might ask, "In that case, what do you pray for? To this they reply: "In the same way, the dust of Your feet remains [upon her]."

"Where that place is, there we desire it"—this is dejection. Or rather: "We have taken refuge in the dust of Your feet. If this is so, then in which path of Your footsteps should that dust be received?
To this they reply: "In the same manner, it is the very dust residing on those feet, accompanied by them. This...
The meaning is as follows: while massaging His feet, they remain there with the saffron powder from His breasts;
that very powder alone is cherished by the servants. Śrī, vying with Tulasī, desires that very same thing. Therefore, there will be no rivalry between us and her. Or else:

The sense is this: because of the feet of Him by whose feet Śrī desired the pollen of the lotus, she remained only in the lotus forest due to that similarity [of color]. Although she obtained a place (pada) upon His chest, what kind of place? A place not frequented by service (bhṛti); it is not served by service, which is rooted in servitude.
Regarding the phrase "attained through service": rather, it is that which is established by its very nature (*svabhāva-siddha*). We too are exactly like that;

and as for the word "ca" (and), it is used in the sense of "tu" (but/rather). Just like her, we have taken refuge in the dust of the feet along with Tulasī; thus, no contradiction is created with her—this is the arising of intense longing (*autkaṇṭhya*).
The variegated state [of the mind] arises from envy, lack of tranquility, dejection, and so forth. (37)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might object: "Since you are of the same lineage as those like me, alas, why do you say, 'How have we touched the soles of your feet? Anticipating this doubt, they speak with extreme humility, being shrouded by the longing for their own desired object, beginning with the word "Śrī. That [Śrī] belongs to whom...

The meaning is that even after obtaining a place upon the chest of Nārāyaṇa, Śrī desired the dust of His lotus-feet; having abandoned the particular longing for service appropriate for a beloved, She chose only that which is fitting for a maidservant. The implication is that for this very reason, She accepted even the crowding together of many maidservants there.

What kind of woman was she? To this they say: "Of her... Having thus stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), they state the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*): "In that same way... Therefore, because it has been said, "This son of Nanda is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.8.13), he is like Nārāyaṇa; and you, who are such as he, are for him.
The meaning is this: although we have sought refuge and attained the status of being worthy of the position of the Beloved (preyasī) through our excellence in noble lineage and other such qualities,
it is solely due to the greatness of Your virtues that she— and we—
experience only a sense of inferiority, despite having obtained such a station.
In this regard, Śrī, relying upon the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of similarity to a lotus, desired the dust of His lotus feet;
we, however, disregarding that adjunct, have taken refuge in the dust of Your feet.
Thus, by means of the metaphors of "lotus" and "non-metaphor," the excellence of His feet and the distinction of ourselves are demonstrated.
This is implied.

[Alternatively: "Is it not the case that, for the reason stated previously, you are intent only upon satisfying your own senses, and not upon the affection that is favorable to me? To this they reply: "Śrī. Because (yat) —]

The meaning is "for that very reason. Thus, the sense of the sentence is: just as she, though authorized by her own husband in matters of such aesthetic delight (*rasa*), yet possesses a longing for the service of that [other] consisting of his attendance, so too do we toward you.
Likewise, during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, just as Śrī abandoned all others to worship Him alone, [so do we].
Thus, it has been made known that even for us, there is devotion to you alone.

Or rather, surely I do not recall touching you even in a dream. Be that as it may, even if there were a single lapse through lack of reflection, it is not proper to commit it again; and that would be an impropriety.

To the objection that [the Lord’s conduct] violates the noble custom of virtuous women and that His own conduct destroys such behavior of yours, they reply by taking Śrī herself— the crest-jewel of virtuous families— as their example, saying: "Śrī," meaning on the chest, that is, in the heart of her own husband.
Although Śrī has indeed attained a station of renown,

she is bewildered by the weight of your matchless sweetness; nevertheless, due to her own sense of unworthiness regarding contact with your limbs, that which is merely the dust of the feet related to Vṛndāvana— this being what [is sought].
He desired: "We too have taken refuge in the dust of Your feet"—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). As it has been said:
"By the desire for whom Śrī, the woman, performed penance" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.16.36);
because such renown is heard, and he himself will say later: "Your birth is supremely victorious."

The repetition of the word "pāda-rajas" (the dust of the feet) in the verse, "Vraja takes refuge in Indirā; for she is eternally here" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.1), should be understood as arising from extreme longing.

As it has been stated regarding both positions, the absence of metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) in both cases should also be understood as being just as before. And that [absence] applies to both positions.
Not only she alone, but Tulasī herself was also suddenly enamored by Vṛndā in her playful form;
for in the Jālandhara-upākhyāna of the Kārttika-māhātmya of the Padma Purāṇa, it is heard that she too became her beloved. Likewise, in the Mathurā-māhātmya of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Vṛndāvana is the twelfth [place], inhabited by the goddess Vṛndā; it is presided over by Hari and served by Brahmā, Rudra, and others. Thus [it is said] in the Vārāha Purāṇa, in its Māhātmya.

"Vṛndāvana is the twelfth [place], protected by Vṛndā; it is dear to me, O Earth, and the destroyer of all sins. Because it is heard that [the Lord] resides there, even dust that has come into contact with His servants is [sacred].
To further distinguish her excellence— even that which remains after being served by the hosts of Your attendants—

they speak of another quality of hers with the words "of whom" (yasyāḥ). Other gods [are merely] at the level of the perfection culminating in love for their own husbands, [which is attained] through their own gaze.

Śrī Viṣvaksena, Garuḍa, and others—even their effort [is directed toward her]. If it is the case that for each of them, she is of such a nature, then what is the fault? This is the underlying sense. Even in the context of divine majesty (*aiśvarya*), the meaning is generally the same as before;
however, whereas previously she was attained through a vision of excellence produced by love, here—on the other hand—[it is attained through majesty].

The distinction lies in the fact that [the former] has attained spiritual knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus, this should be understood as the answer to such statements as "Service to the husband is for women," and so forth; furthermore, this is intended as a prohibition.
Now, one might object: even Śrī and Vṛndā remained in my forest at my request by abandoning their own husbands—what [fault] is there in that?

To the question "Who are you?", they replied: "We are Śrī. The meaning is that we are that very Śrī who, along with Tulasī and Vṛndā, has always desired the dust of your lotus feet here in this forest; thus, out of that longing, she has made her dwelling here.
"In the same way," [they say] "we too have taken refuge in the dust of your feet"—this is said ironically, implying "certainly not."

The meaning is as follows: the fickleness displayed by Lakṣmī, who is renowned for her instability, and likewise the unchastity of Vṛndā—who, though she had obtained Jālandhara as a husband—is entirely appropriate; such behavior is not for women like us. Here too, [the word] "of the husband" [is implied].
This is the answer to that very point. ||37||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O crest-jewel of the noble! Do not sprinkle the fire of the longing in our hearts by offering the nectar of your lips; rather, grant us even mere service unto You. If this is said, [the Lord replies]: "Even so, O simple-minded ones, only one or two of you shall be accepted by Me. Otherwise—"

Fearing that, due to your extreme abundance and the resulting constant rivalry among one another, there will surely be suffering even in the future, they—seeking to avoid that through a simile and desiring only the state of being maidservants in the ultimate sense—said: "Śrī. That is to say, *uta* (even) *api* (though), even when her own glance is the cause [of such rivalry].
"But for all others—everyone else besides you, including the gods beginning with Brahmā—there is effort.
This indicates that envy arises due to such a distinction in greatness. It is suggested by one who cannot endure the company of a rival wife;
this is the intended meaning of the word "others" (*anya*). Thus, his lack of attachment to her is also implied.
Nevertheless, even that Lakṣmī, though accompanied by her co-wife, desired only the dust of His lotus feet;
this was stated by the wives of the Nāgas: "Desiring which, Śrī performed penance as a woman" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.16.36).
And it was also said by Śrī Sanaka and others in the Third Canto:
To him whom prosperity approaches at every moment, while others seeking wealth bear the dust of his feet upon their own heads—
he who is the abode of the fresh tulasī garland offered by the fortunate.
"The world [is like] the pleasure-vehicle of the Lord of the honey-bees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.20).
The reason for this is stated as "frequented by servants";
because it is served by a multitude of servants who are the objects of His supreme affection, it is characterized by *rajas* alone.

The meaning is: "because of the conceit of being supremely exalted. Alternatively, even though Śrī has obtained a place upon the chest of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, she is nonetheless [devoted] to the dust of Your lotus feet; for indeed, she is utterly infatuated by the weight of Your incomparable sweetness.

Just as [the Lord] desired that, so too have we taken refuge in His very dust of the feet by way of seeking shelter; therein, the dust of the feet signifies servitude. And in that regard, out of supreme devotion and with the intent to express one's own lowliness, it is specifically "the dust of the feet" and not the Lord Himself directly.
It has been stated that [the goal] is servitude (*dāsya*). In that regard, because it is extremely difficult to attain, there is a sense of oneness intended to express even a mere fraction of it.
Or rather, it is only when servitude exists that the dust of the feet is obtained; or indeed, only when that [servitude] has been attained.
The desire for the dust of His feet and the state of having surrendered to Him mean that servitude (dāsya) is being accomplished;
because of the eternal connection between "yat" and "tat," the word "tat" brought forth by the word "yat" indicates steadfastness in the sole desire for Him.

Alternatively, since the metaphor of the lotus was previously employed in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), that metaphor was not applied to himself because he lacked the quality of removing all suffering and so forth, which is the intended meaning of *śrī* (glory). Or rather, Lakṣmī desired only the dust of such majestic lotus-feet.

But we are lowly, devoid of such fitness; yet we have taken refuge in that very dust associated with His lotus feet, even though it has fallen somewhere far away. This is an expression of supreme wretchedness.
The repetition of "the dust of the feet" is for the purpose of making known the exclusive longing for mere servitude (*dāsya*). As it is said:
The meaning is: "She did not consider the fault of her being a servant due to her longing for service to You; so too do we.

Alternatively, desiring to request service in the future, they—establishing His supreme excellence by way of His being desired even by Mahālakṣmī, who is worshiped by all—and thus taking refuge in Him alone, say: "Śrī. This is the meaning.
That very same [place]. Let it be qualified by those [attributes] in another way.

Or rather, that which belongs to Tulasī—because she always dwells there due to her fondness for Govinda’s feet—it is "frequented by infinite servants. In this, even the competition among many is shown.
Because of the statement, "The lotus feet of the Essence-beings," this refers to the exertion of others—both the *suretaras*, such as the Daityas and others, and the *surās*. The rest is the same.
By this, the answer to the verse beginning with "of the husband" [24] is given: for service to the husband and so forth is not the supreme [goal].

It is not merely dharma, but rather servitude unto you alone; for even Śrī, whose compassionate glance is sought by Brahmā and others, seeks that very [servitude]. Or else, it refers to Him—Nārāyaṇa—the dust of whose lotus feet Śrī desired.
In the same way, "tat" means "like him," referring to you, whose dust of the feet we have taken refuge in;
for it has been said: "Therefore, this son of Nanda is equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.19). The remainder is entirely consistent.

This is the meaning [of the verse] without resorting to *aiśvarya* (divine power). The intended sense based on *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows: even though she was such [an exalted being], and having obtained such a place, she desired only the dust of his feet—that is, the *Śrī* (Goddess Lakṣmī)—but she did not actually obtain it;
thus her lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) is indicated. By the phrase "of whom" (*yasyāḥ*), some fault has been attributed to her because she was desired by many people.
Therefore, with an awakened mind free from non-duality, it is indeed appropriate that one should desire Your service in that very way;

or rather, for the sake of which— namely, so that Śrī may not look at me even when I am looking at her, nor at others, including the gods and the *sāttvika*s— this effort is made during the time of [her] abiding.

Because she blinded them with wine and other intoxicants, and because she caused them to faint as she departed at the time of her leaving, it was Śrī herself who desired him. On Kṛṣṇa’s chest there is a certain subtle yellow line on the left side, which Garga and others proclaimed in Vraja to be Lakṣmī; it was with this intention that they felt envious of her.
[This is] her speech. And we likewise, being such as we are, what else could we do but become those who have taken refuge in the dust of your feet?
Rather, the meaning is that we, being of sound intellect and steady nature, shall indeed go home for the sake of serving our husband and so forth. ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: Regarding the verse, "Now living beings take pleasure in me" (*bhā.pu.* 10.29.23), [the commentary states]: "O amorous women, you ought to cultivate only that affection which consists of the state of being a lover (*kānta-bhāva*)."
Anticipating the objection that the form of Lakṣmī and others might be intended there as examples, they offer a rebuttal: "Śrī.

For although Śrī is likewise renowned as being upon the chest, even though she has obtained a place on the breast of Viṣṇu, [she does not equal] Your lotus feet which reside in Śrī-Gokula-Vṛndāvana, together with the Tulasī known as Vṛndā.

He desired her; for it is well known among the sages that from the time of your birth, Nanda’s Vraja became a playground for Lakṣmī, and thus the goddess Vṛndā, appearing in the form of Tulasī, made her eternal residence in Vṛndāvana. Of what nature was he? He desired even the dust [of her feet] through his servants.
It is honored by those connected to Vraja through such acts as being held upon their heads and so forth, even though it has been enjoyed [by them].

But of what nature is its majesty? It is such that even for other gods, including their own attendants and so on, there is exertion [to attain] even a glance of compassion directed toward her. The word "ca" (and) implies "we too."

The word "api" (even/also) carries the same sense as a particle indicating a change in tone (*kāku*). Therefore, the meaning is: just as Śrī and Vṛndā are, so too we are indeed simple-minded, yet we have not even truly taken refuge at the dust of Your feet; in fact, we have not done so at all. ||37||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: By means of two verses beginning with "śrī yat," other [goddesses], manifesting this very same meaning, demonstrate their own super-mundane nature as being superior even to Śrī—
[stating] that although Śrī had already obtained a place upon His chest, she nevertheless longed for, indeed desired, the dust of His lotus feet, and not [His chest].

She has obtained [it]. Why has she not obtained it? Because for Tulasī alone, that which is served by Your servant is natural; "bhṛti" means the wage for labor, and the fruit of action is not served by that [wage].
What is she like? To this they say: "of whom," meaning those others who, in their own vision—that is, in their perception of themselves—are [otherwise].
It is merely the exertion of the gods; we are likewise of that same nature, but there is this distinction:
she is indeed only a desire, whereas we have attained the very dust of Your feet through our surrender; thus, we are even superior to her.
Therefore, enough with any other suspicion. ||37||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: When it is said, "They have been delighted by you," one might at times feel perturbed. Having reflected in their minds that those women desire to attain the status of the highest qualification (*uttama-adhikāra*), they pray, "May we become like Lakṣmī, who, having abandoned the pride of her lotus-throne, longs for the dust of [Viṣṇu's] feet. Thus they speak as Śrī.
Thus, even Śrī, who possesses desire, longed to serve the dust of Your lotus feet;
for although she had obtained a place upon Your chest free from rivalry, Śrī— being the supreme heroine and most clever—
considered the extraordinary good fortune of the soles of the feet and served the very dust of the lotus feet.
Abandoning her status as a co-wife, she serves the Lord on His chest together with Tulasi, who is without a rival wife; for there is but one nectar [of love].

Since the soles of His feet are the locus of all nectars, being the very essence of passion (*rāga-sāra*) because they are the support of passion, she thus serves the dust of His feet, desiring the specific sweetness and longing inherent in all nectars within that passion.

If it is asked, "How is there knowledge of these [Vedas] being served by Śrī?", he says in response: These Vedas, having realized their own sovereignty in a previous birth, therefore proclaim that they are to be served by Śrī. Alternatively, the statement regarding their being served by Śrī is based on the words of Garga: "Equal to Nārāyaṇa in qualities" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.13).

Nothing is impossible. Of what nature is the dust of the feet? It is "served by servants" (*bhṛtyajuṣṭam*); that is, it is served by servants who are nourished by a particular essence (*rasaviśeṣeṇa*), namely those twelve forms that have the netherworld (*rasātala*) as their support.
[Objection: If Tulasi is served by others and by servants as well, then how can there be a rivalry with Śrī?

"Was envy not born [in her]? To this he replies: Just as Tulasī, though seeing Śrī Kṛṣṇa being served by other attendants, felt no envy in her heart but served Him with extreme joy, so too for Śrī [Lakṣmī], there was no occasion for envy due to the majesty of Vṛndāvana; thus it is said:

And [it is said], "where there are those whose enmity is natural. The sense is that rivalry finds no room in the minds of those who serve at the dust of the feet—those who are free from envy as if they were strangers to one another, being utterly immersed in the happiness of service. Thus, the firmness of authority comes through service alone, and not otherwise.
