For the sake of beholding her beauty, Śrī looks upon us; for this purpose, other gods such as Brahmā and the rest exert themselves through the practice of austerities. Just as she emerged during the churning of the Ocean of Milk and, disregarding Brahmā and the others who desired her, served only the dust of her feet, so too [does she act].

"Having abandoned husbands and others who desired us for their own pleasure because of our resemblance to Śrī, we too have taken refuge at Your feet; yet we are not of the highest qualification. Rather, it is the duty of servants and maidservants to serve their master, and the duty of those related to or favorable toward the master to serve him."

But our husbands and others are not favorable; on the contrary, they are harmful. Therefore, their abandonment alone is appropriate. Although the Lakṣmī of Vaikuṇṭha, having abandoned the fault of fickleness, always indeed worships the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, nevertheless, [how much more so] the dust of Your feet, O You who sport in Vṛndāvana!

Perceiving the preeminence of virtues in service, she desires to dwell upon the soil of Vṛndāvana and acts accordingly. As it is said: "O King, it became the pleasure-garden of Ramā. And furthermore: "By the desire for whom Śrī performed penance as a woman..."
"Having abandoned desires, she has long maintained her vows" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.16.36).

By this, an answer has indeed been given to the objection that she failed in her service to her husband. Or rather, although Lakṣmī—the wife of Śrī—is desired by the servants who attend upon Him, she did not obtain His lotus feet.

Although her servants remained motionless and she had abandoned fickleness, nevertheless, because they were destitute, no special regard arose for her on account of their mental compliance. For the sake of her own glance—at herself, meaning "upon her own glories"—the servants [longed] for a glance; [as did] the deer.

Because it has been stated that [the Lord's] lotus feet are "the all-in-all" (sarvasva) of them, for that very reason Śrī exerts herself with the thought in her mind: "May I, by their grace, become authorized to serve the dust of their feet when they are pleased. Just like those servants, we too [seek] your dust; indeed, your dust is inherently auspicious.
The sense is that one is exceedingly fortunate by virtue of the connection with his feet. ||37||

Viśvanātha: Thus, you yourself have made us your own beloveds; yet, we express our desire for nothing other than service at your feet, speaking with an illustration: "Just as Śrī Lakṣmī desired the dust of the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa, so too do we [desire yours], even though you are equal to him."

They have taken refuge in the dust of Your lotus feet. Furthermore, since You are equal to Nārāyaṇa according to the words of Garga Muni, it follows by its own force that we too are equal to Śrī; this is the underlying meaning.
Moreover, although Tulasī has obtained a place—the very station—on Your chest, the most excellent of all locations...

Even though the dust of his feet was frequented and served by the attendants of his co-wife— thus resembling a mere throng of men— she desired it; for, casting aside even her natural modesty appropriate for a beloved wife and accepting her own inferiority, she longed for it out of her state as his beloved.
"Even the state of being a maidservant is exactly as we desire;
therefore, even with your red-clad leaf-clad servants, we wish to abandon all shame and massage your feet. Likewise, [we shall perform] the service of the forest-dwelling Pulindī women of Vṛndāvana."
We desire even to smear our own foreheads with the saffron from her feet, which has adhered to the grass, accepting even such a deficiency of our own.
Furthermore, may the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, being well-pleased, grant her [this] for the sake of his eternal residence.

The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is this: "O crest-jewel of connoisseurs (*rasika-śekhara*), you have bestowed [your grace] upon your own chest, yet you do not grant it to us even for a moment, though we are in the vicinity of the soles of your feet;
thus, our own foreheads are truly cursed. If one, desiring one's own fame, [acts] according to the authority of Garga’s words...
"If you wish to become equal to Nārāyaṇa, then carry us upon your chest"— this is a suggestion that touches upon the profound depth of his inner sentiment.
Indeed, just as that Lakṣmī is fickle, so too are you all in the houses of meritorious people.

"Even in the home, you must accept the nature of fickleness"—this playful suspicion was voiced by whom? By the silent one [the Muni]. "The Goddess Śrī is fickle," they say; yet she is supremely steadfast. For it is said that for the sake of obtaining her glance filled with the essence of parental affection (vātsalya-rasa)—a glance directed toward her own [devotees] rather than for the sake of looking upon other gods such as Brahmā and others—[she remains constant].
For those who are like her sons, there is only exertion; yet she generally regards neither that nor them, but rather some power of hers alone bestows upon them the wealth they desire. ||37||
Therefore, O Destroyer of Sins, be gracious to us who have abandoned our homes and come to the root of Your feet, hoping for Your service.
O Ornament of Men, grant the state of servitude to those whose souls are scorched by intense passion upon beholding Your beautiful smile and gaze.

Śrīdhara: O destroyer of afflictions, O remover of suffering! We, whose only hope lies in your service—that is, in your worship—have abandoned our homes and wives and have arrived here like yogis. Our minds are scorched by the intense passion born from beholding the play of your beautiful smile and your gaze.
O jewel among men! Grant me your service. ||38||

Vaṃśīdhara: Because they have taken refuge in the dust of your feet, therefore [they are so]. Or else, "those whose hope is for service to you"—that is, sitting near you; or rather, it is a qualification of the dwelling place: "having abandoned those in which there is the destruction of service to you. [This is the construction] with respect to the yogins.

[These are] the renunciants. Or rather, they address those who are suffering: "The *puruṣabhūṣaṇas* [are so called] because they 'steal' (*muṣ*)—that is, afflict—the heart, which is the 'earth' (*bhū*), the abode of the person (*puruṣa*), the individual soul (*jīva*). Or else, they are so called because they "dwell" (*vasati*) upon the earth of the person (*puruṣabhū*). The sense is that this is appropriate for one who knows both the external and the internal. [This refers to] servitude (*dāsya*).
The state of being a slave; by this, attachment and so forth are indicated. ||38||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "We have no rivalry toward anyone, nor do we possess pride;
our affection is for You alone. Therefore, be gracious toward us.
To this, others said: "That is not so," and so forth. O *vṛjinārdana*, O destroyer of suffering! Therefore, to us... [the rest of the sentence follows].
"Be gracious!

If you say, 'Indeed, I am gracious only toward those who possess nothing,' they replied, 'We too are exactly like that!'—O ornament of men! Grant us servitude; grant us the state of being your maidservants, so that we may be able to perform worship."

Of what sort are we? [We are] those whose souls are heated by You, or for the sake of You; the heat caused by You passes away only through worship of You. O You of beautiful smiles and glances! O You of intense desire!
The meaning is that even intense—that is, sharp—desire is surpassed by You, who are supremely sweet even compared to desire itself. ||38||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, although situated in the third direction, she concludes what was intended with the words "Therefore, not so. For that very reason stated previously, [the Lord] grants grace; they say to Him: "Grant me only servitude (*dāsya*). But are they not intoxicated by fresh youth? Even servitude—
If you say that such a thing is difficult to obtain, they speak with supplication as to how it might be given: "We have attained," and so forth.
The sense is: therefore, by renouncing everything, you ought certainly to fulfill the hope of those who have sought refuge;
otherwise, we shall suffer great sorrow, and that would be unbecoming of you.

They said: "O Destroyer of Sins! And there, their hearts overflowing with their own natural emotion, they said with the intention that service consisting solely of a particular aesthetic flavor (rasa) should be granted: "O Crown of Connoisseurs!
[Your... (tvad...).
Or rather, the meaning is that even for those whose souls are tormented by such gazing, you grant only servitude;

thus, hope for the removal of that very torment has been abandoned. And they say that servitude is indeed appropriate, addressing Him as "O Ornament of Men! (puruṣa-bhūṣaṇa). Furthermore, it refers to those in whom there is the destruction of Your worship—that is, Your service—everywhere.
Thus, by means of a pun (*śleṣa*), there is both a dwelling and a qualification. Or rather:

"O you of beautiful smiles and glances! You say this only out of deceit"—thus, while her inner feeling is being grasped through dissimulation (*avahitthā*), she reveals that feeling through her verbal dexterity: "The passion (*kāma*) which is more intense than yours..."
The meaning is: "For us, whose souls are tormented by Him"—this is the reply to the charge that He is of ill-character (*duḥśīla*).

For those who are scorched by desire for You, how could there be any deliberation or fault regarding His abandonment? Indeed, for those seized by the great serpent of lust, neither of these two [deliberation nor fault] is possible; thus, the purpose is a negation.
Therefore, for our sake, be gracious; the meaning is that you should abandon your insistence.

The word "vṛjinārdā" should be split as "vṛjinārda. Since we, whose hope was fixed on worshipping you, have left our dwellings and reached the base of your feet, therefore [you should grant us this], O You who possess the characteristics such as being beautiful like you, and so forth.
The meaning is: "Grant service to them [the gopīs], but not to us; we have no need for that.

The intention behind the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is that even for those gopīs, because they do not ultimately accept that [service], there is an absence of the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*).
He [Kṛṣṇa] [approached] the men, who were actually his friends, assuming the various costumes of the women of Gokula out of a longing for each of them.

"In you they are adorned"—here too, impossibility is shown. Or rather, *puruṣa-bhūṣ* means "the existence of man," that is to say, the universal of man (*puruṣa-sāmānya*). "O *ūṣaṇa*!"—that is, O tormentor! O defiler of that very species! This is an address accompanied by anger. *Ūṣa*... [text fragment]
Regarding pain: ||38||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, because you have surrendered to passion (*rajas*), grant me grace.
They say this very thing: "Grant me only servitude. If it is asked, "But they are intoxicated by fresh youth!
How can servitude—which even Lakṣmī and others pray for—be granted? then [the answer] is with humility:

They said: "Hoping for Your grace, we have abandoned our homes along with all our kinsmen and attendants and have come to the soles of Your feet. Therefore, You ought certainly to fulfill the hope of us who have surrendered by renouncing everything; otherwise, great sorrow would befall us. This is the sense. Otherwise, there would be immense suffering for us.

And they say that this is unbecoming of you, addressing him as "O Destroyer of Sins! In that regard, with the intention that servitude consisting of a particular *rasa* alone should be granted, they say "O Crown of Rasikas!
And they say that this is indeed appropriate, addressing him as "O Ornament of Men! The rest [is] by them...
This has been explained.

Or rather, [one might object]: "In that case, let the householders perform my worship right there in their homes, just like the community of devotees, by going to their houses along with my servants, the cowherds. To this, [the Lord replies]: "Right there... [and so on].

If it is argued that this is because of the attainment of all those requisites, they reply there with a tone of irony: "Abandon your dwellings. The reason for this is: "In those [dwellings], there is no destruction of the practice of austerity (*tapas*) and worship (*upāsti*); the meaning is that the cultivation of that [tapaḥ] cannot be accomplished there. Furthermore, O Great Deluder! We do not offer service like other devotees.

It is prayed for that which might be accomplished within the homes along with the groups of cowherds; however, with the intention that it be specifically through the service of a maidservant (*dāsya*), they speak with an enactment of extreme distress: "The *puruṣa* is the individual soul (*jīva*); its *bhū* is its place, the heart; that [place] *ūṣati*, meaning it afflicts or torments it. [From the root] *ūṣa* in the sense of pain. O You who are thus!

"By your beautiful smiles and glances"—or rather, "O you with beautiful smiles and glances!"—thus, by means of verbal artistry, she reveals her inner state which is being concealed through dissimulation (*avahitthā*), as if saying: "Therefore, you speak this out of sheer craftiness. [The phrase *tvattas*] means "from you"; [the one] who is tormented by the intense passion (*kāma*) arising from you...

"Since He is our very self, therefore quickly perform the remedy for that [separation]; otherwise, the final stage [of death] will arrive. Alternatively, the sense is: "Grant me the service (*dāsya*) which constitutes that remedy. Or again: "Indeed..."

If it is argued, "The servitude to Me that is naturally established for you through your status as daughters and wives of My cowherd women—the foremost of My devotees—is already a fact; what is the use of praying for it?"—it is true, but [the Lord says] with great urgency: "Grant me that which is extraordinary and appropriate for Us."

They say: the meaning is that which is fit for those with heated hearts is their service (*dāsya*). Or rather, the direct mention of "self" is due to humility, bashfulness, and so forth. Alternatively, the word "not" (*na*) from the previous [verse] is to be supplied.
Or else, out of extreme distress, they say—even if it involves grasping at straw—that this is for women whose hearts are heated, whoever they may be.

"Grant us servitude. The implication is that even when such servitude is attained, there will certainly be a special grace from you. This is the answer to the charge of being "ill-behaved. It is indeed appropriate to abandon even a true master out of a desire for service to You; this principle has been recorded in the Siddhānta.

Thus, and especially because those who dwell there have you as their object of worship, and because they are connected to you through their relationship with their masters, they fall from the path of your devotion and are indeed sinners; therefore, they must certainly be shunned.
Furthermore, for those whose souls are tormented by longing for you, how could there be any deliberation or fault in abandoning them?
"What indeed can there be for those seized by a great serpent? This is the meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*): *vṛjina* means sin.
We have come to the root of Your feet because You are the destroyer of the sins of others as well;
yet now, Your mind is observed to be set upon sin itself, so be gracious. [Forgive] our offense in coming here.
"Forgive me. The meaning is: "Restrain your mind and place it within the holy [Vraja].

Or rather, if one should say, "Surely even Lakṣmī finds it difficult to obtain service to Me; please accept this which is being given out of Your mercy," they reply with indignation: "Those who, having abandoned their homes, hope for Your worship..."
"O Satya, we have reached the root of your feet; we have taken refuge like maidservants.
[The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative: grant servitude to them, whose souls are tormented by intense longing.
For us, who are devoted wives, that is sufficient—this is the meaning. [We seek] only male companions, and not—"

"O you who adorn women! Therefore, what is this to us, or why does it burn our hearts?"—the meaning is as before. The underlying sentiment is: "What then is the point of even devotion toward you? This sequence of the composition has not been explained [previously].
Prīti-sandarbha 332: They conclude the preceding statement with "tan na" (that is not so).
The term "vṛjinārdana" (destroyer of sins) is used here in the accusative sense. O remover of all suffering, therefore, be gracious toward us; the meaning is:
abandon this false perception. But surely you [also]...

Having abandoned their homes and other possessions, they came here and likewise took refuge at my feet; yet there they said, "They did not reach the root of our feet. In that same way, having cast aside what is unreal, those who hope for Your worship have not reached the root of Your feet, which is real; rather, they have done so out of mere curiosity, as if [seeking] the moonlight.

The meaning is that they have come for the purpose of seeing Vṛndāvana. Therefore, grant the service of those very women whose souls are scorched by the intense longing born from beholding You in such a manner, but not that of those like me. Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because there is an absolute lack of giving, and thus no status as a recipient (*sampradāna*).

This is said with the intention that [the gift] "becomes" [something else]. Therefore, the meaning is that even this gift will not remain very stable in this Gokula. Furthermore, the address "O Ornament of Men" (*puruṣa-bhūṣaṇa*) is a pun; it refers to the male friends who have gone to Gokula.

Thus she adorns herself, yet even today she has not adorned even a single woman of Gokula. Therefore, the sense is that these heroines, though their souls are so tormented, exist merely as products of imagination.
Here, because the impossibility [of her doing so] is indicated by another state of being (*bhāva*), it is said: "The forest was seen in full bloom" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.21).
By this, even the intensification of that state has not been overlooked. ||38||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therefore, they say, "Be gracious unto us"—to which [the Lord replies], "That is not so," and so forth.
Thus, by dispelling our other doubts, be gracious to us. O Vṛjinārdana!
O destroyer of suffering! What sort of people are we? We are those who, having abandoned their homes, have hope only for Your worship.

"We have reached the root of your feet; therefore, grant us service"—this is the intended meaning, namely, "grant us [service] for ourselves. Of what sort are we? We whose souls are scorched by you alone. O Beautiful One! O You from whom even intense, exceedingly fierce passion arises through the sight of your smile—that is, by the sight of your smile.
The meaning is that desire, too, is provoked because of this. ||38||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, being unable to maintain their fortitude because their minds are hardened by the rows of flames from the fire of separation, they pray with plaintive lamentation, saying, "May You be gracious to us. For the service of Your foot-dust alone is the ultimate goal of human endeavor.
Following the example of Lakṣmī and out of a sense of conformity, we who remain at home have resolved to serve only the dust of your feet. Therefore, be gracious toward us; be pleased.
By this turn of phrase, [the meaning is]: "Abandon your crookedness. O Vṛjinārdana! O Destroyer of Suffering!

O you who have practiced vows such as the lifting of Govardhana! What kind of people are we? We have reached the base of your feet, that is, the vicinity of your feet. Having done what? Having abandoned our dwellings—that is, having left our homes—those of us whose hope is fixed upon your worship.

If it is asked, "Surely I am staying alone in the midst of the forest in solitude; how can I show favor toward you? they reply: "We have reached the root of Your feet. He who worships at the root of the feet is indeed the recipient of favor. Therefore, having abandoned our dwellings there—

They have returned after having renounced [their lives] through their resolve for spiritual restoration. Furthermore, as you yourself have said: "Moreover, those who have abandoned worldly dharmas for my sake, I sustain them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.46.4). By the word "residences," it is intended that they have renounced all acquisitions along with their belongings.

By the term "destroyer of crookedness" (*vṛjinārdana*), your compassion is expressed; you are compassionate, while we are afflicted. Since the removal of suffering for the afflicted is not accomplished [by others], the reason for abandoning our homes is this: we place our hope in worshiping you, so that, like yogis who have renounced all attachments, we may perform your worship with the cessation of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*).
"We have come because our hope must be fulfilled; otherwise, there will be a violation of your own vow. For you yourself have said:
'In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them' (Gītā 4.11). Therefore, grant us your service. Or else, what kind of dwellings would satisfy our hope for your worship?"

The meaning is that they "syati"—that is, they attenuate or render insignificant—the devotion consisting of service to You; this is according to the rule that the root *so* signifies making thin (*tanu-karaṇe*).
Now, one might ask: why is servitude sought by abandoning the master of the house? To that, [the author] states his own distress:
Desiring only servitude as the means for the pacification of that [suffering], they said:

"Of us whose souls are scorched by the intense passion arising from beholding Your beautiful smile and gaze... Their souls were scorched by that intense, unbearable passion caused by Your beautiful gaze preceded by a smile.

"Of us whose minds [are fixed] upon you; or rather, O one of beautiful smiles, those whose inner self—the individual soul—is scorched by the intense and irresistible passion arising from your cause, that is, from your glance and your looking toward us. [This refers to those] who are deluded by your deceptive smile, and who, by their own example, [have become so] toward you.

Now, for us who understand Your pure nature, who recognize indifference toward You through Your current teaching of the Dharma, and who—precisely because of that—are free from desire for anything other than You, our Beloved—grant us Your service (*dāsya*). When You grant this service, the Lord of Vraja and the others will harbor no envy; for once we have obtained this service, [we shall be satisfied].

The sense is that even one's husband and others will not harbor malice [toward them]. Or alternatively: O Destroyer of Sins! For those who have taken refuge in You, there is the removal of their evil; yet we, though having taken refuge at the base of Your feet, still suffer the torment produced by desire. This very point—
It is wonderful that the very sin by which attachment to husbands and others arose has been destroyed by the sight of your feet;

for you have abandoned even the home, which is the root of sin, and now, for those whose souls are tormented by the intense and incurable passion born from the sight of your beautiful smiles, [your feet alone remain].

For those whose minds are afflicted, you alone are the cause of their heart-disease; the medicine to cure it is nothing other than service to you. Having understood that even before reaching the tenth stage, the body, home, and so forth are the causes of suffering, they have abandoned them long ago. But you, though inflicting the heat of desire, do not allow it to be relinquished.
It is possible. Therefore, the prayer is: "Having granted us servitude, please protect us.

O Ornament of Men! You are the adornment of men—that is, of your friends, the cowherds; you always decorate them with flowers, sprouts, red ochre, and other such things while sporting together with your friends.
The sense is: "In that very same way, please adorn us as well at some time. Alternatively: "O Person! O Inner Controller of ours! You know the pain born within us; therefore, turn [this] away.
O Ornament! We are the objects to be adorned, while you are the ornament itself; therefore, please adorn us."
But female servants, having obtained favor through service to their master, wander about free from fear;
therefore, the prayer is: "Adorn [her] with the state of a servant. (38)

Viśvanātha: Therefore, having abandoned home, family, and so forth, they say, "Like the devotees of Nārāyaṇa, we desire only your servitude"—to this he replies, "That is not so. Since you are equal to Nārāyaṇa, therefore be gracious toward us. [The devotee objects: "But surely, [your grace] is contrary to my own favor..."
The meaning is that there exists for you a suffering not yet seen; how then can there be grace? One might ask, "Does Nārāyaṇa also grant grace everywhere? To this they say: O destroyer of sins!
You alone must destroy even that suffering. For Nārāyaṇa certainly destroys the suffering of those who take refuge in Him.
"And we have come to the root of Your feet; moreover, we have done so precisely out of freedom from any other desire," they say: "having abandoned our homes.
Now, one might object: even after renouncing the happiness of domestic life, must not some happiness necessarily be obtained from me?

"We understand that you say, 'We seek [nothing],' yet they reply: 'Our hope lies only in worshipping you; there is no hope for any happiness whatsoever as a fruit of worship to be granted by you. This is the meaning:
even though our intention is simply, 'Through worship we bring you joy,' [the joy] arising from the sight of your own happiness..."
"If our happiness were accidental, then what would be the fault?
[The Lord asks. "But then, why is that improper? [They reply: "It is true that you alone are the cause even of the flame of the fire dwelling in our hearts; thus they say: 'Of yours...'"
"Grant us only the state of being maidservants—that is, servitude—to those whose souls are scorched by intense passion through Your beautiful smiles and glances;
do not grant us the status of wives. Herein lies the commentary of the venerable feet of Śrīmad Vallabhācārya: "Therefore, we desire only servitude and not [the status of wives]."

They are seeking marriage; therefore, even the requirement of initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth does not apply according to worldly convention—this is the point. Consequently, there is no harm whatsoever to us whether we are unmarried girls or already married; for in either state, service to you is possible. This is the underlying intention in the *Prakṛta-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*.

The venerable Śrī Sanātana Gosvāmī also states: "Even when marriage has occurred, worshiping as a mistress (*aupapatnya*) is a source of supreme, great bliss, more so than worshiping as a wife; this is well known from the *Śrī Bhāgavatāmṛta*, the *Kāvya*, and other works. Therefore, in this context, it is specifically a particular form of *dāsya* (servitude)."
Requested; and now she requests this: "May we become your maidservants.

How so? Because you are an ocean of desire, for you who are a libertine toward women, this very service—characterized by the production of your pleasure through our own limbs—is indeed performed by us young women.

Therefore, even the prayer for the sprinkling of the fire of love within our hearts is itself a prayer for Your worship; for even this fire of desire is primarily an instrument for our service of You. For this very reason, the address is most appropriate: "O Ornament of Men! [of us] fair-limbed women."
All her limbs are adorned with ornaments made of sapphire gems. ||38||
Beholding Your face veiled by curls, with cheeks radiant with the beauty of earrings, and with smiles and glances, and the nectar of Your lips—
Beholding Your pair of staff-like arms that grant fearlessness, and Your chest, the sole beloved of the Goddess Śrī, may we become Your handmaidens.
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask, "Why is servitude (dāsya) being prayed for after abandoning the ownership of a home?

To this they say: "Having beheld" (vīkṣya). [The face] is covered with curls, meaning the face is veiled by the ends of the hair. Likewise, it is that upon which the cheeks possess the beauty of two earrings, and which possesses nectar upon the lower lip.

Beholding that face of yours which grants fearlessness, and seeing your pair of staff-like arms and your chest as the sole source of delight and the generator of passion through its splendor, we shall become your very slaves. ||39||

Vaṃśīdhara: [He] suspects: "Why do you, who are worthy, desire servitude which is fit only for the unworthy?"—this is expressed by the word *nanu*. According to Amara, *alakāḥ* means "curled locks of hair. The sense is that because of your extreme beauty, servitude is indeed appropriate for you, the Lord of All. Some, however, [interpret this as referring to one whose face is covered by curls].
The two earrings possess the nature of a net; the region of the cheeks possesses the nature of a vast expanse;

the nectar of the lower lip possesses the nature of being alluring; the smile and the glance possess the nature of enchantment; the flute-song possesses the nature of the Bhairava raga; the cowherd folk possess the nature of forest-dwellers; and the eyes possess the nature of *khañjana* birds.
"They conceptualize," [it is said]. ||39||
Regarding what was said—that the "Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā" consists of the "Upāsanā-śākhā"—others asked, "What is that like?

[The author replied: "Having beheld Your face veiled by curls," and so forth. Having beheld Your face veiled by curls, Your cheeks, the nectar of Your lips, Your smile, Your glance, Your two arms, and Your chest, we become Your maidservants.
The meaning is: "May we become worthy of their worship. This is an indirect expression (*vakrokti*). ||39||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, you have not been purchased with a price such as wealth, nor have you been given wages; how then can you be maidservants? It is said in reply: indeed, that transaction occurs elsewhere; for you, however, the very act of granting the sight of Your own face and so forth is the price.

And they say "and the support," namely: "having gazed. Having seen [her] specifically, they speak of that very particularity through the qualifiers beginning with "encircled by locks of hair" (*alakāvṛta*).
In that regard, "encircled" means covered by locks of hair shining above the forehead;
"the beauty of the earrings" refers to the upper part [of her face]; and "in which there is a glance accompanied by a smile" refers to both sides.

Regarding the phrase "in the lower and middle parts": thus, beauty is described everywhere by means of the broadness of the cheeks (*gaṇḍa*) preceded by [the description of] the physical form; and by the expression "the splendor of the earrings" (*kuṇḍala-śrī*), their translucence is suggested.
Furthermore, the nectar of her lips is inferred from the arising of a particular longing merely upon seeing them.

And because of the experience of a particular fragrance; likewise, the quality of being most powerful and so forth is indicated by the fact that he granted fearlessness to his devotees through the slaying of the Daityas and other such deeds. By that cleverness, fear from husbands and others was removed; yet in reality, it was through a firm embrace.

The removal of fear regarding desire and so forth is intended. By means of the metaphor of a staff, the excellence of its form—such as its being well-rounded, broad, and long—is indicated; here too, such distinction has been described.
Likewise, by "glory" (śrī), there is the reference to the goddess Lakṣmī, who resides on the left side in the form of a golden-colored streak.

The phrase "in which there is one supreme lover for the agent" indicates that He is a treasury of the perfection of ultimate beauty and other such qualities. The repetition of the word "and" (*ca*) and the reiteration of "beholding" are intended to express the specific excellence residing in His own abode, arms, and chest.
Likewise, for the two subsequent [stages], there is a single action because they produce a single purposeful effect;
for when the glorious face is adorned by such lips as those of a cheek, what is desired is merely a kiss and drink, while for the arms and chest, it is merely an embrace.

From the sequence of the descriptions of Alakā and the others, this is understood: although the sight of her various beauties first arose in his face, he did not look with his four eyes due to bashfulness;
rather, it was out of extreme longing that he subsequently looked with a particular desire, whereby he bit her arms.

But rest is indeed upon the chest; thus the sequence should be understood. In this way, it is implied that the very cause of her state as a maidservant is supreme enchantment (*parama-mohanatā*). Furthermore, in the world, wages and price are seen to be the granting of sense-objects (*viṣaya-dāna*); yet that [is found] in you, who possess the splendor of various forms.

"Since the nectar of her sweet lips, the touch of her alluring arms and so forth, and her chest—the treasury of perfect beauty—have been obtained, [this union] is self-evident; nevertheless, she looked [at him]. By this, even the "bondage of the *khañjana*-birds* that are their own eyes" is suggested (*dhvanita*). In that regard, the hair-locks (*alakāḥ*) possess the nature of snares, and the two earrings... [are like hooks].
The state of being the final coil [of the serpent-power] in her two cheeks; the location of its treasury in her lower lip;
the playful glances of her smile which serve as alluring food;
and the charm of the pair of *khañjana* birds she nurtures, which engenders trust—therein:
The sense is that his pair of staff-like arms possess the quality of granting fearlessness, precisely because they are endowed with sprouts [the hands].
Furthermore, it is indicated that such a chest is a region where one may move about at ease. The rest is by them [the commentators].
Alternatively, according to some, *śrī* is a long vowel [referring to *śrī-mukham*], meaning a face whose beauty (*śrī*) consists of its two earrings.

The reading [is as follows]: And then, having seen—the pair consisting of the two earrings which are the cause of beauty on their cheeks, the nectar of their lips, and likewise their laughter and their glances—thus beholding all of these as being of primary importance, [the word] "sudṛśyam" (well-seen) is used; however, its purpose here is negative (i.e., it means "not well-seen"). Now, if this is so:
"In that case, how is it that you remain there looking repeatedly at my limbs? To this they reply with pride, "We look. Here too, the negation is suggested solely by the intonation (*kāku*). ||39||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, if it is asked, "In that case, those who relish the mood of servitude (*dāsya-rasika*) should generally adopt service like Śrīdāmā, Subala, and others, characterized by such feelings," [the author] states with feeling the reason for requesting a specific kind of servitude: "Having seen" (*vīkṣya*). Having seen Him directly in his presence.
The description of the glorious face, the two arms, and the chest is primarily intended for the purpose of kissing the cheeks, drinking the nectar of the lips, and embracing closely; therein,
the upper portion is covered by locks of hair shining upon the forehead, while the beauty of the two earrings is mentioned.

"In which [face] there is a glance accompanied by a smile on both sides"—thus, beauty is described throughout all parts, including the lower and middle sections. By means of the metaphor of the physical form (*sthala-rūpaka*), the splendor of the two cheeks is suggested as being superior even to mirrors and the like.
"By whom fearlessness was granted to devotees through the slaying of demons and other deeds," and so forth.
The quality of possessing strength and so forth; by that cleverness, fear of her husband and others was avoided.

In reality, however, what is intended is the removal of fear from desire and the like through a firm embrace. By the metaphor of a staff, there is excellence of form such as being well-rounded, broad, and long. [This is] by means of *śrī*, which may mean either fortune or her own natural splendor.

Having made [her] the one supreme, peerless delight— the two *ca*-particles express her ultimate beauty and preeminent splendor— and having gazed [upon her], the repetition [of the verb] is intended to indicate that the arms and chest are as prominent as the illustrious face.

Or rather, by stating that the sole cause of being a maidservant is merely the sight of Him, it is shown that there is indeed supreme enchantment for each respective [aspect]. Therefore, the meaning is: "Since the specific varieties of those rasas are established through direct experience according to their nature by virtue of being maidservants, we shall remain as maidservants alone. This occurs while [the state] is present.

The fifth [point]: This intention is hidden—the enjoyment through illicit love (aupapattya) is a supreme great bliss even compared to enjoying her as a wife once marriage has taken place. And this is found in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*, in works on poetic ornamentation (*kāvyālaṃkāra*), and elsewhere.

This is indeed well-known; for this very reason, it is specifically *dāsya* (servitude/devotion) that is sought here. And now it is further requested: "May we become [your] servants. Other things have been suggested by them.
Alternatively, according to some, it refers to the face which possesses the *śrī*—the beauty—of the two earrings. Or rather, according to the view of some, it is *śrī*.

The reading is long. And thus, there is a dual compound (dvandvaikya) for the two earrings, the two beautiful cheeks, and the nectar of the lips; likewise for the smile and the glance. In this way, the preeminence of all these features is illuminated, and that is indeed suggested by the two forms [of the words]. Having beheld them as truly beautiful.

It is supremely beautiful; or rather, it is that which is specifically "worldly"—meaning visible—to those in the world, because it is captivating even to men. For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Kapiladeva:
"The chest is the dwelling place of the Bull (Ṛṣabha) of great majesty, bestowing bliss upon the minds and eyes of men" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.28.26].
The meaning of this is: "of the Bull" refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the most excellent of all.

Because he manifests his own complete lordship even to men, how much more so to women? The reason for not stating it explicitly in that way regarding the Mother is because she is already mentioned [as such]. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *api* (even). He is the sole lover of Śrī and her place of sport, because he always dwells there; or rather, he is the constant bestower of happiness.
Because of that embrace;
or else, [he is] the one supreme or peerless lover (*ramaṇa*) even of the two splendors (*śriyaḥ śobhe*).
The elision of the *visarga* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣaḥ*). Furthermore, the particle *ca* is used here in the sense of "and" (*anvācaya*) as the first [conjunction].
The second [case] is used in the sense of "also. Thus, from the illustrious face, the two arms are secondary;

even more so than that, the chest—despite its intended possession of superior beauty and comfort—is rendered even more secondary due to the jealousy arising from its being occupied by Lakṣmī, as if it were a co-wife.
Alternatively, by means of the two *ca*-particles, as before, the preeminence of all [the factors] is indicated;

for each one is a cause for servitude (*dāsītva*) by virtue of its own preeminence. Or else, previously, when requesting specific forms of service, worship was intended solely in the capacity of a lover (*jāra*).
"Surely, being by nature fickle, why do they pray for that very thing?

Why do they not all desire to be my wives through the gate of the monastery, like a group of maidens who have performed the vow of Kātyāyanī? To this, they say with cleverness: "Having gazed... [they are] indeed maidservants.
"Let us become [your wives]"; the meaning is: "We shall serve you solely through the state of being born from you. The fifth case ending is used here in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

For by this very manifestation of the essence of overflowing love, there is the perfect attainment of the specific experience of that sweet nectar, as appropriate. And that is stated in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*:

This has already been described and is well known in works such as the *Kāvyālaṃkāra*. By this, the answer to the statement "it does not lead to heaven" (*asvargyam*) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.26] is given: since the state of being an adulterer is produced by gazing upon the beauty of Your face and so forth, what fault indeed can there be for us in that?

Or rather, since by serving Him through a legitimate marriage one attains a specific supreme happiness that exceeds even liberation, even the bliss of the Vaikuṇṭha realm, and even the service of Lakṣmī and others— what need is there to mention anything such as the lack of heavenly merit? Therefore, for noble women alone is it fitting to serve Him along with you.

The meaning of the pun (*śleṣa*) is as follows: even after beholding such things as Your glorious face, we, Your maidservants, would become [Your] "servants" (*karmakāryaḥ*)—the fifth case here denotes possibility—would we? By way of a rhetorical question (*kāku*), the meaning is: "Certainly not. The reason for this is that [Your face] is the sole lover of Śrī alone, and thus [it is inaccessible] to all others.
This qualification applies only to her, who is of a fickle nature, and not to us, devoted wives of stable character, whose delight is in your face and so forth.
Or rather, having seen your face covered by your locks of hair, which possess the beauty of earrings and other such ornaments, you [spoke thus].
Having especially scrutinized and displayed his pair of staff-like arms, and having especially observed and displayed his chest, we have been delivered over to fear;

that is to say, we have been surrendered to fear. Therefore, for the sake of our external destruction, [our] mouths— (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary explaining a verse regarding the display of terrifying forms by a deity to instill fear.)
Be one whose face is free from intoxication. ||39||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: Regarding the passage beginning with "atha śravaṇāt" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.27], they say that by the phrase "mayi bhāvaḥ" ("attachment toward Me"), His own power of beauty is demonstrated; therein they say: "having seen..."
Thus [it is said]. Here too, the final word *ca* is used in an interrogative sense (*kākū*), while the preceding one serves to aggregate each of those aforementioned points.
The meaning is: "Having observed this as well—and indeed even this—we shall become maidservants, yet not in every respect.
From the *Bṛhatkramasaṃdarbha*: "What kind of service will you perform today? For we are indeed maidservants."

Thus, others have stated it as an established fact: "Having beheld," and so forth. Your face is covered by those locks of hair which are beautiful to behold; this is a subsequent *karmadhāraya* compound. It is such that its cheeks possess the splendor of earrings (*kuṇḍala-śrī-yukta-gaṇḍasthala*), and such that its lower lip possesses nectar (*sudhā-adhara*). It is beautiful to behold.
And the compound *vakṣa* is a *karmadhāraya*. Of what sort? It is the sole delight (*eka-ramaṇam*) by virtue of being the cause of Śrī.

The meaning is: "Just as these [attributes] are established by their very nature, so may we also become her handmaidens. Alternatively, [the word] *vīkṣya* means "having looked," using the suffix *lyap* in the sense of prior action; thus, it refers to that which is not exceedingly delightful (*nātisurasam*). (39)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, they ask, knowing that previously they requested [the dust of the feet] as something to be served, but now, by requesting other things as well—following the maxim of a mendicant’s alms-bowl—they are actually accepting servitude under a pretext. "What fault is there in abandoning the home? We shall become your maidservants."

What kind of face? It is one whose two cheeks possess the beauty of earrings, upon which is a lower lip containing nectar. Furthermore, what is it like? It is one in which there is a smile—a laugh—and a glance shimmering with that [smile].
Therefore, in their minds, happiness alone is primarily intended as the object of relish.

Therefore, they describe it as "encircled by bees" (*alakāvṛtam*). By comparing it to a blue lotus surrounded by swarms of bees, the intention is to suggest its drinkability due to the abundance of nectar. By the phrase "the beauty of the earrings" (*kuṇḍala-śrī*), the excellence of the splendor on both sides is indicated through their being covered by a pair of full [cheeks]. [This refers to] the surface of the cheeks (*gaṇḍa-sthale*).
Purity is illuminated. By the phrase "nectar of the lips" (*adhara-sudhā*), the state of being a locus for longing is indicated.

By the phrase "smile and glance" (*hasitāvaloka*), the abundance of the manifestation of grace (*vilāsa*) is indicated. And having beheld the pair of staff-like arms—of what kind? Bestowing fearlessness; it is that which has been granted to devotees.

By that very power of His own, such as the lifting of Govardhana and so forth—since You Yourself have said, "You should not feel any fear here" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.25.21)—and because it has been experienced many times before, He beheld [the mountain].
Of what nature was it? It was the sole lover of Śrī, the generator of her delight; or rather, it was our [source of] splendor through its beauty.

Thus, "delight" refers to an excellence of beauty. Having seen all this as the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the sweet sentiment (*madhura-rasa*), one should accept the state of service (*dāsya*). Even this attire alone is sufficient, let alone all these things being perfectly appropriate. In the state of being the mistress of the house, nothing at all is achieved; whereas in the state of service, everything will be attained. Therefore—

"Thus we shall become slave-girls purchased for no price. Or rather, the reply given there—namely, "It is not conducive to heaven, it brings ill repute, it is trivial, painful, and fraught with fear" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.26)—is applicable only elsewhere; in this case, however, it is not so, for [this union] is not considered contemptible.
Since these defects have been transformed into virtues in Your new servants, who perceive heaven, liberation, and hell as equal in value (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 6.17.18),
the very sight of Your face causes one to see heaven as something to be abandoned; thus, there is indeed the attainment of the desired goal, even in the case of the two cheeks which serve as mirrors.

Because it was accepted for the purpose of beholding her own reflection, the state of being a paramour (aupapatyam) was indeed accepted. Here too, the acceptance of the state of being a paramour is seen from the fact that the nectar of her lower lip—which is superior to that which is enjoyed by the gods—is itself an object of enjoyment. [The phrase] "with a smile and a glance" refers elsewhere to the state of being a paramour in relation to fame.

Therein, impurity prevails; but here, even laughter is radiant, and even the gaze is radiant—even infamy is radiant. Therefore, though it be something else accepted that is trivial and enjoyable for only a short time, because it is protected by the pair of arms of one who grants fearlessness, that hardship is accepted as difficult to overcome.

Furthermore, even though illicit love (aupapattya) is recognized as being beset by many faults because it is served by Śrī [Lakṣmī], it is perceived as consisting of nothing but bliss according to the inclination of our hearts. Although it is loathsome to others, it is not loathsome to us. It is a pleasure appropriate for the home, leading to heaven and bringing fame.

It is easy to achieve and provides happiness to be enjoyed for a long time; yet even such a thing as this has been abandoned by us. For it is said: "Those who see the same purpose in heaven, liberation, and hell" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.17.18). Indeed, fame is the root of heaven—it lasts as long as a person's glory endures.

"He is celebrated as meritorious among the worlds; he rejoices in heaven for so long"—thus, even fame has been renounced because it is a cause for heaven. It is "not leading to heaven" (*asvargyam*) because heaven is not desired [by him]. This is because it has been said: "Other devotees see the same purpose even in heaven, liberation, and hell" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.17.18).
Or rather: that which is worthless has been accepted because it is filled with great happiness, even though it is to be enjoyed for only a short time;

that which is difficult to accomplish has been accepted because it is the cause for attaining Your feet; and that which is loathsome has been accepted because our abandonment will be carried out by husbands and others.
For even that which is enjoyed for a long time becomes insipid in its ultimate transformation. Thus it has been said: "Not even the surface of heaven [is eternal].

For us, this illicit union with other men's wives—which is beset by six defects—has instead become endowed with six virtues. As it has been said: "In some cases, even a virtue may become a defect, and even a defect may become a virtue."

"Virtue arises from the prescribed rule. Just as study and teaching are virtues for a Brāhmaṇa, yet a fault for a Śūdra, so too, when other women— knowing that devotion to you is their duty— desist from sexual union because they perceive it as a fault, our illicit union [is likewise a virtue].

It is indeed a virtue; it is indeed a fault because it has not been tasted by others. Therefore, this instruction applies only to them. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that this intimidation finds no place among us, since your servitude is the means for attaining the supreme goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), whereas [the other paths] are certainly not the means for attaining the supreme goal of human life.
It becomes a means of accomplishing evil. We have been purchased at the price of being gazed upon by [your] face and so forth; we are indeed slaves.
Enjoyment, however, is obtainable only through your grace. Once that has occurred, what is there that cannot be obtained?
Thus, having strengthened our resolve for a paramour by means of the sight of your face and so forth, [you now say] "this is not conducive to heaven."
The sense is: "Are you not ashamed to produce such a primary terror? ||39||

Viśvanātha: Since you have become my servants, were you purchased by me for a price? Or are you my own bestowed employees? [I acquired you] at a price many millions of times greater than what is appropriate for us—a price beyond our sight, hearing, or experience, and of immense value.
Having purchased us at the very onset of our youth with the cintāmaṇi jewel of her smiles and glances,
she brought us to her own bower-palace—
palaces of sapphire consisting of a ground of makaras made of gold, cintāmaṇi jewels, and gems, which serve as the abode for the playful splendor of Lakṣmī and pillars of blue sapphire.

Having displayed their own riches under the pretext of [visiting] Alakā and other cities, they say: "Behold! You feed us daily with nectar that is difficult even for the gods to obtain. When you bind the red, curved turban upon your head, then, as the maidservant pulls it upward with a comb, you too—

Having observed her face— which was partially covered by locks of hair whose roots were visible at the left and right edges of her forehead, yet not entirely concealed— after having carefully raised it with her own finger and drawn it back until it entered within the uṣṇīṣa; and when you bind your topknot, then...

Having observed her face slightly veiled by curled locks that are neither too long on the forehead-tip nor on the left and right sides; and having observed her face completely veiled— that is, fully covered— by those locks during the time of oil-massage and rubbing with fragrant powders, as well as during the height of sexual union.

Having made ourselves filled with the abundance of sweetness being relished by [Your] two eyes, we become Your maidservants. What is the face like? By means of the two earrings—which, at different times, are unobstructed by the curls of hair, slightly obstructed, or completely covered—and which are steady or slightly trembling.
And where there is a distinct splendor from the two [cheeks] that are not fickle;
because at the time of laughing and smiling, the cheeks and the corners of the mouth are spread wide;
and even upon the surface of the cheeks, there is the nectar of the lower lip—that is, a flowing forth due to the sweetness of the lips.

That from whose cheeks the nectar of His lips was being drunk by the cakora-birds of the Gopīs' eyes as He moved from one cheek to another; or, during the breaking of the secret convention, that upon the cheeks of the Gopīs [was reflected] the nectar of His lips; or, that upon the cheeks of the Gopīs [was applied] the nectar of His lips.
Alternatively, it is that [face] wherein the two cheeks possess a splendor consisting of the beauty of the earrings reflected therein;
wherein the lower lip is nectar; and wherein there is a gaze accompanied by a smile. It is a "smile" because of the blossoming of the gopīs and the night-lotuses resulting from that gaze.
Or rather: "But surely, your husbands, unable to endure this, will produce fear in King Kaṃsa for me and for you by means of a roar. To that they replied: "Fearlessness has been granted."

The sense is that since Your pair of staff-like arms is such as it is— having supported the mountain [Govardhana] even against Mahendra, Darpaka, and others— it is Your very staff-like arm that shall be the slayer of the life-breath of the beast Kaṃsa. And thus, by the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) thus suggested:
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) was fully developed.

Indeed, they say: "You do not treat other women as mere maidservants; rather, having forcibly brought even Lakṣmī—the wife of Nārāyaṇa—from Vaikuṇṭha, you carry her upon your own chest. Thus it is said: "by Śrī," meaning by Lakṣmī.
By the agency of the golden line (*suvarṇa-rekhā*) born of her sense of shame, there is that which possesses one primary delight;
therefore, how much age has now passed for you among the fourteen worlds, as well as in the higher realms above them, even in the great Vaikuṇṭha worlds beyond the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)?
It is implied that we know you will not abandon any beautiful woman whatsoever. ||39||
O dear one, what woman in the three worlds would not falter from the noble path, being utterly deluded by the sweet-toned, prolonged song of your flute?
And beholding this form, the good fortune of the three worlds,
the cows, the twice-born, the trees, and the deer all bore horripilation.
Śrīdhara: Now, it was said that illicit love is loathsome; regarding this, they say—"What woman?

O dear Kṛṣṇa, by means of that flute-song which is long and drawn out, consisting of modulated notes and variations in melodic intonation (or, according to another reading, consisting of the nectar of beautiful words), [she is captivated].

What woman, even if deluded, would not waver from her own duty and the conduct of the noble, when even men, deluded by that which is the fortune of the three worlds— since they bore it and have borne it— have wavered? Yet,
merely by hearing the words indicative of you, there has been such an abandonment of one's own duty.
It is appropriate; what need is there to mention your own experience? This is the intended meaning. ||40||

Vaṃśīdhara: To dispel the sense of contempt regarding the previously mentioned paramours, they say: "The words are sweetly distinct. From their own duty, characterized by conjugal fidelity, for those immersed in the bliss born from hearing the singing of melodious words, even the recollection of dharma and adharma does not arise.

The underlying meaning is as follows: cows and other animals possess internal consciousness. Since it is said that even men—led by Śakra, Śarva, and Parameṣṭhin—were enchanted by the sound of his flute, [it follows that] Śaṅkara and the others assumed the guise of women and joined the assembly of gopīs;
what then need be said of ordinary women? Such is the sense.
They say "moreover" (kiṃ ca) to show that this delusion belongs not only to humans but also to others besides them:

"The fortune of the three worlds," meaning this form which has come within the range of our vision, consisting of a configuration composed of most beautiful limbs; such is the sense. [This refers to] the word indicating you.

Merely by hearing words such as "Madhusūdana," "Murāri," and "Govinda," all dualities are destroyed; therefore, because there is an absence of the service of scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, it is proper to renounce one's own duty (nija-dharma) that has descended according to the order of social classes (varṇa). Thus:
"Those whose dualistic nature has been shaken off by even a single taste of a drop of the nectar of the pastimes of His followers have perished [of that duality]," so it is said. Therefore,
whether through hearing or describing His state, may I not become like a servant bound by ritual injunctions.

Thus will the venerable Svāmī-pāda say in the *Bhāvārtha-dīpikā* (10.87.41). Furthermore, the intended meaning is also that "by your experience"—that is, by the direct realization of the Self as "I am Brahman. However, according to the literal text, the sound of the flute, which indicates you, is such that Kṛṣṇa plays this [flute].
"Of such a form," thus [it is said]. ||40||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "But surely this is indeed worship; O blessed one, may there be well-being! [The Lord asks:

"In that case, do you ladies possess passion? [They reply: "No, no, we are Your devotees. Anticipating this doubt, the *madhyā* (middle), *dhīrā* (steadfast), and *prauḍhā* (mature) women say: "O dear one (*aṅga*), what woman is there for You... and so forth. "O dear one! But this [love] belongs to You alone."
This is a fault of both your flute’s sound and your form,
in that even cows, birds, trees, and deer bear horripilation;
for they are utterly enchanted by this sweet-toned, prolonged flute-song, and thus [attain] this beauty which is the fortune of the three worlds.

Upon beholding your form, what woman would not waver from noble conduct, from the vows of her family, from the path of the Vedas, or from the conduct of the noble—waver for the sake of your noble character? Would she not become unstable? By this it is shown that the fault does not lie with women; rather, women possess unconditioned love for you.
Thus, your audacity lies in the fact that you yourself produce a different passion in them by the sound of your flute. ||40||

*Vaiṣṇavatoṣiṇī*: "In that case, you will surely be ridiculed by devoted wives. To this, they clearly replied with both anger and dejection: "What woman? The meaning is: what woman existing in the three worlds would not waver? On the contrary, every single one would waver. And those goddesses were traveling in celestial chariots.

This is indicated by the passage beginning with *bhā.pu. 10.21.12*. The word *kalā* has been explained previously; the word *pada*, moreover, indicates that every single step is of such a nature—as expressed by the term *āyatā*. In this regard, they indicate Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s persistence and, through their own fortitude, prevent the passing of time during that interval, according to the alternative reading (*pāṭhāntare*).
They manifest its supramundane flavor by saying, as if with fear, that "Māra alone exists everywhere"—whether in non-seeing or even in seeing—and thus they say: "Of the three worlds.
This refers to the fortune and auspiciousness (*saubhāgya*) of the entire world existing above, below, and in the middle.

Or rather, the meaning is that "in which [the object] is contained"; thus, by saying "this is perceptible and present," any notion of its being otherwise is dispelled. Or else, the meaning is that "this is such a unique [object].
By the word "having beheld" (*nirīkṣya*), they indicate a *kaimutya* argument: if even by hearing of it one might experience delusion, how much more so by seeing it?

Regarding the word *strī* (woman): the sense is that even men—and indeed the Blessed Lord himself—would be bewildered by her. This is because it will be stated later: "Led by Śakra, Śarva, and Parameṣṭhin, they fell into a state of dejection" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.35.15), and because of the mention in the third [canto]: "and she was a source of wonder to herself" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.2.12). Oh!

Let alone the talk of those who possess such discernment between the essential and the non-essential; for even cows and other animals obtain both hearing and sight of these two forms—the flute and the song—and since they are self-manifesting (*svaprakāśa*), this is not impossible. As it is said: "By this, those who desire the world... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.25).
The reply to this is: "And this is for the purpose of negation.

[Objection: "But if you have no agitation at the sight of my limbs, then why do you wish to depart from here? To that they say: "What woman?"—meaning, what woman is there who possesses even the mere characteristics such as being of that species and so forth?
On account of your noble conduct and virtuous behavior, she would not waver or depart from your presence;
furthermore, since even cows and other animals bristled with thrill [at your sight], who indeed would not depart upon seeing and beholding such a form as this? On the contrary, she would remain.

The meaning is that we shall all depart. For the presence of beautiful women near a handsome stranger is certainly a cause for public scandal. Thus, although they are deluded by him and do not properly perceive his true nature, the intention is: "Nevertheless, we shall withdraw. (40)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, although [these practices] are to be worn upon the heads of the circle of the learned, nevertheless, for the sake of instructing the world, it is certainly fitting to maintain virtuous conduct (*sad-ācāra*) with great care.
Regarding this, they speak with both dejection and anger: "Where? etc. What woman existing in the three worlds would not tremble? Indeed, [all would].

The meaning is that everyone would indeed be moved [from their state], because even Pārvatī and others who rest in the lap of Śrī Śiva have resorted to delusion; and this is well known from the *Skanda Purāṇa* and other texts. Here too, it has been indicated by such passages as: "The goddesses traveled in celestial chariots" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.21.12). Or perhaps at some time...

They say that it possesses transformation (savikāra), stating: "Let the song of the flute indeed not arise; yet its form, supremely enchanting, shines eternally"—this is expressed by the word *trailokya*.
*Trailokya* refers to the good fortune (*saubhāgya*) of the three worlds existing above, below, and in the middle.

Whether it be the quality of being beloved by the people or beauty, that which is present before one's eyes here and now has its potential for change refuted. Alternatively, it is extraordinary; having seen this unique beauty of Śrī Raghunātha, even sages were enchanted and attained a particular state of ecstatic emotion (bhāva).
Thus it is said in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"In former times, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
having beheld Rāma, who is Hari, there with his most beautiful form, desired to eat him."
"They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were then liberated from the ocean of worldly existence," and so forth. And in the Mahākaurma Purāṇa:
"The high-souled sons of Agni attained womanhood through austerity,
and [obtained] as their husband Vāsudeva, the unborn, all-pervading source of the universe. Even from this, a distinct superiority is intended, because it now manifests his own complete divinity.

Alternatively, the meaning is that this is indescribable and supremely wonderful; for even in your case, it is seen in reflections and the like, and it causes amazement by producing a particular state of being. Thus it was said by Uddhava: "It is a source of amazement for oneself" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.12). "Having gazed" (nirīkṣya).

The meaning is that just as there would be delusion even by hearing or remembering the flute-song, who indeed would not tremble upon seeing Him directly? For this reason— that is, from His form— the word "go" (cow) indicates domestic animals such as bulls, calves, buffaloes, and goats, as they too are cattle by nature.
Even those devoid of discrimination [were moved]; by the use of the plural "pulakāni" (thrills), it is indicated that they occurred at all times and on all limbs.

By these, other transformations are also implied, according to such statements as: "The thrill of trees is their lack of movement" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.21.19). This was because they bore [these signs] due to the arising of a particular state of being.
The supreme enchanting power of His form, even more so than the song of the flute, has been described; as will be said by the goddess Śrī Rukmiṇī:
"His form is the attainment of all goals for those who possess eyes and can see" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.52.37);
and as stated by Uddhava: "It causes wonder even to Himself" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.12).

His excellence should also be understood from various statements, because those with vision are capable of perceiving beauty, and likewise, because wonder arises from the extraordinary sight of that crest-jewel of the supremely discerning, due to his state of being established in the investigation of what is real and unreal.

And here, the direction [of the argument] is that even in the absence of those respective [objects], the expression of the transformation of love (*prema-vikāra*) regarding cows and so forth is mentioned. Other points have been suggested by them.
In that regard, since even the men were moved, there was the breaking forth of horripilation (*pulaka-udbheda*) among the twice-born, the trees, and the deer. What [more is to be said]?

Or, it is according to the delusion of the gods and others that will be described in the passage: "Śakra, Śarva, Parameṣṭhin, and the rest fell into a state of bewilderment" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.15). Alternatively, *yat* is an indeclinable;
the meaning is "by which two," namely by the flute and the song. The power of the flute-song to cause delusion is especially...

This has been clearly stated in the twenty-first chapter and will be further explained in the thirty-fifth; the rest is the same. Thus, the supreme enchanting power of his flute-playing, singing, and form has been described. [Now follows] the name of Kṛṣṇa.

The fact that this is a state of delusion is indeed indicated by the word "aṅga" (alas). For nowhere is Śrī Kṛṣṇa directly addressed with the title "Parama-mohana" (the Supreme Deluder). Therefore, the sense is that there is no fault whatsoever in abandoning the conduct of the learned out of such incapacity. However, in reality, for such people...
Because there is no qualification for [the practice of] *sadācāra* (right conduct). This has already been explained previously. For this very reason, the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda wrote:

"Even by merely hearing words indicative of that [conduct], it is appropriate to abandon one's own duty (*nija-dharma*). And because the Lord possesses all powers, for the sake of maintaining the world (*loka-saṃgraha*),...

The observance of virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*) would indeed be possible for him; however, how could that be possible for those who are overwhelmed by love, given their lack of such capacity? In this very way, their extraordinary greatness, though hidden, has been revealed by those very words beginning with, "He is indifferent toward the sage who is peaceful" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.14.16).

This is the general direction. This is the answer to the verse beginning with *anena śravaṇāt* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.27): "Even among men there, and even among sages, and even among cows and other beings in their previous incarnations and here, where there is direct delusion, what talk can there be of those like us? Thus, we are not at fault for the loss of discrimination."
Or rather, since even for cows and other such beings, merely by the sight of Him and the hearing of His flute-song,
such a state characterized by bliss is attained, it follows that for those who experience Him directly according to their capacity,
the supreme bliss characterized by a special form of divine love is surely attained; thus, close proximity is indeed appropriate.

Thus it is said. In reality, however, for one whose realization might occur even through hearing and so forth, that realization would be especially accomplished through direct proximity (*sannikarṣa*).
The intended meaning of the word-play (*śleṣa*) is: what woman, possessing the conduct of the noble ones (*ārya*), would deviate? But rather, none at all. Since...

Beholding [this], cows and other animals experience horripilation; is this beauty of yours not present in the three worlds? (The interrogative intonation implies: "Indeed, it is. Therefore, the sense is that you should not harbor pride because of this.

Alternatively, "O you whose flute-song is drawn out by the sound of the *kalapada*! and "O deluder! O one deluded by passion!"—this expresses a lack of self-control. From whom, then, would she not waver, who would not go home?
From whom? From one of noble conduct (*āryacarita*), most righteous—one says this sarcastically (*solluṇṭham*).

Alternatively, "O Noble One, deluded by the songs of the flute with its sweet-sounding notes!"—this is spoken with the utmost audacity. From your conduct, characterized by adultery, who would not waver? Who would not turn away?
The meaning is: who would accept this? The rest is the same. ||40||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Prīti-sandarbha 332: Now, raising the objection, "If you two are so firm in your vows, then why do you not remain right here for the entire night? they speak again with apprehension: "What woman..."

"Aṅga te" and so forth. Even if it be so, nevertheless, O *aṅga*—O you whose flute-song is sweet and drawn-out, O you who are utterly deluded by the arrow of Kāma known as *sammohana*—what woman in the three worlds would not waver from noble conduct (*ārya-carita*), that is, from virtuous behavior, because of you? Let it be so for us.
News of those who observe the vows of the highest saintly discipline is heard only from afar.

Thus, having described his fault regarding his qualities and his disposition by means of the two vocatives as the cause for departing from that state, they describe his fault regarding his physical form with the words "trailokya... (the three worlds). Likewise, it is from the very conduct of the noble ones...
And seeing this form of the Cause, who would not tremble? For, as it says "O cow and twice-born," the proximity of beautiful women to a handsome stranger would surely lead to public scandal. (40)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, if it is as you say—that you possess an innate sense of pride—then why do you grieve, being ignorant of the intended meaning of my words? To this, others replied: "What woman," and so forth. O dear one! [this refers to] you.

Bewildered by the flute-song with its sweet, drawn-out notes, she would not waver nor falter from the path of your noble conduct. Indeed, your conduct is so alluring that what woman in the three worlds would not waver? Every one of them wavers. In this matter, the fault does not lie with women; it lies with you alone.

The meaning is this: it is not only from your conduct; having beheld this form as well, for because of this form, even cows, birds, trees, and deer have borne horripilation—they become possessed of thrills of joy. ||40||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, if you should say, "Just as I am intent on the welfare of the world, so too must right conduct (*sadācāra*) be maintained by you; this is established by the weight of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa-paṅkti*), and it is not something that can be disregarded," they reply with indignation: By the address "O dear one" (*aṅga*), this is made known—if you...

If you had been born from us, you would not have spoken thus. Therefore, you teach without even knowing our suffering, according to the traditional saying: "One may possess scholarship in instructing others. O noble lady, what woman is there in the three worlds who would not waver from her own duty, the conduct of the virtuous? She would not abandon her own dharma—thus [it is said].

The meaning is: "not at all," such is the sense. They were infatuated by that sweet, indistinct, and melodious flute-song; they were deluded by that song which was *kalāni*—indistinct and sweet. As it has been said: "The goddesses, traveling in their celestial chariots, had their very essence shaken by the god of love. It is not that this reversal brought about by you will occur.

They say it is wonderful. Regarding the term *trailokya*: it refers to the fortune and beauty residing within the three worlds, or that from which the fortune of the three worlds proceeds. Having beheld this form established before their very eyes, even men are bewildered; indeed, upon seeing the beauty of Śrī Raghuvīra, they are moved.
Even the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest were deluded by him. As it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"In ancient times, all the great ṛṣis residing in the Daṇḍaka forest, upon seeing Rāma, who was Hari in a most beautiful form, desired to devour him there."
They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula.

It is understood that they speak solely by the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Or rather, this form is a source of wonder even for you; as it has been said: "it is a cause of amazement for oneself. Or else, O *kala-pada*! [The term is explained as follows: whose *pada* (foot/position/nature) takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) *kaṃ* (bliss), or by whom the flute is [played].

That bliss is such that one becomes immersed in one's own essential nature; thereafter, one wanders elsewhere. O you who are enchanted by the song of the nectar-flute! Since you always play the flute and never cease, why this doubt toward us alone, for even you [are affected] by the flute-song?

"You are deluded. Or rather: "O you who sing with the nectar-flute! O deluded one!"—by these two words, the emergence of a *sāttvika* emotion due to being deluded is indicated. Therefore, it is not surprising that you, speaking so favorably to her while restraining us, cause even those of a different species—the cows, birds, trees, and deer—to become likewise affected.
By the word "cows" (go), bulls, calves, heifers, and so forth are to be understood. "Birds" (dvija) refers to winged creatures;

as it has been said: "O Mother, birds are indeed mostly sages. "Trees" (druma)—"Oh, these are the best of gods," was spoken by the Blessed One's own mouth. "Deer"—"We are blessed, even though we are of dull intellect," [said] the does.

By the arising of a particular internal state, they bore horripilation—those qualities that indicate such a specific state in women like us. Furthermore, having deluded them with the song of His flute, He caused them to abandon their own duty (*dharma*).
Because they were deluded, you attribute the fault of abandoning virtuous conduct to us; yet, the abandonment of *dharma* was brought about by You alone.

Because it was caused by you, the fault would fall upon you alone; for according to the maxim that "the fruit of a scriptural injunction belongs to the performer," there is another point as well. We, however, having recalled the promise we made—"O Śyāmasundara, we are your maidservants"—have become maidservants. For maidservants, by performing what is right or wrong according to the word of their master...

It should be understood that this has already been answered by the statement: "The merits and faults of a master are heard by female servants who are preoccupied with serving him. Why do you not say, "But you, having promised 'I will give these to you,' now refuse to give them and depart"—thus forcibly plunging me into an ocean of suffering? For what reason [do you remain silent]?
The sense is: "We know. ||40||
Viśvanātha: But surely, you have already offered a libation of water to the path of righteousness!
Why then do you defile others according to the maxim, "The shameless man who is himself corrupt seeks to corrupt others"? This particular mark upon my chest is indeed innate.

"The golden line shines; and seeing it, how can you be guilty of offenses even against Lakṣmī—the crest-jewel of devoted wives—by defaming her? We do not defame anyone there; however, you were created by the Creator for the destruction of the dharma of even the three worlds."

"You have been created," he said with angry impetuosity—"Which woman? O dear Śrī Kṛṣṇa! By that flute-song which is nectar-like in its nature, wherein the words are melodious (*kala-pada*). In the reading *kala-padāyata-mūrchitena*, *āyata* means long and *mūrchita* means [melodically] intensified.

The meaning is that she was deluded by the variations in the modulation of notes (*svarālāpa*); thus, it is not the woman who is at fault, but rather the song performed by you. She should not deviate from her own duty characterized by devotion to her husband according to the conduct of noble women (*ārya-carita*), but rather every woman would deviate. You [are the one responsible for] the transgression (*pratyavāya*) characterized by the abandonment of dharma.

The sense is: "You will surely attain it. They say—"In the three worlds"—to show that it is not only your quality (*guṇa*) that destroys *dharma*, but even its very form (*rūpa*). That which possesses auspiciousness (*saubhaga*) alone, even in the material (*prākṛta*) and non-material (*aprākṛta*) worlds situated above, below, and in the middle, and not otherwise...

The sense is that the hatred of some here is caused by their desire to destroy the Dharma. Nor should it be said that even natural desire in women is a cause for delusion; for they say that your beauty and qualities bring about a state of helplessness in all beings, both moving and stationary—because, because...
"They did not bear, nor do they bear, the forms of His songs; therefore, O King, what need is there for much?
Led by Indra, Śiva, and Brahmā, they fell into dejection" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.15).
Thus, from this chapter on the flute-song, it is shown that even those who know the supreme reality were bewildered—a source of wonder for Himself.
