And it should be understood that the statement of Śrī Śuka—"Thus, even for him, a sense of wonder was seen in you"—[Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.12] also occurred. (The commentary on verse 11.81 in the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* should also be consulted.
It is evident that you have been born as a god who removes the fear and suffering of Vraja, just like the Primordial Person, the protector of the world of the gods; therefore,
O friend of the distressed, place your lotus-hand upon us.
And upon the heated breasts and heads of her handmaidens.
Śrīdhara: "Vyaktam" means certainly or definitely. ||41||

Vaṃśīdhara: "Since you are the master of all, you are our lord; and since we are born of the same lineage, a relationship with you is appropriate. Therefore, there is no fault in our union with you, so how could there be any censurability? With this intention, they say: "Clearly," as follows: "Just like the Original Person (Ādi-puruṣa)."

The Protector of the world of the gods, Vāmana, was born; likewise, that very same Primordial Person has now become [the Lord] of Vraja—the entire assembly of devotees. Or rather, He is so called because He removes the fear arising from worldly existence and the threefold suffering (ādhyātmika, etc. belonging to us who dwell in Vraja; thus He is "born" (bhijāta).
It is clear and beyond doubt:
"This one, the delighter of the cowherds and Gokula, will bestow the highest good upon you. O fortunate ones, those men who feel love for him—
"Enemies do not overcome these," according to the words of Śrī Garga Ācārya beginning with this verse.

Here, "enemies" refers to desire (*kāma*) and the like. Since this is so, therefore—because of its innate coolness, because it removes distress, and because it causes bliss to flow—the hand itself is a lotus (*paṅkaja*). Or else, *paṅka*...
He who conquers affliction (*kleśa*) is "born from the mud" (*paṅkaja*); [your] hand is indeed that very lotus. Your hand is a remover of mire;
otherwise, there would be a loss of your status as a kinsman to the afflicted—this is the intention behind the form of address (*sambuddhi*).
The phrase "of the female servants" (*kiṅkarīṇām*) is stated everywhere for the sake of granting fearlessness and for the sake of strengthening their state of servitude. Or else:

The distress of a servant is removed by the master alone; and you are our master. Otherwise, according to the maxim, "How can he who does not listen to what is beneficial be a lord?", how could you possess the status of a lord? Such is the sense. ||41||
The Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā concludes by saying: "It is evident that you... and so forth.

"Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the distress or suffering (*ārti*) of Vraja—that is, its pain. It is "evident" (*vyaktam*), meaning clear and manifest, that everyone knows you have appeared (*abhijātaḥ prādurbhūtaḥ*) for the purpose of removing the suffering of both [the cowherds and the demons]. You are the Lord (*deva*).

While being intent on play, you—though even superior to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Person and protector of the world of the gods—are compared with him alone because no other example exists. Therefore, Vraja is also superior to the world of the gods. Why then do you yourself cause us such distress?
Therefore, O friend of the distressed! place Your lotus-hand upon our scorched breasts and heads; such is the instruction. ||41||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, although situated in the fourth direction, they likewise avoid the fault of *dharma* and so forth within the self, and instead conclude by attributing the very occurrence of the fault of *dharma* to that [self] alone;
they then state precisely what was intended to be said. Furthermore, let that indeed be so.

"Everything," they say; yet, because my desires are fulfilled by virtue of possessing qualities equal to those of Nārāyaṇa, I would have no inclination toward anything else, much less toward such a task. Anticipating this doubt, they say: "Manifestly. Whatever fear the Vraja has from Pūtanā and others, or from forest fires and the like, and whatever terror and distress it suffers from rain, wind, and so forth—all that is for Your sake.

There is suffering, as well as the distress arising from the fear of separation from you; being the remover of both those [sufferings] caused by your absence, the meaning is that you should come to destroy them.
Therefore, my cow-pasture is my refuge, I am its lord, and it is my possession.

"I shall protect them through the yoga of my own self; this is the vow I have undertaken" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.25.18). Having personally reflected thus, he took up the burden of the mountain. According to a certain variant reading, the word *abhijātaḥ* means "the distress of the people of Vraja," referring to all external and internal afflictions, and it also means "born of a noble lineage," i.e., born from a virtuous family.

Even in that case, there is a distinction; for if our destruction were caused by you alone, there would be an even greater fault of unrighteousness (*adharma*) than the violation of a vow (*vratabhaṅga*), since it would result in the destruction of [the vow]. The sense is that even for the Lord, whose desires are fulfilled, such protection of a vow and such a desire are indeed observed.

They say: "He is a god" (*deva*). He is called a god because he plays (*divyati*) and shines forth (*virājate*) in every way. He is the Original Person (*ādi-puruṣa*), the most excellent among all persons; even he, as the protector of the world of the gods, becomes born among Aditi and others by his own will alone as a guardian of those mere people. Therefore, for that reason.

The lotus-like nature of the hand is described only in the sense of its capacity to remove heat; however, since in reality the cause of that heat is merely the non-attainment of her [the beloved], the heat would vanish at the very moment of her commencement.
It is with this very intention that, even upon breasts already heated, those women—though exceedingly tender—made their request for her placement thereon.

Thus it should be understood as before; they have also spoken with humility, saying, "And upon the heads of your maidservants. Furthermore, the intended meaning is: "O friend of the distressed! O Lord who shines forth visibly! It is unbecoming that there should be suffering for your female servants. Likewise:
"Do not place [your hand] out of desire, but rather as a friend to one in distress"—this is the hidden intention:

that even though the passion of love is being concealed by feigned indifference, it will manifest of its own accord through the placing of the hand upon my limbs; and while this is for the purpose of a prohibition, nevertheless, do so by force.

Fearing that he might touch [them] as if they were [ordinary objects], they say: "Clearly" (*vyaktam*). The sense is that in this matter, protection from the aforementioned cause—even from fear of violating the Dharma—is appropriate, but not their destruction. "Do not place us [there], do not place us [there], O kinsman of the distressed!"—thus, through the fear of violating the Dharma, they manifest their own distress, being tormented.

"O you whose heart is tormented by the fire of passion! Place [your foot] upon the heads—even those of your own household maidservants, let alone those like me; do not place it there. How much less, then, upon our breasts?"—this is the meaning. Thus, this section beginning with "Welcome" (svāgatam) should be understood as the *anubhāva* (manifestation) known as *saṃlāpa* (conversation).
A dialogue consisting of a statement and a reply is known as *saṃlāpa*; this is because of the aforementioned definition. ||41||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus sequentially refuted everything stated in those replies, they now, demonstrating the purpose of His descent, pray with supreme longing and a plaintive tone: "Manifested... [The fear of Vraja arose from the forest fire, and there was great distress.]

Because of not attaining you; or rather, fear [arises] from Pūtanā and others, as well as from forest fires and the like, for your sake, and distress from rain, wind, and so forth. Or else, fear arises from the apprehension of separation from you, and distress from your neglect. In an alternative reading, "the distress of the people of Vraja" refers to all external and internal afflictions without exception. This...

This is not agreed upon by everyone. This was said with reference to himself; or rather, it refers even to those people of Vraja who reside on the land of Vraja at some other time—how much more so for us?
Being its bearer, he acts for the sake of its destruction; such is the meaning.
He has arisen—that is, become manifest—through the specific quality of revealing His complete state as the Blessed Lord on all sides.

Although the removal of the burden of the earth and so forth are also purposes, nevertheless, the primary purpose is solely the removal of the fear and suffering of Vraja. In that regard, it is through the very pastimes performed for that purpose that [His glory] is manifested everywhere.
The primary purpose is the accomplishment of the expansion of the nectar of one's own love.

For that sake, they teach by means of an illustration that even the transgression of dharma must be performed out of a special compassion for the wretched: "The Lord is indeed worshipful to the entire world, because He is the Original Person, the cause of the universe."

The Supreme Lord. He too is a protector of the world of the gods (*sura-loka*); "world of the gods" refers to heaven, by which those residing there are indicated. Alternatively, he is the protector of the gods and other people of his own [realm], being their guardian by slaying their adversaries and the like—how he becomes such a protector, as a protector.
Or rather, even though He remains the same in all respects, there may still be a partiality toward His devotees;

likewise, for the sake of us who are afflicted by distress, You must indeed transcend dharma, so that no fault attaches to Him, but rather it becomes a great virtue— even for You— this is the intended meaning.

Or rather, although You are a god, the primordial person (ādi-puruṣa), and the protector of the world of the gods, You are nonetheless the remover of the fear and suffering of Vraja; for this very reason, You are truly born as the son of the illustrious Lord of the Gopas (Śrī-Gopendra-nandana).

And that is manifest, certain, and indeed clear—this is the meaning. Therefore, from that... [kara]... (Note: The final word "kara" appears to be a fragment of a larger term, such as "karoti" or "karotu," which was likely part of the original sentence.)

Thus, because it is naturally cool, because it removes distress, and because it flows with the essence of bliss, first place that lotus upon our breasts, which are heated and overcome by the fever of love; then,
for the sake of destroying that affliction, place it upon our heads, for the sake of universal fearlessness.

Or, it is for the sake of strengthening the acceptance of our servitude. The two *ca*-particles are used in both cases to indicate their primary importance. By removing the fear and suffering of us alone, who are dear to You, there is the removal of the fear and suffering of the entire Vraja. Therefore...
The sense is that even the purpose of Your incarnation—which consists in manifesting the essence of the entirety of the Blessed Lordship—will thus be accomplished.
Now, one might ask: "How can the hand be placed upon those who are suffering? To this they reply: "O Friend of the distressed! Out of compassion for the wretched..."
The sense is that even suffering and the like must indeed be endured.
Now, one might object: "I fear the placing of hands upon the heads of those devoted wives who are intent on their vows.
To this they reply: "Of the maidservants," [meaning] while you, the kinsman of the distressed, are manifestly shining forth.

It is also indicated that it would be improper for the women who are your maidservants to suffer distress. Alternatively, [the Lord says]: "O you who are intoxicated by passion! How can I, who have conquered passion, place my hand upon your breasts?
Therefore, it should be placed only on your heads. To this they reply: "By one who is distressed... [They say: Do not place it out of passion, but rather...

The meaning is: "Place [him] as a kinsman to one in distress. Otherwise, by our immediate falling into the final state [of death], there would be a loss of your reputation for being a kinsman to the distressed.
This is the hidden intention: that the god of love, though concealed by feigned indifference (*avahitthā*), resides within our limbs.

"By the placing of the hand, [the deity] will manifest of her own accord. Now, one might ask: even though there are many such women, how can there be such a prayer directed toward a single one? It is because of the manifestation of a particular power (śakti-viśeṣa) belonging to that [deity].
Or rather, it is with the intention that "place [it] even without following a sequence"—such is the direction [of the teaching].
The implied meaning (*śleṣārtha*) is as follows: You are "well-born" (*abhijāta*), endowed with noble birth because you are the son of the Lord of Vraja;

by the three words beginning with "O God" (*deva*), it is stated that your engagement in unrighteousness is improper. Just as the Original Person (*ādi-puruṣa*) is the protector of the world of the gods and the remover of fear from the world of the gods, so too are you the remover of the fear and suffering of Vraja.
"If we, who are virtuous, are forcibly overcome, there will surely be fear and distress for Vraja because of you;
and that is improper for you, as it would be contrary to your own purpose. By "no," she means prohibition:
"O friend of the distressed! We are not distressed," the implication being that you shall become our protector.

Because of the absence of desire and other such passions due to the phonetic connection with the syllable *a* (*a-kāra*), [place it] on breasts that are not heated; for this very reason, do not place [it there]. Or rather: O "Heated One" (*tapta*)—O you whose heart is consumed by the fire of desire! Or, being yourself heated, do not place, do not offer, your lotus-hand upon the breasts. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "also" (*api*). [This applies] to you.

The meaning is: "Do not place [your foot] even on the head of us who, by virtue of being princes, have attained a state like that of maidservants through our residence in Vraja. Or rather, [it means do not place it] even on the heads of the young maidens who exist as maidservants in the house of the Lord of Vraja, let alone those such as myself.

Thus, having defeated him with this response consisting of ten verses, his own desired object is clearly entreated in this eleventh verse due to the intensity of his distress. Furthermore, the underlying double meaning (*śleṣārtha*) here should also be inferred sequentially as a resolution of the aforementioned double meanings; and that has been written in its respective places.

Alternatively, by means of a particular cleverness regarding the meaning of those ten verses previously mentioned, a response to each of these eleven verses may be inferred. In that regard, there is a repetition, and furthermore, one additional verse exceeding what was stated; therein, the meter is long (dīrgha-chandas), for the sake of its absolute conquest.
Or rather, it should be understood as being due either to the intensity of her lingering affection or to the weight of her immense sorrow.

Nevertheless, O Lord! O Master!—with such words of welcome [18], she spoke to her own maidservants; and even there, she spoke that cruel and harsh speech, "You too," which was a source of neglect toward us.

"It is not even fitting," refers to the line "abandoning all objects"; for what need have we now for news of that? "We are devotees at the soles of your feet" refers to the two verses beginning with "The night... and so forth; because of our taking refuge in you, [we are protected] from terrible beings and the like.

"There is no fear from kinsmen," "they have been seen as devotees"—for this reason too, they have come solely for the purpose of worshipping you, and not for the purpose of seeing the forest. By this, it is established that the very cause of their coming is the worship of you; thus, go there.

[22] Thus, by the refutation of her departure for Vraja and so forth, the specific nature of her own affection is indicated by the words "Serve [Me]. By this, the meaning of "or rather" is expressed: "We have come because of Him alone, and not through ordinary affection like other people. This applies to the two [verses] beginning with "difficult to restrain" and "of the Master."

Because the insistence on serving a husband who has been described through reasoning has been refuted, the avoidance of it is established through a humble entreaty— even though it is already proven by reasoning— that one should not abandon him, as that would lead to a lack of heaven and infamy (verse 26). Furthermore, the reasoning for this has already been demonstrated in the passage beginning with "as the deity" (verse 31).

The specific details for each of those, however, should be understood according to what was previously written; the same applies hereafter. Regarding the four verses beginning with "yat pati" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.32] and "mātaraḥ" [20], as well as "tad yāta" and "bhartur duḥśīla," they are to be employed in all bondages through prayer directed toward that very person.
Because of indifference—[the question being] "what is that [indifference] toward the pleasant and unpleasant?"—it is said, "O Lord, it belongs to You" and "it belongs to the cowherd settlement";

thus, by Your power alone, there is auspiciousness in that place. By this, for the word *rajanī* (night) as well, there is an absence of fear due to proximity to You. Likewise, for the line beginning with *tathā brūta* (speak thus), it is also solely for Your sake.

The meaning is "going," because that is the intended sense; likewise, for the phrase "welcome" (*svāgatam*), as before, such a statement would be inappropriate toward those persons who are to be ruled. "In this way" (*evam*) means that the phrase "or else" (*athavā*) indicates a particularity of his own internal state. Regarding the phrase "in the words of instruction" (*upadeśa-pade*), [the word] "not conducive to heaven" (*asvargyam*) applies everywhere.

For you alone—who are taught as being worthy of worship by all for the sake of all goals—is there the abandonment of all defects and the attainment of all virtues through even a semblance of worship; thus, by the words "dearest" and so forth, even the possibility [of such a relationship] in reality has been refuted. By this, the phrase "from hearing" and so forth is also [refuted], because [the object] is the Supreme Self and so on.
Because of the principle that even the contact with your limbs—which are of the nature of the ultimate reality—is itself of the nature of the ultimate reality;

otherwise, a connection would not be possible, just as between light and darkness. As for the statement "it was seen as most dear," its dearness consists precisely in its being dear to Him, and not through any separate existence. Therefore, what [is there to say]?

"Merely by the sight of him. And here, due to the intensity of the rebuttal mentioned there, and there, due to the love-and-anger repeatedly arising for the sake of conquering him, even the sequence was not required for the purpose of providing a mere reply; so it shall be further on as well.
"‘They perform... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.33)—thus, by the word ‘welcome,’ there is the unfitness of your cruel speech regarding the welfare and the object of our delight;
or rather, because of your arrival in our presence, ‘welcome’ to you, O illustrious one, and we have truly attained our purpose—it is not otherwise."

This is because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). [The word] *pati* [is connected] with *vrajasya*; likewise, as before, [the words] *mātaraḥ* and so forth [are connected] with the four [verses]; *sve ātman* [is connected] with *rajanī*; and because of Your proximity, O Lord of the kinsmen of the life-breath (*prāṇa-nātha-bandho*), there is freedom from fear from any quarter, due to Your being present as the supreme kinsman. O Lord of the Givers of Boons (*varadeśvara*).
"Thus," or rather, "in this way": we have come here specifically because of that particular affection, in accordance with the boon previously granted.

By this, it is also implied by the word "seen": we have come here for that very purpose, and not merely for the sake of seeing the forest. "Be gracious"—this refers to the phrase "not leading to heaven," [meaning] through your grace.

Because when [the Lord] exists, all virtues are accomplished and faults are abandoned; "let him not cut" means "let him hear," which refers precisely to the contact with his limbs. "Because of maintaining hope for a long time" is what should be contemplated. "With ease" means "welcome"; for you, whose form is a mass of bliss, such cruel speech consisting of suffering is not fitting.
"It is fitting" (yuktā), or "as before" (pūrvavat).

The phrase "the mind was stolen" (*cittam apahṛtam*)—referring to the three [verses] beginning with "of Vraja," "of the foot," and "of the night"—is used in the sense that, through the stealing of the mind, the continuity of each respective [recollection] has ceased. This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Their own desire has been clearly manifested. By that [desire], they mean: "Tell her 'it is welcome,'" and since our hearts have been captivated by their feet, whatever is appropriate for them to do toward us is indeed what is dear to us;
thus, "the reason for our coming" refers specifically to the two verses beginning with "Let us do it" and "Therefore, go," and so forth.

By the phrase "the mind" (*cittam*), [it is implied] "due to the powerlessness of karma. Alternatively, this is also established by the words "or rather": "We have come here solely because our minds were captivated by you, and not out of mere affection like other people. By the half-verse beginning with "the feet" (*pādau*), there is an indication of the supreme deluding power of those two [the feet] through the statement "not conducive to heaven" (*asvargyam*) and so forth.

By the avoidance of defects such as one's own isolation (*nijāvivveka*), it is indicated that another action— whether "let us act thus" or "what else shall we do?"— is to be abandoned, while its proximity is to be adopted;
this is shown by the verse beginning with "Siñca" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.35), which is a welcome greeting for those who have arrived.

Because it is appropriate for those of great fortune to act for the benefit [of others]. By this, one should say "this is pleasing," and [bow] at the feet as before. Likewise, even for the word "or else" (*athavā*), the meaning is exactly this: "we have come together for this very purpose;
otherwise, for all the others who are about to die immediately, what is the use of thinking of anything else?"

Regarding the verse beginning with *yarhi* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.36), the phrase "O lotus-eyed one" and "welcome"— which by its very sight removes all suffering— is inappropriate as a harsh utterance. Alternatively,
if You look upon me with Your naturally cool and sweet glance, at that very moment there is welcome.

And [it concerns] his great fortune. Or rather, it is simply from the sight of you, the lotus-eyed one, who are supremely enchanting, that all those events occurred. By the phrase "beloved by the forest folk," [it is implied] that because of the night, he remained by the side of his beloved people, and since there was no fear from any quarter for his beloved ones, he saw this.

The commentary on this is also as before. By the phrase "from that time onwards" (*tat-prabhṛti*) and so forth, the commentary on the verse-quarter beginning with "of Vraja" (*vrajasya*) is as before. Regarding the four lines beginning with "the mothers" (*mātaraḥ*), because they lacked interest in those [pastimes], the phrase "enough with even talk of them" (*alaṃ tad-vārtayāpi*) implies that they were [already] satisfied (*abhiramitāḥ*). As for the word "or else" (*athavā*):

"We have come solely because of the particular nature of our delight in you. By this, it is indicated that delight alone is eternally dear [to Him]. Therefore, when He said, "Speak what is dear," she touched the sole of His foot—the very moment granted by Ramā—[saying], "It is not heaven," and so forth, regarding the two verses concerning the Lord of Ramā.

Since it is impossible for her to be our wife, our attainment [of her] is established only through the state of a paramour; and in that case, since she is the most exalted object to be attained, once our attainment of her is accomplished, what indeed could be called "non-heavenly" and so forth? Furthermore, just as it was with her, so too with us...

Indeed, physical contact would necessarily occur, and by that, the state of being [the beloved] would be fully realized; otherwise, such contact would be impossible during the worship of the assembly of devotees by one possessed of supreme love.
This is indicated by the verse beginning "Śrīr yat... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.37). The word "vrajasya" refers to the feet, and "rajanī" refers to...
Regarding the first two [verses], that [verse] beginning with "tad yātu," and the first two [verses] beginning with "bhartuḥ":

even though the glance of Brahmā and others is sought after, she desired Śrī while disregarding them all; likewise, we too have taken refuge while disregarding everyone else—so what need is there for any other talk? By this [is meant] "or rather" (athavā).
"We have come here solely because of our love for her that is similar to hers. This was observed;
indeed, by considering her own affection for You, just as she possesses the Ocean of Milk and so forth, so too do we possess this Śrī Vṛndāvana. Therefore, there is no need for us to see You alone.

Likewise, regarding the two [statements] beginning with "not conducive to heaven," it is exactly as before. Therefore, with the underlying intention that "our desire is for nothing other than your service," say "it is pleasing" (priyam); this is established even for the feet [of the verse]. For only when that is so are we truly fortunate (mahābhāgāḥ) and worthy of the inquiry "are you well?"—thus, [the word] "svāgatam" [is used].
Regarding the word "pādasya" (of the feet), it is as stated in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.38]: "prasīda" (be gracious) and "svāgatam" (welcome)—the meaning of these two halves is as before.
And by this, in the verses beginning with "priyam" (what is dear), our dearness consists solely in Your grace. Thus it is.

"Thus [is] the arrival": because of the nature of destroying the fear of suffering (*vṛjinārdana*), [the word] "of Vraja" applies to the first half [of the verse], and "of that [Vraja]" applies to the second half as well. "Having reached the root of the feet":
regarding the second half, "having returned," it is because for those who have reached the root of Your feet, departure elsewhere is impossible; therefore, [they remain] right there.
And because of their steadfastness: "Having dismissed the attendants" refers, as before, to the fourfold group beginning with "the mothers.
"We have come for the sake of serving you alone, not to see the forest"—this is the meaning of "our hope is in your worship. By the phrase "O beautiful one," [it answers] the alternative "or else."

"We have come here precisely because our souls are tormented by desire. Regarding the two statements, "O ornament of men" and "it is not conducive to heaven," there is no fault whatsoever in your taking a wife, for you are the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*); in reality, you alone are the father [of all], and you are the supreme goal to be attained. Therefore, through union with your limbs, our devotion (*bhāva*) surely increases.

For the principle beginning with "proximity belongs to mortals" (*sannikarṣo hi mārtyānām*) refers only to other objects. This is seen in the verse *vīkṣya* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.39), which pertains to the four verses beginning with "Having beheld Your glorious face and so forth, we shall become maidservants of Vraja," and to the two verses beginning with "Of our husband."
"For those who have become your servants, what need is there for anything else? By this, the sense of "or rather" (*athavā*) is also established:

"We have come [to you] precisely through the state of being your servants. Regarding the two phrases "the sole lover of Śrī" and "not leading to heaven," etc., they are to be understood as before. Thus, the meaning of the half-verse "welcome" (*svāgatam*) and the quarter-verse "speak" (*brūta*) is also established.
"Service to you alone is dear to us; our coming here is for that purpose alone, and once that is accomplished, there will be the welcome and so forth.
Alternatively, [the phrase] "to whom protection has been granted" refers to Vraja; [the word] "night" and so forth refer to the two [verses]; and [the word] "husband" refers to [the Lord].

And because, through these three [qualities], there is the attainment of fearlessness here in this world from terrible beings and from kinsmen, and in the next world even from Yama and others; and because, by the same logic that "it goes there," service to one's master and so forth would otherwise be rendered useless, and because [the opposite] would bring fault through the abandonment of what has been accepted— [this is] the face.
By the very phrase "having seen," the meaning of "was seen" is also established;
for, by beholding such a glorious face of yours, no desire to see anything else arises, and because of the scriptural declaration that you are the sole lover of Śrī. Everything else is the same.
Regarding the verse beginning with "kā strī" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.40):
for those who have been utterly deluded by the song of his flute, what is the use of such things as a welcome? Or what is the use of inquiring after their welfare and so forth?
Or what is the use of instructing them in dharma and other matters? This refers to the pair of verses beginning with "trailokya" and "asvargyam."
In such a specific enjoyment of beauty, what indeed could there be that is non-heavenly or the like?

It will increase all the more by its own nature. By the word "yad" (which), through the mention of its extraordinary majesty and its transcendental nature, any defect mentioned in worldly logic regarding proximity is also avoided.

In the verse beginning with *vyaktam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.41), the phrase "remover of the fear and distress of Vraja" refers to the feet; the two verses beginning with "O night... refer to the Lord; and the two verses beginning with "He who went there... refer to the husband, all as explained previously because of the absence of any cause for fear. The two verses beginning with "O God... and "not leading to heaven... [refer to the same].

There is no fault here for you either, out of compassion for the distressed; nor is there any fault for us, who have somehow attained the status of primal beings through association with you, a primal being. For in reality, he alone is the husband, and since his union is not of a worldly nature, even the contact of his limbs is likewise non-worldly.

Because all faults have been avoided as before, and because [the Lord’s] state of being the object of attainment has been made known; therefore, say to His feet, "Place us there, O Beloved. Regarding the word *kiṅkarīṇām* (of the maidservants), [it means] "we have come specifically by way of this particular form of servitude. By this, for the phrase *dṛṣṭam* (seen) as well, [it refers to] the maidservants.
The sight of the forest is merely incidental; the primary purpose is the sight of the Lord.
Thinking, "Fulfill here and now that which has been long desired," [the Lord] immediately said, "Welcome," and so forth.
This should be understood as the reply to His foot [the messenger], namely: "May it be truly dear to you. This is the general direction.
Enough with excessive detail; we fear the fault of prolixity in the text.
May the meaning here, at every step, be rendered correctly— or even otherwise— by those whose souls have been delighted by the grace of the lotus feet of the beloved of the illustrious gopīs.
The meaning of his words and theirs is indeed mutually different;
yet, though it is to be known by the heart alone, it has been boldly set down here by my intellect for the delight of the virtuous.

Thus, it is understood that physical contact had certainly not occurred previously; otherwise, the various statements made by him and by them would be untenable. For this very reason, the author of the *Śrī Muktāphala* and others [cite] what was stated in the twenty-first chapter regarding *pūrvarāga* in the twelfth chapter [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*].
The verse beginning with *akṣaṇvatāṃ phalam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.7) is thus summarized. For this very reason,
the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda also explained that even though the primary meaning is "delighted by you" (*tvayābhiramitāḥ*)— meaning made joyful—
in the case of dreams and so forth, [the term is used] by the venerable Śrī Vallabhabhaṭṭapāda and others.

Thus it has been explained. Each of those points has indeed already been written. Likewise, in the fifteenth [chapter], the two verses beginning with "That dust of the cows... (*bhā.pu.* 10.15.42); in the nineteenth, the verse beginning with "The supreme bliss of the gopīs" (*bhā.pu.* 10.19.16); and other similar [passages] from elsewhere.
In that very context, this should be inferred.

Alternatively, even if there was contact with her limbs previously—once or two or three times—it is indeed already chosen because of his singular devotion to her. This being the case, the primary meaning of the word "abhiramitā" (pleased/enjoyed) is maintained. Now...
And when He repeatedly engages in such conduct or in particular amorous pastimes (*rāsa-vilāsa*), one should understand that such speech belongs to Him and to them;
or rather, since their minds are immersed in the nectar of supreme love (*parama-prema-rasa*), even though He stands at their side, [He speaks thus].
Even when they are alone, by the principle expressed in such passages as "nevertheless, at every step, his pair of feet are ever new" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.11.34),
they regard that [pair of feet], though repeatedly performed [in their service], as always fresh, because of the very nature of that supremely sweet reality; and likewise, of that same [reality].

Even for that crown jewel of connoisseurs (rasika-śiromaṇi), such various utterances would indeed be appropriate; consequently, Śrī Svāmipāda’s commentary on the word "abhiramitāḥ" (delighted) is also perfectly consistent.
This has already been explained in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*. ||41||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* 332: Regarding the passage beginning with "This night... (*bhā.pu. 10.29.19*), in the context of the words "you must remain here in my presence," even the possibility of a hostile intent (*balākāra*) being suspected, it is as if stated with praise.
They pray: "It is evident that you are [the Supreme Being]," because you have been born in such a way.

Therefore, O Friend of the distressed! You who protect the people of Vraja even from the fear of falling away from dharma, why do you place your lotus-hand upon the breasts—even though they are not yet heated by longing—of the maidservants, the household slaves, who have conceived a desire for the sight of you?

"Do not place [them] down; do not offer them. Let alone talk of breasts—do not even place them upon their heads! The sense is this: such being the case, you should not even mentally entertain talk of that sort regarding women like me, who are born of noble families and are supremely chaste."

Thus, the meaning consisting of the rejection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s request has been explained. Furthermore, the suggested (vyaṅgya) meaning in the form of a request made by her own self as a special kind of messenger is generally well known. In that regard, the permanence of following her husband and others by virtue of the instructions of the *dharma-śāstra*—

Relying upon the science of knowledge established by the Blessed Lord, they seek to refute it; yet, by the mere movement of their own imagination, they postulate a supreme self-principle and establish that the purport of all instructions lies solely in following that principle, as stated in *yat-paty-apatya* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.32).

Thus: may this statement of instruction regarding one’s own duty (svadharma) find its ultimate purport in You alone among all statements of instruction; that is to say, may it culminate in Your worship. [An objection: How can I be the locus of that? To this they reply: "You are the Self, the Supreme Self. Therefore, this very...

The meaning is that, by the force of such scriptural passages as "By the study of the Vedas, the Brahmins seek to know [Brahman]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), You alone are the locus of that [knowledge].
Now, one might ask: "But from what [source] is my status as the Supreme Self? To this, they respond with insight: "Indeed..."

It is well known that You are the dearest of all embodied beings, the object of unconditional love, the kinsman, and the benefactor who acts without ulterior motive; and these two qualities are the defining characteristics of the Supreme Self, as stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (2.4.5): "But everything is dear for the sake of the Self."
This is well-known in the *Ādijñāna-śāstra*. Therefore, it is established that you alone are the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Consequently, for us who are intent upon your worship, even if we abandon our own duties (*svadharma*) through the instruction of the most powerful *jñāna-śāstra*—namely, "The uncreated is not attained by the created" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.2.12)—the Brāhmaṇa has reached a state of world-weariness (*nirveda*).

The sense is that there is no fault. Furthermore, it has already been shown that their knowledge of His sovereignty is unable to arise due to the excellence of their experience of His sweetness. And in this regard, they specifically cite the authority of the conduct of the virtuous, saying: "For they act... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.33).
The virtuous ones (*kuśalāḥ*) are those who have destroyed [the distinction between] the essential and the non-essential; for this is well-known. The meaning is "especially.

"In one's own" (*sve*) means in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), according to the previous intention. "In your own self" (*sve ātmani*) means in that You who are experienced as eternally dear within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); such is the meaning. Thus.
Or rather, it is with this intention: because they take delight only in You who are thus constituted, and not in dharma and the like which are its causes, nor in the home and so forth;
therefore, what is the use of husbands and the rest to us? As it is said: "O lotus-eyed one... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.36).

In the case of words such as *ramā* and others, they should be explained in the same manner as [the word] *śrī* in the verse beginning with *śrīr yat-pādāmbuja*. Thus ends the explanation of conversation among the verbal *anubhāvas*. (41)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therefore, first we were utterly enchanted by the song of the flute; thereafter, we were bewildered by Your very pastimes; thereafter, having beheld this form, the auspiciousness of the three worlds, we fainted; and even beyond that, we have been intent on speaking with You. From this point forward—

"What is our fortitude? Therefore, do not further delude us. Others, concluding with "Be gracious," said: "It is evident that you... and so forth. It is indeed manifest that you have appeared as the one who removes the fear and suffering of Vraja; O God, protector of the world of the gods!

The meaning is that just as You Yourself exist as the Original Person (Ādi-puruṣa) in Your partial manifestations (aṃśa-rūpa), so too do You protect the world of the gods by virtue of being the Original Person; however, in Vraja, You do so in Your own person—this is the sense of the word "bhavat" (Your). Therefore, it is fitting that Your compassion should be even greater [toward us]. Or else, [the meaning is] that just as the Lord is the Original Person...

"You are the protector of the world of the gods, and likewise, you are the remover of the fear and suffering of Vraja. Therefore, place your lotus-hand upon our heads and upon our scorched breasts, for we are your maidservants. O friend of the distressed!
Since you remove the suffering of Vraja, it is entirely fitting that you remove our own distress"—this is the conclusion.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus restated everything that was said, they, being deeply distressed, describe His purpose for the incarnation and pray for the alleviation of their own suffering, beginning with the words "It is manifest" (*vyaktam*). This is manifest—that is, certain—that You have appeared as the remover of the suffering of the people of Vraja.

Some say that He descended for the protection of the universe; however, the protection of the universe can be accomplished even through other incarnations. It was with the specific purpose of removing the suffering of the people of Vraja that He descended, and by such acts as lifting Govardhana Hill, He removed the external and internal distress of all.
The sense is: "Once you are born, because there will be no removal of our internal suffering, an imbalance will arise;
since those who cause us joy are now in distress, no one at all will show affection toward you.
However, the removal of the earth's burden would occur solely by your own will, as this is generally the nature of an Īśvara.

The removal of the suffering of the people of Vraja through our connection is the primary purpose; indeed, the removal of our own suffering is the very objective. In the removal of our suffering, the protection of the sweet nectar (*madhura-rasa*) will be achieved.
When the sweet nectar is protected, your essential nature, which is full of supreme bliss, remains well-guarded.
The term *bhāva* means "it shall come to be.
What principle do they state? That whoever has taken refuge in someone must be protected and guarded by that person. For example, the Primordial Person, Śrī Nārāyaṇa.

Through incarnations such as Vāmana and others, He is the protector of the world of the gods; He guards and protects the gods and their respective realms. Although the Lord is worthy of worship by all, He deceived the demons by assuming the form of Mohinī and gave the nectar to the gods. Even though the Supreme Lord is equal toward all, [He acts thus].
There is no partiality; nevertheless, He acted thus by manifesting affection for His own.

A *deva* is one who plays (*divyati*, *krīḍati*)—one whose primary nature is play and who is dependent [on others]. How can You deceive us? For You, as the son of the Lord of Vraja, are the object of service, while we are the servants.

If it is asked, "How indeed can there be the removal of suffering? Please explain that specifically," they reply: Therefore, first of all, let this lotus-hand, because it is by nature the remover of suffering and because of its extreme coolness, serve to pacify the heat upon our breasts, which have been consumed by the flames of the fire of love.

"Place it! For the fever of passion in women resides only in the breasts. When the mountain of the heart has been leveled, place your lotus-hand upon our heads; we shall establish the reputation that the purpose of your incarnation was indeed the subduing of our affliction."

If it is argued, "Since my childhood I have been a lifelong celibate student (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī), and I am afraid of touching your breasts and so forth," they reply: "He desires the touch of the breasts of his maidservants; he has no fear of anyone, nor any sense of restraint. This is the fruit of his lifelong vow of celibacy."
The word *bhaviṣyati* means "will come to be. O Friend of the Afflicted! We are afflicted; you are our kinsman, the destroyer of suffering.

If there were still affliction even while you, our kinsman, are present, then your compassion would not be established. Although you are free from desire, nevertheless, by you the most afflicted Gajendra [was saved].
Just as your fame was established there by your renown as a friend to the distressed when you rescued [the elephant],
so now, for the sake of preserving your own reputation, please act with propriety by placing your lotus-hand upon our heads and cooling the fever of our breasts. Or rather, you—
"He who removes the suffering of the people of Vraja" means he is clearly renowned throughout all the worlds as the remover of the distress of the inhabitants of Vraja,
as evidenced by his subduing of Kāliya and other such deeds. "Noble-born" (abhijāta) means that he looks upon us with nobility because he is the son of the Lord of Vraja.

If it is objected: "Surely you ladies have not come tormented by heat, but have come here out of fickleness and the nature of women," they reply: "Therefore, place your head upon your breasts and your lotus-hand upon them; by laying your hand there, let the heat itself be perceived. The meaning is that the heat will become manifest of its own accord.
Regarding the phrase "of the maidservants": the meaning is that if our distress does not depart, no one else will perform service for you.
Thus, through this prayer expressed by suggestion (*vyañjanā*), physical union is itself requested.
Viśvanātha [states]: "Therefore, enough with this display of cleverness; abandon your dissimulation."
They said: "It is clear; that is to say, this narration is not hidden anywhere. What is it?

It is he who removes (harati) whatever fear you have from forest fires and the like, as well as the distress (ārti) and suffering caused by rain, wind, and so forth. There is also a reading: *vraja-janārti-haraḥ* ("the remover of the distress of the people of Vraja"). [He does this] *abhi*, meaning in every respect.

He was born in the house of Nanda; thus he is proclaimed by all the people of the world as "Nārāyaṇa. If these gopīs were to die today in numbers reaching hundreds of millions, how would there not be distress for the people of Vraja, including their fathers and others, and what fear would they not feel, thinking, "How is it that all these have died simultaneously in the middle of the forest?"
The word *bhāva* means "it will come to pass. If so, what is it that you desire? To this they reply:
"Therefore, O friend of the distressed, place Your lotus-hand upon our scorched breasts.
[Objection: But then, this [hand] of Yours is so tender; will it not burn? To this they reply: "Of the maidservants... [and so forth].
The meaning is this: even though these two [the sun and moon] cause heat to us, who are your maidservants, they serve only as instruments for your service;

even for a lotus, the heat of the rising sun is not painful, but rather it is a source of pleasure. Furthermore, by the words "and upon our heads," she intends to convey: "Henceforth, let there be no fear in you regarding my abandonment. (41)
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard this lamentation of theirs, the Lord of the masters of yoga (Kṛṣṇa) [replied].
Laughing with compassion, he who delights in the Self nonetheless brought delight to the cowherd girls.

Śrīdhara: *Viklavita* means lamenting due to helplessness. Having seen the King agitated upon hearing of the distress of the gopīs, Śrī Śuka—the supreme sage accompanied by Śrī, who removes the suffering of others—spoke for their pacification, [he] who holds the flute (*vaṃśīdharaḥ*) and who caused them to rejoice (*arīramat*, i.e., made them sport).
"Thus" means in this manner. "Of them" refers to those gopīs. "Yogins" refers to Sanaka and others; "their lords" refers to Śiva and others;
"the Lord of them" is the son of Śrī Yaśodā. By this, his supreme excellence of compassion is expressed.
The yogins are compassionate; the lords of yoga (yogeśvaras) are supremely compassionate; [he] is the most excellently compassionate of all.

Regarding "Śrī-Kṛṣṇa": with compassion, He personally wiped away their tears and performed other such acts. Even for the gopīs, since the Lord has said, "Their minds are fixed on Me; My life-breaths are they," and because they are of that very nature, the wise should reflect that there is no loss of His self-sufficiency (*ātmārāmatva*). As He will also say: "Just as a child..."

"An illusion regarding one's own reflection" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.17). By the word *pralapitam*, which means "uttered through dependence," that is, being subject to desire, there is the sense of meaningless speech;
for Amara states: "Pralāpa is meaningless speech. By this statement, the Lord’s feet [have also described] those [women].
In reality, "not being so" (atathātva) has been implied; "not being so" means the absence of affliction by desire and the like. ||42||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "Thus," and so forth. Regarding the word "laughing" (*prahasya*): because his eloquence failed when he was about to give another reply, laughter itself arose. By the words "Lord of the Lords of Yogis" (*yogeśvareśvara*) and so on, [the Lord's] capacity to fulfill the desires of all simultaneously is expressed. By the phrase "even though He delights in the Self" (*ātmārāmo’pi*) and the like, His state of being one who finds delight in the Self is indicated.

The meaning is "having abandoned non-attachment. Alternatively, he is called *ātmārāma* because he delights in those who have become his very self; thus, although he himself was already enjoying delight, he caused them also to enjoy delight. ||42||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, having heard this lamentation— which, like her own words, touches upon both meanings and consists of expressions of anger and wretchedness arising from distress— and having fulfilled her own desire by hearing it, she then laughed,
even amidst their jesting.
Because of the arising of a particular state of agitation; because of the accomplishment of hearing what was personally desired from that [person];

because of the excellence of the reply given there, which was consistent with one's own words; because of the disappearance of dissimulation (*avahitthā*) and the subsequent arising of the emotion (*bhāva*) called love (*rati*); and because it possesses a nature that expands the mind to a high degree.
The meaning is that he attained a particular state of emotion characterized by the physical expression of facial serenity well-known in the science of aesthetics (*rasa-śāstra*).

And having heard those very words of piteous supplication full of love, he delighted the gopīs with compassion— that is, in such a way as to be accompanied by a moistening of his heart— and he himself instigated them to take pleasure.
The meaning is that he showed excessive insistence (*atyāgraha*). In this way, his particularity of desire (*icchā-vaiśiṣṭya*) in that regard is indicated.

The sense is that even among children playing together, [the action belongs] to the child who is the instigator (*prayojaka*), just as in the case of the master. For this very reason, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending is used, according to the rule: "after a root that is intransitive when its agent is sentient, [the active voice is used for the agent]."
Because that [rule] is prescribed with reference to the intention of the agent.

Now, is this not a wonder among the citizens? To this he says: "Even though He delights in the Self. Oh, how intense is the power of their love's qualities, since it is said, "And even sages who delight in the Self," and so forth.

The sense is that by the power of Hari’s qualities, he too was brought under his own control, just like the group of those who delight in the Self (ātma-rāma). For this very reason, the word *api* (even/also) is meaningful; otherwise, it would indeed be contradictory. As it is said: "I do not hope for myself even for a moment without my saintly devotees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64).

Although there is a statement that [the Lord] is even superior to the general devotees, nevertheless, because the intention here is to express His specific distinction, such a description is given; thus, there is neither tautology nor futility.
Now, one might ask: "How could He, being a single person, delight countless [beings]? To this he says: "The Lord of the Lords of Yoga."

Even the masters of yoga (yogeśvaras), having manifested arrays of bodies and so forth, are able to perform various activities simultaneously; however, because He is the Lord of even them and possesses inconceivable, innate power, He is able to do so even without such [manifestations]. And it will be stated by the venerable Nārada:
"How wonderful it is that this one man, with a single body, simultaneously married sixteen thousand women individually in their respective homes!"— this is the sense [of Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.69.2].

By using the word "gopī," [the author] recalls their status as the eternal beloveds of Him, which is well-known through their respective great mantras; furthermore, he indicates that even this is not particularly wonderful.
Thus says the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*. This is merely a rambling or a statement of verbal deficiency.

"Because he touches both extremes, he is attached to both; having laughed intensely with compassion"—by this, the deception mentioned in the statement, "Laughter is the illusion that causes the madness of people" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.1.31), is refuted, since it is precisely what they desire that is established by them. Or else, [he laughs] at their agreement with his own hand.

"Having wiped away their tears and so forth, He delighted them. By this, His indifference is discarded and His affection is demonstrated; for the meaning is that the gopīs were worthy of such grace due to their particular intensity of love.
"Laughing"—this indicates their distress because they did not understand His own intention. By that...
And because her own dissimulation (*avahitthā*) was thereby rendered meaningful;

or else, because laughter arises from the pure emotion (*śuddha-bhāva*) due to the emergence of great joy at the reply; or rather, because the emergence of amorous transformation (*kāma-vikāra*) occurs when their dissimulation is removed by those words of his—for laughter is indeed an accessory emotion (*vyabhicārī-bhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that passion (*rati*) is accomplished through mutual attachment and the manifestation of cleverness?
And that would not be possible in her case, because she delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*) and so forth. To this he replies: "Yoga is one-pointedness of mind;
its Lord is the master of those whose yoga has been subdued, such as Sanaka and others; He is the Lord even of them, and though He delights in the Self..."
The meaning is that at that time, neither his steadfastness in yoga nor his delight in the Self remained due to the manifestation of such diverse cleverness.
Alternatively, as before, his status as the Lord of the Lords of Yoga was lost through his agitation, and his delight in the Self was lost through his pleasure-seeking.

The word "apagata" (gone away) must be analyzed; otherwise, it would be impossible for them to take delight in hearing that [sound]. Alternatively, by the word "yogena" (by means of yoga), it is indicated that although He is one, being as if manifold in form, He caused them to rejoice individually and simultaneously. The rest is the same. ||42||

The sequence of the composition: Having heard these words of helplessness, uttered through the power of love in the manner previously described, [the Lord is addressed as] "Yogeśvareśvara"—meaning one who possesses inconceivable power capable of accomplishing various extraordinary deeds. Furthermore, [He is called] "Ātmārāma" (one who delights in the Self).
The intensity of their love and virtue is as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 1.7.11: "And the sages who delight in the Self...
By the phrase "He caused them to take pleasure" (*arīramat*), it is shown that His own attachment there was primary, like that of the instigating child among children playing. (42)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Immediately following that, Śrī Śukācārya reveals what occurred, beginning with the words "iti" and so forth. Although he is the Lord of the lords of yoga (*yogeśvareśvara*) and one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*)—meaning he rejoices in his own bliss within the Self—even being such, what is the meaning of [the word] "prahasya" (having laughed)? It refers to me.

Having cast aside the lordship over the lords of yoga and the delight in the self—which had previously fallen away—he laughed and took his pleasure. Yet he did not merely take pleasure; rather, having discarded the knowledge of being the Lord residing within himself through the method already described, and being free from limitation, he thought: "Let all women, according to their desire, sport with me."
The power of the causative suffix (ṇic). ||42||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, having been rendered speechless by the words addressed to the gopīs, and having become agitated by their lamentations of distress and their *sāttvika* emotion of melting love, he remained restrained there, saying nothing further. Then the Lord of Sages, cognizant of her state, speaks—thus [he says]. Thus.

In this manner, having heard their distress— which was filled with the piteousness of love-born anger and contained prayers that fulfilled their own desires— by means of resisting Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deceptions with corresponding replies, He immediately laughed and said: "But by me, through instruction in dharma and the display of fear..."

In order to examine their true disposition, they display anger through words that are full of inner affection yet outwardly expressive of indifference; disregarding my intention, they communicate with plaintive tones and feigned distress. Therefore, enough of this excessive dissimulation! Having said this and laughed aloud, as for the laughter itself—

It is the indicator of a transformation of the mind. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*: "The state (*bhāva*) of the mind that is otherwise changeless would be its first modification" (1.323). Having manifested the state residing within one's own heart through laughter, in such a way that it becomes full of compassion (*sadaya*); for compassion (*dayā*) is indeed without conditions.

Desiring the abandonment of that which is not suffering, and acting accordingly, even though he was one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*), he set aside that very delight in the Self; and although he did not perceive any particular pleasure with his own eye-organ, he took delight in those women—he caused them to be enjoyed. Of what nature was he? The Lord of the Lords of Yoga (*yogeśvareśvara*). For other yogis indeed...

Those who have obtained the grace of the Blessed One become perfected in the higher knowledges (abhijñā) such as the power of recollection; yet He is the Lord even of them. Although He knew the mental state of the cowherd girls, desiring to hear their words in that manner, He manifested indifference.
Alternatively, "yoga" refers to union; its lords are the Great Lovers (Mahāvilāsins), who are of the nature of supreme power (*parama-śakti*).
The meaning is that their lord is the ultimate limit of supreme artistry, whose form is great power (*mahā-śakti*).
By manifesting indifference, he produces the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*) and thereby brings forth the fullness of the sweet aesthetic flavor (*madhura-rasa*).
The sense is that he acted in such a way in order to experience [it].

Alternatively, other yogins, through the proximity of dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma-pratyāsatti*), enter the bodies of others and experience happiness by means of their very bodies and senses, even without their own bodies.

But this is not so; rather, it is a marvel that while remaining present with his entire body, he delighted those many women in groups. For this very reason, he will say later, "among them, two by two," thereby indicating his presence with his whole being through a specific power and agility.

Regarding the term *viklavitam* (distress): by the mention of "listening," cessation through delighting in the Self (*ātmārāmatā*) is indicated. This hero, however, is the *dakṣiṇa* (liberal) type. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*: "The *dakṣiṇa* is said to be one who is equal toward even many heroines" (*Raṣu.* 1.126). Regarding the word *prahasya* (having laughed): "In the *śuci* (pure) sentiment, there are likewise laughter, the *preyas* (the beloved), and the marvelous."

"O best of friends"—by this, it is indicated that they nourish the sweet nectar [of love]. Furthermore, perceiving my indifference, you have formulated such a response; thus, I myself have embraced that very indifference. Therefore, even though we have abandoned them, we laugh at the gopīs.

Although it has been experienced many times, the concealment of the bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa demonstrates the intensity of their longing and affection. Furthermore, devotees are drawn in by the qualities of the one they worship; likewise, Śrī Kṛṣṇa too, being attracted by the love of the beauties of Vraja, relaxed His state of self-contentment—this is the essential meaning.

Viśvanātha: Having heard the "viklavita"—that is, having heard the speech expressive of distress, and thereby having fulfilled his own desire; *prahasya* (having laughed): "Oh, you passionate women! Every single day, at the time of meeting, you display boundless perversity. But I, on this very day..."
Whatever slight perversity I displayed this very day through feigned indifference was itself infused with courtesy.
Yet, because of that, you—who are so full of agitation—have offered such a libation of shame that you make me laugh.
Therefore, it is by me alone, who am expert at drinking up the ocean of your daily feigned indifference in a single mouthful, [that this is done].

"You are conquered! O you who consider yourselves the crest-jewels of the wise! You are conquered! Therefore, come here in person and, being free from the constraints of shame, self-restraint, and the like, place the golden jewel upon my neck and drink the nectar of my words together with me. For I have long been afflicted by a great thirst."

Laughing, He—He who is the auspicious and benevolent Ordainer—delighted those cowherd women, even though He was one who finds delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), in such a way that it was full of affection. Thus, regarding the cowherd women as being possessed of such love, there is the verse from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (1.7.11): "And the sages find delight in the Self... (*ātmārāmāś ca munayaḥ*).
Just as in the expression "Hari, who possesses such qualities," because the gopīs are manifestations of His own essential hlādinī-śakti, they too are His very self;
thus, sporting with them who are His own self is indeed possible.
Although there are scriptural statements such as, "Neither Saṃkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even the Self is like you" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.14.15),

and "I do not desire myself without my saintly devotees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64), and so forth— indicating that from the Lord's own perspective, His devotees are superior even to Himself— [the devotee still thinks:]...

It should be understood that because these gopīs are known to possess a preeminent capacity for bestowing bliss, and because they are the crest-jewels among all devotees, He—though self-reliant—engages in dalliance with them solely for the sake of increasing His own bliss.
One might object: "But according to the *Kramadīpikā* and other scriptures, He is surrounded by hundreds of millions of women."

Is it not possible for Him alone to enjoy those [women], numbering one hundred crores, all at once and in one place? To this he replies: He is the Lord even of the yogis such as Saubhari and the lords of yoga such as Rudra; whereas Saubhari and others enjoy themselves only after having created a multitude of bodies (*kāya-vyūha*), Kṛṣṇa, however...
Because his conduct is beyond the reach of logic, apart from that which will be stated in such passages as: "O, how wonderful that he, with a single body... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.69.2]. ||42||
Accompanied by those women of noble conduct, whose faces blossomed with joyful glances, Acyuta was filled with delight.
With the radiance of his noble smile like white jasmine flowers, he shone like the moon surrounded by stars.

Śrīdhara: He whose splendor is like the *kunda* flower amidst those [women] whose faces bloom at the sight of their beloved, and who possesses a noble smile and [white] teeth; he is the deer-marked moon. (43)

Vaṃśīdhara: Śrī Rādhā, who dwells together with me (Mayā) and Śobhā, has been reached by these [gopīs]. He is one whose noble activities consist of the touch of his limbs, flowers, and other offerings, as well as the casting of side-long glances. By the words "at the sight of her beloved," the faces are likened to a forest of lotuses and her glance to a single lotus.

The nature of the sun (bhāskaratva) is indicated. [This refers to] those teeth (dvija), which possess a noble smile; or rather, the *dvija-kundas* are the twice-born (teeth) themselves, who are like *kunda* flowers (the *mādhyapushpa*). He is one whose rays (*marīci*) are the light of the *dvija-kundas* through a noble smile—that is, an excellent laugh. For it is said: "The word *bhānu* means a ray (*kara*), and *marīci* is feminine."

*Amara* [states]: "The word *kunda* is not feminine when it means jasmine; it is masculine in the sense of Mukunda, a treasure-trove (*sannidhi*), and the interior. *Medinī* [states]: "It is masculine in the sense of Mukunda, a treasure-trove, and the interior.
*Halāyudha* [states]: "The word *eṇa* refers to a deer, a kuraṅga, or a hariṇa. Thus, he who has the mark of an *eṇa* (deer) as his emblem is so described.
*Amara* [states]: "The words *kalaṅka*, *aṅka*, *lāñchana*, *cihna*, *lakṣma*, and *lakṣaṇa* all mean a mark. By this...
By the radiance of Hari, the concealment of their own radiance by them has been stated. ||43||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Describing the manner of sporting by means of those [four verses] beginning with "by them," and demonstrating the agency that prompts that [sport], [the author] first [speaks] together with them.
He describes the extraordinary beauty of Him as well, through the union of love, by means of an illustration: "By them" (tābhiḥ).
Since it is said that He "caused them to sport" (arīramat) with Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself as the agent, who had come together with them;
therefore, being surrounded and encompassed on all sides by such women as these, He shone resplendently.

He shone with particular splendor. Even there, Acyuta—being free from falling away (cyuti) even in union with each and every one of them—is thus one whose activities are noble (udāra-ceṣṭita). He is one whose forms (rūpa) are such; therefore, the "beholding of the Beloved" should be understood as having either oneself or Him as the agent. By the word "utphulla" (fully blossomed)...
The lotus-nature of her face is manifested because, through the removal of the darkness within her heart, she has attained its own day; this is the intended meaning.
Thus, the particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of those women has been described. He speaks of that [flavor] as well: "She whose smile is noble."

The phrase "whose radiance is like that of the jasmine of the twice-born" describes the superior beauty of his smile through the brilliance of his splendid teeth. Although he possesses an eternal splendor that has naturally reached its highest perfection, the author establishes a specific excellence of beauty through them by means of an illustration: "like the moon. [This refers to] the moon.

Fullness: because the deer-marked one (the moon) is perceived in the form of a deer, he is called the "deer-marked"; just as the full moon shines brilliantly when surrounded on all sides by stars that are themselves radiant, so too does He shine.
In this way, there is a mutual beauty, a state of being most dear, and eternal companionship between Him and them.
From that, its thinness is also indicated. ||43||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Describing the manner of His sporting with them through these four verses beginning with "by them," He first states—with an illustration—the particular excellence of His own splendor resulting from the union of love with them, using the words "by them" (*tābhiḥ*). "By them" means by those who have come into His immediate proximity; or alternatively:

[They are] those who have come together by abandoning such things as feigned anger; or rather, *mā* means splendor—that is, supreme beauty—and she who possesses that [splendor], the supremely beautiful Śrī Rādhā; [they are] those who have gone to her (*itābhiḥ*), meaning they have attained her.
By this, it is implied that at the time of their initial liberation, Śrī Rādhā was not among them, but...
As soon as Kṛṣṇa’s feigned indifference arose, she appeared; thus he was met, surrounded, and encircled by them.
Although Acyuta is unconquered by desire and other such passions—as the Viśvaprakāśa states: "Acyuta refers to one who is unconquered"—he was nevertheless overcome.

Alternatively, he is called *acyuta* because he has not fallen away from any splendor whatsoever; or, because he does not fall away from the flow of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in any way, his state of being filled with all flavors is expressed. For this very reason, he was especially pleasing—that is, he shone brilliantly.

The reason for this is as follows: he is one whose activities—which consist of sublime qualities such as various forms of cleverness that arouse specific aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), which are supreme and bestow ultimate bliss, and which take the form of glances, the offering of the merit of touch, and so forth—are [of this nature]. Or else, it means "having laughed."

The reason previously stated shines forth there indeed. Or rather, he "delighted" (arīramat), meaning he caused [her] to take pleasure (rañjayāmāsa), since the word *rati* has the sense of passion (*rāga*).
And so says the Viśva lexicon: "The word *rati* is used for the beloved of Smara, for passion, and for sexual union. This very point is the reason for their union.

And thus, it should be understood that "one of noble conduct" (*udāra-ceṣṭita*) refers both to the aforementioned means of pleasure and to the cause of radiance. For this very reason, the beholding of the beloved may be performed by oneself or by him.
In this way, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is also shown through a particular power. Toward those [women] who are present on all sides, with equanimity—

Because of the simultaneous observation: by the word "utphulla" (blossomed), the face is suggested as a lotus and the eyes as suns. Thus, the manifestation of their particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) has been described. They speak of that [flavor] also in the case of noble laughter among the twice-born (*dvija*).

And he whose [laughter] possesses the luster of *kunda* flowers; thus, the purity of his laughter and the brilliant radiance of his teeth are described. Alternatively, it means that in his noble laughter, there is the luster of the *kunda* flowers of his twice-born [teeth].
Or again, it means that by which noble laughter possesses the luster of the *kunda* flowers of his twice-born [teeth]; this refers to his glorious teeth.
The superior beauty of the smile through its radiance has been stated.

He establishes, by means of an illustration, that even for one who has naturally reached the highest pinnacle and consists of eternal beauty, there is a specific excellence of beauty produced by those [teeth]: "the moon" (eṇāṅkaḥ). The full moon, surrounded on all sides by the stars...
Just as He shines when surrounded by virtuous women who are themselves radiant, so it is here;
thus, along with them, His mutual beauty, dearness, and eternal companionship are indicated. ||43||

The sequence of the composition: He states the causal agency itself with the four verses beginning with "tābhiḥ" (by them). "Sametābhiḥ" means joined together by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself as the agent. ||43||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He describes that manner [of his appearance] with the words beginning "tābhiḥ" (by them). Acyuta, surrounded by those who had come together—that is, who were assembled—shone resplendent. Whose pastimes and movements (*ceṣṭita*) were noble?
By what kind of women [was he surrounded]? [By those] whose sight was a beloved thing, whether as the agent of the act of seeing or as the object of the act of seeing.
Therefore, their faces are blossomed. That which has an *ut*—meaning excellent—*āra*, meaning expansion;
that is this laughter (*hāsa*). In such [laughter], there is the radiance (*dīdhiti*) of the twice-born jasmine flowers (*dvija-kunda*). Who [is like whom] with what, as it were?
The deer-marked one, the moon, is like [the sky] with the stars (*uḍu*). Of what nature is he? He is noble (*udāra*), meaning he rises upward (*ūrdhvam iyati*).

The movement of whom [is such]. "Priyā" (the beloved) is used as a point of comparison. He whose radiance is like the radiance of the gods and of kunda flowers—[radiance] characterized by a noble and great laugh (*hāsa*) that is *acyuta* (unfailing), lasting through many nights, and pervasive. The term *uḍu* is a gender-specific qualifier, being feminine in this context. ||43||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Describing at the outset their simultaneous union with many [gopīs] and intending to indicate the long dalliance to be performed later, he briefly describes the excellence of the splendor of that amorous play: "With those immeasurable [gopīs], Acyuta..."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa appeared especially radiant; having heard their distressed lamentations while they were weary with the pain of separation, he now laughs, for he has moved far beyond the reach of their former mental impressions. This is the sense: having perceived them, he laughs as they have all come together into his presence. Acyuta.

Free from the loss of charm; in the mind, everything is indeed encompassed within the play (*līlā*). It is especially—and with superiority—delightful because of the plays that are inseparable from the substrata of other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Elsewhere, the play is performed by means of a quality (*dharma*), but here, the play is performed by the possessor of the quality (*dharmin*) himself.
It is permeated by the sweet flavor; for this very reason, the specific distinctions have been stated—namely, that it arises from those of the same class and not from those of a different class.
Alternatively, previously, how was he adorned with excellence through his delighting, and what was the nature of his noble conduct toward all?

For them, there was simultaneously a cultivation of a specific essence of flavor, enjoyable by all the senses, which was skillfully honored; this was [experienced] only by those of the same class, not by those of a different class.

Viśvanātha: He whose activities and pastimes (*ceṣṭita-līlā*) bestow noble joy upon them and grant love to those devoted in spirit (*bhāva-bhaktānām*) through hearing and other such means— he is Acyuta, who simultaneously remains free from falling away from his exclusive devotion to each of them, and who is noble in bestowing happiness upon them.
He is one whose radiance is manifested by the great laughter of the twice-born, which resembles the brilliance of jasmine blossoms. ||43||
Being sung to and singing aloud, the leader of hundreds of female throngs,
wearing the Vaijayantī garland, roamed about, adorning the forest.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Vaṃśīdhara: Being sung of by the gopīs, and himself singing and extolling the moon, Kṛṣṇa sang of the autumnal moon and the bed of white water-lilies in the moonlight. The multitude of gopīs...

"Thus, 'Kṛṣṇa's name' [is to be recited] again and again"—this is stated in another commentary. The word *śata* signifies "many. As for *yūtha*: "O Daughter of the Mountain, ten *arbudas* constitute one *yūtha*."
"Ten arbudas constitute a yūtha; thus those who know the science of numbers understand," so it is stated in the Tantra.
The definition of the Vaijayantī has been stated previously. ||44||
In *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: the connection with the three verses beginning with "upagīyamāna" is by way of transposition.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: having entered the riverbank and gracing the forest, he took his delight.
Otherwise, such enjoyment on a mere stretch of sand would not be charming; therefore, he wandered about.

Thus, the phrase ending with "kriyāntam" constitutes a separate sentence. Regarding the term *vanitā-śata-yūthapa*: *vanitā* refers to a woman who has produced excessive passion; there are hundreds of such women who are *yūthapas*.
A *yūtha* is an immeasurable multitude of beings of the same kind, and one who protects (*pāti*) them is a *yūthapa*. Thus, he is one in whom there are hundreds of such *yūthapas*.

There are a hundred of them; the word "hundred" here also signifies the "innumerable. The meaning is that your principal herd-leaders are innumerable, for when herds are infinite, what need is there to mention their counting? ||44||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, beautifying even Śrī Vṛndāvana by the arising of its particular splendor, He wandered along the path of His journey in order to go to the banks of the Yamunā—which are suitable for amorous play—to kindle His internal emotion (*bhāva*) through singing and the presentation of flowers and other offerings; this he describes with the verse beginning "upagīyamāna."
Singing aloud with joy, illuminating the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) by means of the moon and other such objects;

being sung to by them in the manner of a chorus (*upagāyana*), he is described through those very songs being imitated—since, through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), their meaning is integrated into that very context. And this should be understood as follows: for example.
In the *Śrī-rasāmṛta-sindhu*:

"Victorious is the Moon, the beloved of Rādhā—the embodiment of all nectar of rasa, whose spreading luster eclipses the rows of stars, and who is charming with his dark-complexioned consort. [Bharatārṇava 1.1.1] Thus it is said.

In some cases, it arises from the substitution of one or two syllables; for example: "Behold, this bed of night-lilies shines with a beauty that creates the splendor of night, possessing the pure luster of the moon and the glory of hair-like rays; it resounds with the sweet songs of swarms of bees. [The original verse is: yāminīkṛtaruciḥ śucikāntiś candrakāvalivibhāvikacaśrīḥ | ṣāṭpadālikalitaiḥ kalagītaiḥ paśya bhāti kumudākara eṣaḥ || [The modified version is: yāminīkṛtaruciḥ śucikāntiś candrakāvalivibhāvikacaśrīḥ | ṣāṭpadālikalitaiḥ kalagītaiḥ paśya bhāti kumudākara eṣaḥ || (Note: The modification involves the subtle shifting of syllables within the compound structure to produce a different aesthetic effect while maintaining the metrical integrity.)
