Or else, by singing that [name] with its specific melodies, rhythms, and so forth, while being sung by her, one becomes absorbed in Him alone in the mind; because of this, there arises a singular manifestation of Him in speech. As it is said in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa sang of the autumn moon, the moonlight, and the bed of night-lotuses, while the group of gopīs sang the single name 'Kṛṣṇa' again and again. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.51).
Thus, both meanings therein are to be relished: "Kṛṣṇa" and "name" constitute "Kṛṣṇa-name," which refers to that.

And this should also be explained as: "He spoke thus alone and exclusively. According to Amara, *vanitā* refers to a woman who has produced excessive passion. He is their leader (*tan-nāyaka*), meaning he protects hundreds of their groups (*yūthāni*).
By means of *śleṣa* (double entendre), it is as in the expression "those which drink" (*pibanti*) or "as if drinking with the eyes," and so forth; [here it means] he serves them with attachment.

Or, he drinks [the nectar] directly by means of drinking the nectar from their lips and so forth; thus, according to the similarity of their respective individual dispositions (*bhāva*), they form groups (*yūthatva*) in classes. The *Vaijayantī* is a garland woven from flowers of five colors, for it is said that the *Vaijayantī* consists of five colors. Even though...

Although there exist other ornaments as well— such as bracelets and anklets— as will be mentioned later, she is nevertheless described as "wearing them" because they are appropriate for her limbs during her pastimes in the forest. And she was quickly fashioned and presented by those very ornaments,
or perhaps by Vṛndā herself, the goddess of that forest, for that purpose here and there in the groves and other places.
It should be understood that "sthāpitā" means she was established [there]. "Vyācarat" means she wandered about. ||44||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, beautifying even Śrī Vṛndāvana with the arising of such extraordinary splendor, He wandered along the path of His journey—either to kindle His desire through song and the presentation of flowers and other offerings, or to go to the banks of the Śrī Yamunā, which are suitable for amorous play—as the author says: "He approached... (upa).

Being praised by descriptions of His form, qualities, pastimes, and so forth; or rather, being sung to from four sides with various songs of His praise, He therefore sang aloud with joy. "Vanitāḥ" refers to women who have engendered intense passion in men; as it is said in the Viśva lexicon: "vanitā [means] a woman."

Women have engendered an extreme passion in men; thus Amara says: "The term *vanitā* applies to a woman who has engendered excessive passion. He protects hundreds of their herds—that is, he guards them from all suffering—or rather, he drinks [them in]. As it is said: "as if drinking with his two eyes."

"He serves with attachment as if he were one of them from the very beginning. Alternatively, it means that by drinking the nectar of their lips and so forth, he drinks directly as it were; thus he is so described. Their grouping into "yūthas" (herds) follows the similarity of their respective individual dispositions (*bhāva*).
Among them, some eternal beloveds residing in Śrī Goloka and other realms have descended from there along with him.

Some of them are goddesses who are constituent parts of that [divine nature], with reference to whom Śrī Brahmā and others were instructed: "Let the celestial women come into being" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.1.23). And some attained the state of Gopīs through the means of spiritual practice, by achieving a particular state of being through great effort. The sages are of two kinds.
And the Śrutis are the sages who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest and those great ascetics on the banks of Lake Mānasa;

and some Śrutis are the Mahopaniṣad and others. Their respective accounts are clearly evident in the Padma, Bṛhad, Vāmana, and other Purāṇas. Within that very context, there is a further internal distinction based on specific nuances of meaning.

The meaning is that although they were present individually in this manner, because all of them were for the most part similar in their nature, he delighted in all of them equally. The *vaijayantī* was woven from flowers of five colors, according to the statement: "The *vaijayantī* is of five colors."

Some say it was inlaid with the nine gems. Although other ornaments had previously been worn out of a desire for amorous play—as will be stated later: "The bracelets, anklets, and tinkling bells of the women together with their beloveds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.5), and so forth—nevertheless, that [palace]...

"Carrying [it]" refers to how he generally appeared with a particular splendor because of her at night; or rather, he wandered about, having had it fashioned right there on the spot by her and immediately presented to him. ||44||

The sequential arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): being sung in accordance with his own melodies, rhythms, and so forth, it is sung in the manner of a chorus (*upagāyaka*) by singing his name. As it is said in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"Kṛṣṇa [beheld] the autumnal moon, the moonlight, and the bed of night-lotuses..."
"The group of gopīs sang the single name of Kṛṣṇa again and again" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.51).
Thus ends the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*. First, due to the intensity of their joy, they too began to sing;
in reality, however, this *rāsa*-pastime is primarily characterized by music (*saṅgīta*). And as for that music...

Singing was his primary preoccupation. Therefore, he went for a stroll in the forest himself, desiring to hear how each of them sang among them; thus he says with two verses beginning with "upagīyamāna" (being sung to). "Upagīyamāna" means by those very women. "Gāyan" (singing) means [he was singing] himself.

Those very same women; he whose [retinue] consisted of a hundred female leaders (*yūthapa*), each of whom was to be known as a leader of ten million (*koṭi*) followers—since it is said that he was "surrounded by hundreds of millions of beautiful women"—he wandered about adorning the forest. "Wearing a garland" refers to the manifest splendor of Śukadeva.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Previously, it was stated by the Holy Mouth that "the forest was seen";

since the forest had already been considered as the locus for pastimes during the mental pastimes (*mānasa-līlā*), he now describes the actual wandering (*vihāra*) with the words "being sung to" (*upagīyamāna*). It means being sung to by them in their presence, as previously [stated].

Because they sang with such excessive *anurāga* (devotional attachment) for those who were honored by Kṛṣṇa, that very singing became an inspiration for Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own singing. Therefore, hearing their songs— which centered on Śrī Kṛṣṇa and described His forms, qualities, and pastimes— He Himself also sang aloud, [and thus] of all of them...
Singing with a continuous flow of excellence in the qualities of form, what is he like?

He is the leader of hundreds of throngs of women (*vanitā*). He is one who protects (*pāti*) hundreds—meaning innumerable throngs—of women in whom new passion has arisen. Indeed, this very new passion constitutes the melodic discourse of the *ṣaḍja* and other notes.

The sense is that [the Lord] has manifested as possessing specific distinctions. Some are Upaniṣads, some are sages of the Daṇḍaka forest, some are perfected through worship, some are goddesses, and some are eternally perfected. Thus, He protects by nourishing the aesthetic flavor (rasa) through the equality of their spiritual essence, which is fivefold.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He wears upon his chest a Vaijayantī garland, woven from flowers of five colors, suitable for dancing.
The intended meaning is this: although there are five kinds of ornaments, the five kinds of gopīs are likewise [the ornaments].
The underlying sentiment is that by wearing garlands produced in Vṛndāvana, he has shown honor even to the forest itself.
Therefore it is said that he "wandered about adorning and embellishing the forest," meaning he moved about with great distinction;
by frequenting the thickets concealed by creepers and the like, he brought the sweetness of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) to its highest pitch.

The sense is that he adorned himself by entering upon beds fashioned from flowers, sprouts, and the like, and receiving floral ornaments and other decorations from his beloveds, who were themselves adorned with such things. ||44||

Viśvanātha: [The Lord] being sung by them with excellence through melody, notes, rhythm, and so forth. Therein, the song is performed with three rhythms (*tāla*), as follows: "The face is the abode of sweetness..."
"May that smile of yours, which causes the fame of the lords of elephants to tremble and shatter,
and which is desired by those with beautiful eyes—
may it, along with its companions, protect me incessantly. Thus [it is said].
And they themselves, those most eminent ones such as Śrī Rādhā, Candrāvalī, and others who protect hundreds of groups of women, each sang that very same song in the manner of her followers;
in some places, they sang to one another by modulating a single note, as follows:
Your face is the abode of sweetnesses; alas, therein the playful movements of your glances have attained an incomparable beauty.
"O beautiful one, all those arts of love [are present]. Thus [it is said].
O beloved, the moon, by bearing the guise of a deer, carries only ill-repute bestowed upon it by the rising of your face.
"Or was it that we were ridiculed by the people, or did even this foolish brahmin swallow poison? (Kṛṣṇabhakti 19.70–71).
Here, the author uses "sundarī" where one might expect "sundare," and "kānte" where one might expect "kānta."
The custom is that her beloved attendants sing [this].
Regarding the *vaijayantī*— it is strung with flowers of five colors, according to the statement, "The *vaijayantī* is of five colors"— (o)0(o)— .
Having entered the riverbank, which was like cool sand, he took delight with the cowherd girls in the breeze fragrant with the lotuses of their shimmering joy.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Vaṃśīdhara: Of the river Kālindī. "Hima" means cool; that [place] where there are such sands (vālukā/sikatā) is described thus. It refers to one whose nature it is to gladden by means of the surging waves of intoxication from that river.

*Tat taralānandī* means that wind which possesses the fragrance of water-lilies (*kumuda*) where they are; thus, it is "that wind which brings joy through the trembling [fragrance] of the lilies. Alternatively, it refers to those water-lilies which, by that river, are *tarala*—standing as if dancing—and *ānandī*—fully blossomed.

By the wind joined with the fragrance—the sweet scent—of those tremulous and joyous night-lotuses, the specific qualities of the wind’s intoxicating aroma and coolness are intimated. Now, one might ask: how did he sport upon such a vast sandbank with hundreds of millions of women?
Because everything is easily accomplished through the Lord’s illusory power (māyā), which is expert at bringing about the impossible;
and because Brahmā has seen millions of universes within a single portion of Vṛndāvana. As it has been said:
"That very form of the land of Mathurā, though limited, is nonetheless wonderful."
It may be expansive or contracted, according to the progression of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes.
Right here, even the entire series of cosmic eggs reaches its full extent;
for even in a mere representation of Vṛndāvana, that which has been experienced by the Creator himself exists.
Therefore, in that very sandy bank of the Yamunā during the Rāsa-līlā—
Even hundreds of millions of women perished for you; what is so wonderful about that?
Thus it is clearly stated in the Bhāgavatāmṛta and other works. ||45||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, having brought them to the sandy bank of the Śrī-yamunā, he says with a couplet beginning "Not today" (*nādya*) that they shall be delighted by his exceptional cleverness—*himavālukā* is camphor; [the sand] is like that.
In this context, the term "Śaka-pārthiva" (the Śaka king) and so forth refers to that very [era]. Likewise, in the previous passage, "Vana" also refers specifically to Vṛndāvana.
By the playful waves of that river, there arises a breeze filled with the fragrance of lotuses, bringing joy and pleasant recreation;
thus, even at night, there is the blooming of lotuses, just as there is the blooming of jasmine in autumn.
The languor [of the moon] is due to its being "delighted" (*ānandī*) and "enjoyed" (*juṣṭam*) by the power of the nectar of His (Kṛṣṇa’s) such pastimes.

Its fragrance and coolness are evident. According to some, there is the reading *kumuda* for *ānanda*; and in place of *juṣṭam*, the reading *remam* occurs in some places. For this very reason, a separate section has been made [for this verse]. ||45||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, having led them to the sandy bank of the Śrī Yamunā, He says with two verses beginning "Not today" (*nādya*) that they shall be delighted by the manifestation of His particular cleverness. [He says this regarding] the river Kālindī; and again, having come to the bank of the Kālindī, as it is said: [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.45].

Because it will be described later; and because the specific names of that forest and her [the river] are not mentioned there, as they are easily understood through such descriptions due to their well-known status. Alternatively, he refers to it as a "forest" (vana) with respect merely to its being uninhabited, and as a "river" (nadī) with respect merely to its excellence as a sandy bank (pulina) due to its flowing nature.

"Entering together with the gopīs" means entering with affection. "In which there are cool sands"—by this, its suitability as a bed for amorous play is shown through both its capacity to dispel fatigue and its softness. He was one who delighted in and sported happily upon the surging waves of that river.

And by that wind, which is endowed with the fragrance of lotuses; or rather, by that wind which is possessed of a delightful scent—manifested through the trembling of even those lotuses that are closed at night—that brings joy and produces pleasure. The reading "kumuda" (lilies) is favored by some.

By the connection with "waves," coolness is expressed; by the word "eṇāṅka" (marked by the deer), [the quality of] being frequented is indicated; and by the word "juṣṭam" (frequented/enjoyed), slowness and fragrance are clearly manifested. Thus, the triad of qualities is stated, which in every way expresses the suitability of the riverbank as a place for amorous delight and its power to kindle passion. ||45||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Having done what did he wander about adorning the forest?
To this he says: having come to the riverbank. With whom? With the cowherd girls (*gopīs*). Of what nature was it?

"Like sand with cold grains," where there is an elision of the middle term; "cold-grained" (*hima-bāluka*) refers to camphor, which is well-known by that name. It is also "frequented" (*juṣṭa*)—the word *api* (also) must be supplied here—"by a breeze such as that, which possesses the fragrance of the shimmering, joy-bestowing night-lotuses (*kumuda*). This is [the meaning].
The intention is as follows: first, there is indeed the play of amorous dalliance; after that, the *rāsa-lāsya* dance;

and finally, the water-sport. Thus, this pastime consists of three parts and is an extreme secret. Furthermore, it is not possible on the riverbank because it is exposed to view, and because [the gopīs] would be visible while traveling in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*). Therefore, [it must take place elsewhere].
"The very play of *rāsa* and *lāsya* is to be performed here"; having seen the riverbank, she entered the forest again.
The word "having come" (*āgatya*) indicates a prior action. ||45||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus entered the groves and adorned themselves with garlands, they describe what He did while sporting on the banks of the Yamunā: "In the river...
Because the throngs of women in the midst of the forest were infinite, He sported with some restriction; then, [He went] to the bank of the Kālindī.

Beholding it to be spacious, he entered the sandy bank of the river Kālindī to sport with the gopīs without constraint and took his delight there. Of what nature was it? It was "possessing cool sand" (*himavāluka*), meaning its sands were cooled by contact with cold water; this indicates that due to its softness, it served as a cause of pleasure by the mere touch of it.
Such is the sense. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that in which there is joy from the restless waves of that Kālindī;

the sense is that the power of the moving waves to awaken latent emotions is indicated. Again, of what nature is it? It is characterized by the night, during which the fragrance of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*) that have blossomed prevails.

"Where there is fragrance, by that [fragrance] the wind [is characterized]"—by this, the threefold nature of the wind is stated, as well as its removal of fatigue. In the reading *juṣṭam*, the connection is with the subsequent verse, "he caused [her] to take delight. Through the connection with the rippling river, the coolness of the wind is expressed.

The sense is that because of its proximity to the forest, coolness is mentioned, and because of its connection with water lilies (*kumuda*), fragrance is mentioned; thus, it is indicated that even more than the forest, the riverbank (*pulina*) is a locus for aesthetic charm (*vilāsa*) and an excitant of emotion (*bhāvoddīpaka*).
Viśvanātha [comments]: "It is delightful by means of the tremulous waves of that river" refers to both coolness and gentleness.

And he took delight in that breeze which brought the fragrance of lotuses blooming even at night, for it was a giver of joy. In the reading *juṣṭam*, the connection is with the subsequent verb *ramayāñcakāra* ("he caused to take delight").
In some versions, the readings *kumudāmoda* and *taralānanda* are found instead. ||45||

Through the stretching out of arms for an embrace, the grasping of her thighs, the loosening of the knot of her lower garment, the touching of her breasts, playful jests, and the striking of fingernail-tips;
By means of his playful glances and smiles, he delighted the beautiful women of Vraja, awakening the god of love within them.

Śrīdhara: By stretching out his arms, by embracing, by touching and stroking their hands and other limbs, by jesting and joking, by the scratching of fingernails, and by playful sport, as well as by glances and smiles, he greatly inflamed their passion and delighted them. (46)

Vaṃśīdhara: "Embrace" means a hug. The "touching of the hands and so forth" should be understood as characterized by the release [of tension] prescribed in the Kāmaśāstra. Alternatively, it may be through playful glances and laughter, such as the imitation of a lion's roar, gazing, and gentle smiles. As it has been said in the Māgha-kāvya:
The latent desire within young women was awakened by the scratches of nails and teeth inflicted during the pressure of their arms and the grasping of their breasts.
Māra also slowly opened his eyes. (Śiśupālavadha 10.72) ||46||

* Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Either it refers to the aforementioned demonstration of the Lord of Yoga, who, by the swiftness of His embrace, assumes manifold forms while uplifting and increasing Himself as the Lord of Love for the beauties of Vraja;
or else, it means manifesting Kāma, the Lord of Love, for the beauties of Vraja; or again—
Rati, out of love, caused her husband to take delight in himself. ||46||

The *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* states: "By stretching out his arms and other gestures, he elevates that supreme love—which is called 'Great Devotion' (*mahābhāva*)—the husband of *rati*, characterized by affection appropriate for a lover, even though it is being concealed by natural modesty and the like; thus, there is his attachment to *rati*."
And supreme cleverness has been displayed there; therein, "stretching out the arms" means the commencement of an embrace—or rather, by the stretching out of the arms, an embrace, meaning a firm hug.
"Playfulness" consists of forms such as teasing and so forth directed toward the beauties of Vraja; thus, the beauty appropriate for that is present here.
This is what is intended to be expressed. And by that, according to the maxim "where there is form, there qualities reside," such cleverness is also implied;
furthermore, their mutual delight should be understood as unobserved, due to the specific power of their own enchanting nature. ||46||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "By stretching out his arms and so forth, he causes [it] to stand up" means that even though it is being covered by natural modesty and the like, he makes it manifest;
or rather, that which exists already as the play of a particular form of love, he now causes to increase specifically.

The meaning is as follows. For this very reason, it is stated through *śleṣa* (pun): "the husband, that is, the protector, of Rati," whose sole characteristic is love (*prema*). Likewise, by the term "Lord of Rati" (*ratipati*), it is intended that even for Kāma, whose body had been consumed, completeness was achieved only through rebirth for the sake of the pleasure of Rati; thus, his attachment to Rati and his supreme skill (*vaidagdhī*) are indicated.

It has been shown. In that context, the stretching out of the arms is for the purpose of drawing near those who are at a distance, or it is an imitation of a previous embrace. Alternatively, the meaning is that through the stretching out of their very arms, there is an embrace, that is, a firm hug. The *kṣvelīs* consist of forms such as playful nudging and so forth.

Or [it consists of] forms such as drinking from the lower lip and biting. By the phrase "of the beauties of Vraja," it is indicated that they too possess such very same cleverness; otherwise, there would be no accomplishment in manifesting such cleverness on his part.
And in the act of amorous play, it should be understood that by means of their own particular powers, they [act] simultaneously and unobserved by one another. (46)
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.
Regarding the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: now he describes the first pastime, beginning with "By the stretching out of the arms" (*bāhu-prasāra*), etc.
By means of the embrace resulting from the stretching out of the two arms, [there was contact] of the hands, of the curls of hair, of the thighs, and of the waist-knot.
By touching and stroking their breasts, with playful scratching of his fingernails, with jesting, sport, glances, and laughter, he aroused,
increased, and delighted the Lord of Rati within the beautiful women of Vraja; yet in reality, it was their own natural love that was the cause, and not his.

The meaning is that desire (*kāma*); in its absence, that divine play (*līlā*) would not be flavorful (*surasā*). Therefore, [the Lord] himself increased their desire, even though it was non-existent [prior to that]. And that desire is not worldly (*prākṛta*), but rather that very portion of the Blessed One by which he becomes an incarnation of desire; it is that very same portion [of the Lord] within their minds.

He was possessed [by him]. Or rather, *rati* (pleasure) is the permanent emotion (*sthāyī bhāva*); its "husband" is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). Alternatively, since this is my time for service, he is appropriately the God of Love (*kāmadeva*). "Ut" means with excellence; "paralyzing" means excluding the mere literal meaning of the verbal root. With you as his companion...
"Let it not be thought that this 'play' (līlā) is delightful by itself; rather, its victory [over ordinary play] must be understood as being due to you.

Thus, when the awakening of emotion has occurred through the sight of the sandbank, he speaks to describe the sequence of amorous pastimes performed with them, beginning with "the stretching out of the arms. The stretching out of the arms follows.
Embracing is *parirambha*, which is *āliṅgana*; following that, there is the touching of the hair, the thighs, the waist-knot, and the breasts by Śrī Kṛṣṇa with both hands;

"jesting" (*narman*) consists of the touching—meaning the contact—with the tips of his fingernails of those [parts] located in the abode of desire, namely the hair, thighs, waist-knot, and breasts, as well as the striking with the tips of his fingernails.

By these. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*: "They know that speech in which jesting is predominant as *narma* (amusement)" (*Rasārṇava* 3.45). By those laughs which occur during glances, whether through play in the form of playful taunts and the like, or through play in the form of drinking from the lower lip, biting, and so forth.
Or rather, by stimulating the Lord of Rati with glances and smiles—the meaning is this:
such is the procedure for ordinary desire that it does not increase beyond the discharge of the vital fluids;
but this is a supermundane desire which attains ever-increasing growth even without the discharge of the fluids.
The meaning is that it does not come to rest. ||46||

Viśvanātha: The extension of the arms refers to the stretching out and embracing of their own arms as they have become one with his chest, as well as the touching and grasping of hands and other limbs;
and through jesting and laughter, the striking with the tips of the fingernails, and playful glances.
By means of his smiles, he heightened and inflamed Kāma—the Lord of Rati—who consists of love for them as well as for himself;
with that very same number of self-luminous forms, he delighted each one individually.
For indeed, on that sandbank, despite the great throng of gopīs, there was no lack of privacy due to its openness.

And because of the absence of pleasure-chambers, couches, and so forth, does it not follow that amorous play with each of those hundreds of millions of women individually is impossible? True; however, because the land of Vṛndāvana—like the form of the Blessed Lord—is all-pervading, even a space the size of a sesame seed possesses extreme vastness.
The state of possessing various groves with enclosures, as well as the possession of flower-couches for diverse amorous pastimes accompanied by perfumes, garlands, betel, and the like,
was manifested solely through the power of *yogamāyā*, which is expert at accomplishing the impossible; and at the conclusion of the divine play (*līlā*), it was once again concealed.
And thus, this is indeed a well-joined [treatment]. ||46||
Thus, having received such honors from the high-souled Lord Kṛṣṇa,
those proud women considered themselves preeminent among all women on earth.
Śrīdhara: [It refers to] the Great-Souled One, whose mind is liberated. ||47||
Vaṃśīdhara: Thus, by stretching out his arms and so forth; "those whose minds are liberated" means those who are unattached.

"Of women"—that is, those who are exceedingly beautiful among the beauties within the world of mortals—there are those who are proud, thinking, "We are the most beautiful," and who are thus inflated with pride regarding their beauty and other qualities. (47)
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
Now, erotic union (*sambhoga*) does not attain fullness without the element of separation (*vipralambha*).
"For when cloth and such are treated with astringent dye, the color increases greatly" (Uṇādivṛtti 15.3);

according to this maxim of Bharata, because of the intensification of a particular kind of love, he begins to describe a specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) in order to depict a particular excellence of play ahead: "In this way," [referring to] the Great-Souled One.

The cause for that [attainment] is "from the Supreme," meaning from the Blessed Lord Himself, the Blessed One; likewise, it is "from Kṛṣṇa," meaning from Him who is thus renowned. Thus, the honor—that is, the recognition and good fortune—obtained in the manner previously described through being under the sway of that love.

Having become such [as he was], those proud women who had attained his love— whether they were women on earth or elsewhere— each considered themselves alone to be superior among them all; thus, toward him, those women became proud, their minds filled with mutual rivalry.
The meaning: Regarding that, the definition of *māna* (pride/resentment) is as follows:
"When a couple are both present in one place and mutually attached, yet their desired embrace, gazing, and so forth are obstructed, that is called *māna*. [Uṇī. 15.74]
"The course of love is as naturally crooked as that of a snake; for this reason, the pride of young lovers arises both with cause and without cause. [Uṇī.
15.102] Furthermore, according to the *Rasa-śāstra*, while there is pride among those elsewhere due to the lack of such a hero, among those here—
Even upon attaining such gains, there is a lack of appreciation for obtaining good fortune equal to one's own; as it has been said:

"Pride (garva) is defined as the slighting of others due to being the supreme repository of good fortune, beauty, youth, and virtues, and through the attainment of desired objects and the like" (Bharata-śāstra 2.4.41).
"Those states which are transferred are considered transitory;
they emerge and submerge like waves in the stable ocean.
Thus, according to the system of Rasa, even pride (*garva*) is a transitory emotion belonging to that specific type of permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) which is love for Him.
Because it is a transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*), it should be understood as being identical with that [rasa]; for such indeed is the nature and the excellence of this rasa. ||47||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, due to the intensification of a particular kind of love, [the author] begins to describe a specific form of *vipralambha* (separation) for the sake of a particular pastime, starting with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
In the manner described above, which reveals a specific kind of cleverness, [the Lord] was obtained even from the Great Soul who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*).

Those [qualities] by which there is pride (*māna*) or honor (*sammāna*), which are specific states characterized by the elevation of the mind; therein the cause is "the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ*). The meaning is: for the sake of experiencing a particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), because of the manifestation of His own divine nature (*bhagavattā*). Therefore, [He is] from Kṛṣṇa, who is an ocean of diverse great flavors and who supremely attracts the heart.

Or rather, being proud, they considered themselves superior—the most excellent—among the women existing on earth. Or else, "on earth" refers to the playground (*vihāra-bhūmi*), which is intended as common to all; nevertheless, it means among those very women, the gopīs.

Each one considered herself superior because she was thus delighted by him; therefore, they became proud—or rather, this is a separate sentence. This is because intoxication (*mada*) and pride (*māna*) will be described later.
In reality, however, for the sake of pleasing their most excellent and discerning beloved, those women who were themselves supremely discerning [acted in such a way].
That which consists of the nature of aesthetic flavor (rasa) takes the form of service and playfulness; that is to be inferred. ||47||

The sequence of events: Because of His supreme excellence among all the divine and super-divine Great Souls, the proud women on earth and elsewhere considered themselves even superior; thus, among women, He became one who cherished their affection with pride.

The meaning is that they have maintained pride; the sense is that this is because those from elsewhere have not obtained such a beloved, and those residing there do not recognize their own attainment of such good fortune. 47.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: This pastime, however, is an extreme secret and cannot be described;
nevertheless, Śukadeva concluded by mentioning it briefly with the word "evam" (thus). By "evam," he means "by such a manifold pastime," since it is beyond the scope of speech.

The meaning of the word "dūragamyayā" (by her who is to be reached from afar) is as follows: they had received honor—that is, they had received worship—from the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa. Because he bestows great respect upon those of noble soul and great aspiration, the women—being themselves worthy of honor—considered that which was given by him to be exceedingly significant; thus they thought, "We have achieved our purpose."
They thought. ||47||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having first produced a state of separation (*vipralambha*) merely by going to the forest, and then having nourished it with the sweetness of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), they have now become women who have their husbands under their own control; considering themselves superior due to their own cleverness, they are slow toward their lover.

Having seen [the general state], in order to increase the aesthetic flavor (rasa), Śuka restates the meaning of the context with the words "Thus" (*evam*), indicating that she should subsequently attain a specific aesthetic flavor through the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*). "Thus" means by means of the aforementioned forms of honor, such as the stretching out of arms and so forth, from Kṛṣṇa, who is the very essence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
From what kind of Blessed One? From Him who, having concealed His sixfold opulence (*ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya*), shines with the sovereignty of rasa;

and from such a Great Soul, Kṛṣṇa, whose heart is noble in bestowing the sweet nectar upon all beautiful women—those who have obtained honor, good fortune, and prosperity from Him, and thus have become proud (*māninī*) on this earth.
Among all women— or rather, among their own peers,

the beauties of Vraja on this earth— they each considered themselves superior, thinking, "I alone am the most beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and no other," for they were honored by Him in that very way; thus they were proud and full of self-conceit.
Thus it was said in the *Rasārṇava*:
"Even when a husband and wife are together in one place, though their feelings are unspoken,
that which obstructs the embrace, gazing, and so forth desired by oneself is called *māna* (pride/resentment)."
The course of love is naturally crooked, like that of a snake; for this reason, pride arises in young people both with cause and without cause,
based on their excellence in fortune, beauty, youth, and virtues.
And pride is said to be the disparagement of others due to the acquisition of desired objects and the like.
For pride, too, is included among the transitory mental states (*sañcāribhāva*).
Those which cause a state to move about are considered "transitory" (*sañcārin*) here;
they emerge and submerge within the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), like waves in the ocean.
"Without separation, enjoyment does not attain fullness;
for when cloth and such are dyed with saffron, the disease indeed increases greatly. (47)
Viśvanātha:
Now, erotic union (*sambhoga*) does not attain fullness without separation (*vipralambha*).
For when cloth and such are dyed, the color increases all the more. [Uṇī. 15.3]
Thus, according to the maxim of Bharata, for the sake of nourishing the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), that which was manifested by the power of divine play (*līlā-śakti*) alone—

the pretext of separation (*vipralambha*)— is described with the words "in this way. It refers to the Great Soul (*mahātman*), the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), who is superior even to the hosts of divine and super-divine heroes (*nāyaka*), and specifically to Kṛṣṇa.

Having received honor from Him personally and attained His respect, they considered themselves each individually superior among all women dwelling on the earth by virtue of attaining the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa; being proud,
they were called *māninīs* because of their pride (*māna*) that "I alone am most fortunate."
Those possessed of pride. ||47||
Seeing their intoxication with good fortune and their pride, Keśava vanished right there for the sake of their pacification and grace.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, by means of his good fortune, he subdues intoxication, lack of self-control, pride, and arrogance. He is Keśava because he brings both "Ka" (the body) and "Īśa" (the Lord) under his control. ||48||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the first half of the tenth book of the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the commentary titled Bhāvārtha-dīpikā. ||29||

Vaṃśīdhara: Regarding those beautiful cowherd girls (*gopa-sundarī*): by the name "Keśava," it is implied—through suggestion (*dhvani*)—that who could possibly bring under control one who controls even Brahmā and Śiva, the lords of all? Since we are equal to Śrī Rādhā, and because He regards us as being exactly like Her, therefore, of them...
Seeing the intoxication of good fortune and the pride of Rādhā due to their shared dwelling,

He vanished right there on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā among that assembly of beautiful women of Vraja, in order to pacify that pride and to bestow His grace upon Śrī Rādhā. The meaning is that He became invisible to their sight.
Even disappearance is for the sake of the perfection of enjoyment (*sambhoga*). As it has been said:
"Without separation (*vipralambha*), enjoyment does not attain fullness; oh, how crooked indeed is the nature of the King's love! Thus, the nature of love must be crooked.

Regarding the phrase "He vanished" (*antaradhīyata*), the singular number used here in the subsequent chapter is not to be considered contradictory to the statement "Whose feet are these that have been traversed by the son of Nanda? since it was stated [by the Lord] that this was for the sake of her grace (*prasāda*).
Furthermore, grace is appropriate only when directed toward one person exclusively; therefore, it should be understood that his disappearance occurred together with her alone.

Alternatively, there is oneness by virtue of the intention to express the unity of the two—oneness by virtue of the intention to express the unity of the two—as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Rādhā is eternally of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa is certainly of the nature of Rādhā. And as stated in the *Saṃmohana-tantra*: "From that, light arose in two forms, in the shape of Rādhā and Mādhava. (48)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: “For the sake of tranquility,” and so forth.

This means for the sake of the tranquility and clarity (*prasāda*) of the intoxication of good fortune (*saubhaga-mada*). For when there is the intoxication of good fortune, the mind becomes agitated (*uttālatā*), because in that state, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) takes on a liquid form. Indeed, in such agitation, there is a lack of reality; therefore, [it is said] not [for that].

According to the principle that "enjoyment (*sambhoga*) attains fullness without separation (*vipralambha*)," and so forth, he vanished right there in order to bring about the fullness of enjoyment; he did not go to another place.
The meaning is that he remained right there, merely having become invisible. Alternatively, it means for the sake of grace (*prasāda*), [he manifested] grace.
Clarity of mind increases longing for the destruction of pride and for mutual friendship.
He qualifies him [the Buddha] as follows: "to him from whom tranquility—that is, cessation—has departed. (48)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having specifically observed—that is, having clearly seen—that pride (*māna*) of theirs, which consists of that intoxication (*mada*) caused by good fortune; for Viśva states: "The word *mada* refers to semen, musk, pride, and joy; these two [the latter] are distinct. And having observed that pride therein...

The meaning is: having considered [the situation] as something that cannot be accomplished by other means in the case of pride (*garva*), and having seen it as something that cannot be accomplished even by conciliation and the like in the case of arrogance (*māna*); for the sake of pacifying pride and for the sake of propitiating—that is, winning over—arrogance, he vanished right there. [The root] *dhī* signifies "disregard."
The meaning is that he was seen departing for the divine realm and so forth, but not going elsewhere;

here, according to what will be explained later, his disappearance should be understood as occurring together with Śrī Rādhā alone, and that was accomplished by Yoga-māyā herself once His desire had arisen. Although...

In some cases, the indifference (*upekṣā*) of the Leader is required for the pacification of envy and pride that have a cause; for even that which is born of a cause attains tranquility through appropriately applied means, such as conciliation, sowing dissension, force, bribery, prostration, indifference, and other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*). This is stated in the *Uṇī* (15.112): "Even that which is born of a cause attains tranquility through appropriately applied means, such as conciliation, sowing dissension, force, bribery, prostration, indifference, and other aesthetic sentiments."
However, regarding one who is free from cause and devoid of pride, even if there is no remedy or only a slight remedy,

I should nevertheless remain equanimous for the sake of pacifying that [state], because it would otherwise lead to a deepening of suffering through mutual arrogance; therefore, it is solely for the sake of pacifying the state of both that [equanimity is maintained] toward those two, which are the maturation of love.

Moreover, both of them possess a desire for tranquility, a desire for playful sport born of their own will, and simultaneously, a desire for passion consisting of the bestowal of the Great Rasa (mahā-rasa) toward each other; thus, this separation (vipralambha) shall serve solely for the sake of supreme love. And it will be said: "But I am not [a friend]," O friends [Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
[10.32.20] And so forth. Regarding the disappearance, the fundamental cause is simply her longing for the sport together with him alone.
Here, the word "Keśava" [is used].
"Those rays which shine forth are designated as my hair;

therefore, O best of sages, they call me Keśava because I am all-knowing"—from this statement in the *Bhārata*, the meaning is that he is supremely radiant. And consequently, upon his disappearance...
Even though all forms of beauty were present there, a sudden absence of beauty was manifested. ||48||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By that abundance of her own cleverness; or rather, by that good fortune (*saubhaga*)—that is, auspiciousness—which arises from the manner of dalliance [expressed] by what was said, namely, "I alone am to be delighted by him"; or else, having observed his intoxication caused by that good fortune even though it was for the sake of her own pleasure, [she acted] for the purpose of quelling it.

Otherwise, due to the absence of self-dependence, the success of the desired pastimes of *rāsa* would not be achieved. Furthermore, it should be discerned that upon seeing her pride, He—through the play of assuming the form of pride for the sake of reconciliation and out of affection—manifests a special grace; this occurs because, without His vanishing, there is no attainment of that specific excellence of love worthy of the *rāsa*. Or else, regarding intoxication and pride:
For the sake of tranquility. For what purpose is this tranquility? To that he says: "for the sake of grace," meaning for the sake of a special favor through the *rāsa* dance;
or else, by way of disappearance, as in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.22]: "I am not able... and so forth.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the communication of the excellence of one's own [beauty] and its dependence on that [other], which will be described later. Alternatively, from that [beauty] comes *saubhaga* (good fortune), and by means of that, *mada* (intoxication), meaning either pride or joy. And thus says the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *mada* refers to semen, musk, pride, joy, and the rut-fluid of an elephant. That form of *māna* (pride) is a particular kind of mental exultation (*mānasollāsa*).
Having observed [this], [the Lord acts] for that very reason: for the sake of *prakṛṣṭa-śama-sukha*, which is the bliss consisting of the *rāsa*-pastime;

and for the sake of *prasāda* (grace), in order to manifest His favor—such as not abandoning Him even during invisibility (*antardhāna*) and the special nature of His devotion. And this will be explained further on.
It is evident that this will come to pass; or rather, it is for the sake of *prasāda*—that clarity which leads to tranquility and supreme bliss.
The rest is the same.
Thus, in every respect, the disappearance was solely for the purpose of a particular kind of endearment, and not otherwise.

It should be understood that this is due either to her delighting in the Self (*ātmārāmatva*) or to envy (*asūyā*), because she was not accessible to even the most skillful suitors. For this very reason, he himself will state later: "While I was worshipping Her in Her absence, She became concealed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.21), and so forth. The phrase "in that very place" indicates that she did not go anywhere else in person.
And because he has suddenly vanished from sight; and with the intention that this [disappearance] would otherwise be impossible for him, he states his status as the Supreme Lord: "Keśava. (48)

The sequence of composition: for the sake of pacifying the intoxication of fortune—that is, the pride born of good luck—and for the appeasement of her resentment. It says "for the sake of pacification" (praśamāya) and not "for the sake of indifference" (upekṣā), because according to the treatises on aesthetics (rasa-śāstra), it is improper to employ other aesthetic sentiments (rasas) [such as indifference] in this context. Here, although indifference would be inappropriate due to the nature of the lover's resentment (praṇaya-māna), [the poet avoids it].
Because it is most venerable due to its being a literary work composed by him. ||48||
The Composition of Affection (386): Now, love-in-wrath (*praṇaya-māna*) is without cause.
Its "causelessness" is understood as being due to the absence of any external cause, since it manifests solely through the play of affection. This occurs for the hero as well.

In the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of devotion to the Blessed One, this [love-in-wrath] may also serve as an excitant (*uddīpana*); therefore, it should be cited here by way of incidental discussion.

Just as Keśava, having observed their intoxication with their own good fortune (*saubhaga-mada*) and their pride (*māna*), considers this section beginning with [the verse] "ity ādi" through an alternative interpretation: therein, *māna* refers to the pride of affection (*praṇaya-māna*). Its cause is the intoxication with their own good fortune. Therefore, for the sake of pacifying that pride and for their propitiation, he himself also—
He vanished right there out of affectionate modesty. ||48||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, play with those who are full of pride does not become truly delightful. For the inclination of the mind is what nourishes aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And so it is said: "Sensual enjoyment (*sambhoga*) is not fully nourished without separation (*vipralambha*). Thus, He performed the pastime of vanishing right there.

He said: "Of them," and so forth. Having observed their such-like intoxication of fortune (*saubhaga-mada*) and such-like pride (*māna*), which is an elevation of the mind, for the sake of their pacification—that is, for the cessation of those two—he vanished right there, remaining in that very place; he disappeared. The passive suffix (*karma-pratyaya*) is used with an active sense (*kartari*), as in the case of the "agent-as-object" (*karma-kartṛ*).

In the same way, the agent and the object should be understood. As it is said: "Those whose minds do not undergo transformation even when a cause for transformation exists—they alone are the wise," and so forth. The meaning is that he remained right there, invisible to them. For what kind of tranquilization? For the sake of serenity—that is, for serenity as its very form. Of those two...
Tranquility itself is clarity. ||48||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: In order to cause an increase in aesthetic relish (*rasa*) by means of subduing their pride, [the commentator] describes the manner of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s disappearance, which was His intention: "Of those... and so forth.
He refers to that intoxication with good fortune belonging to those women who had been honored by the stretching out of His arms and other such acts.

Having observed the pride caused by good fortune— and according to the *Viśvakośa*, "mada" refers to semen, musk, pride, and the rut-fluid of an elephant— and having observed her self-importance and independence, [the Lord acted] for the sake of pacifying that pride and arrogance; yet, because the playful amorous sport (*rāsa-vilāsa*) had not arisen within her being (*sattva*), even though she was honored, there was no increase in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Thus it was born. Therefore, when intoxication and pride had ceased, in order to grant a special favor by manifesting His particular grace, charm, and skill, He vanished right there within that very circle of gopīs; having become invisible to them, He did not go elsewhere.

Remaining right there, out of the range of their vision, he intended to hear their loving conversations and bring about the heightening of aesthetic relish (*rasa*). This indeed is a transformation of love: that even though the dearest one stands before them, he is not seen.

Or rather, for the sake of tranquility and happiness, to grant immediate bliss; for the sake of clarity, to produce a special state of affection. Or else, for the sake of tranquility—that is, for the cessation of the distress born from not attaining one's desires—and because pride and arrogance are incompatible with that [tranquility], it is for the sake of their clarity as a result of that, for the pleasure of the lover.

The fruit of that is their favor. And he will state this later: "I am not able [to restrain those who are joined with faultlessness]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.22). If it is asked, "How can the intoxication and pride of many groups be overcome by one? he says in response:

Keśava: He who brings under his control (vaśayati) both Ka and Īśa—these two being "keśau"—is Keśava. By this, his possession of all powers is expressed. Alternatively, he is Keśava because he possesses excellent hair (praśastāḥ keśā yasya). Or else, he is Keśava as the ultimate limit (avadhi-bhūta) of Ka—that is, of happiness—which increases hundredfold at each successive stage, and of Īśa, the controller.
The meaning is "the bliss of one's own nature" (*svarūpa-sukha*).

Now, [the root] *vā* has the sense of "blowing," "going," or "attaining. The verbal root is *vā*, meaning "motion" or "fragrance. However, for the sake of ceasing intoxication and pride, even one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*) [dwells] in a grove (*upavana*) because of his delight in the Self.
"He took delight" has already had its meaning explained; however, by virtue of "delighting in the Self," that [delight] was previously set aside. Thus it was said:
"Pride and intoxication.
Even that which is born of causes subsides into tranquility through the appropriate means as they have been revealed.
"By means of conciliation, sowing dissension, force, bribery, dissimulation, and indifference, as well as other sentiments," [Uṇī. 15.112]. ||48||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, because the Lord dallied with all of them equally, she who was the most preeminent among them—the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu—became proud, her eyes clouded by a sudden surge of jealousy. Consequently, the others, being inferior to her, became filled with pride regarding their own good fortune.
Since there was a doubt regarding this wonder, he states what the Blessed One himself established therein, beginning with "tāsām" (of them).
By the grammatical rule of *eka-śeṣa* (retaining one of two similar terms), the meaning is: "of those beautiful women of Vraja and of that daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.
Having observed, respectively, that [excessive] pride born of her own good fortune and their [own] pride, he—being both he and that... [text continues].

Or there is a compound: *saubhaga-madaś ca tam* ("the intoxication of good fortune and him"). Or the reading is *taṃ saubhaga-madam* ("that intoxication of good fortune"). "For the sake of pacification" means for the purpose of pacifying their intoxication of good fortune, and for the purpose of propitiating that proud woman. *Keśava*: he who (*ka*) is Brahmā and *īśa* (Śiva), and who moreover (*api*) weaves (*vayati*) or governs them both.

The sense is: what effort could there be for him in quelling her intoxication with her own beauty? The sense is that he, the crest-jewel of connoisseurs, certainly possesses the skill to please her by arranging her hair and performing other such acts of grooming. *Antaradhīyata* is an archaic (Vedic) form; it means *antaradadhāt*.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, *dhīn* is a form derived from the root *dhīñ* (meaning "to disregard") belonging to the *daivādika* class.
Here, based on the subsequent text, it should be understood that he took Śrī Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter by force.
The meaning is that he was seen by them only there, and not while going elsewhere. And that [was] his...
When that desire arose, it was accomplished by Yogamāyā herself. ||48||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth [chapter], which is well-connected for the virtuous, within the tenth book of the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the *Pāramahaṃsya-saṃhitā* within the *Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya* of the illustrious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa composed by Vyāsa.
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Rāsa-dance," in the Tenth Book;
now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Regarding the search for Kṛṣṇa during the rāsa-dance,
Śrī Śuka said:
When the Lord had suddenly disappeared, the women of Vraja...
Not seeing him, they suffered like female elephants separated from their herd-leader.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirtieth [chapter], Kṛṣṇa is sought by the gopīs, who, tormented by separation,
wander incessantly through forest after forest like those intoxicated.
Not speaking, not seeing. ||1||

Vaṃśīdhara: "The search" (mārgaṇa) means the seeking of Kṛṣṇa. And that [search] was not necessarily conducted properly. Why? Because they became like those who are mad, as if driven mad by the agitation of separation. This is to demonstrate the intensity of the gopīs' devotion, making known that the natural possession of divine power (yogaiśvarya) belongs to Hari alone and to no one else.

He said: "Śrī Śuka" refers to that Śrī Kṛṣṇa. "Kariṇyaḥ" means female elephants; according to the Amarakośa, "kareṇu," "ibhyā," and "nebhā" denote a female elephant. "Yūthapam" means the lord of the herd, the king of elephants. ||1||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By describing his disappearance, there arises for Śrī Bādarāyaṇa a weight of distress; thus, due to the interruption of the narrative, there is an apparent flaw in the middle of the chapter. [This refers to] Śuka accompanied by Śrī.

He spoke thus, crying out with indistinct and sweet words due to the arising of grief from the disappearance of the Blessed Lord; this should be understood similarly in what follows. Having become composed in a moment, as if lamenting, he said:
"Within," [referring to] "having suddenly disappeared within. This refers to the act of vanishing.
"Because [the cause] was not considered beforehand. Regarding "unexpectedly," Amara states: *atarkite tu sahasā*. This should be inferred as the reason for the intensity of the heat.

By the phrase "the women of Vraja," the propriety and intensity of their fever of separation are intended, given that He is their sole beloved. [The text mentions] the leader of the herd, the lord of rutting elephants.

The simile is based on the fact that, according to such statements as "like female elephants" and "for the elephant is indeed skilled in sexual union," they have him as their sole object of focus; thus, due to the severance of that [union], there is an excess of torment. ||1||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By describing their disappearance, even Śrī Bādarāyaṇa experienced an onset of intense grief; thus, due to the interruption of the narrative, there was a break in the middle of the chapter. Even though such sorrow had arisen, the Blessed Lord took one among them who was supreme in every respect.

Having vanished, and having reflected for a moment upon her good fortune while maintaining his composure, he says: "Antar" (within). [The phrase] "vanished all of a sudden" (*sahasāivāntarhite*) is used because the manner of his disappearance cannot be discerned.
Regarding this, Amara states: "But when something is unaccounted for, it is 'all of a sudden' (*sahasā*). This should be understood as the cause for the intensification of his distress.

By the phrase "the women of Vraja," it is intended that because they have him as their sole beloved, the heat of their separation is both appropriate and excessive. Or, by the comparison "like female elephants [separated] from the leader of the herd, the lordly rutting elephant," there is an illustration of how their suffering becomes intensified due to the severance from him, since he is their sole object of support. ||1||

The sequence of the composition, the extensive sequence of the composition: immediately following that, he describes what occurred with the words "When [the sun] had disappeared," and so forth. Not seeing, meaning not perceiving, they suddenly felt distress; they experienced great anguish. ||1||

The Composition of Affection (389): Now, separation (*pravāsa*). This [separation] is of various kinds, as is the subsequent union with her; these should be illustrated with reference to the illustrious Queen of Vraja and the Revā.
For the sake of understanding their connection, the definition of separation is given therein:
When two youths who were previously acquainted become separated by distance and other such factors,
that which is described by the wise is called "sojourning abroad" (pravāsa).
The meaning is: "This deception produced by that [separation] is called 'sojourn abroad' (pravāsa)" [Uṇī.
15.152-153]. In this regard—
"Anxiety, insomnia, agitation, emaciation, soiled limbs, delirium, disease, madness, delusion, and death—these are the ten stages [of love].
And this [love] consists of going a little distance and going a very great distance; among these, even the former...

It is of two kinds: that occurring within a single pastime (*līlā*) and that occurring during the interval between successive pastimes. The former is as follows—as in the verse beginning "When He had disappeared" (*antarhite*). Likewise, it is explicit in the passage: "Then Kṛṣṇa also disappeared" (*tataś cāntardadhe kṛṣṇa*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.39). ||1||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Although Śrī Śuka was himself deeply tormented by the grief of the gopīs who were distressed by the disappearance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, nevertheless, knowing that Śrī Kṛṣṇa remained within their circle protecting their very lives, he composed his mind and described the pastimes arising after that meditation.

To explain this, he said: When [the Lord], without saying anything at all, suddenly and unexpectedly vanished in order to achieve self-mastery through equanimity (*upekṣā*), and when He had thus become invisible and passed beyond the range of their vision— then, for the sake of perfecting His playful grace (*vilāsa*), [He acted] in that manner toward the Blessed One who is full of the sovereignty of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).

By the phrase "the women of Vraja" (*vrajāṅganāḥ*) having acted [thus], it is indicated that their heat of separation is extreme because they have Him as their sole life-force. Of what sort were they? Not seeing—that is, not perceiving—the one who honors them and who is their very soul, they [suffer] due to His absence, since He is their sole support.

The illustration through the intensity of their heat is as follows: just as female elephants, not seeing the leader of the herd, the intoxicated lord of elephants, become distressed, so too did they suffer. This is the intended meaning: only the elephant knows true pleasure (*rati*), for it is bound by mere touch; yet the female elephants also know the pleasure of touch. Therefore...
Thus, when they do not see one another, there is an intensification of their longing. For these gopīs, this longing—which is essentially of the nature of love—is eternally established;

through the sight, embrace, and conversation with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it becomes the very form of bliss. Yet, in the state of separation (vipralambha), that same longing is perceived as suffering, and not otherwise.
Because the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) possesses a twofold nature. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the thirtieth [chapter], however, the women of the mountain, maddened by separation, questioned Kṛṣṇa;
having enjoyed his pastimes with them, he abandoned them.
Not speaking, not seeing. ||1||
By means of her gait, affectionate smiles, and playful glances;
by her charming conversation and graceful movements in play;
Their minds captivated by the Lord of Ramā, the women adopted various gestures that were entirely focused upon Him.

Śrīdhara: By His gait, by His affectionate smiles, by His graceful glances—those gazes full of charm—and by the delightful conversations, pastimes, sports, amorous gestures, and other such playful charms; by all these, beginning with the gait, of the Lord of Ramā, [the hearts of the gopīs] were captivated.
Those whose minds were drawn [to him], and therefore whose very selves were centered in him alone, took up his various gestures and played by imitating them. (2)

Vaṃśīdhara: By his gait, which is like the playful movement of a young lion; by his affectionate smiles, which are gentle laughs of love. Regarding *vibhrama*, Hema states: "The word *vibhrama* denotes service or uncertainty. Hari Dīkṣita states: "Vibhrama is considered to be the instability of mental states arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)."

She by whom one delights is Ramā; [the Lord] of her, Rādhā, who has Rādhā as His companion. The repetition "tās tāḥ" (those, those) is due to agitation; the meaning is "whatever pastimes were performed previously, those very ones.
This is because the word *tat* refers back to what precedes it. By imitating that—

An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is that which, having first perceived something, is subsequently produced with a form identical to it by means of the same place and so forth; the meaning is: "it is not like that. ||2||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "By their movements," and so forth; "they assumed various gestures," and so forth.

This will be shown later; otherwise, [the verse] beginning with "Singing loudly together of him alone" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.4) would not be consistent. Alternatively, some who were truly absorbed in Him acted in this way.
The meaning is that some, reflecting, wandered from forest to forest. ||2||

The *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* clarifies this very distress through two additional chapters beginning with the verse starting "gatyā" (by her gait, etc.). Here, "gati" refers to a general movement; "anurāga" is the emotion directed toward her own object, a state befitting a beloved;
and there are smiles and amorous glances. In this context, "vibhrama" refers to...
The various sweet gestures of those who have arched their eyebrows constitute *vihāra*, which is a gesture of love (*śṛṅgāra*).

*Vibhrama* is a superior state, a specific manifestation of the emotion of love (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*). As it has been said: "The instability of the mental fluctuations arising from love is considered *vibhrama*. Thus, when there is an instability of the mental fluctuations due to passion for that [beloved], it is mental.
The physical [expressions] consist of movement, smiles, playful glances, and gestures; the vocal is to be understood as speech.

Other states should also be understood as being indicated by these [examples]. Furthermore, movement is mentioned separately because it is general, whereas smiles and the like arise merely from the commencement of passion.
This is a collective expression. Since both conversation and pastimes arise precisely from the birth of amorous confusion (*vibhrama*), they are described as "arising from their union.
Their minds were captivated by those previously mentioned activities—such as walking and so forth—performed together with them.

And consequently, those various true women—who are of that nature and consist of it—assumed and attained all the diverse movements previously described, such as "the stretching out of arms" and so forth.
Among them, the women were by their very nature possessed of an excellence of intoxication, by virtue of their being placed at the forefront of the yogin's task. Why?

Furthermore, the meaning is that they possess love for Him. By the phrase "of the Lord (pati) and Sovereign (adhyakṣa) of Ramā"—who is the presiding power over all beauty, qualities, sweetness, and opulence—the state of being unsurpassed by all is indicated. Alternatively, "Ramā" refers to Śrī Rādhā, as explained previously.

Thus, the aforementioned association with that [Lord] is indicated. All those various gestures previously mentioned, beginning with "the stretching out of arms," were assumed—that is, attained—by them. ||2||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: It manifests the very state of *tāpa* (fever-like longing) through two chapters consisting of more than [the standard] verses, beginning with the words "by movement" (*gatya*) and so forth. By "movement," physical activity (*kāyikī ceṣṭā*) is indicated as a whole.
By "smiles and amorous glances out of passion" (*anurāgeṇa smitaṃ vibhramekṣitāni*), mental activity (*mānasī*) is indicated, because those [actions] are produced by passion.

Through delightful conversations and the like, there is the verbal [service] by means of delightful speech; and through delightful pastimes and amorous gestures, it is threefold, according to their respective suitability. "Pastime" (vihāra) refers to sports such as the lifting of Govardhana Hill or the playing of the flute; "amorous gesture" (vibhrama) refers to the movements of erotic passion. Thus it has been said:

"The instability of mental activity arising from amorous passion is considered *vibhrama* (bewilderment). Among these, each subsequent state is superior to the preceding one. Their minds were captivated by those former deeds;
consequently, being of that nature and absorbed in that, they truly became identical with it. Thus they became of that very essence.

Or it may be a separate sentence. Since both "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*) and "being absorbed in that" (*tanmayatva*) will be explained [later], the phrase "those whose intoxication is intense" (*pramada*) is intended to refer to the previously mentioned "intense pride" (*prakṛṣṭa-māna*). Alternatively, *pramada* means joy. The sense is that although they are of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*), they are truly in the state of supreme suffering. Of Ramā...

"Of the husband of Lakṣmī"—this indicates supreme cleverness; by this, the excellence of the husband and others is also suggested. Alternatively, "Ramā Śrī Rādhā" suggests, as before, her association with them, which will be described later. "Those various [states] are supremely ineffable"—this states the impossibility of imitating them.

Nevertheless, they took them up; or rather, all those various gestures previously mentioned. This playful display of love (*prema-vilāsa*) is entirely natural for city-dwelling women (*nāgarī*). For this very reason, imitation of the beloved is called "play" (*līlā*) in the treatises on poetics (*alaṃkāra-śāstra*). Or else, those various gestures [were taken] from Kṛṣṇa’s various...
The playful activities were the agents; the women, as the objects of those actions, undertook them. Of what nature were the women?
They were "of that very essence," meaning their minds were fixed upon Him. ||2||

The sequence of the composition [is as follows]: "By the movement," and so forth, according to the context. Here, the meaning is "of the Lord Adhokṣaja, the husband of Ramā, who is the presiding power over the abundance of all forms, qualities, sweetness, and sovereignty. Alternatively, it refers to those various [powers] previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "the stretching out of the arms," and so on.
In that regard, it manifests its identity with that. ||2||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Prīti-sandarbha* (324): Thus—"Luster (*kānti*) is said to be beauty itself, radiant with the nourishment of the god of love" (*Uṇādivṛtti* 11.15).
In accordance with the rule: "When *kānti* (loveliness) itself attains an extreme expansion through the qualities of age, enjoyment, place, time, and so forth,
it is called *dīpti* (brilliance)" (*Uṇādivṛtti* 11.17),
both *kānti* and *dīpti* should be illustrated accordingly.

*Līlā* (playful charm) is the imitation of the beloved through beautiful dress, actions, and so forth [Uṇādisūtra 11.28]. Within that, the imitation of her actions by means of dress and action is as follows: immediately after the passage beginning with "When the Blessed One had disappeared" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.1], there is the passage beginning with "With a gait full of passion and a smile" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.2].

*Rasikāhlādinī*: In *saṃyoga* (union), there is the experience of the essential nature alone; in *vipralambha* (separation), there is the experience of the entirety of the divine pastimes (*līlā*). For this very reason, it is said that in *vipralambha*, Kṛṣṇa, pervaded by the entirety of the pastimes, entered into their minds—the verse beginning with "He went" (*gataḥ*) expresses this. Those women [perceived] Śrī Kṛṣṇa with great honor.

They were possessed of intense intoxication. Now, having disregarded Him, they imitated—that is, they replicated—the various activities of the Lord of Ramā during their separation from Him, such as the pastimes of sucking the life out of Pūtanā and so forth. What kind of women were they? Their minds were captivated by the movements and other gestures of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, what kind of women were they?
"Consisting of that" means composed of that; or rather, those for whom He alone is the self, the conscious subject.
The intended meaning is this: in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) characterized by union (*sambhoga*), there was a perception consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

In the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*), however, because of the beloved's entry into her inner being, her own movements were perceived as if she were possessed by a spirit, causing wonder.

Because they were of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, they adopted His very activities. When their inner senses (antaḥkaraṇa) became transformed into His form, their movement was like that of an elephant, as was their mental passion (anurāga), their smile preceded by that [passion], and their playful glances (vibhrama-vilāsa) preceded by those [smiles]; by these, the mind—
Those delightful conversations and secret whispers which delight [the heart];

the dwelling, the play, the particular coquetry, and the particular grace; or else, the various wandering, the going from one bower to another; or else, "coquetry" (*vibhrama*) means a graceful movement. By these [qualities], taken either individually or collectively—
Or [they may be produced] by all [the factors] together. Among these, movement and posture are physical; smiles, glances, and sidelong looks are ocular;

speech is vocal; and coquettish distraction (*vibhrama*) is mental. Thus it is said in the *Rasārṇava*: "Coquettish distraction is considered to be the instability of the fluctuations of the mind arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)."
They are called *ramā* because they delight; they are the goddesses of Vraja. He is their lord (*pati*), meaning their protector;

for this very reason, he has become their very self (*tad-ātmā*) for the sake of protecting their lives. Their minds were captivated by these [qualities] such as his gait and so forth—those whose minds had been led to concealment [of their true nature], though previously they were already so by their very nature.
Formerly possessed of intense passion, they are now devoid of passion due to separation. The prefix *pra-* here conveys the sense of "gone.
They have performed an imitation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. As it is said in the Rasārṇava:
"That which is an imitation of the beloved, preceded by sweet speech..."
That which may exist through gestures or movements is called *līlā*.

Now, it might be objected: was it not previously stated, "O Lord, we are your maidservants"? Is it not improper to imitate the master's actions, as that would result in mere mockery? To this he replies: "Consisting of that" (*tad-ātmikāḥ*). That very [Lord] is within one's own self, in one's essential nature.

"Yāsām tāḥ": those [gopīs] whose self-remembrance was forgotten once their nature as Kṛṣṇa had arisen. If these women were to possess self-remembrance, then this reproach would apply; however, that is not the case.
Therefore, the imitation of the beloved's pastimes for the sake of dispelling their distress has been stated in brief; it will be explained in detail later.
He will say. ||2||

Viśvanātha: Then, he describes the manner in which the transitory emotion (sañcārī bhāva) of madness— which arose in those who were searching for him here and there in the groves but had not found him, and whose suffering of separation increased as they waited— became fully manifest through two verses beginning with "gata-".

First, there was His arrival at her side by the natural movement of the feet of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Ramā and master of all perfection of beauty; and then there were His glances, accompanied by smiles full of affection, wherein the pupils possessed a distinctive, enchanting rolling motion.
They then engaged in a charming conversation: "O land-lotus! Will you give your nectar to this bee who is afflicted by extreme thirst, or not? O bee! The husband of the lotus is indeed the sun."

But it is not a bee. So how will it cause you to drink its own honey? O lotus! This is indeed the very nature of you lotuses, that you cause your own kin, the sun, to drink only your own honey; however, [you cause] the bee, your paramour, to drink as well. Therefore—

Defeated by her very words, she laughed and engaged with me in the pastime of drinking the honey of our lips. Or rather, as you were going toward the base of the *nīpa* tree near me—which is called "the lotus-born"—the serpent Mahādarpaka bit you; its venom spread all the way up to your chest.

Even so, do you not ask me for its pacification simply because you are a woman of noble family? Therefore, out of compassion, I myself shall come before you and, reciting the mantra that neutralizes that poison, I shall touch your body with my palms. O, O snake-charmer! Do not [fear] me!

A snake bit her. As the snake was biting that very limb, he rubbed it with both palms and said, "O noble lady! Although I would have disregarded you even after knowing that your body is overwhelmed by the flames of poison solely from your faltering voice, [I shall not do so]."

"Then the killing of a woman will befall me; therefore, I shall surely pacify that poison. Having said this, he performed the scratching of her chest with his fingernails and so forth. From that arose amorous play (*vihāra*), then sexual union (*samprayoga*), and then the confusion (*vibhrama*) of intoxication with passion. As for that...

It has been said: "The instability of the mental fluctuations arising from amorous passion is considered *vibhrama* (bewilderment). These [fluctuations], intensified by memory during the state of separation, have been projected [onto the senses]. [She says: "Hey! What are you doing here?
Go outside and search for my beloved of life! Having thus rebuked them, she [dismisses them] from her body.

Those by whom their own minds have been drawn out are "those [women]. Since women intoxicate intensely (*prakarṣeṇa mādyanti*), they are so called; and having thus reached a state of madness, they become identified with that—those whose intellect and other faculties have become its very self.
Therefore, they assumed those various gestures belonging to him, such as the deliberate seizing [of objects] and so forth.
The meaning is that they imitated [him]. ||2||
In their movements, smiles, glances, speech, and so forth,
the beloveds were the very embodiments of their lover’s own form.
"Here am I," thus did those women, whose very essence was Kṛṣṇa's playful dalliance, declare themselves.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase *gati-smita* and so forth: those whose forms (*mūrtayaḥ*) are reflected in—that is, permeated by—the gait and other qualities of their beloved; therefore, they possess the playful movements and amorous pastimes (*vihāra-vibhramāḥ*) of Kṛṣṇa himself, such that each thinks, "I alone am Kṛṣṇa," toward one another.
They announced [this]. ||3||

Vaṃśīdhara: He did not merely play by imitating [Kṛṣṇa], but also by becoming identical with Him; thus he says, "And moreover" (api ca). Of the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa. "Possessed" (āviṣṭāḥ) means they were brought to His very form. Since they were possessed by Him, for that reason, O frail women! "This Kṛṣṇa is indeed I. That...
Or rather—the connection is that "the women" are those whose nature is that [of the Buddha], having attained that very form. ||3||
In the *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "This Kṛṣṇa is indeed I"—thus they declared, and they declared it to one another.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). Otherwise, there would be no protection for their bodies; therefore, the Lord Himself appeared within their internal senses (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) in such a way and brought about that state of identity (*tādātmya*). Hence...
Thus it was said, "Right there he disappeared" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.48); that is, right there, within those very [waters], he became an internal presence. ||3||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: In that regard, it manifests His very nature as follows: "In His movements," and so forth. When the movements and other qualities of the Beloved are mentioned, the word "and others" (*ādi*) includes His playful wandering (*vihāra*) and amorous sport (*vibhrama*).

Because these are being restated as already described, their specific previously mentioned attributes have not been explicitly stated here. In those [movements], He is "established" (*pratirūḍha*), meaning He has become identical with them.
"Embodiments" refers to those whose bodies consist of an aggregate of sense organs and so forth;

thus, the attainment of their state both internally and externally has been described. By the phrase "the weak ones, the women," it is implied that it is indeed appropriate for me to imitate the gestures of women. Nevertheless, wherever you have longing, there I [shall be].

Thus, each one of them announced to all the others that he was the resident of such-and-such a monastery (*vihāra*). Of what nature were these women?
