They were those whose wandering play (*vibhrama-vilāsa*) was like that of Kṛṣṇa in the monastery, or those from whom there was the delusion (*bhrānti*) of Kṛṣṇa’s wandering in the monastery; and their state of being absorbed in him (*tanmayatva*)—
With the intention that this occurs solely through the state of being overwhelmed by the pastimes of love (*prema-līlā*), and not through the absorption of *ahaṃgraha* meditation, he says:
"The beloveds of the Beloved. This means: the beloveds are those who possess natural love for him;
and the Beloved is one who likewise possesses such remembered love for them. [This refers to] that which is called the pastime (*līlā*).
And this is its power (*anubhāva*): "Playful imitation of the beloved through charming dress, actions, and so forth," as it has been said.
And thus is the dramatic application (*prayoga*): "She who repeatedly observes the playful adornments [of her beloved], habitually cultivating the thought, 'I am Madhuripu (the Enemy of Madhu)'. (3)
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: In that regard, it manifests the state of being identical with Him through the word "gati" (movement) and so forth.

Regarding "gati" and the others mentioned, the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes "vihāra" (sport) and "vibhrama" (amorous play). Since these are restatements of what has already been said, the various specific attributes previously mentioned are not repeated here. [The devotees] are permeated by the fully manifested pastimes.
"Embodiments" refers to those whose bodies consist of a collection of sense organs, limbs, and so forth;

thus, the attainment of that state both internally and externally has been described. And so it was said by Prahlāda: "One whose disposition and form imitate the state of being that [object]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.7.36).

It is implied that it is only fitting for women to imitate feminine gestures, as they are "weak" (*abalā*). Nevertheless, or rather, being entirely devoid of strength due to the intensity of their feverish longing, each of them individually realized, "I am she," thus expressing their helplessness in separation or their absorption in playful ecstasy (*līlā*). In that regard:

The reason is: "They are true because they consist of that and are composed of that. By the word "that" (tat), either Śrī Kṛṣṇa or His movements and so forth are meant; the reason for not explicitly stating "I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa" is due to being overwhelmed by the agony of separation.
Or, it may be because they consist of Him; and this state of being composed of Him arises solely through the very nature of the weight of the pastimes of divine love, and not otherwise.

With the intention that [the Lord acts] through non-dual knowledge and so forth, he says: "The beloved of the Beloved. He uses the name "Kṛṣṇa" with the intent of expressing His supreme power of attraction. The rest has been explained by them.
Alternatively, even here it should be understood as a mere imitation; and thus, in the preceding verse, the phrase "consisting of Him" [is used].
The perfection of imitation has been explained. He demonstrates that very point with the word "gati" (movement). O young women!
"I am that very Nanda, the lord of those various pastimes"—this is the speech of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this is the ellipsis.
And it should be understood that this was previously spoken by Him on some occasion during playful jesting; for otherwise, why would He speak such words?
In response to the question "Is it completed?", he says: "Consisting of that" means having their minds fixed upon that.
Alternatively, this is again a reason as before, for the purpose of making known the perfection of the imitation.
For this very reason, they possess a playful confusion like that of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, consisting of specific gestures such as kissing, embracing, and so forth.

Or rather, "the playful grace of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasyeva vihāra-vibhramaḥ*) means those whose playful charm is such that their necklaces (*hāra*) have fallen away. Or else, it means those for whom there is a specific delusion regarding Kṛṣṇa’s play; the sense is that they imitate him because it cannot be determined whether it is Kṛṣṇa himself who is playing.
And in the non-completion of her speech, the cause clearly appears to be her agitation due to separation. Alternatively, the meaning is:
"I am she who has been enjoyed many times by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in various ways. Her failure to reveal this is either due to her cleverness or due to her very agitation from separation. In such a confession—

The reason is as follows: the meaning is that they reported that [death] to Him because, in that death which was beyond words, their very selves and minds were characterized by an extreme longing to die due to unbearable suffering; for the meaning is that they were utterly overwhelmed by the remembrance of His pastimes, their bewilderment and madness having been caused by Kṛṣṇa’s amorous sports. ||3||

The sequence of composition: "gati" (movement), etc. Those whose forms—the bodies consisting of an aggregate of senses and so forth—have become similar to, or have been fully established in, movement and the other [states]. And thus, he describes the condition of those who have long since attained their focus. ||3||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Prīti-sandarbha* (325): The meaning is that these are His pastimes described in such passages as "those various outstretched arms" (*bhā.pu. 10.29.46*). Subsequently, the form [is perceived] through immersion (*āveśa*).
That which consists of the cultivation of non-difference from Him—such as in His gait, smile, glances, speech, and so forth.

Even though He thus manifests pastimes that are the very form of His own playful splendor, their own internal disposition remains hidden, as will be stated in the passage: "They strive and yet He remains concealed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.20).

"They are striving. Now, even at this earlier stage, for the purpose of passing the time, those pastimes which were initiated to be sung by them through the intensity of their love—those very pastimes they have become absorbed in;
this should be understood as the cause for their specific imitations of those [pastimes]. And this imitation is generally not...

It is denoted by the word *līlā* (divine play), because states such as childhood (*bālya*) and so forth, lacking a [specific] objective support, do not constitute integral parts of the radiant aesthetic flavor (*ujjvala-rasa*).

In that regard, even though Pūtanā and others possess states that oppose mere affection (*prīti-mātra*), and likewise Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s mother and others possess states that oppose specific forms of their own affection (*nija-prīti-viśeṣa*).

The imitation of activities was accepted as artificial by the friends of the gopīs—who were themselves imitating Śrī Kṛṣṇa—in order to pass the time of their separation and to nourish those various ecstatic moods; it should be understood that this was not done out of actual possession of those specific moods. And some explain it in this way:

When there is an intense absorption in the remembrance of the pastime of the killing of Pūtanā, some women even imitate Pūtanā out of fear alone, suspecting that Śrī Kṛṣṇa might be intent upon them. This is just as in the world,
when one who is crazed by fear suspects his own safety is in danger, he imitates the tiger or other causes of that fear.

It occurs; therefore, even when imitating Him, love alone blossoms toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa as it does toward their own selves, and not hatred. That love remains in them toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the very same manner as it exists toward themselves—as His own form—and thus it continues to follow its natural disposition.

Therefore, in passages such as "Then another bound her with a garland" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.23), the imitation of Śrī Yaśodā should be understood in the same way. For previously, through the intense absorption of remembering the pastimes of Dāmodara, she had attained the ecstatic mood (bhāva) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and from that, her face—

In accordance with the manner described in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (1.8.31), "He led [her] away through the cultivation of fear," fear even arose from Śrī Yaśodā; and by recollecting the nature of his childhood, he imitated her.
Consequently, she herself, through the very immersion in that pastime, became like Kṛṣṇa, while another woman likewise became like Kṛṣṇa.
He bound [her]. Nevertheless, even as before, the very joy appropriate to her own nature remained within her;
for that joy is the supreme substratum of each and every state. Thus, while externally there was the imitation of those various states, in the midst of them lay the state of Śrī Yaśodā.
There is no contradiction, because one's own [ordinary] state is not touched due to the intervention of the state of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||3||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: When that absorption occurred, what transpired? To this he says: *gati-smita* (in their gait, smiles, etc.).

Those whose bodies were "pratirūḍha-mūrtayaḥ"—that is, whose forms were fully entered by the pastimes of their beloved, the object of their affection—and who were therefore "abalāḥ" (helpless) due to being seized by the demon of Kṛṣṇa.
Dependence has been described; for that reason, those whose senses and bodies were possessed by Kṛṣṇa, being of His very nature, announced to one another, "I am Kṛṣṇa.
Now, if it is asked: since a distinction exists between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, how did this statement of non-difference arise?

To this he replies: "Consisting of that" (*tad-ātmikāḥ*) means that because Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself has entered into their bodies, senses, and so forth, [the agency] belongs to Him alone and not to them. Just as a knower (*jñānī*), upon attaining the direct realization of the Self, says, "I am Brahman"; and just as in ritual acts, one says, "In this rite, you are Brahman."

When "Be" is said, he indeed says, "I am Brahman. Just as in that case there is worldly usage based solely on the non-difference of being (*bhāva*), so too here there is the realization of non-difference from Kṛṣṇa; as it has been said:
"The expression of non-difference is seen to be threefold—in knowledge, in devotion, and in action."
"In this matter, the qualified person is one who possesses a sense of difference regarding the fruits.

Furthermore, what are they like? They are "those whose delusions consist of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes"; that is, those for whom there is delusion (*vibhrama*) concerning Kṛṣṇa’s very pastime (*vihāra*), his play. One [gopī] plays just like Kṛṣṇa; seeing her, the others experience delusion.
It occurs as follows; it is stated in the *Rasārṇava*:

"At the time of the beloved's arrival, due to the agitation of the onset of passion, there is *vibhrama*—the disarray of ornaments such as armlets and necklaces through the misplacement of their positions. (Rasārṇava 1.203).
In the movements and other attributes of Kṛṣṇa, His forms are superimposed; likewise, in His forms, the movements and other attributes are superimposed.

Thus, through this mutual adherence to one another's qualities, both the fullness of His pastimes and their manifestation have come into being. Movement belongs to the feet, smiling to the mouth, looking with the eyes, and speaking is the vocal expression—this is the characteristic of His form.
All delusions and the like, as well as pastimes and other forms of bondage experienced during the state of union, having entered the path of memory, become their opposites.
Vātsyāyana states that when there is an abundance of rasa, women attain the nature of men.
Alternatively, they are those whose forms are reflected in the beloved’s own movements and so forth; they are indeed the very essence of the playful amorous sports of Kṛṣṇa—
those [sports] consisting of specific varieties of dalliance such as kissing and embracing— or rather, they are the sporting itself of Kṛṣṇa alone.
"Those whose playful grace (*vibhrama-vilāsa*) was such that their necklaces (*hāra*) had slipped away and broken; or rather,

those who possessed the delusion (*vibhrama-bhrānti*) that 'this is Kṛṣṇa’s own sport,' and thus acted toward one another with the thought, 'It is Kṛṣṇa himself who is sporting here,' because they were of his nature and their minds were fixed on him."

It should be understood that even while their speech was unfinished, they brought about a mutual relish; for the contemplation that "separation alone has made them identical with Him" is indeed their true non-dual knowledge,
yet through love, identity with Him arose at that very moment— had it been truly [previously] so, then...
If the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa had occurred [at that time], such a state would have come to pass. As he will say later:
"Beholding their beloved arrived, the women, their eyes blossoming with love, rose up" [Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.32.3];
thus, there would have been no rising [from sleep]. And so it is said in the Gītagovinda:
Frequently observing the graceful play of her ornaments, she is habituated to the contemplation that "I am the enemy of Madhu" (Kṛṣṇa). [Gītagovinda 6.5]. Thus ends the third verse.
Viśvanātha: When that very madness reaches its full maturity, he describes their condition with the verse beginning "gati" (movement).
Those whose bodies (*mūrtayaḥ*)—that is, their physical forms—are superimposed upon the previously mentioned movements and other attributes of the beloved;
first, there are the movement, smiles, and so forth of the beloved. In each of these [superimpositions], within their own bodies composed of mind, senses, and the rest—

They have ascended. Therefore, the meaning is that their own forms have re-ascended into those [states] such as movement, smiles, and so forth. Then, when unity is attained through intoxication, having abandoned the exclusive states of being such as "I am indeed Kṛṣṇa" or "Kṛṣṇa is indeed I," there arises the realization: "He is I, and I am Kṛṣṇa."

Having attained a state consisting of the maturity of relishing the aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*), they became one with that [flavor] and achieved identity with Kṛṣṇa; it should be understood that this was not merely through the practice of *ahaṃgraha* meditation, as indicated by the statement "the beloved of the Beloved. They "informed" one another—that is, they made it known to each other—but not [that they were] "we."
The meaning is that not even a few of the women of Vraja were aware [of this].
The reason for this is: they were those whose bewilderment and madness arose from remembering the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa. (3)
Singing loudly in unison, they searched from forest to forest like madwomen, seeking only him.
They questioned the trees regarding the Person who exists within and without all beings, like the sky.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the words "singing": while going from forest to forest, they searched—that is, they sought him out. He describes their state as being like that of madmen: they questioned the lords of the forest (trees), [asking about] the Person who exists within all beings, in their midst, and yet exists outside them. ||4||

Vaṃśīdhara: To show that even though they had attained that state [of oneness], they performed other actions as well, he says "And what more?"—namely, "Singing. This was either for the purpose of making their own distress heard to him from afar, or else for the purpose of attracting him, who is fond of song, by means of that [song]. It was directed toward this very Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not toward anyone else.

Something else: they have come together in a compact for the sake of properly seeking [their goal], or for the sake of mutually pacifying their suffering. Regarding trees that bear fruit without flowers and are all-pervading, the question concerning their location speaks nothing but madness.
And whatever worldly object is seen or heard, whether internal or external, Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of it—so says the Śruti. (4)

The Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā: Having come together and become one, they went from forest to forest, searching. They did not merely search; they questioned. [They asked] as if it were empty like space. The sense is that this questioning was not preceded by deliberate intellectual intent. They directed their attention toward the trees.

They questioned Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who, like the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), dwells within all beings both internal and external—just as they would question a person. Since the verb *pṛcch* (to ask) takes two objects, the primary object, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, must be supplied. ||4||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And then, he describes once again the state called "intoxication" (*unmāda*) of those women who had finally regained their composure after a long time, beginning with the verse "gāyantyaḥ" (singing). Here, "singing" refers to that which is famous in Gokula, consisting of the slaying of Pūtanā and other such deeds. And that [was manifested] from the "subsidence of the poisonous waters," etc. (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.31.2).

It is with the intention of protecting herself in the manner that will be described. She sings loudly so that he may hear her distress from afar; or rather, to attract him who is fond of song by means of it; or perhaps, simply due to the nature of the intensity of her suffering, she directs it toward him alone. Even though [she acts] through renunciation...

"He is supremely miserable; nevertheless, he seeks that very thing"—this is the meaning. It is as in the verse: "He counts the multitude of virtues and does not desire even to wander from delusion" (Gītā 2.9). Being joined together, that is, united with one another, they are everywhere for the sake of thorough searching. Or rather, [they are so] through mutual friendship.

It is for the sake of allaying distress; or rather, it is due to the very nature of that particular kind of distress. This simultaneity of singing and searching means that they wander while singing, yet from time to time they ask questions.
The reason for asking the trees is expressed by the phrase "like one who is insane"; the suffix *kan* is used here in its own sense (to denote the state itself).

By this, his lack of restraint regarding his hair and so forth is revealed, even though he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all beings. For this very reason, they questioned him as he existed pervading both the interior and exterior of all elements like space;
for it was only in the form of a human performing divine play (*līlā*), which serves as the object of their own love, that he became the subject of their inquiry.
This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, one might wonder: "Alas! Has all of this for them become nothing but a cry in the wilderness? He says "no"—"ākāśa... (the sky...), and he himself will state later: "By me, while worshiping in their absence" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.19].
Thus [they spoke].
Or rather, they questioned the Puruṣa, their own leader— who exists within and without all beings,
both moving and stationary, like space, as if present in person through his very being.

They questioned Him as He was manifesting Himself. And such a flash of knowledge arose in them solely from a particular transformation of their love, just as it is said: "The forest creepers and trees, as if revealing Viṣṇu within themselves, became rich with flowers and fruits" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.9). In that state, the external manifestation occurs at a distance.

"But 'antaḥ' means from nearby. And the sense is that, since [consciousness] exists there, it is appropriate to pose the question even regarding insentient beings such as the species of trees, because they possess intoxication (unmāda). ||4||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Nor is this merely a matter of imitation or being absorbed in the divine play (*līlā*);

rather, being overwhelmed by the pain of separation, they search here and there and ask everyone they see before them. Thus he says: "Singing" (*gāyantyaḥ*). Their loud singing was directed toward Him from afar.
Is it for the purpose of making him hear of her own suffering? Or perhaps, since he is fond of song, for the purpose of attracting him by means of it?

Or else, is it simply because of the very nature of the weight of her distress? Even though his singing and so forth are not appropriate given his renunciation and his status as the supreme giver, nevertheless, even at that time, she thought, "He loves only this [song]," thus demonstrating his singular devotion to her.

Or rather, it is said that they have the habit of singing together as one. Being united and joined with one another, they are everywhere for the sake of correctly seeking [the truth]. Or rather, for the sake of mutually pacifying suffering through friendship.
Or rather, simply because their very nature consists of specific forms of suffering. This is in response to a question concerning the lords of the forest (trees).

The reason is: "like a madman. The suffix *ka* is used here either in its own sense (*svārthe*) or to denote contempt (*kutsāyām*). By this, the lack of restraint regarding hair and so forth is implied. In that context, both the search and the questioning are refuted by the absence of deliberation;
otherwise, questioning trees would be illogical. [This is understood] from the phrase "from forest to forest," which implies searching in every forest.

From this, his extensive wandering and his search over a long period of time are also indicated. Just as space exists pervading both the exterior and the interior, so too does he exist, pervading all beings—all living creatures—internally within each person in the form of the *puruṣa*. Or rather, [he exists] within the elements (*bhūta*).
Upon reaching the groves and other places, they questioned the trees and such things—though He was present both inside and outside near them—precisely because of their madness;
or rather, the reason for such questioning and searching was that they thought He might be some other man, their own master. Or else:
"Alas! Though He was present everywhere and though they themselves knew Him to be so, those girls, overwhelmed by the intensity of the pain of love born of separation, even questioned the trees.
Thus, being in such a state herself, she says "ākāśa," etc. The meaning is the same as before. Alas, listen!
The nature of being overwhelmed by the intensity of love—such are the contemplations. ||4||

The sequence of the composition: "Singing" (gāyantyaḥ). Here, "singing" refers to that which is well-known in Gokula, consisting of [the deeds] such as the slaying of Pūtanā. This simultaneous occurrence of singing and searching is such that they wander while singing, yet from time to time they inquire about the Person who is the inner controller (antaryāmī) of all. Therefore...
They questioned Him who, like space, exists pervading both the internal and external within all beings;

the reason for this is that He was manifesting among them specifically as the object of their own love. Or rather, they questioned the Supreme Person, their own leader, who, like space, [pervades] all beings—that is, all living creatures.

They questioned Him who exists pervading both the interior and the exterior; the meaning is that they questioned about His presence here and there. It is like asking someone who is inquiring about a certain reflection.
And such knowledge on their part arose simply from the manifestation [of Him] here and there through their love—for the forest creepers and the trees.

As in the passage, "Manifesting Viṣṇu within themselves, as if rich with flowers and fruits" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.9), there is a grand sequence of events: it was not merely that they remained with those various gestures held in their hearts, but rather, preceded by that singing, they wandered from forest to forest; thus he says: "Singing... (gāyantyaḥ).
"Highly," and so forth. "Highly" means that, fearing He might have gone far away at some point, they sing loudly.

Thinking, "Only when we are all together, having met, will no one among us ever be separated from this Śrī Kṛṣṇa," they act like madwomen—*unmattakavat*, where *kan* is used in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). It is not only... [the men].

They were filled with doubt and questioned him. The verb *pracchi* (to ask) takes two objects (*dvi-karmaka*). In this context, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the primary object (*mukhya-karma*). The secondary object (*gauṇa-karma*) is the Self (*ātman*), the Puruṣa who exists within all beings like space, as well as within and without. Since there was no other subject to be asked about therein, they questioned Him.

The meaning is that they questioned [him] having taken him as their object (*lakṣīkṛtya*). Regarding the phrase "existing among beings" (*bhūteṣu santam*), it results in the sense of "having taken the being as the object" (*bhūtaṃ lakṣyīkṛtya*). Regarding the phrase "the lords of the forest" (*vanaspatīn*), the meaning is "towards the lords of the forest" (*vanaspatīn prati*). By that, "singing" (*gānam*) is the direct object (*karma*), while "that one" (*amum*) is the indirect object (*gauṇaṃ karma*); [the same applies to] "the person" (*puruṣam*) and "the lords of the forest" (*vanaspatīn*).

The second case [is used] for the sense of a *karmapravacanīya* [particle]. Alternatively, the meaning is "having reached the trees" (*vanaspatīn prāpya*). For when "the necklace" (*hāram*) is uttered, there is a comprehension of the syntactic connection through the ellipsis of a verb such as "close it. ||4||
The Composition of Joy (345): Madness occurs when the heart is deluded—as in the passage beginning, "They sing loudly together of him alone," and so forth. This is clear. ||4||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Describing the behavior caused by divine madness through the arising of transitory emotions in those who have attained identity [with Him], she says:
"Singing...
Being gathered together and meeting one another, they went from forest to forest, searching here and there, yet they did not find Him who was hidden away, causing them such distress.

Perceiving him to be that very person, they sing loudly; the loud singing is for the purpose of making their own distress known, thinking that he has gone far away. Or else, because fame is exceedingly fond of singers, it sings loudly for him; here the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), as in the word "unmatta" (madman).
They searched while forgetting to cover their own bodies; they did not merely search, but even questioned others. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*:
"Mental derangement (*unmāda*) is a confusion of the mind caused by separation from a loved one or by the loss of something desired."
But in that which arises from separation, the behaviors would be running about and lamentation.
"Incoherent prattle, sleeping, rising suddenly, conversation with inanimate objects, and smiles without cause"—thus it is said.
He describes their conduct as being like that of a madman: "like the sky," being of one and the same nature both externally and internally.
They questioned the peaceful Person who lies within all beings as their inner controller; for this very reason, they questioned the great lords of the forest, the massive trees.

This inquiry was directed toward the trees because they recalled what Śrī Kṛṣṇa had said—beginning with the words, "O best of gods" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.15.5)—and because they had previously witnessed His extraordinary affection for them. This is the question addressed to the trees.
In mobile beings endowed with the activity of the external senses,
[the Self] exists externally and is perceived as immediate through the functioning of the external senses; whereas in stationary beings,
it exists internally, for the Person is established within them alone, just as these [beings] are like guardians of a treasure.
Thinking they were mere mental fluctuations (*vṛttayaḥ*), they questioned; or rather, like those who are insane, being as empty as space, they questioned;

or else, while the distinction exists within all beings—both stationary and moving—they questioned the trees as if they were external. Indeed, due to their insanity, they were devoid of self-discrimination regarding the moving beings.
The meaning is that, having questioned the stationary beings, they asked [the mobile ones]. ||4||

Viśvanātha: When that madness of theirs, having abandoned its own intensity, grew mild, he describes how those women, possessing a partial external awareness, acted—as in the verse beginning with "singing": "We, the women of Vraja, are suffering from separation from our beloved."
"Let us search for him"—this is the outward inquiry. "United," meaning gathered together, they went from forest to forest.
"Like madmen" means slightly intoxicated; the suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of "slightness. They questioned the trees regarding Puruṣa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this is the characteristic of madness.

Surely we know that Kṛṣṇa was then happily sporting with the Queen of Vṛndāvana, who is the foremost of all; however, he may or may not have known of the madness and other states of these gopīs who were maddened by separation from Him. Therefore, He is qualified as being like the ether, both within and without all beings.

It remains pervading [all]. Thus, although the nature of Kṛṣṇa is unlimited, because He is omnipresent, it is indicated that He indeed hears their questions and so forth, even though they are perceived only in their respective locations. ||4||
"O Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha, have you seen him? Has the son of Nanda gone away, having stolen our hearts with his affectionate smiles and glances?"

Śrīdhara: He elaborates on this with nine verses. Therein, with the hope that they might see [Him] because of His greatness, they ask about the *aśvattha* tree and others: "Was He seen?"—meaning, "Having stolen our hearts with glances playful with love and laughter, He has gone like a thief; was He seen by you? (5)

Vaṃśīdhara: That is the context of the question. Among the lords of the forest (vanaspati), these—the Aśvattha and others—are "far-reaching" because of their greatness and their imperishability (acyutatva). Alternatively, because they are respectively the abodes of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, they are therefore also great. Referring to the Aśvattha, they say: "Not by me..."

"It was seen" because of the determination [of its presence] through the movement of its trembling leaves; and "it will not remain even tomorrow" because of their despondency. This has been rightly said. Addressing one another who possess eyes, they say—"O Plakṣa tree!"—referring to that which is devoid of eyes, asking how it can be seen. [The compound *prakṣākṣa* is formed as follows: *prakṛṣṭe akṣiṇī yasya*, where the vowel *a* [is elided].

The state of being a prior form (*pūrva-rūpatva*) is established because [the word *vaṭa*] belongs to the *śakadhvādi* class, and also due to the identity of the letters *ra* and *la*. Now, although he sees, he is unable to speak due to the absence of the organ of speech; therefore, they call that banyan tree his "middle" (*adhyama*). It should be understood that its fresh sprouts are like his tongue. Of the mind...
"Having taken away the state of being a jewel"—that is to say, we do not ask you, who are virtuous, about the thief. ||5||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O" (*vaḥ*)—this is an address to each of you individually out of respect for your being dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Now, for what purpose is He questioned by you?
Regarding this, they say: "He has gone after stealing our mind. By the word "having stolen" (*hṛtvā*), the preciousness of the mind is revealed. Therefore, the sense is:

"We ask you, O virtuous ones, about that thief who has come here as the object of our longing"; for this very reason, although his name is explicitly mentioned out of distress, the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is not explicitly mentioned.
"Even out of envy. By the word "even" (api), it is implied that since the thief's name cannot be grasped [as evidence], the informer might also be subject to that [punishment];

this is what is stated. "Kaccit" is used as an interrogative particle. The sense is: "If he has been seen by you, we shall search for him, having gained confidence that he is wandering in that very direction. ||5||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "By you" (*vaḥ*) means by yourselves or belonging to yourselves. The mention of this relationship is for the purpose of anticipating the vision [of Him], as well as for speaking out of affection. Alternatively, this is simply the very nature of the abundance of love (*prema*), by which one's own state [of being] makes another similar to oneself.
The phrase "is addressed" (*ucyate*) implies that each [tree] is called out individually and separately out of respect for its Vaiṣṇava nature.

In this regard, the Vaiṣṇava character of the *aśvattha* is well known as being a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, regarding the principal form of Śrī residing on the surface of the earth, [the Lord said] to Arjuna in the context of the *vaṭa* tree: "Know Me to be in every *vaṭa*."

This is because it was spoken by the Blessed Lord. Likewise, regarding the *nyagrodha* tree; by their association, some maintain that the *plakṣa* tree is also, respectively, the abodes of Śrī-Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā.
Although such an intention might not seem appropriate given that He questioned them like one intoxicated by the distress of separation, [the following applies].
Furthermore, as for that which has been explained by the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda in various places, it will be made clear that these five chapters are devoted to *nivṛtti* (renunciation),
in accordance with his own initial promise and not in accordance with the mood (*bhāva*) of the Gopīs. Therefore, solely...
Each of those seen before [us] is questioned individually;

nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the consistency between preceding and following statements, something is briefly noted here according to their own commentaries, since such an address is appropriate when speaking to one's own master as "the son of Nanda. Or rather:
This is with the intention of [showing] their state as connoisseurs (*rasika*), and so it is further on as well.
Now, for what purpose is he being questioned by you? To this they reply: "Having stolen our heart, he has gone.
By the word "having stolen" (*hṛtvā*), the jewel-like nature of the heart is suggested. Therefore, he did not come merely as a visitor; rather, he is a thief.

The sense is: "We ask you, who are virtuous. By the word "kaccit" (I hope), a question is implied; the ellipsis is "then, please tell us," for due to being overwhelmed by separation, it is impossible to complete the sentence [otherwise]. Therefore, we shall search thoroughly with effort right here. Or rather, what can be inferred from what has been seen by you?
The sense is that, thinking "he is right here nearby," they have thus become confident and will restrain their breaths to protect themselves.

Alternatively, since it is said "like one who is insane," it should be understood that the sentence concludes in that very manner because, being overwhelmed by extreme distress, there is no possibility of expecting a reply or the like. Thus...
Also at the beginning. ||5||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: "The son of Nanda" is the reason for his own confidence; the meaning of "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) is as follows.
The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha* elaborates on that very point: "He has been seen by you," and so forth.

The *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* are forest trees (*vanaspati*); they are called "forest trees" because they do not flower, according to the rule: "A forest tree is one that is without flowers. Thus [it is said].

Even if they possess the fruit [of their merit] without any apparent cause, these women must surely be fortunate; with this intention, He first questioned them, saying, "Alas! Has He been seen by you? To the objection, "What is the use of asking that to you?", they replied: "If He has gone away having stolen our hearts, then while there are many of you, He is but one."

They asked, "How did he take [our hearts] away? It is said: "The son of Nanda" means the son of Nanda, the king of Vraja; by him, they became weak—that is the meaning. By what means was your mind stolen?
To that they replied: "By means of his loving smiles and glances, he drew our minds from within—the interior—to the outside."
The meaning. ||5||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, in response to the general question, their similarity to madmen has been stated. Now, without accepting that [similarity], he asks—"Is it seen?"—thinking in his mind, "These Vaiṣṇavas, having heard about Śrī Kṛṣṇa, will describe him as he truly is. O Aśvattha tree! O... [he continues].

O Plakṣa, O Nyagrodha! Because the Aśvattha is a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed Lord, as it has been stated that the Aśvattha is the foremost among all trees; because the Plakṣa is also a manifestation of Rudra; and because the Baṭa is also a manifestation of Brahmā—even though this realization does not belong to the goddesses of Vraja—
Nevertheless, the statement should be understood according to the influence of prior impressions (*pūrva-saṃskāra*) characteristic of the Upaniṣads.

"Has He been seen by you? (*vo dṛṣṭaḥ kaccit*) is a gentle inquiry. Alternatively, "your master" (*vaḥ prabhuḥ*) refers to one who is related to you. [Objection: If He has indeed been seen, then what of it?
Regarding this, they say: through love, smiles, and glances, there is entry into His heart; by means of smiles and glances, there is the carrying away [of the heart].

Therefore, the sense is that for Him, nothing at all is impossible. Indeed, according to the well-known saying, "There is nothing hidden from the virtuous," we ask you; for what has not been told to you here?
"Having gone, we shall ask others. ||5||

Viśvanātha: He elaborates upon the question with nine verses. Therein, anticipating that they might certainly see him—even though he is situated at a distance—because of his extreme loftiness, they ask: "Is he seen?
*Plakṣa* is known as *pīlu* or *khanvu*; *nyagrodha* is *baṭa*. For what purpose do you ask? Thus [he asks].
Anticipating their question, they said: "The son of the virtuous Nanda has also gone away,
having stolen our hearts through the gateway of our eyes, accompanied by smiles and glances sent by his servants, which are like a special great deluding herb that maddens all the world with love."

The meaning is that they have entered our inner palace through the gateway of our eyes, stolen the jewel of our minds, and fled. Having stood there for a moment, thinking, "Aha! What are these wretched things? and thus disregarding us, they remain stiff and give no reply; therefore, enough with them.
Having abandoned those who possess small fruits, who are ignorant of the dharma of helping others, who have not blossomed, and whose inner natures are impure, they have gone elsewhere. ||5||
O Kuravaka, Aśoka, Nāga, Punnāga, and Campaka trees: will the younger brother of Rāma, with his smiles that strip away the pride of haughty women, pass by this way?

Śrīdhara: Thinking that great beings are of immense benefit through their own blossoms, they ask the kuravaka trees and others: "Kaccid... O kuravakas and the rest, has he—who possesses a smile that removes all pride—been seen as he departed from here? (6)

Vaṃśīdhara: "He whose sound is *kaurava* (the cry of the Kurava bird) is thus; by this they say he will speak with sound—'O Kuravaka! Others said: "This is where there is a slight (*ku*) sound of bees; therefore, even the bees do not go here. Or rather, because of its bad sound (*ku-śabda*), it increases grief (*śoka*); hence, it is 'Aśoka'."

Ask him who destroys sorrow. He is not fit to speak; his name, however, should be known as that of one born with the nature of a goat, like a kid (*varkara*). "Nāga" means *nāgakeśara* (Mesua ferrea).
Because it possesses filaments (*kesara*) resembling eyelashes (*pakṣman*), he must have certainly seen this with his own eyes. Another...

They said, "This Punnāga tree, which is even taller than this [other tree] and can see from afar, will speak. Then the others said, "He is laughing under the pretext of flowers; he has seen your thief! She said, "He is just as intoxicated as Rāma," referring to him as "Rāmānuja" (the younger brother of Rāma). [She spoke thus] because of the age, beauty, and other qualities of those proud women.
As soon as we became aware of them, we observed that their branch-tips were being shaken by a sudden wind, and they said: "Aha! By shaking their heads, these trees are saying, 'We do not know.'"
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thinking that because they are so great, they would surely not speak out of contempt for us who are insignificant, they ask others—"Is it...? *Kurvaka* is a red, unfading *nāga* [flower].

The *nāgakesara* tree. Has he gone from here? Or rather, was it asked because he was previously seen here and has now vanished? Even now, it might be possible to see him from afar as he goes "from here"; nevertheless, since he would not be easily found, one should follow his footprints right here as he approaches nearby and, by means of those [footprints], find him.

The sense is: "Let us search. Furthermore, in many places where the reading is *gataḥ*, the commentary explains it by supplying the word *itaḥ* (from here), following that interpretation; this is like the term *rāmanujaḥ* (the younger brother of Rāma) being used for Nandasūnu (the son of Nanda).
Now, one might ask: "How was your heart stolen by him, you who are so proud? To this they reply: "Of the proud ones (*māninīnām*)."

The phrase "even such a one as he, whose smile removes their pride" suggests his lack of deliberation; for "pride" (darpa) here means arrogance. At that very moment, by means of that feigned smile, the pride consisting of conceit was taken away. For this very reason, [the gods] say, "We shall search," regarding him who possesses such great power of delusion.
The sense is: "We cannot live even for a moment separated from them; therefore, we ask.

[From the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*]: Thinking that because they are so exalted, these great souls would surely not speak to us lowly ones out of contempt, they ask others—"Is it well? [The flower] is red, unblemished, and fragrant.

"Nāga" refers to the *nāgakeśara* tree. Has he gone from here? Or rather, the question was asked because he was previously seen while staying right here; for now, however, since he has "gone from here," it is possible that he might be seen even from a distance.
Nevertheless, thinking that he would not be easily found, [the searchers] followed his footprints right here as he drew near, and by means of those [footprints], him...
The sense is: "Let us search for him.
Now, one might ask: how can proud women (māninī) inquire about him? To this they reply: "of the proud women" (māninīnām).
Pride would not persist by his mere smile alone; it [would only persist] through their own particular cleverness (vaidagdhyaviśeṣa).
"By that very [smile] our pride was aroused; we have committed no fault therein. Or rather, "At that time, our pride was destroyed by that smile; for this reason, we are searching for Him.
Or rather, "Because of the separation from such a great delusion, we are unable to live even for a moment; therefore—"
The meaning is: "We shall ask. ||6||

The sequence of composition: The form "ita" is the past passive participle (niṣṭhā) derived from the root *iṇ*. By stating that he has "gone" (*gata*)—even though he was one who removed the pride of proud women with his smiles—the poet suggests his lack of deliberation in acting. ||6||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "O friends! He has certainly not been seen by them; because they lack flowers, he did not come near them. Therefore, let us ask the trees that possess beautiful blossoms," they said, beginning with "Kaccit" and so forth. *Kaccit* is used for an inquiry. Who are these Kuravakas and others? [They replied: "The younger brother of Rāma was seen."
Thus, the phrase [beginning with] "ity" must be supplied and turned back to the previous [verse]. Why is such an action improper for him?
To this they say: "Because it is the remover of the pride of us who are proud. For they say: "He is remembered as the remover of the pride of the proud women. (6)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thereupon, thinking that their own self—which is to be attained as the ultimate goal—had been disregarded, they thought, "What will these lowly beings know of the fruit of serving the True One? Thus, out of contempt, they went elsewhere and questioned the fragrant flowers such as the *kuravaka* and others. These five, beginning with the *kuravaka*, are the arrows of Kāma.
They are endowed with flowing blossoms. They say, "It is possible that he will be seen gathering their flowers," and add: "O Kuravaka! O Aśoka! O Nāgakeśara! O Punnāga!
O Campaka! You all, whose very nature is to benefit others, remain here making everything fragrant."

Regarding the question, "Have you seen him? if it is asked, "Whom are you asking?", they reply: "Rāma’s younger brother has gone"—the name is not stated directly out of affection or perhaps out of jealousy. [Objection:
But what has been taken from you, that you, being so proud, should ask this?
Regarding this, they say: "One whose smile removes pride" (*darpa-hara-smita*). His smile removes *darpa*, which is arrogance (*garva*).

Having taken away pride itself, which is his entire possession, he has departed. Pride is the root of honor; when pride is gone, honor naturally falls away. To this, he asks: "If you have seen him, then tell me."
The definition of pride (*garva*) is given in the *Rasārṇava*:
"Pride is said to be the contempt for others arising from sovereignty, beauty, youth, lineage, learning, strength, or the attainment of desired objects" (*Raṣu.* 2.25).

"That crookedness of emotion which, through the persistence of love, binds the heart independently and deeply, is called *māna* (pride/resentment). [Rasārṇavasudhākara 2.112] Thus [ends the section]. ||6||

Viśvanātha: Having entered the flower garden, [he thinks]: "Ah, it is indeed true that these trees, whose inner hearts are pure, serve their guests—the bees—with their own nectar. Approaching the trees, he says: "Is it well? Kuruvaka refers to the red amaranth (*amlāna*). Nāga refers to the *nāgakeśara*. Is it well?
The sense is: has he departed, or perhaps he remains right here, concealing himself?

Anticipating the question, "Why do you ask?", they say: "He whose smile steals away the pride—that is, the wealth of honor—of us women who are rich in pride; thus we have been rendered truly destitute."
At that very moment, seeing those trees with their tips shaken by a sudden wind, they said, "Alas!
We do not know [what has happened]," and shaking their heads, they remarked, "Enough of these harsh species of men," and departed for another place. ||6||
O auspicious Tulasī, beloved of Govinda’s feet! Have you,
together with your circle of friends, beheld that most beloved Acyuta?
Śrīdhara: Bearing you along with the swarms of bees, he is exceedingly dear to you; was he seen by you? ||7||

Vaṃśīdhara: O friends! This Tulasī is exceedingly dear [to Kṛṣṇa]. Therefore, having met her first, she should be questioned; thus they say. She is called *tulasī* because she "removes" (*syati*) "equality" (*tulam*); that is to say, there is nothing else equal to her. The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to the root *syati* according to the Uṇādi rules.
O you who are to be praised! You are the bringer of all auspiciousness merely through being seen, touched, and so forth.
The reason for this is: "you are dear to the feet of Govinda. Just as another person who is dear to Govinda purifies the world through being seen and so forth—
"By the sight, worship, or even conversation with my devotee, one who is burdened with great sins shall become a vessel for auspiciousness. This is from the *Ādi-purāṇa*.
By the word "Acyuta," he [the Lord] expresses that, in reality, there is an absence of passion toward women. (7)
*Caitanya-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: These individuals, being of the human species, generally favor the side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; therefore, thinking that they might not speak out of envy upon learning our assessment, [the author] has not explained them.

Considering her to be one who sides with them because she belongs to the female sex, and inferring from their constant observation of her particular joy that she must possess a special fortune, they imagine that she has seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa and ask Śrī Tulasī: "Kaccit... O auspicious one! Hei!
O you who bring auspiciousness to the world! Or, you who possess supreme good fortune. The reason for this is "Govinda.
You are the beloved of Govinda, the Lord of Gokula, just as in the verse beginning, "The Fortune (Śrī) whose lotus-feet...
Alternatively, the word *caraṇa* here merely indicates respect, as in the expression, "the teachers say" (*ācārya-caraṇā vadanti*).
"And now, with humility, [he shows] respect"—the meaning is "O beloved of the Lord of Gokula.

By this, his necessity for coming is intended to be expressed. The reason for his being so dear is indicated by the word "together" (saha). Furthermore, your attention to that matter might not be possible; therefore, he is exceedingly dear to you.

Through the use of *śleṣa* (double entendre), it is also suggested that those like us have surpassed our beloved; by the phrase "together with the swarms of bees," her excellence is demonstrated, since this indicates that even the bees are worthy of following her. Alternatively, her extreme dearness is revealed, for because of that very dearness, even those arrows (*śilīmukha*) are not turned back.
Because of this indication, it is also suggested that it is impossible for those intoxicated [bees] to conceal themselves with their humming.
Therefore, the sense is: "He has certainly come into your presence and has been seen by you. By the pun on the word *acyuta*, it is further reinforced that he shall never be separated from you. (7)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thinking, "These servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, being of the human species, might not speak out of envy upon recognizing our identity," and regarding them as if they were their own friends, and anticipating a meeting through their exceptional good fortune, they ask Śrī Tulasī: "Kaccit... (Is it well?)... [and so forth].

Thus: "O Kalyāṇī! O you who bring auspiciousness to the world, or rather, O you who possess supreme good fortune! The reason for this is: she is addressed as such because her two beloved feet belong to Govinda, the Lord of Gokula, who is intent upon manifesting His own entire sweetness; or else, [she is so called] because she is dear to those two [feet].

Even greater good fortune than that of Mahālakṣmī is indicated. This is because, despite great effort, even for one desiring Lakṣmī, the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—which manifest His complete divinity—are naturally dearer. The absence of metaphors such as "lotus-like" (for His feet) is due to jealousy arising from His being so beloved.

Therefore, even though you are accompanied by swarms of bees (*ali-kula*), he who bears you—even now—having first held you as part of his *vaijayantī* garland or having recently plucked you to wear you in the form of a wreath and the like; for this very reason, because of your extreme dearness to him, have you been seen by him at all? [The phrase] "by swarms of bees" refers to her constant state.

The state of being composed of *makaranda* (honey/nectar) implies that he is never to be abandoned; likewise, it is indicated that his buzzing cannot be suppressed by those who are intoxicated. Therefore, the sense is that since he has necessarily come into your presence, he must have been seen by you. "Acyuta" means one who is never separated from you.
The statement "it becomes so" serves to reinforce that very point. By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), the phrase "by swarms of bees" implies:
"He supports you—who have many lovers—out of affection, yet he does not support us, who are devoted to him alone; therefore, we are surpassed by those who are dear.
Alternatively, it may mean: "He is one by whom everything previously dear has been surpassed"—this is a speech of envy and malice.

The structural arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): O you whose two feet are dear to Govinda, the illustrious Viṣṇu! Or rather, the word "feet" (*caraṇa*) here merely indicates respect, as in the expression "the feet of the teacher" (*ācārya-caraṇaḥ*).
And this respect is now expressed through humility as "O beloved of the Lord of Gokula. (7)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "O friends! These [companions] of His, being mostly like that [Lord], will not speak even upon seeing [Him]. But Tulasī, because of her feminine nature, has a tender heart; therefore, it is likely she will indeed speak, for she has seen Him and, out of affection for Him," so [it was said]. Tat...
"Let us ask her as it were," they said—"O Tulasī," and so forth. "O auspicious one! O long-lived one!
The reason for her being auspicious is: "O you who are dear to the feet of Govinda! Has Acyuta, who is exceedingly dear to you, been seen?
The reason for his being exceedingly dear is: "bearing [or holding] you. Just so, along with the swarms of bees.
Because of that love for you, she carries you even when you are swarmed by swarms of bees. ||7||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Trees such as the *aśvattha* are without flowers, while others such as the *kuravaka* are without fruit; these men do not know suffering, and they are the objects of their beloved’s trust, following him in private. If, when this is made known, agitation arises in him, then who can know?

Thinking, "What would happen? they did not give an answer. [They thought: "Tulasī is of the female species; she is dear to Kṛṣṇa even in the absence of fruits and flowers; she will understand our suffering. Thus, anticipating a vision of Kṛṣṇa, they asked: "O Tulasī! O auspicious one! O you whose form is auspicious! O you who are ever possessed of good fortune! Therein—

The word "hetu" (cause) is a qualification of the womb (*garbha*) for one who is dear to the feet of Govinda. It is an address to her whose feet of Govinda are dear, or who is dear to the feet of Govinda. "Govinda" refers to him who is bound by his vow to protect Gokula. This too is a means of attaining [him] for us; even more so than Lakṣmī.

"Your good fortune is greater," [she said], "because he dwells solely upon her breast. For this very reason, though you are followed by swarms of bees and have many lovers, he has abandoned you; and though she has but one lover, she has not abandoned us."

What kind of person is so exceedingly dear to you? Or rather, he by whom those who were previously dear, such as myself and others, have been surpassed; or else, he by whom the pleasure of love (*ratimukha*) has been transcended due to his independence. Even now, having abandoned us, he continues to engage in amorous play with you, free from any lapse in his graceful dalliance. This is the underlying meaning—as follows:
"Even though Lakṣmī is present, his excessive affection is directed toward you alone; likewise, even in our presence, he will show affection toward you alone.
Why then is this hidden by Vāta? There is no harm whatsoever in telling it to you, so let it be told by you. (7)

Viśvanātha: "These women, who support our side and understand the heartache caused by the Cupid residing in the hearts of women, will be compassionate; therefore, let us ask them. Having approached them, he [addressed] Tulasī, the most preeminent among them.
They asked: "Is it well? [The reply is: "O auspicious one!"—we are inauspicious due to our separation from Kṛṣṇa;
you alone are well. The reason for this is: "O Govinda! Alternatively, the word *caraṇa* here merely indicates respect, as in the expression "the teachers say" (*ācārya-caraṇā vadanti*).

"Are you not also lovers of His feet? "True," they replied, "but she alone is the fortunate one because of her superior virtues and because there is no separation [between them]. "He departed while indeed bearing you. "In that matter, the very cause is the excellence of your fragrance."

They manifested [this]. The sense is: we conclude that our failure to grasp you—despite your being borne by one who is fond of fragrance and who disregards even the agitation caused by thousands of bees along with swarms of bees—is solely due to your lacking such a fragrance. ||7||
Have you seen Mālatī, Mallikā, Jāti, or Yūthikā?
Has Mādhava departed, bringing joy to you with the touch of his hand?
Śrīdhara: Although he possesses an abundance of virtues, they ask out of humility, thinking, "Perhaps he might see us"—thus, "O Mālatī," etc.
O Mālatī, Mallikā, Jāti, and Yūthikā: was he seen by you?
Did he depart, generating affection for you by the touch of his hand? Here, [the distinction between] Mālatī and Jāti...
A further distinction is to be observed. ||8||
Vaṃśīdhara: Only those who are humble despite possessing beauty, wealth, and learning are beholders of the Blessed One, and no others.
[This is stated in the verse: "By means of birth, deeds, age, form, learning, sovereignty, wealth, and so forth..."
"If he were not possessed of such arrogance, this would be my favor toward him"—thus it was said.

Regarding the phrase "even though these possess an excess of qualities": *mālatī* is so called because Rādhā’s delight (*rati*) is in her; since *ra* and *la* are interchangeable, and because it belongs to the *bahv-ādi* group, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. By this, because she is dear to him, she is also dear to him. *Mallaḥ*.

She is called *mallikā* because she possesses a fragrance superior to all flowers. According to the *Medinīkośa*, the word *malla* refers to a vessel, a skull, a species of fish, or a powerful person; thus, she is dear to him as one who possesses a most excellent fragrance.
Furthermore, she is called *jātī* because, like the *jāti* caste, she is beloved by all. This term does not end in the suffix *ktin*.

However, she possesses a cluster in the form of a bunch; thus, *yūthikā* means "one who has a hundred petals" (*śatapatrīkā*), according to Vijayadhvaja. He began to take a cluster of her flowers for the sake of his beloved, and was certainly seen by her. May that supreme Ramā and her husband, the beloved Mādhava, [protect us].

Like the spring season, he is a bringer of light; and it is indicated that among the female servants who were in bloom, he engaged in playful jesting with jealousy through the touch of his hand and the marking of nail-scratches and the like. ||8||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not commented upon.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Nevertheless, thinking that she might not speak out of her own pride in being honored, [the author] has indeed bowed down and offered flowers, for she is surely a servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Free from pride, these very women ask: "Mālatī? Each is addressed individually due to their agitation;

therefore, [the question] "What of it? has been explained by them. In that context, "What of it? carries the sense of the continuing word "kaccit" (I hope). At least the sight [of her] has already occurred; in that regard, was there even a touch?

The intention is that we ask specifically about the fact that [the child] has been born. Alternatively, it means they consider the sight of those flowers possible through the agency of Śrī’s hand picking the most excellent blossoms.
And the intention is that by saying "you have gone," it is indeed appropriate for them to tell us this because of their shared suffering.
Thus, regarding those female slaves in their menses, the intended jest was one characterized by jealousy, indicated by such things as nail-marks. ||8||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Fearing that she might not speak to him due to her co-wife status, the maidservants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa ask—"O Mālatī! Addressing each one with affection because they consider them all to be maidservants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by offering them fine flowers, "Va" is as before; "Have you gone? is asked by them.
This has been explained. Alternatively, they imagine that vision of them as before—namely, "joy.
The phrase "having gone" means by the touch of the hand; that is to say, by the gathering of your excellent flowers through the hands of Śrī. Therefore, his coming to your side [is justified].
The sense is that this is indeed possible. By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), the scratching with fingernails upon those maidservants is intended as a playful jest.

They speculate on the purpose of gathering flowers—since the flowers are being cut by the very nails—saying, "Mādhava. The meaning is: for the sake of sporting with honey, that is, for the sake of sporting with sweet flavor (*madhura-rasa*).
"Lakṣmī’s husband" means for the sake of Lakṣmī; this is a statement of jealousy.

In reality, however, as before, she is Śrī Rādhā herself, and [the ornaments] are indeed for her decoration. And that occurs either by the course of destiny, or through pure nature, or spontaneously, even in the absence of their conscious awareness of her.
It should be understood that it emerges spontaneously from its own mouth as a manifestation of everything. ||8||
The sequence of composition: the intention is that Mādhava is the spring (vasanta) because of his fondness for flowers. ||8||

*Bṛhatkrama-sandarbha*: "O friends! He has been seen by her; it is not being told even from the very moment of his arrival. Therefore, let us ask Mālatī and the others, for among these, they are like our own sisters.
Thus they inquire: "Mālatī," and so forth—"O Mālatī! O Mallikā! O Jāti! etc.

"O Yūthikā! 'Mādhava has departed, bringing joy to you with the touch of his hand'—by this reason, indicated as if by a *siddha* (an accomplished being), he was seen; this is beyond doubt. The word 'kaccit' is used solely for the purpose of address. Therefore, let our words be told exactly as they are: by which path did he go?"
The meaning of the state [of being]. ||8||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thereafter, not having obtained [an answer], they reflected: "She is jealous because of her co-wife status;

she has not spoken because she considers herself too proud to be compared to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thinking thus, and seeing a flowering creeper ahead, they considered: "She will surely speak [of Him] with these flower ornaments, free from pride."
They said: "O Mālatī! O Mallikā! O Jāti! O Yūthikā!

Have you all seen him? Tell me! Having seen the gathering of flowers along with their stalks, she asks out of agitation born of jealousy: "By the touch of your hands [have you seen him]? regarding your flowers.

By gathering flowers with her glorious hands, she produces for you pleasure and happiness; has she followed this path? Since she plucks the flowers with her very nails, it is through jest that the nail-marks themselves have been revealed.
They imagine the gathering of flowers to be for a specific purpose—namely, Mādhava, because he is the Lord of Lakṣmī—for her sake.

The gathering of flowers is for the purpose of binding her hair; or rather, he is the lord of that splendor and abundance, and thus the gathering of flowers is for the purpose of adorning his own limbs, which are composed of blossoms. Or again, Mādhava is like the personified springtime, and for that very reason there is the gathering of flowers—just as [he would adorn] us with the touch of his hands, embraces, and so forth.

Having brought comfort, he cast the sinners into some ocean and departed somewhere; likewise, having bestowed pleasure upon you by the touch of his hand, the scratching of his nails, and so forth, he has gone from somewhere, for he is no longer seen. Therefore, you too experience the sorrow of separation. Thus it is said:

The sense is that because they are overwhelmed by a burden of suffering, they lack the capacity to grant a reply. Having reflected, "What will these classes of women say, being devoted to their own interests with minds concealed by affection? For it would be fruitless," these trees and others have been obtained as benefactors of others through their fruits.

"Like sages devoted to meditation, let us ask them. Having gone forward, Viśvanātha asks the mango trees and others: "Alas! Intoxicated by the pride of her great beauty, she does not even look at us; therefore, let us ask these women like myself, who are devoid of such beauty, about her rivals. Thus he speaks, turning elsewhere.

Having gone, they said: "Mālatī. By that touch with the hand for the purpose of gathering your flowers, the internal distinction between the *mālatī* and *jāti* species should be observed through the signs of their being in full bloom during the rainy season and autumn respectively. ||8||
the mango, the priyāla, the jackfruit, the āsana, the kovidāra, the rose-apple, the arka, the bilva, the bakula, the mango, the kadamba, and the nīpa;
May others who exist for the sake of others and are well-disposed toward us praise the path of Kṛṣṇa for us, whose minds are devoid of devotion.

Śrīdhara: [He asks] "May these [trees], which satisfy all living beings with fruits and so forth, see [the Lord]"—thus he says, "The mango... and so on. There is a distinction between the sub-species of mango (*cūta*) and mango-grove (*āmra*), as well as between *kadamba* and *nīpa*.
O mangoes and the rest, and others who exist for the sake of others—that is, those whose very birth (*bhava*) is solely for the sake of others.

Those dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā— meaning those residing near its shores— are you who should describe, that is, tell us, the path of Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇa-padavī), the way of Kṛṣṇa, for us whose minds are desolate and whose hearts are empty. ||9||
Vaṃśīdhara: Due to the difference between the qualities of sourness and sweetness in the mango and the *cūta*, there are intermediate species:

the sour-mango species and the sweet-mango species. The *nīpa* has few flowers, while the *kadamba* has many flowers. The *priyāla* is the *rājādana*. The *panasa* is the thorny-fruited tree. The *asana* has yellow heartwood.

The *kovidāra* is the *kañcanāraka*. The *jambū* has black fruit and glossy leaves. The *arka* is well-known, as is the *bilva*. The *bakula* is commonly known as *maulasarī*. The meaning is as follows:
the sense is that by the power of austerity in the form of serving sacred sites (*tīrtha*), they are capable of warding off the suffering of others.

"Deprived" means separated; "whose souls are struck" refers to those gopīs whose very selves are [lost]—or alternatively, it means those who have been abandoned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for whom Kṛṣṇa Himself is their soul.
Among these, even the sun, though devoid of excellent flowers and fruits, is mentioned because of its being dear to Śiva. Or else:

If you yourself declare that you belong to Śrī Vṛndāvana, then we shall establish you alone as being situated above all others. As for the repetition of the mango, *āmra*, *nīpa*, and *kadamba* trees, it should be understood as arising from the instability of the mind. ||9||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Fearing that they might not speak of this out of devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they inquire of other authorities who are like sages, beginning with the word "cūta. *Cūta* is a species of creeper; *āmra*...
This is the class of trees. In the very same context as before, however, poets do not apply the term "creeper" (*latā*) to the mango tree;

yet in regions such as Madhyadeśa, those [trees] are seen to have the form of creepers. Furthermore, regarding the *nīpa*, it should be understood that it is a large-flowered tree characterized by abundant pollen, according to the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon which states: "The word *nīpa* may refer to the *dhūlikadamba*. As for the *priyāla*:
Its seed alone is consumed because it is renowned for its excellent seeds. The *panasa* has thorny fruit.

The *asana* is the yellow *sāla*. The *kovidāra*, which has twin leaves, is well known in the Vindhya region and elsewhere as *koyilāva*. This is a variety of *kāñcanāra* similar to the *kāñcanāra*. The *arka* is extremely inferior.
By the word "asked," their extreme longing is made manifest.
[An objection: "But what is our purpose in telling that to you? To this they reply with the word "para" (supreme).
Here, according to the opinion of Śrī Svāmipāda, the reading is *bhavakāḥ* without the vowel *i*. *Bhava* means birth.
This is because of the explanation. In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the reading containing the vowel *i*—namely *bhavikam*—is seen everywhere;
therefore, its meaning is "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*) or "prosperity" (*abhyudaya*). Its meaning is also that very same thing.
Nevertheless, [the name] "Yamunopakūlā" is used because, by virtue of dwelling at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), she is truthful and compassionate.

The sense is that truth alone is to be proclaimed, not deception. The analysis of the compound is as follows: those whose banks (*kūla*) are near (*upa*) are *upakūlāḥ*; and "those on the banks near the Yamunā" is *yamunopakūlāḥ*.
Anticipating the objection, "Why do you not simply search for and seize him yourselves?", he [responds] by making known his own distress.
Generating compassion, they speak with a sense of dejection—the meaning being that their consciousness is struck by the pain of separation because they are devoid of self-control.

Therefore, the implication is that, as if dead, they are unable to seek [him] themselves. Previously, inquiries about his whereabouts were made to almost everyone; however, among these [ladies], no response was obtained from the earlier ones.
Having ascertained the fourfold [path], one merely prays for the indication of its route. ||9||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: These [trees] are servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa or Lakṣmī. Fearing that they might not speak of Him, they ask other trustworthy persons—beginning with "the mango" (*cūta*). There is a distinction between the mango and the *āmra* due to the difference in their juice, and a distinction between the *kadamba* and the *nīpa* due to the difference in their color and other qualities. The *priyāla*...

The *sālabheda* is the *asana*, the yellow *sāla*. The *arka* tree, though lacking superior flowers and fruit, is mentioned here because its flowers are dear to the illustrious Śiva. Others include the *pīlu*, *karīra*, *madhuka*, *nāgaraṅga*, *nārikela*, *pūga*, *tāla*, *kadalī*, *lavalī*, *badarī*, and so forth.
[Objection: "But what purpose do we have in speaking of that to you? To this they reply with the word *para*.

In the opinion of Śrī Svāmipāda, the reading here is *bhavakāḥ* without the vowel *i*, because he explains *bhava* as "birth. The form *bhavikāḥ*, containing the vowel *i*, is seen everywhere in the context of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

And thus, "bhavika-maṅgala" means prosperity; its meaning is the same as that [of *abhyudaya*]. Nevertheless, by the phrase "on the banks of the Yamunā," her inability to endure the suffering of others is indicated. Furthermore, because her brother, the illustrious Yama—the son of the Sun—is the one authorized to punish the worlds for their sins.
Because she had become like that through association with one who had descended [into the world] out of an inability to endure the suffering of others,

this story is indeed well-known in the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Śrī Yamunā-māhātmya*. Alternatively, the sense is that, by virtue of residing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one must speak only the truth and must not deceive.

Anticipating the objection, "Why do you not simply search for and seize him yourselves? they speak with dejection, generating compassion by making known their own suffering—the meaning being "of those whose souls are bereft," that is, whose consciousness is destroyed by separation;
or alternatively, "of those who have abandoned the Self," meaning Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the Beloved.
The implication is that we are as if dead and thus unable to seek [him] ourselves.

Previously, inquiries regarding his vision were made concerning all [the sages]; however, in these cases, because there is the possibility of ascertaining his vision due to their specific qualities, one merely requests instruction on the path to him. ||9||

The structural arrangement [of the text] is as follows: the *cūta* belongs to the class of creepers (*latā-jāti*), whereas the *āmra* belongs to the class of trees (*vṛkṣa-jāti*). In the former case alone, the state of being a creeper (*latātva*) is applied. Regarding the term *nīpa*, it should be understood from the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon that "the *nīpa* occurs among the *dhūli-kadamba*"; thus, it is to be known as a great-flowered tree characterized primarily by its pollen. Even though the *arka* is extremely lowly...
By the word "asked," the intensity of their longing is made manifest. ||9||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "O friends! They have been forbidden by him for this very reason;

since they do not speak, what is the use of obstructing them? These [gopīs], moreover, are residents of a sacred ford (*tīrtha-vāsī*) by virtue of dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā, and are speakers of truth due to their altruistic nature."
"Thus [are] the trees. Let us ask them," they said, and so they questioned others again, beginning with "O fallen one," and so forth.

The *kadamba* and *nīpa* are mentioned separately because of their internal differences. As for those others whose names were not grasped, in order to dispel their pride, [the text says] "on the banks of the Yamunā," indicating their residence at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

"Those who bear the burden of others' welfare and those who are skilled in the welfare of others must certainly speak"—anticipating the objection that "we are silent ones," they say: "the path of Kṛṣṇa. For it is possible to describe a path even without the employment of speech, through activities such as [pointing with] sprouts and so forth. Therefore, [they mention] the path.
Tell him only the way, but do not reveal your own wretchedness by being devoid of selfhood. ||9||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: "Cūta... and so forth. The distinction between the mango (*cūta*) and the *āmra* is by way of their taste. The distinction between the *kadamba* and the *nīpa* is by way of their color. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "the term *nīpa* may refer to the *dhūli-kadamba*.
A *nīpa* is characterized primarily by its pollen and possesses large flowers, whereas a *kadamba* has flowers of equal proportions [to its leaves].

The *priyāla* is known for its beautiful seeds; the *panasa* is the jackfruit tree (*kaṭaṅkī-phala*). The *asana* is called the yellow *śāla*; the *kovidāra* is the *camarika*, according to the *Amara-kośa*. The *bṛhat-patra* is known as the *kāñcanāra*. The *jambu* and others are well-known indeed.

May the Madhūka, coconut, Karīra, betel nut, Tāla, Tamāla, and other such trees all proclaim the path of Kṛṣṇa to us. If it is asked, "What benefit will there be for us in speaking of Kṛṣṇa? [the answer follows].
Regarding this, they say: "Those whose existence is for the sake of others" means those whose birth (*bhava*) is solely for the benefit of others, that is, for the purpose of assisting others.
If the reading is *bhāvikāḥ*, it means that which is auspicious (*bhāvika*) solely for the sake of others—that is to say, a praiseworthy protection (*praśastāvaraṇa*). Of these, they...
The constant practice of what is commendable and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—this indeed is declared to be auspiciousness; it is auspiciousness itself, brought about by oneself.

Furthermore, for the sake of further narration and to offer them praise, those dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā have been sprinkled with its water as if she herself were personified devotion. Therefore, let those very devotees, who are compassionate and dwell along the Yamunā’s shore in order to behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa, speak.

If it is asked, "Why not seek [the Lord] by oneself? What is the point of asking? they reply: "For those whose souls are abandoned" means for those whose minds are empty and who are terrified, being unable to search on their own. Alternatively, it refers to those from whom the Self—the venerable Kṛṣṇa—is separated or devoid.
"May they describe the path of Kṛṣṇa—the means for attaining Kṛṣṇa—for us who are wretched, having been abandoned by Kṛṣṇa.
The intention is: 'Please tell us that very same means by which Śrī Kṛṣṇa was attained by you.
Viśvanātha: "Oh! These [gopīs] [are speaking] regarding their co-wife Tulasī and from that Kṛṣṇa..."
"Though they know [the truth], they do not speak out of fear, thinking, 'Enough with these who are dependent on others. Therefore, let us go elsewhere;
these very people dwelling at the Yamunā-tīrtha must be those whose remembrance of Viṣṇu is inferred by their very stillness; thus, they are not liars."

They said, "We shall speak," and the people of the world replied, "The mango tree. There is a distinction between the mango (*cūta*) and the *āmra* based on their classification as a creeper and a tree, respectively.

The *nīpa* is the *dhūlikadamba*, which has large flowers; the *kadamba* has small flowers and is extremely fragrant. The *priyāla* is a species of *śāla*; the *asana* is the yellow *śāla*; and the *kovidāra* is a species of *kāñcanāra*.

The arka tree, though lowly, remains ever near Him because he is dear to the Lord of the Gopīs. As for others, such as the coconut and breadfruit trees—you who are like us, devoid of self—tell us the path of Kṛṣṇa!
To what purpose indeed would we tell it? To this they reply: "It is only for the sake of others that it is auspicious."
Those for whom there is prosperity; those for whom [the river] Yamunā is on the near bank—these belong to the *gaḍvādi* group. (9)
O Earth, what austerity have you performed that you shine with the hair on your body standing erect from the thrill of the festival of touching the feet of Keśava?
Was it born from the foot, or from the stride of the wide-striding one (Viṣṇu), or perhaps from the embrace of the one in the form of a boar?

Śrīdhara: O Earth, O you who are cherished by the earth, what austerity have you performed, such that you possess the festival of the touch of Keśava’s feet—that is, for whom there is a festival through the touch of Keśava’s feet? Why is this so?
Because you shine, O dear one, with your limbs thrilled and bristling with horripilation. In this regard, there is a specific distinction:
He asks: "Is this festival arising from Your feet now produced merely by the touch of one part of Your foot? Or rather, it is not merely that;
for even before the strides of the Wide-strider (Urukrama), all was traversed by the foot of Trivikrama. Oh, or else—"
It is not merely this; rather, even before that, by embracing the body of the Boar.
Therefore, you must surely have seen him—show him to me! ||10||

Vaṃśīdhara: To announce their lack of caste, they fell down helplessly and said, "O Earth... [The absence of the *guṇa* vowel change is an archaic Vedic usage]. He raises the doubt, "How was the festival known? with the word "kutaḥ" (from where?). [It was known] by the hairs (*aṅgaruhaiḥ*) growing on their bodies. There, at that festival, [the fragrance] arose from the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet in one particular spot. Now...
The word *vā* indicates the second alternative; *āho svid* indicates the third alternative in this sense.
