Or rather (*yad vā*): because he nourishes the *āhava*, the battle of amorous play, therefore [he is superior] to that very youth Nanda. Here, by the word *Keśava*, the cowherd girls refer specifically to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who possesses excellent hair.
"Because another meaning is not intended," says Vijayadhvaja. (10)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "What penance have you performed, O Earth? and so forth. "O Earth"—the word *kṣiti* is derived from the roots *kṣi* (to dwell) and *gam* (to go);

the suffix *ti* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules, meaning "that in which one dwells. From that, the feminine suffix *ī* is applied; thus, in the vocative case, it becomes *kṣite*. What austerity has been practiced by you, such that...?

She is one for whom the touch of Keśava’s feet is a festival. He states the sign of that festival: "O fair-limbed one, you shine forth, thrilled with horripilation like trees with new shoots. The word *api* functions as an interrogative particle. Is this festival born from the feet of Keśava, who resides in only one part [of his body], or rather from the heroic stride (*vikrama*) of Urukrama?

By the extraordinary stride of Vāmana, or rather by the fortune of being embraced by the one in the form of a boar; otherwise, this fruit of your asceticism would not have come to you from this [source]. This is the intended meaning. (10–13)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, by praying for the path and remembering the path, one casts one's gaze upon the ground; perceiving its all-pervasiveness, one envisions the sight of it, and considering the emergence of tender *dūrvā* sprouts and the like as a thrill of horripilation (*pulaka*), which belongs to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Having honored him with the very festival of the touch of her lotus-feet, they describe her great good fortune while indicating his supreme excellence—“What of him? Here, *tapas* refers to action that generates merit.
The word *api* implies: “Is this festival born from her feet [not enough]? Is Viṣṇu not also threefold?”

It was not because of the treading of the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu—the Trivikrama described in the Vedas—who manifested His divine opulence for the purpose of traversing the three worlds, that all things were overcome; rather, it was certainly not so, for at that time there was no such extraordinary splendor of festival. Or perhaps let it not be so.

Or rather, they say that even in the direct enjoyment of the Lord—who manifested as the Great Boar for the sake of their deliverance through the mere touch of His foot—it was not accomplished; thus they say, "Ah!
Or else, they consider austerity itself to be a festival arising from the touch of Keśava’s feet.

"Was it due to the touch of Trivikrama’s foot? Or rather, was it due to the embrace of the Varāha-form?"—this is the implied meaning of "Tell me that. By thus surpassing each [previous incarnation], the specific greatness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indicated. Therefore, [the question arises]: "How shall we endure separation from Him? Or rather: [the rest of the verse follows].
The meaning is: "You are supremely fortunate, whereas we, being devoid of that, are indeed unfortunate; therefore, out of compassion, please show us correctly the path to that state. ||10||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, by making known his own distress, he fell to the ground, overwhelmed by the arising of excessive sorrow; or rather, by praying for the path and remembering that path, he fixed his gaze upon it.
Seeing the emergence of tender durva grass sprouts and perceiving that her body was covered in horripilation born from the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet,
they recognized her supreme good fortune and, out of extreme distress, said: "Why [is this]?"— "O Keśava!"— [they cried].

The state of being the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratva*) is as previously explained. Alternatively, by the etymology "one who possesses excellent hair" (*prakṛṣṭāḥ keśāḥ santi asya*), supreme beauty is indicated. By the phrase "shining forth specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa bhāsīti*), it is intended that the festival has a unique cause consisting of a particular splendor.

The employment of metaphors such as "lotus-feet" is intended to express the festival [of joy] arising from the mere touch of those very surfaces, even without regard for qualities such as softness. Such a festival would not occur through the mere connection with the feet alone, but rather through sexual union (*sambhoga*) itself; this is another perspective.
They said, "Ah! By this, something else was suggested by them.
Or rather, by beholding such splendor and by the very touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, they celebrated that festival as being the most excellent of all, thereby indicating her supreme good fortune.
They describe it as follows: "Even so. This festival has arisen from the feet [of Viṣṇu].

Was it perhaps because of the foot of Śrī Viṣṇu—who manifested his divine power for the purpose of traversing the three worlds—that all was traversed? But no, certainly not; for at that time, such a specific splendor of a festival had not yet been attained. Oh, no!

Or rather, let it be; they say that even in the direct enjoyment with the Blessed One— who manifested the form of the Great Boar for the sake of their deliverance by the mere touch of His foot— it was not accomplished, as indicated by the word "āho."

Or rather, the festival arising from his feet occurred because of the touch of the foot of Trivikrama; or else, it came about by reason of being embraced by the form of Varāha—this is the implied meaning of "tell that. Thus, in every way, the specific greatness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in relation to those various [deities] has been indicated. Therefore:

"How can we endure separation from that? Or rather, the underlying intention of the sequence of verses is: "Since you are supremely fortunate, while we are unfortunate being deprived of him, please show us his path out of compassion"—this is the meaning of "What of you? (10).

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: O friends! These [ascetics], being absorbed in meditation upon Him alone with such motionlessness, do not even hear our words; how much less will they speak? Therefore, let us go past them and ask the Earth herself. She, at least—
"Wherever she goes, let her go; there is nothing that shall not be within her range, and that very region shall be seen by her.
Thus they act, thinking, "The bristling of her hair indicates that she is traveling to that place"—[and so they ask], "What have they done?
and so forth. O Earth, what austerity has been performed by you? Indeed, an austerity has been performed.
"How was it inferred? To this they say: "O, [the word] *harṣe* means 'in joy'; you are one for whom there is a festival (*utsava*) through the touch of Keśava’s feet. [The questioner asks:

"How was it inferred that you yourself are a festival? To this they say: "If you shine while being thrilled (*pulakitā*) by trees consisting mostly of the hairs of your body, then your own good fortune (*sva-sukṛta*) is something that cannot be told by yourself. If [you object]: "That is so," [we reply: it is indeed so.
"If you do not speak of that, then let it be told by her [the Earth] herself; listen," they said—"even... and so forth.

By the "striding" (vikrama) of the Wide-Strider (Urukrama), Vāmana—that is, by the touch of his foot—or else by the "embracing" (parirambhaṇa) of the Lord in the form of the Boar (Varāha), that is, the incarnation as Varāha; by either one of these two causes.
It must have been one or the other: either the touch of one's foot or the embrace of all.
Therefore, you have seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa; tell us, where is he? This is the remainder of the sense. ||10-13||

The Essence of Affection (312): It is indeed the very nature of the highest excellence of affection that it causes its own object to be experienced as preeminent in every respect. For instance, by Bharata’s love for the deer, even the earth was described as being of great fortune due to the touch of its hooves—what more need be said?
"The ascetic practice performed by this ascetic woman is such that this earth... and so forth;
likewise: "What has been done for you, O Earth? and so on.

Here, in the first half [of the verse], there is a statement regarding the greatness of the sweetness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa out of love; in the second half, by that same [feeling], there is a statement regarding the worthlessness of everything else. And here, the word "api" (even) is used in the sense of "kim" (what/why). Consequently, this transformation of joy arising from his feet is [due to] the stride of Urukrama, that is, Trivikrama.

Or was he born from the lifting of a foot? Or—*āho* being used here as an alternative—is this birth from a foot produced by the act of embracing due to the lovely form of the Boar? Indeed, it was not so; such is the meaning. *Api* may also be used in the sense of "even," as in the expression "there might even be [something] from clarified butter. And therefore:
Even from the wide-striding prowess of Urukrama, this transformation arising from his foot would be only slight; such is the meaning. ||10||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Not finding anything further beyond this, they say—presuming that because the earth has come within the range of their vision through the description of her path and because she is horripilating, Śrī Kṛṣṇa must certainly have been seen by her: "What was done by you? O Earth! What austerity was performed by you, since...?
"You are possessed of supreme good fortune.
[The interlocutor asks: "How indeed was this known by you? To that they reply: "O Keśava! [This means: He who dwells within both Ka (Brahmā) and Īśa (Śiva);
what need is there to mention anyone else? Or, it refers to Him who is endowed with excellent hair.

You shine forth as she for whom there is a festival at the touch of his feet; therein the sign is that you are "romāñcitā," thrilled with horripilation by the hair on your body—by the sprouts of grass and the like—and thus you look exceedingly beautiful. Seeing this horripilation, the arising of an emotion (*bhāva*) is inferred, for horripilation does not occur without an emotion.
The arising of a feeling does not occur without the touch of the feet;
therefore, surely there is no touch of the feet. Regarding this, they imagine—"api" (even)—in the sense of possibility:
"this festival is now such that the touch of the feet is possible. It is not merely this much; why is that?
This festival is not conceivable as arising from the mere touch of your feet, which are softer than even fresh butter,
since you are indifferent to qualities such as softness;
or rather, it is not merely this much that has occurred previously, for the sake of traversing the three worlds through the strides of the Wide-Strider (Urukrama).

Nor can this festival be said to be caused by the treading upon all his limbs with the foot of the manifested Trivikrama form, for such splendor was not present at that time; or rather, it is not produced merely by the touch of the foot,
but rather [by the touch] of the Varāha form manifested previously for the sake of your upliftment.

There is no doubt that this festival arising from his feet consists of an embrace or a full-body caress upon all the limbs of the Blessed One; we ask for the specific reason why you, who are supremely fortunate, out of compassion for us unfortunate ones, reveal this path. ||10||
Viśvanātha: Oh! Are these people not hearing my question because they are absorbed in meditation upon Viṣṇu?
Or rather, are even these residents of the holy place (tīrtha) so heartless that they do not answer at all?
Alas! These residents of the holy place have not ascertained the truth, wondering "who knows" or "who does not know him."

How is it that they are needlessly censured? When someone said, "Let him who saw that person—who has thus become certain of the truth that he knows him—be questioned," she was asked by all: "Dear friend! Who indeed is that person? Do you know him? Thereupon, she pointed to the earth with her forefinger.

He revealed it. And then [Kṛṣṇa said]: "It is indeed true that you say, 'Wherever He exists, there is this very earth'; thus, there is no separation from Him even for this earth, nor for Kṛṣṇa’s own groups of fathers, friends, beloveds, and servants."

Because she is unfamiliar with the suffering of separation, the earth alone is fortunate; therefore, a question regarding her does not arise as it did for those who preceded her. Rather, reflecting on how even they might become entirely free from the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa by performing the same penance, they ask, desiring to know her ancient austerity: "What..."
Thus:

O Earth, O dweller of the earth! What austerity have you performed, such that you shine as one for whom there is a festival through the touch of Keśava’s feet, since [your surface] is covered by hair-like sprouts of grass rising up?
Wherever he stays, his body is covered with horripilation from the most excellent thrill;

there he remains as if touching you with his very feet. Since the bliss of contact with Kṛṣṇa’s limbs has pervaded you day and night, you ought to describe that austerity. As for us, we are unfortunate women separated from him. Therefore—
The sense is: "Even by merely hearing this, we shall have our purpose fulfilled.
Observing her as she remained silent, he himself infers from the recollection of past events, beginning with the word "api":
"From the stride of the Lord Trivikrama (Urukrama), that which was born from His foot..."

The attainment of the feet (aṅghri-prāptiḥ) occurs upon the attainment of the earth (bhū-prāptau); "saṃpūraḥ" means that if there, [there is] that very austerity characterized by the endurance of His great burden—this is the meaning. "Vai" is used for certainty or as a verse-filler (pāda-pūraṇe). Or rather, [is it not] by the embrace of the one in the form of the Great Boar (mahā-varāha-vapuṣaḥ)?

The meaning is: why is that very austerity—which is characterized by the attainment of pain arising from his firm embrace—[considered penance]? Furthermore, even that austerity which is the means for you to attain this festival [of union]—which is difficult for others to obtain—is composed of nothing but pleasure, because for you, a woman, it is characterized by union with a man; thus, it is not [penance].
The meaning is that someone other than you is fortunate. ||10||
O friend, has Acyuta come here with his beloved, the female deer, bringing complete delight to the eyes by displaying his limbs? May he grant you bliss.
The fragrance of the jasmine garland belonging to the head of the family blows here, colored by the saffron from the breasts of his beloved as she clings to his body.
Śrīdhara: Anticipating that Kṛṣṇa might have been seen due to the proximity of the doe's gaze, they say: "api" (could it be?).

O friend, O wife of the deer, has He approached? Has He come near with His beautiful limbs, such as His face, arms, and so forth? This indicates what was previously mentioned regarding His being with His beloved. Of the beloved...
The fragrance of a jasmine flower garland, stained by the saffron from the breasts of the noble lady as she was embraced by his limbs, is wafted by the wind toward the householder Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||11||
Vaṃśīdhara: O wife of the deer, O consort of the antelope!

[The breasts] are those whose two nipples have been reddened—that is, turned crimson—by the saffron from the breasts of the beloved; or else, as before, it refers to the saffron from the breasts of her who has had contact with the body of her beloved, Hari. Of the beloved.
"Or of the lovely one," [it is said]. The Lord of the Gopīs is the Kulapati (the leader of the clan). "Gandha" means that which possesses fragrance;

thus, "gandhavān" refers to the wind. The suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). The statement that the fragrance wafts here while its presence is not itself seen is an expression of the poetic figure *vyaṅgya* (suggestion). ||11||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, the following is considered here: Did the Blessed Lord disappear after taking someone with Him? Although this will become clear later, the Lord of Sages himself did not [state it] previously.
He has clearly stated this intention: that even though there are various manifestations of the Lord, he has a particular insistence on the Lord Himself in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, even though there are various respective retinues, his [insistence] is on those very inhabitants of Vraja; and likewise, even though there are...

Even among those very queens of Vraja, he was even more [beloved] than they; this is a secret that everyone indeed knew. However, even while they were present, they did not know that he was most exceedingly so in Śrī Rādhikā alone. This is the gradation of my own persistent insistence.

It is solely due to the varying degrees of excellence in each case. My mind falters to directly reveal this supreme secret; out of fear of appearing ignorant, I wish to inform you even by means of the words of her companions, since it is not perceived there even by those who are opposed to it.
We shall reveal it from time to time through the very function of the suggestive word (*vyañjanā*) as the occasion arises;

and if we should ever reveal it by our own impulse of inspiration, even then we shall not state its name directly. Let that be so for this [work], but let it be the same for others as well. Furthermore:

In all cases, it is only the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*) that reveals various aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), not the primary [denotative] function. And if that [suggestion] is elevated for the sake of expressing a specific nuance once the context has been determined, it would be exceedingly wondrous. Having this in mind, [the poet] first [expressed this] through the medium of a female friend.
When the Blessed Lord suddenly vanished after taking her with him,

the friends of that friend remained full of doubt; yet, although they were intent on searching for Subala’s younger sister and were somewhat overcome by madness, they remained occupied with searching for that couple even while accompanying her.
Because they were situated in separate groups, their efforts—manifesting from afar due to their lack of concentration on that [search]—were in vain as they wandered about;
yet, even without seeing the footprints mentioned below, they somehow perceived something here and there. For instance, their speech is as follows: "O female deer... and so forth.
In this case, the meaning understood from the entire sentence—even from all its individual words—is precisely that which suggests approval.

Consequently, their friendship directed toward that couple is perceived, and the longing to behold them constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). The word *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). This, then—
The meaning is "we honor [him]. Alternatively, *api* is used in the sense of a question; thus the meaning is "we ask this.
What is that? To this they say: "O friend! Acyuta has come near you, having arrived at your presence."
"Is it not indeed a wonder that he, who dwells in the forest, has come into our presence, we who are newcomers?
To this they reply: "Together with his beloved.
Indeed, that is certainly a wonder; however, wherever there is a sight of him, there is she as well.

What wonder is there in the fact that through association there is even greater happiness? Regarding this, they say: "By her alone, together with her limbs—which are variegated by various emotional expressions (anubhāvas) manifesting such bliss—there arises for you, for her, and for the eyes of those belonging to you, a state of perfect rest (sunirvṛti) that belongs to him alone."
Even from a mere glance, you spread—that is, extend—the supreme bliss upon seeing him in his company;
therefore, you ought not to conceal this from us. For we are his intimate companions, knowing his innermost nature, and we are able to know everything concerning him by the mere scent of him.

They say: "From the limbs of his beloved," and so forth. First, indeed, this very fragrance clearly reaches here with a plaintive tone—from the touch of that noble lady's limbs upon those [limbs] of the head of the clan, from the saffron clinging to her breasts there, and from the jasmine garland smeared with it there.
There, they spread a longing through words of high esteem.

By the term "eṇa-patnī," there is praise for her vision based on her very species; by the term "eṇa-patnī," according to Pāṇini’s traditional rule [Pāṇini 4.1.33], *patyur no yajña-saṃyoge*, it indicates that the eṇa deer are used for sacrificial purposes, and thus she [is the wife of such a sacrificer].

The praise [of the husband] is intended to show that the status of being the sacrificial wife (*yajña-patnī*) has been manifested; the praise of her fortune is expressed by the word "approached" (*upagata*), meaning he has come near her; furthermore, by the use of the word "beloved" (*priyayā*), there is an excellence of praise for both the seer and the object seen; and by the phrase "having attained an extraordinary state through the mutual union of their limbs," [the intimacy is emphasized].

"O friend, as before, you extend such perfect bliss to our eyes"— by these words, the excellence of her vision is shown. Furthermore, where there is such praise of the object of sight by the beloved, without any hesitation, saying "It is Acyuta," there [the same excellence] belongs even to those women who are attached to your lordship.
The praise [of her] is for the purpose of seeing that such a state is fitting:

first, as "the beloved" (kāntā) for that visible woman; then, as "the saffron from her body" (tad-aṅga-saṅgā) for the visible beloved who has attained what is difficult to obtain; and finally, as "the saffron" (kuca-kuṅkuma) for the visible saffron which has acquired its fortune through contact with her.

"Of that which is colored by it" means of the jasmine garland (*kunda-sraj*) which, through its connection with it, has acquired an excellence of beauty and is visible; "by its whiteness" refers to its own nature as being suitable for the splendor of its arising; and "of that very same [garland]" is implied.
"Of the head of the family" refers to the visible beloved. "Here" refers to that which has acquired the fortune of his fragrance.
Because it pervades the visible object and its location, it is called *vāta* (wind); having assimilated even that wind into itself, it moves of its own accord in every direction.
Thus, due to its association with various specific qualities, it is designated as "fragrance" (*gandha*)—the play of scent—and its excellence is thereby understood. ||11||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Just like Śrī Tulasī, she is also his eternal beloved; however, out of co-wifely jealousy, she might not speak [of his condition] unless prompted by His own will. Therefore, trusting her as a friend, they ask the female deer with the word "api" (also).
O wife of the male deer, you too surely know the pain of separation from a beloved; therefore—

The sense is: "Let it be told. There is a singular number (*ekatva*) because, due to the intensity of the pain of separation, her gaze falls upon only one person at a distance; and there is a plural number (*bahutva*) in the words *dṛśām* ("of the glances") and *vaḥ* ("to you"), because of the honor shown by the approach of Acyuta.
Alternatively, the singular number refers to the class [of glances] as a whole. Or else, [it refers to] her who stands nearby among those many women.

Because the question is directed primarily toward one [beloved] alone; and because of the phrase "with a beloved," whether it be with Lakṣmī or some particular gopī, he truly brings supreme bliss—that is, perfect satisfaction—to the eyes through his limbs, as if out of jealousy. Otherwise—

The failure of those with wide and serene eyes—what else could it be, since such a vision would otherwise be impossible? The prefix *su-* is intended to express its superiority even over the bliss of liberation (*mokṣa*);
by this, an ultimate and final vision is also intended. Otherwise, there would be no attainment of perfect peace (*sunirvṛti*).

He [addresses her] as "friend" (sakhī) because of her affectionate gaze toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa or because of their shared pastimes in the forest; thus, the meaning is that He should not practice deception toward us.
He is called "Acyuta" (the Undeviating One) in order to extend our complete peace of mind, or else to indicate that there is no falling away (vicyuti) in coming here.

This is the underlying state. They manifest that very state by saying "the beloved" (*kāntā*). For, according to the maxim "those who know it recognize it," they possess familiarity with its fragrance. Thus it was previously stated: "wearing the Vaijayantī garland" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.26.44). And therefore, together with you...
From the phrase "bearing [garlands] with swarms of bees" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.7), the *tulasī* garland is understood;

and now, by the phrase "and jasmine wreaths," a triad of garlands is thus implied. Alternatively, since *tulasī* occurs elsewhere in the *Vaijayantī* as well, its wearing [is prescribed] because of the great splendor of the jasmine wreath during the moonlit night.
It should be understood that by now she wears that very same [garland], having abandoned the Vaijayantī.

It belongs to the Kulapati, the Lord of Gokula; or rather, to the Master of the host of Gopīs. She does not mention it directly out of modesty or perhaps out of cleverness. Therefore, for us—who have him as our sole husband—his absence [is felt].

The sense is: "Tell [him] quickly by all means, lest there be a loss of life. Through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), it is an expression of jealousy: "It is only fitting that she should associate with one who is the husband of a person who takes—that is, accepts—what is contemptible. The rest has been explained by them. Alternatively, he was approached—that is, united—with his beloved.
"He is indeed here.
"Well then, let him be sought out and seen? To this they replied: "With [his] limbs"—meaning he is seen only by your most blessed eyes, but not by us to behold.
The meaning is that "it is possible. Now, they say: "In that case, it does not exist here at all," [answering] with the word "beloved" (*kāntā*). The rest is the same. ||11||
The sequence of the composition: "Even so" constitutes two [verses], 11–13.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, having obtained an answer from the stationary beings and having reached a conclusion regarding the mobile beings, she saw a doe standing nearby and [addressed her] with friendship.
Having rested, they ask: "O doe, is it so? O doe, O mate of the black antelope (*eṇa*), you too know the pleasure born of union with a husband and the sorrow born of separation; therefore, speak!
Perhaps at some time, having come with your beloved, you saw someone near you.
They speak with envy: "What is he doing? Spreading great bliss for the eyes through his limbs—the parts such as hands and feet—otherwise, the gift of life to the eyes would not be established;
for elsewhere, in the absence of extreme proximity, such exceedingly intense pleasure is not known. O friend! Thus [they say].

Addressing him by name, they ask with confidence, anticipating his affection for Śrī Kṛṣṇa; for it is well known that the friendship of the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together. Therefore, deception is unbecoming of you. By the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*), they imply that he is "Acyuta," meaning one who never falls away from his amorous play with his beloved. [Thus they address] the Lord of the Family.
Of the Lord of Gokula—that is, the Master of the cowherd community—or rather, of the Lord of the assembly of gopīs;

the fragrance of the jasmine garland (*kunda-sraj*), that is, the wreath of jasmine flowers, wafts here, coming toward us. Previously, the wearing of the Vaijayantī was mentioned: "Wearing the Vaijayantī garland" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.44).

Thus [it is said]. Now, because she who was hidden from view fashioned and offered it, the wearing of the jasmine garland is described as being out of affection; they state the evidence for this on account of its extreme fragrance—“by her beloved,” and so forth.
It is colored by the saffron from the breasts of his beloved through contact with her body; that very sport [of love] is present in the contact of her limbs.

The saffron (*kāśmīra*) from the *kuṅkuma* on her breasts that has adhered to her— its very scent makes known its state as *kuṅkuma*, due to the emergence of a *sāttvika* emotion, or because of the immediate manifestation of a particular arrangement [of the powder] at that very moment. Although the fragrance of the *kunda* flower is slight, nevertheless...
The excellence of its fragrance is indicated by its contact with the saffron on her breasts; that is something we cannot endure.
But you were seen sporting with that beloved woman who is so fortunate, and you even smelled the fragrance; yet, because of your lack of envy, everything has turned out well for you.
"Envious speech," thus [it is said]. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Then, alas! How could she, whose limbs were variegated with the marks of his own beloved such as the banner, thunderbolt, and goad, and who was blinded by the great pride of one whose husband is under her control, speak of him as "not me"? Having gone forward and observed a certain doe, they said: "api" (even).

"O friend! O wife of the deer! Why has your beloved approached and come into your presence?"—from the very association with the vocative term "by you" (*tvayā*), the word "you" is understood here. The sense is: although you are the wife of the deer, you are like us; yet you consider him alone to be your beloved.
Since he was spreading great bliss—an intense joy—through his limbs, face, arms, and so forth, providing supreme satisfaction to the eyes;

the plural number in "vaḥ" (to you) and "dṛśām" (of the eyes) is used out of respect. By the term "Acyuta," the sense is that because you followed him out of a longing for the bliss of your own sight, he did not fall away from you. Therefore...
Observing her proceeding ahead by her very nature, she says as if speaking: "O, what shall I say? 'He has been seen'!
I am indeed showing him to you; come along my path!
Thus saying, she goes forward, yet repeatedly turns her neck and looks at us. Is he not being seen? So it seems.

When questioned, some said: "In that case, Kṛṣṇa must be right here somewhere; however, the doe, fearing Kṛṣṇa, has hidden herself somewhere to avoid the fault of betraying her own location. As they were speculating thus, they experienced by chance a divine fragrance and exclaimed: "Aha! This is truly it, this is indeed it!"

"Truth! they exclaimed repeatedly with joy: "The fragrance of jasmine garlands, colored by the saffron from the breasts of their beloveds as they cling to their bodies, is wafting forth. Here, the fragrance of the two bodies of the lovers, of their breasts, of the saffron, and of the jasmine belongs to them.

The meaning is that it is determined by her very nose. The sense is: "O Kulapati, you who delight the community of cowherd women"—for the Kulapati has now abandoned his many wives and is sporting with only a single beloved;
therefore, behold his injustice! ||11||

Having placed his beloved arm upon her shoulder and holding a lotus, the younger brother of Rāma was surrounded by swarms of bees, blinded by intoxication, that hovered around the clusters of *tulasī* flowers.
As you walk here, do these trees welcome your salutation with their affectionate glances?

Śrīdhara: Seeing the trees bent by the weight of their fruit, and thinking that they too had bowed down upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, the women, together with their beloved, imagine His graceful movements and ask: "The arm...
[He is] here followed and pursued by swarms of bees from the *tulasī* plants, which are blinded by the intoxication of its fragrance.
"While walking," [it is said]. ||12||

Vaṃśīdhara: While it may be somehow useful to question those who have adopted the profession of a *viṭa* at the time they wish to go near Mālatī and others with the desire to gather flowers, how is questioning the *aśvattha* tree and so forth useful? Therefore, [the author] shows the possibility of that [usefulness].

They said: "An arm. Referring to the *aśvattha* and other trees which rescue one from *saṃsāra* through prostration, circumambulation, and so forth, they said to them: "O trees! Rāma’s younger brother, accompanied by one blinded by pride, has placed one arm upon his beloved's shoulder with the other..."

Having taken up a lotus to ward off the bees greedy for the lotus-face of his beloved—or rather, with a lotus held in his hand—he welcomes and accepts your prostration with affectionate glances. By the phrase "or rather" (yad vā), the intensity of devotion even among immobile beings is suggested. ||12||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, perceiving her silence to be a state of paralysis arising from the onset of a heavy burden of distress—both from the longing for her own vision of Him and from the pain of His absence—he abandoned her.
Having observed the trees bowed down by the weight of fruits, flowers, and so forth, and perceiving them as full of humility and affection,
they ask all of them— "O arm!"—
here too, approval through praise for each [tree] is suggested by the meaning of the sentence, just as in the case of "O... [the address].
"O trees! Does Rāma’s younger brother greet your salutation, or rather, does he welcome it with affectionate glances?
Having thus indicated that they were worthy recipients of his own affection and their grace, [the author] raises the doubt:
"How could he not welcome the praise of their virtues? Anticipating this, [he says] regarding them...
They say that the cause for her immersion in sweet amorous play is her knowledge of that [state], and they say that the cause for that knowledge is,

as before, her own intimate awareness of her internal qualities through the mere scent of her— beginning with the words "the arm" and so forth. In that regard, the general cause for her rejoicing is expressed by the word "moving."
The meaning is that he was intent on going to various places for pastimes.
Now, one might ask: "He wanders and sees us everywhere at all times; what is the distinction today?
To this they reply: "Having placed his arm upon the shoulder of his beloved. [This refers to] his beloved, who is supremely affectionate toward him.
"Placing her on his shoulder"—meaning, having placed whatever is soft upon his shoulder.

Anticipating the objection: "Surely he has come to show her to us; why then would he not welcome our prostration? they say: "Followed by swarms of bees from the *tulasī* groves, and holding a lotus for his beloved..."
The meaning is that he is intent on shaking his toy lotus with his right arm in order to ward them off;

the implication is, "In that case, how could he welcome them? Here, however, by the phrase "by the swarms of Tulasī bees," [it is meant] the all-pervading fragrance of the Tulasī flowers from his playful face.
The excellence is thus illuminated. And so it will be said: "Intoxicated by the divine fragrance of *tulasī* and honey" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.35.10).

For this very reason, even though they were blinded by intoxication from drinking that nectar, they followed him; thus, through the friction against the limbs of their beloved, the manifestation of a particular fragrance was revealed.
Thus, in this manner, here too, as before, the praise of each respective element has been shown. Furthermore,

regarding the Vaijayantī garland mentioned in the phrase "wearing the Vaijayantī," and specifically that which was described in the passage beginning with "Is there perhaps a tulasī in the middle?"— since the excellence of that [tulasī] has already been introduced by the statement "wearing you" (tvāṃ bibhrat), and...

The *tulasī* garland was indicated; furthermore, by the mention of the *kunda* wreath, those very *kunda* wreaths were shown, and now the causes for their slipping away and their various sports have been suggested. Thus, through the meaning of the sentence and the praise of each [item], approval alone is suggested.

Now, the meaning of the words should also be connected as before. Thus, the very friendship of the crooked ones has been obtained; and by means of the apparent contradiction in the verse beginning with "these [words] of hers cause us agitation," that very same [friendship] is indeed determined. (12)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Observing that the deer had become motionless due to the intensity of their gaze and their own perception of the pain of separation, and seeing that they too were overcome by a weight of distress, He left them and beheld the trees, which were bowed down by the abundance of fruits and flowers and full of humble devotion.

Considering them all to be most virtuous, they ask all of them about the arm: "The arm. Having surmised that she had come with her beloved because of the previously mentioned scent of her body, and that there was the fragrance of the beautiful arm mixed with the fragrance of the woman's shoulder upon which the beloved arm rested, and so forth—thus [they inquire].

Having perceived the fragrance of the lotus moistened by the scent of the Lord’s hand, as well as the fragrance of the *tulasī* on His body mingled with the scent of bees, He spoke thus; or rather, He spoke in such a manner by way of reasoning, thinking that perhaps this might be the customary practice of the women of Nāgara.

"By the swarms of bees from the *tulasī* plant"—this is because of the particular sweetness of its fragrance on all sides. For this very reason, the specific nature of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is revealed by the phrases "pursued by those blinded by intoxication" and "his arm," and so forth. Likewise, there is the good fortune of the *tulasī*, and through that connection, the bees [attain it].

And it has been indicated that he wanders here for the purpose of avoiding them— those blinded by pride— by means of an intervention such as yours, fearing that their own concealment might be disrupted by their own great clamor;
or rather, to transfer [the pollen] onto your flowers.

Or rather, by virtue of His being of a stationary species and thus equal to the *tulasī*, it is possible that even toward you He may extend His grace at this particular time, out of consideration for His own purpose; therefore, the sense is that He is moving about right here specifically because of His affection for those who bow down to Him.

Does she welcome [you] with affectionate glances, or does she accept [you] with approval? Since such [reactions] are extremely rare for them, the question "or what? implies a sidelong glance; the ellipsis is "therefore, tell me that.
Something else has been indicated by them.

Or else, having seen those glorious footprints there on the left joined with their own feet, and seeing the trees on the right bowing even more deeply as if to obtain consolation, he imagined that his glorious right hand had grasped a lotus; and in some places, [the footprints] fell forward rapidly as if out of fear.
Having observed her beloved’s footprints deeply imprinted and disarrayed,

and having inferred that she had been followed by bees blinded by intoxication; or rather, having seen on every side the drops of honey issuing from the mouths of bees upon each of those various footprints, he spoke thus and thus.
This should be understood;

or rather, those various statements are made solely out of madness, and not as a result of any philosophical inquiry or investigation into doctrines— thus they are the words of a madman (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.14).
Because it will be stated later [that they follow him out of intoxication], the phrase "they follow him" is used through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) to mean that they are indeed blinded by intoxication;

thus, because of their connection with him, he too is "blinded by intoxication"—this is a statement made in feigned anger (*praṇaya-kopa*). Alternatively, the sense is: "It is truly improper that this man is followed by us, who are blinded by intoxication and have therefore lost our pride."
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: [The commentary notes that] because of their natural restlessness, when the female deer have moved to another location, they consult with one another, wondering, "What will these [deer] say regarding what they themselves have experienced?"

Considering all the virtuous sons of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who, like trees, are bent down by the weight of their fruits and flowers—to be benefactors of others, they ask about His arm: "The arm... [They speak thus] because He is sporting with a certain woman, recognizable by the scent of saffron on Her body;
out of fear that She might stumble against Him, He has placed His left arm upon Her shoulder as a support.
"He stands still because of his languor from the weight of his amorous play. With his right arm he holds a lotus;
furthermore, he is followed—that is, pursued—by swarms of bees belonging to the *tulasī* plant.
This indicates that they are blinded by the intoxication resulting from drinking the nectar of that *tulasī*.

Having attained this fourfold fragrance— the fragrance of the arms, the fragrance of the beloved, the fragrance of the lotus, and the fragrance of the *tulasī*— and having been observed by the rows of bees situated in the same place, the bees [were moved] upon hearing the humming born of their amorous play.

Having considered even the slightest possibility [of her presence], and having mentally envisioned this triad—the good fortune of his beloved, the good fortune of the *tulasī* plant, and the good fortune of the bees—and seeing the humility of the trees, he asks: "O trees! Is your bowing to me performed with affectionate glances?"

Does he rejoice and approve? Having reflected in his mind, "He is one who benefits us and who conceals our amorous dalliances," he treats you thus. Or rather, while asking with a sidelong glance, "Is it new?", what is he doing as he sports in this manner right in your presence?
It is simply a lack of appreciation. Repeated questioning is a sign of affectionate intent. By this, ingratitude toward him is attributed to me.
This is the meaning of the phrase "having taken the lotus."

The intended meaning is as follows: it was stated that the bees were wandering among the trees because they were drawn by the fragrance of the wind carrying the beloved’s breath; therefore, being preoccupied with warding them off, it is certain that she was merely welcoming your prostrations.
[Objection: "But surely, although the question 'Is she dear to the mango tree? was previously asked, no answer was obtained;
why then is the question asked again regarding the trees? [Reply: The question was asked again because she is overwhelmed by the affliction of separation.
As it has been said: "For those afflicted by love are naturally wretched toward both sentient and insentient beings; therefore, tell me!"
The sense is: "Having been told by you, we shall search for the truth with confidence.

By the term "Rāmānuja," his fearlessness is expressed; it is also indicated that there is no hesitation regarding anyone. By the word "madāndhaiḥ" (by those blinded by pride), it is meant that only those blinded by pride follow him; we, however, are free from pride.
"What purpose or goal will be accomplished?"—this thought was momentarily sustained by despondency due to the agitation caused by separation. ||12||

Viśvanātha: While He is present right there, she perceives another characteristic as well and, seeing the trees bowed down by the weight of their fruits and flowers as if they were prostrating themselves, she speaks with deliberation: "The arm... O trees! Kṛṣṇa is moving about here.

Does he welcome with affectionate glances the salutation of you who, in the form of subjects, bestow fruits, flowers, and other offerings? Alas, alas! How could there be any opportunity for him to look upon such virtuous and pure-hearted people as yourselves with favor? [Thus he speaks] with envy.

They say: Rāma’s younger brother was intoxicated; even there, having rested his left arm upon the shoulder of his beloved, he became slack and weak from the fatigue of their union. Making that very tender arm resting upon his beloved’s shoulder his pillow, [he lay there] because of the bees rising up at the fragrance of her face.

Holding a blue lotus in his right hand precisely for the purpose of putting [others] to flight—this is the sense: that for him, whose mind is entirely intent on serving Him, there is no possibility of a glance falling anywhere else.
He is followed by swarms of bees from the groves of tender *tulasī* plants; [he goes] to the *tulasī* plants.

"Having abandoned [him], let him be sought right here; the sense is that he is wandering somewhere here or there, hidden right in this very place. Now, one might object: "In that case, let us follow the swarms of bees themselves"; to this they reply: "by those blinded by intoxication. For indeed...
The sense is that it is fitting for noble persons to follow those blinded by intoxication. ||12||
"—O! (o)0(o)— Ask these creepers that have embraced the arms of the forest tree;
surely, touched by his fingernails, they now bear horripilation, alas!"

Śrīdhara: Some say, "O friends, these creepers have surely been united with Kṛṣṇa; therefore, ask them. But surely, union with him is difficult to achieve for one already united with her own husband. [They reply: "No!
Even though they were embraced by the arm of their husband, the lord of the forest, oh, what great fortune it is that they were touched by his nails!"
For they bear horripilation; the sense is that such a manifestation of horripilation does not occur upon union with one's own husband. ||13||

Vaṃśīdhara: Because she was united with Kṛṣṇa, for that reason. Here he raises a doubt with the word "nanu" (surely). That union is the union with Kṛṣṇa. It is not impossible—that it is difficult to achieve—he says "no. As for how the touch by his nails—the nails of Kṛṣṇa—was known, they say: "because... [referring to] the blossoming [of her body].
"The hairs stand on end. They say that otherwise this would be impossible, with the words "for not," etc. The underlying meaning (*bhāva*) is as follows:
the joy that women experience upon the touch of another man is exactly the same as that experienced in union with their own husband; this is the intended sense.
Showing yet another characteristic, they say—"Ask," etc.—"O friends, these creepers..."

Ask those who bear the marks of union with Kṛṣṇa; for it should not be said that union with Him is difficult to achieve when one is already united with one's own husband, since, oh, how great is the surge of passion even when they have firmly embraced the arms of their husbands, the trees! Indeed, they are surely bristling with horripilation from being touched by His fingernails.
They bear [this state], for such horripilation could not occur even when united with their own husbands.
Therefore, because that characteristic is visible to us, they will be able to falsely claim, "We did not see him, just as we did before. This is the intended meaning.
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: It is understood that all of this did not even become an object of attention for those who will say, "Whose words are these? [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.27].

Because doubt is impossible, some women, though they have fixed their attention on something, display only what they themselves desire— as if not hearing it at all— due to the absence of passion and aversion; and here the Lord of Sages, manifesting his indifference toward this matter, demonstrates the diversity of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) acquired in previous lives by saying, "Ask these creepers."
Ask these very creepers, for they have embraced even the arms of their Lord, who is in the form of a *vanaspati* (tree). [Objection:

If this is so, then how can their union with Him be conceived? To this they reply: "Surely" (*nūnam*)—the word expressing conjecture—means they were touched by the fingernails of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa. [Objection: But how is even this so?

Was this reflected upon? Regarding that, they say: "Ut" means "highly"; they remain bearing horripilation (*pulaka*) in the form of sprouts; "aho" expresses wonder at its unprecedented nature. Indeed, the meaning is "in this way, previously. (13)
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Indeed, these are His devotees who follow His doctrine; surely they would not speak [of this].

Therefore, let us ask our own creepers here because of their female nature," they said to one another—"Ask! All that follows, beginning with "embraced by the arm," is according to their own internal disposition. (13)
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
*Prīti-sandarbha* (286): An example of the indifferent (*taṭasthā*) [heroine] is as follows: "Ask these...
Here, even though she has heard the words of her friend, her indifference toward him is clearly manifested by her remaining aloof. Thus...
"Surely He has been propitiated by her," following these words of a friend, and also in such statements as, "Oh, how blessed are these companions! (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.29). ||13||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Once again summoning her fortitude, she disregarded the trees in her agitation, reflecting:

"These trees, born of the bamboo species, are hard; why would they speak in favor of him? Then, considering that these creepers, being female, are acquainted with such suffering, she imagined they might speak [on his behalf]. Thus she conversed with them one after another.
Consulting with one another, they say: "Ask them!

Ask these creepers why, even though embraced by the arm of their husband, the lord of the forest, they bear horripilation—evidenced by the appearance of sprouts and so forth—as if touched by his fingernails. This is certainly the case.

While she was searching for a flower to bind as a crest-ornament for her beloved, she came into contact with Him; therefore, she said, projecting her own experience onto them: "She is blessed, whereas we are unfortunate," implying that such a manifestation of horripilation cannot occur without the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. From this point on, they ceased because no further reply was received.
The meaning. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Showing another definition, they say, "Ask"—meaning, O friends! Ask these very creepers, who bear the marks of union with Kṛṣṇa. Nor should it be said that union with him is difficult to achieve when one is already united with one's own husband;
for behold, even while firmly embracing the arms of their husband, the lord of the forest, there is such an overflow of passion!
Surely, touched by his nails, they alone now bear horripilation;
for such horripilation could not occur from union with one's own husband.
Therefore, because that characteristic is visible upon them, they will be able to falsely claim, "We did not see him, just as we did before"—this is the intended meaning. ||13||
" Thus the cowherd girls, distressed in their search for Kṛṣṇa,
imitated those various pastimes of the Lord, having become absorbed in Him.

Śrīdhara: The statement that they questioned Him like madmen has now been elaborated upon. He now elaborates on what was said in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.2: "The gopīs, becoming one with His nature, then adopted those various gestures of the Lord of Ramā"—this is indicated by the word "iti. "Unmatta-vacaḥ" means the words of the madman; and "unmatta-vacasas tā gopyaḥ" means those gopīs who possessed the speech of the madman.
Distressed and extremely overwhelmed by their search for Kṛṣṇa, they imitated him; that is, they acted like him. ||14||

Vaṃśīdhara: Having elaborated upon one promised point, he proceeds to the second—in accordance with the manner stated above. To explain how [the Lord] remained established within himself amidst the flames of the intensified fire held in imitation, he says: "consisting of that" (tad-ātmikā). ||14||
"Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: 'Thus the words of the madman,' 'the gopīs,' and so forth. These become the words of the madman;

likewise, those various [gopīs] who are of that same nature are the true [consorts] of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, being favorable toward Him. Those who are unfavorable, such as Pūtanā and others, however, are of the nature of identity with all names.
Because they exist as modifications residing in the intellect, they should be understood as being entirely favorable. ||14||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, the gopīs—whose speech was like that of a madman according to the manner previously described—were distressed by the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa while searching for him; the meaning is that they were unable even to perform that [search]. Accordingly, it is said: "Then the truthful ones sang aloud" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.4).

The meaning is that they also performed, from time to time, those various pastimes such as the slaying of Pūtanā, which had been obtained through the continuity of their singing in accordance with the original [performance]. The reason for this is: "tad-ātmikāḥ.
This means those whose very self—their consciousness—is centered on Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa; that is to say, they were intensely attached to Him. In that regard:

The imitation of Kṛṣṇa is indeed manifest through the state of being identical with Him. And therein, because there is no mention of effort—as in the phrase "He raises His arms with effort"—there is no appearance of non-difference from Him while not abandoning one's own nature; for [Kṛṣṇa Himself says] "I am Kṛṣṇa, behold My gait" in every instance.

Furthermore, because the word "that" (tad) is employed for the purpose of establishing blackness; and because the imitation of Pūtanā and others arises from fear caused by Him with respect to Kṛṣṇa, it occurs precisely through identification with His nature,
as He is encompassed by the sentiment of childhood— yet this is due to the excellence of the general nature of their love.

Because the state of being Kṛṣṇa has been attained, out of fear of that [state], there is no touch of the state of being a mother due to the absence of the latter; rather, it is through the state of being Kṛṣṇa alone. Thus, there is no union of two states that are mutually incompatible by their very nature. All of this occurred suddenly at that time because of the presence of intoxication (*unmāda*) within them.
It was attained; and it should be understood that it was nothing other than this. ||14||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: [This is] according to the manner described above. Alternatively, "unmatta-vaca" (those with mad speech) is a restatement of those gopīs whose words were of such a kind; this is for the sake of strengthening the previous statement that their various utterances were merely due to madness, like a madman. In that regard:

"Because they asked questions even of those who were unworthy, and because they asked various such questions there as well"—this is the reason for the phrase "they imitated [him]": they were distressed by separation from Kṛṣṇa, the supreme attractor. Therefore, it was solely due to this distress that...
This means imitation of this or that [pastime], and not by means of a cognition of pleasure and so forth according to one's own whim.

The reason for this is stated: "having that as their very self" (*tad-ātmikāḥ*), which means their minds have been captivated by that. Alternatively, by the word "that" (*tat*), the pastimes (*līlā*) are referred to; and thus, through attachment to the imitation of those [pastimes]...
Righteousness (samyaktva) is intended here.
Or rather, surely even by the mere remembrance of His pastimes, the lives of those afflicted by the pain of separation are difficult to sustain;
how then could their own selves remain in their hearts, when the flames of the fire of separation have been fanned by the very imitation [of His deeds] and by ghee?
Anticipating the question, "Did He remain [there]? he says: "Those whose very self is in Him.

Therefore, due to the connection with that ocean of exceedingly cool nectar, He did not depart. Otherwise, while remaining in His own place, He would surely have been consumed; this is the meaning. [Thus they are described as] "those whose minds were possessed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
The meaning is that each such imitation occurs solely through a lack of autonomy, and not by one's own free will. ||14||

The sequence of the composition: In the manner previously described, those gopīs whose speech was like the words of a madman, being distressed by their search for Kṛṣṇa, were as if terrified; the meaning is that due to the pain of separation, they were unable even to do that. Thus being, they sang aloud [Bhāgavata Purāṇa].

Following this and other [verses], the meaning is that whatever pastimes such as the slaying of Pūtanā were attained through the continuity of the song, those too they performed from time to time in the midst [of their play]. ||14||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, having questioned each one individually and failing to receive an answer from anyone, when madness arose, Kṛṣṇa did not go elsewhere; rather, he entered into me alone, and so there was a realization of identity with the thought, "I myself am Kṛṣṇa"—thus it is shown.
"Like the words of a madman," and so forth. In this manner, like the speech of a madman, being distressed by their search for Kṛṣṇa, they imitated those various pastimes of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa.
"Those various" refers to those previously experienced. The reason for the imitation is that they were absorbed in Him—that is, they attained identity with Him.
They have gone. ||14||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: It was previously stated that they questioned even those who were unworthy, like madmen; yet, considering it improper to question insentient objects, they determined that emulating His pastimes was the means to attain Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and thus they imitated them—this is what is meant by "like madmen."

Those whose speech was like that of a madman in the manner previously described were the "mad-spoken" gopīs. And those gopīs, being disregarded by the Blessed One— who was resplendent with his mellows and activities— imitated those various well-known pastimes of his sixfold group, such as the sucking of Pūtanā’s life-breath and so forth.
Since they were "timid regarding the search for Kṛṣṇa," this is the primary reason for their imitation, and not out of independence.
It was also performed as a means of cooling the fever of separation through the recollection of His pastimes. If it is asked how this was done through the imitation of pastimes, he says in response:
*tad-ātmikāḥ*—those whose very self (*ātman*) is that [pastime] within their own minds; or rather, those whose self is centered in Him alone.
"Those for whom the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is the *jīva* (individual soul); he alone is the protector of their life. This is the meaning:

if their *ātman* were to remain in its own body, then it would surely be consumed by the fire of separation; however, because it resides in Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is like one who has died due to the coolness [of his touch]—it is not burned. These are their bodies.

Thus, by entering into that [state], he imitates His pastimes; however, his own self is not [merely an imitation] because it has been embraced within the very self of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, nothing is inconsistent here. ||14||

Viśvanātha: These [women] say nothing at all because of their blissful stupor; thus, even though they are insentient, they possess speech like the words of madmen, characterized by the appearance of a desire to question and so forth. Consequently, being timid even in the search for Him, some among them reflected individually as follows:

"Now, by imitating His very form, gestures, and so forth, I shall manifest myself in the form of Kṛṣṇa and bring about even momentary relief for these most distressed women as well as for myself"— having thus resolved in her mind,
she sequentially brought to mind all of His pastimes, beginning with the pastime of the slaying of Pūtanā.

Those whose minds were fixed solely upon Him imitated Him; and therein, the imitation of those who were adverse was performed by Yoga-māyā alone, having assumed the form of a gopī right in their midst for the sake of accomplishing those various pastimes. It should be understood, however, that it was the gopīs themselves who imitated those who were favorable.
"Do not speak of them in our assemblies"— though thus forbidden, he,
being overcome by bliss, found them truly delightful here;
yet, I shall not proclaim their names in this place.
Thus the sage now resolved within his mind. ||14||
One, acting like a *pūtana* demoness, drank from the breast of another who was acting like Kṛṣṇa;
another, acting as a child, cried out and kicked one who was acting like a cart.

Śrīdhara: By the four verses beginning with "kasyāścit," the imitation [of Kṛṣṇa] is elaborated; then, by the [next] four verses, his absorption in that state [is shown], and finally, by one verse, the imitation [is concluded]. This is the distinction. Acting like Pūtanā—that is, behaving as Pūtanā did—she drank from the breast while acting like Kṛṣṇa. Having acted like a child (*toka*), she behaved like a child.
Having made oneself [the object]. ||15||

Vaṃśīdhara: "She acts like Pūtanā" is *pūtanāyate*. From the form *pūtanāyate*, by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ sa-lopaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied; then, although the suffix *śānac* would normally follow after a verb ending in *taṅ* (ātmanepada), the use of the *śatṛ* suffix here is archaic (*ārṣa*). By the rule *śyap-śyanor nityam*, the augment *num* is added. *Tokam*...

"Tokāyate" means "he acts like a child" (*toka*); it is formed as *tokāyyate*, and having thus derived *tokayitvā*, the suffix *ktvā* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), according to the rule "the *avyaya*-suffixes [including *ktvā*] denote the state.
In the form *śakātāyatīm*, the absence of the nasal augment (*num*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: If that is so, [what about] Pūtanā and others? To the question "To what does this identity belong?", he says:

"Of a certain one," and so forth. Now, identity (*tādātmya*) indeed arises from love reaching its ultimate limit, through the absence of any other mental state, resulting in becoming absorbed in that [object]. In that case, how can it occur with respect to those who are of a different nature (*vijātīya*)?

If it is argued that because there is an absence of love in Pūtanā and others, they lack identification with Her due to a lack of attachment—and since the *līlā* necessarily requires the existence of its opposite—the claim that they are "of Her nature" (*tad-ātmikā*) is inconsistent; furthermore, this contradicts actual experience. Then, in this case, one must investigate as follows: regarding the phrase "of someone," it is to be understood as before.
Because every noun functions by residing within the intellect (*buddhistha-vṛttitvāt*). Here, by the word "what" (*kiṃ*), one should understand *yogamāyā*.

"Having resorted to *yogamāyā*"—this alone is its defining limit. Until that point, by the power of the Lord’s will, *yogamāyā* became the provider of all assistance for them, both in union and in separation. Therefore...
Because they possess that very nature, in their imitation of His pastimes, they manifest a distinct state of being through the very convergence of the requisites for those pastimes. ||15||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He describes the expansion of that imitation by means of its identity with Him through nine verses, beginning with "pūtanāyantyā. The meaning is: even so, she acts like Pūtanā while remaining established in her own true nature, and not by assuming any state contrary to that [nature]. Thus, "kṛṣṇāyantī" (acting like Kṛṣṇa).

In this context, however, according to what will be stated later—namely, "the state of being a child of Kṛṣṇa"—it is understood that they perform those actions even through their inner disposition (*bhāva*). The same applies to the subsequent cases as well. Furthermore, the phrase "he drank from the breast" is merely an imitation, since that specific act itself is disregarded [in its literal sense]. *Śakaṭāyatīm* means "acting like a cart."
And suchness consists in remaining high above while supporting the earth with both hands and feet, with the face turned downwards. ||15||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: It elaborates upon imitation itself with the words "of a certain [woman]"; the distinction of that [imitation] has indeed been manifested by them. And there, although it was said "they imitated," when the elaboration of imitation itself is to be performed, the elaboration of being absorbed in that [state] is also merely the elaboration of imitation.

"For the sake of awakening to rightness" (*samyaktva-bodhanārtham*). In that regard, first of all, there is a threefold imitation: primarily, the imitation of physical activity by means of physical activity itself; and likewise, the imitation of activity associated with speech by means of [speech] activity itself, and similarly, the imitation of activity associated with the mind by means of [mental] activity itself. Among these—

Although imitation occurs almost everywhere through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone, it is nevertheless divided into three types according to the predominance of this or that element in various instances.
Among these, he first describes the imitation in which bodily movements predominate in three verses, beginning with [the verse on] Pūtanā.

The imitation of Pūtanā and others by one acting as Pūtanā is accomplished solely through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), perhaps accompanied by the performance of certain gestures (*mudrā*) and so forth, but not through dress or other external trappings, because such things are entirely impossible in this context.
For this very reason, it will be stated: "the visualization of the infant Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.16). That too...

Although it might not be easily accomplished due to the helplessness caused by separation, it should be understood that it is nonetheless achieved of its own accord through their intense absorption in those various pastimes, driven by the very nature of the weight of the pain of separation. In this regard,
although it is not appropriate for those supreme Vaiṣṇavas to imitate the Daityas, nevertheless, by some means...
Overcome by a most difficult-to-master variety of emotional states, they imitated the very pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.

Their dear friends, perceiving those girls to be possessed by various such emotions, performed those same pastimes right there in order to dispel their great suffering by engendering a similar state of mind within them.
All the gopīs, overwhelmed by separation and absorbed in Him, made themselves composed of His pastimes; therefore,
because they were the instruments of those various pastimes, their imitation of the demons and others was entirely appropriate, and thus everything they did was beyond reproach.
The phrase "he drank from the breast" is merely an imitation and not literal, for it is the imitation itself that is intended.
The same should be inferred for other instances that follow. *Śakaṭāyatīm* means "acting like a cart.
Similarly, in what follows, there is an imitation of the sound *śaka*, as if acting like a cart upon the child (*tokāyamānāyāḥ*).
The manner of its abiding should be understood in some way. ||15||
The Sequence of Events and the Great Sequence of Events: Since it was stated there that "those various [pastimes]," all the pastimes are thereby established;
thus, when the imitation of pastimes such as the liberation of Pūtanā arises from the very beginning, he says that very thing—starting with "of a certain [cowherd woman]," and so forth.

By many [means]. Now, "consisting of that" (*tad-ātmika*) means partaking in identity with that (*tādātmya-bhāj*). Identity, however, is the state of being absorbed in that (*tan-mayībhāva*), characterized by the absence of other mental functions through the boundary of love. Nor can it be said that "consisting of that" means "consisting of the pastimes" (*līlātmikā*); for those various pastimes of the Lord were indeed performed [by them].
Because of this statement, it is not possible that they became pastimes and then performed pastimes;

rather, through the possession (*āveśa*) by Kṛṣṇa, there was identity with Kṛṣṇa itself. In that case, how could there be an expression such as "acting like Pūtanā," given the absence of any attachment (*abhiniveśa*) toward hostile beings like Pūtanā? ||15||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: It elaborates upon the imitation of the divine pastimes (*līlā*) with the words "of a certain [girl]," describing the threefold nature of the pastime—mental, verbal, and physical—and states that within two of these types of pastimes, there is the manifestation of Pūtanā and others as the counterparts. "Acting like Pūtanā" (*pūtanāyantī*) means behaving like Pūtanā. Of a certain [girl]...
"Acting like Kṛṣṇa, behaving like Kṛṣṇa"—thus it is said. Regarding this verbal pastime, I am Kṛṣṇa;
I have been told by someone that this is an imitation of Pūtanā’s drinking from her breast and so forth.
Nevertheless, just as she became fulfilled by placing Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon her lap, so too does she act like Pūtanā.

Placing Kṛṣṇa on his lap, he experienced great happiness. The sense is that Pūtanā’s imitation was due solely to the touch of Kṛṣṇa. As stated in the previous verse, "those whose nature was identical to His imitated Him"; thus, He alone became their very self. Therefore...
Because they lacked independence, Kṛṣṇa acted in that very manner for the sake of protecting their lives;

thus, as a pastime (līlā), Pūtanā was treated by His dear friends for the sake of perfecting those qualities. Just as one possessed by a spirit has no independence, the spirit itself enters his body and acts according to its own will.
She performs such movements; in that same way, this is called *līlā*. This should be inferred in other cases as well.

He describes the *śakaṭa-bhaṅga-līlā*: another certain cowherd lady, having made herself like a child (*toka*) and acting like a cart (*śakaṭāyantī*), meaning behaving like a cart, struck it with her foot as if she were hitting it.
The sense is that she followed behind him like a female partridge, desiring the touch of his feet. ||15||

Viśvanātha: Thus he describes the imitation with four verses. She who was acting like Pūtanā (pūtanāyantī), that is, behaving as Pūtanā did, drank his breast, imitating the act of drinking, just as Kṛṣṇa had done. Having become a child (tokāyitvā), that is, having made herself into a child. ||15||
Acting like a Daitya, one [demoness] carried off another who possessed the consciousness of Kṛṣṇa’s child;
while another dragged his feet, she made him roll about with the sounds of her tinkling ornaments.
Two, however, acted like Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, while some others protected [the children];
another there killed Vatsyāyatī, and yet another killed Bakāyatī.

Śrīdhara: Having acted like a demon (*daityāyitvā*), that is, having made himself like the demon Tṛṇāvarta, he carried away another [gopī] who was contemplating the childhood of Kṛṣṇa—that contemplation which meditates upon Kṛṣṇa’s boyhood (*arbha-bālya*).
Vaṃśīdhara: He rolled about and moved along on his hands and knees with terrible roars.
Together with the sounds of anklets and other ornaments. ||16||

"They act like Kṛṣṇa and Rāma" is expressed as *kṛṣṇarāmāyete*. From that, by adding the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), one has *kṛṣṇarāmāyita*. In that context, among them, one woman followed behind, acting like Kṛṣṇa. ||17||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is that she displayed an imitation of his seizing [the child] out of an obsession with fear, [she who] possessed that very childhood disposition—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy. *Ghoṣāḥ*.

Their tinkling bells, by means of their sounds, were either accompanied or served; and this was because the anklets were actually present upon their feet as well. This refers to the imitation of the graceful movements of their dancing, as described in passages such as *ghoṣa-praghoṣa-ruciram* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.22). ||16||
The two of them played. Among them, some acted as cowherd girls and some acted as cowherds and they played.

Then, because the calves were being tended by the boys themselves, He describes another pastime in that very assembly, beginning with the word "vatsa" (calf). Another girl, acting like Kṛṣṇa, while he was there, struck one who was acting like Kṛṣṇa.
It imitates the imitation of killing; the meaning is "he killed. ||17||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Or rather, they are accompanied by the sounds of *ghoṣas*, which are small bells (*kiṅkiṇīs*). And this is because those [bells] themselves are indeed present on their feet in the form of anklets (*nūpura*). This is supported by such passages as: "Resplendent with the ringing of the *ghoṣas*" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.22).
The imitation of the graceful movements described above. ||16||

"Gopāyanti" (they protect) should be understood as "gopa-bālāyanti" (they act like cowherd boys), because at that time the calves were tended by children alone. By the force of the word "ca" (and), he also strikes (*hanti*) or struck (*ahan*) the one seeking to harm (*aghāyatīm*). The use of the present tense (*vartamānā*) here denotes immediate proximity; the sequence of the *bṛhat* [Sāman] has not been explained.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: He describes the pastime of Tṛṇāvarta with the words "daitya... and so on. One certain woman, acting like a demon (*daityāyitvā*) and making herself out to be Tṛṇāvarta, stole the thought of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood; that is, she made [the others] perceive Kṛṣṇa as a child. Another stole [him], [placing him] upon the chest of Tṛṇāvarta.

The intended meaning is that she acted in such a way out of a desire for the touch of Kṛṣṇa. They imitate the pastime described in the sacred tradition: "Crawling along, they dragged each other's pair of feet" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8.22). A certain girl, acting like Kṛṣṇa, by means of the sounds of the jingling bells and other ornaments—
Dragging her feet, she crawled; she moved on her knees and hands. ||16||

He said something else as well: In the region of Vṛndāvana, two gopīs, concealing themselves and imitating the forms of calves, acted like Kṛṣṇa and Rāma. In this way, having made them their leaders, they all played exactly as we had played; another [gopī] did likewise.

She killed one who was acting like a *kṛṣṇa* (crow) against one acting like a *vatsa* (calf), imitating the act of killing. Among them, one who was acting like a *kṛṣṇa* killed one acting like a *baka* (crane), imitating the act of killing. ||17||
Viśvanātha: She who, acting like the demon Tṛṇāvarta—that is, behaving like the demon Tṛṇāvarta—nurtures Kṛṣṇa’s childhood (arbha), which is his boyhood (bālya). ||16-17||
Just as those who have gone far away call out to one who follows after Kṛṣṇa,
so others, playing and sounding their flutes, say, "Well done! to her.
Śrīdhara: *dūragāḥ* means the cows situated far away. *Yadvat* means "just as"; [the phrase] *yathā kṛṣṇas tathāhūya* means having called out to Kṛṣṇa in that same manner.
Alternatively, there is a reading: *taṃ kṛṣṇam anuvartamānām*, meaning "imitating him," or "following after that Kṛṣṇa. (18–19)
Vaṃśīdhara: Following might occur even without imitation; therefore he says, "or 'imitating'. ||18||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, only the imitation has been described. Now, regarding the imitation of the various pastimes performed during the summer preceding the slaying of Pralamba:

Because of the manifestation of her youth, which is the form of the *ālambana* (objective basis) for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), he again describes the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) called *līlā* (sportive play), which consists of imitating her beloved, in two verses beginning with "Having called... (*āhūya*). Regarding the phrase "going far" (*dūragā*): because the rule [that she would return] was not constant, the meaning is "those who had gone far. Others, thinking themselves to be cowherds (*gopa-manyāḥ*)...

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, about to describe the imitation of [the Lord's] speech through five verses, he first speaks of the imitation of the various pastimes performed during the summer season prior to the slaying of Pralamba, using two verses beginning with "āhūya. Here, because it is an imitation primarily of speech, what is being imitated?
Because they gradually attained complete absorption and became one with Him, the phrase beginning with "becoming Kṛṣṇa" was not mentioned previously.

The term "dūragāḥ" (those who go far) has already been explained by them [the commentators]. Alternatively, it means that just as Kṛṣṇa calls the gopīs residing in Vraja and other places from afar by the signal of His flute-playing, so too did He call them. Thus, she followed after Him.
One was playing, performing pastimes such as singing; it should be understood that the others had assumed the state of being cowherds. ||18||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: "They imitate the pastimes performed in the *sakhya-rasa*" means "having called out"—just as Kṛṣṇa calls out to a cow standing at a distance; or else, it refers to the cows staying far away in Vraja.

Imitating Him as He called the cowherd girls with the sound of His flute, and acting like Kṛṣṇa Himself, she played the flute while sporting with her companions who acted like Her friends; others, acting as Her friends, praised Her, saying, "Excellent! (18)

Viśvanātha: Just as Kṛṣṇa calls the cows that are far away—those situated at a distance—the reading is also "anuvartatīm," meaning she follows after that very Kṛṣṇa, imitating him by calling out in that same manner. ||18||
Placing her own arm upon the shoulder of a certain woman, another walking along said,
"I am Kṛṣṇa; look at my graceful gait," her mind entirely absorbed in Him.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Vaṃśīdhara: [She spoke] to Lalitā, who was exceedingly beautiful; with her mind fixed on Him, that is, with her heart set on Kṛṣṇa, she said. ||19||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: the movement, the dance-play. (19)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Indeed, he has spoken with certainty; therefore, the sense is that when He says "I am Kṛṣṇa," no doubt should be entertained. Alternatively: "O cowherds or O cowherd girls, behold my *gati*—my movement or my departure—which is *lalitā*, enchanting. [She who is] *tan-manāḥ*, her mind fixed on Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s desire.

This is the meaning. By this, the fault of thinking "I am Kṛṣṇa" is dispelled. [He says: "I am Kṛṣṇa, complete with all qualities, forms, and so forth; therefore, look at the cowherd girl named Lalitā, who is my very support. This was said by him, the sense being: "Oh, why do you not remember her? And that [occurred] once upon a time.
