It should be understood as being "as before" (pūrvavat), since it was previously stated by someone that [the statement] exists. Now, one might ask: why was the sentence not concluded? To this he says: "With their minds fixed on Him, their hearts stolen by Kṛṣṇa. Alternatively, by this, the very perfection of the imitation is intended, just as before. (19)
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: She describes the bodily pastimes (*daihika-līlā*) with the words "In a certain [cowherd girl]... Another girl, acting like Kṛṣṇa, places her own arm upon a certain girl who was acting like a cowherd boy, and while walking, says: "I am Kṛṣṇa. O... [he continues].
"O cowherds! Behold my graceful gait," they said; for their minds were fixed on Him and their hearts were solely intent upon Him—so Viśvanātha [states].

Consequently, even though those other women desired to imitate His pastimes, due to the intensity of their meditation on Him and the powerful onset of the transitory emotion of madness, their self-awareness departed.

He describes his identity with Kṛṣṇa through four verses, beginning with "In a certain [place]...": "I am Kṛṣṇa, whose arm is placed upon the shoulder of Subala; therefore, [I describe] my own graceful and exceedingly beautiful [form]. (19)
"Do not fear the wind and rain; a protection for that has been prepared by me.
Having said this, with one hand he held up his garment while making an effort.
Śrīdhara: Making an effort, exerting herself, she raised up her garment, that is, her upper cloth (*uttarīya*). ||20 ||21||
Vaṃśīdhara: Therefore, protection from wind and rain is "protection" (tat-trāṇam). ||20||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "By means of wind and rain. This is because, through immersion in those respective pastimes, the wind and so forth manifest directly. Similarly, later on, [the Lord says] "Look at the forest fire," which is due to an excess of fear.
Because it would cause the contraction of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), that illustration of her playful charm is not [appropriate]. ||20||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "By means of wind and rain"—this should be understood as occurring either through mere speech by virtue of imitation, or as if manifesting wind and so forth directly through immersion in those respective pastimes. Likewise, in the subsequent passage, "Behold the forest fire" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.22), they are also said to be "striving."
The loss of strength due to the pain of separation is indicated. "Unnidadhe" means she raised [them] up, or as it were held them firmly aloft like Śrī Govardhana. ||20||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: It describes the pastime of lifting Govardhana with the words "Do not fear.
A certain [gopī], acting like Kṛṣṇa and behaving like a cowherd, speaks to another [gopī] who is acting out various transitory emotions (*vyabhicāri-bhāva*).
Even while being afflicted by wind and rain, she herself endures the suffering and says:
"Do not fear the wind and rain; I have provided that protection for you. Having said this, she exerts herself and performs it with one hand, holding up the garment like Mount Govardhana.
She drew up her upper garment; that is, she held it aloft. ||20||
Viśvanātha: Making an effort, exerting herself, she raised up her garment—that is, she held her upper cloth aloft. ||20||
—o)0(o— Having mounted it, O King, one stepped upon it with a single foot while another stood upon its head, saying:
"Go on this evil day; indeed, I am born as the wielder of the rod of punishment for the wicked."
Śrīdhara: Not explained. Vaṃśīdhara: Of the wicked who are unrestrained. ||21||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is "having ascended by means of stepping upon [the throne]. Now, [the particle] *nanu* is used either for emphasis (*niścaye*) or as an address (*sambodhane*). In the reading *nṛpa*, it is an address expressing wonder (*āścaryeṇa*), O wicked one (*duṣṭāhe*). Thus [ends the commentary] of Kālya.

The address is by way of a threat: "Go away from here; otherwise, I shall inflict punishment," he says—"O you who are born! Indeed, this sentence is certainly intended as a representation of that very pastime (līlā), either through imitation of the state [of the speaker] or through the remainder of the intention of the sentence situated therein. ||21||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Nanu" means either in certainty or as an address. If the reading is "nṛpa," it is an address expressing wonder. He says, "O wicked Kāliya! Go, depart from here; otherwise, I shall inflict punishment"—this is expressed by the word "jāta. "Nanu" here signifies certainty. ||21||
The *Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha* have not been commented upon here.

In the *Rasikāhlādinī*, the pastime of the subduing of Kālīya is described with the words beginning "āruhya" (having mounted). One [gopī], acting like Kṛṣṇa and desiring to touch the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, speaks to another who is acting like Kālīya, having set her aside.

He addresses her: "O wicked woman, go away from here! Have I not certainly become the wielder of punishment for villains such as you? Having done what? She says, "Having stepped upon my head with your foot. The word "O King" causes the audience to pay close attention to this marvelous report. This...

The intended meaning is as follows: Transient emotional states (*bhāvas*), being perceived in some cases like *pūtanas* and in others like forest fires or Kāliya, are causes of suffering. Therefore, effort is directed toward their pacification; thus, there is nothing contradictory here. ||21||
Viśvanātha: Not explained. —o)0(o— There, one said: "O cowherds, look at the fierce forest fire!"
Close your eyes quickly; I shall provide you with security directly.
Śrīdhara: Close [your eyes]; close them. ||22||
Vaṃśīdhara: Among them, for you (yuṣmākam). ||22||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Regarding the phrase "and there" (*tatra ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) provides the connection.
The meaning is: "but in the imitation of the pastime of subduing Kāliya. In that regard, one [commentator] reads the text as: "O cowherds! (*he gopāḥ*).

However, in many instances, the word *re* is not favored because it is unpleasant to the ear. Thus, it is understood that Śrī Kṛṣṇa also commanded the closing of the eyes there; the statement "seeing the fierce forest fire" (*dāvāgniṃ paśyatolbaṇam*) is the explanatory reason for this, meaning that the fierce [fire] robs the eyes of their luster (*tejo-haram*). And that—

It is precisely under the pretext of closing [the eyes] that [this is said]. It should be understood that what pertains to the Muñja forest is likewise to be connected [to this], and thus it was not described separately. Regarding "apidadhvām," although one would have expected "apidadhvadam" because the substitution of *bhaṣ* for the reduplicated syllable is required by the rule "dadhas tathoś ca," it is stated as "apidadhvam."

The change to *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirated stops) or the fourth letter of the class is either an archaic reading or due to the scribe’s negligence. *Añjasā* means "without effort" or "easily. ||22||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Regarding the phrase "and there" (*tatra ca*): the connection with the word "and" (*ca*) means that this was done there even while imitating the pastime of subduing Kāliya; for it is stated [in scripture], "the eyes," and so forth. Furthermore, in the Muñja forest as well, the two-fold protection from the forest fire was likewise imitated.
Thus it should be understood. Or rather, among those [women], from that [state], there is merely the imitation of the Maunja forest-dwellers. The alternative reading is quite clear.
*Añjasā* means without effort (*anāyāsena*). ||22||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: regarding the pastime of drinking the forest fire (*dāvāgni-pāna-līlā*), it says "therein" (*tatra*). On the day of the subduing of Kāliya, at night on the bank of the lake, remembering the forest fire that had arisen as a cause for the destruction of the people residing in Gokula...

A certain woman said: "In reality, it is merely the wandering forest creatures that are non-consuming; having formed the notion of a forest fire regarding them, one who acts like Kṛṣṇa spoke to her who was acting like a cowherd:
'O cowherds! Behold this most intense and terrifying forest fire with your eyes quickly!'"
"Close your eyes and shut them; by drinking the forest fire, I, Viśvanātha, shall provide for your welfare, O wicked one! O Kāliya! ||22||
There, a certain slender woman with beautiful eyes, having tied another garland around an *ulūkhala* mortar,
covered her mouth in fear and displayed a mockery of terror.
Śrīdhara: [The Lord] covered her beautiful face with his beautiful eyes; or, "sudṛk" means a lovely-eyed woman. "Bhīti-viḍambanam" means the imitation of fear. ||23||
Vaṃśīdhara: Since she may possibly be among them, he says "having beautiful eyes" (*varākṣī*) to provide a qualification even for a woman. ||23||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Thus, with the verse ending "some woman bound [her hair] with another garland," he speaks of a dissimilar case.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Otherwise, because she had previously spoken thus, the slender lady, merely imitating the movements of the Queen of Vraja, immediately became emaciated due to the pain of separation; in that context, "in the imitation" means in a certain woman who was imitating a mortar. "With beautiful eyes" (*sudṛk*) means even with her two eyes.

The meaning is that he imitated fear by means of startled glances and so forth. By covering his face with both hands, he manifested the natural disposition of a child’s fear; he assumed the imitation of Kṛṣṇa’s state of being frightened, including trembling and slight weeping or speech. Thus...
The imitation of other divine sports (līlās) should also be inferred as appropriate for each case. ||23||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, he describes the imitation of those for whom mental activity is predominant—beginning with the word "baddhā" (bound). Alternatively, by another woman who is distinct from them, who has arrived later in the form of a messenger (*dūtī*), and who follows their opinion; or rather, by another who is extraordinary compared to the world.

The meaning is "with one that is supremely soft. This is because previously she was bound by her mother even with ropes made of extremely delicate cow-hair and the like; or else, she was previously bound with one garland and subsequently bound again with another of the same kind, for the sake of multiple bindings as before.
Even their flower garlands possess the capacity for binding and the quality of following His will.

Emaciated by the pain of separation, she immediately attained a state of leanness; it was precisely because of her extraordinary love that she imitated the pastimes characterized by the specific quality of being subject to the devotees of the Blessed Lord. In that imitation—
Or rather, "in them" (*tāsu*).

"In a mortar" (*ulūkhale*) means in some [place] that imitates a mortar. "With beautiful eyes" (*sudṛś*) means they mimicked fear even with their eyes through such acts as startled glances; [this is said] while covering their mouths.

And with his own hands, he [performs] this mockery of fear characterized by the natural timidity of a child—such as trembling, horripilation, slight weeping, and faltering speech. Thus, it is generally indicated that there is merely an imitation of mental gestures through fear and so forth; for fear has the mind as its object. In this way...

The pastime of Śrī Dāmodara, consisting of His absolute submissiveness to His devotees, is the most excellent among all pastimes; therefore, it is mentioned at the very end, according to the maxim that one should conclude with sweetness by imitating that [pastime].
The killing of Dhenuka and Pralamba is not imitated because it was performed by Śrī Baladeva; likewise,

the stealing of the maidens' garments and the dragging away of the groups of sacrificial wives is omitted either out of modesty, or because such pastimes culminate within one's own self alone, rendering those external details irrelevant.
Furthermore, the "breaking of the Yamalārjuna trees" is not treated as a separate pastime because it is included within the "pastimes of Śrī Dāmodara";

thus, there is a departure from the previously stated sequence of pastimes. This is due to the description of their agitation caused by separation, through which even Śrī Bādarāyaṇa attained such a state of emotion that his analytical investigation [of the sequence] ceased. Or rather:

According to the principle of the written record (*likhita-nyāya*), among the three—namely, effort (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth—each is present in the subsequent one; thus, it is stated that there is a sequence regarding their being either isolated or combined, and even therein, their relative deficiency or predominance. Alternatively, it is precisely in those [three] that isolation, combination, and so forth occur in this very order.

This is because of the vivid manifestation of those various pastimes; or else, due to being distressed by separation or being absorbed in thought, there is an absence of recollecting the sequence [of events]. This is the general direction of the argument. ||23||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: therein, there is no sequence of the pastimes because they are like the state of one intoxicated; thus, there is sometimes a forgetting of a particular pastime, such as the non-mention of the slaying of the demon [Naraka]. Likewise...

The abduction of Vatsa and the slaying of Pralamba have not been mentioned; because they were consumed by the flames of the fire of separation, no imitation of them occurred. Although the sport of binding [him] to the mortar happened at the very beginning, it has only now entered the path of memory. This former sport was of the nature of happiness, as follows:

Thinking, "Just as he was bound by Vrajeśvarī with a mortar and became subject to her control, so too shall he become subject to our control through this pastime," they imitated her at the end. "Bound" refers to a certain slender girl who, possessing the same disposition as Yaśodā, acted like Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Tied with a garland by someone acting like a mortar, she—her body emaciated from the fever of separation—became so heated that the fire, fearing she would burn it, resorted to a mere imitation of fear, a transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*), by mimicking her form;
thus, the beautiful-eyed woman, covering her face, engaged in a mockery of fear, an imitation of terror. *Sudṛk*.

Or, Sundarākṣī performs the breaking of the twin *arjuna* trees and so forth; it was not mentioned separately because it is included within [the general category of] pastimes, or perhaps it was forgotten due to her being overwhelmed by the pain of separation. In that opinion, it is said to be equal [to the others].
In this way, the imitation of other pastimes is to be inferred. ||23||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, when the intensity of her sudden madness subsided, even her identification with Kṛṣṇa became weakened. Consequently, she perceived herself as a gopī and was intent on imitating the pastimes of breaking pots and stealing fresh butter.
Perceiving this to be the work of Yogamāyā herself appearing as Śrī Yaśodā, [the Lord] acted in a manner appropriate to her; thus it is said: "Bound...

The grammatical construction is as follows: having said, "I bind you with a rope made of fresh butter," she bound him with another kind of garland; then, covering his beautiful face, she resorted to a feigned display of fear—an imitation of terror. ||23||
Thus questioned by Kṛṣṇa, the creepers and trees of Vṛndāvana pointed out to him the footprints of the Supreme Soul within that forest region.
Śrīdhara: Thus once again, in Vṛndāvana, the creepers and trees, inquiring after Kṛṣṇa in a certain part of the forest—that is, in a specific forest region—beheld him. ||24||25||
Vaṃśīdhara: "In a forest region" means in a woodland area. ||24||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: It should be understood even in the case of existence—as "thus," and so forth. Thus, those [entities] under discussion are real by virtue of their identity [with consciousness]. ||24||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is that they were asking questions characterized by those very modes, in a manner consisting of the repeated singing and imitation of those various pastimes. It is a matter of wonder that they beheld the footprints of the Supreme Soul—the original source of all—within that forest region.
Even in the Veda, the sages merely conjecture that words are of the nature of sound by way of indication;
yet in that very place, in the forest region of their own pastimes, they beheld those very footprints in the form of actual foot-marks. Oh, how remarkable this is, even in this mere aspect!

The meaning is this: even all of us sages cannot attain equality with them, much less that particular portion consisting of their eternal belonging to Him and so forth, which is attained through such extraordinary love. In the commentary on the section beginning with "He disappeared," first there is mere distress, and secondly—

The sequence is as follows: first, searching accompanied by singing; second, the imitation of the slaying of Pūtanā and so forth; third, searching once again; and fourth, the sight of the footprints. In his own commentary, he states: first, mere distress; second, the imitation beginning with the stretching out of the arms; and third...

One should discern that there is searching accompanied by singing, and within that very process, the occasional imitation of the slaying of Pūtanā and other such acts, as well as the fourth stage, which is the manifestation of the footprints. ||24||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "In this way" means by the manner of the previously mentioned question; or else, by the repeated imitation of those various pastimes in the manner previously described. The reason for this is that they explained the words "Kṛṣṇa, the attractor of the mind," [and] again, "the Abundance."

"They described him specifically by the casting of their gaze" means that while previously they had spoken only through mere imagination regarding such statements as "the festival of touching Keśava’s feet," now they saw him directly. And in the case of direct vision, even those things which were previously seen directly [are now described with greater clarity].
Due to being overwhelmed by separation (*viraha*), there is an absence of mental connection (*anusandhāna*); therefore, they would be as if unseen. For this very reason, they were not pursued.

And now, because of the imitation [of them] through identification with them (*tanmayatva*), and due to some slight subsiding of that [separation], the meaning is that he saw them preceded by a mental connection (*anusandhāna*) by means of the intellect (*buddhi*). For this reason, the prefix *vi-* is used.
"Of the Supreme Self, who is most beloved"—this is the reason for seeing Him even at night by means of His characteristic marks. The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].
Or else, when the evening has passed and the moonlight of the autumnal full moon has spread far and wide, even from a distance...

The vision of that [reality] is clearly [attained]; or rather, the passage beginning with "thus" (*evam*) and so forth is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to indicate the perception of the words right in the midst of the question. ||24||

The sequence of the composition: the meaning is that it is wonderful how the words [of the Lord], who is the Supreme Self and the fundamental nature of all, were made manifest in the forest region. In the section beginning with "When He had disappeared" (*bhā.pu.
10.30.1*), according to the commentary of Śrīdhara Svāmin, there is first of all mere distress (*tāpa*).

The sequence is as follows: second, searching accompanied by singing; third, imitating [acts such as] the slaying of Pūtanā; fourth, searching once again; and fifth, the sight of the footprints. In his own commentary, he states: first, the heat [of longing]; second, the imitation beginning with the stretching out of the arms; third...

One should discern that there is searching accompanied by singing, and within that very process, there is the occasional imitation of Pūtanā and others, followed by the fourth stage, which is the manifestation of the footprints. ||24||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: "In this way" (*evam*). In this manner, by means of the practice of the pastimes (*līlā*) as previously described, sometimes there is a question directed toward the trees, sometimes toward the creepers, and sometimes...

Imitating past pastimes— sometimes those forgotten— they again question the vines and trees of Vṛndāvana because, due to the intensity of their distress from separation, they lack the capacity for recollection. Repeatedly asking about the footprints of the Supreme Soul, His most beloved, in that forest region suitable for pastimes, they search.
They observed—that is, they saw—the footprints; [they concluded] that this was indeed the fruit of imitating her playful movements.
They observed them by first examining them and then seeing them clearly, having reasoned thus. ||24||

Viśvanātha: "In this manner" (*evam*) means by this method. Regarding the phrase "questioning Kṛṣṇa," this refers here to the intensity of the madness of deceptive separation (*vaipralambhika-unmāda*). When self-forgetfulness occurs, there arises an identification with one's own dearest beloved. As it has been said: "The dear ones [belong] to the Beloved."

"His form having become fully ascended, 'I am he'" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.3), and "I am Kṛṣṇa; behold my movement" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.19), and so forth—this is an imitation occurring when there is some degree of self-identification while being in the intermediate state. As it is said in the account of Pralāda: "In some instances..."
"Endowed with that bhāvanā, absorbed in that, he indeed imitated Him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.4.40). Here too it is said:
"Acting like Kṛṣṇa, he drank from the breast," and so forth.
When that very self-contemplation is prevalent even in its mild form, there arises a question regarding even insentient things such as trees and shrubs.
These footprints of the high-souled son of Nanda are clearly visible,
for they are marked with the signs of a banner, a lotus, a thunderbolt, a goad, a barleycorn, and so forth.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Vaṃśīdhara: "Clearly" means manifestly. How is it known that this [sacrificial rite] belongs to the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa? To that he says: on the banner, up to that extent, having placed her upon His very lap by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself...
Because it leads [to liberation]. ||25||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then they said to one another—"The footprints. Indeed, by means of the banners and other [emblems], those footprints of the Son of Nanda are clearly and distinctly perceived. By which [emblems]? By the banners and so forth.

The meaning is that the banner and so forth are well-known; that is, they are indeed established there. The reason for the presence of the banner and so forth is that [the Lord] is the Great Soul, the Supreme Person (parama-puruṣottama). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), other things are also included.
Regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa in that context, it is stated in the *Pādma Purāṇa* in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:
Indeed, exactly sixteen marks were seen by me on his feet:
eight marks on the right foot and seven on the other.
The banner, the lotus, likewise the vajra, the goad, and the barley grain;
the svastika, the upward line, and likewise the eight-cornered [figure].
O best of Vaiṣṇavas, I shall now describe seven other [forms]:
the rainbow, the triangle, the pitcher, and the half-moon.
The garment, the fish-mark, and the cow's footprint is remembered as the seventh;
likewise, listen, O best of divine sages, to the sixteenth mark, which is seen here and there in the shape of a rose-apple fruit. Thus it is said.
In the *Kramadīpikā*: "The fish, the goad, the lotus, the banner, the barley-corn, the lotus, the thunderbolt... (*Kraḍī* 3.14).
In the *Śrīgopālatāpanī*: "His two feet are marked with the conch, the banner, and the parasol" (*Goṭā.u.* 2.59). In the *Ādivārāha*, in the *Mathurāmaṇḍalamāhātmya*:
"In that place, which is of the nature of Brahman and beyond the material qualities (guṇas), Kṛṣṇa sported as he pleased, his feet marked with the discus.
Thus, there are nineteen marks, including the additional ones of the discus, conch, and parasol. However, in the Skanda Purāṇa, it says:
Only the group of six beginning with the discus has been mentioned, and that indeed pertains only to Śrī Viṣṇu and others; for it is stated in the *Pādma-purāṇa* in the context of the sixteen marks:
"O learned one, whenever these marks are seen..."
There is no doubt that the Supreme Brahman, known as Kṛṣṇa, has been born upon this earth.
"O best of Vaiṣṇavas, two, or three, or four, or even five [disciples] are indeed seen in some way during an incarnation.
Regarding their rule, it is as stated there:
In the center, the banner is to be known; the lotus is three finger-breadths in measure.
The vajra is indeed on the right side, and the goad is indeed at its front.
There may be a barley grain at the base of the thumb, or a svastika mark anywhere;
beginning from the forefoot, it extends as far as the middle of the foot.
Furthermore, O dear child, in that which is called the *pādma* [mandala], an upward line is indeed prescribed;
its eight-cornered [figure] has a measurement of eight finger-breadths.
The sages indeed have declared that [the first] is indicated on the right foot;
now, I shall describe here the positions for the other [feet].
One should know that the rainbow occurs at a distance of four finger-breadths from the fingers; otherwise, it would never appear anywhere else.
A triangle is indicated in the center where there is a jar;
with a measurement of eight finger-breadths, that shall become a half-moon.
The *bindu* and the fish-mark (*matsyacihna*) are indeed specified at the beginning and the end;
the "cow's footprint" (*goṣpada*) with two hooves is to be known by the measurement of the first finger-joint.

"Thus, O sinless one, this is the characteristic; therein the banners are said to be lotus-shaped, with a triangular tip at the end," and so forth. It is explained that [the measurement] is by three *aṅgulas*. The meaning is: having set aside a measurement from the tip of the middle finger, according to the reasoning to be stated hereafter. [The banner] bears the flag beneath the lotus.
This is also because of the dialogue in the *Skānda-purāṇa*. "In any place whatsoever" means wherever it is most beautiful, that is, in many places.

"The beginning" refers to the foot; from there, extending as far as the middle—the space between the thumb and the forefinger—that is the extent of its eight-cornered [mandala], which should be understood as measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

The meaning is: "having left a space of eight finger-breadths in front. Regarding the measurement of its own form, there is no inclusion [of the feet] within that space; for it is well-known from the *Hayaśīrṣa*, *Matsya Purāṇa*, and other sources that the length of the foot is fourteen finger-breadths and its width is six finger-breadths, and [the placement] follows accordingly.

It has also been explained as being three finger-breadths (try-aṅgula) in measure. Furthermore, it will be explained elsewhere that because it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva) and consists of such colors, it possesses the nature of Indra’s bow (the rainbow); thus, by means of a measure of four finger-breadths, it is said to be abandoned from that measure because it resides below the middle finger. Likewise.
Regarding the object of knowledge in terms of its length as well, for the sake of aesthetic beauty, that which is indicated in the middle is situated in the middle of the feet;

the meaning is that it is located below the triangle with a measurement of eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*), because the two corners of that [triangle] slightly overlap the triangle. The *bindu* is a synonym for *ambara* (space). And this—

It consists of two mandalas, external and internal, as it is stated in that very [text] regarding its characteristics: "endowed with two lines. Above all the symbols is a dot (*bindu*), and below all the symbols is a fish; the cloven-hoofed and the solid-hoofed [animals] are at a distance of two finger-breadths from the first dot.

The meaning is "the rainbow and so forth. That [line] which has a triangular mark at its end—resembling a whirlpool in the shape of a lotus—and which occupies the position of a banner (patākā), is formed by the elision of the locative case-ending (*aluk*);
and this triangular mark is to be understood as being on the right side only, because on the left side it is struck by an upward line; thus, the sixteenth sign is to be known as being in both feet.

Because it was stated without a fixed rule, by the description of its being equal to a *jambū* fruit, that mark consists precisely of that color and that shape, and not in the form of lines; as for the disc and the conch—
having beheld one spot of ground, a certain cowherd girl, a beautiful woman among the cowherds, said:
With every limb bristling with horripilation, her lotus-like eyes blossomed wide.

"O friends, look at these lines marked with the signs of a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus; these are the footprints of Kṛṣṇa, who moves with playful grace. Thus says the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Then they said to one another: 'Footprints' means the marks of the feet."

"Clearly" means with certainty. These belong to the Son of Nanda alone and not to anyone else, for they are distinguished by the banner and other marks; therein they state the reason: "of the Great-Souled One," meaning because of his being a Mahāpuruṣa.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the discus, conch, and so forth are included. A specific detail regarding this is found in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Beholding the ground, one cowherd woman, a beautiful wife of a cowherd, spoke,
her entire body bristling with horripilation and her lotus-eyes blossoming.
"Behold this line, O friend, marked with a banner, a vajra, a goad, and a lotus;
these are the footprints of Kṛṣṇa, who moves with playful grace. Thus it is said.
The purpose for bearing the banner and the other symbols is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The Unborn One bears a wheel at the base of the big toe of his right foot;
there it serves to sever the fierce cycle of worldly existence for those who bow before him.
At the base of his middle fingers, Acyuta holds a lotus,
exceedingly beautiful for enticing the bees that are the minds of those who meditate upon him.
Below the lotus, she holds a banner—the banner of victory over all misfortunes;
from the base of the little finger, she holds a vajra that shatters the mountain of the devotee's sins.
In the midst of the Vārṣṇis, he bears the goad that subdues the elephants of the devotees' hearts;
it consists of the fullness of enjoyments and rests upon the joint of his thumb like a barley grain.

Likewise, from the base of the big toe of his left foot, that Blessed One slightly opens his mouth for the illumination of all sciences; he also bears the marks such as the lotus there, just as on his right foot. Thus [ends verse 25].
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.
*Prīti-sandarbha* (310): *Padāṅka*—"These words are clearly those of the high-souled son of Nanda," and so forth. ||25||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: First, she speaks in order to determine for one another [the identity of the footprints], saying "these are the feet"—meaning, these are the feet of Nanda’s son and not of anyone else. This is clearly ascertained. Regarding that, they state the identifying marks: they are characterized by the banner, the lotus, the thunderbolt, the goad, the barley-corn, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), other [marks] are included.
Furthermore, there are signs [indicating this]. As it was said by Brahmā to Nārada:
"Those by whom the Lord, the Blessed One who is affectionate toward His devotees, is thus known—I know them; I do not know the speech of others. This which I have spoken is the truth."
Indeed, sixteen marks were seen by me at that place:
eight marks on the right side and exactly seven on the other.
The banner, the lotus, likewise the vajra, the goad, and the barley grain;
the svastika, the upward line, and likewise the eight-cornered [figure].
O best of Vaiṣṇavas, I shall now describe seven other [forms]:
the rainbow, the triangle, the jar, and the half-moon.
The garment, the fish-mark, and the cow’s footprint are recorded as the seventh;
O wise one, these are the signs that appear to you whenever they do.
And hear, O best of divine sages, about the sixteenth sign:
wherever it may be seen, it has the appearance of a jambū fruit.
"The Supreme Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa has indeed been born on earth; of this there is no doubt.
The sinless sages say that this is declared to be the sixteenth mark.
Thus [it is said]. And then two, and then three, and then four, and even five.
"O best of Vaiṣṇavas, [the marks] are indeed seen in some way on the avatāra.
Thus, the state of being the cause for wearing [the marks] is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The Unborn (Aja) bears the discus at the base of the big toe of His right foot."
There, for the sake of cutting through the sixfold group of enemies of humble people, he—
At the base of his middle finger, Acyuta holds a lotus,
most beautiful for enticing the bee-like minds of those who meditate upon him.
Below the lotus, one holds the banner, the banner of victory over all aims;
from the base of the little finger comes the vajra, which shatters the mountain of the devotee's sins.
In the middle of the heel, he bears a goad that destroys the fear of worldly existence in the minds of his devotees;
and on the joint of the big toe, he bears a barley grain consisting of the perfection of enjoyments.
Likewise, from the base of the big toe of his left foot,
that Blessed One emits an excellent ray of light for the illumination of all branches of knowledge.
The footprints are also signs there; just as with the right foot, the others should be inferred in the same way. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Having thus described the threefold types of insanity, immediately thereafter, having observed the footprints of Kṛṣṇa appearing quite spontaneously, they speak with joyful reflection, beginning with the words "The footprints. The locations for bearing the banners and so forth, as well as their purpose, are stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The Unborn One bears a wheel at the base of the big toe of his right foot;
there, for the sake of cutting through the sixfold group of enemies of those who bow before him.
At the base of his middle finger, Acyuta holds a lotus,
exceedingly beautiful for enticing the bees that are the minds of those who meditate upon him.
Below the lotus, she holds a banner—the banner of victory over all misfortunes;
and from the base of the little finger, she holds a vajra that shatters the mountain of the devotee's sins.

"In the middle of the heel, he bears a goad—the cause for subduing the elephant of the mind through devotion—consisting of the attainment of enjoyments; on the joint of the thumb, he bears a barley grain;
indeed, there is a thunderbolt on the right side, and a goad at its tip. Thus it is said.

Since this was stated specifically regarding Kṛṣṇa in the Skanda Purāṇa, the traditionalists say that the goad is at the base of the little finger and the thunderbolt is on its palm. However, the goad on the heel should be understood as belonging to Nārāyaṇa and others.
Thus, the six emblems of Kṛṣṇa are the discus, the banner, the pitcher, the thunderbolt, the goad, and the barley grain.
Having observed other marks on the right foot from the *Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī*, they are now recorded:
an upward line beginning from the joint of the thumb and forefinger extending to the middle of the foot;
an umbrella on the sole of the foot; and [another] on the middle of the sole.

There are four svastikas situated in the four directions; at the four junctions of the svastikas, there are four jambū fruits; and in the center of the svastikas, there is an eight-cornered [figure]—thus there are eleven symbols.
Likewise, starting from the base of the big toe of the left foot, there is a trident facing that [foot], for the illumination of all vidyās.
"The Blessed One bestows this. At the base of the middle finger is the sky, consisting of two mandalas, internal and external. Below that is a bow without a string.
Below that is a cow's footprint. Beneath that is a triangle. Surrounding that, in some cases, is a quartet of jars.
And three [figures] are seen:
on the base of the triangle is a half-moon touching two corners of the triangle at its two tips; below that is a fish. Thus, including these, there are eight [figures], totaling nineteen. ||25||
Following that path with various footprints,
those women, distressed and looking ahead, saw the tracks closely intermingled with those of their daughter-in-law and spoke thus.
Śrīdhara: "Supṛktāni" means well-mixed or thoroughly blended. ||26||

Vaṃśīdhara: [This is] the speech of all of them—"by those various... meaning "equipped with banners and so forth. Of Him, Kṛṣṇa; the path, the track. Seeking, searching for. By the footsteps, the placements of the feet, of the bride, the woman. Afflicted by jealousy. ||26||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By those various [objects] adorned with banners and so forth; the repetition (*vīpsā*) is due to the desire to express a multiplicity of locations, because of the interruptions on the ground made of *dūrvā* grass and other materials here and there. In front...
Thus, up to that point, because Kṛṣṇa himself had placed her on his lap and carried her away,
the women— though weakened by separation and searching— seeking and hunting for the path, the track of that Kṛṣṇa, [followed] that very one, the bride Śrī Rādhā.
Because she is to be established as one possessing supreme good fortune. ||26||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By means of various signs such as banners and the like—the repetition (*vīpsā*) being intended to express either their great number or their exclusivity—even though they were "weak" (*abalāḥ*), being deprived of strength by both separation and searching, they sought and searched for the path, the way, of that Kṛṣṇa ahead of them; [the phrase] "having looked ahead" (*agrato vilokya*).

Or [it refers to] a certain bride who is to be kept secret; or rather, because she is by her very nature inclined toward modesty, she is like a daughter-in-law (*snuṣā*) in that she is entirely withdrawn; or else, she is called "bride" (*vadhū*) due to a particular desire of Śrī Yaśodā;
or perhaps she is known as a "bride" in Gokula because it has issued from her own mouth.

The reason for not explicitly mentioning her name—that of Śrī Rādhā herself—has already been written. The definition of the term *vadhū* (bride) has been stated. In the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "A certain woman of great merit, languid with passion, went along with him."
"And these are her footprints, and the riches are meager. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.32).
The word *pṛktāni* means "well-mingled" or "joined," because her forearms were placed upon her shoulders.
Thus, it is refuted that he was hidden by their movement due to self-absorption (*ātmārāmatva*) or out of envy; for among them, there was one—

Because of leading her away; and that [leading] should be understood as occurring because she, having remained right there with them, was led out from that place by some secret signal, and met him—who had appeared at a distance for that purpose—after traveling only a few steps forward.
They were distressed because, by abandoning their own [comfort], they accepted only her. Or else:
Though afflicted by separation, they did not speak [out of distress], but rather, preceded by right reflection and so forth, they said to one another: ||26||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus determined that these footprints belong to Śrī Kṛṣṇa by means of such extraordinary signs, she says "by those various [marks]" (*tais tair*), implying that they went elsewhere along that path. [The marks] of the banner and so forth on the ground...
Again and again, while searching for him by following his footprints— the marks of his feet—

they were disregarded by Kṛṣṇa because their pride had been stripped away by internal meditation. Then, in a certain place ahead, they saw the footprints of a particular bride, a goddess of Vraja, situated in the same locations as his own.
Beholding them closely entwined, the distressed women spoke to one another, saying:

"Although that name was known by the Lord of Sages, he did not speak it in the assembly because it was improper to utter the names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds at that time, being overwhelmed by the pain of separation."

Since they were already overwhelmed with distress while searching for her, the sight of footprints accompanied by those of a woman became the cause for the further intensification of that distress. Therefore,
the meaning is that even their obstruction in searching ahead arose solely due to the influence of jealousy.
For it is precisely from the renunciation of one's own [interests] and the embracing of those [of others] that envy and the other [defilements] arise. ||26||
Viśvanātha: "Supṛktāni" means mixed together. ||26||
Whose footsteps are these, left by one who has gone with the son of Nanda,
her forearm resting upon his shoulder, like a female elephant with a male elephant?
Śrīdhara: She whose forearm was placed upon his shoulder; [the word] *kareṇoḥ* means "of the female elephant. ||27||
Vaṃśīdhara: Of which fortunate woman? The *prakoṣṭha* is the part at the base of the palm. ||27||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Regarding that, all [commentators] ask—"Whose? Here, it should be understood that the knowledge of her being female is derived from the lightness of her feet, as well as from her being characterized by a low gait and limbs appropriate thereto.
"By the son of Nanda"— as before, the ellipsis is "let these footprints be identified as belonging to whom.
And although the placing of her forearm upon His own shoulder by the Blessed Lord was indeed due to a particular sentiment of aesthetic rasa (*rasa-viśeṣa*),
it was nevertheless for the purpose of ensuring Her comfortable movement at night, or for the purpose of leading Her away by force when She might stumble.

And this indicates her excessive affection for Him. They express that very point through an illustration: "of the female elephant" (kareṇoḥ). Because those two also move in that same manner out of affection due to the intoxication of passion, [the author] asks "Of whom? and so forth, ending with "the fixed one" (dhruvam), in order to satisfy the great Vaiṣṇavas.
The remainder of the sentence is: "Let it be discerned whose footprints these are, belonging to her who traveled together with the son of Nanda.
Furthermore, the placing of her forearm upon His own shoulder by the glorious Lord was due to a particular sentiment (*rasa*);
or else, it was for the sake of her walking comfortably as she stumbled at night, or for the purpose of leading her forcibly to a distance.
By this, her excessive affection is indicated. They express that very point through an illustration: "of the female elephant" (kareṇoḥ).
For even they proceed in that same manner out of affection due to the intoxication of passion. ||27||
The sequence of composition: "Whose feet? and so forth. ||27||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Up to this point, they had been searching for [the Lord], imitating His pastimes and posing questions to insentient objects according to their respective inclinations, without mutual agreement. Now...
Upon seeing the footprints of the bride, many transitory emotions arose; overcome by a weight of distress and desiring to determine [the owner], they asked one another, "Whose are these footprints?
Whose wife is she, who possesses such exceeding affection for Śrī Kṛṣṇa?"
"But how was He recognized by you? To this they replied: "By the Son of Nanda.

This indicates His lack of awareness regarding the suffering of others. The sense is that, by abandoning our company, He did not allow Himself to be constrained by us, even while acting as our helper out of respect for the Lord.
Of her who had placed her forearm upon his shoulder— that is, she whose forearm was resting on his own shoulder as its point of support—
they imagine that, due to wandering through distant lands and the arising of *sāttvika* emotions born from the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body, her limbs have become relaxed.
The meaning is that Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself placed His own forearm upon her shoulder because her footprints were incomplete and because He did not hold them properly.
Alternatively, these are indeed Her footprints, and they were placed— that is, established— by Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon Her very shoulder.
The meaning is that because of the touch of her forearm—the region of the wrist—the sattvic state (sāttvika-bhāva) arose;
thus, by the sign of her stumbling line of footsteps, it is understood that an excess of love for him had been born.
For if there were not such single-minded absorption in that object, then [the heart] would have been paralyzed by the sattvic state.
"It could not have been otherwise. This is known from the completion of the action: that she was led away by her very gait, with her feet moving in unison.
Nor should it be said that some woman from our own herd has just now joined her, for it is a marvel that she has acquired the power of invisibility even without any display of playful charm.
Regarding this, they provide a corresponding illustration: only an elephant knows the pleasure of touch;

therefore, they take it as an example—just as the trunk of a male elephant (*karin*) is placed upon the shoulder of a female elephant (*kareṇu*), so too [is the experience]. Just as pleasure is obtained by the male elephant through contact with the body of the female elephant, so it is here.

Or rather: "Therefore, let it be understood that some woman staying right in the midst of our herd has gone along with him; her footprints alone have been frequently observed and are now being recognized. ||27||
Viśvanātha: "With her arm placed upon [his]" means that the left forearm of the son of Nanda was placed upon her shoulder. ||27||
"Surely the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, has been propitiated by her,
since Govinda, being pleased, has led us away from here into solitude."
Śrīdhara: "Raha" means a secluded place. ||28||
Vaṃśīdhara: Having recognized that daughter of Śrī Vṛṣabhānu by her footprints,

[he recalls] the words of her friends— or rather, the word *vāsudeva* is derived here from the sense "she leads away" (*nayati*) or "steals" (*corayati*), with the suffix *ḍa* according to the Uṇādi rules— by her, who is stealing our very essence, even Hari himself...

"Even though he is the Lord who takes away everything, he was propitiated and brought under control; Govinda," [the Lord] says, expressing his affection for his devotees. The sense is that for one by whom even the tending of cattle was accepted in order to discharge the debt of devotion, there is nothing else whatsoever that cannot be done. (28)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Following the doubt as to whose words these are, they determine it—by this [verse]. By her being led away, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa was propitiated (*rādhita*).
He spoke of Rādhā; he describes Rādhā; he pleases (*rādhayati*)—this is established from the root *rādh* with the suffix *kta*.
For among all [of them], her affection for this very one is the greatest; thus, she is Rādhā in his company. ||28||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: In this regard, because her friends possess an intimate connection with her due to their depth of feeling, while the opponents are superficially permeated by sorrow and the bystanders lack such attachment, it is her friends alone who speak first: "By her... The word *nūnam* expresses either conjecture or certainty; [the subject is] Hari.

The Blessed Śrī Nārāyaṇa is the remover of all suffering; He is the Lord, capable of bestowing the desires of His devotees, and though independent, He has been worshipped by Her alone and brought under Her control, not by us. Furthermore, the reason for the name "Rādhā" is that She pleases (rādhayati) or worships (ārādhayati).

This has been shown. The reason for this is: Govinda, having specifically abandoned us (*naḥ*) and left us far behind in the forest at night—even there, in a secluded spot (*rahaḥ*) inaccessible to us, a solitary place—he led her away. Or rather, even though he was departing after leaving all of us, he led her alone into seclusion.
The meaning. ||28||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Afterwards, having recognized those footprints as belonging to the goddess Śrī Rādhā, they became reassured and joyfully spoke of her good fortune by means of the etymological derivation of her name—beginning with the words "anayā. The word *nūnam* expresses either deliberation or certainty; *hariḥ* refers to the remover of all suffering.

The Blessed Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Controller, capable of bestowing the desires of His devotees, or He who is independent. He was propitiated and brought under control by Her alone, and not by us; otherwise, our suffering from the pain of separation from Him and so forth would be impossible. She is called Śrī Rādhā because she pleases (rādhayati) or propitiates (ārādhayati).
The naming ceremony is also shown: since Govinda,

although equal to her and to us in being the lord of Gokula, has specifically abandoned us and taken her far away into the depths of the forest at night— even there, into a secluded spot inaccessible to us— there he led her.

Or rather, it is Govinda himself who has been propitiated by her. To demonstrate her supreme good fortune, they specifically praise Govinda—[describing him as] the Blessed One intent on manifesting his entire sovereignty.
Therefore, Hari is the remover of all suffering; or else, he is the Lord who captivates the hearts of all through his form, qualities, and so forth.
He is the lord of the lives of the people of Vraja; therefore, the implication is that the experience of Him was brought about by her alone.
The rest is the same.
The two occurrences of the word *yat* (which) are for the purpose of strengthening that very reason. Or rather, [it means] "since He is pleased," therefore...

This should be construed by imagining two distinct sentences: "yām anayat" (whom he led away) and so forth. The same should be inferred for what follows as well. Alternatively, it may mean: "while going in secret" ||28||
The sequence of composition, the extensive sequence of composition: "because he is pleased with that"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||28||
Prīti-sandarbha 109: Now, regarding Śrī Rādhā-devī in that very place, it is said in the Ādi-purāṇa: "In the three worlds, the earth is blessed; therein, Vṛndāvana is further blessed;
even there, O Pārtha, are the gopīs, and among them is she named Rādhā, who is mine."
In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the *Kārttika-māhātmya*:
"Just as Rādhā is dear to Viṣṇu, so too is her pool dear;
among all the gopīs, she alone is the most beloved of Viṣṇu. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the superiority of that [devotion] alone is described in the Āgneya Purāṇa, as in the statement cited in the Vāsanā-bhāṣya:
"At dawn, the gopīs questioned Uddhava, the follower of Kṛṣṇa."
"And the pastimes and sports of Hari there, [she perceives] without Rādhikā alone;
Rādhā, absorbed in His state, has ceased from the latent desire (vāsanā) [for such things].
Thus, because she has reached the ninth stage, she has ceased from the latent desire for questioning and so forth, being incapable of it in that state.

The meaning is as follows: therefore, among all the goddesses of the cowherd settlement (*sarva-vraja-devī*), by virtue of the signs of preeminence and so forth, she must be Śrī Rādhikā alone—she whose extraordinary fortune was described in the passage beginning with *tābhir eva svayaṃ kasyāḥ padāni* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.27) during the Śrī Rāsa-vihāra. Hence, she is designated by that very name.
They indicated this, saying: "He has been propitiated by her.

The meaning is that by means of this *rādhā*, the Blessed One was propitiated (*rādhita*), accomplished, and brought under control. The word "surely" (*nūnam*) expresses conjecture; and because she propitiates (*rādhayati*), by way of etymology, her name also became "Rādhā."
The state [of being pleased]. The reason for his being propitiated is expressed by "since not... Govinda is the Lord of Śrī-Gokula. ||28||

Prīti-sandarbha 285: Now, each one of them, according to the distinctions of their states of amorous play (*līlāvasthā*), assumes eight names: the woman who goes to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*), she who prepares her bed (*vāsaka-sajjā*), she who is full of longing (*utkaṇṭhitā*), she who is abandoned (*khaṇḍitā*), she who is deceived (*vipralabdhā*), she who is separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*), she whose husband is away on a journey (*proṣita-bhartṛkā*), and she who has her husband under her own control (*svādhīna-bhartṛkā*). Likewise, [there are variations] of these internal emotional states (*bhāva*) toward one another.

Similarity is of four kinds: complete similarity, slight similarity, and indistinct similarity; and this [similarity] is further divided into four types based on opposition: the female friend (*sakhī*), the male friend (*suhṛt*), the neutral party (*taṭasthā*), and the adversary (*prātipakṣikī*).

The distinctions among these emotional states (*bhāva*) are to be understood from the analysis of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*). Among them, the female friend is as follows: even though she is the mate of a deer...

Passages such as these (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.33.11) should be shown before the two [heroines]. For here, by the words "O friend, spreading complete satisfaction for the eyes," her own desire to see Him is revealed.
By addressing her as "friend" (*sakhi*), she is invested with the status of a friend through the equality of sharing in the fortune of enjoying the bliss of His vision.
By addressing her as "beloved" (*kāntā*), there is a clear indication of friendship, through the expression of approval for the excellence of her good fortune in being united with Kṛṣṇa.

For this very reason, the approval of Her pastimes is also expressed in passages such as *bāhuṃ priyāṃsā-* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.12). An example of a friend is seen in the statement, "She has worshipped Him. And of her—
From the praise of his fortune alone, his friendliness is clearly manifest. ||28||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, perceiving the presence of faults in themselves through the sign of their abandonment, and perceiving the absence of faults and the presence of virtues in her through the sign of their acceptance, they describe her good fortune in many ways and say to one another: "By her..."—by whom [the Lord] was concealed within.

Pointing with their fingers to the trail of footprints, they said, "She whose footprints these are has surely propitiated the Lord; indeed, through the propitiation of the Lord, she has become fortunate.
Of what sort? She is distinguished by every happiness through her connection with Hari, provided that she was propitiated by us."

Nevertheless, she has obtained the fruit of her propitiation, which we have not attained; this is because of our knowledge of the specific manner [of her service]. For it is precisely because he was not propitiated by us that we experience the suffering of separation. Had he been propitiated by us, then for us—
It is inferred by means of *kriyātivṛtti* (the non-occurrence of an action) that the suffering born of separation would not have occurred;
for Govinda, the Lord of Gokula— who is equal toward all— yet being pleased, revealed his own affection by taking us away to a secluded place beyond the range of our sight.

Alternatively, *bhaga* means fortune; possessing that [fortune] because he is the son of Nanda, Hari is filled with all happiness. He is by nature one who removes the suffering of the entire Vraja through such acts as drinking the forest fire. He is the *īśvara*, capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise. For instance, when the herds had gathered together...

Because she is capable of distributing the sweet nectar (madhura-rasa), and because we have come here to become her handmaidens without any price, we are able to accept this state of servitude; thus, although our situation is the same, this reversal has occurred for us,
as Govinda’s qualities are so exceedingly favorable toward us.

"They have been born; by our misfortune, they have become adverse. Once it was known that she had performed the worship of Govinda, the intended meaning is: "We too must perform it in that same manner. ||28||

Viśvanātha: Having recognized that daughter of Śrī Vṛṣabhānu solely by the marks on her feet, and being inwardly reassured, they— acting as if they were strangers amidst the great throng of gopīs there— addressed their friend [Rādhā] by means of an etymological explanation of her name.
They say that good fortune is accompanied by joy—by means of her. "Nūnam" (surely) is used in the sense of certainty.

Hari—the remover of the suffering of his devotees, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign capable of granting the desires of his devotees—has been propitiated. Yet, by us, he has departed from us. Thus [they lament].

And so, because she pleases and propitiates, the name "Rādhā" became manifest. The sage applied great effort to bestow that very name upon her, yet it emerged spontaneously from the moon of her face, as if out of compassion to sound the drum of her good fortune.

Or rather: O you misguided ones! You who, out of a vain sense of rivalry with her who is most exalted, have become unrighteous; surely this Hari has been won over—he has come here for Rādhā (rādhitaḥ). Due to the *śakandhv-ādi* rule, there is a single substitute for the following vowel. The Blessed One, beautiful and afflicted by desire, [seeks] his own fame...
Or [the word *bhaga*] is a proclaimer; for the *Amara-kośa* states: "Bhaga refers to fortune, desire, majesty, heroism, effort, the sun, and fame.

*Īśvara* means one who is capable of deceiving you. For, because of that, Govinda—having abandoned our beautiful women (*sundarīḥ*)—finds (*vindati*) or causes to find (*vindayati*) the cows, which are her senses, for the sake of pleasure. Thus he is [called Govinda].
And her footprints are described according to the commentary on the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*:
at the base of the big toe of the left foot is a barleycorn; beneath that, a discus;
beneath that, an umbrella; beneath that, a bangle; and starting from the joint of the forefinger and the big toe, they follow in a curved path.

Up to the middle of the foot are upward lines; on the surface of the middle toe is a lotus; beneath that is a banner with a pennant; above that is a creeper and a flower; on the surface of the little toe is a goad;
on the heel is a half-moon—thus there are eleven [marks]. On the right foot, at the base of the big toe, is a conch.
On the surface of that [ring finger] is a mace; on the surface of the little finger is an altar; on its surface is an earring; on its surface is a spear;

on the surfaces of the joints of the fingers beginning with the index finger is a mountain; on the surface of the mountain is a chariot; and on the heel is a fish—thus there are eight. Altogether, they number nineteen. 28.
Oh, blessed indeed are these particles of dust from the lotus feet of Govinda,
which Brahmā, Śiva, and the goddess Ramā bear upon their heads for the destruction of their sins!

Śrīdhara: O dear friends, oh, how blessed and most meritorious are the dust-particles of Govinda’s lotus feet! The reason for this is expressed by the word "yān" (those which...). The sense is that even we may attain Kṛṣṇa in the same way by being sprinkled with those very particles. ||29||

Vaṃśīdhara: According to Yādava, the word *āli* refers to a sacrificial session (*satra*) or to rows of female friends (*sakhī-paṅkti*). The blessed ones (*dhanyāḥ*) are those who are indifferent (*nirapekṣāḥ*), capable of purifying the men associated with them even without any other means of purification. According to Yādava, "one who is full of virtues and indifferent [to worldly things] is called blessed (*dhanya*) by the wise. This refers to that state of being blessed.

The meaning is that for those whose every sin has been destroyed by bearing the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet upon their heads, and whose inner hearts are purified, the attainment of Kṛṣṇa is not difficult to achieve. This is the statement of bystanders; however, those who take the position of bystanders, not applying themselves there, [use] the words "Kṛṣṇa... [and so on].

Observing this, they said, "Blessed indeed! For at the time of their arrival at the cow-pen every afternoon, during the hour when Kṛṣṇa’s companions were playing, those [gods] would descend daily from heaven and place [the Lord] upon their heads for the destruction of sins—that is, to remove the suffering caused by separation. Brahmā and the others did so for that very purpose.

Those who grasp the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet are indeed seen; as it will be said: "His feet are being saluted on the path by the elders," and "The hosts of demigods are His bards. Our feeling, however, is that simply because we are unable to grasp it out of shame, we thereby incur sin.
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "For the removal of evil"—by which we also take upon ourselves suffering (*agha*);
for in the bright moonlight, the mark of the foot is clearly perceived. (29)

The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: Then those standing on the bank said, "Blessed! The address "O these friends" is used because, due to their shared suffering, there is generally a single state of mind among all of them; thus, they are addressed simultaneously for the sake of expressing an extraordinary sense of wonder. The use of the past tense in "they bore" (dadhuḥ) [indicates the completion of the action].

This is for the purpose of making the certainty known. One should infer that among Brahmā and the others, excellence increases progressively. As for the qualification "on the head" (*mūrdhni*) applied to Ramā, it is intended to indicate her preeminence and thus makes known the abundance of her devotion. *Agha* means sin, offense, or the suffering of separation and so forth. It is the cause of [her] blessedness.

In the word *govindāṅghri*, the elision of the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-luk*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*), according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). The meaning is that [we] are blessed by virtue of our connection to Him. Therefore, even the dust particles from His feet are blessed by obtaining such a connection; the sense is that we, however, being devoid of that, are more insignificant than even them. And this—

The cultivation of the majesty of the dust of His feet is produced by love alone; for love expands even non-existent majesty, how much more so that which is real? Consequently, an excellence in that [love] results in an excellence in that [majesty] itself. As it is said in the *Ādibhastacarita*: "Or rather, what kind of austerity has been practiced by this poor woman, such that she..."
In the prose passage beginning with "The earth... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.8.23), the good fortune of the earth is described by that touch of his own deer-footprint. ||29||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "O these friends!"—this is the address. In this context, for the sake of establishing unanimity among all, or for the purpose of generating a particular devotion, and with the intention of expressing the preeminence of all [the ornaments] during their wearing, it should be inferred that they possess a progressively superior excellence despite the absence of the word "ca" (and).

Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods are always seen by them as they grasp the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet; therefore, this is described based on what is actually perceived, and not with the intention of attributing sovereign power [to them]. The word "goddess" (devī) is used for the purpose of distinguishing her from Śrī Vṛṣabhānu-gopa’s daughter [Rādhā]. Or rather, it is because of her grasping that dust.

Due to the arising of devotion toward Lakṣmī, it was said: "The Goddess is the object of worship. Alternatively, because the words for Śrī Rādhā and Lakṣmī are generally synonymous, the doubt is resolved by the word "Goddess" (devī); for as a goddess, Lakṣmī does not touch the earth. Or else, the "Goddess" is the Goddess of Vraja, Śrī Rādhā herself. [Regarding the word] "on the head" (mūrdhni):
They manifest an abundance of devotion. "Agha" means sin, offense, or the suffering of separation and so forth;
therefore, they are indeed "anagha" (sinless). The sense is that because we maintain [the Lord] through devotion, our own sin has already been cast off.
The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].

Or rather, the very dust particles are blessed and supreme, for they are worthy of receiving the gift of the supreme wealth that is Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form. Or else, those who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms, or those previously seen by the Lord of the cowherd settlement, are indeed blessed if they have not been touched by Her feet. This is a statement of envy. Or else—
These particles of dust are base, yet these grains of rice are blessed; because they were led by Govinda, their plurality is due to their venerability.
Thus, by way of this illustration, it is intended that she, like the particles of dust, is likewise blessed. ||29||

The sequence of composition, the extensive sequence of composition: those who rejoice in the dust of Her feet said, "Blessed," and so forth. *Agham* means suffering; *tannuttaye* means for its destruction. "Blessed" (*dhanyāḥ*) means those who bestow happiness. Those whom Brahmā and the other gods bear upon their heads—from them, we too [are blessed].
The meaning is "tortoise. ||29||
The Composition of Affection (311): "The dust of her feet is blessed"—here, it is *prema* alone that conveys its excellence, and not the knowledge of [her] sovereignty. ||29||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Their consciousness overwhelmed by the intensity of the pain of separation, they—possessing hidden envy—rejoice in her good fortune and, adopting an air of indifference, say to one another, "Blessed!
(addressing them as) "O friends! O companions! regarding the holding of the pollen.
This is for the purpose of emphasizing universal consensus. "Aho" expresses the attainment of something rare and difficult to find.

These dust particles currently being seen, which are connected to Govinda’s lotus feet, are *dhanya*—meaning they are supreme and meritorious. Alternatively, *dhanya* means "carrying wealth," implying that those who bear these dust particles obtain wealth.
It is so. Herein, what wealth is there that is the gateway to delight? That has slipped from our hands;

the intended meaning is that by bearing this dust, its attainment will come to pass. As for those particles of dust, Brahmā—the lord authorized over the cosmic egg—and the Lord (Īśa) authorized over dissolution, as well as Ramā, Lakṣmī—[all these are contained within it].

The Goddess, who is the presiding deity over the granting of all prosperity, shines resplendent as their wife. Regarding the dust particles they placed—that is, bore—upon their heads, they state the purpose: for the removal of evil, meaning for the destruction of sin.
Even though no particular sin is perceived in them, they nevertheless reflect thus: For indeed:

What is the sin of Brahmā? It is the granting of boons to the Asuras who were hostile to the Blessed Lord; that is its defining characteristic. The sin of Rudra is characterized by the promotion of heresy. The sin of Ramā is characterized by the bestowing of her divine power (*vibhūti*) upon the Asuras and Rākṣasas. [This verse] is for the removal of that [sin]. What...

Or rather, because they are created from the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory emotions) of Brahmā, the sin of these states belongs to Rudra—the destroyer of darkness; and because he did not provide assistance to us, the sin belongs to Ramā. For the removal—that is, the destruction—of these sins, these [deities] beginning with Brahmā deposited the dust upon us. Our...

The sense is: "Since sin is impossible [for us], for what purpose shall we wear these? Or rather, they speak again, anticipating the same logic applied to themselves: "Just as these [trees] have become free from sin by bearing dust, so too shall we [be freed from the fruit of our base conduct characterized by pride—the suffering of separation]."
This is experienced through the consecration of this rasa; it is thus suggested that for us, who are free from sin, the suffering of separation will cease of its own accord. ||29||

Viśvanātha: But those who take the side of the indifferent (taṭastha), not paying attention to that point, observe only the words "Kṛṣṇa" and say: "Blessed are they... [referring to the verse] "brahmādyā agha-nuttaye," meaning that in the afternoon they bear Him upon their heads for the removal of sin—that is, for the dispelling of the suffering caused by separation.

At the time of returning from the cow-pasture, those [Vandins] are indeed seen daily descending from heaven with the boys who are Kṛṣṇa’s companions to grasp the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet—as will be said: "His feet were being saluted on the path by the elders," and "The groups of subordinate deities (upadeva-gaṇas) who are the Vandins. As for us, however, it is out of sheer shame...
The sense is: "By that very fact which we are unable to restrain, we incur sin. ||29||
These high words of hers cause us great agitation,
for she alone has carried off the Gopīs and enjoys the lip of Acyuta in secret.
Śrīdhara says: Others say—"of her. She is the very essence of all the gopīs. The meaning is this: it would indeed be so if her footprints were not present; however, they cause us great sorrow. (30)

Vaṃśīdhara: The others are the opponents. [Objection: But surely, for those who have taken up the dust of Kṛṣṇa, how could there be sorrow? To this they reply: "Of her" (tasyāḥ). The meaning is as follows: even if such an absence of sorrow were possible, it would not exist [in their case]. The sense is that the happiness of a co-wife is unbearable. [The word] *acyutam*...

"Her lower lip is nectar constantly flowing"—thus, by remembering the falling of his teeth upon her lip, we experience agitation. The friends of the rival [cowherd] say: "Of her... They cry out loudly;
they produce [this agitation]. For all of us gopīs, the lower lip of Acyuta is the sole object of enjoyment in private.

Having distributed [the food], he eats it. The sense is: "By some means, that very beloved woman has brought him under her control and made us believe she loves us, thus leading Kṛṣṇa this far away. (30)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "These are hers," and so forth. This is the statement of others.
These particles are indeed fit to be taken up; however, because these footprints of hers cause us great agitation, they should not be taken. What offense has she committed?

He said: "Yaikā" and so forth. She is the most eminent of all; she alone did not count [herself]. How so? Thinking, "I am but one among these friends of his own, yet I shall go with him today along with his retinue," she did not count herself in this way. [She went to] the lip of Acyuta, which is the wealth (*dhana*) of all the gopīs; for the root *dhivi* means "to please," and the word is formed by an *auṇādika* suffix.
In secret, in solitude, she eats alone. ||30||

The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī states: The opponents say, "Of her," and so forth. "Excessively" means more than usual. "Agitation" means extreme suffering. "Having taken away" refers to enjoying her company in secret while she was alone. Alternatively, because he was led away by that deceitful woman through theft, he has come here leaving us; otherwise, how could he have come?

Such is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "of all the gopīs in general" is used; however, the reading "our very own wealth" (*asmākam eva dhanam*) occurs in some places. That reading likely arose without consulting their commentary, which explains it as "universality. The reading *rahaḥ* (in secret), on the other hand, is found everywhere. [It refers to] the lip of Acyuta, who, having abandoned her, did not go elsewhere at all.
Thus [ends the section]. ||30||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The speech of Śrī Candrāvalī’s friends—“of her” (tasyāḥ). “Excessively” (uccaiḥ) means with great agitation, distress, or, as previously mentioned, a loss of composure;
or else, it means that out of pride (garvāt), [the flowers] were placed even higher than us, upon her head. “Having taken away” (apahṛtya).

Because he enjoyed her company in secret while alone; or rather, because she led him away by stealth, he has come here leaving us behind—otherwise, how could he have come? This is the underlying thought. The reading "of all the gopīs" (*gopīnāṃ sāmānyataḥ sarvāsām eva*) is accepted by them, as it is explained by the term *sarvasvam* (all one's possessions).

Otherwise, it would have been explained simply as "the object of enjoyment for the gopīs. Regarding the word *adharam*: since Acyuta did not go anywhere else after leaving her, [it refers to] his lower lip. Alternatively, because she is *acyutā*—meaning unseparated from him—long-term enjoyment is intended. By way of pun (*śleṣa*), [it may also mean] that he has not fallen away or slipped from our mouths.

The phrase "that which is low" indicates that she enjoys her own leftovers. Regarding the statement, "Are these dust particles, O friend, and these [flowers] blessed?"—if taken literally, it means: "Do even those things which are high [in status] cause agitation by transgressing over us? [This is said] with a tone of irony (*kāku*), implying, "On the contrary, they certainly do not. Thus, this is the speech of all of them.
It should be understood. ||30||

The sequence of composition, the extensive sequence of composition: others said—"Of her," and so forth. These particles are indeed fit to be worn upon the head; however, those feet of hers cause us agitation. What offense has she committed? They say: "She who alone," and so forth.

When it was said, "It is not fitting for the principal lady that she alone should eat the food—having taken away the wealth [in the form of milk] from the lips of Acyuta—which all the gopīs have contributed; therefore, one should not eat a desired thing alone," [she desisted]. (30)

The Composition of Affection (287): Now, as for the counteractive [affection], it is as follows—"of her" and so forth. Furthermore, since jealousy is indeed manifest, there is a distinct difference from those [other types]. Likewise, in the *Śrī-Harivaṃśa* and other texts, regarding Satyabhāmā’s [reaction] toward Śrī-Rukmiṇī during the seizure of the Pārijāta tree. This is clear. (360)

Envy (*asūyā*) is hatred toward the excellence of others—as in the verse, "These [qualities] of his cause us agitation" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.30), which delights those who relish the aesthetic flavor (*rasika*).
Such is the majesty of the dust from the lotus feet of Govinda when he is alone;
it does not possess such power when combined with that [envy], because of its resulting bitterness, like food mixed with honey and poison.
Thus examining them, they said: "Those footprints of hers cause us agitation;
the meaning is that they give us a pain even greater than the sorrow of separation. Or else:
"Her footprints are 'high' (*uccaiḥ*), for they were placed with a special grace upon the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and thus they are 'high' for us."
They cause excessive agitation; the meaning is that they inflict a suffering even greater than the pain of separation.
They cause us agitation—the loss of fortitude and the obstruction of our search.
Regarding this, they state the reason: because she is that one [Gopī] who is the very everything (sarvasva) of the cowherd girls, though it is always well-guarded.

"Having stolen [it] by stealth in secret, he enjoys her lower lip—which is not accessible to us—even for a moment without losing its charm, and that too without even asking us! This is a statement full of longing and jealousy. Therefore, the implication is that it is not fitting for us to wear this pollen.

Viśvanātha says: Regarding the friendship with the rival [gopīs], they say: "Of her"—meaning that very passionate woman who, having alone stolen and consumed the lip of Acyuta, which is the object of enjoyment for all of us gopīs and which she produces to be raised high, has by some means brought him under her control and made us full of love.
The intention is that Kṛṣṇa, having caused her to abandon [her pride], will lead her only this far. ||30||
the footprints here are not visible because they have surely been covered by sprouts of grass;
her beloved lifted up his beloved, whose well-formed soles were causing her pain."

Śrīdhara: Seeing them searching for nothing but the pure dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, which were not mixed with anything else, she was again deeply distressed. She expresses this in three verses beginning with "They are not seen.
She lifted onto her shoulder her daughter, whose well-formed and delicate soles of the feet were suffering.
He has caused [it] to be mounted. ||31||

Vaṃśīdhara: He describes her distress regarding those who are "unassociated" with her—that is, not touched by her feet. Even though he looks with his eyes, he does not see her because of the absence of contact with her radiance; yet, such grief arises from the thought, "This kind of love is not found in us. (31)
The *Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā* states: "It was not explained.

The *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* says: "They are not perceived. They [the commentators] explain that because it was spoken out of malice, he placed it upon his shoulder. In this context, "having seen them" means "having seen them as being unassociated with that."

Or rather, even the friends said "no," precisely because they were the words of friends—the meaning is that she was one who caused excessive joy to her beloved, as indicated by the phrase "khidyat" (distressed) and so forth; "unninye" means she took him up with both hands and carried him to her lap. ||31||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "He raised her up" means he placed her upon his shoulder; this is explained by them in accordance with what will be said later: "Let her be mounted upon the shoulder" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.39).
"Preyasīm" means the most beloved; "priya" is a sarcastic remark (*paiśunyoktiḥ*). And in the alternative interpretation, it refers to each other.
