By the word "dear" (*priya*), and even more so by "beloved" (*preyasī*), it is indicated that her affection for her exceeds that for all others;

thus, the act of lifting her up is entirely appropriate—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, it should be understood that she was lifted up with both hands and carried away after being placed upon her lap. Only when this is the case...
Through the perfection of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of such embraces and so forth, her status as the "beloved" (*preyasī*) is thoroughly established. ||31||

The sequence of events, the extensive sequence of events: Having gone how far did she not move further, since the soles of her well-formed feet were pained by the sprouts of grass? How was this inferred?
To that they say: "They are not seen," and so forth. Because of her being beloved and her being the dearest one, this is entirely appropriate.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having gone to another location and not seeing those [footprints], they reflect:

"Up until this point, her footprints were seen together with the footprints of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; beyond this, they are no longer visible. They speculate on the reason for this: 'Only her footprints are not seen.'"

"Therefore, we shall hold onto the dust [of her feet]," they observed; yet they did not perceive her true nature, and out of envy, they imagined a cause for it. She whose well-formed soles were distressed by the sprouts of grass from wandering through regions as if covered with thick weeds—he lifted her up with both his hands.
"Utkṣipya" means he lifted her up; likewise, "satkṛtya" means he bestowed upon her specific pleasures such as embracing and kissing. "Svayam api priyā" [means she was dear even to him].
Now, one might ask: if she were his mistress (*prabhū*), how could he have lifted her? To this they reply: because she was dearer to him than women like me.

An excess of affection is indicated. Viśvanātha says: "O you who are seized by the great disease of envy! Do not grieve; there is no [fault] here on her part. For he himself is dear to her, and by merely fulfilling her desire, their mutual love has been manifested through such a journey to a distant place—this is the sense.
Her dear friends said, "There are footprints," to which she replied, "No.

To them alone, other friends, with joyful side-glances, spoke softly and reflectively, "Surely... [The meaning is: she lifted her up with both arms and placed her upon her own chest; for she was her most beloved, being the object of her supreme affection.

This is because the pain from the soles of her feet is unbearable. Indeed, it should be understood that here the two kinds of happiness experienced by her friends arise: one from seeing her such great good fortune, and the other from seeing the suffering of her rivals. ||31||
"O cowherd women, look at these extra-large footprints of Kṛṣṇa as he carries his beloved bride, though he is already burdened by her weight."
Śrīdhara: Since they both performed the treading of the earth by means of their forefeet, for that very reason, look at their feet as being incomplete [in their reach]. ||32||
*Vaṃśīdhara*: Not explained in *Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now the opponents say with malice, "These... The sense is that this is perceived by you, O clever cowherd girls (*gopīs*). [They are] lustful.
The meaning is: [this applies] to one who is dependent solely on lust, but not to one who is connoisseur of the essence of love. ||32||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: They state its definition as "these [signs]... The sense is that, O gopīs, this is indeed perceived by you who are so clever. The term "desirous ones" (*kāminaḥ*) is used because otherwise such signs would be impossible; this is a statement of jealous reproach (*īrṣyokti*). In reality, however...

By the very fact of being joined with desire (*kāma*), the excessive longing for the self and its objects is indicated; furthermore, attachment to that [longing] is intended by the final word. This verse is not found in many manuscripts. (32)

The Sequence of Composition (*krama-sandarbha*) and the Great Sequence of Composition (*bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*): "O friends! This reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*). For that [person] has gone somewhere here, and thus her footprints are not perceived.
It is not so, because she is being led away. Look, look! This reason is indeed inconclusive. For instance:

They say: "These," and so forth. If [these marks] are deeply impressed on the bridegroom as he carries the bride, it is because he is overcome by emotion. The reason for carrying her is that he is a lover (*kāmin*). Having gone some distance elsewhere and observed another kind of footprint, they say with certainty: "Here," and so forth. For the sake of the beloved—that is, on account of the beloved—at this spot.
He performed the gathering of flowers. He indicates his identity by that mark: "Behold him on the uneven, broken ground.
Of what sort? "Upon those treading with the tips of their feet"—*prapada* means the tip of the foot; *ākramaṇa* means the pressing down or support provided by it.
[The commentary for this verse, titled] *Rasikāhlādinī*, is not available.
Viśvanātha: "O you who speak without reflection! Why do you say, 'Do not grieve'?

The opponents, indicating that even the sight of his feet is more painful than not seeing them at all—and implying that our very lives will cease if he is not seen—say: "These... [referring to] "the bride."

The sense is that even though Kṛṣṇa was not formally married to her, he made her his own wife in this forest. For this very reason, householders burdened by weight—namely, burdened by the weight of their wives—indeed wander here and there; the sense is that they are merely lustful, not truly loving. This is because we have abandoned even those who possess love.

Therefore, for this very reason, desire alone should drive him or her; otherwise, how could the son of the King of Vraja—who is indeed exceedingly delicate—be the mount of a cowherd girl? Such is the meaning. ||32||
Here, the beloved was made to descend by the high-souled one for the sake of flowers;
here, the gathering of blossoms was performed by the lover for the sake of his dear one.
While he was stepping with his toes, these two saw him standing on his entire feet.
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Vaṃśīdhara: The grooming of the hair is the decoration of the hair. In this context, [it refers to] a woman who is exceedingly beautiful; [even] by a lover, though he be possessed of full bliss, [this is done]. *Dhruvam* means certainly.

That place is now famous as Śṛṅgāra-vaṭa. This speech of the female friend has not been commented upon in Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā. In Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī, however, the friends speak again with the half-verse beginning "atra," [referring] to the Great Soul.
The meaning is "by Vidagdhaśiromaṇi. Furthermore, this half-verse is not seen in some [manuscripts]; therefore, no numbering has been assigned.
Then other friends said: "Give birth here! [The word] *preyasā* means by one who causes excessive delight.

Regarding the previous [verse], they state the indicative mark (*liṅga*) with the half-verse beginning with *prapade*. [The word] *pade* implies "at every flower-tree" as the ellipsis. For this very reason, there is plurality [of trees] in the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"Dāmodara certainly gathered flowers here on high, by which the footprints of that Great Soul were left here as soon as they were stepped upon" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.34).
Thus says the *Bṛhad-Vaiṣṇava-Toṣaṇī*: "Later, having seen her footprints ahead, they said: 'Here...'"

The meaning is "by the great-souled Vidagdhaśiromaṇi. Through *śleṣa* (punning), it is also an envious remark: "one whose self—that is, intellect—is 'great,' [meaning] massive like a mountain. This half-verse is seen only in certain places.
By the phrase "for the sake of the beloved" (*priyārthe*), it refers back to the previously mentioned "the beloved woman" (*preyasīṃ priya*).

By means of this reversal of expression, it is indicated that their mutual affection is indeed equal. Alternatively, whereas she was previously called "the beloved" (*preyasī*) in relation to her leading [him], she is now called "the lover" (*preyas*); thus, the intended meaning is that the gathering of flowers was performed by her according to the command issued out of her status as the most beloved. In that context, the word *pade* (on the feet) is in the dual number.

For even by staying in one spot within a single flowering tree situated in Śrī Vṛndāvana, the gathering of abundant flowers is accomplished; or rather, because many words that have arisen in various places are seen twice or thrice in one location. Therefore, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Dāmodara certainly gathered flowers here from on high, for the footprints of that Great Soul here are seen as soon as they are stepped upon. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.34).
Thus ends the sequence of steps; the "Great Sequence of Steps" has not been explained.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Furthermore, having gone forward and perceiving the tips of her feet, they imagine the gathering of flowers and say: "Here. Here, in this place of play (*kṣāva-pradeśe*), the beloved, having been commanded by his mistress for the sake of her own adornment, out of respect for that command—honoring what was ordered by her for the sake of his own beloved and for her satisfaction—[proceeded].

The gathering of flowers has been performed; thus, a state of mutual harmony is indicated. Observe the incomplete and uneven foot of one who, while gathering flowers situated in a high place, steps upon the ground with the foreparts of the feet (*prapada*). This is because the parts [of the body] have become manifest.
And because among many words, two by two are not seen together in one place, this was stated as a possibility; thus it was said by Parāśara:
"Dāmodara certainly performed the high gathering of flowers here."
"Wherever the footprints of the Great-Souled One were merely stepped upon here"—thus says Viśvanātha.
Again, the friends say: "here. The meaning is: by the Great-Souled One, who is the crest-jewel of the clever;
or else, by him whose soul (ātman)—that is, his mind—is fixed on that festival of adornment for the sake of the flowers.
The meaning is that this *aśoka* tree was planted for the sake of flowers; having received the touch of her feet, it blossoms immediately, with the intention: "May I adorn her with these flowers.
For this very reason, the great-souled one, possessed of great intelligence, [performed] the gathering of flowers here at the *aśoka* grove.

Thus, the intended meaning here is that for this very reason there are no flowers [on the tree]. Because of the crushing of the earth by your feet as you stepped with your forefeet to pluck the flowers from a branch some distance away— one that could not be reached by the hands— therefore, they are incomplete, since no full marks of those two [feet] are seen upon the ground.
Here, the lover has arranged the hair of his beloved;
surely he sat here while she was adorned with those locks as her crest-ornament.

Śrīdhara: Seeing the mark upon her as she sat between Kṛṣṇa’s knees, they said, "It is the sign of hair-dressing. Having fashioned those flowers into a crest for his beloved, he must certainly have sat down while binding them in imitation of a topknot. (34)

Vaṃśīdhara: The grooming of the hair, the dressing of the hair, and the adornment of the hair—[all performed] in this place. Of the beloved woman, who is exceedingly beautiful; even by the lover, though he is possessed of full bliss. "Dhruvam" means certainly.
That place is now famous as Śṛṅgāra-vaṭa (the Banyan Tree of Eroticism). ||34||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having seen the falling of the flower-cluster called *garbhaka*, the opponents speak again with the half-verse beginning "Keśa...". The word "tu" (*but*) marks a new beginning. In the reading "hī," it expresses certainty.
The purpose of the adornment is indicated by the words "of the amorous woman" (*kāminyāḥ*) and "by the lover" (*kāminā*). The meaning is: for the sake of the pleasure of amorous play.
Having seen such a sitting posture, the female friends said [the verse] beginning with "those" (*tāni*).
It should be understood that the knowledge [expressed by the command] "make them crest-like" (*cūḍayata*) arises from having frequently seen such a style of dress in one's own country.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The grooming and refinement of the hair is performed with one's own fingers or, for that purpose, with a comb placed upon one's own head. The word *tu* marks a change in the introductory topic. In the reading *hi*, it means "certainly. The purpose of the grooming is as follows:

It indicates: "by the lover of the beloved. The meaning is: for the sake of the pleasure of amorous play. Or rather, it is like the previously mentioned "lover" (kāmin). "Certainly" (dhruvam) means "definitely," because its specific characteristic is directly manifested. ||34||

The sequence of composition, the extensive sequence of composition: Then, having gone somewhere and observed the signs of sitting down, some say—"the arranging of the hair," and so forth; this is certain. Here, by that lover, the arranging of the beloved's hair was performed. Regarding that, they state the reason: "those," and so forth; those...
The flowers have been gathered; he is seated here—let him certainly be seen face to face;
this is the meaning. ||34||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Then, observing the movement of petals that had fallen and become scattered on all sides while another garland was being woven, they speak, imagining it in another way, beginning with the words "Of the hair... (*keśa...*). Here, seeing the mark of the weight of her hips, they infer that Kṛṣṇa’s beloved sat down.

While her ornaments were being arranged by her beloved and she was longing for the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s hand, the arrangement of her hair was performed by pressing the braid with His hand. This was done by the lover—meaning one full of longing for kissing, glances, and so forth—in order to demonstrate amorous play; such is the meaning of "it was done."

They state the specific meaning expressed by the word *tu* (but/however). By the word "elsewhere" (*anyā*), they indicate another location; here, in a secluded place (*rahaḥ-sthale*), he was seated adorning his beloved’s hair with those flowers, weaving them into her crest—this is certain (*dhruvam*) and there is no doubt, because the characteristics [of that act] are directly manifest. Thus...
For the sake of increasing passion, her secret approach, the gathering of flowers, and her adornment have been described. ||34||

Viśvanātha: Having observed the mark on her who was seated between Kṛṣṇa’s knees, the opponents spoke again: "It is understood that the dressing of her hair was done with a comb given by the forest deities of this place.
This is the act of a lustful woman, not of one possessed of love; for she has even deceived her own friends to meet a lover."

Because they had gone into seclusion; by a lover, but not by one possessed of true affection, for even we who possess affection do not consider the pain of separation [for them]. And therefore, here, by those [men] who were "cūḍayantaḥ"—that is, making their beloved woman wear a crest (cūḍāvatīm) as a joke to manifest their manliness with those flowers or hair—[the following occurs].
The sense is that because he was seated firmly [on her lap], even talk of secret dalliance occurred; [in the compound] *vinmator luk*, there is the elision of the suffix *matup*. ||34||
Though he delighted in her, being self-rejoicing and finding delight in the Self, he remained unbroken;
yet he displayed wretchedness to those who lust and the wicked nature of women.

Śrīdhara: "He took delight," and so forth, is the speech of Śuka. "Self-delighting" (ātmarataḥ) means satisfied by himself; "sporting in the self" (ātmārāmaḥ) means finding his play within himself. "Unbroken" (akhaṇḍitaḥ) means that even though he was not attracted by the amorous charms of women, he nevertheless took delight. To the question, "If that is so, why did he take delight? he says: "Of those who possess desire" (kāminām). ||35||

Vaṃśīdhara: If it is so, and He is not drawn away—if there is doubt in that regard—he says the reply: "of the lovers. He *reme*, meaning he experienced the play of amorous union. He is *rata* in the bliss of his own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*). He is one for whom there is *ārāma*—that is, sport—in the Self. This is according to the Śruti: "He delights in the Self, he sports in the Self" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.4).
By these two qualifications, the sage indicated the prohibition of the conduct of a libertine (*viṭa*).

Here, the gradation of love is indicated through the gradation of devotion, knowledge, and so forth, which are the means for attaining the pleasure of the Blessed Lord. Thus, other gopīs are merely functions of the senses, whereas she alone is devotion led by Kṛṣṇa.

Or rather, it is the intellect (*buddhi*) that is to be known. One should be satisfied with the fact that the words of that [intellect] are to be applied by the intelligent person as signifiers of their respective meanings. Furthermore, grief and so forth have the *guṇas* as their cause. For this very reason, it is said to be "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*). ||35||
* Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "He took delight with her, though he was delighted in his own self," and so forth—this is the statement of Śrī Śuka.
Its meaning is this: although he was delighted in his own self, finding pleasure in his own self, and although he was undivided [from himself], he took delight with her.
One might ask: how is it that, despite being endowed with such qualities as finding pleasure in the Self, he abandoned everything else and took delight with her alone?

To this he says: "Of those who possess desire," and so forth. Those who possess desire are wretched; as for those who are women, they are of evil nature. This one is not a seeker of desire, nor are these women of the nature of ordinary women. These, indeed, are of the form of the power of consciousness-bliss (*cid-ānanda-śakti*). There is no distinction between them.

Or rather, he is "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*) because his delight is with the Self through identity with the Self (*ātma-tādātmyena*), even while these women have been abandoned; thus, there are no heroines characterized by distinctions of state or name, for there is no such thing as a "broken" condition. This teaches that delighting with even one woman alone is indeed delighting with all of them.

He who [possesses this power] therefore delights those women as well, and he himself sports with her. Beyond this lies his inconceivable greatness; by showing the wretchedness of that lover, it is demonstrated that ordinary lovers indeed cannot do such a thing because of their common nature, nor can they perceive the wickedness of women. And women...

These are evil-minded people; for they do not worship me who am of such a nature, but instead worship a living corpse. Or rather, though I delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), I am "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*)—meaning that nothing is broken within me—and though I am of a single flavor (*ekarasa*), I display to lovers the wretchedness [of separation] and the agitation of falling at my feet and so forth. Nevertheless, her grace...

Perceiving that he was not born [of a noble lineage] and observing the wicked nature and intractability of women, the more he displays despondency, the more she too manifests aversion; thus, manifesting and accomplishing both [these points], she says: "How can my friends have been abandoned?"—revealing her anger. In this very manner...
He manifests a pastime of being under the sway of His devotees;

or rather, showing that He takes pleasure by becoming attached to Himself even as He displays the wretchedness of those who are lustful. Thus, [He showed] the wickedness and the state of suffering of the gopīs who had been abandoned by their husbands.

Demonstrating this, the meaning is as follows: "I am thus completely under your control; if you harbor pride here, then you will become like her"—this is a hint at a future consequence. Or else, whoever is lustful is miserable; just as the lustful one is, so is he who is not thus [not lustful], just as I am.

"In this way, whatever women there were, they were all wicked-souled; whereas those who were not like [ordinary] women were not like that, as in the case of the Gopīs"—thus, by means of negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*), he showed the wretchedness of lustful men and the wicked nature of ordinary women, and took his pleasure. The meaning is that he took his pleasure in such a manner as to be extraordinary (*aprākṛta*).

Regarding the term *strīṇām* (of women): for womanhood (*strītva*) does not consist in the possession of hair and breasts; rather, it is established as the state of being a cause for binding by virtue of covering (*ācchādakatvena*), derived from the root *stṛ* with the suffix *ṅīṣ*. This is precisely the meaning of the etymological parts (*avayavārtha*). Otherwise, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Devahūtī and others, who possessed such physical traits yet had already attained the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Or rather, he took delight in such a way that the wretchedness of those possessed by desire arose; and he considered the women who had been abandoned as being outside [of himself]. ||35||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, having praised that pastime together with her through the very mouth of the Śrī-gopīs, he himself also praises it: "He rejoiced. By means of his own manifestations (*vaibhava*), which are forms of his own portions (*svāṃśa-rūpa*), and by way of the causes consisting of the Lakṣmīs and others belonging to Vaikuṇṭha, as well as the beloved wives (*preyasī*) and others connected to the cowherd settlement (*goṣṭha*).

Being devoid of dependence on anything else, he was delighted in his very own self, which is the substrate of all those various aspects; the meaning is that by himself alone his desires were fulfilled. Even being such a one, he was likewise *ātmārāma*—the meaning is that he was intent upon immersion in the bliss of his own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*). Even being such a one, for that reason he took delight; that is, he rejoiced, disregarding all those [external objects].
In this context, "by that" means by her as the cause. Because the word "that" (tat) manifests a distinction residing in the speaker's mind, the meaning is:
"by way of being the object of that supreme love which is the locus of all [other loves]."

In the reading "reme tayā cātmarataḥ," because the word *ātmārāma* would result in a redundancy (*paunaruktya*), it is understood that he is "delighting in himself" precisely because his nature consists of having all desires fulfilled by her. Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) indicates that just as she imagined his delight with her, so too did he delight [with her]. Thus it is.
The intended meaning remains exactly as before.
Now, one might ask: "Is he not seen enjoying himself even with those beloveds such as Lakṣmī and others?
To this, he replies: "Unbroken"—meaning that by reason of her [the primary beloved], he is not broken here and there as he might otherwise be.

The meaning is this: just as a woman whose husband has been unfaithful might mentally stray from him, he [the Lord] never strays from her for reasons such as Lakṣmī and the like; therefore, because he is conquered by her love, it is revealed by him. Such is her love for him.

Even such a person was brought under his control; indeed, he possessed such power that even [the state of] delighting in the Self (ātmarāmatā) was eclipsed by it. Thus, in this way, those who lack such an object of focus, self-love, and subjection [to the Divine] are merely lustful men and women.

He says that [these things] are shown as being cast aside by its own majesty: "showing to those possessed of desire. "To those possessed of desire" means to those whose nature is characterized by desire in the form of a longing to satisfy the body—which is nourished by food, water, and so forth, which transform into impurities such as excrement and urine—and not [to those who see it] as having the form of existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*).

The meaning is that they are self-satisfied, and not characterized by such qualities as being understood as the cause for his own delight, namely *sattva*, *cit*, and *ānanda*. Furthermore, their fitness for illuminating Him will be stated later in the passage beginning with "by them, whose sorrows have been dispelled" (*bhā.pu. 10.32.10*).

The meaning is that [he displays] the wickedness of other women, having brought under his control such a wretched leader and his own corrupt nature characterized by joy, pride, and so forth. As it was said by the venerable Queen Rukmiṇī:
"Within, he is covered with skin, beard, body hair, nails, and hair..."
"Flesh, bone, blood, worms, feces, phlegm, bile, and wind—
a woman who does not smell the nectar of your lotus feet is deluded and possesses the mind of a lover for a living corpse" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.45).

In this regard, the extraordinary nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has indeed been stated. Furthermore, by the verse beginning with "yā te padābja... and so forth, it is made known that only certain individuals who are capable of experiencing His extraordinary nature become similarly extraordinary themselves.

Thus, by demonstrating their wretchedness and her wicked nature through a clever turn of phrase— just as in the verse, "The moon, bearing its mark, shines forth from the face of Ramā, thereby suffering defeat," and as in,
"She was seen by the eyes that steal the beauty of the lotus" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.2)— he reveals this.

By this, only the excellence of the extraction of those respective [qualities] from Himself is established; however, because He is not preceded by a conscious intention (*buddhi-pūrvikā*), when such qualities as delighting in His own Self are perceived, even an imitation of them—like a person mocking others by displaying the wretchedness of a lover—is not possible for Him. Otherwise, it would not be so.
This has been explained. Furthermore, being under the sway of love for the devotee is indeed well-established in many passages such as, "I do not hope for myself... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.4.64). ||35||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "In himself, by himself, and of his own accord"; or alternatively, "delighted (rataḥ) simply by his own nature (ātmanā). In the reading *ca*, the particle *ca* serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for what has been stated, meaning "and he rejoiced.
Thus, even though he was already delighted and satisfied by himself alone, he nonetheless rejoiced. Such a state [of being satisfied by oneself] does not exist now.
The meaning of "remained" (*sthitam*) is as explained previously. The repetition of that statement is for the sake of strengthening it.
Therefore, the intended sense is that he was satisfied by her alone, delighted by her alone, and captivated by her delusions.
Thus, it is indicated that because he was conquered by love, he surrendered his entire being to her. And that—
For that supreme one who is affectionate toward his devotees and who is overwhelmed by love for his dear ones, there is no fault whatsoever;

on the contrary, it is nothing other than a great virtue that manifests the very essence of his own divine nature. This has been written many times before and has indeed been explained in the *Śrībhāgavatāmṛta*.

Alternatively, they were equal to himself because of his friendship with them. Or rather, the meaning is that even while being devoted to those gopīs who were dear to his own self, he remained unimpaired and complete, and thus enjoyed himself fully through total engagement of body, mind, and speech. The rest is the same.

And it is not only His own beloveds who were thus delighted; He also performed a benefit for others, as He says: "of those possessed by desire. The meaning is that He instructed the people that they should not be under the sway of lust nor under the sway of women. In this regard, just as the Blessed Lord [acted] toward men by means of His own conduct...

She instructs [him]; likewise, his beloved wife also instructs [him] and thus displays her wicked nature, as the author says: "And she... Although such conduct and pride are not due to wickedness, but rather serve solely to increase the mutual love between these two great city-dwellers, and especially...

While it is certainly not appropriate for [the Lord] to have a husband who is under his own control, nevertheless, pride and the specific speech uttered by him toward the Lord are indeed improper; thus it is explained by those devoted to the scriptures on the worship of Viṣṇu.
Even that fault is entirely dispelled, because those two [scriptures] are intent upon instructing the world.

Or rather, it shows the wretchedness of lustful beings such as Indra and others by demonstrating their state of envy due to the absence of the happiness of blossoming and so forth toward their beloveds; and it reveals the wicked nature and poor intellect of women because they serve husbands other than Śrī Kṛṣṇa who are contemptible; or else, it is a display of wretchedness toward those who are lustful.

And by showing [this] very wickedness toward women, he is instructing them; this is the sense. The underlying idea is: if there is a relish for amorous play, then men desiring to sport must remain undepressed even while being thus subject to women; and likewise by women, in matters such as sexual union.
Having abandoned modesty and the like, and having brought a man under their control,

they should be intent on wicked conduct characterized by independence; this is evident from the speech and behavior of those two that will be described hereafter, or rather, from the intention behind the aforementioned behavior.
Alternatively, this very manner of lovemaking mentioned here has been demonstrated; and thus,

through a particular cleverness, there is a display of feigned helplessness and wretchedness by means of various postures described in the *Kāmaśāstra*, such as placing both of the woman's feet upon the two shoulders.

And [such acts] as biting the lower lip, seizing the hair, and acting the part of a man upon the chest of a man are to be understood [as occurring] in relation to specific sages established in knowledge and so forth; likewise, the employment of words such as "wretchedness" and "evil nature" [is used] with reference to them.
But in reality, it occurs through the particularity of their own aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and by way of a specific mode of expression alone.

Alternatively, "ātmarataḥ" may be taken as ending in the locative case; thus, it is construed with both [of the preceding terms]. Consequently, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). By showing to those who possess desire that in one devoted to the Self there is only wretchedness—which is indeed suffering—since the enjoyment of desires and so forth cannot be achieved through such devotion; and by showing to women that in one devoted to the Self there is only wickedness.

By demonstrating this, service to her Lord and so forth could not be accomplished by her; for this very reason, disregarding his own self-satisfaction, he himself took delight with her—this is the general direction of the matter. Enough with further elaboration.
In this way, those words of his are consistent with the sentiments of those illustrious queens of Vraja.

Even in the knowledge of the reality of the Śrī-Bhagavān, because it consists of a specific aesthetic relish (rasa) through the non-deviation of one's own internal state, there is a sequential composition; thus, He Himself praises that pastime along with her: "remire" ||35||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now Śrī Śukadeva introduces the account of that very same [gopī] with the words "He took delight with her," and so forth. The meaning is: "with her who was led away, having abandoned all others.
They say, however, that there was no partiality on His part: "While these gopīs were separated from Him, He, who finds delight in the Self, [remained] with Himself, that is, with His own mind."
"Rata" means delight; here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). He took delight together with her, who had been brought [there].

[An objection: "But how was this known? To this they say: He is one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*) and possesses inconceivable supreme sovereignty. For this very reason, he is "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*), meaning his love is unbroken, incomparable love—this is the sense. This is because he is a "generous hero" (*dakṣiṇa-nāyaka*). By me... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
This is because of his own statement: "She was hidden from view while he was worshipping her in her absence" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.21).

Therefore, the pleasure with them was mental, whereas with her it was physical. What was he doing? He was demonstrating the wretchedness of lustful men and the wicked nature of women, making this understood through the application of inference.

For instance: whoever is desirous is miserable, because of being powerless; wherever there is powerlessness, there is misery, as in the cases of Purūravas, Yayāti, and others. Whoever is not so [powerless] is not so [miserable], as in my own case. Thus, by means of an inference based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), the misery of those possessed by desire is established. In this way...
The gopīs and others are not evil-minded, because they possess contact with my limbs. Wherever there is contact with my limbs, there is no evil-mindedness, as in the case of Lakṣmī and others.
Those who do not possess contact with my limbs are evil-minded, such as...

The women, such as the gopīs, are distinct [from ordinary women]. This means that by means of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he demonstrates the wicked nature of ordinary women. By this [he shows]: "I am not a lustful man, nor are these women wicked by virtue of being female; rather, their hostility and so forth arise from their feminine nature for the purpose of my pastimes. My...

The meaning of the sentence is that following after them is merely His pastime (līlā). He is called "one who delights in the Self" (ātmārāma) because He takes pleasure in the gopīs, who are as dear to Him as His own self. ||35||

Prīti-sandarbha (288): Now, when separation has arisen, it is only through their dejection that there is a perception of wickedness on their part, but not because of actual wickedness, since [their nature] consists solely of the playful manifestation of love. The Lord of Sages (Śrī Munīndra) also, in accordance with that very state of theirs—
He repeats her words, having heard what was spoken by her, beginning with [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.42].
However, he himself had previously rejected the fault in that intoxication of hers, as in: "He took delight with her, though he is delighted in the Self."

Although he was delighted in his own self, satisfied by himself, finding delight in the Self, and playing with his own being, he remained unbroken; yet, being constantly attached to her, he took pleasure in her. If he were such a one, why did he become so attached to her and take such delight? To this he says: "By her," as in the verse: "Hari, possessing such qualities... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.7.10).

The meaning is: "by virtue of having such qualities," that is, by being the very essence of the entirety of her love. Therefore, since it is impossible for anyone else to possess such [qualities], this manifests as a specific form of love (*prema-viśeṣa*) and not as mere desire (*kāma*).
And that specific love is so powerful that, just like desire, it produces wretchedness and other such states in the two of them.

He says "kāmitām" (the state of being desired) to reveal this: by means of his own self, he demonstrates that very wretchedness well-known in the world which belongs to lovers toward the love of beloved women— which is essentially composed of intoxication, pride, and so forth— by way of transferring the excellence of that [divine] love onto them.
He took delight while manifesting [this].

Or rather, he says "of the lovers" (kāminām) to show that by her very play (*līlā*), all others who consider themselves refined (*nāgara*) were rendered insignificant by her alone. By the greatness of her own play, she brought about the wretchedness of ordinary lovers.

He shows the deficiency in the excellence of their aesthetic flavor (*rasa-sampatti-hīnatva*) and the wickedness—the state of having a corrupt nature—of ordinary women through their devotion to another besides Him, just as [the moon] shines with its stain shaken off after defeating the moon, as in the verse: "The face of Ramā shines, having vanquished the moon. (35)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: They state that for whose sake all this was done: "They took delight. Having thus established the pastimes as determined by the conjectures and personal experiences of the queens of Vraja, Śrī Śuka describes to Parīkṣit how Śrī Kṛṣṇa is solely subservient to love through the path of aesthetic relish (*rasa*).
He explains: "He delights in [the Self] (remā). The word "api" (also/even) is to be supplied everywhere. He is one who delights in the Self;
even though he delights in the Self—that is, in his own essential nature—or alternatively, he is one who delights by means of the Self (*ātmanā*), that is, by his own nature;
or even though he is one who delights in the group of beloved ones, being endowed with affection for them; or alternatively, he is one who delights in the Self, that is, in the mind (*manasi*).

Though contented, though devoid of expectation for sense objects, and though one who finds delight in the Self—meaning one whose pleasure and play (*āramaṇa*) is in the Self alone; or rather, one whose garden (*ārāma*) is with the Self and thus requires nothing external—even so, he took delight with her. He took delight, disregarding his state of being delighted in the Self and his habit of finding delight in the Self.

This is the intended meaning: knowing the degree of happiness found in delighting in the Self (*ātmarati*) and in being delighted by the Self (*ātmārāmatā*), He took delight in that [Self]. What pleasure is there in delighting in one's own body and senses? That delight and that pleasure—which belong to the body and senses—how could they exist in the Self, which is devoid of senses? For this very reason, He is omniscient.

The one possessed of knowledge thus performed the discernment of all flavors; for, being unbroken and complete, he took delight. This is the meaning: prior to sporting with the gopīs, there was neither self-delight nor the state of delighting in the Self.

Because both [qualities] are not inherent [in the individual soul]. Nevertheless, although self-delight (*ātmarati*) and self-repose (*ātmārāma*) are attributes of consciousness (*caitanya*), the act of delighting in one's own [objects] is an attribute of the embodied being (*vigrahin*) as qualified by the body and senses. Thus, there is no contradiction even though both [sets of attributes] reside in the same substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as it is in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*).

There is no contradiction between knowledge and ignorance, or between merit and demerit; it is the same here as well. Therefore, just as there is a gradation between knowledge and ignorance, or between merit and demerit, so too, having understood the gradation between being a lover of the cowherd women (*gopī*) and being one who delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*), he experienced his own bliss through sporting together with the cowherd women who were of a similar nature.

He manifested his own skill in the arts through the path of aesthetic rasa, and he also manifested his own indivisibility; otherwise, how could one man possibly be the consort of so many leaders of herds, were it not for the perfection manifested by his *yogamāyā*? Just as another...
A hero (nāyaka) is considered "broken" when, while awaiting the arrival of his beloved at a rendezvous, she does not come;
however, this one is not broken because he has many consorts, for he is called "Acyuta" (the Unfallen).
This is due to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s status as a "right-hand hero" (dakṣiṇa-nāyaka). As it is said in the Rasārṇava: "Even though there are many heroines..."
"It is said that the right side is equal [to the left]. Furthermore, oh, what beauty and love!
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having been captivated by her, took his pleasure with her, disregarding his own self-delight and his state of being one who delights only in the Self.

Having stated his own purpose, he states the purpose [of the work] with the words "for those who possess desire" (*kāminām*). For others—namely, ordinary people who are merely vessels for excrement and urine—the state of being *dainya* (dejection), *pāravaśya* (subservience), and *prasādana* (appeasement) arises through the surge of the mind due to the perception of the roughness on the beloved’s face, which brings about the emergence of transitory emotions (*sañcāribhāva*). It is precisely for such people that [this work is intended].
He took delight in demonstrating the wickedness, the nature of suffering, and the mounting of joy, pride, and arrogance that women possess due to their husbands being under their own control.

This is the intended meaning: Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda-vigraha); [the gopīs] are of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda-rūpā).
Therefore, the exclusive devotion of the Vraja-gopīs is not merely an imitation, but is indeed ontological.

This is stated by way of *kaimutya* (the logic of "how much more so"): even in worldly matters, the state of being mounted upon pride and arrogance—which is characterized by being established in honor—is found among the wicked; how much more so, then, in the case of Kṛṣṇa, who is the personified essence of the sweet nectar of rasa?
"Lest there be dejection or absorption in that [worldly state]"—

this was the intention of Śrī Śuka, which has been explained by the Teachers (Ācāryas) even for those who are unacquainted with such activities and unacquainted with the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; [it concerns] His independence and the stainlessness of the gopīs.
To establish their ignorance by means of the example of other women, He said, "of those who are lustful.

Therefore, there is nothing inconsistent; this is the intention of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Just as the words "Welcome to you, O fortunate ones" produced a certain understanding in them according to the literal meaning, so too here [the word] "kāminām" [is used].
He taught people by his own conduct that those who desire should not be under the sway of women;
he established the wickedness of women through her behavior. Although such pride was not due to wickedness, but solely for the sake of increasing the mutual love between the two.

While this is indeed appropriate for one whose husband is under her own control, nevertheless, it is the established law (*dharma*) that in the practice of the path of *maryādā*, speech characterized by pride—which causes disregard for the Lord—is improper. Thus, while instructing her in the path of *maryādā*, He likewise instructs her in the path of *rasa*: "If you have a desire for amorous play (*riraṃsā*) in the sweet sentiment (*madhura-rasa*), then..."

Those who possess aesthetic sensitivity should be humble and subject to the influence of women if they desire devotion through skill in the arts of love; conversely, if they possess such skill, they should, having first cast aside modesty, bring their husbands under their control and act with independence—yet women who are overcome by pride and arrogance should be taught that such behavior leads to wickedness. Thus, there is instruction in both cases.
This secret was not revealed by looking into the mouths of sages devoted to knowledge, ritual action, and so forth.

Therefore, disregarding his state of self-repose (*ātmārāmatva*) in accordance with the *kāma-śāstra*, he took delight with her; for through self-repose alone, no particular pleasure arises—thus it is sufficient. ||35||

Viśvanātha: Having thus demonstrated the excellence of her good fortune through the very words of the gopīs, he himself establishes it as well—[with the verse beginning] "He took delight. Although he is one who finds delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), he took delight with her.
The reason for this is: "delighting in his own Self" (*svātmarata*). He is one whose own delight is made beautiful by being together with her.

He: the meaning is that he would not experience such happiness in the state of delighting in the Self as he would in sporting with her. This is how it must be explained, for if the reading were *ātmara-taḥ*, it would result in a redundancy with the word *ātmārāma*. The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). He whose delight—his sporting—is with that very Self through effort.

"He" refers to the Self (*ātman*). According to the *Amara-kośa*, [the Self] is "the mover, fortitude, and intellect. The sense is that such great effort is made precisely because there is no attainment of such bliss in the state of delighting in the self alone (*ātmārāmatā*).
Now, does this not imply that it [the state of delighting in the self] is complete? To this he says: "unbroken. That too is complete.
Thus, it is not fragmented; the sense is that because it is the *hlādinī* power, it constitutes His very nature (*svarūpa*).

Even though it is the *hlādinī* power, because it is of the nature of that supreme limit—namely, *mahābhāva*, which is the essence of all joy consisting of love—and because the Blessed Lord delights in Himself (*ātmārāma*), [He remains whole].

Even compared to delighting in mere joy, there is indeed a superiority in delighting with Her, who is the very essence of the greatest joy. As it is said in the Tantra: "The Hlādinī is the Great Power, the most excellent among all powers."
"She is the very essence of that [Kṛṣṇa], known as Rādhā;
she is the embodiment of the Great State (mahābhāva), most excellent by virtue of her qualities.
And therefore, although he delights in the Self, he finds delight in his own self together with her; and though he delights in his own self, he remains undivided from her.

The grammatical connection is: "Pūrṇa alone took delight. And by that, he acted for the benefit of those who do not know the reality of the Blessed One but are capable of worldly discrimination, while simultaneously concealing from them the truth of his own divine play;
thus he says: "Of the lustful"—meaning those under the sway of desire and those under the sway of women—"let there be no [such state]," so he made the world think.

The meaning is that He taught them. The Lord and the beloved of the Lord provide the authoritative proof for the principle that when men are under the sway of desire they become wretched, and when they are wretched, women become wicked;
for they wander here and there prattling, being the very causes for the concealment of the reality of the essence of radiant love.

The sense is that they "became [thus]. This should be explained by the two words *eva* as follows: "showing [this] very way" and "concealing the true essence of the sentiment of love (*prema-rasa-tattva*).
Alternatively, it may mean "showing wretchedness in relation to lovers"—thinking "the world is like myself."
The meaning is that, by way of logic, those who were lustful saw him as truly wretched, and those women who were lustful saw him as truly evil-minded;
or rather, "displaying the wretchedness of the lustful" means that he was seen by the lustful as one rendered wretched by their petitions for sexual union and the like.

It must be so; showing that there it must be with wicked women acting without consent, he makes known to those who appreciate aesthetic flavor (rasika) that in this way alone is the nourishment of rasa, and not otherwise—this is the intended meaning. ||35||
O!"—thus speaking as they showed him, those bewildered cowherd women wandered about;
for Kṛṣṇa had led away that particular cowherd woman from the forest, leaving behind all the other women.

Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "And she," he describes the wicked nature of women. Thinking, "I shall abandon those gopīs whose vehicle for coming—that is, their means of arrival—is desire, and instead worship me," he considered himself superior. ||36||
Vaṃśīdhara: He states the nature of the demoness’s intellect—thus, it has not been explained [here] according to the previously mentioned view of Caitanya, the *Mañjūṣā*.
Vaiṣṇavatoṣiṇī: And that is so; for in such a state, their condition of proof is twofold.

It is possible: when there is the manifestation of only the beloved, it consists primarily of the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) such as joy; when there is somehow the manifestation of another [object], it consists primarily of the stable emotion such as pride. Therefore, because of the predominance of intense passion (*gāḍhānurāga*), it consists of the manifestation of that alone, persisting for a long duration.
She was born consisting of joy and other such emotions; now, however, since she has somehow become external, she is "other" (parā).

The reason for her being superior to the self is that he—possessing an ineffable and manifold majesty, supremely independent, and exceedingly difficult to attain—has abandoned all the gopīs, even those who were desiring him there. This is the meaning.
Even there, being beloved and acting with exclusive love for Me alone, he worships and remains devoted.

Here, even when others appear, the manifestation is that of the gopīs alone, and not of ordinary women as in the previous cases; thus, a specific distinction has been shown in this respect as well. (36)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "In this manner" means according to the method already described. Such characteristics of their mutual play should be understood according to their respective order or meaning.
Thus, even while speaking and demonstrating in this way, they were afflicted by the pain of separation; for that very reason, they were bewildered.

The gopīs were truthful, for they had lost their discrimination; thus, being under the sway of exclusive love for Him, they wandered here and there, or else, they were overcome by the pangs of separation. ||36||
*Krama-sandarbha* and *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Again, describing the manner [of the Lord's pastimes] through all the paths, and intending to describe the *vipralambha* (separation) caused by her pride and resentment, he speaks of the events occurring in private, beginning with "Thus... (*ity evam*).

Thus, imitating the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and displaying to one another the marks of their amorous play therein, they became bewildered and wandered about, moving as if they were real. Having thus described their state of agitation, [the text describes] her pride (*māna*) which was fashioned in a manner identical to his own.

He describes: In a forest region suited for amorous play, having abandoned other women whose desires remained unfulfilled, she led the gopī—who felt the fault of pride born from her husband—to a secluded place. ||36||

Viśvanātha: Having described the portion of the most preeminent and radiant *sambhoga-rasa* (the rasa of union) belonging to the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, he now establishes the seed for describing the portion of *vipralambha* (the rasa of separation), beginning with the words "yām" (her whom...). ||36||
And she then considered herself the most excellent of all women, thinking:
"Abandoning the other gopīs, my beloved is wooing me."
Śrīdhara: Not explained. Vaṃśīdhara: "Variṣṭham" means the most excellent, the supreme of all. ||37||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: And she, Rādhā, having recollected all her friends, reflected in her mind.
What was that? She considered herself the most excellent among all women. What is the meaning?
"I am the foremost of all; this [behavior] is not fitting for me. To explain what that was, he says: "Having abandoned," and so forth.
That she abandons everyone and devotes herself to me alone—this is unbecoming for one of such high standing. (37)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Here, the two half-verses beginning with "evam" (thus) are not accepted by them [the followers of the *Sātvata-tantra*], because if the first half-verse were present, the phrase "remed tayā" (she sported with him) would be inconsistent as a statement by Śuka; and if the second half-verse were present, the phrase "sā ca" (and she) would be inconsistent as a reference to the mother's rising. Thus, having praised their mutual love in this manner...
He describes that very nature of pride consisting of such playful dalliance, as well as the act of propitiating Him and so forth,
for the purpose of nourishing that [pride]. By the two verses beginning with "And she" (sā ca) and "And she at that time thought" (sā ca tadā mene),
he shows that even though she was among them previously, she possessed such intoxication.
It is understood that [the beloved] did not exist [before], but has only now been born;
and thus, when such a state exists, two conditions for their measurement (cognition) are possible:

when there is the exclusive manifestation of the beloved, it consists primarily of stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as joy and the like; whereas when there is some manifestation of another [object], it is otherwise.
"But somehow, when he appeared externally, she went away"—this is the reason for her considering herself superior.

Even there, having abandoned all the gopīs who were longing for him, he—whose greatness is indescribable and manifold, who is supremely independent, and exceedingly difficult to attain—is the beloved; this is the meaning. Even in that situation, he remains the beloved.

Being one whose love is directed toward Me alone, He worships and follows [the gopīs]. Here, even when others appear, there is only the manifestation of the gopīs and not of ordinary women as in previous cases; thus, uniqueness is shown even in this respect. ||37||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Some explain that although she was among them previously, she did not possess such pride (*māna*) at that time, and that it arose only now. In reality, however, the meaning is "when such amorous play (*rati*) was occurring. Or else, [it means] "she [was one who had been] thus enjoyed by him."

He is the cause of the pride of all women, specifically the women of Vraja; for he has abandoned all the gopīs, even those who desired him and sought his love. He is one whose wondrous majesty is indefinable, supremely independent, and exceedingly difficult to attain—this is the meaning. Furthermore, he is the beloved who bestows his singular love upon me alone.
Or rather, although he is dear to all of them, he devotes himself to me alone and follows me with affection.

And it is entirely appropriate that this [state] nourishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the mind of a preeminent clever woman whose husband is under her control; thus, a corresponding favor from him will surely follow hereafter. ||37||

The Sequence of Composition: Thus, having praised the love described by her in that manner, he describes the actual manifestation of that very [love] which is the subject at hand—beginning with "And she" (sā ca). By the phrase "at that time" (tadā), it is understood that although she was previously among them, such pride (māna) did not exist in her before, but has arisen only now. That...
And thus, when such a state exists, two conditions of pride (māna) are possible for them:

when only the beloved flashes forth, it consists solely of the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva); when there is some flash of another [object], it consists of the stable emotion enriched by transitory emotions (sañcāribhāva) such as arrogance (garva). Therefore, because of the predominance of intense passion (gāḍhānurāga) in her—
Having existed for a long time as something consisting solely of a stable state within me, it has now somehow arisen externally; such is the view of the opponent. ||37||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, she, Rādhā, having abandoned everyone else, felt a sense of impropriety in her own mind, thinking, "He is devoted to me alone," and what she did next is described in the passage beginning with "And she" (*sā ca*).
That Rādhā considered herself the most excellent; she was indeed most excellent, yet she thought so. As for that which she thought...
It has been said; this is its intended meaning: "I am the foremost of all, so it is not fitting for me that this should happen. What is that?

He says: "Having abandoned," and so forth. Having abandoned everyone else, he is devoted to me alone; this is not fitting for a person of high standing. Well then, I shall delay right here until all have assembled.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: At that time, she considered herself the most excellent among all women; as long as she remained in the midst of the group, her pride had not manifested, but now it has arisen on account of Kṛṣṇa’s honoring her—the meaning is that she began to feel amorous desire. Alternatively, *kāmayamānā* means "the vehicle of desire" (*kāmasya yānam*).
The meaning is that those [other women] are "abodes of desire" because they lead one there. Having abandoned them, this beloved of mine attends to me alone;

for although he is equal toward all, his heart is drawn by my virtues, and he follows me out of subordination to me. Thus, I have become one whose husband is under her own control and possesses every authority. (37)

Viśvanātha: "And she too. Previously, all [the gopīs] were possessed by the intoxication of good fortune (*saubhaga-mada*), and now she is as well. The reason for this is: "having abandoned," etc. "Desiring" (*kāmayānāḥ*) means longing; or rather, those for whom desire (*kāma*) is the vehicle (*yāna*), the means of arrival. For this very reason, that which is caused by the good fortune of other gopīs—
The former pride has arisen; that too has been pacified without remainder. ||37||
Then, having gone to a region of the forest, the proud woman said to Keśava:
"I am unable to move; take me wherever your mind desires."
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Vaṃśīdhara: He shows the sense that [the Lord] is attainable through devotion and not otherwise by saying "tataḥ" (therefore). "Therefore" means because of the conceit arising from thinking [herself] superior; "dṛptā" means arrogant. "Keśavam" means the Lord of all. "Na pāraye" means I am not able.
"I am entirely dependent on you," she said, [expressing this] with the words "Do not... (verse 38).
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "In that case, I shall do this: when he says, 'I am unable to move,' he will remain right here;
meanwhile, they too will come and meet him. With this intention, she said:
"Therefore, having gone to the forest region, the proud woman spoke to Keśava, but not to his presence. I am unable..."
"Calitum" and so forth. If you are unable [to go], then what shall happen? To this he says: "Naya mām" and so forth.
Where will you lead me? Wherever your mind is—meaning, to the side of my companions who have been abandoned by you. Thus, I am unable to go far away, having left them behind.

It is in accordance with what was said before. Your mind is fixed on that very place; I know this only through your mere presence there. Nevertheless, the secret is that I feel an intense longing to go there immediately. ||38||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: After that, following the measurement, she went with him in due order toward a particular forest region; having gone ahead, being proud and haughty, she braided—that is, knotted—his hair. Therefore she asked: "What? To which they replied: "I cannot finish it."

"Because you are exhausted from wandering so much"—this is an indication of a reason based on a pretext. Now, if it is argued: "O innocent one! You must go to another charming place far ahead of them," he says in response: "Do not. The meaning is: "Placing her on your lap as before, you yourself must lead her. (38)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, following that [measure], or from that measure, or from the place of amorous play, being proud and haughty, she went ahead toward the forest regions—the places consisting of the forest—in the manner of going together with him; or else, thinking, "He will certainly become my follower."

Out of pride, she went of her own accord even to Keśava, the Supreme Lord; or rather, because he was intent on performing acts for the welfare of Vraja by slaying Keśin; or else, according to the logic already stated, because she was infatuated by his beauty—this is the sense. Therefore, what did she say? That...

They said, "I am not able," the implication being that she was exhausted by passion; she did not state it so directly out of modesty. Or perhaps, she spoke thus precisely because of her pride. If one objects, "O charming girl! You must go to another delightful place far ahead of them," she replies, "No."
The meaning is: "Having placed [it] on the numerical mark and so forth as before, you yourself must lead it. ||38||

The sequential arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*) and the extensive sequential arrangement (*bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*): Now, because she had kept this very thing in mind, she spoke with distinct syllables, beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*). Having gone to the forest region—that is, into the middle of the forest—she spoke to Keśava.
Of what nature was she? Arrogant and fearless. What was that? He says, beginning with "Do not" (*mā... nayeti*). I...

"I am not able to move. Her intention is this: "If I do not move, then he too will not move; meanwhile, all those others will gather together. Thus, what was well said—"I am not able"—is appropriate. Anticipating the question, "If you are not able, then what should be done?", she says: "Lead me," and so forth. [Me...]
"Lead me; where shall I be led? Wherever your mind [desires]. The meaning is: "Let your mind go wherever it wishes.
But your mind is fixed only upon those women who are separated from you, whereas toward me, it is fixed only on your glorious form (śrī-vigraha).
This is a *vakrokti* (an ironic or indirect expression). Therefore, lead me right there. What is the use of this excessive, selfless exertion?
"By way of conventional usage" means that there is an external manifestation of the "I"-notion. ||38||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: He speaks of the ripening of her pride (*māna-paripāka*)—beginning with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). From that place of love (*rati-sthāna*), suspecting the arrival of other women being sought there, she went to another part of the forest (*vanoddeśa*).
Being arrogant (*dṛptā*) and proud (*garvitā*), [she thought of] Keśava, the subduer of Brahmā and Śiva; how much more so, then, of this woman? Since...

Or, "he perfumes the hair," meaning he makes it fragrant by the offering of incense; thus, the meaning is "one who is supremely amorous. He spoke to him. What did he say? That is stated: "I am unable to move.
Because she was distressed by the fatigue of passion from wandering through the forest region, she was unable to go on her feet due to her nail-marks.
"I cannot.
"But surely all of them will come here; should you not go to a place suitable for dalliance?
To this he replies: "Wherever your heart is, there you must go; lead me there. Out of modesty...
Without speaking directly, she spoke thus, intending in her mind: "Having cast me aside, she will take [him] herself by means of insinuation";
she said, "Lead me," meaning "bring me there. ||38||
Viśvanātha: Having gone to an excellent spot in the forest, Keśava is weaving her hair into a variegated braid as she unties her crest—the tuft of hair that reveals her natural playfulness;
therefore, pride itself brings aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) to her, for she is a proud woman who has her lover under her control.

The meaning is: "I am unable to move" means that I have become exhausted from wandering through the vast forest; this is the sense. Now, if it is argued, "O innocent one! You must go further ahead to another charming place far from those [trees]," he says in response: "nayā" (do not lead). The meaning is: "carrying me as before. Now, what...?

"Shall I lead her to a flower-couch within a bower in the area ahead, which is inaccessible to other people, or to the flower-garden for the sake of floral ornaments? To this he replies: "Wherever your mind [is inclined].
Thus addressed, he said to his beloved, "Climb onto my shoulder," and then Kṛṣṇa vanished; that bride was filled with remorse.

Śrīdhara: He shows the wretchedness of those possessed by desire with the words "Thus addressed. He states her unbroken state with the words "And then. The meaning is that she had vanished just as she was about to climb onto his shoulder. ||39||
Vaṃśīdhara says: To demonstrate the nature of pure awakening, he states, "That bride.
This means that immediately after being permitted to ascend onto his shoulder; the sense is that he has thus made known her own sovereignty. (39)
The Chest of Caitanya’s Teachings: The Lord, though knowing this, in order to shatter her pride regarding her own preeminence, acted out a contrary understanding and said:
"If you are unable to walk, then mount upon my shoulder; only this much remains."
"All other conduct exists; let this also be performed," he said. He did not merely say this, but vanished as well—as he says: "Then he disappeared," and so forth. ||39||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, having heard her speech—which consisted of feigned laziness and the like, appropriate for one whose husband is under her own control—the Lord Himself also vanished with a smile; this he states with the three quarters beginning with "evam."

"Mount upon my shoulder," he said; and he spoke thus to his beloved merely as a jest. For indeed: that which is a wicked word in another's mouth is itself a joke when uttered from the mouth of one's dearest; what is smoke born of common fuel is incense when produced from aloeswood. Or else, "skandha" [means]...

According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*, "kāya" refers to the trunk and the region of the roots of the arms; thus, because it is logical, "kāya" here refers to the chest—this too is merely a jest. "Tataḥ" means immediately after that. The particle "ca" is used in the sense of "tu" (but), indicating a change in the subject of the sentence; or, it serves as a conjunction in the phrase "antardadhe ca" (and he disappeared). [He departed] from her presence.
Even in this disappearance, one should understand that the absence of jealousy among the co-wives and their unanimity are also intended purposes;

for even in the previous disappearance, that too was desired. Thus, by accomplishing many difficult tasks through a single action, supreme cleverness is demonstrated. Oh, how wonderful! Upon and upon...
The sense is that the intellects of these women move as the intellects of sovereign mistresses. Thus,

having shown the pinnacle of love consisting in being one whose husband is under her own control— accumulated through shared enjoyment— he now demonstrates, even within a playful separation (*vipralambha*), its other pinnacle, which consists of supreme wretchedness and delusion.

That very excellence [of the sight] is indicated by the words "she" (sā) and "with a quarter-verse" (sapādena): she, whose sole life was that vision, was consumed with grief and lamented repeatedly. (39)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He says, "Let her mount upon my shoulder"—this is said as a joke toward his beloved. Or else, *kāya* refers to my chest, or my waist, or even the collective whole; the meaning is the group of gopīs. And so Viśva [states]: *skandha* means a trunk... [etc.].

"And on her body, at the base of her arms"—thus [it is said]. Therefore, let her be mounted; for at that time they were situated in a high place, or in the region of the Śrī-Yamunā's outflow. Or rather, it is intended to express their height by means of that measurement; such is the direction [of the argument]. Thereafter, or from that place, of her—

Or [it is] from his presence; the particle *ca* is used in the sense of *tu* (but/rather). Or, as a conjunction in a distinct syntactical opening, it means "and he disappeared," for the purpose of disappearance has already been stated. He indicates that very point: "Kṛṣṇa, whose form is a mass of supreme bliss"—the meaning is that it is solely for the sake of a particular kind of bliss. Therefore it was said:

Regarding the word "beloved": here there is a specific detail mentioned in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Having cast aside her, who felt pride born from the honoring of the flower-garland, the son of Nanda the cowherd departed by this path; behold!"
When another woman follows behind, she—sluggish from the weight of her hips—is unable to proceed;
yet when she must go quickly, she moves with her toes planted firmly on the ground.
O friend, by that [stealing] he goes with his hand placed upon the top;
thus the trail of footprints is observed, with its placement of steps not under control.
By the mere touch of his hand, this woman was insulted by the rogue;
because of her despair, her slow-moving steps are seen to have turned back.

"Surely she was told, 'I am hurrying; I shall return to your presence,' by that Kṛṣṇa because of whom this trail of footprints is so swift. Thus, proud as she was, yet with her very life dependent solely upon seeing him, she lamented repeatedly and grieved deeply. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.35–39)

The structural connection (*krama-sandarbha*): Thus, having heard her joking words—which, though consisting of feigned laziness and the like, were appropriate for one whose husband is under her control—he himself also vanished with a joke; this he expresses with the three quarters beginning with "evam. In this way, [he describes] that state belonging to a woman whose husband is under her control, which is suited for sexual enjoyment.

Having shown the highest limit of love, he now indicates its very excellence by showing, even through a playful separation (*vipralambha*), that highest limit consisting of supreme wretchedness and delusion; he does so with the verse beginning with "She" (*sā*) and its accompanying quarter-verse. ||39||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Although the Blessed Lord understood that intention, He acted by simulating a contrary understanding; this is described in the passage beginning with "Thus addressed," etc. He said to His beloved Rādhā, "Mount upon My shoulder," to which she replied with words of feigned anger. By Him...

For if he did not effect his disappearance, his own statement would result in futility; thus, the fact that he was perceived as being deceptive is itself the truth. He does not merely say this, but also says, "And he disappeared," beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and so forth.
The meaning is "then, right there," where the suffix *tasil* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*). Otherwise, it would follow that he were merciless. [He himself...]
She sees, yet she does not see; thus, as it were, she disappears—this is the meaning. Immediately thereafter, that bride felt remorse. ||39||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: What happened after her boastful speech? He says: "Vam. Having been addressed in this way, he said to his beloved: "Climb onto my shoulder. Thus, having been raised up by her—who was proud of her good fortune and possessed the fault of pride—and having been addressed with a glance, he spoke these words to his beloved with playful humility.

He said, "Please climb onto my shoulder. Seeing her, out of delusion, desiring to do so without understanding his jesting words, Kṛṣṇa immediately thereafter vanished from that place of enjoyment; having produced a state of separation for the sake of increasing the aesthetic flavor (rasa), he became invisible to her sight. Who was she? Her—[whose...]

Was she honored by having her hair adorned and so forth? Having been addressed as "bride" (vadhū) because she was accepted by Kṛṣṇa, she whose very life is Kṛṣṇa alone felt remorse; she later experienced regret, thinking, "I spoke these words without knowing his independence. ||39||

Viśvanātha: Thereupon, Kṛṣṇa reflected thus in his mind: "Alas! She has indeed abandoned her own natural duty (*svadharma*). For a virtuous heroine (*sannāyikā*) does not grant her consent to the hero regarding a bed of flowers by means of her eyes alone. If she has abandoned her own duty in the form of such feigned resistance (*vāmya*),"

Then even I, as a true leader, must indeed abandon my own duty characterized by courtesy, which consists in following the beloved with whom I have enjoyed intimacy; for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not truly delicious when there is courtesy or dissimulation on the part of only one of the two. Nor am I to be censured here by those who appreciate aesthetic flavor (*rasika*), for *rasa* is indeed...
It would indeed be best to follow the established sequence regarding the heroine;
moreover, my long-standing desire to witness directly the particular state of this woman, who possesses great love, brought about by her separation from me, will be fulfilled on this occasion.
The excellence of her good fortune born from union with me has indeed been experienced by them;
let them now be submerged in an ocean of supreme wonder upon seeing her extraordinary state, which manifests the highest intensity of love born even from separation from me. Of her—
In the presence of the flames of the submarine fire of my separation, let their own separation from me act like the flame of a lamp.

Furthermore, through these two—union and separation—of the most perfect kind, let the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) also attain its state of perfection today. And in her separation, which was brought about by me...

Reflecting upon many such purposes, he thought: "Immediately after the pacification of all separation, when there is unanimity among them all, the Rāsa dance intended for today will succeed; otherwise, if things were different, their pride—which is so deeply attached to union with me—would be entirely impossible to quell today."
Desiring to vanish suddenly, He said, "The shoulder. The meaning is that while remaining right there and still looking at her, He vanished from the range of her vision.
Here, in the mind of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter, who was saying, "Lead me where Your mind is," [this thought arose]:

She reflected: "I am exhausted from the fatigue of sporting and wandering through the groves; I have a desire for sleep for a moment. For him too, the passing of the entire night without sleep would be unfortunate and result only in unhappiness. Therefore, if he wishes to take me to the flower-couch, let him take me; we shall both go there."

Thinking, "We shall sleep," he did not express his disagreement there. It should be understood that in that situation, the Lord's knowledge of the inner workings of his heart was concealed by the very power of his pastimes consisting of the essence of divine love (*prema-rasa*), for the sake of the successful accomplishment of those particular pastimes. He lamented repeatedly and wailed aloud. (39)
"Alas, O Lord, lover, dearest one! Where are you, where are you, O mighty-armed one?
To me, your wretched maidservant, O friend, reveal your presence!"
Śrīdhara says, expressing remorse: "Alas, O Lord! (39).

Vaṃśīdhara: Alas, I am despondent in the forest! "Alas" (*hā*) is used in the sense of dejection, sorrow, and affliction—so says Amara. O Lord, bestower of hope! O Beloved, bestower of delight! O Dearest, most exceedingly dear! O Mighty-Armed One, protector from the fear of terror! [This is] for Your maidservant, who is worthy of instruction, wretched, and worthy of compassion; O Friend!
Thus [he spoke]. He said that the duty of a friend is not to abandon one's friend in a place of danger. ||40||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: It expresses lamentation alone—“O Lord! (*hā nātha*). *Hā* denotes either grief or an address of distress;
thus it should be applied everywhere. O Lord (*nātha*), protector by virtue of being the Master! O Beloved (*ramaṇa*)!
"O bestower of the happiness befitting my beloved! O dearest one who expands the love in my heart directed toward you!

Where are you? Though you were so affectionate toward me, where are you now, all alone? Alas, alas! My heart is agitated by the ignorance of your whereabouts"—this is the underlying sentiment. The repetition (*vīpsā*) is used again due to her agitation.

As if fainting from the recollection of the particular beauty of her limbs— which kindles her own rasa and reminds her of her own good fortune such as embracing him— she says, "O you with mighty arms. Then, out of extreme dejection, she says, "Of a maidservant," and so forth.

Fearing that he might be seeking my presence once again in order to obtain my embrace and other such favors, she says, "No, no! Friend, you who have been granted the good fortune of your own companionship, show me even your very presence; let me know it. (The phrase *sāhabhāya sannidhim* means "the proximity of companionship.")

The sense is: "Show me even your own presence and let me know it; for now, since my misfortunes have been brought about by you alone through the granting of your companionship, I shall not accept them there. But if you remain here, I shall become at ease, having reached a firm certainty even in my mind."

The reason for this is as follows: although she was unfit for the friendship of a maidservant and the like, by Your very grace she was forcibly brought into a state of exclusive conformity to Your happiness; thus, the term "alternatives" (paryāya) is used. Furthermore, she was wretched (*kṛpaṇā*), meaning she was unable to endure this suffering and did not know how to avoid it. Therefore, it is not...
The sense is that she should neither practice deception toward me nor sow the seeds of her own remorse.

This is the majestic demeanor (*audārya*) known as a "greatness" (*anubhāva*); as it has been said: "The wise declare that majesty is modesty present in all circumstances. And so, alas, she fell to the ground in a swoon.
This is to be understood, because it will be stated later that she was deluded. ||40||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He expresses her lamentation itself with the word "hā" (alas). "Hā" is used in the sense of grief or as an address to one in distress;
thus, it should be applied everywhere [in the following vocatives]. "O Lord! (nātha), O Master of my life! "O Lover! (ramaṇa), O Husband! "O Bestower of delight! (rati-dāyaka)!
"O Dearest! (preṣṭha), O Most Beloved! "O Long-armed One! (mahābhuja)—the meaning is "O Giver of firm embraces. Of these...
Each subsequent term is indeed the cause of the preceding one.
Or rather, O Lord, O Master! It is not only thus; but O Bestower of the bliss of dalliance, or rather, O Performer of various sports! Therefore, O Beloved by Your very nature, even of Yourself—
