The meaning is "most beloved" (parama-priya) because of [his] presence; for, O mighty-armed one (mahābhuja), the meaning is that you are the embodiment of the dense mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda-ghana-mūrti).
Alternatively, [the address] "O performer of supreme enjoyment" (parama-bhoga-kartṛ) indicates the constant attainment of happiness such as erotic love (rati) and so forth.
Or alternatively: she calls him "Nātha" because he is the Lord of Vraja; there too, she calls him "Ramaṇa" because he fulfills the desires of her husband;
there too, she calls him "Preṣṭha" because he is her lover; and there too, she calls him "Mahābhuja" because of his supreme beauty and other qualities.
Or else, she laments on the ground in great agitation, crying out in the utmost distress, "Where are you? Where are you?"
Falling down, desiring his embrace and remembering him, she said, "O you of mighty arms.
She did not say, "I am here," while remaining at a distance; rather, she said, "Show me your presence"—the meaning being, "be present before me. Why? Because she is a servant, and even so...
[She says this] out of pity; otherwise, she intends that if her final state were to occur, you would surely regret it, and thus she says: "O friend, O most beloved!
Or rather, she says "O friend" so that, upon seeing him present, no deception as before should be practiced anywhere.
"O you who are the object of my supreme trust! Or rather, O beloved! It may be that you think, "I have not gone anywhere leaving you; I am right here by your side.
If so, then, O simple one, I do not see you at all. You [behave] with such friendship...
Thus he says, "of the maidservant," in order to manifest himself. The rest is the same.

Although, due to the absence of coherence caused by the impairment of separation, one might not require logical consistency in the lamentation—and even such inconsistency would be a merit—nevertheless, for such [women], even a fragmentary sentence contains every meaning.
"She served" means that her devotion is described here; this should be understood in the same way for what follows.

And thus, it should be understood that she, becoming bewildered, alas, fell to the ground, because it will be said later, "she was deluded" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.41). Alternatively, it refers to the statement, "Let the shoulder be climbed upon" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.39).

Because of her state of mental distraction caused by the intensity of her love (*prema-utkaṇṭhya*), she did not perceive Kṛṣṇa even though he was standing right before her; thus it is said, "Kṛṣṇa disappeared. In reality, however, he remained there in silence simply out of curiosity. Thereupon, remorse arose in her, who was possessed by that mental distraction of love.
Likewise, seeing other gopīs present there, it should be understood that Kṛṣṇa had indeed vanished from her sight. ||40||
The sequence of composition, the extensive sequence of composition: he describes the manner of repentance, saying "O Lord!

O mighty-armed one! Show Your presence. Although Your presence is inferred here—since You are right here and have not gone anywhere—even so, show it; this is the meaning. [He addresses Him as] "O mighty-armed one."

It should be understood that [the lover], having vanished while indicating the experience of the pleasure of the touch of his arms, remains there embracing with both arms; and that is like the embrace of a friend obtained in a dream. "Where are you?
Where are you?"—only the touch of the arms is experienced, but not you; yet you are behind, in front, or at the side.
You are not perceived. Therefore, the meaning is: "Show your presence even though it exists. ||40||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Just as such a state occurred for them during the *vipralambha* (separation), so too did it happen for her;
thus, he describes her lamentation with the words "Hā nātha! (Alas, O Lord!). "Hā" is used to express distress.
"O Lord! O Master! O Lord of my life! I have acted improperly; you must forgive me."
"For you are indeed our master; I am your servant and must not be abandoned by you. "O lover!

You are the enjoyer who bestows delight, while we are the objects of enjoyment. Therefore, for the sake of ensuring that there may be pleasure, you must remain right here by my side. "O dearest one! Most beloved one, thus..."
Even though you have acted thus, you remain the sole object of my affection, and there is no other object of my love.

With words faltering due to the manifestation of intense anguish, she says: "Where are you? With the intention that he might lift her up as she is submerged in a great ocean of suffering, she says: "O mighty-armed one! [Hold me] firmly with your long arms!"
"Only you are capable of embracing and lifting [me] up, not anyone else.

If it is asked, "But I am right here; why do you lament? he says in response: "Show me the proximity of your maidservant (dāsī), for servitude is possible only upon seeing one's own closeness to her. O friend! by the virtuous...

Because of the saying, "Friendship lasts for seven steps," I am your friend and long-time companion; therefore, I am not to be deceived. Since I, being wretched, am unable to abandon you, this treasure of yours is my own true wealth, situated here in my presence as I lie in the tenth stage of illness.
"Show me your lotus-face before the tenth stage [of pregnancy] arrives; otherwise, if it is lost, you will later regret it. Therefore, show it quickly. (40)

Viśvanātha says: He utters a lamentation itself, beginning with "O Lord!"—"From this body of mine, which is being consumed by the great fire of separation from you, my vital breaths have now almost departed; they cannot be preserved by me even with effort. You alone are their lord; therefore, grant me your vision and protect them quickly."

[The inner] state is as follows: "I do not pray for their protection for my own sake alone, but rather for yours alone," she says: "O Rāmaṇa!"—referring to me, whom you have brought so far into this secluded place, having abandoned all other gopīs, for the sake of the particular pleasure of dalliance.
The meaning is: "When she has died, not finding such pleasure in love elsewhere, you too will remember me and lament in sorrow.
[An objection: "Let my sorrow be; what does that matter to you? To this he replies: "O dearest one (he preṣṭha). It matters to you.
Because he is my dearest, that suffering of his will multiply a millionfold and ripen upon me alone.

I shall not be able to endure that suffering of yours—even at the cost of death—for even a single portion of the toenails of your lotus feet is worthy of being wiped by millions of my own lives. Therefore, please remain present and [bear] that very [suffering].

The sense is: "Remove my suffering. Now, one might object: "If my life-breaths have already almost departed, how shall I be able to turn them back? To this he replies: "O you of mighty arms!"—referring to your arm.

The sense is that as soon as this body is restored to health and its natural composure through the mere touch of the life-restoring medicine, the vital breaths will return and remain of their own accord.
Now, if you know my destination even without me, [then tell it] to the prince...

"Lead me, who am most delicate and worthy of honor, wherever your heart desires"—did you provoke her by speaking such words? To that, she replied with a tone of reproach and agitation: "I am but a wretched slave-girl of yours. At that time, I spoke thus because I was overcome by exhaustion from amorous play, sleep, and lassitude; forgive me.
The sense is that [the lover] becomes angry.

Furthermore, she says "O friend" to indicate: "It was precisely because you formed such a firm friendship even with me, though I am unworthy, that I spoke to you in that manner. O beloved, I have therefore become appeased.

"If you say, 'Come near me,' I am now blinded by the pain of remorse; I do not see where you are," she says—"Show yourself! It should be understood that after lamenting only this much, she fainted and fell to the ground due to the agitation caused by her separation. [The phrase] "she was deluded" follows next.
Because it has been stated [so]. ||40||
Searching along the path of the Blessed One,
the cowherd women saw from nearby their friend, who was distressed and bewildered by separation from her beloved.
Śrīdhara: *Anvicchantyaḥ* means searching; *avidūrataḥ* means nearby. ||41||

Vaṃśīdhara: The "gopīs" (those who protect or guard the cow) are the functions of the senses, which guard or protect the "cow"—the faculty of sight—by preventing it from wandering toward improper objects; these are the subjects of the scripture. To show that prior to enjoyment, the manifestation and disappearance of direct perception may sometimes occur, he says: "Upon separation from the Beloved."

"Afflicted with suffering"— this indicates that she is indeed miserable by means of the streams of tears mixed with profuse sweat and blood from wounds caused by dust and thorns clinging to her as she rolls upon the ground. ||41||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Not far" means not very far;

for if it were too far, there would be the presence of an intervening obstruction. Even though it is distant, [it is perceived] due to its particular splendor that surpasses the beauty of the full moon.
Because her sight was possible [to them]. She was suffering, and for that very reason deluded and fainted;

because they perceived her abandonment even while she was all alone through their cultivation of shared sorrow, and because envy had departed due to their extreme unanimity, she is called a "companion" (*sakhī*), yet [this applies] specifically to one's own companions.
In this regard, a particular intensity of the immersion of love is to be understood. ||41||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "From afar" (*vidūrataḥ*) means from a very great distance; they saw her previously because of her extraordinary luster. Alternatively, "seeking from afar" means having gone a long distance ahead while searching. Or else, by eliding the vowel *a*, it means "not far" (*avidūrataḥ*), that is, nearby.

Thus they saw her; and it should be understood that, due to the intensity of their own distress, they did not hear her cry of pain even though she was nearby at first. She was distressed by the separation from her beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa and subsequently became bewildered.

Because the signs— such as the entire body being smeared with blood from wounds caused by dust and thorns while rolling on the ground, the profuse flow of tears, and the lamentation— and such a state of delusion cannot otherwise be accounted for except through separation from him; this is indicated by the word "mohitām" (deluded).

A special degree of affection for her over all other women has also been shown; for while they suffer the pain of separation, she imitates their pastimes, and her delusion is equal to that of her final state. Seeing her in such a condition when united with her friends, those friends, possessing an identical affliction, feel it especially so.

The meaning is that all [the women], experiencing their own feelings doubled [in intensity], turned around and wept. Consequently, the previously mentioned envy and other such emotions vanished of their own accord from all of them at a distance;
thus, afterwards, through great efforts and various clever maneuvers, she regained her own consciousness and composure.

They brought her there slowly and gently. Then they asked her about that event; this should be understood as the sequence of the narrative, the "Great Sequence" (*bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*). Now, he states what she had previously thought:
"Searching," and so forth. The cowherd girls were distraught due to their separation from their beloved.

They saw that friend Rādhā. Of what sort? She was first inferred or conjectured: "If she is she, how is she alone? If she is not she, then who is this other? Thus they first inferred her and afterwards saw her—that is, they recognized her. But they did not see her as distressed, like themselves.
The meaning is that they did not see [the Lord] as one subject to the suffering of separation, because He was in constant contact with the limbs of the concealed Lord. ||41||

Prīti-sandarbha (288): Now, one might object that mutual antagonism among the devotees of the Lord is both impossible and unpleasant. Furthermore, in passages such as *tāsāṃ tat saubhaga-madam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.48), even the Śrī Bhagavān is seen desiring to remove their jealousy, pride, and arrogance.

Likewise, the illustrious Sage himself has also employed the word *daurātmya* (wickedness) there in relation to them. To this it is replied: indeed, every pastime of the glorious Blessed Lord proceeds solely for the nourishment of His own bliss; He engages in such pastimes that, upon hearing of them, one becomes absorbed in Him.
"May it be... and so forth; the meaning is "even having heard.

In this regard, the very nature of her amorous play is that it indeed brings forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the accompaniment of the various diversities of emotional states (*bhāva*), characterized by jealousy, intoxication, pride, and the like.

It nourishes [the devotee], for it is described by poets in that very same way, and is accepted by the illustrious Lord Himself in His own pastimes. Even within Himself, the state of being a hero with fourfold divisions—namely, the clever, the compliant, the deceitful, and the bold—is manifested in its proper place. Therefore, it is indeed the power of His pastimes (līlā-śakti).

In those [moods], she assumes various states; and it has been shown that she does so precisely in accordance with those states. Therefore, when there is separation from Him for all of them, because they then attain a state of being of one kind through dejection, only the mood of friendship (*sakhya*) is manifested everywhere.

As in the passage, "Seeking the Blessed One," here the indication of their former friendship is present; and the play of their separation serves solely to increase the intensity of their longing directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the crest-jewel of the citizens, the increase of those [pastimes] is exceedingly pleasing.
As it has been said: "But I, O friends, do not [bestow my favor] even upon beings who worship Me" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.10), and so forth.
Therefore, even separation occurs in the midst [of these pastimes]. At that time, there is the playful diversion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s intoxication, pride, and so on.

Even if one were to transgress [the bounds], there would still be a firm resolve toward them; therefore, for the sake of pacifying intoxication and pride, and for the sake of the serenity that consists in the excellence of craving for their own objects—this is the meaning of the phrase "their good fortune" (*tat-saubhagya*).
It is for the purpose of the entire collective *rāsa* pastime, and for the pacification of intoxication and pride.

"Prasādāya" means for the sake of serenity, or for the purpose of producing clarity; therefore, the desire to increase that [serenity] is also an incidental consequence—this is the same [as previously stated]. (This should be seen in the latter part of the commentary on verse 10.30.35 of the 288th section of the *Prīti-sandarbha*).

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Then, overwhelmed by the pangs of separation, she fell to the ground. When there is the expectation of what happened next, he describes her attainment [of Kṛṣṇa] through the search for her among the other gopīs, while explaining that this is the very nature of the manifestation of love (*prema-vivarta*). This indeed is the manifestation of love: that even though He is standing nearby...

They do not see their dearest one, as in the lamentation of the female osprey (*kurarī*). Therefore, out of some curiosity, remaining right there in their vicinity within that circle, he watches in silence;
he remained listening to their conversations of love. Hence it is said: "And then Kṛṣṇa disappeared."
Thus it is said in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.39. Furthermore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa will say later: "I remained hidden while they were worshipping Me out of sight" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.32.21).
Now He describes the manner of their meeting with Him, beginning with the words "anvicchantyaḥ" (seeking). Thus...
Seeking the path of the Lord in the manner previously described, all the gopīs, while searching from afar, saw their friend fallen on the ground in a nearby place;
because her suffering was identical to the sorrow born of being abandoned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she was recognized as a friend due to that equality of suffering.

Even the departure of her envy arose spontaneously. They beheld her—who was deluded by separation from her beloved, deluded by the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa her beloved, and who had attained a state resembling him—suffering and having reached the fruition of her pride. ||41||

Viśvanātha: Seeking—that is, searching for her—they saw her even from that distance because of her lightning-like radiance; they called her "friend" because even her rivals felt affection for her upon seeing her in such a state. Furthermore, this is the very nature of the *ujjvala-rasa* (the erotic sentiment).

When it is known that one's beloved is free from attachment to any woman other than herself, there arises among women an absence of jealousy, hatred, and the like, as well as mutual affection. As it has been said: "For this very reason, their particular affection for [their own] beloved shines forth. (41)
Having heard what she said regarding the honor she had received from Mādhava and the insult she suffered through his wickedness, they were filled with the utmost amazement.
Śrīdhara: Then, accompanied by her as well, they entered the forest to search for Kṛṣṇa. Thereafter, they desisted from their search for Hari. ||42||

Vaṃśīdhara: By that friend; the attainment of pride characterized by climbing onto [her] shoulders. In the alternative sense, characterized by direct perception. Due to wickedness—that is, arrogance—[she experiences] humiliation characterized by abandonment. ||42||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "Due to wickedness"—that is, from the conceit that the self is primary. (42)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Therefore, it should be understood that after hearing what was said by her, there followed a question regarding the manifestation of the sign of weeping; [the Lord] spoke: "I did not know how I became separated from you, but from afar I performed self-investigation (*ātmanusandhāna*)."
Having heard all such accounts of what had occurred, and having also heard there that even Lakṣmī herself—

due to her husband’s possession of all virtues and other perfections— longed for him as her lover, and that she had attained supreme good fortune and honor through him quite spontaneously, [she remained] right there.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) begins with: "Having heard of the characteristic of pride arising from her own wickedness, and the characteristic of abandonment consisting of insult, she was struck with wonder. Here, however, the use of the word *daurātmya* (wickedness) is for the purpose of echoing her words of wretchedness. In reality, however, she is one whose self—that is, her body—is far removed from Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

"Dūrātmā" refers to one for whom the Self or Śrī Kṛṣṇa is distant; "daurātmya" is the state of being such, meaning from that state of being far removed due to separation. This also connects with the triad beginning with "paramaṃ vidmayam" (we know You as the Supreme) and ending with "tayā kathitam" (spoken by her), encompassing all His activities, including His disappearance along with Her.

Because even his conduct when accompanied by himself is difficult to conceive; because even in that case, such pride would arise; because among his own people, he has never been seen even in tens of millions; and because, that being so, it is absolutely impossible for him to feel contempt even toward her. ||42||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "And then" means that everything was told by her; or rather, out of fear of the recurrence of sorrow, even though not asked by those friends, she herself described that event in the form of a lamentation upon meeting with them—this is the sense. Thus, this constitutes a single, distinct sentence.

Or rather: and thus, having heard of his attainment of pride, the two *ca*s (conjunctions) illuminate the preeminence of both [Mādhava and Lakṣmī], because he delights in various ways with each of them, and likewise because he vanishes suddenly at the very moment of aesthetic relish (*rasa*). [He is superior] even to Mādhava, the beloved of Lakṣmī; or else, by means of *madhu* (spring/wine).

The sense is: "She always sports with sweet rasa; therefore, there is another person entirely who is worthy of receiving honor even more than I am, but not I. Nevertheless, she has attained such honor solely through the greatness of His compassion, and not by her own qualities. Thus, it is well said.

It should be understood that everything inauspicious arises solely from one's own faults, due to the very qualities such as the compassion of the Blessed Lord; thus He instructed even the saintly ones. Alternatively, "durātmā" refers to the state of being one whose self—or indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself—is far away.
Therefore, there is wickedness; the meaning is that it proceeds far from that [virtue]. There is supreme astonishment immediately through such acts of grace and suppression. (42)

The sequence of the composition is as follows: the connection is that [the speaker] heard what was said by her, heard the attainment of pride characterized by the act of leading her away to that very place, and heard the insult characterized by abandonment;
here, however, the use of the word *daurātmya* (wickedness) is due to the repetition of her words of wretchedness, whereas in reality...
"Daurātmyam" refers to the state of being one whose self—that is, the body—is distant from Śrī Kṛṣṇa; it is for that reason [that she speaks]. ||42||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, when they met, she was questioned by them and told everything; this very point is stated with the words beginning "by her" (*tayā*). "It was told by her" is one sentence, meaning that everything was told by her in due order. In that narration, regarding Mādhava...
The meaning is that, having heard of the attainment of pride, they were filled with astonishment. ||42||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: In response to the inquiry, "What was done upon seeing her?", he says: "By her. [She was] awakened by many [friends] through the mood of friendship; for this very reason, she emerged slightly from her delusion. First, she was asked about her own situation, and afterwards about Kṛṣṇa's. Then, she spoke.

Having heard from Mādhava—the husband of Lakṣmī—of his dalliance, such as the gathering of flowers, the arranging of her hair, and so forth, or of the insult he received; by this, his particular cleverness (*vaidagdhyaviśeṣa*) is indicated. Or else, [it refers to] the contempt characterized by neglect that he suffered from embodied Spring (*mūrtād vasantāt*), due to his own wickedness characterized by pride and the like.
"Having heard this, they were struck with supreme amazement"—
the meaning is that their amazement arose from the possibility of humiliation upon reflecting on his conduct, such as his simultaneous disappearance and the grooming of his hair. ||42||
Viśvanātha: Then, when her awakening was carefully brought about by her friends through loud weeping and service with fans and other means, she was asked by them, "O dear friend!
Tell us your own story," and although she spoke, how [could she tell it] to her dear friend?
"I was separated from you all," I thought, "but being deluded and dependent on others, I did not realize it.

However, I am certain that both the attainment of honor and dishonor arise solely from one's own wickedness; for, having disregarded you—more than a thousand loving women—and having set me ablaze with the fire of separation from you..."
That one woman was granted such good fortune is indeed her own misfortune;

for even though I am wretched and simple-minded, I could not bear to move toward that prince of ill-conduct, saying, "Take me away"— this, however, is my own misfortune, since such great humiliation has resulted from it.

"Whether he has attained [it] or not, in either case there is only great mental suffering for me. Thus, in her private quarters, she sequentially manifested envy, modesty, and dejection toward them. Here, the use of the word *daurātmya* (wickedness) by the illustrious Lord of Sages was merely a repetition of his own words; in reality, however—
"She whose self (ātman) is far from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, or from whom Śrī Kṛṣṇa is far, is 'dūrātmā'; the state of being such is 'daurātmya'—the meaning is: due to that separation.
"They attained supreme astonishment"—O dear friend! Your good fortune is indeed fitting.

There is no wickedness here; even for you, who are weary of pleasure and have your husband under your control, to issue a command to your lover is not wickedness, but rather something that heightens the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). However, it is the transgression of a command by a beloved woman who has already been enjoyed by a compliant lover [that constitutes such].

And this bringing about of such a miserable state was itself an act contrary to [His] aesthetic flavor (rasa), revealing His own wickedness; alas, alas! they were struck with supreme wonder, thinking: "How could He, the crest-jewel of great connoisseurs, the possessor of great love, and the ocean of mercy, have desired to act in such a way?"
Then they entered the forest as long as the moonlight could still be discerned;
perceiving that it had entered into darkness, the women then turned back.

Śrīdhara: Not explained. Vaṃśīdhara: "Tamaḥ" (darkness). Having perceived that darkness had entered her eyes due once again to the pain of separation; or else, [having perceived] Śrī Kṛṣṇa who had entered the forest thicket of dense darkness (*tamas*).

The meaning is "having known. The intention is that on the full moon night, because the moon shines throughout the entire night, well-known darkness is impossible. This suggests that they exerted effort toward the study of true scriptures, having turned away from false ones, for those [scriptures] are the objects of their learning. In reality, however:

Having perceived—that is, having known—Him who has entered the cave of the heart, indicated by the word "darkness," according to the Vedic scripture: "He who knows Him hidden in the cave"; they desisted from the worship of Hari and attained His very nature.
As it is said: "By devotion one comes to know Me truly, as who I am and how great I am."
For there is the traditional teaching (smṛti): "Then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter" (Gītā 11.55);

the Vedic revelation (śruti) beginning with "He who has supreme devotion for the God" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23); and the Vedic revelation stating, "Devotion alone leads one to Him. Regarding the word "women"—it refers to women.

The meaning is that [he was unable] to enter the forest enveloped in darkness. The reading *hareḥ* is approved by the Master (*svāmī*). This is because, in order to resolve the redundancy of the word *tataḥ*, he explains that very word *tataḥ* as "from the searching for Hari. Otherwise, [the purpose of] the word *tataḥ*...
There would be an unsuitability for the preceding qualification, and there would be a lack of excellence in the syntactic connection (anvaya) such as "of Hari from that. ||43||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, with her supported by her friends due to extreme agitation, they searched for her once again along with her; thus he says—"Then," up to "the forest."

The meaning is that, having pervaded the forest, the moonlight was perceived—that is, as they entered the forest, they searched for Him. Having inferred that Śrī Kṛṣṇa had entered the extremely dense darkness by means of footprints and other signs, they then withdrew from that forest. And so it is said:
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the dense forest; his footprints cannot be seen here.
Turn back! This is not within the range of the moon's rays. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.43) Thus it is said.

"Women" means that women lack the capacity to enter a forest of darkness, due to their nature being permeated by apprehension and affection. Because he was suspected of having entered there— having come from his own people to his own beloved— he [was rescued] from that place difficult to traverse.

The meaning is that they were intent upon departing; "of Hari" (*hareḥ*) is a reading held by some, but it appears to be disapproved of by the authors of the commentaries (*ṭīkā*). This is because the word "thence" (*tataḥ*) is repeated for the sake of providing a resolution, and because "thence" itself is explained as "due to the searching for Hari. Otherwise, the purpose of the word "thence" would be...
Prior to that, there would be an incapacity for qualification. ||43||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Nevertheless, due to the agitation caused by supreme love, they searched for him once more along with her; thus he says, "Then," etc. As far as the moonlight was perceived—that is, observed—pervading the forest, so far did they enter the forest. Having entered, they searched for him.

The meaning is as follows: Perceiving that [the path] had entered into darkness because of the extreme density of the forest and was filled with gloom, they turned back from that forest. And so it is said in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the thicket; his footprints cannot be seen here."
"Turn back; this is not within the range of the moon's rays. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.43). Regarding the word "women" (*striyaḥ*), the meaning is that women lack the capacity to enter a forest in the dark.
As for the reading *hareḥ* ("of Hari"), that is the opinion of some, but it is not accepted by the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda.

It is observed that because the word "tataḥ" (therefore) is repeated for the sake of providing a resolution, it is explained specifically as "from the searching for Hari. Otherwise, if "tataḥ" were explained merely as "from searching," its prior mention would be illogical. Furthermore, such an interpretation would result in a lack of elegance in the syntactical connection between "Hari" and "tataḥ."
The sequential arrangement and the extensive sequential arrangement: therein, having become one,

and by means of the sequence of movement through the process of investigation right there, thinking, "That forest where there is no entry of moonlight has been reached," he turned back from there and arrived at the very same sandbank seen previously.
Thus he says with the three verses beginning with "Then, entering... (43).

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Then, it is said that they again conducted a search together with her, who had dispelled their distress; this is expressed by the word "tataḥ" (then). After that conversation, for the purpose of searching for him, they entered—that is, they went into—a forest of sparse shade along the path indicated by her, together with her. As far as...

Pervading [the sky], the moonlight was perceived and shone forth; having surmised his entry into the forest, they searched for him. Thinking that Śrī Kṛṣṇa had entered the darkness ahead—unnoticed due to the density of the trees and the similarity of color—they desisted from their search for Hari and turned back.
Thus it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the thicket; his footprints are not seen here.
Turn back! This is not within the range of the moon's rays. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.41)

Because women possess the nature of trees and because they are incapable of entering darkness; "tataḥ" (from that) is used with the sense of all case endings (*sārva-vibhaktika-tasi*). Thus, there is no tautology in the phrase "of that Hari.
By this, a specific transitory emotion (*sañcāri-bhāva*), namely despondency (*nirveda*), has arisen. They did not go home, nor did they remember [him].
Because the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) called love (rati) possesses firm roots. ||43||

Viśvanātha: And then, with her hand supported by her friend out of a sense of detachment, they all together searched for him; thus he says, "Then... Even on a full-moon night, darkness exists only because of the dense shadows of the trees, as far as the moonlight can be perceived. As it has been said:
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Kṛṣṇa has entered the dense forest; his footprints cannot be seen here.
Turn back, for this place is not within the range of the moon's rays. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.41) Thus it is said.
In truth, O friends submerged in an ocean of grief, in this darkness as black as a rain-cloud, he—
whose body is as dark as a rain-cloud— remains hidden out of fear of being seen;
do not shrink back, for wherever you go, he is surely elsewhere.
"He will flee; enough of this endeavor to cause exhaustion to one whose body is so exceedingly delicate"—having reflected thus, they turned back. ||43||
With their minds fixed on him, their speech directed toward him, their movements centered on him,
and their very selves becoming him, they sang only of his virtues and did not remember their own homes.

Śrīdhara: Even though they had not yet reached their own homes, they did not remember them at all; they were "of that nature," meaning those for whom He alone was the Self—i.e., they were absorbed in Him. ||44||

Vaṃśīdhara: The meaning is as follows; the purport is that they have attained identity with Him through meditation. He describes the nature of those whose intellects are fixed on Him: "tan-manaskāḥ" (those whose minds are absorbed in Him). This means those for whom His conversation—that is, His narration—is their primary concern. "Tad-guṇān" means His virtues, and not His faults. "Gāyantyaḥ" means where My devotees sing.
"O Nārada, I abide there," he said, because the Blessed One is fond of song. "Self-dwellings" refers to the houses of the body. (44)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "With their minds fixed on Him," and so forth.

By the phrase "those whose minds [were directed] toward Him" and so on, since all [the senses], beginning with the mind, share a single substratum, the distinctness of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has indeed ceased;
this is the intended meaning. Therefore, because they had that as their sole substratum, they did not remember their own homes. (44)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Furthermore, having turned back from there, they became immersed in supreme sorrow due to the fear of pain—according to the manner to be described later in the verse, "Does nothing distress him who has entered there?"—even though he was not actually tormented by thorns and the like. Thus, the author says: "With their minds fixed on Him."
Those whose minds were fixed on entering that very same place where he was confined;
then those whose conversation—consisting of talk and recollection of his suffering—concerned that very same object;
and then those whose actions, prompted by that very same cause, were directed toward the possibility of his escape through other efforts.

Those whose nature consists of circumambulating [Him] on all sides; therefore, those states of being in which the self-exertion is directed toward Him alone— being thus truly merged within Him and having become the cause [of His manifestation]—
manifest through that [devotion] solely the qualities characterized by compassion and so forth, which consist of such mastery, and nothing else.

But they, singing of the faults such as the abandonment of their own [families], made him hear them through their song; they did not even remember themselves, let alone their homes—this is the meaning. ||44||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Nevertheless, what need is there to say that they would go to their own homes? And it is said that even though they were mindful [of their duties], they did not do so; thus he says: "with their minds fixed on Him. This means that they did not attend to their own various riches of happiness, nor, by the force of habit, to the household chores.
Or rather, "those to be approached" (*gamyāni*) refers to the self, the body, or the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). "Dwellings" (*āgārāṇi*) refers to houses, or the body and home;

thus, the enjoyer, the means of enjoyment, and the objects of enjoyment have been mentioned. The reason for not remembering them is stated by the three phrases beginning with "with minds fixed on that": attachment of mind, speech, and body toward that [object] is expressed.

In that regard, attachment of the mind occurs through the recollection of its qualities and so forth, or through various conceptualizations concerning it; that of speech occurs through mutual conversation about it, or sometimes through calling it by name and so forth; and that of the body occurs, as before, through the imitation of its gestures.

[This is achieved] by prostrating like a staff for the purpose of salutation, and by weaving garlands of flowers for that purpose, preparing beds and coverlets, and so forth. For this very reason, they are of His nature and consist of Him; or rather, their selves have been offered to Him in the manner described. Therefore, [they praise] His qualities.

Thus it is said, yet they do not sing of faults such as cruelty even regarding His renunciation; for singing is appropriate because the Blessed Lord is fond of song. And so it was said by Him Himself:
"I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis."
"O Nārada, I abide wherever My devotees sing.

Thus, because singing is the means for captivating the glorious Lord, its preeminence over all else is intended. Alternatively, at that time, due to their lack of such focused contemplation (*anusandhāna*), it was merely...

This is due to the very nature of the intensity of the pain of separation. Nevertheless, because it is mentioned at the very end, and because it is remembered as being formed with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), its preeminence is established by its primary status.
Furthermore, since speaking and singing cannot occur simultaneously in that state, there is speaking at one time and singing at another.
This is to be inferred. [It should be understood that for some there is conversation and for others there is singing.
Alternatively, by the four phrases beginning with "intent upon Him" (*tan-manaskāḥ*), their eternal nature has been described.
Therefore, they are now singing due to the pain of separation; thus, they are "of that very nature," as before.

Or, it is for the sake of avoiding the final stage (antya-daśā). Or rather, he distinguishes them precisely for the sake of avoiding that [final stage] by means of their nature as an increase in the pain of separation, or through an absorption in that [pain]. They are those whose minds are like his mind—free from fear and so forth—or whose speech is like his speech.
Those whose speech consists of playful conversation preceded by profound and sweet syllables and meanings;

those whose movements consist of various actions such as embracing, which are like his own; and those whose bodies are as captivating as his own through the imitation of his three-fold bend (tribhaṅga) and other gestures—even so, they [praise] only his virtues.
"Sing" indicates their inherent nature. Furthermore, it is suggested that through each [of these acts], their longing for attaining Him increases rather than subsides. The rest is the same. ||44||
The composition of the sequence (*krama-sandarbha*): singing only of His qualities, and not even their own suffering and so forth.

The composition of the great sequence (*bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*): those whose minds are fixed on Him, whose conversation is directed toward Him, whose activities are solely for His sake, and whose very support is He; they sing only of His qualities.
In truth, they did not even remember their own bodies as their dwellings. ||44||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, one might ask: "In their despair at not having attained Kṛṣṇa, why did they not go home?

He states the reason for this: "With their minds fixed on Him" (*tan-manaskāḥ*). They did not remember their own homes—that is, they did not recall their own bodies (the *kṣetrajña*) or their houses (*āgārāṇi*, meaning *gṛhān*). The suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of identity (*ātma-ka* means "whose nature is the self").

Or rather, those whose minds possess that very same pleasure of amorous delight; or those whose minds have that very thing as the object of their play; or those whose conversation consists of that very thing, meaning their mutual exchange of speech and counter-speech; or those whose discourse is that very thing.

This has been stated in this very same work: "With voices as deep as clouds, they call the cattle by name from afar" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.15.13). Alternatively, those whose singing consists of his very conversation in the form of meditation, their various bodily movements are for his sake alone.

Those [gopīs] whose nature consists of the gathering of flowers and so forth, and the fashioning of garlands, staffs, balls, and the like; or alternatively, those whose various activities consist of hiding and other such pastimes as before—that is to say, they are absorbed in that; or rather, those whose very self and inherent nature is centered on Him, and not on their homes; or else—

Those whose very selves were of the nature of that same playful manifestation; for this very reason, because Kṛṣṇa was fond of singing, they performed only songs of His qualities and forms, and not remembrance of their home. ||44||

Viśvanātha: By means of fixing their minds on Him alone, when the intensity of their madness had subsided as before, they addressed Him with words such as "O Aśvattha tree, have you seen [Him]? When the madness reached its middle stage, they manifested His specific gestures by imitating His actions, as in "She cried out 'Kṛṣṇa! and "She drank from His breast."

When madness reaches its full intensity, they become one with that state; through self-forgetfulness, they have become absorbed in Him, like those who say, "I am Kṛṣṇa! Behold my gait! And by the force of previous impressions alone, they sing loudly of His very qualities, as if saying, "Behold this very one! ||44||
Returning once more to the bank of the Kalindī,
those whose hearts were absorbed in Kṛṣṇa gathered together and sang of Kṛṣṇa, longing for his arrival.

Śrīdhara: However, having come to that very bank of the Kālindī where they had previously met with Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, they meditated upon and contemplated Kṛṣṇa. Thus, those who were longing for Kṛṣṇa’s arrival gathered together and sang only of Kṛṣṇa. ||45||

Vaṃśīdhara: Regarding why they sang while wandering here and there, he says—"But what? (kiṃ tu). On that bank (*pulina*) where [the flute] was abandoned, for the reason that He must have surely come there out of compassion to console us, He has come back again; this is the meaning. "Assembled" (*samavetāḥ*); there is no sorrow with the five.
Because of the statement "together," they have attained a state of oneness. ||45||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: To the question of what they did then, he says "again," and so forth.

Just as the bodies of those who delight in the Self wander here and there by chance, so too did they come to the riverbank—not through deliberate intention. Thus, there is no contradiction with what was previously stated. (45)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, even there, fearing that he might be obstructed by his own [attendants], she abandoned every path for searching him; thus, we all gathered together and went to that very *līlā-pulina*, where the sound [of her voice] reached us clearly from afar.

Having perceived their loud singing filled with wretchedness, reproaches, and so forth, they performed it while meditating that Śrī Kṛṣṇa would surely come quickly out of compassion; thus he says, "Again," etc., from the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Again" refers to their returning to the riverbank. There, He was abandoned by us.

Thinking that Śrī Kṛṣṇa must have surely come there out of compassion to console them, or else, due to the absence of His vision, out of a desire to see the very place of His pastimes along with Himself; for this very reason it is said: "Kṛṣṇa is the one who draws the heart toward Him, or He is the bestower of supreme bliss."

Meditating [on Him], thinking that He had gone there, or perhaps reflecting on the sport they had performed together, they gathered together; this was for the sake of hearing from Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own lips [the news of His return], according to the maxim "there is no sorrow when accompanied by five," or else due to the very nature of their separation, [thinking of] Kṛṣṇa as the embodiment of the mass of supreme bliss.

The sense is that, indeed, her life-breaths did not depart solely because of her singing. For those [women], only her arrival was desired; thus, no other desire whatsoever arose, nor did the longing for her arrival cease.
And in that context, by the word "arrival," it is meant that through the agony of extreme separation, they desired merely the sight of her.
But it is not anything else; such is the meaning. ||45||

The sequence of the composition: Proclaiming once more the reason for their arrival at the sandy bank, those whose thoughts were fixed on Kṛṣṇa considered Him to have gone there; yet again, from afar, they were such that His arrival was longed for by them through the very vision of emptiness. ||45||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: The word "again" (*punar*) refers to where they previously went with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Their "arrival" (*āgamanam*) means their manifestation (*āvirbhāva*). "Those who longed for it" (*tatra kāṅkṣitam*): the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning those whose longing was directed toward that [manifestation].

"Assembled" (*samavetāḥ*) means they were in communion with Him in their hearts, because they shared a single latent impression (*vāsanā*). This is because their contemplation (*bhāvanā*) was fixed upon Kṛṣṇa.
They sang for Kṛṣṇa in that manner; it should be understood that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, though invisible and hidden from sight, remained right there with them. ||45||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: In response to the inquiry as to what they did then, he says—"Again. Having returned once more to that bank of the Kālindī where Śrī Kṛṣṇa had sported, [one might ask]: "But how could they go again to that very place where they had been abandoned by Kṛṣṇa? If this is asked:
To this she replied: "Those whose thoughts are fixed on Kṛṣṇa have come here with the hope that Śrī Kṛṣṇa will take delight upon this sandbank, thinking, 'This sandbank will grant us His company.
By whose and whose good fortune has Kṛṣṇa appeared here, seeing no other means of attainment, and filled with compassion for our wretchedness?"

Having perceived his loud singing, they thought, "He will surely come himself," and with their hearts fixed on Kṛṣṇa, who is personified beauty itself, they sang aloud. Longing for His arrival, they abandoned all faults through the singing of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities; and when those faults were removed, Kṛṣṇa Himself [appeared].

Thinking, "He will appear," and having determined that Kṛṣṇa would become fruitful upon the banks of the Yamunā at that time, those women who longed for His arrival sang as they awaited Him, for Kṛṣṇa is fond of singing. ||45||

Viśvanātha: Alas, alas! Wherever we go in search of him, he will flee from there. Therefore, what is the hardship of wandering through the forest? We shall instill in him a desire for it; without such a desire, he cannot be obtained—for "he is obtained only by that which he chooses" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23).

Thus, as if taking the sacred revelation (śruti) as their authority, and as if revealing the established conclusion that in his philosophical system compassion alone is the cause [of his teaching], and in that compassion, the proclamation of his own deeds is the cause,
they returned to that very place where they had previously met with him and spoke to him.
He says: "Again" (punar). ||45||
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the thirtieth chapter here in the tenth book has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous.
Thus ends the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, known as the Pāramahaṃsī, in the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The thirtieth chapter, titled "The Search for Kṛṣṇa," in the Rāsa-līlā of the Tenth Book.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter,
titled "The Narration of the Song of the Gopīs."
The gopīs said:
By Your birth, Vraja is supremely victorious;
for here indeed Indirā dwells eternally.
O beloved, look at your own people in all directions; with their hopes fixed upon you, they are searching for you.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirty-first [chapter], having lost all hope, they returned once more to the riverbank;
singing only of Kṛṣṇa, they prayed for His arrival.

"Victorious! [He says: "O beloved, by your birth, Vraja is victorious—that is, it exists in a state of supreme excellence—just as it becomes exceedingly so. Because you have been born here, Indirā (Lakṣmī) indeed takes refuge here;
she dwells having adorned Vraja. Thus, while all of Vraja rejoices, here..."
"Your own people—the cowherd women—whose very lives are somehow sustained for your sake alone, are searching for you;
therefore, please look upon them, let yourself be perceived by them. Or else: "May you be seen by us," or rather: "In this way, may you be seen by them as they search."
Vaṃśīdhara:

*Caitanya-mañjuṣā*: "Victorious," and so forth. The word "victorious" (*jayati*) is employed at the outset for the sake of auspiciousness. Although the earth alone is victorious, nevertheless, the victory of Vraja is superior.

Thus, the word *adhika* (excessive) is employed. By "birth," meaning manifestation; the root *jan* is established in the sense of manifestation with the suffix *mani*. At the very same moment as Your manifestation, Śrī also manifested. They say that she is unable to remain even for a moment without You—"She takes refuge," and so forth. Together with Śrī...

"What is the use of your dwelling with me?"—this is indeed the truth; however, they say, "We do not desire to dwell with you, but rather desire only to see you"—for in the verse beginning with "O beloved" (*dayita*), [the sense is: O beloved, you are not very far away; since you are indeed nearby, let you be seen.
They investigate; this root *ci* is transitive (dvikarmaka), meaning "may you become visible.

In every direction (*dikṣu*, i.e., in each quarter). Alternatively, from the form of the root *diś* with the suffix *kvip*—meaning "in the assigning" (*atisarjane*)—there is the substitution (*ādeśa*) [of *diś* for *diś*];
in those assignments, they are yours (*tāvakāḥ*). Not only are they yours, but those whose life-breaths are fixed in you are also yours.
The word *janāḥ* is masculine; otherwise, it would belong exclusively to you (the feminine). ||1||
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī:
Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī:
Who now remains in this world of humans who does not possess devotion?
If separation occurs, to whom does it not happen? And when separation exists, who can live?

By such statements as these, they say that although beloved women might not live during the separation from their beloveds, it is true that they do not die because of you alone— the meaning is that they hold onto life with you as its cause, living on in the hope of attaining you.
Or else, the meaning is that regarding you as their object, their lives do not perish because they have been entrusted to you.

The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained. The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, since the singing of the Lord is endowed with supreme excellence (*sarvotkarṣa*), it is appropriate to begin it with the word "jayati" (He triumphs), which expresses that supreme excellence.
They say the same thing: "He conquers," and so forth. By your birth—that is, by your manifestation—the cowherd settlement (Vraja) conquers even more.

It was already victorious because it is a terrestrial Vaikuṇṭha; now, through your manifestation, it conquers even further, because it has become both a terrestrial and a non-terrestrial Vaikuṇṭha. The reason for this is that Lakṣmī, Indirā, is indeed ever-present here.

The meaning is: "He takes refuge right here; he stays right here. Therefore, while Vraja possesses such supreme excellence, it is improper that we who dwell in Vraja should suffer such misery. Thus, the meaning is that they pray for a vision of You in order to dispel this [misery], just as one says, "He gathers fruit from the tree."

Because the root *ciñ* is transitive (*dvikarmaka*), the intention is: "May you become visible. It is your very sight that is desired; otherwise, the word *adhika-jayati* would have to be interpreted [in a strained way]. As for the fact that Indirā (Lakṣmī) takes refuge [in you], what does that have to do with our fulfillment? Is it so, or not?—this is the meaning of the sentence. ||1||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha;
in the thirty-first [chapter], there is the fragrance of the honeyed voice, rhythm, and so forth of divine love.
The row of lotuses that is the Gopī-gītā shone forth, attracting the bees that are Kṛṣṇa.
Repeated obeisances to the eternal masters, the glorious gurus,
whose remnants alone are the sustenance of my life, by which I now strive for auspiciousness.
It was previously stated that "they sang"; what exactly did they say? To this, he says: "The gopīs said.

"O Beloved! By Your birth, Vraja is victorious. The meaning is that, by not specifying a particular relationship, it exists with excellence over all worlds indeed—even in the world of Vaikuṇṭha, such [a state] does not exist.

To exclude that [possibility], they say: "In such a way that it may be superior" means that Vaikuṇṭha is indeed the most excellent, whereas Vraja is the most excellent of all. They state another indicative mark as well: Mahālakṣmī, known as Indirā, "constantly resorts to" (śrayate)—that is, she serves (sevate)—Vaikuṇṭha; for the root *śri* is used in the sense of service (*sevā*).
The implication is that because she alone is served [there], Vraja is more full of all prosperity even than Vaikuṇṭha;
thus, we ourselves are the beloveds of You in Vraja, which is so completely filled with great happiness caused by her.

"We do not pray to you for protection from this supreme, unbearable suffering—which we experience and which has never been seen, heard of, or undergone by anyone else in all the worlds—but rather, having seen [you] but once, let our eyes be fulfilled;
thus they say: 'here in Vṛndāvana,' for this is indeed certain."
"Look! What is there to see? Your own people are searching for you. They said this so that one might not doubt how these people, though possessed of such intense longing, could perish; [they said]:
"Those by whom the life-breaths were held and entrusted to you, and who were driven mad by you—if they were indeed ours, then [why do they perish] among us?"

"I would have always remained among them, even though they were consumed by the fire of separation; it would have been better to die at this very moment so that we might have been happy. But since you, our own lord, are supremely happy, their happiness follows yours—how then could their bodies perish while there is such happiness for their lives? Therefore [she says]:

The sense is that your happiness, which consists in witnessing our suffering, is indeed eternal. In this verse, there is identity of the second syllable in each quarter, as well as between the first and seventh syllables; likewise, this is generally the case in other verses as well, though occasionally.
It exists in some places, and it has been explained by the authors of the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā*. ||1||
With eyes that steal away the splendor of the autumnal lake, which is like the interior of a lotus filled with a multitude of excellent and virtuous bees.
O Lord of Surata, you who grant boons, this girl is your slave without price; for one who subdues her, is there not death in this world?

Śrīdhara: Here, because independent arms are acting as speakers, the introduction "others say" (*apare āhuḥ*) is applied to every verse; nevertheless, the connection (*saṃgati*) is now stated. If it is asked, "What is there for me to investigate? they reply with the word "autumn" (*śaradā*). [The phrase] "well-born in an autumnal lake" (*śarad udāśaye...sādhu jātam*) refers to that which has arisen properly in a lake belonging to the autumn season.

O Lord of divine pleasure, O Master of enjoyment, O Giver of boons and desired objects; by that eye which steals— that is, takes away— the beauty residing within the interior— the womb— of the perfectly born, blossoming lotus, you are slaying us, who are your priceless slave-girls.

Is this killing being committed by you in this world not [killing]? Is killing only killing when done with a weapon? Does it not become killing even when done with a glance? Indeed, it does. Therefore, the sense is:
"Look upon him so that his life, taken away by your glance, may be restored. Look upon him.
Thus, this remainder of the sentence applies everywhere as far as possible. 2.
Vaṃśīdhara:

*Caitanya-mañjūṣā*: "If you do not appear, then even the killing of a woman will occur," they said—beginning with the words "śarad-udāśaya" and so forth. That which is well-born in a lake associated with autumn...

The lotus is excellent; whatever splendor resides within its interior, that splendor she robs away with her gaze. If even by such a glance killing is not difficult, then what wonder is there that she, who steals the beauty residing within the heart of a lotus situated in the midst of water, will take away the life of us who dwell on dry land? Even though you [look] with your gaze...
Even though you inflict death, she alone is to be seen as beloved; that he should pray for her again is indeed like the maxim: "the medicine for poison is poison itself. ||2||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: +++ *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: +++ *Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: not commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, since Vraja is so exalted and Indirā herself resides there eternally, the slaughter of a multitude of women is utterly improper. Or, if you say, "I shall not kill you," that too is not acceptable; for is killing by unarmed means not considered killing? Thus [it is].
They say: "The autumnal pond," and so forth. O Lord of amorous play (surata-nātha)! Or rather, O Lord who is well-delighted (suṣṭhu-rata)!

Is there not slaughter here on this ground of Vṛndāvana for those who have become slaves—not purchased with money, but slaves acquired by the very glance [of Your eyes]? Indeed, even in a place of ordinary merit, a person [is slain].
"She does not commit murder, but you, even here"—such is the power of the word "here" (iha).

Thinking that [the Lord] had appeared in person as if by the force of the previous statement, "O beloved, look!", some women, experiencing inner agitation through the good fortune of their own eyes, spoke thus. With what kind of gaze?
In a lake that serves as a resting place in autumn—that is, in a lake existing during the autumn season—there is a lotus (*sarasija*) that is well-born, truly arisen, excellent, and sublime;

the "splendor" (*śrī*) within its interior is such that it steals away [all other beauty], and thus [the body] is described by that term. The meaning is that even the limbs of a thief are themselves thieves.
Alternatively, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *dṛk* (vision), ending in the instrumental case, meaning "those who have not perceived such a vision.

It is like saying "they die because of food," which means "because of the non-perception of food. Or else: "O Giver of Boons (*varada*), O Giver of Desires! Therefore, let [me] be seen; for if that is not done, is this killing here not truly killing? Thus [it is said].
You alone are the Lord of the virtuous, and you are also the bestower of boons. O Bestower of Boons!
The killing of one who acts as a bestower of boons is utterly improper. ||2||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says: "Indeed, do I wish to give you sorrow that you should thus indicate it?
In that case, you yourself will surely strike us," they say—beginning with the word *śarad*. ++...++ [The commentary continues from here.]
— from the subsiding of poisonous waters, from predatory beasts and rākṣasas,
from rain and wind, and from the fire of lightning;
O Ṛṣabha, we have been protected again and again by you, the son of Vṛṣamaya, from fear on all sides.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, having protected them out of compassion from many deaths, why do you now send Manmatha with your glance to have him killed? To this they say: "viṣa... etc. O Ṛṣabha, best one!
From the destruction (*apaya*) by water and so forth which is like poison (*viṣamaya*), and likewise from the serpent-demon Aghāsura and from the wind-god Vāyu for a year...

The sense is: "Since you have protected [the cows] from the fire of lightning, from the fall of thunderbolts, from the bull Aṛṣṭa, from that son of mine [Kamsa], from the sky, from everything else, and from all fears by means of the subduing of Kāliya and other deeds—why do you now neglect them? ||3||
Vaṃśīdhara:

Caitanya-mañjūṣā: Now, if your sole objective is indeed our execution, then they ask: "How was [the Lord] previously protected from those very causes of death that had approached him?"—beginning with the verse starting with *viṣa-jalāpyāyāt*.
And so forth. ||3||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: ...
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: ...
*Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Regarding the word "vṛṣa": from Vṛṣamaya-ātmaja, that is, from Vatsāsura, the son of Vṛṣa.
The meaning is: "from my own son Vyomāsura. ||3||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, if your sole objective were indeed our destruction, then how is it that we have been protected by the successive causes that presented themselves?
They demonstrate this with the verse beginning "From the swelling of the poisoned water," and so forth. [The phrase] *viṣa-jalāpyayaḥ* refers to the swelling of the poisoned water.
The Yamunā lake was turbid with mud; Vyāla was Aghāsura, who was indeed a *rākṣasa* because he had devoured a body; Varṣā and the others are well known, as they were created by the enraged Śakra;
Vṛṣa was Ariṣṭa; and Mayātmaja was Vyomāsura. What need is there for more? It was out of fear of him on all sides.

Even there, repeatedly and again and again—surely it need not be asked why these [demons] became the cause of Your death, or why you were protected; for the protection of those residing in Vraja is itself our protection. By that...
When Vraja attains excellence, our own excellence ought to follow as well; therefore, the intention is that if this does not happen, it will cause us distress. (3)
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha: What? (o)0(o)
Indeed, you, the delight of Gopikā,
who perceive the inner self of all embodied beings,
have been requested by Vikhanas for the protection of the universe.
Sakha was born in the lineage of the Sātvatas.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, with the intention that it would be utterly improper for you—who have descended for the protection of the universe—to neglect your devotees, they say: "Not indeed," and so forth. O friend, you certainly (*khalu*) are not the son of Yaśodā; rather, you are the witness of the intellects of all living beings. [The interlocutor asks: But is he visible?
Regarding this, they say: having been entreated by the Brahmin Vikhanas for the protection of the universe, he arose and was born into the lineage of the Sātvatas. Thus it is said. (4)
Vaṃśīdhara:
[Objection: "If it is argued that He protected them from those [demons] with the thought, 'I shall slay them myself,' even that is not so;
for they say that You have descended into the family of the Sātvatas solely for the protection of the universe—certainly not [for Your own sake]."

And so forth. Indeed, O Blessed One! You are truly the delighter of Gopikā; in being the delighter of Gopikā, you possess the nature of a cowherd (gopa). Being a cowherd, you are ignorant of our suffering, for you perceive the inner self of all embodied beings.
Thus entreated by Vikhanas for the protection of the universe, you, the Friend, have arisen in the lineage of the Sātvatas. And so on.
If you had been cognizant of the suffering of others in the manner that is expounded by those learned in the scriptures,
you would have become intent on concealing [the truth] from people like us; for, being present within the universe, you are likewise one who gratifies the Vaiṣṇavas.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Krama-sandarbha*: Alternatively, having inferred the wonder according to what preceded, they speak for the sake of praise with two verses beginning with "Not indeed" (*na khalu*). (4)
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, some say that You are indeed the son of the cowherd girls;

others say You are the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of all living beings; and others say You have descended for the sake of protecting the universe—thus three well-known views exist. Among these, You behave toward us as if You were distinct from each of those three views.
To show what this "play" (*līlā*) of yours is, they say: "Certainly not," and so forth. "O Kṛṣṇa!
You are certainly not the son of a cowherd woman; for if that were so, you would have shown compassion toward us, who are of the same kind.
Nor are you the witness of the inner self of all embodied beings; for if that were so, [you would have shown compassion] toward us as well."

Otherwise, there would have been no knowledge of the suffering within the inner self; nor would You have been entreated by Brahmā, the son of Vikhanas, nor would You have arisen in the lineage of the Sātvatas for the protection of the universe. Had that been so, there would have been protection even for us who dwell within the universe. Therefore, this incarnation of Yours is truly wonderful.
The state of being. ||4||
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
O beloved leader of the Vṛṣṇis, for those who have approached Your feet out of fear of worldly existence,
Your lotus-hand grants their desires while bestowing fearlessness.
Place the grasp of Your glorious hand upon our heads.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, they say, "Fulfill this fourfold prayer of us, your devotees," with the four verses beginning with *viracitābhayam*. O foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, for those living beings who have reached Your feet—that is, those who have sought refuge—out of fear of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*), You have fashioned [protection].
O beloved, do not place upon your head that lotus-hand of yours which has granted fearlessness, which likewise bestows desires and boons, and which grasps the hand of Śrī. 5.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjūṣā: "O gopīs! Indeed, you speak quite the contrary when you say, 'I am the witness of the self of all and the protector of the universe'; if that is so, then act accordingly."
They said: "One who has manifested fearlessness," and so forth, with many [epithets]. ||5||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: ...
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
... *Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Out of fear of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*) and of everything connected therewith.
O You who directly grasp the hand of Śrī, as it were, by bringing all prosperity under Your control within Your own cowherd settlement; [this is] Yours. ||5||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: If it is argued that, according to the three views mentioned above, "I am exactly as they describe me in those ways, and not otherwise—this should not be doubted," then let it be so;
thus they say: "O you who have bestowed fearlessness," and so forth. O leader of the Vṛṣṇis! O you whose supreme concern is the protection of the universe!

"He has arisen in the lineage of the Sātvatas for the protection of the universe"—this address is based on the view that his purpose is dedicated to the protection of the world. The underlying sense is: "May the protection of all of us be performed.
In what manner is that to be done? To this they say: "O Beloved! Place Your lotus-hand upon our heads; then..."
The meaning is: "We all indeed live. Of what kind [is He]? One who has manifested fearlessness (*viracitābhaya*). For whom?
For those who have gone to Your feet (*te tava caraṇam īyuṣām*). From what? From the fear of *saṃsṛti* (transmigratory existence); that is to say, [He is] fearless.
Of what kind [is He]? That by which there is the grasping of the hand of Śrī, the Goddess Lakṣmī; thus [He is]. Of Śrī...
"It has the mere grasping of the hand as its purpose. But for us, it grants desires and bestows all that is wished for.
By saying "on the head," there is first of all a request for only a small amount in the manner of a beggar; by this, wretchedness is also suggested. (5)
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
O Hero who removes the suffering of the people of Vraja, whose smile destroys the pride of Your own kinswomen— O Friend, please favor us, Your maidservants! Do not treat us with disdain.
Show me your beautiful lotus-face.

Śrīdhara: O Hero, O destroyer of the suffering of the people of Vraja! O Friend, whose smile destroys—that is, annihilates—the pride (*smaya*) of Your own people, please favor (*bhaja*) us, Your maidservants; "sm" means certainly. First of all:
Do not show us the beautiful lotus-faces of those women.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjuṣā: not explained.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: +++ [incomplete]
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: [The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, if it is the case that you live merely by the placing of hands upon your heads, [then...]

"Then close all your eyes; I shall place my hand upon your head. They said, "Not so," beginning with the words "O Vraja... This is an address based on a reason: "O remover of the suffering of the people of Vraja! O Hero!
O All-capable One! If that is so, then just as you are capable of indifference, you are likewise capable of concern.
"In that case, am I indifferent? No, O You whose smile destroys the pride of Your own kin!
Accept us as Your maidservants.
Is 'acceptance' merely labor or service? No," they said, "reveal Your lotus-face."
The meaning is that beholding one's own face is indeed worship (*bhajana*). The genitive case in *yoṣitām* is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), meaning "among women, who are not maidservants?
Alternatively, O people of Vraja—those very inhabitants of Vraja who are his attendants (*parijana*)—O dispeller of the distress of women! O hero! [Thus he addresses them.]
Or a regional affectionate address. ||6||
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
Your lotus feet, which destroy the sins of those who bow before You, which follow the grazing deer, which are the abode of Śrī, and which rest upon the hoods of the serpent— [I worship them].
Make us free from evil deeds; cut away the disease that dwells in our hearts.

Śrīdhara: Your lotus feet—which, without distinction, destroy the sins of embodied beings who bow before You, which follow even the grass-eating cattle out of compassion, which are the abode of Śrī through their auspiciousness, and which are placed upon the hoods of serpents due to Your supreme valor—place those feet upon our breasts. Make them rest there.
For what purpose? "Hṛcchayam" means desire; "kṛndhi" means cut or sever it. ||7||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjūṣā: not explained.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: +++ [incomplete]
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, if you have already achieved your purpose merely by seeing my face, [why do you ask further?]
If you say, "Since that was already seen previously, why then do you feel such longing?"—it is not so;

for we desire nothing other than the sight of Your face. Yet, they say—"Bowing down," and so forth—they wish to place Your lotus feet upon their breasts: "Place Your lotus feet, O Lord, upon our breasts."
"Do so. Anticipating the question, "What will happen then? they say: "Cut away the heart-dweller, the torment of the heart.
[An objection is raised: "But where is it well-known that Your lotus feet are the cutter of the heart-dweller?
To this they reply: "They are the draggers-away of the sins of embodied beings who bow down. For there is nothing superior to the dragging away of sin.
The destruction of the heart's desire [is possible], because that [desire] is adventitious.
But surely, since they have bowed down, it is done accordingly? This also is not so;
for even the following of grass-eaters—that is, of animals that eat grass—is merely a natural consequence of their nature. In this very same way, his [behavior] is simply innate.
Compassionateness.
[The opponent objects: "But surely it is improper for you to set foot upon your breasts, which are smeared with saffron paste and other substances and are exceedingly beautiful.
[The Gopīs reply: "No," they say—"for they are the abode of Śrī, the source of splendor; by contact with them, our breasts [become auspicious]."
There will be an exceeding beauty, like a golden full pitcher covered by a lotus.

Indeed, I speak the truth: how can your feet, tender as lotuses, be placed upon your hard breasts? To this they reply: "Placed upon the hoods of serpents"—that is, upon the hoods of the serpent Kāliya.
"Placed upon hoods hardened by jewels—how can there be any doubt about that?
This is the conclusion from *Rasikāhlādinī* by Viśvanātha. Others say: "O you who are bowed down to... [The verse continues: "Place your lotus-feet upon their breasts. Why? [Because...]

For what purpose? O Hṛcchaya (Dweller in the Heart), cut—meaning sever—Kāma (lust). Here, by these women who possess love that is incapable of [worldly] pleasure, who are endowed with great affection, and who are devoid of knowledge regarding the removal of their own suffering or the attainment of happiness, whose physical, vocal, and mental activities have as their sole objective the bliss of Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone... [of Him].

In order to kindle the pleasure of amorous union, those who are supremely clever generally do not diminish the verbal expression of love by disclosing their own beauty, youth, and pangs of desire; rather, they express only their passion,
just as one might address a friend who is a glutton for food when that friend is feeling hungry.

When a person, desiring to feed him out of affection, exerts themselves in preparing the four kinds of sweet foods, even when questioned by him, says only for their own sake, "I am going for my own purpose, not for yours"— that very thing is heavy love. If, however, [the person thinks], "This much effort of mine is solely for the sake of your happiness," [then it is light].
If one says that love is for one's own sake because of being free from desire, then that love becomes trivial. As it is said in the *Prema-sampuṭa*:
"Love between two connoisseurs is like a lamp."
"It illuminates the chamber of the heart and shines perfectly still;
however, if it is expelled from the mouth through the gates [of the senses], it quickly extinguishes or becomes light. Thus it is said.

In this regard, their lack of intent toward their own pleasure is understood precisely from the Lord’s own words, "I am unable," which manifest His being under their control. It should be known that His state of being subject solely to their love is what is seen in all the scriptures, and not a state of being subject to desire.

"Do I not fear sin? To this they reply: "For embodied beings who are prostrate before you, how could there be any apprehension of sin from you? The sense is this. Furthermore, "Will my delicate lotus-feet not suffer pain upon your hard breasts? To this they reply: [They are like] cows, which follow those that graze on grass; [the breasts are like] them.

For cows indeed follow even onto hard ground as they graze on grass; if there is endurance for your feet even there, then what need be said of our breasts? The sense is that the hardness of the breasts, far from being painful, is actually a source of pleasure to him.
"Is it not improper to place one's feet upon your breasts, which are adorned with various jewel-ornaments?
To this they reply: "Since these breasts are the 'abode of Śrī'—that is, of beauty—this [placing of the feet] will indeed become their finest ornament. This is the intended meaning.

"Am I not afraid of your husbands? To this they replied: "You do not fear even the serpent Kāliya when he has placed his hoods upon you; how much less, then, would you fear them? This is the intended meaning. ||7||
O lotus-eyed one, with your sweet voice, your charming speech that is pleasing to the minds of the wise!
O Hero, satisfy us who are bewildered by these ritual acts with the nectar of your lower lip.

Śrīdhara: O lotus-eyed one, with that speech of yours which is sweet, containing charming words, and which is pleasing to the minds of the wise—meaning, heart-stealing and profound—do you, with the nectar of your lower lip, satiate and revive these bewildered female attendants who carry out your commands. ||8||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjuṣā: not explained.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: +++ [incomplete]
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, you whose speech is inconsistent have previously stated—

"Place your lotus-hand upon our heads; then show us your lotus-face; and then place your lotus-feet upon our breasts"—having thus resolved, let it be said: "If you say, 'I shall do exactly that,' we reply:
'With sweetness,' etc. O lotus-eyed one! [those of us] who are fainting with infatuation..."

"O you who perform our rites, while these servant-girls are approaching, satisfy and revive us with the nectar of your lower lip—that is, by making us drink the honey of your lower lip—and then offer it back to them. You must not let them drink from your lower lip in silence; rather—"
They say [the words] begin with sweet speech—that is, with a sweet voice: "Do not fall into delusion;
drink, drink from the lower lip. This is by means of tender words; the instrumental case is used here for qualification.
Of what kind [is this voice]? It is one wherein the speech is *valgu*—beautiful—and which consists of a collection of words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other [syntactic] qualities.

Because the authority belongs precisely to such a word; therefore, for the wise—that is, for the learned, meaning those who are discerning—it is "delightful," that is, pleasing. This alone is the limit; nothing further need be requested. ||8||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha: "O you who are the sole beloveds of my life, O beloved jewels! I am not indifferent toward you who are the very essence of my existence; [be gracious] toward me, your servant."
"How can you be distrustful toward one who is bound by a golden chain of constant love for gold? Trust me! Know me to be right here at your hand's mark, like your own bracelet.
Hearing those words as they were uttered, another said: "In a sweet voice... [and so on].
By that speech— which is sweet because it is composed of syllables that manifest sweetness, which is pleasant to hear,
and which is delightful to the wise and the learned due to the variety of its charming words and meanings— these deluded female attendants of ours, who carry out our commands, are being enchanted.

"Further refresh her, who has attained a state of blissful delusion from the intensity of tasting its sweetness, with the nectar of your lower lip.
