Or rather, since we have attained delusion, cause us to drink even the nectar of your lower lip; that is to say, cause us to attain delusion once again. (8)
O Lord, the nectar of Your speech, praised by poets, is the life-giver to those scorched by suffering and the remover of all impurities.
Those people who give much are proclaimed on earth as auspicious listeners of the glorious and far-reaching [teachings].

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, they say that although death was already attained by us in separation from you, we were merely deceived by those fortunate ones who drink the nectar of your stories—expressed in the verse beginning with "tava.
Your story itself is the nectar; the reason for this is that it is the "life-sustainer for the distressed" (*taptajīvana*). This indicates its superiority over the well-known [celestial] nectar.

They say: "It is praised by the poets and even by those who know Brahman as being unassailable; yet that nectar which is the enjoyment of the gods has been rendered trivial by them. Furthermore, that nectar of yours removes impurity and destroys desire and karma, whereas the [other] nectar is not such. Moreover, it is auspicious to hear, bestowing blessings merely by being heard. That [nectar of yours].

Moreover, it is dependent upon practice; furthermore, it is glorious and profoundly peaceful, yet it is intoxicating. Those people on earth who thus recite and describe this nectar of your story in its full extent are "givers of much"—that is to say, they bestow life. Or rather, such [is the nature of your story].
Those on earth who recite the nectar of your story are "givers of much," meaning they have given much in their previous births;

that is to say, they are virtuous. This is what is intended: those who merely recite the nectar of your story are already exceedingly blessed, how much more so those who behold you! Therefore, we pray [to you].
"Let it be seen by you," [he said]. ||9||
Vaṃśīdhara:
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "Your story is nectar," and so forth. Your story alone is nectar;

however, here the word "nectar" (*amṛta*) refers to poison through the figure of speech known as "contrary indication" (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*). As it is said: "Much benefit was done there... [and so on].

[From the *Sāhitya-darpaṇa* 2.11], and so forth; for this reason, it is a "heated life" (taptam jīvanam), because it has been praised (*iḍitam*)—that is, lauded—only by poets who are authors of technical treatises (*śāstra-kṛdbhiḥ*), and not by those who know love. Therefore, it is "removing impurity" (*kalmaṣāpaham*), but not "extinguishing the fire of separation" (*virahāgni-haram*). It is "auspicious upon hearing" (*śravaṇa-maṅgalam*), meaning that the very act of hearing is auspicious, but not...
It bestows happiness, yet not through mere experience. It is "spread" (*ātatam*) by the pride of glory—the independence born of sovereign power.
Even in the case of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), it is likewise distinct from other forms of nectar. Therefore, they recount that story to me;
[the word *bhūridā*] is derived from the root *do* meaning "to cut," thus implying they are "cutters of much" (*bhūri-cchedakāḥ*), which is a form of censure.
For the other meaning is indeed quite clear. ||9||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
+++ *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: +++ In the *Sanātana Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* (10.534): "The story itself is nectar. The reason for this is as follows:

It is called "the life-giving heat" (*tapta-jīvana*). Poets, including Brahmā and others, have declared it superior even to the well-known nectar (*amṛta*); while that nectar enjoyed by the gods was praised by them, it has been rendered insignificant by this [nectar]. Furthermore, it removes impurity—that is, it dispels the impurity of desire—whereas that other nectar is not of such a nature. Moreover, [The text continues: *tapta-jīvanam | prasiddhāmṛtād utkarṣam āhuḥ kavibhir brahmādibhir apīḍitaḥ stutam | deva-bhogyaṃ tv amṛtaṃ tais tucchī-kṛtam | kiṃ ca, kalmaṣāpahaṃ kāma-kalmaṣa-nirasanaṃ tat tv amṛtaṃ naivam-bhūtam | kiṃ ca* [Translation: It is the "life-sustaining heat. Poets, including Brahmā and others, have stated that its excellence surpasses the celebrated nectar; for while the nectar enjoyed by the gods was praised by them, it has been treated as trivial by these [poets]. Furthermore, it is the remover of blemish—the destroyer of the blemish of desire—but that nectar is not like this. Moreover,

The auspiciousness of hearing [Your stories] bestows auspiciousness by the mere act of hearing, without depending on the performance of various other rituals. Moreover, that nectar of Your stories is glorious, profoundly peaceful, and intoxicating. Those on earth who recite it in such a manner—spreading it as widely as possible—[attain the highest good].
They discern this: those people are "givers of much" (bhūridāḥ), meaning they are givers of much, in the sense that they give life;

and now, due to the lack of such people, we are as if dead—this is the underlying thought. Or else, those who recite such nectar of Your stories are "givers of much," having given much in previous births.

The meaning is "those of supreme merit. Therefore, the sense is: "In the absence of such unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), we are unable to chant Your stories; how then shall we live? Or rather, they say: "In separation from You, we are as good as dead due to the particular vividness with which Your stories manifest," thus saying: "Your story alone is our death."

Death is direct death itself. Why? Because life becomes scorched, overwhelmed by heat, due to this particular love which, by its nature as a supreme burner, produces instantaneous death. Nevertheless, it is praised by poets, the authors of poetry, because it removes all impurities. Moreover—

It is auspicious for the ears and brings happiness. Furthermore, it is spread—that is, extended everywhere—by those such as Brahmā and others who are intoxicated by their own opulence (*śrī-mada*). In reality, however, the fault is indicated that the auspiciousness of the ears is actually spread only by those who are intoxicated by opulence (*śrī-mada*). Therefore, those who [drink] the nectar of Your stories which is of such a nature...

On this earth, those very people who "bhūri-dyanti"—that is, who cut off, sever, or crush [other matters]—are the ones who praise [the Lord]. Thus, in truth, it is indicated that the specific fruit of the narrations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed great; such is the direction of the argument. ||9||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: "If this is so, I shall act accordingly; let there be a moment's delay."

If it is argued, "Let it be done," they reply: "There is no conviction in your words"—referring to the verse beginning with "Your nectar-like speech" (*tava kathāmṛtam*). Your speech alone is the nectar (*kathāmṛtam*), not the action. The meaning is that you satisfy [us] through your speech in a way that you cannot through action. Therefore, [the phrase] *taptajīvanam* means "the life of one who is scorched."
Because it is their livelihood; since [otherwise] no purpose would be served, such talk results only in the heating of one's life.

Therefore, it is praised by poets and authors of treatises, but not by those who know love. Consequently, it removes only impurities, but does not quench the heat of the heart. Thus, it is auspicious only for the ears.

The hearing [of that tale] is auspicious, yet it does not grant joy to the heart, for it is expanded by *śrī-mada*, the intoxication of power and sovereignty, acting according to its own will. Therefore, those on earth who recite that story are "givers of much" (*bhūri-dā*) but "cutters of much" (*bhūri-chedakāḥ*); the root *do* means "to cut," thus implying a reproach. But as for your story—

"Life is sustained by heat," "praised by poets," and "removing impurities"—through such praise, this *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect eulogy) delights the connoisseurs. Thus, considering these four prayers to be difficult to attain, they say that one should take refuge in the nectar of Your story alone. In our separation, life is not something unattainable for us; however—

They speak of the excellence of the narrative, saying: "It is certain that [liberation] is to be accomplished by the nectar of Your story; as there is power in You, so too is there power in the story. Of what nature is this nectar of the narrative? It is "the life-giver to the tormented," for it revives those living beings who are scorched by the heat generated by desire and other passions—namely, the seekers of sense-objects.

Having rendered [the mind] empty of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects such as desire, one brings it to its own natural state (*svaniṣṭha*). This indeed is the very nature of the nectar of poetry (*kathāmṛta*). It is "praised by poets" (*kavibhir īḍitam*), which means by those who are liberated and have realized the truth.

It has been praised—that is, extolled—by them as being fit for their own service; this was stated by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* regarding its fitness to be served by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
They say: [The Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam] removes impurity; it destroys the impurity of sin which consists of ignorance and is the very nature of saṃsāra.

Having thus described its being served by those who are liberated and those desiring liberation, they state that it is to be served by pure devotees other than these three categories, as it is "auspicious to hear."

There is nothing else for them to be accomplished; thus [the author] says that it is, by its very nature, the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The meaning is that it brings about the glorious fortune of *bhakti*. "Pervasive" (*ātata*) means extended as far as Vaikuṇṭha. Even in Vaikuṇṭha, there is only the nectar of this narrative.

Because it is heard that [this nectar] is to be served upon the earth, the phrase "attaining what was unobtainable" is an expression of its excellence; those people who praise—that is, recount—this are givers of much, for they give away their very selves.
Or rather, they declare the nectar of the narrative to be superior even to the nectar enjoyed by the celebrated gods.

"Scorching life," and so forth; this is because it has been explained by the teachers. Alternatively, for us who are separated from our beloveds, the nectar of their story appears in a contrary manner; thus they say that the moon, sandalwood, and other things—which are causes of coolness for all people—appear in our experience as causes of heat. This is because of the manifestation [in us] of their being causes of torment.
Likewise, while the nectar of their discourse prevents the death of others, for us, our very speech is as good as dead,
because death is imminent upon hearing it. While their life is a "heated life" that provides nourishment to others scorched by the heat of saṃsāra, ours is the opposite of that.
In our heated hearts, this life-giving account was cast like water into hot oil;
just as water poured into hot oil causes an increase in flames, so too this story became the cause for an intensification of the fire within our hearts— it was truly as if it were dead matter.

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "praised by poets" (kavibhir īḍitam), meaning lauded through the attribution of non-existent qualities; for it is perceived as such by poets such as Nārada and others. It is "removing impurity" (kalmaṣāpaham), because it is perceived as removing the sin of those entitled to perform expiation (prāyaścitta); and even when one partakes of the nectar of its narrative, the fruit of that sin—namely suffering—is removed.

The meaning is: "The cessation of our suffering is not seen; therefore, we are not qualified. Alternatively, by the power of the Vedic scripture, *tyāgenaike amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ* (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 12.14), for those who have arrived here through the renunciation of attachment to husband, sons, and so forth, there is not even a trace of connection with sin.
Therefore, they are not qualified for atonement (*prāyaścitta*); the sense is that we shall not hear it as being an atonement.

"Auspiciousness by mere hearing" means that it produces happiness simply by being heard, yet it is ultimately inauspicious because it produces suffering through its ultimate consequence. [This refers to] the nectar of the narrative (*kathāmṛta*).

If it were of the nature of happiness by its very essence, then it would have been perceived by us alone, like the news of the birth of a son; whereas for us, there is the opposite, such as the observation of a loss of fortune. Or rather, it was spread abroad by those who are illustrious and endowed with Lakṣmī.

"We are destitute and possess nothing; therefore, since we have not yet reached the tenth stage [of life], we are already fully capable of service. Those people who thus proclaim and narrate this nectar-like story—which is widespread and extended throughout the land of Vṛndāvana by means of songs, recitations, and so forth—are truly blessed.

"Bhūridā" means givers of much, yet not those who discriminate between worthy and unworthy recipients; the sense is that they give whatever they have. Alternatively, it may mean "abhūridājanāḥ," which is a compound of "abhūridāḥ" (those who give little) and "ajanāḥ" (non-persons); the intention is the curse "may you be non-persons who give little," namely, those devoid of rebirth, accompanied by the snapping of fingers. ||9||
Viśvanātha: Who could describe the greatness of the sweetness of the story composed by Him?

They say that even a story concerning You, when told by another, is sweeter and superior to the two nectars—referring to "Your" [story]. Why is Your story alone nectar? Because of its similarity to it for those who are tormented.

It revives those scorched by great diseases and the like, as well as those tormented by *saṃsāra*; and because it revives even those scorched by separation from you, its superiority over the nectar of heaven and the nature of liberation has been declared by poets such as Dhruva and Prahlāda in verses beginning with: "That bliss which belongs to embodied beings... and so forth.

"The other two nectars are praised: O Lord, let them not exist even within the self-glorious Brahman; rather, let them belong to those falling from their celestial chariots after being shaken by the sword of Antaka (Death). By such statements as these, [the former two nectars] were not found pleasing.

They remove impurities—sins that persist until the exhaustion of *prārabdha*—but they do not destroy the nectar of heaven; rather, because they increase desire and other passions, they actually produce them. Furthermore, even the nectar of liberation does not destroy the sins of *prārabdha*, for it is to be tasted through hearing alone and serves as the means to achieve one's ultimate goal.
But those two auspicious things are not like this:

they do not bestow the abundant wealth culminating in divine love, nor are they pervasive and expanded by speakers at every moment; yet those who speak and glorify them obtain that very abundance in great measure.
The sense is that even though they give their entire possessions to them, they are not able to repay that debt.
Or rather, your speech is sweet only when accompanied by the sight of you; otherwise, however...
They say it causes great harm; the meaning is that even your mere mention is like death, being the cause of dying.
Why? Because life becomes heated, as there is a pun suggesting it is like water poured onto hot oil and the like.
[An objection: "In that case, why is it praised in the Purāṇas and other texts? To this they reply: "By poets such as Vyāsa and others..."
The meaning is that it is "praised by poets" because it is described even by those whose nature consists merely of description.
The meaning of "removing impurity" is that through the experience of suffering, past impurity is indeed destroyed.
It is that which brings about one's own welfare and the destruction of obstacles simply by being heard by the world. If...

The meaning is that wise people, having reflected upon the suffering that results from hearing that [teaching], will not listen to it; and then, even that [teaching] will surely perish. With the thought, "Let the world perish through the very people who are intoxicated by the pride of wealth and blinded by the intoxication of riches," they have spread [the teaching] throughout every country and village at the expense of their own wealth.

Having established reciters of ancient tales in villages, [the Dharma] has been spread abroad; therefore, those who proclaim them on earth are "givers of much" (bhūridāḥ), yet they cut, shatter, and kill many worlds of listeners. Consequently, by spreading a web of stories and sitting there as if they were gentle, they are even worse than a hunter who kills men.

The sense is that these [other topics] should be disregarded from afar by the wise, as will be stated in the passage beginning with "the pastimes performed by Him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.18). In reality, this is a "disguised praise" (vyāja-stuti) intended to manifest the supreme excellence of both the narrative and its narrator. ||9||
Your laughter, O Beloved, Your loving glances, and Your playful wandering are the auspicious objects of meditation.
O deceiver, those secret intimacies that touch the heart truly agitate my mind.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "Surely you are satisfied merely by hearing My stories; what is the use of seeing Me?
[Reply: No; our minds are agitated by Your playful charms, and even there we find no peace.
Thus they say: "O Beloved, O Deceiver, O Hypocrite, regarding Your secret amorous intimations... [and so forth].
Vaṃśīdhara:

Caitanya-mañjuṣā: Others say that it is not only such a story [that causes agitation], but something else as well—namely, "the smile" and so forth. For even these things certainly cause agitation. The particle *hi* has the sense of *eva* (indeed/certainly).
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: +++ Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī:
+++ Krama-sandarbhaḥ: not commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Not only is Your story of such a nature, but even Your other acts, such as smiling and so forth, agitate our minds; thus they say, beginning with "prahasitam" (Your smile), etc.
O Beloved! Your *prahasitam* is Your laughter, Your *viharaṇam* is Your wandering about, and *rahasi saṃvidaḥ* are Your secret intimacies.

For conversations with those who are not one's own kin certainly agitate the mind. The meaning of the sentence is that those [conversations] which were previously known for giving pleasure to the mind have now, due to their changed nature, all become causes of mental agitation. There are three qualifiers for each of the three [objects]. Of what kind was the laughter?

Wherein is the gaze endowed with love? What is the manner of wandering? It is the auspiciousness of meditation itself—the auspiciousness of meditation alone, and not of the meditator, because [the latter] causes agitation of the mind. Of what nature are the perceptions? They touch the heart; they touch the vital core (marman). For you are, by your very nature, a deceiver.
"You are renowned for being full of deceit"—this is a fitting address. O deceiver!
O master of guile! Therefore, it was indeed rightly said that your nectar-like words are "life-giving to the parched," and so forth—words that delight the connoisseurs.

Viśvanātha says: "But for us, without the sight of you, even mere objects related to you cause extreme pain"—thus they say, "the laughter. "Viharaṇa" means sexual union. And those intimacies—the playful conversations that touch the heart—though one might wish to forget them because they cause such pain, they cannot be forgotten.
The sense is that these can be forgotten. Even by meditation, [one realizes] that auspiciousness bestows supreme happiness;
thus it qualifies all four. They agitate and disturb the mind.
Having entered the mind and granted immediate pleasure, they bestow great suffering at the very next moment.
Therefore, O deceiver! even those baṭakas given by a deceiver, though sweet to the taste at once, are extremely burning and life-destroying in the long run; this is the meaning. ||10||
O Lord, when you walk from Vraja tending the cattle, your foot is as beautiful as a lotus.
O beloved, our mind falls into a state of agitation, thinking that it might perish amidst the sprouts of the grass of moral conduct.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, they say in two verses that their hearts are moist with excessive love for you, yet for what reason do you practice deceit toward them? "You move," etc. O Lord, O Beloved, when (*yat*) you move from Vraja while tending the cattle, then that lotus-like, beautiful, and tender [foot] of yours—

Our minds become turbid—that is, they fall into a state of unease—thinking, "He will suffer and be distressed by stones, awns, grass, and sprouts underfoot. Such are we, our hearts anxious with fear for your suffering. ||11||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya’s Casket: You alone are merciless toward us; for if you did not sometimes perceive even our faults, how could you have rebuked him? We, however, are not so.

Others say: "We burn day and night with love for you alone"—beginning with the words "You move," and so forth. Therefore, you are indeed a mere animal (paśu), since you do not perceive the agitation of our minds.
How is it that you do not perceive it? To this they reply: "Your feet, as beautiful as lotuses, are being crushed by stones and grass-blades."
"Alas, what misery!"—this is the underlying sentiment. ||11||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbha*: these have not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "It is not only now that you bring us to the forest and torment us;
even your pastime there was a source of agitation for us," they say, beginning with the words "You move" (*calasi*).
O Lord! When you go forth from Vraja to graze the cattle, even from that lotus [of yours]... [your movement causes us distress].
O beloved, even though the ground is beautiful, our mind falls into agitation—a state of dense suffering—thinking that it might be trampled by blades of grass and sprouts;
therefore, it was well said: "And his wandering is auspicious only for meditation," but not otherwise.
It is an auspicious omen for the one who meditates. ||11||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says: Furthermore, you cause us pain not only now, but moreover, having caused yourself pain as well, you strive to give us sorrow; thus they say, "You move... and so forth.

Whenever, at whatever time, [the mind] perceives that even more beautiful and delicate than a lotus, it might wither or suffer due to stones, husks, grass, and sprouts, it attains a state of mental turbidity and unease.
Alternatively, *kalila* means that which takes (*lāti*) or seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) strife (*kali*) or quarrel; the state of being that is *kalilatā*.
The meaning is that it creates strife within our own minds along with us. And as for that strife, it is as follows:
"O mind! If he becomes weary from wandering in the forest, then, having departed from Vraja, [remain] eternally..."

"Why does he go there? Therefore, why do you distress yourselves in vain? "O witless cowherd girls! His two soles are even more delicate than a land-lotus. Yet, in the forest, there are indeed stones, grass-blades, sprouts, and pebbles."
"How could there be no suffering? "O simpleton! He wanders only on a path of very soft sand. "O you who lack discernment! Do cows graze only on grass along the path?
"O you blinded by love! How could he, possessing sight, place his feet upon stones, grass, and the like?"

"O you who are devoid even of the scent of love! If, through the force of agitation or by mistake, a foot were to fall upon them, what would happen? "O brother mind! You speak the truth; we were created by the Creator to experience just such suffering. "O miserable ones!"
"Indeed, you shall live; however, I shall now depart from your bodies along with your very lives. ||11||
At the close of day, he bore a lotus-face covered by his dark locks of hair.
O Hero, repeatedly displaying a dense cloud of pollen, you instill passion within our minds.

Śrīdhara: But you, at the close of day, in the evening time, bear a face with dark locks of hair covering it, thick with pollen, sprinkled with the dust of cows, and like a lotus whose face is blooming in the forest, its surface strewn with the pollen from swarms of bees; and that [face] again and again—
The meaning is: by repeatedly manifesting [yourself] in our minds, you instill and bestow only the god of love (Smara), yet you do not grant union;
thus, you are a deceiver.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjuṣā: Thus we burn throughout the entire day from the time of leaving Vraja until our arrival at the forest;
yet when you approach Vraja from afar, you remove that very anguish, or perhaps not even so.
On the contrary, others say that this is actually a form of torment, beginning with the words "at the close of day" and so forth:

"O Hero! O All-Powerful One! At the close of day, at the time of Your arrival at Vraja, You bestow love (smara) upon our minds. In reality, however, there is no love in our minds other than [the memory of] You."
By the power of that very [beauty], you yourself cause her to be superimposed [upon others] and then deprive her of her distinctness; yet even therein, it is not always easy [to distinguish].
Even when covered in part by dark locks—by those curls of hair which are intensely black like powdered collyrium—the identity is still recognized; for these are "kuntalas" and "cūrṇakuntalas. 12.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbha*: these have not been commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: At the time of departure, suffering is indeed appropriate; however, even when returning, He does not grant such happiness [as one might expect]. Thus they say: "At the close of day," and so forth. O Hero!
At the close of day, at the time of returning from Vraja in the evening, [the face] covered by dark locks of hair—

By showing us Your forest-born face, You bear Love (smara) within our minds; that is, having held Love even though it was non-existent within our hearts, You deliver it to us. Even though He does not come of His own accord, You draw Him forth by force and deliver Him—this is the intended meaning of the word *bibhrat* (bearing). O Blue-Black One! Or else:

He is called *nīla* because he intensely impels (*ilayati*), from the root *ila*, meaning "to impel. "Enveloped by locks of hair" indicates the fatigue of herding cattle. The meaning of the word "charmingly" (*cāru*) is that she shows [her face] in a beautiful manner, or, being enveloped by locks of hair, she reveals it by drawing those locks aside. Thus it was well said: "O deceiver! (*kuhaka*)!
They do not disturb the mind. ||12||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says: Furthermore, they say that even in union you do not wish to grant pleasure—at the end of the day, at evening time—with dark locks of hair and curling side-locks.

It was covered by clouds tossed by gentle breezes; it was "dusty with wealth" (dhana-rajasvala), meaning sprinkled with the dust of cows, according to the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon which states that *dhana* refers to both cattle and riches. It bore a face like a forest-born lotus—a face resembling a fresh lotus, lovely with its swaying garlands and sprinkled with a profusion of pollen. And that [face]...

Repeatedly showing himself here and there under the pretext of tending the cows and searching for His dear friends, and then turning back to come within the range of our vision, He reflected— knowing that His very appearance brings joy to all people— that He was thus plunging us into an ocean of suffering; and [thinking this], He [disappeared] from us.

"You restrain Smara (the god of love)!"—the meaning is: "He who, having inflamed us like the flames of poison by following the path of the family dharma, has brought us here to the forests and thus makes us weep. O Hero! Your discharge of the arrows of Smara was undertaken solely for the purpose of destroying the dharma of the women of Vraja. 12.
One who grants the desires of those who bow before him, worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā,
the ornament of the earth; he is to be meditated upon in times of distress.
O our Beloved, O destroyer of afflictions, place Your most peaceful lotus-feet upon our breasts.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, they now pray with two verses—beginning with "praṇata-kāmadam"—that He should act in this way, abandoning all deceit: "O Adhokṣaja, O Rāmaṇa! You who are worshipped by Padmaja (Brahmā), who are to be meditated upon in times of distress, who remove calamity by mere meditation, and who are most peaceful."
"Even during the time of service, may Your most blissful lotus-feet be placed upon our breasts to pacify the heat of our desire. ||13||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjūṣā: Indeed, sir, that which has passed is indeed gone. What should be done now? Anticipating this doubt, others say: "O Beloved! [Take] the lotus-feet."
Place [it] upon our breasts! It is to be meditated upon in times of distress and in separation. It grants the desires of those who bow;

are we not those who bow? It is worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā; why is it not worshipped by us? Since it is called the "ornament of the earth," it must indeed wander incessantly upon the earth; let it also become the ornament of our chests.
Thus is the objection. ||13||
The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī,
the Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī,
and the Krama-sandarbha have not been commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therefore, at the time of departing from Vraja, there can be no pacification of the suffering caused by remembering her feet—which had become weary from treading upon the sharp blades of grass used for grazing the cattle—except through the touch of those very feet as they rest upon her breasts. Thus it is.
It is proper to do so; likewise, since even at the time of her arrival,

the pain born from the offering of one's heart— whose locus is the mind and whose instrument is the beholding of her lotus-face— does not depart without the granting of the nectar of her lips, it is equally proper to act in that very manner.

In order to extinguish the two types of suffering, they state the two means sequentially in two verses, beginning with "praṇata-kāmadam. O Lover! O Destroyer of mental anguish! Place Your lotus feet upon our breasts. Of what nature are They? Most peaceful (*śantama*) and most auspicious (*kalyāṇatama*). Peace (*śam*...).

The word "Śabda" is indeclinable, as seen in such examples as "Śaṃyu. It is "Iṣṭa" (desired) because it grants the desires of those who bow down and bestows what is wished for. It is "Durlabha" (rare/attainable with difficulty) because it is worshipped by Padmaja, Brahmā. It is "Karunā-makaranda-niṣyandi" (overflowing with the nectar of compassion) because it is the ornament of the earth. It is "Sarvāpad-vināśaka" (the destroyer of all calamities) because it is to be meditated upon in times of distress. ||13||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha: Now, if you conclude that "I always cause only suffering," and thus think, "Enough of me for you," fearing such resentment—alas, alas!
Thinking, "Blinded by the suffering that is the fruit of their own karma, they have attributed faults even to you," and feeling remorseful,

they praise him as the giver of all happiness in order to appease him; and making it clear that "our purpose is fulfilled by you alone," they pray for the alleviation of their own suffering with the two verses beginning with "praṇata-".
The meaning is: "Even though you have become the offender against those who are bowed down in submission—such as Kāliya, his wives, and others—you are the granter of desires;

therefore, since you were worshipped by Brahmā (Padmajā) for the sake of pacifying his own offense, may our offense be forgiven. By the phrase "the ornament of the crest-jewel of the earth," [he implies] that even our breasts are among them.

The sense is: "Adorn [us] by placing Your feet [upon us]. By the phrase "the refuge" (*apadī*), it is meant that "you shall easily cross all difficulties," according to the saying of Garga; thus, the sense is: "Protect us from calamities. The reason for this in every respect is that [the Lord] is most peaceful (*śantama*), the embodiment of all auspiciousness, and the embodiment of all happiness.
"Ādhihan" means "to destroy mental anguish"; moreover, there is no effort at all for you in placing your feet upon their breasts;

on the contrary, it is indeed a pleasure. Thus they say: "O lover! For you who desire to sport, through that very act, the fulfillment of your desire will surely come to pass"—this is the sense. ||13||
Increasing passion and destroying sorrow,
it was beautifully kissed by the whistling flute.
O Hero, bestow upon us that nectar of your lower lip which causes men to forget all other passions.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, O Hero, grant us—that is, give us—your nectar of the lower lip; "well-kissed by the flute resounding with a *svarita* note" means it is perfumed by the nectar of sound. It causes men to forget other attachments—that is, the desire for other pleasures, such as those of a universal emperor (*sārvabhauma*) and so forth.
It causes one to forget and it causes one to dissolve; thus it is so called. ||14||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mañjūṣā: If you do not place your lotus-feet as an ornament upon the earth by resting them on [our] breasts, then the earth has no connection with the nectar of your lips; therefore—
"Grant us the nectar of your lower lip," other women said with a playful taunt, beginning with the words "increasing [the pleasure of] amorous union.

[The Lord replied: "O Hero! You move [it] especially (viśeṣeṇa īrayasi), thus [you are so called]; grant that nectar of your lips. If it is argued that it was drunk by the flute, they say: "It was not properly drunk by it," [adding] "by the well-sounded flute (svarita-veṇunā suṣṭhu)."

"It was kissed, not drunk! You wish to drink the remains of the bamboo [flute]! Oh, what shamelessness on your part! Anticipating this objection, they say: "It is desired to drink that which destroys sorrow (*śokanāśana*), even though it is such [by nature]; no further investigation (*upadhā*) is made. It is not only the destruction of sorrow; [it is also] sexual union (*surata*)."

The increase of that [love] is the bliss of love. For an elixir (rasāyana) is indeed twofold: one which bestows vigor upon the healthy, and another which cures the disease of the afflicted. This, however, is both. Therefore, it causes the forgetting of other diseases and dispels desire for anything else. ||14||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*;
*Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Even for men, the nectar is found in the chewing of betel and the like; how much more so [for the Lord].
[This refers] to women; therein, there is a metaphorical identification between the lower lip and its [the lip's] flavor. ||14||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: To destroy further suffering, they state another means, beginning with "surata" and so forth. O Hero! Bestow upon us the nectar of Your lips. Of what nature is it? It is that which increases love for amorous union (*surata-prema*), because it destroys grief. If it is argued, "But was that not already drunk by the flute alone?"—no.

Therefore, she merely kissed him well, but did not drink [him] thoroughly. If it is argued that it is improper to drink what has been left over (ucchiṣṭa), they say in response: "The remedy for the supreme elixir is the forgetting of other attachments.
For regarding a medicinal drug, such deliberation is not made; it is like honey and the like. Since you are departing from Vraja...

Regarding the two acts—bestowing the nectar of her feet upon her breasts and so forth, and bestowing the nectar of her lips—described as the means for pacifying the two types of suffering taught in the two verses beginning with *dina-parikṣaye* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.12): "Place [the nectar] upon our breasts; cut [our bonds]... [and so on].
There is no tautology with these two verses, namely *hṛc-chayam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.7) and *adhara-sīdhunāpyāyasva naḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.8). ||14||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says: Furthermore, O you who are like Dhanvantari himself! O crest-jewel of physicians!
Grant us some medicine, for we are fainting from the disease of love.

They say it is "the enhancer of pleasure. Its capacity to bring nourishment, its destruction of grief, and its removal of pain have been declared of it. Nor should it be asked how that which is so highly precious can be given away without a price; for you, a hero of generosity, must restore life even to one who is utterly degraded and breathless.
They say it is indeed given away even without a price: it was thoroughly and perfectly kissed—that is, tasted—even by the *kīcaka* flute, which resounds with a *svarita* note.
Indeed, attachment to wealth, people, family, and so forth is precisely what constitutes an unwholesome diet here; this [state] is for those who possess such [attachment].

"It is not given there," they say—"it causes the forgetting of attachment to other things. The sense is: "This is a marvelous medicine which, by turning men away from evil paths, causes one to forget—that is, to cause the fading of—attachment and clinging to other objects; this we have seen through our own direct experience. [Thus it is] bestowed upon women of the human race.
"Give, O hero! Whether you be a hero in generosity or a hero in compassion. (14)
When you wander through the forest during the day,
even a moment passes like an eon for those who do not see you.
O dull-witted one, you have gazed upon your beautiful face with its curling locks and the lashes that frame your eyes.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, having seen that there is suffering even for a moment in not seeing you, and happiness in seeing you, we—like ascetics who have abandoned all attachments—experience a truṭi or half a kṣaṇa as being like an entire yuga. Thus, the suffering of not seeing you has been described. Moreover, somehow at the end of the day...

For those whose eyes were gazing upward at your glorious face, O Śrīman, Brahmā—the creator of their eyelashes—was indeed dull and sluggish; for even an interval of a single blink was unbearable to them. Thus, the bliss of the vision is described. ||15||
Vaṃśīdhara:
*Caitanya-mañjūṣā*: "If it is so, how long a delay should be made? To this they reply with the verse beginning with *aṭasi* and so forth:
"For those who do not see you, a moment (*truṭi*) becomes like an eon (*yuga*). Because of the general reference in the phrase "those who do not see you" (*apaśyatām*), [the meaning applies to all].
The meaning is: "If this is true even for a mere living being, how much more so for us who are devoted to you?
This applies to such phrases as "with curly locks" (*kuṭila-kuntalam*) and so forth. ||15||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: these have not been commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Regarding the different ways in which you cause various kinds of suffering—by departing from the cowherd settlement in the morning and by returning to it in the evening—they say "You wander," and so forth, describing how you are even more a source of pain during the intervening time. It should be understood that the address "O Beloved" (*ramaṇa*) is used here.

Whenever you wander through the forest during the day, for those like me who do not see you, even a moment— a *truṭi*— acts like an eon (*yuga*) because of the resulting suffering; or if at some point immediately thereafter a sight of you occurs, even then a blink of an eye (*nimeṣa*) feels as long as an eon— this is the intended meaning.

Out of resentment toward the Creator, they say: "Crooked," and so forth. For those of us gazing upon Your glorious face, the Creator who fashioned our eyelashes is indeed dull-witted. What can we say to him?
Therefore, the sense is that we possess no well-being whatsoever in any state. ||15||
The Composition of Joy 92: Their very inability to endure even a moment’s separation—from [the verse beginning] "O crooked one" ||15|| (392).
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, it is our own misfortune alone that brings suffering; what part do you have in that?

They say: "He wanders. When you wander—that is, go—to the forest of Vṛndāvana, then for us gopīs who do not see you, even a *truṭi*—the two hundred and seventieth part of a moment—becomes equal to an entire *yuga*. The neuter gender [of *truṭiḥ*] is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

The sorrow of separation from you, which for all the people of Vraja lasts for three months during the day, for us becomes three watches [of the night] equivalent to hundreds of millions of yugas; what other cause could there be for this, were it not for some past misfortune? And furthermore, somehow...

At the end of the day, for those very cowherd women who gaze with longing at Your glorious face, the Creator—the fashioner of eyelashes—is dull and devoid of discrimination; he causes them suffering (this is the ellipsis). Thus, in the absence of seeing You, the ocean of sorrow is indeed difficult to cross, yet in Your sight—

Even that blinking of the eyelashes, which obstructs vision, lasts for nine hundred *truṭis* yet feels like nine hundred ages; thus, the sense is that suffering occurs in both ways solely by the power of adverse karma (*duradṛṣṭa*).
The time it takes to consume three *trasareṇus* is known as a *truṭi*.
A hundredth part of that is a *vedha*, and three of those are known as a *lava*.
A *nimeṣa* should be understood as three *lavas*, and three of those are traditionally taught as a *kṣaṇa*. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.11.6–7)
Maitreya:

Or rather, the root *kṛt* means "to cut. May that clever and intelligent person—who is a cutter of the eyelashes of his own eyes—behold with excellence the splendor of your illustrious face as he gazes upon it; but not we.
The sense is that they are not clever. ||15||
Having utterly transcended their husbands, sons, lineage, brothers-in-law, and kinsmen, they have finally come to Acyuta.
O Gambler, who would abandon at night those women skilled in seduction, who are themselves deluded by your song?
Śrīdhara: Therefore, O Acyuta, having completely bypassed our husbands, sons, lineages, their relatives, brothers, and kinsmen, we have come into your presence. Of what nature are you?
You are the knower of our course—meaning, you know of our arrival—or you are the knower of the paths of song (the Vedas), or we are the ones who know the way.
O rogue, O deceiver! Who would abandon such women as these, who have come of their own accord at night, enchanted by your loud singing and high-pitched song? The meaning is: no one at all. ||16||

Vaṃśīdhara: Because your separation is unbearable for us, for that reason [he says] "O Acyuta"—the intention behind this address is: "Are you a eunuch, being devoid of the emission of semen (vīrya-cyuti)?
[He speaks thus] to one who is wise and knows that our arrival is solely for the purpose of amorous dalliance. [He refers to] the movements of song.

[The powers] consist of forms such as attraction and enchantment. Even if our coming here is for the sake of seeing [you], your singing is nonetheless intoxicating; therefore, we should not be abandoned. We have come knowing full well that you, who know all paths, will not leave us once we have arrived. "O deceiver! [she says].

We know your deceitfulness from your alteration of your own true nature; the sense is that there is no need for such deceit toward us. By saying "niśi" (at night), the implication is that the abandonment of timid women at night is improper.
The meaning is this: the abandonment of a thing already in one's possession is indeed unjust, even for one who is free from attachment.
For it is said: "Indeed, opposition to a desire that has already arisen is not praised; how much less so for one who is attached to desire, even if they have otherwise abandoned all attachments. (16)

*Caitanya-mañjūṣā*: Anticipating that if this were the case, they would not tolerate any delay and would therefore go home immediately, some who had cast off their bodies composed of material qualities and possessed transcendental forms said: "O husband, son," and so forth.
"O rogue, O deceiver! Having utterly transgressed [the duties toward] husbands and sons... [and so on]. Specifically...

Having transcended that [body] and abandoned even the mere connection with it through the relinquishing of that body, they have come to you—whether having arrived or departed. O Acyuta, thinking "we shall not fall away again from this non-material body," they have gone to you; they have attained you, O Knower of the Goal, by means of this.
"Those who know the goal," means those who know the reality of You; they are deluded by Your exalted song. ||16||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: This being so, they say that what has been done today is extremely improper—[expressed by the word] "pati" [and so on]. "Relatives" (*bāndhava*) refers to mother, father, and others. Because of the transgression of their words, because of the abandonment of affection and so forth, and because of the total disregard for dharma and other values, it is done with excessive distinction and with a firm foundation.

The sense is: "Having leaped over and transgressed [the boundary], you have come here because you were deluded by our singing, like female deer"—this is the underlying meaning. Furthermore, they say "those who know the way" (*gativedaḥ*) to show that this singing was not accidental, but was indeed preceded by knowledge; the sense is that they knew of our arrival.
Or rather, one might ask: "Are you not indeed supremely wise? How then were you enchanted by a mere song?

To this they reply: "Because we know the specific nuances of the melody," meaning those [nuances] by which even Śakra, Brahmā, and the supreme lords are led astray (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.15). Or else:
"You ladies are clever; since you even know such a nature of mine, how is it that you did not become cautious?

To this they replied, "We are indeed knowers of your nature. The implication is that this is because your speech is like a spell for enchantment (*mohana-mantra*). "Oh, let that be! Women have been led astray by their own accord."

Furthermore, as for the question "who would abandon [her] at night?"—the sense of the potential suffix (*liṅ*) is that no one would do so. Therefore, O deceiver! O you whose nature is to trick! By this [statement], it is implied that even another deceiver—who, like her, establishes his own livelihood solely through the wealth obtained by means of deception—would not abandon her.

The sense is that even in that case, there is a distinction [of superiority]; therefore, O Acyuta! "O You who do not deviate from Your own qualities"—this is Your name endowed with its true etymological meaning. ||16||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Relatives" refers to paternal and maternal kin and others. According to the logic previously stated, by abandoning each preceding one in favor of each subsequent one, it should be inferred that there is a progressive superiority among them. "Exceedingly" (*ati*) means with an excess and a particular distinction due to the transgression of their words and the abandonment of affection and so forth.
Having disregarded [ordinary] dharma and so forth, and having transcended [all things] by virtue of being rooted [in You], the reason for [Your] coming is:

"O Acyuta!"—the meaning is that because of Your majesty in delighting those who have taken refuge in You, etc., there is no possibility of Your ever falling away. Furthermore, You know our own nature and that of Yourself.

"Knowers of the goal" (gati-vidas). Alternatively, they are "knowers" (vidas) because they know your knowledge—that is, your super-knowledge (abhijñatva)—and your own greatness, such as your adherence to excellent vows, and they know that our sole refuge is you alone; thus they are "knowing ones" (vidatyaḥ).
Or rather, the meaning is that they know your essential nature, which consists of compassion and other such qualities. Furthermore, [the text continues:]
"Deluded by the song! O gambler! O rogue! Because you have altered your own true nature, [you act thus].

At night—meaning in the darkness—it is simply improper for cowards to abandon women; this is the intended sense. The use of the optative suffix in *tyajet* expresses a possibility: even a gambler would not abandon her, let alone anyone else."

The meaning is that even for a rogue, the abandonment of women at night is simply not possible. Therefore, the implication is that in your case, far from mere roguery, there would result an extreme lack of gratitude. Alternatively, [the reference is] to those who were previously lured and brought near by means of singing at night in a secluded place out of a desire for dalliance.

The meaning is that because you abandoned the beautiful cowherd girls afterwards, you were indeed a rogue (*dhūrta*). Therefore, the sense is: "Now that your roguery has become manifest, grant us a sight [of yourself]. The rest has been explained by them. Or else: *kitavāḥ* means rogues! Or rather: "Are these women yours, the rogue? Like you, we too are rogues."
"We know all of your cunning; enough with this deceit toward us. This should be understood as the cleverness of requesting an audience. ||16||

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. As for the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: the daytime excursion is indeed just as described; however, the nighttime excursion does not become free from turbidity, nor is it so [described], because [the Lord] brought [her] to the forest by the sound of the flute.
"Having abandoned [us], you vanish"—those women who had cast off their bodies at that moment and were immediately reunited spoke thus:

"O husband, son," and so forth. "O gambler (kitava)!"—the term *kitava* refers to one who steals away another's entire wealth; this is an address to him. Likewise, [they speak of] surpassing the husband and the others...

The meaning is that they have specifically transcended—that is, having abandoned their respective bodies associated with those [worlds]. Capable through extremely clear practice, they have come into your presence. O Acyuta! By this address, it is fitting that upon coming into the presence of the Acyuta, one should indeed become Acyuta himself. In that regard, who...

Who other than you would abandon women at night? Of what sort are they? Those who know your ways and are enchanted by your songs. Or rather, of what sort are you? One who knows their ways and is a refuge for them. (16)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: "O you who are the daughter of my husband! etc. Having utterly transcended—here meaning having disregarded by taking account of—their status as husbands and so forth; they have come into your presence, near you, as those seeking refuge, O you who know the *gati* (the goal), that is, you who know the *gati* consisting of the state of intoxication and amorous sport. Or else:

"Knowing our arrival," or rather, "knowing Your nature, which consists of the state of being a lover (*ramaṇa*)," or rather, "knowing Your *gati*— that is, Your departure or lack of stability," as it is said in this very same place:
"Blessed are these does, though their own course is that of the deluded" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.11).

By this it is said: they indeed know your course; or rather, knowing your course externally as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), but internally as being of the nature of amorous play (*vilāsa*); or else, knowing your course—that is, your craftiness—they have come into your presence.
"Indeed, if you know my true nature, then why have you come?

To this they replied: "We are enchanted by the song You sang. As it is said: "The goddesses, traveling in their celestial chariots, their very essence shaken by the god of love, repeatedly loosened their braided hair as flowers fell from them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa).

By this [verse], it is stated: "If even the delusion of the goddesses has been described in this way, what need is there to speak of the delusion of unrefined people like me? The underlying sentiment is: "Oh, the greatness of your song, which consists of a spell for enchantment!
This is the intention: if they had come of their own accord, then abandonment would have been appropriate; however, by that [song] of theirs...

They say this is a logical principle: "By now abandoning us—who were brought here under those very names—he manifests his deceit by performing a mockery. O rogue! O deceiver! Even another gambler practices deception before seeing the heroine, but once she is seen, he reveals only his pleasure.

Regarding this, they say: "Women come of their own accord even at night"—the meaning is that during the night, who other than you would abandon them? No one at all, provided there is the possibility [of union]. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing his own livelihood, even another gambler resorts to deceit; that very same deceit belongs to him for his own purpose, and it belongs to you as well.

"Since deceit does not result in one's own benefit, such deceit is indeed futile. Therefore, having abandoned your husband and others to come here, and now leaving us, how are you not ashamed? Thus, we pray that you abandon this artifice and grant us your vision. (16)

Viśvanātha: And those who had been confined within their inner apartments by their husbands at the time of the flute-playing spoke with jealousy, beginning with "O husband! (pati). We, who know our own final gati—the tenth stage—are now *anti*, having come into your presence (*tvad-antikam*). O Acyuta! Even here you have become *cyuta* (fallen/deviant); what [is that]?
The intended meaning is that you bear the name "Acyuta" (the Immovable) only by way of a contradictory definition. If it is asked, "In that case, why have you come?

they reply: "We have been enchanted and robbed of our discrimination by your song. If this is so, then [they say], "O fools! Endure this agony! To this they respond: "O rogue! O deceiver! Such women as these at night—"
A timid woman has come to you of her own accord; who, indeed, would abandon you except for one devoid of compassion? The meaning is: "No one at all.
Or rather: O gambler! O intoxicated man! What young man indeed would abandon the young women who have come to him at night?
Therefore, the sense is that even though you are a deceiver, you yourself have been deceived. For a gambler is a man who is intoxicated.
"Vaṃcaka means 'called gold' (kanaka)," according to the Medinīkośa. ||16||
With a secret understanding, with the arousal of love in his heart, with a smiling face, and with loving glances;
Beholding your broad chest, the abode of splendor,
my mind repeatedly becomes bewildered by excessive longing.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, with the intention that you alone might provide the medical treatment for the heart-disease of ours—which was caused by our previous longing to see you but has now been abandoned by you—they speak in two verses beginning with "In secret" (rahasi). [The verse says: "O Abode of Fortune, Your chest is vast and expansive... and so forth.
Upon seeing it, excessive longing arises; likewise, the mind becomes repeatedly deluded. ||17||
Vaṃśīdhara:

Caitanya-mañjūṣā. Therefore, they say that even for those who possess a longing for the sight of Him, the result is only suffering—beginning with the words "rasasi" and so forth. Having repeatedly beheld Your abode, people feel an excessive longing, yet their minds are not satisfied.

The mind becomes deluded in such a way that it becomes empty; it is "over-touched" (*atispṛṣṭa*) by him because it desires excessively. Of what kind [is she]? She possesses the splendor of a broad chest; the meaning is that she is seen there even in secret. Or, [it means] she is seen with her broad chest. Of what kind is that? It is the abode of beauty (*śriyaḥ dhāma*). And of what kind are both of these?

One whose purity (*śuddhi*) is perfectly distinguished by consciousness (*saṃvid*); [the word *viśiṣṭa*] is established by the root *daip* in the sense of "purifying" (*śodhane*) with the suffix *kvip*.
— *Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī*: *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī*.
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon. As for the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: then the young maidens said—"In secret," and so forth. "In secret" (*rahasi*) means in a private place;
"consciousness" (*saṃvit*) refers to the act of perceiving—that which was stated in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.27]: "With me, you shall enjoy these nights."

Having observed what was commanded, having understood it, and having seen her loving glance and her broad chest, the meaning is that an intense longing arose in him again and again. Therefore, his mind is bewildered—it becomes deluded.
The sense is: "How can you act in such a way? What is this loving glance like?
From whom arises the desire that dwells in the heart; whose very face is a smile that delights; or rather, having beheld his smiling face—of what kind? Whose glances are full of love.
Of what nature is his broad chest? It is the abode of Śrī. (17)
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—

O dear one, Your manifestation as the forest-dweller of Vraja is sufficient to destroy the sins of all and is the source of universal auspiciousness; yet, please grant even a slight measure of Your grace to us, whose souls long for You.
Which is the eradicator of the pain in the hearts of one's own kin.

Śrīdhara: And Your manifestation—Your full revelation—is, without distinction, the destroyer of the sins of all the inhabitants of Vraja and the forest, the dispeller of their suffering; thus, You are the auspiciousness of the universe and the embodiment of all auspiciousness. Therefore, for us whose souls long for You and whose minds are fixed upon longing for You...
"Give up even slightly, abandon even a little"—by this he means "abandon the objects of desire without acting out of miserliness. What is that?
It is the medicine that cures and eliminates those things which are most strictly hidden from the hearts of one's own kin; you alone know that [remedy], O Vetasa—this is the hidden intention. (18)
Vaṃśīdhara:

Caitanya-mañjuṣā: Others say, "Your indifference toward us has been released"—referring to the inhabitants of Vraja and the forest. Now, we possess both the status of being residents of Vraja and the status of being forest-dwellers.

Therefore, it is entirely fitting for you to be the destroyer of our sins; thus, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that you should abandon whatever causes pain to the hearts of your own people. The meaning is: "Abandon even the slightest thing that destroys us—those whose very souls long for you—and which acts as a source of harm. (18)
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī; Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī;
Krama-sandarbhaḥ: Now, what indeed are those heart-pains? Or rather, what is their eradication?
Regarding this expectation, they say: "Go," and so forth, as well as "That which is yours," and so forth. Illnesses are merely delusions;
and that [remedy] is simply placing [the hand] slowly upon the breasts, which is the very destruction of those [delusions]. Therefore, the sense is that this alone is repeatedly entreated. ||18||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Therefore, they say this is not appropriate for You, beginning with the words "of the forest-dwellers of Vraja" and so forth. O dear one! Your manifestation (*vyakti*)—Your appearance—is the destroyer of the suffering (*vṛjina*) of the forest-dwellers of Vraja; it is exceedingly sufficient (*alam*) as the auspiciousness of the entire universe. Thus, by virtue of being the inhabitant of Vraja...
And since You are included within the universe, Your manifestation is indeed the destroyer of our sins.
Therefore, please abandon even slightly—that is, relinquish—that which is a destroyer or a killer of those whose very nature is longing for You;

the meaning is: do not do that. O Friend of Your own people! Of what sort are we? [The answer follows: "O Lord, we are those who have been abandoned by You. "Of those whose heart-pain is in the heart," or rather, "that vision which is the destroyer (nisūdana), the annihilator, of our heart-pains—that, grant (tyaja) even a little of; that is to say, bestow it. Here, the root *tyaj* has the sense of "giving. In the compound "of the heart-pains of one's own people" (*svajanānāṃ hṛd-rujām*), it may be taken as a single word. ||18||
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha — o)0(o—
O beloved, that your well-formed lotus-feet, which we place gently upon our rough breasts out of fear,
now wander through the forest— is it not for this reason that they suffer?
The intellect of us whose lives are spent in worldly existence wanders like a quail and other such birds.

Śrīdhara: Overcome by excessive love, they weep and say: "That which... O beloved! We, fearing that your delicate lotus-feet might be bruised upon our hard breasts, would hold them gently; yet you wander through the forest with them. (In the reading "ṅayasi," it means "you go.")

Whether it be cattle, or some other [creature], or even yourself, you lead them—that is, you cause them to reach—that lotus foot; does it not perhaps suffer from small stones, pebbles, and the like? How indeed could it not suffer? Thus, the intellect of us whose life is yours wanders in this way.
"He becomes deluded. ||19||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Let there be our narration of suffering; there is no purpose in it whatsoever.
What is the use of wailing in the wilderness? No, rather, it is because we faint upon recollecting your suffering.

Concluding with the words "thus [you] break," they say: "That which is yours," and so forth. Your heart alone is hard, not your limbs such as the beautiful arrangement of your body. Therefore, as you wander through the forest with those very tender feet, why does it not cause you pain? Thus our minds are bewildered. You are life...
The sense is that for those whose lifespan is eternal, their bodies do not fall even by such suffering. ||19||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

The Composition of Affection (392): In this regard, the passage beginning with "from the poison and the submersion in water" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.3] expresses the intention that He should protect us now, viewing the entire Gokula as something to be protected by Himself. "From the son of Vṛṣa" means from the calf; "from the son of Maya" means from the demon Vyomāsura. And again:

Aiming at those various extraordinary deeds, this praise consists of superimposing the status of the Supreme Lord upon You through a display of wretchedness in the manner of a beggar, as in the two verses beginning with "O Son of the Gopīs, You are surely not... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.4). Therefore, even from the perspective that the entire universe must be protected by You, now for us...

"Protect us," as before. Even there, because He descended into the lineage of the Sātvatas—the Vaiṣṇavas such as the venerable Nanda and others—there is a particular excellence justified by the fact that He attained our friendship during His childhood.
This is the meaning. [Regarding the phrase] "the leader of the Vṛṣṇis" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.5), even among them...
Because he was born in the Yadu lineage. Thus it is said in the *Mathurā-māhātmya* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*:
"And Govardhana is the Blessed One, where Govardhana was lifted up;
all the Yādavas were protected by warding off the rain of Indra."
In that very same place, elsewhere, in the context of the *Śrī-Govinda-kuṇḍa*, it is said: "Where the Blessed One was consecrated by Maghavan, the enemy of the Yadus.
Or else, after praising with the words beginning "From the immersion in the poisonous waters" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.31.3), it continues: "Again..."
They say this with affectionate jealousy, using the half-verse beginning "na khalu" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.4). Thus,
by neglecting us who have fallen into such a wretched state, you are indeed the son of the Queen of Vraja,
the protector of all the inhabitants of Vraja, including the cowherd girls and ourselves.

He does not exist [as a separate entity], yet there exists the Supreme Self— the beholder of the inner self of all embodied beings— who, being untouched by the happiness or suffering of anyone, perceives the pure individual soul. Even so,
because He has indeed descended to protect all through His detachment from the essential nature of the Brahman-seeker, He does not [neglect] us.

"It is right for You to show indifference," they said again with humility, using the half-verse beginning with "By Vikhanas" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.4). With that same intention as before, he also spoke the verse beginning with "The one who has fashioned fearlessness" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.5),
and the phrase "Of embodied beings who have bowed down" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.7), [referring to] the abode of Śrī.

The meaning is this: even for those such as prostrate beings, [the Lord’s] action—consisting of the removal of sins and so forth—is understood by us precisely because He is composed of supreme compassion; thus, it is fitting for Him to perform the cutting away of the "heart-dweller" (lust) even within our own breasts. For that which is the cause of the heart-dweller, there must be a corresponding alternative remedy.

And they said: "With sweet [voice]... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.8). The meaning is: surely, since your voice—which intoxicates the mind—is sweet precisely because it is suffused with fragrance, that very nectar of your lips must be the medicine for this [intoxication]. Oh! How could such nectar of your lips be easily obtained by those devoid of such merit?

Since that sweet voice may well be far away, and since we have fallen under the restrictive bond of the assembly of elders (*guru-goṣṭhī*), even the nectar of your life-story—which is being proclaimed through the succession of people even in other contexts—is difficult for us to obtain; thus he says: "The nectar of your story" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.9).

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, those who praise You have become givers of much to us. But why is there such great affection for You on the part of you all? To this they reply with the verse beginning, "Your laughter" (*prahasitam*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.10).
How is it that my laughter and so forth possess such a nature? To this they reply: "O Deceiver" (*he kuhaka*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa...).

[10.31.10] Thus it is said. The meaning is: "You alone know that certain kind of hypocrisy which exists within you. In this manner, other [verses] are also to be applied accordingly. They speak with the highest excellence: "That which is well-born in you... (19).

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, the first group of speakers themselves conclude with the words beginning "yat te" and so forth. O Beloved! We, having placed that well-formed lotus-foot of yours upon our hard and firm breasts, slowly bear it; by means of that lotus-foot, [we traverse] the forest.
"You wander; why then does it not cause you pain? Indeed, it does cause pain. By what means? By thorns and the like.
Therefore, our intellect—the mind of us whose life-force is you—is wandering, becoming unsettled.
Hence, desist from this further wandering in the forest; let yourself be revealed. This is the conclusion by way of the meaning of the sentence.

"Having gathered together, they sang to Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.45). Thus, at the end of the preceding chapter, by the verb "jaguḥ" (they sang), it is established through the verses that their activity was indeed singing (*gāna*), and not merely that which was uttered by them has been composed in verse by the poet.
Therefore, this is a song accompanied by *rāga*, *tāla*, and *svara*. And therein—

One must understand the intermediate skill (*kauśalam avāntaram*): the second syllable of the first quarter (*pāda*) is the same as the second syllable of another quarter. In the verse "jala-ruhānanaṃ cāru darśaya" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.6), it is necessary that the second syllable be the letter *ja*. That...

In the passage *jaḍa udīkṣitam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.15), the substitution of the letter *ḍa* for the letter *ṭa* should not be accepted as a fault of corruption (*skhalita-doṣa*), because they belong to the same varga; rather, this is a stylistic peculiarity (*vaicitrya*) of the singing. ||19||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:

Viśvanātha says: "O connoisseurs! As for that which you request, my lotus-feet are currently immersed in the bliss of wandering through the forest; therefore, there is no room for them to remain upon your breasts."

He obtains [this]. Regarding that, they say "sa-rodana" (with weeping), namely: *yat te* ("that which is yours"). We are indeed terrified even by that lotus-foot of yours (*caraṇāmburuha*)—so exquisitely well-formed and delicate—which we would place upon our breasts; for with that very lotus-foot you wander through the forest. This is expressed through an interrogative intonation (*kākūkti*). Alas, alas! What a calamity!
The sense is: "You are performing an incomparable feat of daring.

Now, one might ask: "How is it that you are afraid? To this they reply with the word "karkaśeṣu" (in the hard ones). The meaning is that the very hardness of the breasts is the cause of fear. Then, why is there such delay? To this they say:

"He loves you" means that He delights in placing His feet upon those very breasts; the sense is that He does so solely because He perceives Your happiness. Furthermore, at that time, although Your pleasure was directly perceived through the pressing of the breasts with His foot, we were filled with apprehension that pain would inevitably arise for Him due to the extreme delicacy of His feet.
Since weariness indeed arises, they say, "Let us proceed slowly. This state of being distressed by the fear of pain even during that happiness is a characteristic of *mahābhāva*;
therefore, the underlying suggestion (*dhvani*) is that even in union with you, suffering has been inscribed upon our foreheads by the Creator himself.

"What should be done by us through austerity? If we pray for the softness of your breasts, there would be no comfort for you; yet if they are hard, there would be pain to your feet. Thus, in both ways, there is a dilemma for us"—this is the underlying suggestion (*anudhvani*). Let it be so for us in this state of union and separation.

"How painful! But what pain do you endure even in your own independence, that you wander through the forest? Is this lotus-foot of yours fit for wandering in the forest?"—thus is the reproach implied.
[She replies: "Indeed, when something comes to my mind, then I do it; what is it to you ladies in this matter?"

Therefore they say: "That limb does not suffer; rather, it certainly suffers. But you alone are as merciless toward your own limbs as you are toward us. Or rather, these [limbs] become pained even by my pain;
therefore, by me who has set out to cause them pain, my own suffering [is being ignored]."
Do you endure even that suffering with the intention that it must be done and must be borne?

Or rather, do you consider even that suffering to be nothing but pleasure because you derive great joy simply from seeing our misery? Or perhaps, according to the maxim that "faults and virtues arise from association," [is it due to your proximity to us?]
Previously, your heart was as delicate as a flower; that very same heart has now become hardened by contact with our firm breasts.
Just so, your foot too has become hard through contact with the breasts, and therefore it is not pained even by thorns and the like. Or rather—

By the majesty of the touch of Your feet, even thorns and the like become truly soft. Or rather, out of extreme compassion—or perhaps out of a longing to taste Your sweetness—the Earth herself raises her tongue at every place where Your feet are set down. Or else, You [are greater] than even we...

"By the power of fate, the ocean of love has become tormented by separation from us; wandering about, he has reached a state of madness and does not even attend to the pain in his own feet. As we reflect on such various reasons, our minds wander; they do not find certainty anywhere.

[The opponent says: "This is merely a manifestation of your own suffering! As for me, I do not consider that suffering to be true suffering, since my life-breaths remain. To this, they reply: "Of your long-lived self," [meaning] it belongs to you.

"Of those whose lifespans reside in you alone"—the meaning is that while you, O auspicious one, remain, there shall be no destruction of our lives even by such great hardships. This is the underlying thought: Fate, which has set out to afflict us just as it has you, considers these lifespans of theirs to be [now]... at present.

"I shall establish them in these very states; then, their lifespans scorched by the extreme torments bestowed by me, they will die instantly. After that, from whom else shall I inflict suffering? Therefore, having deposited their lifespans in Kṛṣṇa—who shares my nature and is my kinsman—these women, not dying, shall [attain] the shoreless [bliss] as they desire."

"Thinking, 'In this way I shall cause suffering,' for that very reason we do not die; or rather, it is only the intellect that wanders due to uncertainty regarding that [death]. But our vital breaths certainly depart from the body—see this for yourself now! Now, one might ask: while life still remains, how can there be destruction?"
Regarding this, they say: "O Lord, we have now surrendered our own lives to you—our lifespans being entrusted to you—so that you may sport for a long time in Vraja; such is the meaning. (19)
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the thirty-first [chapter] has been appropriately concluded here in the tenth [skandha] for the sake of the virtuous.
Thus ends the tenth book in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā known as the Pāramahaṃsyā, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Gopīs' Song.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The Consolation of the Gopīs: Śrī Śuka said:
Thus the gopīs sang and lamented in various ways.
O King, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, they wept with piteous voices.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirty-second [chapter], Hari, his heart moistened by the pangs of separation from their conversation, appeared there and consoled those gopīs, honoring them. i.
The son of Nanda has arisen, ever delighting the cowherd women whose hearts are overwhelmed by the surging waves of the nectar of his own love. ||ī||

"Thus [they were] to be hidden," meaning from that point onward; "in many ways" means in various manners; those who possessed an intense longing and great desire for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, crying out in beautiful voices at the top of their lungs. ||1||
Vaṃśīdhara:
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: the word "iti" expresses a manner; therefore, it means "beginning with this."

This is the meaning: singing loudly at times due to the intensity of their overflowing love, or perhaps speaking at length; or else, due to the agitation of separation, prattling somewhat incoherently. The word *citrathā* (in various ways) connects with both what precedes and what follows. [They sing] in a beautiful voice.
The meaning is "with a long, compassionate voice. The vocative "O King" is an address of distress, appropriate for one who yearns intensely upon seeing him. ||1||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, after the singing, there arose lamentation, and subsequently even weeping; thus he says "iti" and so forth. Singing intensely, being permeated by passion (*rāga*) and other emotions, they lamented in various ways like those who are mad, speaking emptily so that it might be with a beautiful voice (*susvara*).
Thus they wept; their melodious voices were natural, not produced through conscious effort. ||1||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, after the singing, lamentation arose, and subsequently even weeping occurred; thus he says "iti" and so forth. [The women] were singing intensely, being permeated by passion (*rāga*) and other such states.
Prattling in various ways like madwomen, they wailed into the void with such sweetness as was possible; this natural melodiousness was innate, not produced by conscious effort. ||1||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, Śrī Śuka describes the manner of weeping of those who, situated in another stage—the tenth—were uttering some meaningless prattle. In this way, by the aforementioned method beginning with that, they were singing loudly, and at one point, in the midst of it...

"Pralapatyaḥ" means speaking meaningless and incoherent words; "of this kind" refers to what has been described by me. The term "variously" (*citradhā*) is connected to both [the preceding and following phrases]. Furthermore, when even this did not manifest, then [they cried] with a beautiful voice, accompanied by a tone that evokes compassion.

Thus they wept; "O King" is their address, intended to draw your attention to the excess of the pain of separation they feel. Considering that all other efforts have proven fruitless and that weeping alone remains as the means to attract Kṛṣṇa, they did exactly that. In this regard:

The cause is that they were intensely longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa—those whose yearning and eagerness were fixed on seeing Kṛṣṇa, and not on serving their husbands and so forth, nor on the protection of the body and such matters. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the thirty-second [chapter], Hari arrived; his own limbs were honored by the words of Śuka, and having returned their honor with words of love, he made them feel indebted to him.
Singing in various ways—through such modes as *āścarya*, *tāna*, and *ālāpa*—and uttering cries out of an excess of extreme helplessness, they wept with melodious voices. ||1||
To them appeared Śauri, his lotus-face smiling,
wearing yellow garments and garlands, the manifest destroyer of the God of Love himself.
Śrīdhara: "Directly the churner of Manmatha" means that he is the manifest deluder even of Kāma—the one who deludes the world—who himself has arisen as desire within the mind. ||2||
Vaṃśīdhara: Among those gopīs, [he who was] born in the lineage of Śūra and is firm (karkaśa)—even after witnessing their great suffering—did not manifest for all this time; thus he says "Śauri.
Or, because he conquers desire, Śauri manifested; that very point he states with "sākṣān-manmatha" (the manifest Manmatha). The mind...

He churns and agitates, thus he is called Manmatha. The word is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. He is designated as Manmatha because he acts as a churner through the mind alone, even without a physical body. As it has been said:
"This is an unprecedented science of archery belonging to the great-souled Manmatha."

"Having left the body unharmed, he pierces the mind within"—this is the meaning. Since it is said that "when the mind is conquered, everything is conquered," and because desire has the nature of subduing the mind, its conquest is metaphorically attributed [to the self]; and one who conquers the mind is a conqueror of all.
Because desire also deludes that mind, the Blessed One is the "Mathematics of Love" (Manmatha-manmatha).
