The intention is that even Desire was deluded by the sight of the Blessed One’s form, which possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids. Furthermore, [He appeared] for the purpose of wiping away the streams of tears falling from their faces.
Or rather, he is called "the wearer of yellow garments" because he bound his hands in order to ask for forgiveness for his offense;

or else, it means that for the sake of seeking pardon for his transgression, he grasped the hem of the garment with his hand as if it were a blade of grass, and tied a garland around his neck like a cloth. ||2||

*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "Wearing yellow garments," and so forth. The meaning is that, due to having traveled from afar, either out of love or through a particular state of emotion, he holds with his left hand the yellow garment that has become loose;
or else, while remaining right there, by means of a dramatic display of haste as if he had just arrived from a distance, [he holds] the yellow garment.

"Pītottarīyaka-deśa" means that part of his body where the yellow upper garment is slipping down to the ground; "sragvī" means wearing a dangling forest garland. "Madana" is so called because he intoxicates (madayati) or churns (mathnāti);
"manmatha" is Rudra, who churns even that Madana—his intoxication (mada)—and thus [the Lord] churns even the intoxication of Manmatha.
"Manmatha," thus [it is said]. ||2||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Of them who were thus weeping—now, due to the apprehension of my own suffering, their lives have almost departed because of this particular state of wretchedness resulting from their crying. This is the meaning of "of those being so conjectured. Thus, through that specific state of wretchedness arising solely from concern for Him and regardless of oneself, there is the attainment of Him.

Thus it has been shown. Although Śauri is well known as one manifested from the lineage of Śūra, he appeared specifically for them; the meaning is that his manifestation was unprecedented in every respect. And so it will be said: "Bearing a body that is the sole abode of the Fortune of the three worlds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.14).

Regarding the statement, "There the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.7), what austerity did the gopīs perform, such that they attained His form— the very essence of loveliness, unsurpassed and not achieved by any other means?

In such passages as, "They drink with their eyes the ever-new and difficult-to-attain [nectar]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.44.14), there is likewise a specific statement regarding the Śrī-gopīs; and in such passages as, "These [are supreme]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58), and "That which the sages, fearing worldly existence, and we ourselves desire" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58).

According to the established doctrine of Śrī Uddhava, such a state is indeed appropriate for those women who possess the greatest love; he demonstrates this very point through the maxim, "Just as for one who is eating while being pursued... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.42), and so forth, stating: "The direct enchanter of Manmatha."
Among the various manifestations of the Caturvyūha, such as Vāsudeva and others, those who are directly Manmatha— that is, Kāmadeva himself,
and not merely ordinary Manmathas who are possessed by a portion of his power (śakti-aṃśa) and thus possess only an indirect form— their [Manmatha] is also Manmatha,
in the sense that it reveals their nature as Manmatha, just as in the expression "the eye of the eye" and so forth. Of those...

The meaning is that this [deity], being a partial illuminator of the specific qualities of form (*rūpa-guṇa-viśeṣa*), illuminates all of them entirely. For this very reason, there exist one-syllable and other mantras as well as meditations (*dhyāna*) for him in his capacity as the Great Manmatha; however, in those meditations, the assumption of another form is solely for the purpose of manifesting his nature as Manmatha.

It is implied that, by means of the etymological function (*yaugika-vṛtti*) of the word *manmatha*, He exists even for them in the form of an agitator and so forth. Thus, it is shown that such a form serves as the supreme objective support (*ālambana*) in the primary rasa (*ādi-rasa*) and is inaccessible through any other form of devotion. In this way, the unprecedented nature of the manifestation of His essential form is established.

Having spoken thus, he speaks also regarding the playful attire (*vilāsa-veśa*) with the three qualifying adjectives beginning with "smayamāna. Therein, by the use of the present participle in "smayamāna," there is an intention to convey its occurrence at that very moment; thus, a distinction from a natural smile (*sahaja-smita*) is perceived. Furthermore, since the intended meaning is already established by the term "pītāmbara" (clad in yellow silk) alone, [the following serves to further specify].
The application of the suffix *dhāraṇa* is indeed distinct, because it conveys at that time the cognition of another as being qualified by that [suffix].
Likewise, in the case of *sragvī*, since the suffix expressing the sense of "possessing" (*matvarthīya*) is prescribed in the sense of praise.
Furthermore, by means of the smile, one's own state of being well-pleased and the fact that the renunciation consists of jesting are indicated.

By wearing the yellow garment and covering himself up to his head, he indicates his state of mental contraction resulting from the abandonment of them. By being adorned with a garland, it is made known that because he is solely attached to her, he finds no pleasure in any other company without her. And thus, for the purpose of entering into the hearts of the listeners:
This is a description of the beauty at that moment. ||2||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, immediately after hearing their such weeping, he appeared at that very moment because he was unable to endure it; thus [the author] says, beginning with "tāsām" (of them). Regarding the word *śauri* here, the term *śūra* is not used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), but rather in its etymological sense (*yaugika*). Even for the son of Śūra, there is nothing beyond this.
He was not merely capable of the pastime of disappearing, but rather manifested visibly before them;
for this very reason, his lotus-face was smiling. His smiling nature arises from the thought, "Beyond this, I possess no further fortitude.
He is described as "wearing yellow garments" (*pītāmbara-dhara*), meaning that due to a particular emotional state, his yellow garment was slipping.

The meaning is that he holds [it] with his left hand. Alternatively, having grasped a portion of his yellow upper garment (*uttarīya*), he conceals his smile. Or else, because his upper garment has slipped, a portion of his yellow garment (*pītāmbara*) is slightly visible at his waist; otherwise, this would have been established by the term *pītāmbara* alone.

Wearing a garland, he possesses a never-fading forest wreath. He is the "Manmatha" (the churner of minds) because he churns the minds of Manmatha (the god of love) and others; or alternatively, "Mad" refers to intoxication or the act of churning, thus "Madana" is he who intoxicates or churns;
and he is the "Manmatha" (churner of Madana) because he churns even Rudra’s pride and arrogance by appearing in the form of Mohinī.

"He has taken away their pride"—thus it is said; the meaning is that even though he was such [a great being], he himself was drawn by their beauty. Or rather, he is the manifest God of Love, the very Love-god even of the embodied God of Love. ||2||

The sequence of composition: Although Śauri is renowned for having manifested from the lineage of Śūra, he manifested from those very [gopīs] alone; the meaning is that his manifestation was unprecedented in every respect. He is Manmatha himself—the Manmatha of those Pradyumnas who abide in the various fourfold manifestations (caturvyūha). He is the eye of the eye [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad].
[4.4.18] The meaning is that it is like this: it reveals the state of being the Mind-born (Manmatha). ||2||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, immediately after hearing their such weeping, being unable to endure it, he spoke at that very moment, saying "it has become [so]"; this is expressed in the verse beginning with "tāsām" (of them). Regarding the word *śauri*, here the term *śūra* is not used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), but rather in its etymological sense (*yaugika*). Even for the son of Śūra, there is nothing beyond this.

He was not merely capable of the pastime of disappearance (*antardhāna-līlā*), but had actually manifested before them; therefore, his lotus-face was smiling. His smiling nature arises from the thought, "Beyond this, I have no further fortitude.
He is "wearing yellow garments" (*pītāmbara-dhara*); due to a particular state of emotion, his yellow garment is loosened.

The meaning is that he holds [it] with his left hand; or else, holding a portion of his yellow upper garment (*uttarīya*), he conceals his smile; or else, because his upper garment is loose, the yellow garment—meaning a portion of the yellow garment—is upon the earth, otherwise the state would be established by the term "yellow-clad" (*pītāmbara*) alone. He is garlanded (*sragvī*).

Wearing a forest garland that never withers; she is the "mind-disturber" (manmatha) of even Manmatha (the god of love), because she churns his mind just as he does. Alternatively, *madana* means one who intoxicates (*madayati*) or churns (*mathnāti*), or one whose mind (*manda-math*) is intoxicated;
yet Rudra is called *manmatha* because he does not churn [her], for she, in her form as the Enchantress (*mohinī*), churns even his pride (*mada*) and arrogance.
"He destroyed pride" means that even he himself was drawn by their beauty. Alternatively, he is the direct Manmatha—the Manmatha even of the embodied Manmatha. ||2||

The Composition of *Prīti*: Now, the *ujjvala* [rasa]. Here, the *ālambana* (the substratum) is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who manifests as the beloved and is the object of the state of being the beloved (*kānta-bhāva*). The supports (*āśraya*) are those of the same class of emotion (*sajātīya-bhāva*) and His supreme favorites. Among these, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is exemplified as follows: "To them appeared the son of Śūra... (*tāsām āvirabhūc chauriḥ*).

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now they say that even weeping has become the means for attaining Kṛṣṇa—referring to the words "of them" (*tāsām*). He by whom their hearts were consumed by the flames of separation, by him [Kṛṣṇa] was wept for; among those women who were supremely distressed and standing on the verge of the tenth stage [of love-in-separation], Śauri appeared to all.
The meaning is that he descended into the lineage of the Śūras for the purpose of dispelling suffering and manifesting his own virtues.
"Appeared" means he became visible. His lotus-face was smiling for the sake of removing their grief; the smile was [directed] at himself alone, solely for the purpose of concealing his own fault.

"Because of being guilty": he wears yellow garments (pītāmbara) for the purpose of concealing his horripilation and other signs. Having covered his entire body with the yellow garment, he has appeared. "Garlanded" (sragvī): it is said that in her absence, he wears a garland as a cause of coolness to quench even his own heat.
Or rather, he has now manifested after considering that there was neither aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) nor fame (*kīrti*) in his mind [previously].

By the term "Pītāmbara" (Clad in Yellow), the wearing of yellow garments is indicated through the similarity of its color; by the term "sragvī" (Garlanded), the protection of fame is suggested through this wearing of a garland. Of them—

It was for the sake of adornment. Alternatively, he manifested his world-enchanting form in order to cause the speech of those who had risen up out of envy to be paralyzed—those who thought, "He possesses garlands woven from the flower-strings of Vṛndāvana. Thus, by manifesting the sweetness of his graceful movements, [he captivated them].

He is the direct destroyer of Manmatha. That Manmatha, however, is merely material and agitates only those who are material, but not the non-material beloveds of Kṛṣṇa. This one, moreover, is the manifest form;
the meaning is that he is the deluder even of Manmatha, who deludes the world. If even Kāma has become deluded—

In that case, what is the wonder in their being enchanted? It is because ordinary desire (*prākṛta-kāma*) lacks the power to enchant them; the meaning is that He alone is the enchanter. This is the intention:
for as long as Kṛṣṇa performed the pastimes of the *rāsa*, for that long, even [ordinary] desire...

Cessation has arisen; because he is immersed in his own essential nature (svarūpa), he has become inactive. Having reflected, "During the time delimited by that [state], may all people not achieve their own self-interest through being inclined toward me," he intentionally deluded them. This desire, however, while abiding in the essential nature of Kṛṣṇa, is composed of consciousness (cinmaya).

"He is to be served by the gopīs" (gopī-jana-sevyaḥ). By such statements as "These [gopīs] alone are the true possessors of bodies" (etāḥ paraṃ tanubhṛtaḥ), it is clearly seen that they are worthy of being saluted even by Uddhava and others. ||2||

Viśvanātha: "Śauri" is an expression of resentment toward Kṛṣṇa by Śrī Śukadeva, who sides with the gopīs. Precisely because he was born of the kṣatriya caste with a crooked heart, Kṛṣṇa manifested his prowess by inflicting such great suffering upon these loving women. If...

The meaning implied is: "If he had been born into the cowherd caste with a straightforward heart, then this would not have happened. Therefore, even in their suffering, their faces are blossoming; in reality, however, their lotus-faces are made to blossom solely for the sake of his joy, as they are smiling.

He whose heart-lotus is indeed scorched; he who, having draped the yellow garment over both shoulders, holds it with his two hands—the sense being that he does so to beg forgiveness for his offense. He is "garlanded" (sragvī)—the sense being that he shows the very garland his beloved had caused him to wear.
He was one who churned the mind even of Manmatha himself—the aggregate of all desire—so that he churned it.

She brought about such a transformation of the approaching Kandarpa, who was intent on deluding even the world, into a feminine form that she deluded him as well; for upon seeing Kṛṣṇa’s beauty, even he became tormented by the arrows of love.

The meaning is that she was bewildered. By this it should be understood that Kṛṣṇa and His beloveds were [bewildered] precisely because He—who is Cupid incarnate—is not subject to the influence of that [passion]. At that time, by being the direct "enchanter of Manmatha," He manifested His own sweetness which is supremely enchanting, even for them who were experiencing such suffering of separation.
To clarify that it is for the purpose of causing forgetfulness. ||2||
Seeing their beloved returned, all those slender women, their eyes blossoming with joy,
rose up simultaneously as if their very life-breath had come back to them.
Śrīdhara: The body consists of the hands, feet, and so forth. (3–4)

Vaṃśīdhara: [He refers to] that Kṛṣṇa. Because of the metaphorical treatment of the part as non-different from the whole, the word *tanū* here refers to the limbs, or else to bodies. The word *prāṇa* intends a singular sense in its general application. *Tanvaḥ* refers to the hands, feet, and so forth. The repetition of the word "arrived" (*āgatam*) is for the sake of emphasizing them.

In order to clarify that the rising of those who had fainted was caused solely by her arrival, a certain woman whose name is not specified [speaks]. By mentioning the hands and so forth with the words "hands etc.," she indicates that Hari is attainable through devotion alone.
"Smeared with sandalwood" means adorned; the verbal root *ruṣ* is used in the sense of adorning. [This applies] to all the gopīs.

He describes the love-expressions appropriate to the individual natures of some of the principal [gopīs] with five verses beginning with "A certain one" (*kācit*). Because she is filled with devotion, she speaks through the explanation of the latter half [of the verse], referring specifically to her right lotus-hand.
The underlying sentiment is that this arises both from her friendliness characterized by humility and from her eagerness for touch. This [is the first gopī].

This [woman] is full of affection, possessing a love sustained by a touch imbued with respect; she is devoted to her beloved and is skillful; and because she was the first [to serve], she is the eldest of all. She has anointed only her left arm with sandalwood paste, which is smeared with streaks of devotion, for it is appropriate that she remain on the left side of her own beloved. This is she.

With an embrace initiated by herself that bore the scent of respect, she was like honey mixed with a touch of affection; her friendship was manifest, her lover was somewhat under her control, and she was *dakṣiṇā* (courteous). Thus, she received him with joined palms (*añjali*).
She is mostly friendly like a servant, submissive to her beloved, and compliant. ||3-4||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained. *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: [He who was] first arrived with longing, and immediately thereafter, having appeared from afar, reached his own presence by the process of approaching; and thus:
In the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Then they saw him approaching, his lotus-face blossoming" (*Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 5.13.43).

For this very reason, it is said that they "looked specifically" or "beheld," because due to their helplessness from weeping, there was no certainty even when seeing him slightly; or rather, because even though he was seen, the supreme mortals lacked conviction.

The meaning is: "only after looking closely. Although all the women were unable to rise due to their exhaustion from separation, they all rose simultaneously. The reason for this is expressed by the word *preṣṭham* ("the most beloved"):
because he is their sole beloved, he is the singular cause of both their death and their life. He establishes this very point through an illustration: *tanva...* (O slender one...)
The repetition of the words "thus arrived" is made for the sake of clarifying that arrival is the sole cause for his rising;

this is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) known as *vilāsa* (graceful playfulness), which consists of the movements of gait, standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as the actions of the face, eyes, and other limbs.
"But the excellence arising from union with the beloved at that very moment is *vilāsa*," as stated in [Uṇī. 11.31]. ||3||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "He has arrived. This is according to their intention; or rather, He manifested in their midst. Or else, the meaning is that having first appeared at a distance, He reached His own presence by way of approaching them. Thus, in the *Śrī-viṣṇu-purāṇa* [it is said]: "Then they saw..."
"Coming with his lotus-face blossoming" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.43). For this very reason, it means "having looked specifically," that is, having seen him;

for due to the helplessness caused by weeping, there was no seeing at all even when there was a slight glimpse. Or rather, even though he was seen, because of a lack of confidence on account of her extreme distress, the meaning is "only after looking thoroughly. Therefore—

With their eyes blossomed wide and fully opened in intense joy, those women—who were unable to rise due to their physical exhaustion from the pangs of separation—all rose up at once. The reason for this is stated: "Because he was their dearest."
Now, one might object: "Even so, how could their simultaneous rising in such a manner occur all at once, as if they had reached their final state?
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes this very point by means of an illustration—the verse beginning with *tanvā*.
The sense is that, because He alone is her most beloved, He is the sole cause of both her death and her life. As for what follows...

Or rather, at first their eyes blossomed with joy; afterwards they stood up—just as even for subtle things there is first vibration and so forth, and only afterwards engagement in their respective functions. By the repetition of the word "arrived," it is indicated that arrival was the sole cause of their rising. (3)
The *krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
The *bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: regarding that which occurred when He had appeared, he says "Him," and so forth.
"Arrived" means manifested, not having come from anywhere; having vanished right there.

Because they were already standing; even those who were weak and unable to rise rose up exceedingly. "Simultaneously" means that because there was no sequence in their seeing [the Lord], He appeared before each one individually.
By this, it should be understood that they sang while remaining seated as before. In this regard, the illustration is: "tanvaḥ" (their bodies).

"Like breath returned": *prāṇa* is the self (*ātman*) because it causes [the body] to breathe; having reached that, the bodies—meaning the physical forms—are referred to in the singular due to their identity with the Self, though they are plural in number. Thus [it is said]. ||3||

The Composition of Affection (*prīti-sandarbha*): Immediately following this, an illustration of *sambhoga* (enjoyment) is also shown by such verses as "Beholding him, her dearest, who had arrived" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.32.3). (393)

Vilāsa is the momentary distinction arising from union with the beloved, manifesting in the movements of walking, standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as in the actions of the face, eyes, and other limbs.
As it is said: "Upon seeing her most beloved arrived... This is clearly evident. (326)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: First, she describes how they became filled with agitation upon seeing him appearing from a short distance within their field of vision; thus she says, "Having beheld him," as it was stated by Pārāśarya: "Then they saw him approaching, his lotus-face in full bloom" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.43).

For that purpose, having searched for everything—including songs and even weeping—and having understood them to be means for attaining Him, [the women] saw Him from afar, beheld Him clearly, and recognized Him; thus, although it causes the heat of the fire of separation, they considered it the best of lives because of its being the cause [of His arrival]. [The women were] weak.

Although their physical strength was impaired by the pain of separation, all of them rose up from their seats at once with great agitation; for, fearing that he might show himself but once and then become invisible again due to a lack of trust in them, they had risen together in haste. Thus, they arrived immediately after their emaciation.

Those whose eyes were blossomed and fully opened—regarding them, he provides an illustration: just as the limbs, such as the hands and feet, rise up and become endowed with consciousness upon seeing that life-force has returned, so it was in their case. ||3||
Viśvanātha: "Limbs" refers to the hands, feet, and so forth. The repetition of the word "arrived" is intended to clarify that their rising from unconsciousness has that arrival as its sole cause. (3)
One woman joyfully grasped Śauri’s lotus-hand with her own lotus-palms;
another placed his arm, smeared with sandalwood paste, upon her shoulder.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: Not commented upon.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Previously, through the wretchedness of separation and by means of similar words, the attainment of equality for all [the gopīs] was shown. Now, as they have regained their respective supports and are following their own individual natures, he describes the distinctions in their internal states (*bhāva*) through the differences in the activities of the principal [gopīs], beginning with "A certain one... (*kācit*).

With five [qualities]: he took the lotus-hand of the intoxicated one because it was appropriate for such conduct to support him who was weary from wandering in the forest, and because of his longing for touch. And the rightness of the hand is due to the second [goddess] holding his arm upon her own shoulder.
Because it is appropriate for her to stand on the left side by virtue of being situated alongside her beloved,

and because it is appropriate to grasp the right [hand] in that manner; and because it is appropriate for the second woman, who holds his arm upon her own shoulder, to stand on the left side by virtue of being situated alongside her beloved, [the right hand of the first woman is grasped].
For it is appropriate to grasp [the hand] of the *dakṣiṇā* woman alone; in this manner, each subsequent type should be understood.

From the mention of "with joined palms" (*añjali*), it follows that she is gentle, primarily a friend, a servant, dependent on her lover, and *dakṣiṇā*. She is "smeared with sandalwood" (*candanena rūṣitam*), meaning covered with streaks of devotion (*bhakti-ccheda*), because she is worn by being drawn [to him].

She is sharp-witted, her friendship is manifest, her lover is somewhat dependent on others, and she is clever. Here, betel nut has been placed in every bower by the illustrious Goddess Vṛndā along with garlands and other articles; or perhaps it was accomplished by Yogamāyā herself.
"Of Śauri" is understood from the context. (4)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, describing through six verses the departure of the heat of separation for all of them and their supreme festival and so forth resulting from His arrival, [the author] first speaks of the amorous gestures of the eight well-known principal gopīs individually—beginning with "A certain one... (kācit).

With five [hands]: one is a lotus-hand for the purpose of holding a garment with the other, as such a practice is beautiful; by the metaphor of the "lotus," her natural ruddiness and other beauties, as well as her power to remove distress, are suggested.
The term "with joined palms" (añjali) indicates a particular intensity of devotion; "with joy" (mudā) signifies the cessation of the suffering of separation.

This [phrase] is to be understood as following throughout all subsequent instances. His—or that—arm, which is indescribable due to its beauty and other qualities; the term "of Śauri" (the Lord) continues to apply here as well. The same applies further on. By the word "smeared with sandalwood" (*candanena rūṣitam*), meaning "anointed with streaks of devotion," both its beauty and its quality of removing heat are expressed. ||4||
The sequence of composition: the group of six beginning with "A certain woman" (kācit), etc. ||4||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, having described how He appeared, the text speaks of what various women did upon seeing Him with many verses beginning with "kācit. One woman, full of respectful affection, held His lotus-hand;
some call this lady Candrāvalī; another supported His arm (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.32.4).
Thus she was preeminent in friendship and full of affection. ||4||

The Composition of Love (*prīti-sandarbha*): This [love] exists with many varieties. Indeed, in a single state of being, there is a particular mutual regard between a couple. Among those, for beloved women, due to an excess of the conceit of belonging to you, toward their lover—

In the *pāratantrya* (subordination) form of *vinaya* (discipline), there is an abundance of courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*); elsewhere, there is an excess of possessiveness (*madīyatva*). Where there is an abundance of the appearance of crookedness in jest (*narma-kauṭilya*) due to the lover being under another's control (*paratantra-kāntatā*), and where there is an awareness of the inner vital points (*antar-marmajñatā*), these two pairs—distinguished by their differences in many parts, few parts, and their mutual commingling—are found in other [types].
And [the state] is manifold. These aforementioned states—as in the six verses beginning with "A certain [woman] her lotus-hand"—are as follows:
here, the previously mentioned state consisting of a particular intensity of reverence is first stated in the verse beginning with "A certain [woman] her lotus-hand.
And because this stands at the very beginning of all, it is described first; from this, it is understood that she is the eldest (*jyeṣṭhā*).
And thus, at the very beginning, there was a meeting with her alone;

likewise, from that very fact, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own extraordinary regard for her is understood. Similarly, by her grasping his hand with folded palms (añjali), her own devotion toward him is made manifest, as well as her state of total dependence upon him.
And she occupies a middle position; therefore, this first example is indeed appropriate.
Now follows the second example, consisting of an excess of "mine-ness" (*madīyatva*): "One [woman], knitting her brow," and so forth.
Indeed, by virtue of being described in the middle, she is understood to occupy a middle position.
Her position as the central figure reveals her supreme rarity;

from this, it is understood that she possesses a particular state of being (*bhāva-viśeṣa*). And the direct indicator of that state is none other than the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth, which conveys the excellence of her sense of "mine-ness" (*madīyatva*) and other such qualities. And she is indeed Śrī Rādhā herself.
This is to be known.
Such indeed is her disposition, as seen in the *Bhaviṣya* Purāṇa passage cited in the *Vrata-ratnākara* regarding the occasion of Kārttika:
And on that day, at night, the Blessed One went to Rādhā’s house;
she, being angry, bound him around the waist with her girdle-string.
Kṛṣṇa, however, having announced the great festival at his own home, sought to appease his beloved; then she spoke to him thus:
"Then, once her disposition had become established in such a way that [she thought], 'Rādhā is my beloved,' and so forth..."
In accordance with the statements of the *Padma Purāṇa* and others, and following such passages as "He was surely worshipped by her" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.30.28),

the greatness of that very state of being is clearly perceived due to its own majesty. It is precisely because of this corresponding state of being that even Śrī Satyabhāmā [attained such results] in Dvārakā.
It is praised in every respect. In that regard, the similarity of nature and the state of being praised in every respect are as described in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"If those words of yours are true—that you are exceedingly dear to me for the sake of truth—"
"Then let this tree be taken for the sake of making my home manifest its true purpose.

(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.30.33). And as for the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the *Pādma-kārttika-māhātmya*: "None is dearer to Me than you," and so forth. Furthermore, the statement of Vaiśampāyana in the *Śrī Hari-vaṃśa* confirms that very point regarding her good fortune (*saubhāgye*).
And it became superior.

Now, that which was previously characterized by existence would also be the heroine who is its opposite, by virtue of being a state opposed to that state. And it is well known that she is indeed Candrāvalī. Thus it has been said:
Śrī Bilvamaṅgala,
having arrived from the temple of Rādhā-mohana, spoke to Candrāvalī;
upon hearing his words, "O Rādhā, may there be well-being," Candrāvalī replied.
"O Kaṃsa, in this heart full of well-being and yet bewildered, where have you seen Kaṃsa?
Where is Rādhā?"—may Hari, smiling with his face bowed in embarrassment at these words, protect you all.
Here, a certain woman whose disposition is similar to that of Candrāvalī is described by the verse beginning with "with folded hands," and so forth. One.

And by the verse beginning with "tad-aṅghri-kamalam" (His lotus feet), it is established by the learned that these two are Her friends, Padmā and Śaivyā; they possess a disposition similar to that of Śrī Rādhā, as described in the verses beginning with "aparinimiṣad-dṛgbhyām" (with unblinking eyes) and "taṃ kācid" (A certain woman [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.8]). He is mine.
Thinking, "She will experience me herself," because there is an absence of grasping, touch, and so forth on her part, she experiences it through the touch of resistance (*vāmya*).
Therefore, these two are her friends; and they are likely named after her, because they follow along with her.

From the textual reading, Anurādhā and Viśākhā should be [the two names]. Indeed, regarding those who say "Viśākhā is the perfection of meditation" (dhyāna-niṣṭhikā), there is the established consensus among experts that in the *Bhaviṣyottara* as it is recited—"Rādhā and Anurādhā"—it is Anurādhā herself who is called Lalitā. Furthermore, a certain woman, characterized by a state of emotional fusion (*saṅkara-bhāva*), maintained [this identification]: "O Rādhā and Anurādhā... (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.32.4).
Thus it has been stated in the aforementioned passage. By holding that [garland] upon the shoulder of the right arm, it attains equality with the southern [direction];
therefore, this is indeed known among the learned as Śyāmalā of the north. Furthermore, the eighth [form] is described here as stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman was filled with great joy;
she cried out, 'Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44).
Because her emotional state is not yet fully manifest, this is "detachment" (*tāṭasthya*). And this woman is "Bhadrā."

The establishment through authoritative tradition (*abhiyukta-prasiddhi*). He demonstrates that those entities have the nature of nothing but supreme bliss (*paramānanda-ekarūpatva*) with the words: "All... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.9]. (367)
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, when the heat of separation has been dispelled for all of them,

the activities previously contemplated by those leaders of the group— which emerged from their mouths during their conversations about separation— are now presented through dramatic enactment (*abhinaya*), distinguished individually according to the principle of "seizing by the horns" (*śṛṅga-grāhikā-nyāya*) as various states of emotion arise.
"She shows [herself]"—this is expressed through five verses. The name of "a certain woman" (*kācit*) is not mentioned because she is a beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śuka says: "A certain woman [belonging] to Śauri," referring to her who, at the moment of his disappearance, had thought only of the touch of His lotus-hand.
By saying "a certain woman [offered] her lotus-hand," the fact that it was the cause of coolness is suggested by the gesture of the joined palms (*añjali*).

With both hands joined together, she expressed her humility with reverence and joy, her heart overflowing with delight; yet, harboring a hidden intention— fearing she might vanish once again within her own home,
or fearing a dispersal due to wandering through many places.

Or, it may be that she grasped his lotus-hand out of a desire to obtain the bliss born of touch. A certain woman, casting aside all reserve, placed his arm upon her shoulder; for she did so either with the hope, "I shall become intimate," or with the hope, "I shall be constantly embraced. By this—
Because he wears yellow garments (*pītāmbara*), the cessation of former afflictions (*kleśa*) is indicated by the word "rejoices" (*mudeti*). Of what kind is the arm?

It is "adorned with sandalwood" (*candana-bhūṣita*), meaning it is smeared with sandalwood paste applied in some pattern of decorative lines (*bhakti-ccheda-racanā*) for the very purpose of removing the heat of separation upon her shoulder, which had been scorched by the fever of longing. In that regard—

The qualification "adorned with sandalwood" (*candana-bhūṣitam*) is used in the sense of being "smeared" (*rūṣitam*); this is the meaning according to Viśvanātha. [The author] speaks of the love-expressions appropriate to the individual natures of certain gopīs who are foremost among all the gopīs in five verses beginning with "A certain [gopī]... (*kācid*). [He describes her] lotus-hand...

The phrase "only the right [hand]" becomes clear from the explanation of the latter half [of the verse]. The sense is that she took [it] out of her loving-kindness (*maitrī*) consisting of discipline (*vinaya*), and out of a longing for touch.
This [hand], through its affectionate contact full of respect, is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in its oily tenderness (*sneha*); it belongs to him and is dependent upon her beloved.

And because she was the first, she is the eldest of all; her left arm alone—smeared with sandalwood paste and marked with streaks of unguent—is placed upon the left side of her own beloved, as that is the proper position;
this [arm] is slightly [pressed] by an embrace performed by herself, which bears the scent of respect.
She who possesses the affection of ghee mixed with the sweetness of honey, whose friendship is manifest, and whose lover is somewhat under her control, is the *dakṣiṇā* type. ||4||
A certain slender woman took the chewed betel from his hand with her joined palms; another, tormented by love, placed his lotus-feet upon her breasts.
Śrīdhara: With the *añjali*, that is, with the two hands joined together. ||5||

Vaṃśīdhara: He placed [the water] upon her breasts, which were scorched by heat, in order to dispel their burning; that water was either the chewed remnant of betel, the residue spat out and discarded, or the liquid itself. (5)

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "That lotus-foot"—having sat down, while he was still standing, she raised one foot out of the power of her affection and placed it upon her breasts; her subsequent sitting down will be described later. (5–9)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "She took [it] with her joined palms," as before. Here, however, there is eagerness for the nectar of the lower lip. This heroine is gentle, characterized primarily by the mood of service (*dāsya*), devoted to her beloved, and *dakṣiṇā*;
she placed her right lotus-foot upon her breasts with her left arm.

Because she has attained the state of having her body’s parts placed upon his left foot by leaning against her beloved; and because he is currently standing, as will be described later in relation to her sitting down; therefore, while she is indeed seated, she holds his feet. The reason for placing them [the feet] upon those two [her thighs] is that they are "heated" (santapta).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by means of the emotion called *rati* consisting of separation. In the reading *hṛdaye*, the meaning is the same.
This [heroine] is *prakharā* (sharp), primarily characterized by servitude (*dāsya*), a friend [to her lover], dependent on her beloved, and *dakṣiṇā* (accommodating). ||5||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "With folded hands" is as before. Alternatively, she constantly chews betel leaf out of a desire for its abundant flavor, or perhaps due to the fear that it might fall [from her mouth], since she is slender and extremely emaciated by separation; for this very reason, the betel is being chewed.
Because it consists of the supreme essence, betel was formerly brought by the Śrī-Bhagavān himself, the crest-jewel of the urbanites;

or rather, it should be understood as that which was offered by the goddess Śrī-Vṛndā and others. That she placed one lotus-foot between her breasts should be understood as her sitting down for that purpose.

The Lord’s seating in front will be described later with the words, "He sat there" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.14); the reason for His being placed between those two is given as "santapta" (tormented). Otherwise, the departure of the heat of separation and the fever of desire would not occur. Even if the reading is "hṛdaye" (in the heart), the meaning remains the same. ||5||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "A certain [woman] with folded hands"—this refers to the chief among the young maidens.
"One [woman], her lotus-feet..."—this refers to one possessed of humble affection. She, indeed, was a certain [woman] who maintained [that state].

In the verse beginning with *tad-bāhum* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.4), the position of the Lord is described as having one foot loosely placed on the shoulder of a certain woman who holds His arm upon her own shoulder; for this very reason, she sat down herself and rested His loose foot upon her breasts, yet at that time the Blessed One did not sit down.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Just as it was requested in the verse, "Grant me even the nectar of Your lips" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.31.8), she, with her two hands joined in *añjali*, accepted the chewed betel-roll together with the nectar of His lips.
How wonderful is she, whose slender limbs were emaciated by the pangs of separation during the intervals between drinking that nectar of His lips!
Was there not one who prayed: "O most peaceful lover, place your lotus feet upon our breasts to destroy our suffering" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.13)?
To fulfill her own heart's desire, she placed His lotus feet upon her breasts, which were heated by the fire of separation and tormented by the fever of love.
The implicit meaning here is that she sat down there amidst the throng of those women after having placed [the lotuses] down;
otherwise, it would have been impossible to place her lotus-feet [upon them]. ||5||

Viśvanātha: "He took [it] with joined palms"—thus this [act] is characterized by a friendship consisting primarily of servitude (*dāsya*), and is both *kāntādhīnā* (dependent on the beloved) and *dakṣiṇā* (gracious). Having grasped the right lotus-foot with her own two hands, she sat upon the ground and placed it between her breasts; thereafter, she rested her left arm upon the shoulder of her beloved.

It should be understood that Kṛṣṇa stood supporting the earth with his left foot. This [left foot] is characterized by devotion consisting primarily of friendliness (*maitrya*), while the right is characterized by servitude (*dāsya*) under the influence of love (*kāntā*). Therefore, these two are the companions of the first [devotion], which is filled with the ghee-like affection of *tadīyatā* (the sense of "belonging to Him"). ||5||
Frowning with one eyebrow raised, overwhelmed by the intensity of her passion,
she looked at him as if striking him, biting her lip.

Śrīdhara: Having knit her eyebrows—having made them crooked—and being overwhelmed by the intensity of her love, that is, possessed by a lover’s anger, she, biting her lower lip, looked as if striking him with the reproaches found in her side-long glances. ||6||

Vaṃśīdhara: By the mention of a portion of a name, as in the word *bhīma* for Bhīmasena, the term *kaṭa* should be understood as a reference to *kaṭākṣa* (a sidelong glance). Regarding the phrase "as if striking": the intention is that she thinks, "O rogue, you have abandoned me too! Thus, she is perceived as being Rādhikā. ||6||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: being overwhelmed by the intensity of her love, knitting her brows, biting her lips, she looked [at him] as if striking him with side-long glances.

"By the casting of side-glances" means by the movement of sidelong looks. "Sandaṣṭā" is a reading found in some versions. From the context, it refers to the game of *śārī*. By saying "as if striking," it is suggested that she causes agitation even to him; and by the fact that he was held by them, it is suggested that he remained there merely out of courtesy. Likewise, by his stubbornness (*vāmyena*).
By the phrase "even though she was standing at a distance, with an outburst of love," it is shown that there is supreme bliss in beholding her. As it is said in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"A certain woman, having made the surface of her forehead curved by her eyebrows [in a frown] toward Hari..."
"Having gazed with the two bees of her eyes, she drank in the lotus of his face" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44).

Here, the secondary emotional state (*anubhāva*) known as *bibboka* (coquettish disdain) is demonstrated. As it has been said: "Even toward a beloved, *bibboka* is a display of disregard due to pride and arrogance. Likewise, there is also that which is called *lalita* (graceful charm), as it has been said:

That in which there are graceful movements of the limbs through various postures, captivating with the play of the eyebrows, and characterized by delicacy, is declared to be *lalita* (the graceful). [Uṇī.
11.56] This woman is spirited, a very dear friend, entirely submissive, charming, and beloved. (6)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "With an outburst of love, she knit her eyebrows completely; thereafter, she became overwhelmed by that very outburst of love—this is the implied meaning. This is to be connected with the subsequent word 'aikṣata' (she looked). And so it is stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:"
"One, having arched her brow over the surface of her forehead and gazing at Hari with her bee-like eyes, drank in the lotus of his face" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44).
And another looked as if striking him with the discharge of side-glances; here too, it is simply the intensity of love.

The reason should be understood from the statement "having bitten her lip" (*nirdaṣṭa-daśana-cchada*). Alternatively, because the word "love" (*prema*) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse], the sequence of composition has not been explained.
Regarding the extensive sequence of composition: "frowning with one eyebrow" (*ekāṃ bhru-kuṭim ābadhya*) indicates she is possessed of affectionate anger (*praṇaya-krodhavatī*); so some say.
They call this Śrī Rādhā. ||6||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: As it is said in the verse beginning with *pati-sutānvaya* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.16), that one leader of the group, distinguished by a particular playful anger (*praṇaya-kopa*), stood at a distance; with guile, she knit her creeper-like eyebrows, bending them into a frown by the contraction of her brows.

Mental crookedness was observed. Through the intensity of her love, there was an outburst of anger caused by the paralysis of all her senses; because she was thus overwhelmed, she bit her lips—that is, she firmly bit her lower lip. Previously, this was for the purpose of restraining greed.

Her eyes were filled with the playfulness of granting what had been promised; for the sake of restraining her own nature, she cast glances of passion and impetuosity. Or rather, "ākṣepas" are those arrows which are cast (kṣipyante) all around (ā); with these, she seemed to strike [him].
It is indicated that she struck him with side-long glances for the purpose of abolishing his independence and bringing about his subjugation. As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"A certain woman, having made the surface of her forehead curved by her eyebrows [in a frown], [looked at] Hari..."
"Having gazed with his bee-like eyes, he drank in the lotus of her face" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44).

Just as it was thus thought, so too in the verse, "O dull-witted one, your face with its curly locks is being watched by those whose eyes have eyelashes," the mere sight of the face is what is prayed for.

Viśvanātha: Having knit her brows and thus made them crooked— meaning, having drawn back the strung bow with an arrow fixed upon it— she, overwhelmed and rendered helpless by the intensity of her love and the onset of a lover’s pique, [pierces] Kṛṣṇa with the discharges, that is, the castings, of her side-glances which serve as arrows.

"O crest-jewel of deceivers! Having applied the hālāhala poison of your own love toward me as if striking at my very life, you have made it perfectly effective; why do you now draw near again to burn the vital breaths that have already almost departed from my body? You have indeed been well recognized!"—thus she implies.

He looked. Biting her lip—an expression of anger manifested by the grasping of her own lower lip with her joined palms—she was possessed of a crooked pride arising from the honey-like affection of my devotion. (6)
With her unblinking eyes, she took delight in his lotus-like face; though she had drunk it in, she was not satiated, just as the virtuous are never satiated by his feet.
Śrīdhara: Although she had drunk him in—that is, had fully beheld him—with her unblinking eyes, she did not reach satiety as she continued to enjoy him again and again. ||7||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: [not commented upon].

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Juṣāṇā" means serving or beholding with affection; it is suggested that even the eyes themselves have become like cups, meaning they have been fully beheld with supreme love. "Santas" refers to those solely devoted to love and devotion, [indicating] either sweet love (*madhura-prema*) or love-devotion (*prīti-bhakti*).

Only a partial similarity regarding the absence of satisfaction is intended here; however, in the verse beginning with "the lotus feet of the deer-eyed ones" (*sāraṅgāṇāṃ padāmbujam*), their devotion is directed toward His glorious lotus feet. And for these beloved consorts, because of their longing for the nectar of His lips and so forth, their affection is generally directed toward His glorious face itself—thus a specific quality of their love is indeed indicated. Therefore, for them...
Because the softness and other qualities of the glorious lotus-feet have not been directly experienced, there is the employment of the metaphorical forms "lotus" and so forth. (7)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "With her two unblinking eyes" means she is motionless with the bliss of vision, naturally straightforward. (7)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: That other leader of the group, delighting her eyes with his lotus-face, partook of it; by describing the eyes as the "instrument of drinking," it is indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the nectar in the form of beauty within the lotus-face is worthy of being drunk, just as a liquid enters into the interior.

"Drink" refers to the characteristic of drinking. In this context, "drinking" is precisely the entry of the beauty of her lotus-face into the heart through the gateway of the eyes. Even though it was "well drunk"—meaning well-beheld—with supreme affection, she was not satiated; she did not think "enough," as indicated by the word *alam*. This is what is meant by "she did not consider it sufficient."
The beauty of the object is the cause of engagement; the absence of a purpose is not an obstacle. In this regard, there is an illustration: "just as the virtuous [follow] His feet.
It is said that for the deer, He is the lotus of His feet; thus, they follow His lotus feet. Just as they do...

Even while constantly serving His lotus feet, they do not consider it "enough," for there is no satiety; indeed, this is the illustration. For the saintly, there is always something yet to be attained. While all [the devotees] possess a share in the lotus feet, no one possesses a share in the nectar of His lips; therefore, its excellence is absolute.
It has been indicated. ||7||
Viśvanātha: With her unblinking eyes—eyes that do not close due to the paralysis of bliss—as if they were two bees [hovering] over his lotus-face; or rather, this is well known [from tradition].
Because she had been shattered by the arrows of his side-long glances, she was agitated and tormented by fear and remorse.
Even though its sweetness has been properly tasted and drunk, they continue to enjoy and relish it again and again;

thus, the lotus-face possesses boundless sweetness by its very nature. Furthermore, this is enhanced by the strike of the arrows of the sidelong glances from the Queen of her own herd, which are most dear to her.
Due to the mixture of transitory emotions (*sañcāribhāva*) such as contraction, shame, despondency, and dejection, that [feeling] then became manifold and greatly intensified;

consequently, because of the excess of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) therein, she was not satiated. Having shown the illustration through its complete form, he states the illustration by means of a single part: "The virtuous ones" (*santaḥ*). Here, there is the striking with the arrows of side-long glances (*kaṭākṣa*).

At that time, Kṛṣṇa’s vision was entirely fixed upon her and his mind was completely absorbed in her, not even to a single degree on anyone else. Precisely because he perceived her lack of attention toward him, and thus no shame arose in her, she gazed with both eyes— meaning with her full vision— entirely of her own free will.
Therefore, she who beholds his face from all sides should be known as truly fortunate, for she alone rains down the arrows of her sidelong glances.
A certain woman, having taken him into her heart through the aperture of her eyes, closed them.
With their fingers bristling with horripilation, they were embraced by joy, like yogis overwhelmed by bliss.
Śrīdhara: "Having made it his heart" means having brought it into his heart. ||8||
*Vaṃśīdhara*: *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*—not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Having placed Him within the heart through the aperture of the eyes"—meaning, [He is] in her heart. Regarding Him...

In a clear medium, the supreme attachment of the original object (bimba) alone is indicated; therefore, due to her manifest emotion, she closed her eyes out of bashfulness, and with her limbs covered in horripilation from the power of that emotion, she remained for a long time as if embracing—meaning she remained just so, imitating an embrace. The phrase "like a yogi" is an illustration for the internal manifestation [of the experience].

Alternatively, "yogī" is an adverbial modifier meaning "in such a way as to be in yoga. She is tender with modesty due to the aforementioned reason; she is a good friend, one who has her lover under her control, and she is charming. Thus seven types have been described; the eighth, however, is mentioned in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman, filled with great joy, cried out, 'Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44). This [woman] is both sharp-witted and straightforward; herein, this must be analyzed: first, there is the emotion (*bhāva*) known as *rati* (love).

It is of two kinds: one consists of the lover’s lack of courtesy and so forth, arising from the sentiment of "belongingness to him" directed toward the self; the other consists of the self's stubbornness and so forth, arising from the sentiment of "belongingness to me" directed toward the lover, which makes the lover dependent on her. Thus it is.
Through the varying degrees of the mixture of these two states, other diverse states are also manifested.

Among these various states, there may be friendship between those of the same kind because of their agreeableness, while there may be enmity toward those of a different kind because of their disagreeableness. This applies specifically to states of the same kind.
Friendliness (*sauhṛdya*) may arise from merely wishing for the welfare of others due to some degree of agreeableness;

however, there would be neutrality (*taṭasthya*) toward those whose distinctions of genus and so forth are not very clear— either because they are excessively mixed or because they are extremely subtle—
due to the absence of a cause for focused attention.

For those women whose minds are inclined solely toward their respective individual emotions regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it is most appropriate that the arising of [their roles as] friends and so forth has Him alone as its root. Among the two primary emotions consisting of "His-ness" (tadīyatā) and "My-ness" (madīyatā), the latter is superior due to the greater intensity of possessive attachment (mamatā).
For indeed, there occurs an excess in the flow of profound love.

From that very cause, there arises the appearance of crookedness—which is another synonym for perversity (*vāmya*) and is a transformation (*vivarta*) of that [love]—according to the maxim of Bharata: "The movement of love, like that of a serpent, is naturally crooked" (*Uṇādisūtra* 15.102). Therefore...
Even a beloved husband may fall under her power; and thus Rudra says:
"The wilfulness of women, their elusiveness, and their resistance—that indeed, I consider, is the supreme weapon of the Five-Arrowed One. [Uṇī. 1.20]
As it is seen concerning Śrī Satyabhāmā in the *Śrī Hari-vaṃśa*:
"Endowed with beauty and youth, the queen, proud of her own good fortune and full of self-importance, fell under the sway of jealousy upon merely hearing [of Rukmiṇī]. (HV 2.65.50)
"Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, was the mistress of the household;
Satyabhāmā was the most excellent among women and excelled in good fortune. And thus it is said.
For this very reason, the description of the first four [wives] occupies half [of the space] each, while that of the latter three [occupies] the other half.

By the phrase "one by one," even a preference for [the first] is observed. Among these three, that very one which was described as "knitting her brow" is the most excellent, both because of the distinctiveness of its emotional state (*bhāva*) and because of its presentation at the outset;
moreover, such an entirely extraordinary state of being belongs to her alone when she abandons herself.

Since the Śrī Bhagavān himself manifested His own extraordinary excellence by bestowing His fortune upon her— who was brought into His own company through the renunciation of everything else— it must be she;
furthermore, among the first four, she alone is the eldest and most excellent because she stood at the forefront.

Surpassing all others from the very beginning through the touch of her beloved and because of her exceedingly sweet gestures toward those on the right, she is to be known as the counter-position (*prātipakṣikī*) to the one of a different nature who is the most excellent among the northern group. Now follows the consideration of these groups: therein, for the first of the northern group, there are two friends immediately following her.

However, for the first *prathamā*, there are two [cases] starting from the third case, which is separated by one; this is due to the similarity of their state (*bhāva-sāmyāt*) and because they abide on the left and right, following their respective positions. As for that which is the first *dvitīyā*, although it remains having entered within the end of the first group, it is indeed somewhat separated.

Furthermore, because her conduct transcends that [of the former], she should be understood as not a "friend" (*sakhi*) of the first type— due to her husband being dependent on others— but rather a "companion" (*suhṛd*) of the latter type due to some degree of similarity.
Now, as for the one mentioned in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, she does not belong to either of the two aforementioned categories because her emotional state is not very clearly defined.
And because they were not described by Śrī Śuka, they should be understood as merely peripheral.

Now follows an investigation into their names. In that regard, in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, within the context of the Malla-dvādaśī festival, during the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira, their names appear as follows:
O King of kings, learn from me the names of the gopīs according to their prominence:
Gopālī, Pālikā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā, Dhyānaniṣṭhikā, Rādhā, Anurādhā, Somābhā, Tārakā, and likewise Daśamī. Thus it is said.

In some readings, the name is given as *viśākhānyā* or *dhaniṣṭhikā*, and "the tenth" (*daśamī*) is also mentioned as a single name; this is recited at the very end because it is etymologically significant. Alternatively, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) means that the tenth star is also indeed named after [the goddess] Tārakā. Furthermore, this Gopālī must surely be the one who practices the *gāyatrī* as described in the *Padma Purāṇa*.

In the *Skānda-Prahlāda-Saṃhitā*, within the *Dvārakā-Māhātmya* during the section on the Lake of Māyā (*māyā-saraḥ*), regarding Uddhava’s return— just as upon the arrival of the Beloved himself— the eight names are specified along with expressions of that state, because one's own true nature is manifested even upon receiving a messenger of the Beloved.
However, because these are composed of extreme suffering, they are not to be seen on occasions of aesthetic rasa;
yet, since they may be required during moments of reflection, they are written here out of necessity, as follows:
Having heard those words of his, Lalitā was overcome with anger.
Then, with tears in her eyes, she spoke to Uddhava while weeping.
Śrī Lalitā said:
"He is untruthful, a transgressor of boundaries, deceitful, and fond of cruel people;
do not speak of that undisciplined soul in our presence."
Fie, fie upon him of sinful conduct! Fie upon that cruel-minded fool, who has abandoned the womenfolk and gone toward Dvāravatī!
Śrī Śyāmalā said:
"What use are these sorrow-inducing stories of that unfortunate one with his meager merit?
O friends, do not speak of him; tell other stories instead."
Śrī-Dhanya said:
"By whom was this messenger of the wicked man brought here? May that sinful wretch go by such a path that he shall never return again."
Śrī Viśākhā said:
He whose character, lineage, birth, and deeds are not known is a base man;
association with him regarding human goals is useless.
Śrī Rādhā said: For him who felt no fear of committing sin when killing Pūtanā,
O virtuous ones, there is not the slightest apprehension regarding the killing of a woman.
Śrī Śaibya said:
"Tell the truth, O fortunate one! What does the best of the Yadus do?
Surrounded by the women of the city, what conversation does he hold with us?"
Śrī Padmā said: O Uddhava, when will the mighty-armed descendant of Daśārha, beloved by the women of Nāgarī and possessing eyes as broad as lotus petals, come here?
Śrī Bhadrā said:
"Alas, Kṛṣṇa, best of cowherds! Alas, beloved of the gopīs!
O mighty-armed one, deliver the gopīs from the ocean of worldly existence! Thus she spoke.

Some, however, consider Candrāvalī alone to be among the eight and not Dhanyā, because of her extreme fame in the world. In that case, the view enumerating ten does not support a single meaning here due to the discrepancy in number; even between the two views that enumerate eight, the position favoring Dhanyā [is preferred].

It cannot be reconciled there, because among those five—Śrī, Lalitā, and the others—the left-hand [deities] are predominantly fierce (*prakhara*). Here, however, since it says "one frowns" (*bhrūkuṭim abadhyeti*), this would apply to only three;
thus, the position of Candrāvalī would be consistent, as she is the foremost of the right-hand group.

Or rather, because both groups— the left and the right— are to be established as having three members each, making six; and with the addition of the two others, Śyāmalā and Bhadrā, the number eight being thus completed, there would be perfect consistency.

This being the case, that first member of the subsequent group which was described as "the single frown" and so forth is indeed Śrī Rādhā herself, because she has reached the ultimate pinnacle of the excellence of supreme being.
Just as Rādhā is dear to Viṣṇu, so too is her lake dear to him.
"She alone among all the gopīs is the most beloved of Viṣṇu," according to the statement in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
[She is] Rādhā in the forest of Vṛndāvana, according to the *Matsya Purāṇa*, the *Skanda Purāṇa*, and others.
"The goddess Rādhikā, who consists of Kṛṣṇa, is declared to be the supreme deity."

"She should be meditated upon as holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, served by all the deities, consisting of all prosperity, possessing all beauty, the supreme enchantress"—thus it is stated in the *Bṛhad-gautamīya*. And:
"The Lord Mādhava is with Rādhā, and Rādhikā is indeed with Mādhava."
"Vibhrājante janeṣu" [is found] in the *Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa*;
and it has been described in that very same way by Umāpatidhara, the preeminent minister of the great king Lakṣmaṇasena and a companion of Śrī Jayadeva.
On the road, as he was being honored by one with the movement of her creeper-like eyebrows, by another with the opening of her eyes, and by another with the moonlight of her smile—
[he beheld] the face of Rādhā, which, though possessing the beauty of modesty, was characterized by pride, disdain, and a sense of distinction.

"The glances of the enemies of Kaṃsa, falling [upon Him], conquer the affectionate attachment of those who possess bliss. This was explained by my elder brothers, the illustrious Rūpa Mahābhāgavatas, in their commentary on the *Sthāyibhāva* (the permanent emotion) in the *Ujjvalanīlamaṇi*: "Therefore, that which is called 'Gāndharvī'..."
In the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpinī*, they consider that very [form] to be the primary one, based on the evidence of its preeminence.
In this *Prahlāda-saṃhitā*, it holds a middle position due to its skill in expression relative to the preceding texts.
And here, even on occasions of anger, there is a boldness manifested solely through specific divine pastimes (*līlā*).
The status of being "middle" (madhyā) is likewise the same when considered in relation to Bāhudhāriṇī and others.

Now, she who is described as a friend by the verse beginning with *atha yā aparānimiṣat* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.5) is understood to be Śrī Lalitā, due to the similarity in her stubbornness (*vāmya*) and intensity (*prākharya*). At present—
However,
due to the excessive joy arising from witnessing the agitation produced by the blow of the sharp glances cast by her own dear friend,
she is either the one recited as Rādhānurādhā in the *Bāhya* and *Uttara* [sections], or rather, she is simply another synonym for that same person.
And there, since the sequence of the verses and the names is understood to be in pairs, here too the equality of the groups is established;

furthermore, the primacy of the group of friends is attained because of the similarity in their attainment, as expressed in the opening words of the verse beginning with "Then a certain friend of hers [described him] through the aperture of her eye" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.8). Now, that friend of his was described in those words.

But she is generally Śrī Viśākhā herself, due to the similarity between her and [Viśākhā] in terms of both stubbornness and gentleness. In the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā* as well, that statement beginning with "not her character" (*na śīlam*) and so forth is exactly like that.
Now, she who is the first of the first group is indeed Śrī Candrāvalī; for:
The historical tradition regarding her preeminence shines forth alongside Śrī Rādhā; and thus the venerable Bilvamaṅgala says:
"Having come from the temple of Rādhā-mohana, he spoke to Candrāvalī."
"O Rādhā, is all well here? Hearing these words of his, Candrāvalī said, "Is Kaṃsa well, O you of bewildered heart? Where have you seen Kaṃsa?
And where is Rādhā? May Hari protect you—smiling and with downcast face, feeling abashed. Thus it is said.
Due to the predominance of similarity in meaning, this one might be known as Bhaviṣyottarā, or she may indeed be Somābhā.

Furthermore, she who was described by Śrī Rādhā’s friends in the passage beginning with "Then a certain second [gopī] of hers conceived... (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.32.4) would be Śyāmalā. In the Prahlāda-saṃhitā, among the group of Lalitā and the others—

Having entered [her confidence], one perceives her character through the giving of beneficial advice; for while friends engage in lamentation over shared sorrows, the act of offering beneficial counsel is seen to occur only when there is some degree of separation [from such emotional outbursts]. This very point was stated by the venerable Madhvācāryas:
The state known as *līlā* (pastime) is characterized by the manifestation of an internal intent directed toward the Beloved.

Now, regarding the two friends of Candrāvalī described in the verses "Then a certain one with folded palms" (*bhā.pu.* 10.32.5) and "One at His feet" (*bhā.pu.* 10.32.5), as well as those who stand on the bank in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:

These have been described in sequence as Śaibyā, Padmā, and Bhadrā; they are similar because, like servants, they desire to approach with humility and because their specific emotional states are not overly manifest.
This has been written, for the most part with logical reasoning, in accordance with the consensus of those of great spiritual stature.
In that matter, Kṛṣṇa and his followers were the masters of the course of policy.
They might feel abashment because of the names of my confidential pastimes;
let them, whose names have thus been concealed by the sage, forgive my rashness. (8)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: A certain woman, bowed down by qualities such as supreme modesty, being unable even to look directly at Him for a long time again and again, therefore closes her eyes— having taken Him into her heart through the gateway of the openings of her eyes— as if to experience His every bit of beauty with its manifestation throughout all her limbs within her mind.
For when one limb alone is grasped by the eyes, it is impossible for others even to appear in the mind;

or rather, as if out of fear that [the Lord] might depart through the gateway of the eyes. In reality, however, it is simply due to the nature of being completely overwhelmed by various forms of love. Therefore, having embraced him and drawn him close to her heart, she says:
From the word "ca" (and), it is understood that they were chanting "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Thus, it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa:
"A certain woman, seeing Govinda approaching, was filled with great joy;
she cried out 'Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.44).

Regarding the phrase "a certain [gopī] knit her brows," if only one gopī is explained here, then she should be understood as the eighth mentioned by Parāśara. Being utterly immersed in the rasa of bliss, she remained; the meaning is that she remained for a moment.
A yogi, through the yoga of concentration, has attained one-pointedness of mind upon the Blessed Lord. Thus...
And in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"A certain woman, having beheld Govinda, closed her eyes;
meditating upon his very form, she shone like one who had ascended to yoga. (*Viṣṇupurāṇa* 5.13.46).

The illustration refers merely to the absence of external mental activity; therein, by the phrase "through the aperture of the eyes," its distinction even from that state is indicated. Because it is a direct vision rather than a mere meditative visualization, it yields supreme bliss.
This has indeed been explained in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*. There too, it is said: "a certain [vision]..."

This is due to the particularity of their state as women. For this very reason, it is indicated that from embracing them, there arises a specific bliss even greater than from direct vision—both from the Lord’s associates and others, as well as from the group of Śrī Gopīs and others.
This is the general direction. I bow to Candrāvalī, Bhadrā, Padmā, and Śaivyā, in their respective order.
Śyāmā, Viśākhā, Lalitā, and Rādhā—these are her eight beloveds.

The reason for not mentioning their specific names has already been written previously. Although a great degree of gradation in their love is not possible— since each and every one of them reaches the highest pinnacle in that regard— nevertheless, in matters such as grasping [the Lord's] lotus-hands, theirs...

Their activity proceeds either according to their own inherent natures or according to their contemporary desires; nevertheless, just as with the liberated souls, the qualities, and the worshipful foremost associates of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha, so too among these [energies], by some manner of conceptualizing gradation, there are eight who are renowned as primary, and even among them—

Because the Goddess Śrī Rādhā is universally renowned for her preeminence and excellence above all, there is a vast abundance of her moods (bhāvas) and her various activities; it is for this very reason that they have been described separately in eight distinct ways—this is the general direction of the argument. ||8||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "A certain woman [pierced him] through the aperture of her eye," and so forth; though innocent, she was possessed of profound love. (8)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: For instance, in the verse "You are indeed not the son of the cowherd women" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.31.4), it was previously suggested that for the former [the *sakhī-rasa*], merely seeing [Kṛṣṇa] is required;
however, for this [the *vatsala-rasa*], there is a distinction due to the arising of a specific quality, while for the former, there is simplicity, as indicated by the sign "with unblinking eyes."
Out of innocence, a certain gopī remained at a distance, having abandoned the company of other gopīs who distracted her from meditation;

she was described as being so intent on grasping the beauty of every limb of Śrī Kṛṣṇa that, in his absence, she became devoid of all discernment. She held that Kṛṣṇa within her heart through the division of the beauty of all His limbs.
Having performed this and stabilized it in her own mind, he speaks there regarding the method of entry: "through the aperture of the eyes.

Again, she closes her eyes out of fear that [He] might depart externally; however, in reality, there is neither a continuous perception nor a specific aim within the transformation of her love, yet there is nonetheless her intense longing born of passion.
Her cleverness is indicated. By this, it is stated that the activities of all the senses are restrained within her own heart alone.

When Kṛṣṇa has entered her heart, an experience of all the objects of the senses arises while they remain within that very heart. Therefore, embracing Him, she remained in her heart alone, holding Him in an embrace, silently.

She became immersed in an ocean of bliss; for the meaning is that when the embrace occurred, her body was covered in horripilation such that even a spy could not perceive it. Unobserved by others, she experienced supreme bliss.
Indeed, one might ask: "How can there be the attainment of bliss without direct physical contact? To this, her own experience is the proof.
Is there a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that state even in the absence of external perception? The internal fullness of bliss is illustrated by the example of the yogi.

Just as a yogi becomes filled with inner bliss through the power of meditation (*dhyāna-yoga*) due to the absence of external sensation, so too this [state] is born of bliss and devoid of external perception.
And it was so, because there is an absence of pursuit of any further task; for indeed, when one is filled within with bliss, no desire whatsoever remains. ||8||

Viśvanātha: The sense is that she has brought this fickle lover to her heart, having taken him there out of good fortune, with the thought, "May he not depart again. And the sense of "closing [her eyes]" is that she does so out of the apprehension that he might escape once more through the very opening of her eyes. Thus, her limbs are covered in horripilation.

With the thought of attaining the unimpeded enjoyment [of union], "having embraced you"— this refers to the embracing performed by oneself— because of the departure of fortitude due to excessive thirst resulting from the attainment of the Great Joy (*mahāsukha*) subsequent to the joy of passion (*rati*), and because shame does not arise there since one has seen the nature of the world. These are indeed three.

Or, because she goes to the side of her beloved, she may think, "Let him come to us and meet us, but let us never go to him and meet him"; thus, due to her possessing the honey-like affection of selflessness, she is to be known as a "good friend" who has brought her beloved under her own control. Among those three types, the first is as follows:
The Queen of the circle (yūtheśvarī), who surpasses all the gopīs, has two companions, the second and third.

Thus, according to the perspective of Śrī Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī, the names of these seven are understood to be, in order: Candrāvalī, Śyāmalā, Śaivyā, Padmā, Śrī Rādhā, Lalitā, and Viśākhā. As for the eighth—

"Seeing Govinda approaching, a certain woman, filled with great joy, cried out, 'Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and uttered nothing else. According to this passage from the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, she should be understood as the one named Bhadrā.

These eight, whose names are renowned in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya* of the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā* as cited in the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*, should be known as the foremost among the three hundred million gopīs. If one desires to know the gradations of excellence among them, the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* should be consulted.
Śrī Rādhā alone is the foremost of all;
as it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "Just as Rādhā is dear to Viṣṇu, so too is her lake dear to Him. Among all the gopīs, she alone is the most beloved of Viṣṇu."
"The Goddess Rādhikā, the supreme deity, is said to consist of Kṛṣṇa;
she consists of all Lakṣmīs, is all-beauty, and is the supreme enchantress. Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhad-gautamīya*.
"By Rādhā, the god Mādhava [is manifested], and by Mādhava alone, Rādhikā."
And it should be understood from the statement in the *Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa*: "They shine forth among the people. (8)
All of them, finding supreme bliss in the sight of Keśava,
abandoned the torment born of separation, just as people do upon meeting a wise man.

Śrīdhara: Just as people seeking liberation reach the wise Lord; or just as worldly beings reach the wise knower of Brahman; or just as individual souls in the states of Viśva and Taijasa reach the wise state of deep sleep (sauṣupta). ||9||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: [not commented upon].
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:

*Krama-sandarbha*: Just as the conscious witness of deep sleep remains in deep sleep, so too, because of its hidden state, there is the suspicion that [the soul] might again abandon [the body] while possessed of ignorance. ||9||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, all those who were rendered beautiful by their various emotional states according to their respective natures abandoned the torment of separation upon seeing him; so he says, beginning with "all," etc., just as people [behave] toward a wise man.
The meaning is that by attaining a devotee of the Blessed One, one abandons the torment of separation from the Blessed One; it is just so. ||9||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: For this very reason, its excellence is stated in the conclusion; it is said that not only was the desire of these leaders of the groups fulfilled, but that of all of them as well—thus he says, "all. In this way, when the desired object has been attained by the leaders of the groups, [it is attained] by all of them.

Now, he shows the manner in which bliss was attained: those women who, as if fainted by the fire born of separation, were [restored] by Keśava—one who possesses excellent hair—or rather, by him who subdues *kāma*, the touch of *ka* (bliss); for he is explicitly called the "maddener of the mind-maddener" (*manmatha-manmatha*). Thus it is said at the outset.

It has indeed already been stated: "Having observed their intoxication with that good fortune and their pride, Keśava... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.48). Thus it is said that when their intoxication and pride had ceased, He manifested of His own accord. The sight of that Keśava, or the supreme delight caused by Him, was performed by Him.
