The meaning is that, through that supreme bliss, the virtuous women became tranquil and abandoned the fever born of separation, as if they had forgotten it.

This is because the teachers have explained that "the wise one" (*prājña*) refers to the Lord, or the knower of Brahman, or the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). Alternatively, having attained the "wise one"—that is, the knower of essence (*rasajña*)—people who desire to know that essence [attain their goal], just as...
In the same way, it abandons its heat. ||9||

Viśvanātha: People tormented by the cycle of worldly existence, scorched within their homes, and filled with despondency, [seek] the wise and supreme devotee, just as [one seeks] the arrival of people from the land of Acyuta at the onset of the rainy season; such is the description of the monsoon. (9)
O dear one, with those women whose sorrows had been dispelled, the Blessed One, Acyuta, the all-pervading Lord,
shone forth even more brilliantly, like the Supreme Person accompanied by his powers.

Śrīdhara: Just as the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), the Paramātman, [shines] through His powers such as Sattva and the rest; or else, as the practitioner (upāsaka) shines through knowledge, strength, heroism, and so forth; or else, as the latent person (anuśāyī puruṣa), enveloped by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as Prakṛti, shines forth with increasing splendor—so it is likewise here. 10.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not explained.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: Then, even the Blessed Lord [attained] supreme bliss.

He says "by them" (tābhiḥ) because an exceeding beauty has arisen through the manifestation of the Blessed One's essence. "By them" means by those whose grief—the internal torment born of separation—has been shaken off or destroyed; and that specific quality was described by Śrī Parāśara:
"Then Mādhava brought some to reconciliation with endearing words, some with glances and the knitting of his eyebrows, and others by the touch of his hand" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.13.30). Thus,
although the Blessed Lord Acyuta is complete in every respect, he is in that context somehow not subject to any lapse.
He especially delighted in them in such a way that each was more excellent than the one preceding it;
even for one such as He, the fact that they were likewise so is illustrated by the very manifestation of those [powers].
Thus he says: "The Person" means the Lord. Just as He, by means of His powers, [manifests] in the form of the Blessed One...

The meaning is that He shines forth even more intensely when surrounded by His own essential powers consisting of lordliness and the like, but not when covered by them in His form as Brahman; likewise, He too shone forth even more intensely when surrounded by those essential powers consisting of specific forms of divine love.

The address "Tāta" is used in the sense of supreme compassion. Since the word *tāta* has multiple meanings—referring both to one who is to be pitied and to a father—it is precisely because you are worthy of supreme compassion that I reveal this secret to you. (10)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, it is said with the words "by them" (*tābhiḥ*) that even for the Blessed Lord, a greater splendor arose through His supreme bliss and the manifestation of the essence of His divinity. Their specific quality is also described: they were those by whom sorrow—the internal torment born of separation—was shaken off, that is, destroyed.
Śrī Parāśara says: "Then Mādhava brought some to reconciliation with endearing words, some with glances and the knitting of his eyebrows, and others by the touch of his hand" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.13.30).

Therefore, although the Blessed One is endowed with all sovereign opulences, and although Acyuta is somehow, at any time, and from any cause free from falling away from His splendor, He shone— that is,
appeared— most excellently and specifically through them. Or rather, the word "Bhagavān" serves as the reason for His excellence in shining.

The meaning is: because by that very [act], the entirety of his own inherent divinity (*bhagavattā*) is manifested. For this very reason, he establishes through an illustration that even one who has reached the supreme pinnacle of all splendor shines even more intensely when surrounded by them—using the word "person" (*puruṣa*). [For] the individual soul (*jīva*), by virtue of being Brahman, is inherently...

Even though He is endowed with all powers, He shines forth even more intensely through those powers of the senses and so forth when they are manifested; otherwise, there would be a state equivalent to unconsciousness or the like. Likewise, His excellence is due solely to His being surrounded by the circle of His own beloveds through the manifestation of qualities such as sweetness and compassion.

For him too, there would be splendor; otherwise, even by virtue of being served by a multitude of devotees, there would follow the consequence of a complete fulfillment of the essence of the Lord’s nature, which consists of all-encompassing splendor—this is the direction of the argument. For this very reason, he is addressed as "Father" (tāta), either out of wonder or because of his fitness for that realization. Or else, it is due to the remembrance of Him.
Precisely through the helplessness caused by love, as before. ||10||

The sequence of the argument: The person (*puruṣa*) is the reality of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat-tattva*); he shines forth preeminently when surrounded by the forms of the Blessed Lord—that is, by his own essential powers (*svarūpa-śakti*) consisting of sovereignty and the rest—just as [the sun shines] when enveloped by its rays, but not when enveloped by those [powers] in the form of Brahman. Thus, he [shines] by means of them.
The meaning is that He shone forth even more intensely, surrounded by His own essential potencies consisting of the specific varieties of divine love. ||10||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, the Blessed Lord also spoke thus because He had not previously shone in that manner;
he says, "by them [He was] shaken," and so forth. The meaning of the sentence is that He shone by means of them.
"In a superior manner" means that previously He did not shine in such a way, due to His being alone.

In this regard, there is an illustration: just as a person whose powers are dormant does not shine forth in the same way as one whose powers are intensified, so too the Lord (Īśvara) does not manifest in that manner when His powers are dormant. By this, it is shown that the powers possess both a state of dormancy and a state of intensification; however, they never undergo destruction, because they are eternal. Thus it is said, "O Father."
An address [is made] when there is an excess of wonder and joy. ||10||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, by virtue of their association with Him whose distress has been dispelled, an excellence of splendor has arisen even in Śrī Kṛṣṇa; so he says: "by them" (*tābhiḥ*). By those who have abandoned intoxication and pride (*mada-māna*), and who have now had their grief shaken off by the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Free from the perception of unfulfilled purpose": the state of having one's aims unaccomplished is itself sorrow;

because that has ceased, a supreme radiance has arisen. For this very reason, he is "surrounded"—that is, encompassed—by those women who are fit for dalliance. Or else, [he is surrounded] by those through whom, by means of worshipping Kātyāyanī, dalliance preceded by the attainment of husbandhood [is achieved].

Having been entreated and requested for a vow, He granted a boon, promising: "You shall enjoy these nights with Me" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.29). Having acted upon that promise, He shone even more intensely than those who were eternally perfected; for although the Blessed Lord is distinguished by His divine sovereignty, He remained non-different from them.
Because he had accepted them, he shone even more through his sovereignty when chosen by them; for Acyuta is one whose affection never wavers toward them.
Alternatively, it refers to the enjoyment described previously [in the section on] "the stretching out of arms" and so forth, prior to the separation (vipralambha).

It shone even more intensely than that; for, through the *vipralambha* (separation), the fullness of the *sthāyībhāva* (permanent emotion) was revealed, indicating a weight of splendor. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the Sovereign (*īśvara*), does not [diminish] his capacity to benefit all through his illuminating powers (*śakti*) such as *māyā* and others, which are favorable to his body.

It shines forth; likewise. Or rather, the primordial person, the individual soul (jīva), being endowed with the powers of action, knowledge, and so forth, is resplendent; he becomes capable of attaining the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) beginning from heaven and ending with liberation.
In the absence of those [powers], he would be nothing at all; similarly, the Blessed Lord, though full of all desires, [would be nothing without His own essential nature].

Without union with the beauties of Vraja, He did not attain the ultimate pinnacle of sweet rasa during His disappearance; even though people were authorized to witness that rasa, they found no fulfillment until now, when they saw Him embraced by them. "Father"—this address is my own personal experience as I speak it.

"Pay close attention to that. Since the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is not attained by being alone, Śrī Śuka—associating with those women for the sake of increasing that flavor and with the intention of revealing his own vision—shone forth and spoke of his personal experience. ||10||

Viśvanātha: By means of their powers—the powers of all the senses—a person shines forth more intensely. However, when there is a deficiency in those powers, he does not shine as much; in the very same way, Kṛṣṇa also, when they are distressed, becomes distressed and does not shine as much. But when they are free from sorrow and possess great relish, [he shines even more].

"He too finds this even more pleasing. Just as for a person, pleasure consists solely in the happiness of his own senses and pain in the suffering of his own senses, so too for Kṛṣṇa, pleasure and pain arise solely from their pleasure and pain. Thus, His state of possessing love directed toward the gopīs and their being His very own essential nature (sva-svarūpa-bhūta) are established.
It has been made known in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, as follows:
"Sixteen thousand *gopīs* assembled there;
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, Janārdana, is indeed considered to be the *Haṃsa*."
O Goddess, these sixteen powers of his are proclaimed;
Kṛṣṇa is considered to be the form of the moon, while they are remembered as being the forms of its digits.
"Mālinī, the sixteenth digit, is their complete orb.
Of that sixteenth digit alone, there are sixteen fair-faced gopīs; each one of them is further divided individually into a thousand distinct forms. Thus it is said.
According to the scriptural statement that [the Lord] is surrounded by hundreds of millions of young women, there are thirty million *gopīs*;
among them, sixteen thousand are the principal *gopīs*; among those as well, one thousand are the most eminent;
and among those very ones, these eight are the most preeminent. Among even these eight—
Rādhā and Candrāvalī are the two most preeminent; even between those two, Śrī Rādhā is the most preeminent of all—this is the conclusion of the scriptures on devotion (bhakti-śāstra). ||10||
Taking them with him, the Lord went to the sandy bank of the Kālindī,
where the breeze was fragrant with blooming kunda and mandāra flowers and filled with bees.
Auspicious, with the darkness of its faults dispelled by the mass of rays from the autumn moon,
its soft sands were strewn about by the hands of Kṛṣṇā as she moved restlessly.
Śrīdhara: [It is] that [place] where bees are present because of the breeze made fragrant by blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers;

[it is] that in which the darkness of the night—the darkness of the faults—is destroyed by the masses, the multitudes, of the rays of the autumnal moon; therefore, it is auspicious (*śiva*), bringing happiness. By means of hands...

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: he shone even more, surrounded by them, having taken them to such a sandy bank (*pulina*) which was covered and strewn with soft sand by the rolling waves (*tarala*), and having enjoyed it with them. ||12||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: [not commented upon].
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
Regarding the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*, he states "having taken them up" (*tāḥ samādāya*) and so forth to explain what was done that caused it to shine.

By two [verses]. Having composed those [two verses] and entered the sandy bank of the Kālindī, this is the primary introductory lamp (ādi-dīpaka). He qualifies that [lamp]: where the breezes are fragrant with blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, and where bees cling to them, thinking, "Kṛṣṇa will come here and play"; thus, for the sake of Kṛṣṇā...

In this verse, he describes the specific excellence of the ground which shone forth, where the soft sand was properly swept and smoothed with her hand so that it became as shimmering as possible, delighting those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*rasika*).
He states what she did for the sake of the *rāsa*-dance play, beginning with the word "tā" (they). Of those [gopīs]...

In order to dispel their pride and arrogance, He remained concealed; then, taking them up with a hand-holding and other gestures imbued with the sentiment of laughter and the touch of His nails, He grasped them perfectly.
Desiring to make even more spacious that very sandbank where the singing had been performed, He shone forth.
The connection is with the preceding [verse] alone. By the word "of the Kālindī," the abundance of the flow of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is indicated.
By the word "the Lord" (*vibhu*), His capacity is expressed through His presence everywhere and His honoring of all [the gopīs].
Because the riverbank is an excitant (*uddīpana*) of the erotic sentiment, it is fit for the playful pastimes of the *rāsa*.

He specifies [the nature of the breeze] with the word "blooming" (*vikasat*). The *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers are blooming; by that fragrant breeze, the bees are drawn. Through its connection with the Kālindī, the coolness of the wind is expressed;
through its connection with the *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, its fragrance is expressed; and due to its proximity to the forest, its intoxicating quality is expressed. By this—
Thus, the perfection of the conditions that most intensely inflame [the passion] has been indicated. ||11||

Describing how this entire collection [of factors] kindles desire, he speaks of its brilliance: "In autumn," and so forth. The mass—that is, the multitude—of the rays of the moon belonging to the autumn season;
by that, the darkness of the night (*doṣātamaḥ*) is destroyed. By this, [he indicates] the autumnal season.

Brilliance and the quality of being a cause for clarity are indicated. The fullness and brilliance of the moon are also indicated. By the name "Kṛṣṇā" and by similarity of color, her assistance in playful dalliance and her companionship are indicated. Regarding the word "hastā," they are tremulous like hands.
In which [place] the waves were covered by them, and where the soft sand was marvelous for its lack of unevenness (neither high nor low);
by this, it is indicated that due to its softness, it provides comfort to the feet merely by touch. ||12||

Viśvanātha: And then, having properly taken them by means of laughter, grasping their hands, and so forth, and having enjoyed them and entered the sandy bank (*pulina*), she shone—this is to be connected with the preceding [verse]. He describes the sandy bank with a half-verse:
from the breeze fragrant with blooming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, the bees...
In which [place] that [darkness] exists— wherein the coldness of the wind is [diminished] by its connection with the sandy banks, its slowness by its being the abode of bees,
and the darkness of the night (doṣā) is destroyed by the masses of rays from the autumnal moon;
which is therefore auspicious and pleasant, and strewn with the flickering waves of the Yamunā that serve as her hands.
That in which the sand is soft. ||11-12||
With the pain of their hearts dispelled by the joy of seeing him,
they reached the fulfillment of their desires, just as the Vedas reach their ultimate goal.
With their own upper garments, marked by the saffron from her breasts, they prepared a seat for their kinsman.

Śrīdhara: "And they reached the end of their desires; they became fulfilled in their wishes. [The phrase] "just as the Vedas" means this: just as in the Karma-kāṇḍa the Vedas, not seeing the Supreme Lord, become as if incomplete due to their attachment to various desires, but in the Jñāna-kāṇḍa, [having seen] the Supreme Lord...

"Having seen that, they become filled with joy and likewise abandon their attachment to desires. He says "by their own [desires]" to show that even those whose desires were already fulfilled worshipped Him out of love. "Acīkÿpan" means they fashioned [offerings]. "To the inner controller (antaryāmin), the kinsman of the self. ||13||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: [not commented upon].
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:

*Krama-sandarbha*: Regarding the phrase "tad-darśaneti," the analysis of the compound begins with "by the sight of that Lord, who is characterized by a particular eagerness for play. It refers to the arrival there together with Him who is of such a nature.
The long-lasting state consisting of the *rāsa*-pastimes and so forth has been determined, as the previous doubt has been dispelled;

furthermore, the attainment of supreme bliss has also occurred, as he says: "to the end of their desires. In this regard, there is an illustration: "just as the Vedas [attain their goal]. Through the experience of those pastimes, [this occurs] in both cases.
The phrase "because of having achieved the supreme goal" indicates the object of comparison, which is made manifest by the word "yathā" (just as). ||13||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Having observed Śrī Kṛṣṇa desiring to sit down after arriving there, they all prepared a seat; thus he says, beginning with "tad-darśana... (at the sight of Him). The word "tāḥ" (they) is to be supplied.
They caused a seat to be fashioned for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their own kinsman. By what means? By their own upper garments (*uttarīya*).

Each one individually drew out her upper garment, placed it one above the other, and made a very high seat; such is the significance of the plural number. Of what kind were they? Marked with the saffron from their breasts. By this, the worship of the seat is also expressed. The meaning is that because the seat was so high, it was easy for everyone to look upon [the Lord]. Of what kind were they?

With the pain of their hearts shaken off by the joy of seeing Him, there is an illustration regarding this state of having the heart's pain shaken off: "Just as the Vedas reached the end of their desires. The Vedas—that is, the Upaniṣads devoted to the Blessed Lord—just as they reached the goal consisting of attaining His lotus feet after practicing for a long time.
The gopīs reached the end—that is, the fulfillment—of their desires by means of his form as Kṛṣṇa;

the meaning is that they became such that even the pain in their hearts was shaken off. It should not be thought that all of them were left without upper garments because he fashioned seats from their own *uttarīyas*; for at that very moment—
By means of yogic illusion (yogamāyā), the upper garment was produced as before. ||13||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now he describes their activities as manifested through love, beginning with the words "Upon seeing Him" (*tad-darśana*).

Their dust of the heart—the afflictions of the pain born of separation—has been shaken off and destroyed at its very root by the joy and bliss arising from the sight of Him, even though their minds were slightly intoxicated [by that vision]. Or else:

Their vision, knowledge, and deliberation— meaning their determination that "this is the place suitable for the *rāsa*, in this very forest such a pastime must be performed, and here in the Yamunā such a water-sport must be performed"—
had completely destroyed the pain in their hearts; from this point forward...

The meaning is that they harbored the constant thought, "He will not be born. Their desires reached their limit—that is, they attained the ultimate peak of all longings—due to the certainty regarding the future event.
Just as the Vedic hymns (*śruti*), while not perceiving the Lord in the section on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*), remain distressed.
In the section on knowledge (jñāna-kāṇḍa), it is said that having seen the Lord, they reach the end of their desires and become those whose desires are fulfilled;
or rather, the Śrutis, having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who eternally dwells there, stands in the midst of that assembly, and possesses the form of a youth—desired Him. Then...
A boon was granted to them: "In the former Sārasvata Kalpa, you shall become gopīs in Vraja.

Those very girls, who were of the nature of the Upaniṣads, have been born [again]. Just as these [gopīs] reached the end of their desires—that is, the conclusion or fulfillment of their longings—and became those whose every wish was satisfied, so too shall it be for others.
All her desires, though seemingly endless, reached their fulfillment because this rāsa-vilāsa was performed by Him.

For this very reason, she had them prepare a seat with their own upper garments—fine and soft—which they placed upon her breasts. She speaks of the purpose for arranging the seat out of a desire to know [His intent].
Because they had desired to ask something, their breast-saffron was marked by the water of perspiration born from the exertion of searching;
for this very reason, it is said "marked by the saffron of the breasts. Alternatively, it is because the upper garments were moistened by streams of tears shed due to the pain of separation.
The fact that [the Lord] is marked with the saffron of her breasts is mentioned; by this very fact, her own extreme devotion is also indicated.

Now, one might ask: "If he is to be worshipped as the object of affection appropriate for his dignity, then how is it that she prepares a seat for him with her own upper garments? To this, he says: "to her own kinsman" (ātma-bandhave). And the self...

To Him who is the cause of kinship (*bandhutva*) and the bond of love that reaches its ultimate limit; or rather, to Him who binds His own mind, uniting it within Himself; or else, to the intimate kinsman of the *ātman*, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). For this very reason, the conception of His seat is [the seat] of consciousness alone.

Alternatively, based on the indicative mark "marked with the saffron of her breasts," the meaning is that she imagined her own passion itself to be his seat under the guise of the saffron from her breasts. ||13||

Viśvanātha: Regarding that, he describes their loving service, which is appropriate for friends: with the bliss of seeing Kṛṣṇa, all the mental sorrows of the beauties of Vraja were dispelled; they [offered] to Him, their own kinsman, their own upper garments—the very fine cloths situated above the bodices of their breasts.

They prepared a seat such that even the great Upaniṣads, which are the very source of sacred revelation, reached the limit and the ultimate pinnacle of their desires— attaining that state beyond which no further desire can exist. Seeing this, we too, having become gopīs in Vraja, [long for it].

The meaning is that they became filled with longing, thinking, "When shall we sport together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa in this way, by offering Him garments moistened with the kuṅkuma from our own breasts? For this very reason, the Śrutis performed intense austerities to manifest their following after Him in order to attain the state of being gopīs.
The story of Bṛhat and Vāmanī:

"O Lord of Serpents, our minds are fixed upon Your staff-like arms; we too are equal to them, for those who see with equanimity find the nectar of the lotus feet of the Equal One. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.23)
And their statement is as follows:

"In that regard, those Vedic scriptures who had previously witnessed the descent of Kṛṣṇa and thus attained their long-cherished desire became the gopīs in this present kalpa; at this time, however, it is these [gopīs] who have attained their desire."
It should be understood that in the next kalpa, the Vedas will become gopīs because of the infinity of the Vedas. ||13||
There the Blessed One sat down; that Lord had his seat prepared within the hearts of the masters of yoga.
Having entered the assembly of the cowherd women and being worshiped, He shone,
bearing a form that was the singular abode of the splendor of the three worlds.
Śrīdhara: Having arrived at the assembly of the gopīs and being honored by them, he shone, that is, he was resplendent;
for his body was the sole abode and locus of all the beauty and splendor found throughout the three worlds, which he displayed as he revealed it. (14)
Vaṃśīdhara:
*The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "On a seat imagined within the heart of Yogeśvara," and so forth.
The meaning is that even though he was in such a state, he shone while seated there upon a cloth stained with the saffron from the breasts of the cowherd girls.
The meaning is that he does not shine while seated within the heart of the Lord of Yoga (Kṛṣṇa).

Regarding this, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested: he appears as if bearing a physical form—the very embodiment of the sole abode of the Fortune of the Three Worlds (*trailokya-lakṣmī*). That is, he is like the primary abode or the very resolve (*vyavasāya*) of the Fortune of the Three Worlds personified. Alternatively, he is the sole abode of the Fortune of the Three Worlds in the form of the bodies of the cowherd girls (*gopī*).
The states [of mind] are "embrace" and so forth. The meaning is that he was honored by them, as if with the flowers of words blossoming through affectionate jests. ||14||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbha*: these have not been commented upon [here].

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, it is said that while seated upon that throne, the Blessed Lord shone forth exceedingly; this is expressed by the words beginning with "tatra" (there). Seated there on that throne, the Blessed Lord was radiant. Of what nature was He?
"Gopī-pariṣad-gataḥ" (joined by the assembly of gopīs) is a qualifying attribute based on a specific cause; "arcitaḥ" means He was honored and treated with hospitality by them.

The meaning is that for one whose seat has been fashioned within the heart by the lords of yoga, because it is a mental construction, it does not shine there in that manner. What is it like? To this he says: "the body which is the sole, primary station and mark of the Fortune of the Three Worlds"—that is, the body which is the very sign of the splendor of the three worlds.
"Carrying" (*dadhat*) means "bearing" (*dadhāna*). Or rather, "assuming a form" (*vapuḥ dadhat*) means "assuming a physical body" (*vapuḥ dadhānam*), that is to say, being embodied.

Such a one is the "sole abode of the Fortune of the Three Worlds" (*trailokya-lakṣmy-eka-padam*), meaning the singular embodiment of the splendor of the three worlds. [The word] *pada* is used in the senses of resolve, protection, place, fortune, foot, and object.
Thus, from the section on words with multiple meanings. ||14||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Otherwise, he might disappear once again; therefore, having sat upon that seat, the Blessed One—even setting aside his own divine nature as the Lord of lords and casting aside his sovereignty—shone and glowed, having entered the assembly of the gopīs. On all sides...
The gopīs sat in a circular formation, and the Blessed Lord sat in their midst as the presiding master of the assembly.

Alternatively, "Bhagavān" means one who possesses *bhaga*, which is fortune; otherwise, the upper garments of the gopīs would not have served as a special seat for such exquisite aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Of what nature is this Lord? He is possessed of inconceivable power (*acintya-śaktimān*); otherwise, [this would not be possible].

It may be that [the Lord] honors ten million groups with a single body. Although He is easily accessible to the gopīs, He is difficult for others to attain; thus, even by the great lords of yogis—the perfected ones such as Sanaka and others—He is conceived through meditation as if in their very hearts, and there too, He has prepared a seat.

This refers to Him in His state of manifest glory (*vaibhavāvastha*), and not to His direct essential nature (*svarūpa*). Alternatively, the Blessed Lord is called "Īśvara" because He was worshipped by them due to being the son of the King of Vraja, and honored through the massaging of His hands and feet, playful smiles, and so forth; for previously, having been disregarded due to pride and arrogance, they had abandoned Him when He departed.
Now, being highly esteemed due to the fear that [the Lord] might vanish, he possesses a body that is the sole abode of the splendor of the three worlds— namely,
the splendors from the upper limit of Vaikuṇṭha throughout the three worlds,
the splendors from the lower limit of Pātāla, and the splendors upon the earth throughout Bhūrloka.

And among all those [beauties], He assumes that single foot, place, and form; the meaning is that there is no other place in the three worlds for such excellence of splendor, which is the very essence of all things. As it has been said in this very same work: "This is the fruit for those who possess eyes" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.21.7). ||14||

Viśvanātha: There, he sat down upon many cloth seats placed one above another, which had been prepared by them for each of their respective groups individually. [An objection: "But how can one person sit upon that many seats? To this, he says: "The Lord."

The reason why He possesses self-manifestation unperceived by each of those [seats] is that the Blessed Lord is "possessed of *bhaga*"; according to Amara, *bhaga* refers to fortune, desire, and majesty. Having perceived his desire to sit upon all those seats, by His sovereign power alone, through the medium of *yogamāyā*, that many manifestations [appeared].

The meaning is that they have been revealed. Furthermore, he is one whose seat—difficult to obtain in the three worlds, unimpaired, and priceless—has been fashioned within the very core of the heart by the lords of yoga, such as Śeṣa, Śaṅkara, and others, because it was brought there by the mind alone. By these [qualities]...
On a seat prepared right outside his heart with the garments and fragrant substances discarded from his own body, he sat and shone forth; indeed,

that Blessed One himself, who is accessible only through hymns of praise and the like on the shores of the Ocean of Milk and other sacred sites, was present there amidst an assembly of Brahmā, Rudra, and others.

Manifesting in the mind, though remaining beyond direct perception for a mere moment, that very Acyuta—who is free from any falling away—himself went to the assembly of the gopīs and remained there even for a long time.
In the reading "arcitaḥ," it means he was honored with betel, playful smiles, side-long glances, and so forth. To do what?

Has He gone? Even while bearing that very body which is the sole, non-dual abode and support for the various splendors and riches of all things— from the ordinary and extraordinary worlds of the lower, middle, and upper realms, down to the infinite portions of His own self— He has gone to those gopīs.
Nourishing [the assembly] with the sweetness of his limbs, luster, smiles, side-long glances, and so forth; or rather, remaining seated right there,
distinguished by such a manner of sitting and so on, having mentally prepared a seat within the hearts of other masters of yoga (*yogeśvara*),
from that very moment he was surrounded by masters of yoga such as Mahārudra and others, situated in the midst of the circle of gopīs.

The meaning is that Kṛṣṇa was brought into his own heart through meditation as he was specifically distinguished by such a posture, such splendor, and various playful conversations and the like. ||14||
Having honored that Anangadīpana with playful glances and the graceful movement of her eyebrows accompanied by a smile, she— (o)0(o)— [honored him].
Having praised him by touching his hands and feet, which bore the marks [of royalty], they spoke while being slightly provoked to anger.
Śrīdhara: [They were] characterized by the eyebrows, which possessed a playful grace through a glance full of smiling charm; [and they were affected] by contact, that is, by being massaged. ||15||

Vaṃśīdhara: Having honored—that is, having paid respect to—that Kṛṣṇa; [he is] the kindler of the bodiless god of love (Anaṅgadīpana), who inflames desire; by massaging the feet and hands placed upon his lap or bosom;
having praised—that is, having extolled him; "slightly angry" refers to the smallness of their anger due to the very nature of the abundance of their love.

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "Having praised" means that even when they were angry, out of fear of abandoning [the Lord], they spoke only after first offering proper praise; though inwardly enraged, they spoke with only a few words. ||15||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And therein, by way of their affectionate nature, he describes the arising of their concealed anger: "Having honored him"—meaning, having respected him in the manner previously described—"they spoke," the word "they" being understood as the subject. Being of what sort? To that he says: "slightly angry. But surely, such [anger]...
If they have already been honored, how then could they allow even a slight lapse?
To this he says: "an inflamer of the bodiless one" (anaṅgadīpanam). The meaning is that it manifests various amorous sports for the sake of inflaming him.
[The implication is: having previously abandoned her and departed, he now behaves in such a manner.
The sense is: "by reflecting upon the nature of our affection.

Now, since it had already occurred that her own [garment]—by virtue of being covered by the saffron-stained cloth from her breasts—served to kindle his passion, why did he ask about its power to kindle that [passion], in order to manifest his anger even though it was already present?
How do they deserve [this]? To this he says: "Having praised by touching the hands and feet marked with the signs.

With such [intent], preceded by those various touches, He—whose faults are manifest—would appear to be one whose own voice praises His manifold qualities; thus, by means of such a play of the eyebrows which reveals crookedness of mind...
The meaning is that his crookedness has become manifest. The intention is that this crookedness will become evident through the sequence of questions;
thus, the transitory state (sañcārī) called *avahitthā* is manifested. As it has been said regarding the *anubhāva*:
"Concealment (*avahittha*) is said to be the state [of mind] for the purpose of hiding. *Avahittha* is also feminine in gender.
Likewise:
"There may be a certain cause, something to be concealed, and someone who conceals it."
Thus, the application of these three internal states (bhāvas) is observed here.

As for the cause (*hetu*) here: when there is crookedness (*kauṭilya*), it is indeed jealousy (*asūyā*) consisting of resentment (*amarṣa*). It is called "concealment" (*gopana*) because one conceals by means of it; and that [jealousy] is present here in such a manner through various touches and praises.

The deceit of joy and the deceit of intellect, along with their simultaneous occurrence, are both made manifest by this very [act]. Thus, here too, it is the majesty of *yoga-māyā* alone that is displayed, because such behavior occurs through all [faculties] simultaneously. The dual number in "of the feet and hands" applies to each individually.
With respect to genus. ||15||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Having honored" (*sabhājayitvā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of the question, intended to express the honor properly; or rather, it means "having especially honored.
For [the Lord] kindles even desire—which was previously limbless (*anaṅga*, devoid of limbs)—by making it possessed of limbs (*sāṅgīkṛtya*), and thus causes it to shine forth even more than before.

The meaning is that it thus increases their intense passion (*kāndarpa*) to the utmost. Therefore, regarding his feet and hands—whether they were placed on their laps by them, or by him upon theirs—the meaning is "of the foot and the hand," or alternatively, "of the foot and of the two hands. [This was done] through a thorough touch.

By means of various sequences, slowly and with gentle massage, thus too was sovereignty displayed as before. Having thoroughly praised by means of all [the fingers] through the simultaneous contact of either both limbs or four [fingers], it was for the sake of a specific question and for the sake of obtaining its answer.

"Slightly angry" means that the anger was slight due to the very nature of the abundance of love; or else, because it was internal, it was unmanifest externally; or rather, they spoke "briefly," that is, concisely, because of their supreme eloquence.
And thus, they were "angry" because of the experience of prior suffering; or else, [because of] his...

Because it prescribes an excess of speech; or rather, because without anger, due to a lack of understanding his intention, no reply could be obtained from her heart—this is the general direction. The rest has been explained by them. Or else, having kindled the bodiless god (Kāma) with such a frown; or perhaps, having honored him with that very [frown], by means of those [women].
With the intention that such honoring of him alone is appropriate, he says "anaṅga" (bodiless). This should also be understood as a reason for his anger and his speech. ||15||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, after Śrī Kṛṣṇa had sat down upon that seat, they questioned Him slightly while first caressing His hands, feet, and so forth; this is stated in the passage beginning with "Having honored [Him]," and so on.

Having honored and gratified Him by the touch of His hands and feet— He who held Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon His lap— and having offered praises, they spoke only a few words, as if out of fear of losing Him; yet in truth, being inwardly angry, they spoke but little.
It is of great significance. Of what nature is it? It is the kindler of the bodiless god (Anaṅga) through the playful movement of her eyebrows and her smiling, amorous glances.
"Anaṅga" means that which is not a limb; "Aṅgī" refers to the body, and thus it is the kindler of love for that [body]. ||15||

*Prīti-sandarbha*: Regarding the concealment of the outward appearance [of anger]: “Having honored him, who kindles the god of love” (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.32.15), and so forth. Here, the covering of anger is achieved through acts such as honoring. (353)
Now, in the interval between those two, there is the separation characterized by jealous anger (*māna*). Regarding this, it has been said:
"The course of love is naturally crooked, like that of a serpent;
for this reason, jealous anger arises in young lovers both with cause and without cause" (Uṇī. 15.102).
Likewise:

"That which is called 'measure' (māna) because of the statement 'not this, not this' regarding the causeless [Brahman], its very cultivation would be the supreme state of measure. [Uṇī. 15.76] Thus it is said.

Then, since there are these two divisions—namely, that which has a cause and that which is causeless—the cause is also stated as follows: "When a lover brings about a distinction in one who is otherwise the opposite of jealous and so forth, this emotion, primarily characterized by affection, attains the state of *īrṣyā-māna* (jealous anger). [Uṇī. 15.77] Thus it is said.
And as it is said:
"Without affection there would be no fear, and without intimacy there would be no jealousy; therefore, this form of pride reveals the love between the two. (Uṇī. 15.78)
Therefore, in the Harivaṃśa it is said:
"As if imagining that the Goddess was angry, and as if out of affection,
the joy of the Yadus entered very slowly, trembling with great fear."
"Endowed with beauty and youth, the queen, proud of her own good fortune and full of self-conceit, fell under the sway of jealousy upon merely hearing [of the other woman].
Therefore, based on the inference of a breach in the affection shown by the beloved, this becomes "jealousy-pride" (*īrṣyā-māna*) along with its cause. And this...

Even for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, His pastimes are the source of supreme bliss; as He Himself said to Śrī Rukmiṇī: "O lady, desiring to hear Your words, I wish to see Your playful conduct [Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.60.29] and Your face, with its lips quivering from the intensity of love [Bhāgavatapurāṇa...]"

And so forth. Furthermore, her lack of distraction even toward Śrī Rukmiṇī is evident in passages such as, "O elder brother of Gada, your speech is dull-witted" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.40) and others.
And this is appropriate, because one perceives that state of being [toward Kṛṣṇa] as something that nourishes the love known as the absence of any other beloved.

And because it is approved by the tradition of both ancient and modern poets, the emotion known as *māna* (pride/resentment) is indeed worthy of respect. In this regard, due to the simultaneous abandonment of all [other emotions] and the primacy of *saṅga* (attachment), even a trace of that *māna* arose in a concealed manner among the queens of Vraja during the *rāsa*-dance. And that—
It should be understood as being caused solely by renunciation and jealousy—as in the passage beginning with "having honored," and so forth.

(384) *Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, their minds having been previously corrupted by the instruction on dharma, they harbor a hidden resentment born of love, thinking in their hearts, "This is mere scholarship in giving advice to others," while appearing as if they were desirous of knowing the dharma.

Being unable to speak directly of his fault with their own mouths, they remained silent; now [the author] describes the preliminary stage consisting of their inquiry, beginning with the words "Having honored..."— having honored him in the manner previously described by themselves, [they addressed] that Kṛṣṇa.

The "inspiring of passion" (*manu-gāpanam*) has been described. By means of a playful, smiling glance and a wandering brow—meaning by that brow which wanders, moving here and there, while accompanied by a playful, smiling glance—in that context of inflaming desire, there are five instruments like the five arrows of Kāma: laughter (*hāsa*), playfulness (*līlā*), the glance (*īkṣaṇa*), the wandering (*vibhrama*), and grace (*vilāsa*).

And "the brow" (*bhrū*) refers to the place of non-perception among these four; the meaning is the manifestation of various graceful gestures (*vilāsa*) for the purpose of kindling desire. By means of these instruments, one constantly kindles the bodiless one (*anaṅga*) into a state of being a limb—that is, a lack of concern for one's own body—or alternatively, even though he is bodiless...

It illuminates even that which is devoid of limbs by manifesting it through the state of being possessed of limbs. For this very reason, through the contact of the feet and hands placed upon the lap— meaning those feet and hands set there by her— and through the manifestation of various kinds of clever artistry...
By massaging with the soft hands of one who destroys fatigue, and by praising his virtues through eulogy—
surely, for what reason should even such honor, praise, and extreme respect be suspected regarding the subject at hand?
If it is asked, "Let the duties pertaining to the playful amorous sport (*rāsa-vilāsa*) be performed," they respond there,
concealing their own intentions and slightly provoked: "What is the use of this playfulness?"— the particle *nu* here implies reasoning—
and having reflected within their own minds that it is indeed nothing but suffering, they manifest its faults upon their own faces.
Thinking that their amorous play would thereby become more firm, they spoke as if manifesting a slight pout of affection;
or rather, at that moment, having honored him with playful glances and the graceful movement of their eyebrows accompanied by smiles.

"That itself is the true honor. This has been stated in this very same work: "Having attained that honor, he entered the cow-pen with bashfulness, laughter, and humility, casting glances from the corners of his eyes" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.15.44).
Laughter, playful gestures, glances, and so forth, however, serve as concealers of anger. Or rather, in this way, with his whole being...
Thinking, "You abandon even those who have sought refuge," they spoke as if in dispute, slightly provoked by their perception of a fault in Kṛṣṇa, and they questioned him. ||15||

Viśvanātha: Consequently, he describes the behavior of those women who desired to give pleasure to him as he was desirous of sporting—beginning with the words "having honored. With a brow characterized by playful movement (*vilāsa*) through a glance full of smiling grace, he [or they] illuminated his own passion, which kindles the god of love (*anaṅga*), or rather, that which inflames their own desire.
Having honored him with feelings appropriate for that occasion and having shown him respect, she— thinking, "He previously abandoned us and departed,
yet now he behaves in this manner"— in order to conceal her feigned anger (*praṇaya-kopa*),
[touches] his feet and hands, which were formerly placed upon her lap or held by her in her own lap.
Having praised him by touching him— "Oh, how unprecedented is the coolness of your hands and feet,

since by their touch our burning heat is extinguished! Therefore, you are truly one who has never known the suffering of torment, always happy, and indeed free from affliction"— this was a slight [insinuation] through the figure of speech known as "ironical praise" (*vyājastuti*).
The meaning is that, by the very nature of the bliss arising from seeing him, their anger was destroyed and only a remnant of their state as Bhagavats remained. ||15||
The gopīs said:
"O One, You reciprocate with those who worship You; O One, You do the opposite with others;
and O One, You do not even reciprocate with both. Please tell us this clearly."

Śrīdhara: There, wishing to demonstrate the Lord’s ingratitude by means of His own words, those of hidden intent ask about worldly affairs as it were: "They worship" (bhajataḥ). [This refers to] living beings who worship.
"Afterwards" (anu) means subsequently. Some worship in accordance with their previous devotion to Him; others do this.
Just as the opposite occurs, so too do others, even though they do not rely on those [qualities], come to rely on them because of their association with them; yet others rely on neither. ||16||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: [not commented upon].
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Krama-sandarbha*. In that regard, those desiring to establish the Lord's hardness of heart ask: "He worships" (verse 16).

The Composition of the Great Sequence: To the question "What is that?", he says: "They worship," and so forth. In these few words, there are three questions. O Blessed One! May it be well with you; tell us this—speak so that it becomes clear. Some follow those who worship; others do the opposite.

The ellipsis is "they act. "They resort to those who do not resort [to them]" means they resort to them. Others do not resort to either those who resort [to them] or those who do not resort [to them]. "But you do not resort to us, even though we resort to you"—this is a question full of longing, directed toward the goal to be accomplished, expressed with feigned indifference (*avahitthā*).
The question is formulated by combining [the two]. ||16||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having reflected upon three alternatives in their minds, they ask: "They worship" (*bhajante*).
Do they worship in accordance with the one who worships (*bhajataḥ*)? Some worship even the one who does not worship (*abhajataḥ*), which is the opposite of that.
Others do not worship either the one who worships or the one who does not worship. To whom do these three questions refer?

"Please tell us this clearly, so that it may be well understood: who are the qualified candidates here, what is their fruit, and how great is their renown? Having analyzed all of that, speak to us in such a way that it becomes perfectly clear. The address "O! (*bho*) is used to indicate friendship.
Or rather, their names are not mentioned because they are exceedingly dear.
In that regard, according to their devotion, as for those who worship: are they rogues or are they truly authentic?
For example, suppose someone performs a foot-massage for another, and that other person [also] acts toward him...

If one performs the massaging of the feet, what would be the fruit? In the view that "this very thing must be done," there is the fruit of that alone and nothing else. However, an independent action, not partaking in doubt as it were, will not be undertaken. Even in the undertaking of a determined matter, a fault sometimes occurs, as for example:

The example is that the service of a desireless yogi is like the service of a lustful woman; in this regard, it is evident that the fruit is determined as being sometimes a benefit, sometimes a desired object, and sometimes merit. It must also be stated what the fruit is for one who does not serve him when he is being served.

Viśvanātha: In this regard, they reflected within their own minds as follows: "Since today this crest-jewel of lovers has brought us to such a wretched state, he himself must be questioned thus: 'O Kṛṣṇa! Do you have affection for us, indifference, or hostility? These are the three possibilities.'"

Even these possible positions, when examined, do not hold together. Herein, is this love conditioned (*sopādhi*) or unconditioned (*nirupādhi*)? It cannot be the first; for one who possesses conditioned love surely gratifies those people who fulfill his own desires, rather than alienating them. You, however, [have cast] us into the fire of your own separation...

You have indeed burned [us] for the sake of killing; nor were you indifferent, because you abandoned us in the midst of the terrible forest at night, which would not have caused you fatigue even though you were a witness to our suffering;
nor was it apathy, since you were seen to be the one who brings about our happiness and sorrow; nor was it malice—is that something permanent?

Is it based on hostility? Not the first, because such a thing is simply not observed. Nor is it the second, because there is no hostility toward you on our part. Rather, you are providing an example of some extraordinary malice characterized by the desire to kill a trusted attendant. Thus it is with you.

This initial matter must not be stated clearly by us in our own words; rather, something should be asked in the form of a riddle (*prahelikā*), such that he himself, providing the answer according to the facts, might explain this very meaning— since, being connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), we share the same reflections in our minds.
Then they said: "O highly wise Kṛṣṇa! Explain to us one of our riddles concerning wealth.
[The answer is: People worship only after having aimed at those who are themselves being worshipped; some people worship with expectation.

The meaning is as follows: here, since they do not even resort [to others] when there is the acquisition of an object that requires dependence, it follows that their affection is conditional (*sopādhi*). To show the opposite of this, some "resort [to Him] even while not resorting"—the meaning is that they resort to Him without dependence. This is because, in this case, they have no aim for any other fruit based on self-interest.

"Or from the abandonment of devotion" means that disinterested affection has arrived; "others do not devote themselves to either" means they devote themselves neither with expectation nor without expectation, and thus indifference has arrived. "Hatred and malice would also constitute non-devotion"—since these two have also arrived, it is explained as follows.
The Blessed One will indeed clarify even this somewhat further. "Tell us this": the meaning is, "Who indeed are these [people], and what is this worship or non-worship? Tell us that.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase *ete ca etac ca*, the word *etad* is neuter; it is used in the singular when combined with a non-neuter term.

And by the rule *cāsyānyatarasyām*, there is a single-remainder (*eka-śeṣa*) for the singular number; the meaning is: "Speak properly and exactly according to the facts, abandoning the grammatical disagreement (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). ||16||
The Blessed Lord said:
Those friends who worship one another do so because their efforts are solely directed toward their own self-interest.
In that regard, neither friendship nor righteousness exists; for that [action] is solely for the sake of one's own interest and not otherwise.

Śrīdhara, understanding the intention, gives the reply: "Mutually" (mithaḥ). O friends, those who serve one another out of a desire for mutual benefit do not serve anyone else, but rather only themselves. Why? Because their exertion is directed solely toward their own self-interest. In that regard:

And because there is no friendship, there is consequently no happiness; nor is there any merit, since [the action] is for the sake of visible ends, like the tending of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth—this is the meaning. ||17||
Vaṃśīdhara:
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: "Self-interest" here refers to those who enjoy their own seen and unseen [results].

According to the maxim, "Even the gods [are like] those very gods," the deities who have been gratified by sacrifices and other rites grant heaven and the like, just as cows, buffaloes, and others yield milk and so forth. Those whose exertion is directed exclusively toward that— being fixed solely upon it— possess no friendship for that which is called "dharma."

The meaning is that we consider even those two well-known [goals], though they are for the sake of human ends through the independence of dharma, to be subject to exceptions according to the method to be explained; for there is the consequence of their being diverted by wealth (artha) and pleasure (kāma), and because they consist of hypocrisy in the eyes of the connoisseurs (sahṛdaya). Indeed.
In the case of certainty; otherwise, in a manner different from what was stated...
[from] the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
Vaṃśīdhara.

The sequence of the composition: here, one's own interest is seen as the visible fruit. Those who, striving for a visible fruit, serve one another, they serve only themselves. For since service cannot otherwise exist, there is neither friendship nor righteousness therein. (17)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: The Blessed Lord, having understood their intention, gave a fitting reply beginning with "In secret" (*mithaḥ*). "O friends" (*he sakhyah*) is an address full of affection. In worshiping Him in secret, there is neither friendship nor religious duty; for that worship is directed toward one's very own self.
Because it is conditioned by mutual compatibility. In the reading "for the sake of one's own self" (svātmārtham), it means for the purpose of one's own self. ||17||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Regarding that, he states the fruit determined by the first question: "Those who worship one another are those whose efforts are solely for their own self-interest. "Self-interest" (*svārtha*) means having as its sole motive a result visible only to oneself; it does not belong to any single [divine] entity alone. Therefore, they are those whose efforts possess such a nature, having as their fruit a state of stagnation (*niṣṭhā*).

But they, having abandoned [their own kin] and recognized one another, associate with each other according to their relative degrees of excellence; for them, effort is directed solely toward their own self-interest. Therefore, in such mutual association, there may arise friendship, affection, and even a sense of duty.
As it has been said: "In whatever manner people worship the gods, in that very same manner the gods treat them."

It is indicated that, like the tending of cows, buffaloes, and so forth, there is an expectation of a return favor; thus, there is an absence of affection for the Dharma and an absence of gradation [in its value]. This is because when no benefit is rendered, one perceives some fault in the form of indifference, just as one neglects cows, buffaloes, and the like when they lack milk. Therefore, where—

There is also an expectation of a return favor there, yet it is not true friendship; rather, it is merely a semblance of dharma. By the word "hi" (indeed), he asserts with certainty that such service, being perceived as having no purpose other than adharma, is for one's own sake alone—he says:
"That service is solely for the sake of one's own interest. Otherwise, it would be of a different kind than the manner previously described.
"It does not exist. "O friend" is the address; "for the sake of non-deception" means that this manner [of behavior] arises from our mutual devotion to one another. ||17||
Viśvanātha, having understood the intention, gives the reply beginning with "mutually" (mithaḥ).
Those who associate with one another out of regard for mutual benefit and counter-benefit,
and whose exclusive effort is directed solely toward their own interest— the attainment of their own visible and invisible fruits— they are indeed certainly [so].
They worship only their own selves and no other; that mutual worship of theirs could not be otherwise.
Therefore, the meaning is that they are intent on their own self-interest and are merely possessors of desire, finding pleasure within themselves through conditioned adjuncts (*upādhi*).
In that regard, there is no friendship or love among them. Regarding the word "dharma," from the perspective of the meaning of the subsequent verse, it is beyond reproach.
And the Dharma does not [exist] for its own sake; in the reading "for its own purpose" (*svātmārtham*), this is an adjective qualifying the word "that" (*tat*). ||17||
Those who are compassionate indeed honor even one who honors them not, just like fathers;
O slender-waisted ones, here dharma is beyond reproach, as is their mutual affection.
Śrīdhara: Those who worship one who is not being worshipped are of two kinds: compassionate and affectionate.
In that regard, he says that according to their respective order, they possess the desire for Dharma and for pleasure—thus Vaṃśīdhara says: "They worship one who is not being worshipped."
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not commented upon.
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī:
Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
The *krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: the answer to the second question begins with "Those who worship" (*bhajanti*), etc. Those who worship those who do not worship are indeed compassionate (*karuṇāḥ*) and merciful (*kāruṇikāḥ*), just like parents; [the compassion] of those two is exclusive.

There is indeed affection toward children even for one who does not worship [the Lord]. In this regard, he provides the answer to the second question—concerning that blameless dharma and friendship which delights the connoisseurs—by saying, "Those who worship," and so forth. The word "yathā" (as) applies to every instance. Those who worship even one who does not worship [them], by virtue of their extreme childhood and capability...

Those Vaiṣṇavas who, being compassionate and merciful, nourish those people who serve them— even if those people do not serve Vaiṣṇavas themselves— by granting their needs without expectation of any return; in this regard, they are like me,
and the illustration is that just as parents, out of affection and even through religious duty, serve [their children].
These are observed. In this regard, the necessity of a friend is primary, while the duty [of supporting them] is secondary. As it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"When one's mother and father have grown old, a virtuous wife, and an infant son..."
"Even after committing a hundred wrongs, [the wife] must be maintained," so Manu has declared.

Herein lies the faultless, uncontradicted, and complete Dharma. For this very reason, since assistance is necessary in matters of Dharma or friendship, there is no room for suspicion regarding the devotion of one's counterpart.

The meaning is that due to its noble nature (*āryabhāva*), Dharma is beyond reproach and faultless. Furthermore, like a cow supporting the mud [beneath its hooves], some do not accept even an act of worship being performed toward it, as they disregard any reciprocal benefit;
for precisely because of this lack of expectation, there is no relationship of "subject" (*anuyogin*) and "counter-subject" (*pratiyogin*) even in the case of friendship.

There is an absence of equality. For the subject (*anuyogin*), however, it is seen to be endowed with a property (*dharma*); for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), however, the property is neither a *dharma* nor a non-*dharma*. This is precisely because its nature is relative. "O you of slender waists" is an address intended to inspire confidence in the matter stated; in this same manner, one should proceed everywhere according to the dictates of one's own heart.
Thus it should be understood. ||18||

Viśvanātha provides the answer to the second question: "Those who worship Him who does not [ordinarily] accept worship" means they worship Him without expectation. They are of two kinds, distinguished by being either unrelated (*niḥsambandha*) or related (*sasambandha*). Regarding these, it is said: "like compassion, like parents. Among them, the compassionate ones are pure devotees (*śuddha-bhaktas*), such as Prahlāda and others.

"Because one observes the arising of compassion that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi-karuṇā*). Due to the two-fold nature of the examples, both types of persons—those who do not expect a reciprocal favor and who experience suffering or happiness based on the suffering or happiness of others—do not abandon their devotion even at the cost of their lives; the former are superior, while the latter are inferior. Among these two groups:

In this way, the Dharma is beyond reproach because it is free from desire for fruit, and thus it is imperishable; likewise, friendship and love are beyond reproach. "O you of beautiful waist" (*sumadhyamā*): by means of *śleṣa* (punning), this refers to those whose middle question is indeed excellent. Because the first and last questions are cited as examples of what is censured (*vigīta*), the meaning is that the first and last questions are censured. That which...
Or rather, the meaning is that those very [examples] which are excellent, middling, and superior serve as illustrations for this middling counter-argument. ||18||
Even those who worship Him do not truly worship; how much less so those who do not worship?
For they delight only in themselves, their desires are already fulfilled, they are ungrateful, and they betray their gurus.
Śrīdhara: Regarding the answer to the third question, "even though they worship," the meaning is as follows:

those [devotees] are of four kinds. Some are those who delight in the Self (ātmārāma) and have no longing for other things; some are those whose desires are fulfilled (āptakāma), who, even while perceiving sense objects, are devoid of the desire for enjoyment due to their state of fullness; others are the ungrateful and the deluded.

Others, however, are exceedingly cruel toward those who harm their gurus. According to the maxim, "He is a father who nourishes," one who provides assistance is equal to a guru; thus, those who harbor malice toward such a person are so described. (19)

Vaṃśīdhara: He provides the solution to the third question, which is of the form "others resort to neither," stating: "This is the meaning. They are those devoid of resorting to both. Some are *mūrkhāḥ* (fools). They do not perceive external objects beyond themselves, but rather perceive only the Self.

Those wise ones with eyes turned away from the external see [it]; some are its specific manifestations. Those whose desires are fulfilled—[they see it] as being filled and established in immovability.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires. [Gītā 2.70]

Because of such traditional teachings (*smṛti*), the wise have no arising of desire; others are worldly (*prākṛta*). They are deluded (*saṃmūḍha*) and utterly foolish (*atimūḍha*). Others are different from them. Intending to show that malice toward gurus—who wish one's welfare—does not occur except through extreme hardness, he says: "those who hate their guru," meaning they are exceedingly hard-hearted (*atikaṭhina*). (19)
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Indeed, those who do not worship Him at all—knowing that such ungrateful people are ignorant and that their failure to worship was intended [by the Lord]—those who nevertheless do not worship Him, they... [are truly ignorant].
He says "endowed with every fault" [to explain this]. "Guru" means those who disregard their teacher (*gurūpekṣaka*).

Just as in the case of Brahmins and others deserving the punishment of death, neglecting such a person is itself an act of malice (*droha*). However, there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) in this literal sense; rather, by means of a figurative function (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), those who neglect one who has rendered assistance are understood.
It should be understood that this implies their lack of regard for benefit, righteousness, friendship, and compassion.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Vai" means indeed; "naiva" means not at all; they do not worship [Him]. "Hi" is used in the sense of a reason or for certainty.

They are ungrateful (*akṛtajñāḥ*) because they do not recognize or keep in mind that worship which was performed for them, even though they possess expectations regarding worldly matters and the like.

The meaning is that even though they possess the capacity for reciprocation, because they do not act upon it due to ignorance, they are indeed fools; thus, their non-worship is intended on account of their ignorance. But those who, despite knowing [the capacity] and possessing the ability, do not worship them, are truly most wretched; thus he says "guru" (heavy). Such is the case with them.

In response to the questions posed in three quarters (pādas) with three verses, their own exceptional greatness is further emphasized through the specific qualities of their concise and other statements, so that [the listener] might not forget it. Thus, in their view, the Blessed Lord’s state of being self-sufficient through His manifold divine play is established.

Furthermore, the fulfillment of all desires would simply not be possible. By employing the term "guru," it cannot be understood that one has been taught by a teacher; since the pain of separation makes devotion impossible, neither of the first two positions is tenable.
Therefore, only ingratitude remains as the conclusion, and so it will be shown further on.

It will be stated: "one of ungrateful mind," and so forth. In the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, within the *Śrī-Balarāmāyaṇa*, it says: "For he is indeed the banner of ingratitude" (*Viṣṇu-purāṇa* 5.24.16). For this very reason, they too have explained that ingratitude reaches its ultimate limit through his own words alone.

And even in that case, the status of being the final limit would indeed apply. Alternatively, they have explained the term "one who betrays the guru" as meaning "extremely cruel"; thus, it is precisely here that the state of having reached the final limit is consistent. ||19||

The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained. The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: the answer to the third question begins with "Even those who worship... and so forth. Some do not worship even though they are capable of doing so, let alone those who do not worship at all. To the question "Who are they?", he says: "Those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāmāḥ*)."

First: those who delight in the Self because nothing else appears to them; those whose desires are fulfilled because they are complete; those who are ungrateful because of their ignorance; and those who betray their guru because their mental states are governed by sin—these four alone are such [unfit recipients]. (19)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: He provides the answer to the third question with the words "Even toward those who worship... (*bhajato'pi*). Certain great souls do not even worship those who worship them; what then to say of those who do not worship? And they are of four kinds.
The *ātmārāmas* (those who delight in the Self) are devoid of [external] inquiry because they find delight in the Self alone; therefore, even while [others] worship their body...

They do not pursue worldly affairs; what then can be said of worshiping the body? Others, having attained all their desires, have no room for further longing and thus do not require the worship of others, as they are already fulfilled in every desire. It is like saying "Eat! to a man who has already finished his meal.

The statement "Eat" would be meaningless. Therefore, since the purposeful nature of dharma is not established here even for those who partake of both, this is merely a description of the essential nature of these two. For this reason as well, neither self-delight nor the fulfillment of desires is logically consistent. [This is] because of the indifference toward those two, which constitutes mere sport.
Because it has been accepted.
He states the third position: "ungrateful" (akṛtajñāḥ). This means they do not recognize worship or assistance performed by another;
even though they are capable of returning the favor and even though they depend upon that person's assistance, [they do not acknowledge it].
They worship [the Lord] by virtue of being agents who provide assistance to the community; for them, ignorance alone is the cause of their failure to worship.
They are ungrateful, yet I am not ungrateful. The answer to this will be stated in the following verse: "He worships me in my absence."

He states the fourth position: "But those who, despite possessing the capacity [to serve], do not resort [to the Lord] even after knowing [Him], they are exceedingly merciless"—thus he says, "those who betray the Guru" (*guru-druh*). Whoever accomplishes one's desired ends and whoever is one's nourisher is a *guru*, and he is worthy of worship; yet they betray him alone. As for those who [commit] betrayal...

The two-fold nature [of their grief] arises from either the taking away of life or the taking away of all possessions; both of these have indeed come to pass according to their intention. For, since the tenth stage of separation (*vipralambha*) is imminent, even the taking away of life is possible, and the taking away of all possessions has already occurred.

Because the happiness of home has been snatched away; or rather, because even his entire wealth and its enjoyment have been taken from him. Furthermore, because suffering cannot be averted by such treachery toward one's teacher, the meaning is that these traitors to their teacher are exceedingly cruel, as they are devoid of any regard for righteousness or friendship.

The meaning is that this is the very expectation [of the Lord]. He will state the refutation of this argument in the following verse: "But I am not [the cause], O friends. Since three positions have now been presented, treachery toward the Guru remains as the only possibility; for this reason, he will describe himself as having reached the final extreme.
In the *Bhramaragītā*: "But he of unrefined mind let go that which ought to have been maintained" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.47.16).
Furthermore:
"How indeed does Padmā serve His lotus feet?"
"Alas, indeed, his mind has been stolen away by the prattle concerning the Lord of Excellent Renown" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.13).
"Oh, alas! Without knowing [the truth], how can he serve the lotus feet of Śrī?"—thus it was explained by the Teachers.
And likewise, He will speak further ahead, in the assembly of the Gopīs during the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra: "Even..."
"Are you perhaps reproaching us out of suspicion that we are ungrateful?"—thus it was accepted by his own mouth.

For this very reason, the charge of ingratitude falls upon him. He will also provide a remedy for that, simply because he is unable to give a fitting reply due to his incapacity to offer a corresponding return favor; it is not otherwise.

By the words "I shall cross over," he explicitly affirms his own capacity for fulfillment and their state of perfection; among these, it is stated that he is none of them, signifying the absence of the four defects.
Yet, having mentally conceived his own fault, he says: "May that [fault] return to you."
"Very well," he said.
But surely, according to the order of the words, it is the offense against the teacher (*guru-droha*) alone that constitutes the final limit. To this, he provides the resolution:
the order of meaning (*artha-krama*) is more powerful than the order of the words (*pāda-krama*). [As in the case of: "He offers the *agnihotra* oblation; [he cooks] the rice-gruel (*yavāgū*)."
It should be understood as being like the expression "he cooks. ||19||
Viśvanātha: He provides the answer to the third question, beginning with "Even though they worship" (*bhajato’pi*).

These are of four kinds, each succeeding one being inferior to the preceding. Some are "delighting in the Self" (*ātmārāma*), having no outward vision. Others have their desires fulfilled; although they possess outward vision, because their desires are inherently complete, they do not seek enjoyment from others. Others...

The ungrateful (*akṛtajña*) do not recognize the assistance or similar favors rendered to them by others, even though they themselves desire enjoyments from others. Others, the betrayers of their gurus (*guru-druh*), do not merely disregard the assistance or similar favors rendered to them by others; on the contrary, they betray those very gurus even more severely. These are the causelessly hostile.

Since it is established by the logic of "a fortiori" (*kaimutya*) that [the former] includes the latter as having a cause for enmity, it is indeed included within that. Likewise, being a protector and being a teacher—thus, "one who harms a teacher" refers to those who betray the trusting;
this threefold enmity is also simply non-devotion. And therefore:
There is one example for the first question-and-answer, two for the second question-and-answer, and six for the third question-and-answer; thus, there are nine in total. (19)
"O friends, though I favor living beings who devote themselves to me, I do not favor them for the sake of following their ways."
Just as a poor man, having lost wealth he had acquired, remains preoccupied with that thought and perceives nothing else.

Śrīdhara: Having perceived the Self as having reached the ultimate limit here, and seeing those women with their faces hidden by mutual secret smiles through the contraction of their eyes, He said: "I am not 'you'. O friends, I am none among them; rather, I am the supremely compassionate and the supreme well-wisher. How so? Of these...
I do not worship them for the sake of following their conduct or for the purpose of engaging in uninterrupted meditation upon them.

He states this with an illustration: "Just as... [He is] "concealed" (nibhṛta), meaning filled or pervaded by the thought of that wealth alone; he does not perceive anything else, such as hunger, thirst, and so forth. ||20||

Vaṃśīdhara: Here, having considered—meaning, having known—the Self as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who has reached the final limit among these four and entered the ultimate stage; [he beheld] those gopīs, whose faces were marked by mutual secret smiles and slight movements of the eyes—that is, by the subtle twinkling of their eyes—and who were smiling with faces hidden from one another.

Seeing them, Śrī Kṛṣṇa says, "Not me"—meaning not even one among those four. But rather, out of supreme compassion and so forth, He wonders, "How [can this be]? regarding those who worship Him. This is the account: a poor man, destitute, having come together with Me once...
Furthermore, he vanished from his sight for the sake of his own intense joy:
"O sinless one, this form which was shown to you once is for the sake of desire; however, the virtuous man who desires Me gradually abandons all heart-born passions" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.6.23).
Thus, from my words addressed to Nārada: the underlying meaning is that my divine play (līlā) exists solely for the purpose of destroying the cycle of rebirth for my devotees. ||20||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "But I am not," and so forth. "But as for me—I am not even one among those who delight in the Self (the *ātmarāmas*)—why do you look at one another with smiles?
If that is so, why do you not accept us? To this he replies: "Just as wealth [is sought] for the sake of following [others]," and so on. (20)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, according to their view, for one who delights in various pastimes with her and others, the two qualities of being self-satisfied (*ātmārāmatva*) and so forth are simply not possible.
This is because [the Lord] would cause the pain of separation [to his own devotees], and it does not apply to the previously mentioned worship that is both with and without dependence.

It has been explained with the following intention: since discernment (*vijñatā*) is manifested through such cleverness in replying and so forth, one does not act ungratefully; therefore, the state of being a teacher (*gurubhūktva*) results in nothing other than sheer hardness (*kāṭhinya*). Or else, [the phrase] "with the winking of eyes" is intended for the purpose of producing that hardness.

Thus, this effort of inquiry is to be explained. Now, [the Lord] says "no" to the question: "Even if there is no worship of Me, why is My state of being the object of supreme worship superior to that of all those who do worship, let alone those who actually worship? The word "but" (*tu*) marks a new beginning. Even though I am devoid of the fourfold categories such as those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), I am [superior] even to the one who worships.
I do not associate with ordinary people;
I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis. O Nārada, I abide wherever my devotees sing my praises.

The meaning of these and other words spoken by me is this: although I am standing near them, I do not reveal myself to them. The placement of the negative particle (*nañ*) at the very beginning of the sentence is due to the extreme agitation caused by the constraint of my own speech. By addressing them as "O friends! (*he sakhyah*), I have established that I am devoid of self-absorption (*ātmārāmatva*) and similar states.
