The sense is: since I speak thus of "living beings" (jantūn) without distinction, my conduct is of this same nature everywhere and not directed toward you alone;
therefore, one should not suspect indifference on my part toward myself. Why do you not worship me?
To that he says: "of these" (amīṣām). It is for Him from whom there arises the activity of these continuous meditations (anuvṛttīnām), that is, uninterrupted contemplations.
The meaning is: "for the sake of the excellence of continuous love.
If it is argued, "But surely our disposition of devotion toward you exists at all times," [the author replies: "True;
nevertheless, it is for the sake of distinction" that he speaks with an illustration, beginning with "just as" (*yathā*), in the case of something that has been specifically lost or discarded.
Thus, a specific kind of agitation has been shown. For this very reason, he is intensely filled and pervaded by the thought of that [suffering].

Therefore, although there is equality—due to his mastery over all things through his form, qualities, and so forth; due to his being complete in all aims; and due to his lack of dependence on any reciprocal benefit, requiring only love—[he is nevertheless distinguished] by his compassionate fatherhood.

Furthermore, having transcended even the desire for one's own welfare, [the Lord] has demonstrated His own desirability, His power of self-mastery, and the gift of His love— which is the crest-jewel of all human goals—
thereby making known the excellence of relishing the nectar of the beloved’s love, due to His constant longing to increase it.
It should be understood that this is also for the sake of enduring the suffering of separation from that [state]. ||20||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The word *tu* (but/however) marks a new beginning.

Even though I am devoid of the fourfold types of devotees, such as those who delight in the Self (*ātmārāma*), I do not worship [the Lord]. The placement of the negative particle (*nañ*) at the very beginning of the sentence is due to the extreme urgency caused by the self-imposed restraint of one's own statement. O friends! Thus [he says].

It is precisely the absence of self-indulgence and the like that has been established; otherwise, friendship would be impossible. By the word "living beings" (*jantūn*), the absence of specific deliberation is intended; otherwise, their constant following [of You] would be established by its own nature. If it is objected, "But our inclination toward You always persists," [the reply is: True.

He says "as follows" (yathā) with an illustration to show that it is for the sake of attaining that [state] in a special way. By the phrase "especially lost," the possibility of regaining it is ruled out; therefore, he is "completely filled" (nitarāṃ bhṛtaḥ), meaning pervaded. ||20||

The sequence of the composition (*krama-sandarbha*): He provides an illustration of that very specific compassion. Anticipating the doubt that the conclusion there might have some ulterior motive, he says to those who were closing their eyes to one another: "It is not I," [this being] the extensive sequence of the composition; rather, it is you who are failing me regarding the aforementioned attributes (*dharma*).
"They worship [Me]" indicates their own compassion. And lest one suspect me of ingratitude, He says:

"But I," and so forth. "But I," meaning furthermore, although I am one who delights in the Self and whose desires are fulfilled, nevertheless—neither by virtue of those two qualities nor by virtue of being ungrateful and so on—I [do not] abandon even living beings who worship Me, O friends!

I honor even a mere living being; however, if I were to honor these creatures only for the sake of their continued service—that is, for the sake of constant compliance—then, out of pride in their own perfection, they would no longer perform that service. [Objection: But what if they do not honor You?

If they were to become dispassionate [toward their own bodies], what would happen? It is not so; thus he says "Just as" and so forth. "But I am the wealth of all. No one becomes dispassionate toward wealth. Herein lies the example by way of contrast (*vyatireka*): just as when wealth—which has been obtained by some means—is lost again.
Because of that thought, she does not perceive nor know anything else, remaining silent and attentive;

therefore it was well said: "their functions consist of following after [him]. However, this refers to ordinary beings, not to those such as yourselves, for you are my friends. Regarding the friendship of a friend—toward me, her friend—[she acts thus].
They possess my nature. ||20||

The *Prīti-sandarbha*: By means of an illustration of worldly pure love (*laukika-śuddha-prīti*), he himself confirms it to be exactly so with the words "mutually" (*mithaḥ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.32.17–18). Furthermore, he declares the distinctiveness of his own love with the words "not I" (*nāhaṃ tu*, 10.32.19). In the phrase "they worship" (*bhajanti*) and "he worshipped" (*abhajata*), there is no room for compassion (*karuṇā*) or other such motives.

There is an expectation of relishing the affection [directed toward] objects such as the pitiable; likewise, it follows that the affection which those objects, such as the pitiable, feel toward [the devotee] as an object of compassion and so forth would constitute their very life of devotion to compassion and the like. However, in this context, the effort is directed toward the arising of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own extraordinary love for His devotees; and when that [love] arises, [it results] from the relishing of that [affection].

The wonder of love directed toward the devotee becomes exceedingly great; thus, even when He displays indifference toward His own devotees, their love alone increases—this constitutes its unique distinction.
(71) Rasikāhlādinī: Now, having pointed out Your own faults through Your own mouth, You cast them upon another.
Perceiving that they were indicating one another through smiles, he, seeing this, spoke to avoid it: "I am not.
By the word "but" (tu), his distinction from these four types is demonstrated. I am none among those four kinds who are unfavorable to dalliance; rather, I am beyond them.

One should not suspect that he is either merely compassionate or lacks lordship; thus he says, "O friends! Since it is said that friendship exists among those of equal character and disposition, and because he entered into their common purpose, he—who, though delighting in the Self, delights others—was directly the destroyer of the God of Love himself.

By this, it is shown that even desire produces delusion solely for the sake of firm delight; otherwise, under the subjection of desire, one would become helpless through the discharge of the final element (semen). For this very reason, there is no ingratitude. And those who have renounced worldly duties, I sustain them for my own sake.

By the statement "I am" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.46.4), His omniscience is declared; thus, even offense against the Guru should not be suspected in Me. Although the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) are perceived as painful during separation, they do not constitute actual suffering, because in their ultimate result they nourish the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). As it has been said: "The erotic..."
The underlying meaning is that since deception does not thrive without nourishment, one should not suspect me of any fault;
if it is asked, "In that case, how did he remain hidden? he says in response: "Relying upon whom alone is the style [established]."
He said to her: "I, however, do not favor living beings even when they worship me, for I have indicated that there is no distinction [among them].
Even while worshipping them in their absence, I never manifest my worship of them in their presence.
Others, on the other hand, are seen worshipping one another in the form of mutual benefit and return. But I, however—
The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is: "I am not like that, but rather different.
If it is asked, "If so, why is it done in this way? he states the reason there: "Of these" (amīṣām).
This is for the sake of the continuous meditation of these devotees who worship me; however, because I am the friend of all, this [is done].

This refers to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). The meaning is that one should not even suspect that [this convention] is seen to have its fruit in exactly the same form for everyone, and that it belongs to you alone. He clarifies this matter, which is a matter of observed experience, by means of an illustration: "Just as a person without wealth... That is, just as one who was previously without wealth (*adhana*), being destitute, later acquires it...

When wealth has been lost or stolen, one who is "filled with" (nibhṛta)—meaning intensely occupied and immersed in thought—by that concern, knows nothing else, not even hunger, thirst, or the like. This is a well-known worldly fact; for example, after I had shown myself to Nārada once, I vanished again.
Then his continuous devotion arose; the meaning is that for you as well, upon my disappearance, there will be exactly such devotion. ||20||
Viśvanātha: In the examples of the answers to the first and second questions, you are not present.
If you ask which one it is among the examples of the answers to the third question, listen, O you who desire to hear my own defeat at my own hands! [It is] through my very mouth. Mutual [debate].
O friends, you who are foremost in the art of dancing with smiles, playful side-glances, and flirtations, listen!

Although he is one who delights in the Self and has all his desires fulfilled by virtue of being Nārāyaṇa, because he is the son of Nanda, he appears not to delight in the Self and to have unfulfilled desires; and because he is a cowherd boy who has not studied the treatises on ethics, he appears ungrateful.

Even though you are Nārāyaṇa himself, you are all-knowing and grateful; yet, despite your repeated acts of kindness through your playful pastimes and other favors, you abandoned us after only a single instance [of offense] and were thus a betrayer of your gurus.
Nevertheless, because you grant the bliss of your own vision once again, you are not a betrayer of your gurus. If that is so, who then is truly a betrayer?
If you say, "But [you do]," he says in response: "Not me" (*nāham tu*).
The word *tu* indicates a shift in the subject. Although they worship all living beings (*jantūn*), I do not worship them;
what, then, is the difference from the previous case? To that he says: for those who worship them, their continued devotion is my own worship; of that...
"For the sake of livelihood, O weak ones! You who are unable to understand my intention! Alas, alas!
I make the very same effort, yet that very same effort becomes fruitless. Therefore, there is not even a trace of grace from Kṛṣṇa toward me, a sinner; fie upon me!"—thus [he thinks] at every moment.
Through the increase of detachment, humility, and so forth, and by not succumbing to desire, anger, and the like, devotion becomes inflamed;

for those in whom love has not yet arisen, it leads to its birth, while for those in whom love has already arisen, it results in continuous practice (*anuvṛtti*) and attachment to Me. I do not worship for the sake of a livelihood;
even after granting them vision [of Myself], I vanish. From that very [vanishing] comes their continuous practice and attachment.

It increases further. In this regard, there is an illustration for those in whom love has arisen, namely "as follows" (yathā). He is "concealed"—meaning filled and pervaded—by the very thought of that wealth; he does not perceive anything else, even hunger, thirst, and so forth. Therefore, for those who worship me, my own service alone is desired, and because of its preeminence, [it is the highest goal].

"Even though I am manifesting my non-devotion, I am in fact truly compassionate, thinking, 'I am devoting myself even more intensely, though not openly. As for the second question, since you are the very example of it, devotion and non-devotion consist solely in the giving and taking of your own vision."

In the passage to be explained, the sense is that the proposition regarding the subject matter—namely, "In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11)—is such that it cannot possibly be otherwise. Thus ends the commentary on verse 20.
Thus, O women, for the sake of following me— who have abandoned worldly life, Vedic injunctions, and my own kin for your sake— [you have acted].
O beloveds, you should not feel resentment toward that which was hidden while I was away from you; for it was done for your sake.

Śrīdhara: Thus, for those of you who have abandoned worldly life, the Vedas, and your own kin for my sake— having abandoned worldly life by disregarding what is proper or improper, the Vedas by disregarding dharma and adharma, and your own kin by renouncing affection— for such as you, may there be "parokṣam," that is, invisibility or disappearance from my sight.

Thus, while you were serving Me and listening to My loving conversations, I remained hidden by means of my power of disappearance (antardhāna). Therefore, O women, O beloveds, you ought not—meaning you are not fit—to find fault with Me by imputing defects. 21.

Vaṃśīdhara: [The former] consists of disregarding what is proper or improper, and abandoning the fear of public censure regarding virtuous conduct; [the latter] consists of disregarding dharma and adharma, and taking the form of abandoning one’s own husband to serve a paramour. "Listen" is an elliptical expression for [listening to] the conversation of love.

While listening, singing songs of praise for his virtues, and remembering his extraordinary nature, he remained right here solely through his power of invisibility. If there is a lack of faith, one should ask Yamunā and the others; nevertheless, having not observed a smile upon their faces, once again—
He says: "What offense have I committed by this? Therefore, let this transgression be forgiven.

Thus he says, beginning with "by me": "While you were worshiping [the Lord] in His absence with your minds, you yourself have obscured Me; you ought not to be resentful toward Me, you ought not to harbor malice toward Me. Why? Because He is dear."
The offense of a beloved is forgiven only by those who are beloved. ||21||

The *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* states: "And this very day, I have been standing right here near you," thus He spoke. In the manner described by "some approached while milking" and so forth, the phrase "for my sake" and "O weak ones" indicates the difficulty of abandoning those various [duties]. Regarding the word *māsūyitum*: *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "And this very day, I have been standing right here near you," thus He spoke. In the manner described by "some approached while milking" and so forth, the phrase "for my sake" and "O weak ones" indicates the difficulty of abandoning those various [duties]. Regarding the word *māsūyitum*: [the commentary continues as follows: In the phrase *māsūyitum*, the root *asūya* means "to envy" or "to find fault with. The prefix *pra-* implies "excessively" or "intensely. Thus, *prāsūyitum* means "to be excessively envious" or "to find fault with [something] in an extreme way. The suffix *-tum* denotes the infinitive mood, indicating purpose or intention. Therefore, the compound *māsūyitum* signifies the act of being intensely envious or critical toward something. In the context of the verse, this likely refers to the Lord's intention to provoke a sense of jealousy or longing in the gopīs for Him, or perhaps to indicate that He was about to depart, thereby causing them to feel resentment or a sense of loss. The inclusion of the prefix *pra-* emphasizes the intensity of the emotion or the gravity of the situation. Thus, the passage suggests that the Lord, aware of the deep attachment of the gopīs, spoke in such a way as to evoke their intense emotional response—whether through a display of indifference (*māsūyitum*) or a desire to inspire their devotion further. This rhetorical device serves to highlight the profound nature of their love and the difficulty they would face in parting from Him. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full commentary on *māsūyitum* would typically provide further grammatical analysis and contextual interpretation based on the specific verse in question.)

He also states the specific reason: "dear one, dear one. Here, *hi* is used for emphasis (*nirdhāraṇe*). Alternatively, in this manner—as in "possessing wealth" and so forth—it was concealed by me solely for the sake of maintaining your devoted conduct toward me. These words are clearly those of the high-souled son of Nanda.

The meaning is that, in accordance with your previous words, he came into the range of your vision while remaining right in front of you or by your side. What was he doing? He was worshiping you in secret, approving of your loving conversations and so forth. The reason for such favor is stated as "for my sake."
Alternatively, even if they were to deny my two-fold affection (*mādvaya*), you should not yet feel resentment toward me, who am characterized by such love;
rather, the meaning is that since you have been granted suffering by me, you are indeed worthy [of it]. Why?
Because you are dear to me (*priyāḥ*). The meaning is that it is improper to act in such a way toward one who is dear. This...
And there is the skill of conciliation. ||21||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The word "evam" (thus) connects with the word "ity anuvṛttayaḥ" (these are the continuations). "O weak one" (*abalā*) indicates a natural lack of power. "The beloved [speaks] to the beloved" (*priyaṃ priyā*) implies that, because of our mutual affection, my offense such as separation should not be taken to heart. The rest is clear.
They have explained it thus: alternatively, the word "evam" (thus) is connected with "mayā" (by me);
the meaning is "by me who am restrained by such thoughts. The reason for this is given as "mad-artham" (for my sake).
Therefore, even though [the Lord] is beyond perception, one should worship Him while listening to His loving conversations and singing His songs of qualities.

The meaning is that, remembering your particular state of being, He remained right here by means of mere disappearance alone. Alternatively, it was said "for the sake of continued attendance"; as to what kind of attendance that is, He states it by way of an illustration with the word "just as. Therefore, this connects only with what precedes it. O friends!

By this [statement], he reveals what is implied—that this is not being said with reference to you because of our innate friendship—namely: "In this way, do I not honor you? (with an interrogative intonation). For indeed, even for your sake, so that you might continue to follow me, why should I not honor you in this manner?

But rather, it is not at all so. The reason for this is: "for my sake. Or else, even for the sake of your continued devotion toward me, it is certainly not so. Why? Because, due to being restrained by such thoughts, you have abandoned—that is, disregarded—the worlds, aiming solely for my sake and nothing else.

The fourteen worlds, Śrī-Vaikunṭha, and so forth; therefore, even the Vedas [are disregarded] because of their disregard for the ritual acts taught therein. For this very reason, those women by whom their own husbands, sons, and others [are disregarded], even though they act thus, [the Lord remains unaffected] because their conduct consists of an uninterrupted flow of pure atoms (paramāṇu). Such is the meaning. Thus...

The distinction between these [types of devotees] and those who seek liberation (mumukṣus) as well as those already liberated has been shown, because the latter lack that specific longing and possess no such disposition.
Now, one might ask: "For what purpose, then, did You strike down those who were striving? To this He says: "By Me," meaning secretly.

"I was not gone anywhere; rather, while remaining right here in your presence, I was occupied with various affectionate conversations and the like—which were dear to you—perceived by you through a mind that did not grasp my true nature. The suffix *śatṛ* is used in the sense of the infinitive *tum*, meaning "to hear. Thus, [it was done] by the woman who is a gambler... who?
The passage beginning with "one should abandon" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.16) has been refuted.

Alternatively, by eliding the vowel 'a' (akāra-praśleṣa), the meaning is: "even while one is worshipping Him directly and face-to-face, He remains concealed, existing merely as something not perceived by you. Nevertheless...

If it is argued that this must indeed be a fault because it causes suffering to beloved ones, then [the author] says—with the intention that it should nevertheless be endured—"The dear one, the dear one.
Or rather, [one might ask], "For what purpose is even that? To that he says: "The dear one, the dear one"—meaning, by means of beloved women.
The sense is that it is indeed improper for one who is dear [to me] to do so.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "toward me, whose beloved is that worship in my absence, with a natural rasa of curiosity. Oh, how wonderful! This curiosity is truly excellent, in that—

If it is argued that this is "playing with the lives of beloved persons," he says in response: "beloved" (priyāḥ). The meaning is that even that [death] would serve only to intensify love through affection.
Alternatively, although that is so, the two instances of the word *mā* indicate a negation of the primary sense.

The meaning is "by an Arhat. Why? Because it is improper for those who are dear to act thus toward one who is dear, or toward those who are dear; this is the skillfulness of conciliation. The rest is the same as in other places. ||21||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not commented upon.

The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: nevertheless, since this was done by me in such a manner, one should not feel resentment toward that; thus he says "evam" and so forth. O weak women! [Those who] take away (*lānti*) the inferior (*avaram*) or base (*vāmyam*) [nature].

Likewise: "You ought not to be resentful toward me; you should not be impatient. Surely he has departed after abandoning us who were devoted to him; why then should he be resented? To this he says: "By me.
It was by me, while remaining hidden from view, that he vanished. The meaning is: even by remaining concealed, devotion was shown by me to you. [Not] directly...
Devotion through worship is indeed the indicator of love, for you are beloved, whereas ordinary beings are not;
I am beloved, whereas those who delight in the self (ātmārāma) and others are not. Thus he says: "The beloved [are] the beloved ones. Now, one might ask:
if that is so, how is it then that [the Lord] remains concealed? To this he replies: "For the sake of following after you."

It is for the purpose of continuing the engagement, so as to increase the longing again in you who consider yourselves fulfilled by the festival of contact with my limbs. If it is argued that [the body] was indeed concealed at that time, and one asks what proof there is for the statement "worship me," the answer is: my very nature is the proof; for I am...

Thinking, "I am indeed grateful," he reveals his own gratitude toward them by means of a qualification: "mad-artham" and so forth. "If I were not to honor you—who have thus abandoned worldly life, Vedic study, and your own selves for my sake, on my account—then I would be ungrateful."

In order to avoid their own faults, they have indeed performed worship in secret; and since that worship takes the form of a visual audience which is not seen by you during fanning and other such services, the implied meaning (*dhvani*) of the words "worship in secret" is this. Therefore, it was rightly said: "Do not be envious," and so forth. (21)

The Composition of Affection: And this [pride caused by abandonment and jealousy] is pacified by means of praise and so forth. For instance, he praised them with two verses beginning with "evam" (thus). ||21||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus stated the reason for her own devotion in all respects, she speaks of a specific form of devotion in the present context with the words "In this way" (*evam*). In this manner—that is, by the method beginning with "some women, desiring to serve their husbands," and so forth—they have abandoned the worlds acquired through karma for my sake, that is, out of desire for me.

Because they have disregarded the dharma of those who have taken hold of their hearts— starting from heaven and ending with the world of Brahmā— and because they have disregarded the injunctions and prohibitions of the Vedas, and because they have abandoned affection for their husbands, sons, and others; for the sake of following even you who have renounced these things, and for the purpose of uninterrupted meditation upon you.

Regarding "worshiping while out of sight": having kept in mind how women must be avoided at night, one practices worship in person for the sake of uninterrupted meditation, and worships from afar for the sake of protection at night. By performing both of these, she remains hidden, staying beyond the range of vision.

He speaks that which awakens recognition: hearing such loving conversations as "O rogue, who would abandon his woman at night? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.16) and so forth, while demonstrating recognition by saying, "In this place, the gathering of flowers was performed by my beloved for the sake of his dear one" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.30.33), [he sees her] in front and at his side.
Or, while remaining invisible behind you, he performed the protection of your lives;

or rather, while remaining visible, he protected you from all sides during the night; or rather, while remaining out of sight, he cleared away thorns, pebbles, and the like, performing the preparation of the path.
It is not hidden, nor is it situated sideways; rather, it stands directly in front.

The answer has been given to the question you asked: "Why do they all worship Him alone?"—namely, that your worship of Me is direct (*aparokṣa*), whereas my own worship is indirect (*parokṣa*); this is the only difference. O weak ones! Thus [He spoke].
By this address, it is made known that the devotion of you ladies is not like that of others;

rather, it is indeed supernatural (*alaukika*) in its accomplishment. By this, the two positions regarding non-devotion, though they may have been entertained in the minds of the cowherd girls, are refuted; otherwise, even envy might arise. Therefore, for that reason...

"You should not find fault with me by attributing defects such as ingratitude. What kind of person am I? I am dear—that is, an object of affection for you—and you are my beloveds. For even if a beloved is wicked, it is improper to make them an object of resentment; rather, one must abandon such resentment because it is impossible to do otherwise."

The manifestation of defects such as ingratitude (*akṛtajñatva*) toward an object of affection is inconceivable; on the contrary, it is appropriate to conceive of it as a virtue. One who knows the *akṛta*—that is, the unartificial (*akṛtrima*)—disposition is "grateful" (*akṛtajña*);
the state of being such is "ingratitude" (*akṛtajñatva*), which means the knowledge of one's own natural mental disposition. This is the sense.

Otherwise, there would be a coexistence with indifference when the manifestation of faults occurs. Now, if it is argued that in indirect worship there is no similarity to one's own worship because the manifestation [of faults] is a cause of suffering, then you ought not to be envious of me, for I am beloved even with my defects.

"You should not point out my fault; for by pointing out the fault of one who is already at fault, such as myself, you too will become known as being at fault. By this conciliatory speech, "It must indeed be forgiven," he manifested his own partiality. With the words "dear to the dear one," he [alluded to] the fault.

Even though they manifest [their anger], they cannot be abandoned by me; likewise, since I am unable to abandon my beloved, she is unable to do what is improper toward those who are dear to her—this is the underlying sense. ||21||

Viśvanātha: Now, while it is indeed right that you treat your devotees—both those in whom love has not yet arisen and those in whom it has—in such a manner, we fear that because you treat us in exactly the same way, we too have been counted among the common folk.
Anticipating this speech of theirs, which is accompanied by regret, [he says:]
"O friends, you who are the atoms of dust upon my life, my very breath, my supreme beloved’s lotus feet—
forgive this wickedness of mine that I have today treated you as if you were common to others," she says with the word "thus."
Alternatively, the word *amarokta* means "as stated [in the Amarakośa]," namely, "just so" (*tathā eva evam*). Thus, the meaning is "in that very manner.

Consequently, the world has been abandoned for my sake, because of the failure to regard what is appropriate or inappropriate; the Veda has been abandoned, because of the failure to regard dharma and adharma; and one's own self, possessions, wealth, and kinsmen have been abandoned, through the renunciation of affection.
By those [words], for the sake of the continued devotion of others who possess the aforementioned characteristics— just as it was for their own—
and so that there might be a perception of continued devotion in others who worship You in Your absence,
such that they hear Your conversations of love while You remain hidden from view, [the word] "tirohita" (hidden) was used; therefore, this was an extreme impropriety.

This is the meaning. For devotees of the past, present, or future could not possibly exist in this way; nor is there any increase in the degree of devotion beyond this level of constancy. Indeed, no one can hope for a decrease or an increase in the size of an atom or the vastest of things. Therefore, [this applies] with respect to those devotees who love others.

The underlying sense is: "May this indiscretion of mine, consisting of the desire to make known the great excellence of the power of our love in separation, be forgiven. Since this is so, you ought not to be envious of me—that is, you should not look upon me with the attribution of fault. In this regard, the reasons are "because he is dear" and "because she is dear."
The meaning is that those who are dear indeed do not take to heart the faults of one who is dear. ||21||
O you who are united with the blameless! Even with a lifespan as long as that of the gods, I am not able to complete your own virtuous deeds."
May that [liberation], which those with difficult-to-break chains of household life resort to after having completely severed them, return to you through your virtuous conduct.

Śrīdhara: Let this be; however, he says "Listen to the ultimate truth" with the words "No. O wise ones, even by means of your long-lived selves—for a long period of time—I am not able, nor can I, to perform a good deed in return for you, that is, to repay your favor. Of what kind [of you]? [He continues: "Of those who are... [The text here describes their qualities.]

"O ladies, those bonds of the household which are so difficult to overcome and ageless—having severed them completely and cut them away entirely, do not fail me by clinging to them. However, my heart is not fixed on one alone because it is filled with love for many. Therefore, that virtuous deed of yours is indeed a virtuous deed for you."
"Let it return; let there be a return. The meaning is: "I shall be free from debt to you through your very good character alone, and not by means of a reciprocal favor performed by me. ||22||

*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Then he said, "I am a debtor," beginning with "I am not able," and so forth—even by the lifespan of the gods, that is, by the duration of time measured as the life of a deity. (22)
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*;
*Krama-sandarbhaḥ*: "I am not able; I am not capable. (22)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Although you have indeed performed worship, He says "I am not able" and so forth, as if he were indebted to you. [The word *niravadyā* means] faultless, unconditioned, or free from wrinkles;
[the phrase *saṃyuktānām* refers to] those who are joined together. Even though I am the Lord (*īśvara*), [I am unable to repay] your own virtuous deed—that is, your own righteous action.

"I am not able to purify" means "I am not capable. Alternatively, it means "I am not able to perform your duty in such a way that it is well-executed by my own efforts. He says "no" even to the idea that he will be able to do so after some delay, even within the span of the lifespan of the gods (*vibudhāyuṣā*), which is the measure of time for the life of a deity. Why? It is as follows:

He said: "I did not resort to you—you who had severed and cut through the difficult-to-break chains of the household—just as you, having severed the difficult-to-break chains of the household, resorted to me; the meaning is that I likewise did not resort to you. (22)
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus cleansed their resentment, He consoles them in order to manifest His own freedom from debt toward those who worship Him, saying: "I am not able... [and so forth].
For those whose union is with the faultless One, they are themselves faultless in that union, according to worldly perception.
The meaning is that even though desire appears to exist by virtue of the power of sense objects, it ultimately culminates in freedom from desire.
This has been stated by the Blessed Lord Himself: "For those whose intellects are absorbed in Me, desire does not lead to further desire" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.26).
Such a connection with desire is the cause of worldly existence.

The ellipsis "to return the favor" (*pratyupakāram kartum*) is to be supplied. "I am not able" (*na pāraye’ham*) means I am not capable, even with the lifespan of a *vibudha*—that is, even with the lifespan of Brahmā. Alternatively, it means that I am not able to perform properly and correctly my own respective service (*kṛtyam*) toward you, which is your worship (*bhajanam*).

"I am unable. Or rather, the ellipsis to be supplied is: "I am unable to describe your own unique, virtuous deed—that is, your sincere devotion—for no one is capable of doing so. The meaning is that this is because of the disparity between you and me; for one who is truly satisfied by water [never thirsts again]."
"It ought to be similar to the satisfaction derived from water in a mirage.
He states the reason for this: "That which is difficult for you to digest," meaning it is unconquerable and indestructible.
By the word "home" (geha), there is meant that which takes the form of a collective whole, consisting of affection toward husband, children, and so forth.

Or rather, these activities, consisting of the accumulation of all household duties, are impossible even for sages to sever; this very point will be clarified further on: "The bond of affection among kinsmen is very difficult to abandon, even for a sage" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.5). External iron chains may indeed be severed.

The chains of intense affection situated within cannot be severed by anyone; for me, however, because this internal bond of affection is impossible to abandon, there is thus an inequality between you and me. Having completely cut asunder such chains—the very causes of bondage—[one becomes free].
The meaning is "having abandoned" in the sense of not returning [to the path].

Regarding the phrase "that which is not shared": just as your worship is focused solely on me, my worship of you is not shared because it is not focused solely on you; therefore, there is no equality, owing to the great intensity of [your] love.

The sense is that because they are distinct, they cannot reside in one and the same [person]. Your devotion to them—this being a statement emphasizing the state of being (*bhāva-pradhāna nirdeśa*)—let it proceed with goodness;
let it be a reciprocal service, for you are unable to devote yourselves to them due to your total independence from all else. "In whatever way people approach Me... [and so forth].

"Those I favor in accordance with their own nature" (Gītā 4.11); thus, even though there was the possibility of violating my own vow, my state of being free from debt has been established. Henceforth, now that you have attained the status of having husbands under your own control, please command me according to your pleasure—this is the intended meaning.
May that Kṛṣṇa, who is constrained by the love of the gopīs and who, through his own mouth, spoke these distinguished words and accepted his debt to them, be the bestower of love upon me.
(22) Viśvanātha says: "Listen to that which constantly arises within my mind"—thus he speaks with the word *na*.

"Blameless" means those whose union is characterized by the absence of attachment to sense objects, ritual actions, worldly concerns, or the codes of scripture; for you, whose union is thus free from limiting conditions, that which is "good" is good by its very nature, not "good" because of contact with some external object that produces goodness. That I am unable to repay.

"I am able. Even with the lifespan of the gods (*vibudhāyuṣā*), meaning even having attained the life-span of the deities; by the singular number in "task" (*kṛtyam*), the meaning is "even a momentary task of yours"; she who has devoted herself to me, having severed—even if difficult to break—the chains of affection for husband, mother-in-law, father, brothers, and other kinsmen.

"Having cut them off entirely"—by way of a pun (*śleṣa*), the meaning is that even though they were severed like those of an immature yogin, they did not attain the state of being "chains" (*śṛṅkhalā*); that is, they did not bind him at all. As for me, however, I feel affection for my parents, for my own brother, and even for my kinsmen; and I serve you as well. "In whatever way people approach Me, in that very same way [I reward them]."

"Even though I have made my own vow, 'I worship [those to whom I am devoted]' (Gītā 4.11), I have fallen away from it"—this is impossible according to my system. This meaning is also obtained through *śleṣa* (punning): "Having severed [the connection], that which I did not worship you. Here, the conjunction of the letter *na* and the letter *du* occurs by means of *para-savarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound).

Therefore, let that [debt] be repaid to you by means of my very goodness; let it be returned through your own virtuous conduct. The sense is: "By your excellence of character alone shall I be freed from debt to you, yet in reality, I remain indeed a debtor to you. And then, they reflected thus within their own minds regarding him.

Since He is the Supreme Lord, although He is fully endowed with all auspicious qualities, is entirely free from even a trace of defect, and is the Knower of the essence of our love, why does He abandon us? It must be for the sake of exalting us by His own love, while degrading Himself and becoming our debtor; such is His abandonment of us on account of our own karma.
"Desiring victory over this one who wishes to overcome us, we ourselves, being unable to remain thus unfortunate, have indeed been conquered by him through the fruit of his love. ||22||
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the thirty-second [chapter] of the tenth [skandha] has been properly concluded for the virtuous.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Consolation of the Gopīs," in the tenth book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, which is the commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras, the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa-dance," in which Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, having heard the most beautiful words of the Blessed One, the cowherd girls—
whose blessings were fulfilled by his very presence— cast off the fever born of separation from him.
Śrīdhara:
Then, in the thirty-third [chapter], Hari, situated in the midst of the circle of gopīs,
delighted those beloved ones with sports in lakes and forests.
Therefore, O King, at that time—alternatively, those whose blessings were augmented and perfected by the limbs, that is, the body or the members such as the hands and feet, of that Blessed One. ||1||
Vaṃśīdhara: After that, following the praise of the gopīs; "those" refers to those staying on the banks of the Kālindī.

"Hradinī-keli" means water-sports. "Vana-keli" (forest-sports) is an elliptical expression for land-sports and so forth. Then, after the consolation of the gopīs; this is indeed the effortless path, as opposed to a laborious construction.
Thinking it appropriate, he said, "Or else" (*yad vā*). According to Dharaṇi, the word *aṅga* is used in the senses of a limb, a part, a means, a place, and what is dear.
Alternatively, it is an epithet of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). In that case, there is a compound beginning with "by their limb" (*tāsām aṅgena*), and so forth. ||1||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
Victorious is this Rāsa-līlā, the sole enchantress of the world.
In which the majesty of the illustrious goddesses of Vraja is manifest even through their splendor.
In this way, such exceedingly beautiful and supremely captivating [words],

by the report that even in separation there was no abandonment [of her] and especially by the demonstration of her own indebtedness and so forth, dispelled the heat born of both past and future separation— even when, by chance, a further severance occurred.

And because of the removal of the doubt regarding ultimate abandonment; therefore, although it was mentioned previously, it is stated here again with the intention of describing the complete renunciation of distress at this very moment. Furthermore, they have their desires fulfilled by means of embracing, grasping the hands, and so forth, which are its constituent parts (*tadaṅga*); or else, [it refers] to the Blessed One himself.
The qualification [of the gopīs] is that their limbs have accumulated blessings by virtue of being the cause of her most beautiful speech; thus says the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
"Victorious is the Śrī-rāsa-līlā, the sole enchantress of the world."
By whom the greatness of the illustrious cowherd women exceeds that of Lakṣmī herself.

Thus, by such words and other means of the Blessed One, he reveals his own entire devotion to the Blessed Ones; therefore, these [words] are most elegant and supremely captivating. They dispel the heat born of separation, both past and future. Although this has been stated previously, it is repeated here; for even in separation—

Because they do not abandon Him; because, through that [love], they specifically demonstrate their own state of indebtedness and so forth, and because they contemplate the non-interruption [of that love]; and because, with the desire to now properly abandon all distress, the Gopīs have minds overwhelmed by the nectar of innate love—this is the meaning. Furthermore, "tad-aṅga" (His limbs) [is used].
The meaning is that they were those whose desires were fulfilled through such acts as embracing and grasping the hands;
or else, this is an epithet of the Blessed One himself, meaning that the blessings for those gopīs were accumulated by his own limbs, which serve as the cause of his most charming speech. ||1||

The sequence of composition: separation, both past and future, and that which arises from it; because even in separation [the lover] does not abandon [the beloved], and because of the acceptance of one's own debt [of love]. ||1||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, he says "Thus," and so forth, to show that by that very conciliation of the Lord, their heart-burning ceased. "Supeśalāḥ" means very affectionate; "āśiṣaḥ" refers to the pleasures augmented by His limbs—that is, the limbs of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Having spoken thus, they [did so] all at once.
The implication is that he embraced each and every one of them individually. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the thirty-third [chapter], there are the sports of the rāsa dance, the lāsya dance, and water-play;
furthermore, the questions and answers between Parīkṣit and Śukadeva are recounted.

Those [women] whose blessings—meaning their desires—were fulfilled by the touch of His limbs and so forth, being most beautiful and exceedingly captivating; or rather, this is an epithet of the Blessed One Himself, meaning "of the bliss born from the touch of the gopīs' bodies.
And by that, at the conclusion of the question and answer, through the pacification of her pride, there occurred pastimes such as embracing and kissing.
It is indicated that they are near. ||1||
There Govinda began the rāsa-dance with his devoted followers,
accompanied by those jewel-like women who were full of joy and joined their arms with one another.

Śrīdhara: *Rāsa-kriḍā* refers to the sport called *rāsa*, which is a particular kind of dance involving many female dancers; [the Lord performed] that sport together with those whose arms were mutually bound and interlaced. (2)

Vaṃśīdhara: *Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth; the qualifiers for the term "strī-ratnaiḥ" (by the jewels of women) are: "anuvrataiḥ"—those by whom the vow was followed, namely the Kātyāyanī-vrata; [and] "prītaiḥ" (by those who were pleased).

"Delighting" refers to those who have arrived with their beloveds and other various gopīs drawn by the sound of the flute, whose arms are "well-bound" or firmly interlocked with one another. At first, it does not seem possible for one gopī to be with one Kṛṣṇa; however, [the phrase] "with jewels" implies that this applies to all of them.
Because of their equality. ||2||
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī; Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī; Krama-sandarbhaḥ: these have not been commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, having become gracious toward them, He commenced the *rāsa* dance characterized by the previously mentioned attributes; this is stated in the passage beginning with "there" (*tatra*). Regarding the phrase "with the jewels among women" (*strī-ratnaiḥ*):
among women, those who are like the sovereign Lakṣmī herself are the "jewels. Even among those [who are like Lakṣmī], they are the jewels.

And by groups of young maidens who followed the vow that has become a jewel; and by other groups of cowherd women who had arrived, drawn by the sound of the flute, being joyful—having attained joy (*prīti*) through that delight—and with their arms interlocked with one another. What were those young maidens like? With their arms bound to each other.
The maidens, with their arms interlocked one with another— either meaning that one maiden is linked with one other, and so on, for the sake of variety— or else,
having entered between two circles, they follow along [the path]. ||2||

Viśvanātha: With those who were devoted to that sport consisting of the *rāsa*—the assembly of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) such as dancing, singing, kissing, and embracing—and who at that time were mutually harmonious through their mutual agreement, with their arms entwined and linked together. (2)
— o)0(o— The Rāsa festival has commenced, adorned by the circle of gopīs;
with Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, in the midst of them, [he dances] with each two [gopīs].
Having entered, he took the women by the neck and brought them close to himself.

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates that literary composition through a performance with one and a half verses, exceeding four syllables: "In the rāsa festival," [referring to] those who are situated in the form of a circle, with Him having entered between each pair, embraced from both sides as they hold Him by the neck.

In what manner? It means that he has entered between each pair [of women] for this purpose, so that all the women might think, "He has embraced me alone, who am near him. But how can one person enter in such a way, or even if he were present everywhere, from where [would his individuality arise]?
The conceit that they were each individually close [to Him] arose from them; therefore it was said—"by the Lord of Yoga.
This means "by the one of inconceivable power. ||3||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Krama-sandarbha*: Yoga is inconceivable power. ||3||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He describes its manner [of occurrence] with the words "the Rāsa festival," and so forth. That place where the festival named Rāsa took place was a specific location suitable for the *rāsa* dance and graceful play (*lāsya*). It manifested as having been graced by the circle (*maṇḍala*) or circles of gopīs, and it was also graced by Kṛṣṇa.
Thus it should be understood. "Then set in motion by Kṛṣṇa" means initiated by him.

By the Lord of Yoga, who possesses inconceivable supreme sovereignty, having entered between each pair of those women held by the neck, with a whirling skill of extreme velocity—by this [the text] demonstrates his status as the Lord of Yoga.

It has been made manifest. Alternatively, between two mandalas—by one who has entered among those women who are positioned between the two mandalas and have grasped his neck—the women would consider him to be near them. "The women" means...

They abide in the middle of the two mandalas; this alone is the state of being a Lord of Yoga (*yogeśvaratva*). In reality, however, there is only one who is proximate to all, and not as a plurality. For this very reason, they thought—and indeed believed—that he was near to themselves, yet plurality is not real, for there is only the Lord of Yoga.

The capacity to manifest a multitude of bodies—that which, without having done so, manifests as a single entity pervading all—is itself inconceivable supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*). If that is so, how is it consistent with the statement: "Having made Himself as many as there were cowherd women" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.33.19)? True.

The explanation here is as follows: to whatever extent—that is, according to its measure, its constituent parts, and its substratum—it manifests by means of that same measure, that same dimension, and that same substratum. At that time, "the entire sky" means the whole of space; for it is said that *yāvat* and *tāvat* denote totality. [This applies] to those who possess the Real (*sadārāṇām*).
The meaning is that [the sky] was crowded with hundreds of celestial palaces of the gods; those whose very selves were filled with intense longing to behold them. ||3||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, with one and a half verses containing four additional syllables, he expresses his deep absorption in the *rāsa*-pastime which he himself had initiated. *Rāsa* is a specific festival consisting of dance that manifests aesthetic rasa; it proceeded perfectly. He states the reason for this: [because it was performed] by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in person.
The meaning is "by means of the erotic sentiment" (śṛṅgāra). He clarifies His perfection: "adorned by the circle of gopīs.
This means He is adorned or embellished by the circle of gopīs; or alternatively, it means that the circle of gopīs is adorned by Him.
Thus, by Him—who is the form of eternal bliss—their circle, as they stand arranged in a circular formation, is embraced on both sides at their necks.
"Of those taken hold of, two by two" means that they are said to have their necks grasped because they stood on both sides of Kṛṣṇa. This was also stated by Parāśara:
"Though bound within the circle of the rāsa dance, she did not leave Kṛṣṇa’s side."
And the community of cowherd women did not remain with their minds fixed on a single place.
Taking each gopī by the hand one by one, Hari led her into the circle of the rāsa dance, while his touch caused her eyes to close.
Then there proceeded a delightful song of praise, following the sequence of autumnal poetry, accompanied by the tinkling of moving bracelets. Indeed,
having entered between each pair [of women], he was embraced by both at their necks.

If it is argued that a multiplicity of essential forms (*svarūpa*) is perceived there, he says in response: "whom they might think [to be Him]. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the gopīs' perspective, a multiplicity of essential forms appears as if it were real. With this intention, it should be understood that within the circle of the gopīs, there is only one who stands like a central pivot (*śaṅku*).

Otherwise, if there were a multiplicity of essential natures (*svarūpa*), there would be no statement regarding the perception of being near to Her alone, as one might think oneself near to whichever [form] is close; for if the essential natures were manifold and illusory (*māyika*), then [the attainment of Her] would occur through similarity resulting from sincere worship of them.

And there would be a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) that culminates in the destruction of happiness. For this very reason, the Teacher will state: "In the midst of the jewels" (*madhye maṇīnām*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.7), just as the singular number and the lack of repetition in the middle are intended from the perspective of the gopīs' vision.

Now, how can one person simultaneously enter between two pairs— that is, have his neck grasped on both sides while maintaining a state of oneness? And how is it that envy and other such emotions do not arise in those standing face-to-face with him, who see Kṛṣṇa grasping their necks from both sides?
To this he replies: "By the Lord of Yoga. Yoga is a specific, inconceivable, and marvelous power;
its Lord is the controller who is capable of effecting omnipresence. As he will state later:
"How wonderful! That by a single body, simultaneously and separately..."
In each of his homes, he married sixteen thousand women.

Just as Nārada had directly perceived there that a single form possesses inconceivable power and is complete in every respect, so too in this case, there is both identity of essential nature and omnipresence.

It is wonderful; for this is not too much of a burden for the Blessed One’s power of *yogamāyā*. It has already been stated that he "resorts to *yogamāyā*. Otherwise, it would not be fitting to display many deceptive forms toward those who worship His single essential nature with sincere love—this is the underlying sense. ||3||
Viśvanātha: He demonstrates the genre of that literature with the words "the Rāsa festival.
[It is] by more than six syllables less [than the full meter]. The Rāsa itself is the festival;
it is truly and perfectly the bestower of the nectar of bliss to the cātaka-birds of the eyes and minds of the devotees.

He proceeded. By whom? By Kṛṣṇa, who had entered between each pair of those gopīs who were situated in the form of a circle. Here, because the word "set in motion" (sampravartita) is not used, he assumes the role of the instrument himself while bestowing independent agency upon that very rāsa dance.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa has manifested that the Rāsa alone possesses supreme excellence over all His potencies and all His pastimes; therefore, it should be understood that even Lakṣmī and the others longed to attain it, yet they did not obtain it. Of what nature were they?

By that very same [act], they were grasped by the neck and embraced from both sides; here, in the subsequent verse, although the word "in the middle" (*madhye*) and the singular term "emerald" (*marakata*) appear— as in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.33.7, where it says "just as a great emerald is [surrounded] in the middle of golden jewels"— the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) has not been used here in this verse.
By the use of the word "entered" (praviṣṭena), it is shown that Kṛṣṇa, standing in the very center as the pericarp of the circle of gopīs,
manifested such lightness of movement that he danced as if he had entered between every two of the gopīs situated in the circle.

It should be understood that his swiftness of movement was even greater than that of a whirling firebrand (alātacakra), for in the mere time it takes for a single atom to move, he came from the central region, embraced the three hundred million gopīs standing in the circle while dancing, and returned once more to the central region.
For at that time, everyone saw him situated in the pericarp of the mandala; in this very manner:
between every woman was Mādhava, and between every Mādhava was a woman.
"When the mandala had been thus fashioned, the son of Devakī, standing in its center, sang with his flute.
Thus it was said by the venerable feet of Śrī Bilvamaṅgala Mahānubhāva. In that regard, [the following is] pregnant with reason:
He qualifies [the Lord] as "the Master of Yoga" (yogeśvara), because He is the treasury of all arts and is thus a great expert in the means thereof;
for Amara states: "Yoga is used in the senses of armor, means, meditation, conjunction, and reasoning.
Alternatively, "Yoga" refers to the Great Power (mahā-śakti) that is exceedingly skillful in performing difficult feats through Yogamāyā, and He is the Master (īśvara) of that.

Perceiving the eagerness of all the gopīs to embrace him simultaneously, he revealed himself in as many manifestations as there were and thus satisfied them. Here, by the use of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "having entered between each pair," it is understood that he entered into the midst of every single gopī, that is, into the space between each and every pair of gopīs.

They explain as follows: when it is explained that He enters into the midst of each individual gopī, one should not suspect that it is improper for two manifestations of Kṛṣṇa to touch the shoulders of a single woman from the perspective of Yogamāyā; for it is Yogamāyā herself who [manifests] Him to each one individually.
Because it bestows the manifestation of light and touch, there is nothing at all inconsistent in explaining [the verse] as referring to two pairs of gopīs. ||3||
They might think that the sky was so crowded with hundreds of celestial palaces belonging to the gods and their wives, whose minds were captivated by intense longing.
Śrīdhara: At that very moment, the sky became crowded and congested with hundreds of celestial chariots belonging to the gods and their wives, whose minds were filled with eager longing. ||4||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*.
*Rasikāhlādinī*: For this very reason it has been said—"whom they might regard... And it has also been stated: "The greedy see the world as consisting of wealth; the lustful, as consisting of women;
but the wise who seek the supreme truth perceive it as consisting of Nārāyaṇa. Just so.

It is not surprising that they considered their own proximity [to the Lord]; moreover, as it is said: "The residents of Vraja considered each their own wives standing by their side" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.38).
In this case, the cause is indeed the inconceivable power of the Blessed One; how much more so, then, in their estimation of being in close proximity to Him alone?

Thus, the reason for the body's marvelous and unlimited nature is that it belongs to the Lord of Yoga (*yogeśvara*). Other yogis as well, possessing the capacity appropriate to the grace of the Blessed One, are present everywhere; how much more so, then, the Blessed One himself?
This is the meaning of "the Lord of Yoga."

The meaning is that when the Rāsa festival commenced, hundreds of celestial chariots [arrived]; for others were not permitted entry there, yet even the women with their husbands desired to see [the spectacle]. Therefore, the state of those whose souls were carried away by eagerness and curiosity—their minds being drawn [to the scene]—is described as an excitant (*uddīpana*).

For those awaiting the Rāsa festival, there was the sound of hundreds from hundreds of celestial chariots (*vimāna*); here, "hundreds" (*śata*) signifies the "innumerable," meaning by countless [chariots]. Viśvanātha states that the sky was filled with them even to the extent of an *aṅgula*. He [Kṛṣṇa] is the one whom the women would consider to be near them—this refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

The meaning is this: although He was indeed embracing her right here, the fact that He is seen everywhere led them to think, "This must be some kind of dramatic art (*nāṭya-vidyā*) of His. Regarding this, they say that the Son of Devakī stands in the center together with the Sovereign Lady of Śrī-Vṛndāvana alone, because she alone possesses the highest excellence (*sarva-śraiṣṭhya*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause of the rāsa-play and so forth," this is seen from the *Śatanāmastotra* [of Kṛṣṇa]. At that very moment, the sky became filled with hundreds of celestial chariots. Of whom? Of the inhabitants of heaven, such as Brahmā and others, due to their eagerness for this;
however, this refers only to the portion of Kṛṣṇa’s dancing, and not to the playful display of rasa itself.

Because they were unfit due to their status as servants, whereas there was no such impropriety regarding their wives, for this very reason it should be understood that in the *rāsa* dance, both in heaven and on earth, the men saw only Kṛṣṇa and not the gopīs, because they were concealed by Yogamāyā. ||4||
Then the kettledrums resounded and showers of merit fell;
the lords of the Gandharvas, accompanied by their wives, sang his stainless glory.

Śrīdhara: They sang that pure, stainless fame of the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus says Vaṃśīdhara. "Then" means immediately after the commencement of the Rāsa festival. That fame consists of the glory of Kṛṣṇa and the glory of the gopīs, taking such forms as: "Oh, the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Oh, the good fortune of the gopīs!"
But the rain of flowers is for the sake of softening the surface of the stage. ||5||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, from those inhabitants of heaven; or rather, immediately thereafter, they themselves sounded [the instruments], because of their divine nature and because their very essence consists of great auspicious festivals. Thus, even further on, at the beginning...

The sound of the drums was for the purpose of auspiciousness and for the gathering of their respective groups. "They fell down profusely" (*nipetuḥ*)—by the word *ni-* (down) it is understood that there was rain, and by the plural number, it is indicated that a carpeting of flowers indeed occurred upon the arena floor. [He was] accompanied by women, celestial nymphs (*apsarases*), and co-wives.

It is stated that for all [beings] there is exclusive devotion to that alone; because impurity does not remain, they are called "pure," for at that time even their [remaining] all-pervasive latent tendencies (*durvāsanā*) have been eliminated. ||5||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus described the festival performed by the gods, the *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha* states their eagerness: "Then the kettledrums... and so forth. (5)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Regarding the intoxication of those authorized for the flower-rain, song, and instrumental music in the midst of that [pastime], he says "Then" (*tataḥ*). Then, at the commencement of the *rāsa*, kettledrums resounded, indicating the auspiciousness of the world;
as if to kindle the enthusiasm for the dance, they produced a great sound of majesty and so forth. By the authorized ones...

Showered flowers fell; they fell with extreme continuity, precisely at the conclusion of each rhythmic beat of the *tāla*. The lords of the Gandharvas—the chief Gandharvas who hold office—sang His glory. Accompanied by their female companions, [they sang] this song of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, wherein the singing of the Gandharvas [reached its peak].

The companionship, assistance, and incitement [of the women] are indicated. In the singing of the cowherd women, the companionship, assistance, and incitement of those women are indicated. Regarding their fame and his fame—what is it like? It is stainless, capable of dispelling latent tendencies such as lust. Therefore:

By the mention of witnessing the Rāsa festival and so forth, the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects is also indicated; the underlying meaning is that such witnessing does not constitute a fault. Furthermore, it is suggested that the entry of objects of the same class as those useful for that occasion serves to intensify the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), whereas the entry of dissimilar objects does not. ||5||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Of the bracelets, anklets, and small bells of the women.
A tumultuous sound arose from those accompanied by their beloveds within the circle of the rāsa dance.
Śrīdhara: "Of those with their beloveds" means together with Kṛṣṇa; "tumula" means crowded. ||6||
Vaṃśīdhara:

"Valaya" is masculine in the sense of a neck-ornament (kaṇṭharāga), and neuter in the sense of a bracelet; thus says the Medinī. "Nūpura" refers to an anklet, and "kiṅkiṇī" is a small bell; thus says the lexicon (kośa). "Tumula" refers to a tumultuous battle.
The earth. ||6||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus described the festival performed by the Lord, [the author] speaks first of the musical instruments in order to describe the instrumental music and singing suitable for the *rāsa* dance, beginning with the words "of the bracelets" (*valayānām*). [This refers to] the small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) situated on the waist-bands and other ornaments.
By the phrase "of the women" (*yoṣitām*), it is indicated that bracelets and so forth exist by their very nature as women.

By the phrase "with their beloveds" (*sa-priyāṇām*), the word "bracelets" and so on is intended even for the Śrī Bhagavān, who manifests in that manner for the sake of their pleasure. [This refers to] the circle formed by the *rāsa* dance.
The formation of a circle occurs therein. ||6||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus described the festival performed by the gods, [the author] speaks first of the musical instruments in order to describe the instrumental music, singing, and so forth suitable for the *rāsa* dance, beginning with the words "of the bracelets" (*valayānām*). [The phrase] "of the women" (*yoṣitām*) refers to those women who possess small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) attached to their waist-bands and other ornaments; it is used in this way because they are women in general.
It is understood that the bracelets and other ornaments exist [on Him] not for the sake of beauty, because they were taken as decorations;

for previously, when He departed from their homes, they had looked toward them with longing. The phrase "together with His beloveds" implies that even the Blessed Lord went there for the sake of their pleasure, as if He Himself were one of them.
By this, the word *valayādi* (bracelet and so forth) is intended. Regarding *rāse yan maṇḍalam*: it is the formation of a circle (*maṇḍalī-bandha*) during the *rāsa*;

or else, *rāsam* means "belonging to the *rasa*," referring to that circle; or alternatively, it means a collection of *rasas*, which is the sequential arrangement [of the verses]; this has not been explained [in detail].

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Then, imitating their speech, as they moved here and there within the circle with their beloveds, a sound arose from their bracelets and other ornaments that was perfectly rhythmic; thus he says, beginning with "of the bracelets," etc. Because they were mingled with one another, the sound was tumultuous. (6)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described the instrumental music and other performances provided by the Gandharvas and others situated in the sky, [the author] now speaks of the various musical instruments suited for the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) that were used specifically within the circle of the Gopīs—beginning with the words "of the bracelets. The sound of the bracelets of the women, that is, the Gopīs, arose; by this...
The phrase "of the hand gestures (*hastābhinaya*) and so forth" indicates that the various distinctions therein produce the arising of the word "vala.

The phrase "of the anklets (*nūpura*)" indicates that the various distinctions in the movement of foot placement produce the sound of the anklets. The phrase "of the small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*)" indicates that the various movements of the hips produce the sound of the small bells.
And it will be stated further on: "With the placement of feet and the waving of arms" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.8).

Thus, it is indicated that the sound of internal musical instruments serves as a specific stimulant for the aesthetic flavor (rasa) within the upper, lower, and middle pathways. In the phrase "of his beloveds," the beloved is treated as a subordinate element.

Because they alone are predominant among the musical instruments such as bracelets and the like; "rāsa-maṇḍala" means a circle (maṇḍala) from which the manifestation of rasa (rasa-abhivyakti) arises—such a circle being the circle of the gopīs. Alternatively, that particular dance from which the arising of rasa occurs is the rāsa, and its maṇḍala is the formation in a circular shape. Or else:
*Rāsa* is a collection of *rasas*; it refers to a region within that circle. It is crowded with tumultuous sounds;

for this very reason, words such as *kuñcita-akṣa* (with eyes contracted) are suitable for the dance, and likewise, words such as *vatta* and so forth are not perceived separately from the rhythm (*laya*) therein, just as they are not perceived by others standing at a distance.
In such a way that there was no perception of differences between other doctrines, so did the tumult arise. ||6||

Viśvanātha: [This refers to] those accompanied by their beloveds and by Kṛṣṇa. Here, by the use of the word "ca" (and), the *anaddha*, *śuṣira*, and *tumula* instruments are also included. Since these are mentioned by the word "ca," their subordinate status is indicated, and it is thereby suggested that bracelets and the like serve as qualifiers (*upamāna*) for the eyes and so forth. ||6||
There, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them,
like a great emerald in the midst of golden jewels.

Śrīdhara: Like a great emerald among golden gems, He shone while being embraced by those women of golden complexion. Or, with the intention of referring to the glances of the gopīs, the singular number is used even without the repetition of the middle word [in a bahuvrīhi compound]. (7)

Vaṃśīdhara: In that *rāsa*-dance, by those gopīs; [he who is] the son of Devakī and the delight of Yaśodā. "Haimānām" means "made of gold" (*hema*); the form is correct through the elision of the suffix *ṭi*.
[They were] fashioned by a goldsmith. Alternatively, "haimāḥ" refers to yellow gems produced on the Himālaya mountains.

With regard to the intention of the Gopīs' vision, the word "in the midst" (*madhye*) should be repeated, because the Gopīs dance with many forms and positions. He says— "or even without"— to show that since the one who stands upon the pericarp in the very center is singular, the repetition of the word "midst" is not necessary.

The son of Devakī, though born of the Kṣatriya caste and the Lord endowed with the sixfold opulences, shone exceedingly there in the midst of women of the cowherd caste. Although Kṛṣṇa possessed the hue of a sapphire, through his blending with their fair complexions he appeared emerald-colored; even so, a unique beauty was perceived therein.
Some say that the word "great" (mahat) has been employed [as a prefix]. Others maintain that this word "marakata" denotes the indranīla gem;
there is also a reading as "mahāmārakata. ||7||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: As the son of Devakī, the Lord is renowned among you; yet, although He is endowed with the full weight of all opulence and all splendor, He shone most intensely there in the circle of the *rāsa* dance with those gopīs. Or rather, He shone most intensely there in His state as the son of Yaśodā, and even therein—

The meaning is that he shone exceedingly because of them. Even for one such as he, [the author] establishes the excellence of his splendor through an illustration—with the word "in the midst" (*madhye*). The singular number is used with the intention of expressing a collective sense; the meaning is "in the midst of all.
Therefore, even though situated in the center of the circle, he should be understood as a single light. He...
Indeed, by placing Śrī Rādhikā by His side and wandering while playing the flute,
He exceedingly adorns the entire rāsa-maṇḍala;
and this should be understood according to other descriptions of the rāsa found in works such as the Krama-dīpikā.
In the performance of the rāsa-dance pastimes fashioned by throngs of women with hands joined to one another,
even a jeweled stake [was traversed] by him in this very form.
[He who has] manifoldly manifested his own divine body.
"O beautiful one, with the two arms of your beloveds clasped around you, you stand between us both, yet within each of us separately"—
thus, having stated that she is situated upon the jeweled pillar, that very same subject is described again by way of qualification.
Immediately following [the description] "situated in the center of a large, radiant, crimson lotus upon a stake fashioned from jewels," [it continues]:
"meeting in an embrace with the breasts of a young woman..."
"His chest was red as saffron, and his gait was like that of a bull" [Kraḍī 5.61].

Thus it has been said: "Standing in the center of the circle, he played the flute. Because the jewels made of gold—that is, products of gold—are globular in shape, they are generally referred to as "made of jewels," just like emeralds (*mahāmārakata*).

Likewise, there is the singular expression "megha-cakram" (the circle of clouds). From what will be said later—that even for a great emerald gem, its splendor would be greater only by virtue of being situated in the midst of gold gems—the meaning is that for him too, his splendor would be greater only through the embrace of beloved women; the rest [of the description] was provided by them. In that regard:
The word *marakata*, preceded by the word *mahat*, should be understood as denoting the indranīla gem.

Alternatively, because they have acquired the color of the emerald gem (*marakata-maṇi*)— which is not excessively dark— through contact with the mass of luster from those women who are fair as refined gold, they are called "great emeralds" (*mahā-mārakata*).
And therefore, there is merely a particular capacity for dancing, but no particular divinity whatsoever. ||7||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Although the Lord is already endowed with the full weight of the splendor of all opulences, He shone most intensely there in the circle of the *rāsa* dance.

Even though He has by Himself reached the ultimate limit of all beauty, [the author] establishes His extraordinary splendor through them by means of a previous illustration, beginning with the word "in the midst" (*madhye*).

Of those that are golden—either made of gold or possessing a golden hue; just as even a great emerald gem gains greater splendor only when set in the midst of a golden gem, so too his splendor would be enhanced only through the embrace of his beloved. The reason for this is: "the son of Devakī."

Thus, because He was born of Devakī out of affection for His devotees, the sense is that the fullness of His splendor is attained precisely through the expansion of the weight of love directed toward His dear ones. It has already been stated previously that [He is called] Devakī and Yaśodā; the rest has been explained by them.

Alternatively, "the great monkey" refers to the actual oneness of the Blessed One; or else, it is according to the intention of those in the middle for the purpose of playing the flute. On this point, some say: although he has the color of a natural sapphire gem, by his skill in the movements of dance, he appears as if simultaneously—
Because it revolves, pervading all of them individually by seizing their necks and so forth,
and because it acquires the color of a great emerald through contact with the mass of luster from those [mountains] of fine gold and iron, it is called "the Great Emerald" (mahāmarakata).

And therefore, it is merely a specific power of dancing, not some distinct entity created by the Lord; this is the direction of the sequence of the composition: Devakī is indeed Yaśodā as before. //7//

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: By means of the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), he illuminates the singular nature of the Blessed Lord in the manner described above—beginning with "There... and so forth. He shone exceedingly (*ati*). Why?
Because of those [ornaments] acting as causes, amidst golden gems, there was a great *mārakata*, a sapphire (*nīla-indra-maṇi*).
Thus, because of the indication in the singular number, there is no plurality. //7//

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, one might object: "If, while they are thus dancing, Kṛṣṇa becomes a subordinate among them, then there would be a deficiency in His splendor. Anticipating this, [the author] states that His splendor was even greater than before, beginning with the word *tatra*.
In that circle of the *rāsa*-dance, the Blessed Lord, disregarding His own sovereignty, [was surpassed] by those among them...
He shone even more intensely with those who possessed a golden complexion, as if with the *Ṛgveda* itself.

Through their company, he personally experienced the bliss born of the manifestation of beauty. The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indicates that what is intended is not merely an increase in the splendor of his sovereignty, but rather [the joy] arising first from the extension of his arms.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the extreme abundance of the splendor of the forest-dwelling is indicated. The rule is that superiority arises only from that which is of the same class (*sajātīya*), not from that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*). Alternatively, *bhagavān* means one who possesses *bhaga*, which is fortune; he states a qualifying attribute containing a reason: "the son of Devakī."
"The wife of Nanda had two names, Yaśodā and Devakī;
therefore, a friendship arose between her and Devakī, the wife of Śauri.
This means he was the son of Yaśodā. Consequently, because he was being cherished with such affection, he became exceedingly well-nourished.

The capacity for the movement of multiple aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) is illuminated. Alternatively, by means of the two qualifiers, his possession of the qualities (*guṇas*) characterized by steadfastness and grace is indicated. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*:
"Completely entrusted by his parents to a state of carefree ease, he is under the influence of his beloved."
He is mature, possessed of fresh youth, and endowed with the qualities of steadfastness and grace.
By the reason of his freedom from anxiety, an abundance of charm (*vilāsa*) is indicated. Regarding this, he states a corresponding illustration:
"in the midst of gems. [This refers to] being in the midst of gems made of gold, shaped like fingers.
Just as such a leader in the midst of a great army of enemies [shines], so too does he shine when embraced by the two rows [of women] on both sides;
for among those women adorned with ornaments, his splendor is not fully realized without their presence.
In the same way, he alone shines apart from the gold and jewels of the central leader.
