By the use of the singular number, the oneness of the Lord’s essential nature is indicated; thus, through His inconceivable power, He is present everywhere. By the word "in the center," it is shown that even while standing in the middle of the circle, He remains one and the same.
Just as the radiance of a great emerald enters into gold and jewels situated in its midst.

Just as they distinguish beauty through its wonderful and marvelous nature, so it should be inferred here. The teachers have also explained that, with the intention of the gopīs' gaze, the singular number and the non-repetition of the middle word [in the compound] signify the pride of being uniquely close to Him. And thus it has been said in the *Kramadīpikā*:
"Situated in the center of a large, radiant, crimson lotus, with a glistening pin (śaṅku) made of jewels at its core," beginning thus [Kraḍī 5.58],
and so forth.
"With a chest reddened by saffron mingled from the embrace of a young woman's breasts, moving with the gait of a bull"— thus [it is said]. And the statement of Bilvamaṅgala is as follows:
With a woman between every two Mādhavas, and a Mādhava between every two women—
when the circle was thus arranged, he stood in the center.
"The son of Devakī played upon the flute" (Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta 2.35).

This indicates His presence in proximity to the gopīs, according to their perspective, just as it is said in the *Kramadīpikā* that He is "situated in the midst of the lotuses. His stationing in the center of the circle is indicated by one [verse].

"By its own nature" means that just as the moon situated in the sky becomes simultaneously visible to all eyes on earth, so too should the mind be composed. And it is not by the Lord's personal entry, but rather because of the manifestation of His yogic power (*yogamāyā*). Otherwise...

Because of the risk of falling into the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*), and because sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) has already been disregarded previously. Furthermore, just as yogins have the power to move everywhere due to their proximity to all things through the perfection characterized by attainment (*prāpti-lakṣaṇā siddhi*), so too [is the case here].
This is according to Vyāsa’s Sūtra: "Because reasoning is not established" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*). Moreover, those entities which are indeed beyond reasoning...

"One should apply those [reasons] through logic" means that, according to the Dharma, the fact that phenomena are determined by what is beyond logic—that is, their being undetermined—is not at all inconsistent. Thus, there is nothing improper here. ||7||
Viśvanātha: Although the Lord was born into the Kṣatriya caste and was endowed with the six divine opulences, He shone exceedingly there in the midst of women of the cowherd caste;
though Kṛṣṇa was the color of a sapphire, through the blending of their fair complexions, He appeared the color of an emerald.
Some say that the word "great" (mahat) was employed there because its distinct beauty was observed;
others say that this word "marakata" denotes the indranīla gem. There is also a reading: "mahāmārakata. ||7||
With the placement of her feet, the waving of her arms, her smiles, the play of her eyebrows,
her slender waists, the swaying of her breasts and garments, and her earrings dangling against her cheeks;
Sweating, with the knots of their chief braids and waistbands loosened, the dark-complexioned brides sang of Him and shone like flashes of lightning within a circle of clouds.
Śrīdhara: To show how he was graced by them, and likewise how they shone because of him, he says:

"By the placement of feet," and so forth. By the shaking of arms—that is, by the movement of hands—and by the waists being bent, and by the moving breasts and garments; and by those flickering on the cheeks—that is, those moving upon the cheeks.

"Perspiring" means those whose faces are perspiring, that is, emitting sweat. "Those whose knots in their braids and girdles are firm," or alternatively, "those whose [knots] in them are not-knots," meaning the knots are loose. Therein, Kṛṣṇa, who possesses various forms, is like a circle of clouds.
These [emotions], however, are of many kinds; like lightning, sweat is like frost, and song is like thunder—this should be inferred according to what is appropriate. ||8||
Vaṃśīdhara:

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: "By the placement of His feet," and so forth. [The word] "Kṛṣṇa’s wives" is used, not "the cowherd girls. By this, it is shown that they danced in an entirely unhidden manner, singing only of that very Kṛṣṇa.
They shone like lightning in a circle of clouds.

Regarding how he was not only greatly beautified by them, but they were likewise beautified by him, the author says "pāda" and so forth: the placements of his feet [were accompanied] by dances and songs.
By those methods of stepping upon the ground, and by the specific shaking of the arms— that is, the hands— through various movements of the hands;
for although such shaking of the arms would not be possible if the arms were bound to one another, nevertheless, at times, it occurs precisely by relinquishing that state of being bound.
With playful movements of the eyebrows accompanied by smiles, and with the grace of dancing that manifests various aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), their waists—
naturally slender and especially so due to the turning and other motions for the sake of dance— are as if undergoing a breaking; or rather, "breaking" (*bhaṅga*) refers to the state of being bent.

"Kuṭilyam" means crookedness; the sense is "by means of their middle portions becoming curved. The word "muhuḥ" (repeatedly) should be understood in every instance. "Kucapaṭāḥ" refers to their own respective upper garments (*uttarīya*) which were repeatedly gathered up when the Blessed One arose. By others, however, [the term refers to] something else. In this context, it is precisely the "knots" that are meant.
The word-division is appropriate, but not for that which lacks a formal structure (*agranthaya*).

However, passages such as "the wives of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇavadhvaḥ*) and so forth should be explained in this way: singing of that Kṛṣṇa, they—by virtue of being illustrative examples—shone forth as the various wheels of Kṛṣṇa’s manifestation. Where? In what [manner]?

Like lightning within a circle of clouds; indeed, the previously mentioned analogies such as "in the midst of jewels" and so forth do not apply here, because those various adventitious relationships exist through the union of husband and wife (*dāmpatya*), whereas this [present case] lacks an inherent relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). Anticipating this objection, the secret is [revealed] through the manifold variety of bliss (*ānanda-vaicitrya*).

He makes this clear with the words "the wives of Kṛṣṇa. Similarly, here too, the sense is that their status as a married couple arises from a natural relationship alone. For this very reason, even without any special practice, they possess the highest excellence in each and every one of those qualities. ||8||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He did not shine alone because of them, but rather they shone because of him; thus he says, "By the placement of the feet," etc. By the placements of the feet—the modes of treading upon the ground through dancing and movement—and by the specific shaking of the arms, that is, the hands.
By means of the movements of the hands;

for although the shaking of the arms might not be possible while the arms are bound to one another, nevertheless, it is done by both arms joined together while bound to each other, or alternatively, at times, by abandoning that state of being bound for that purpose.

Alternatively, even for arms that are bound to one another, those [gestures] are to be understood solely through the specific postures of dancing movements; in the same way, everything further on should be known accordingly—this is the general direction. [They are] graced by smiles accompanied by the playfulness of the eyebrows and by the skillful artistry of dancing that manifests various aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*).

Their garments and bodices appeared as if they were breaking due to their natural thinness and especially because of the specific movements such as dancing and whirling; or rather, when the glorious Lord rose up, they repeatedly took up their own respective upper cloths for Kṛṣṇa.
The meaning is that the fair-limbed wives of Śyāmasundara are embraced by him and have him as their sole refuge;
this is also clearly suggested by the simile.
Alternatively, [the phrase] "the wives of Kṛṣṇa" means his beloveds, implying their various corresponding clevernesses and other qualities that resemble his own.
The sense is that being deluded by love for Him is indeed liberation; therefore, they sing of Him alone. And the manner of that has been described by Śrī Parāśara:
"Kṛṣṇa is like the autumnal moon to the lily pond of the Kaumudī festival."
The group of gopīs sang the single name of Kṛṣṇa again and again;
thus they shone and were especially beautiful through the mutual blending of the artistry of their dancing and other expressions with the intensity of their love for Him.

Because the abundance of her splendor arises from the very identity of her sovereignty and her worldly nature, her own beauty is indeed implied by the simile "like lightning" through their mutual radiance. Furthermore, the term "wheel" (cakra) suggests a state of manifoldness as if attained through her skill in the movements of dance or through her own particular power.

Or rather, by the intention of describing the clouds as a multitude (ghaṭā), otherwise there would be an absence of beauty due to the lack of intense blackness and so forth; following that [clouds'] extreme beauty, the description of their extreme beauty is intended to show the attainment of a specific excellence of beauty through the rāsa-play, even for those who have reached the ultimate pinnacle of supreme splendor.
Because of its supreme wonderfulness. ||8||

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. Regarding the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, since it is established that the *rāsa* consists of dancing accompanied by song, instrumental music, formations (*bandha*), rhythm (*tāla*), and so forth, involving a large circle of women, the "circle" (*maṇḍala*) has been described; the "formation" (*bandha*) has also been described.
And instrumental music for their bracelets has been described in passages such as *vādyaṃ ca valayānām* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.6).

Now he shows the rhythmic timing (*tāla*), singing, and dancing with the words beginning "by the placement of feet" (*pāda-nyāsaiḥ*). By the term "Kṛṣṇa’s wives," he precludes the notion that they were merely cowherd women (*gopa-vadhū*). Singing of that Kṛṣṇa, they sported and danced.
This is the meaning. Where is she like what? Like lightning in a circle of clouds.

Just as lightning dances within a circle of clouds, so too does she appear in the midst of the circle of dark splendors spreading out from all sides of the Lord situated in the center—within the mandala, in the form of a mandala, unable to exist outside of that mandala.

Due to its density, there is a superimposition of the nature of a circle of dark clouds; and this is to be understood from the meaning of the sentence as well as from the context, since it is not expressed by a word. [This occurs] through the placement of feet that imitate the sound of rhythmic beats (*tāla*), through foot-strikes on the ground accompanied by sound, and through the shaking of arms.
Through a specific movement of the gait, there is a modulation (*mūrcchanā*) by means of swinging the arms, or by the trembling of the arms suited to the abandonment of the tempo (*tāla*).

Even when the arms are bound to one another, the sequence is that at the moment of abandoning the tempo, following the trembling of the two arms, they are bound again. By such a dance as well, there is a breaking of the circle and its obliqueness.

Or rather, it should not be pursued as being "so" [in that specific way]. This is due to skill in the placement and maintenance [of the gaze], through the playful movements of the eyebrows, the imitation of rhythmic beats (*tāla*), and the casting of glances by the eyebrows—of what kind? Accompanied by smiles, and with brows that seem to break at their midpoints, as if they were actually breaking.

With their waists becoming objects of apprehension for fear of breaking due to the swaying of the front halves of their slender vine-like bodies at the moment of abandoning the specific rhythmic tempo; with the very cloths of their breasts—moving despite such effort, but not the breasts themselves;
and likewise, with earrings that were especially dangling from their cheeks despite such effort.

The third [verse]: Their faces alone perspire, but not their entire bodies, because they are untiring and because they are excellent women (*varāṅganā*). Those whose knots are upon their braided hair (*kavara*) and their waist-bands (*rasanā*), because they do not loosen even with such exertion. By the word "singing," one should also understand musical instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) that are conducive to singing.
Because it is brought about by *yogamāyā*. Although this dance has faith as its very constituent, nevertheless musical instruments are indispensable.
In this matter, the Blessed One is the witness alone. That "the gopīs danced together with the Blessed One" will be stated only later.

The dance together; this, however, is the maṇḍala dance. And that is of two kinds: that which revolves by one's own agency and that which revolves by the agency of another. The first is also of two kinds: clockwise (savya) and counter-clockwise (apasavya). The second is characterized by a wheel; and that is performed in reverse order.
In the *anuloma* [order]: if the wheel rotates to the left, then the dancers rotate to the right;

likewise, if the wheel is to the right, then they are to the left—such is the sequence. However, in that case, the rotation follows the turning of the wheel, while the dance remains according to its place. But here, the rotation...
And the dance performed by oneself has no fixed location. As it has been said:
"This *rāsa*-maṇḍala is of two kinds: stable and unstable.
The stable resides in a specific gross form; the unstable rests upon the *cakra*."
When the wheel is stationary, the whirling motion resides in the agent and occurs to the right or to the left;
when it is not stationary, that motion produced by the wheel partakes of both counter-clockwise and clockwise directions.

Just as a dance performed there while remaining in one place appears, when whirled around, to be in various places, so too do the women who are the dancers appear [to be elsewhere]. Thus [it is said]. (8)
*Rasikāhlādinī*:

Viśvanātha says: "Just as He shone with them, so too did they shine with Him"—this he expresses with the words *pāda-nyāsaiḥ*. The *nyāsas* (placements) of the feet are those performed again and again in accordance with the song, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and the rhythm (*tāla*).
They manifested various dances and songs through the vigorous shaking of their arms,

with diverse tremors even of those arms interlocked with one another; moreover, at times, having released the state of their arms being bound together, they performed through the distinct movements of their hands with extreme agility.

By means of the movement of hands, the dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) for the meanings of song-lyrics, smiles, laughter, and various types of facial expressions and postures; for the purpose of expressing aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and demonstrating their respective skills;
with waists that are naturally slender or bent through the turning and movements of dance.
With their moving midsections appearing as if broken due to the shifting breast-cloths—the garments over their bodices—which were gathered up again after the Lord had risen;
these were the wives of Kṛṣṇa, women to be enjoyed. (The term) *vadhū* refers to a wife, a daughter-in-law, or a woman in general.

The Section on Various Meanings: Here, if the word *vadhū* were explained as signifying "wife," it would contradict Bhīṣma’s statement, "He indeed returned to his original nature, like the cowherd’s wife" (*gopa-vadhū*).
Therefore, it should not be explained in that way. [Rather,] the fair-limbed women were embraced by that one, the dark and beautiful Kṛṣṇa.

Because they share that same single refuge and because they are the objects of enjoyment for that same one, they are like brides; thus, she is called "Vadhvā" (the Bride), which is the name of the *Prakṛta-Vaiṣṇava-Toṣaṇī*. ||8||
Dancing with sweet voices and fond of pleasure, they sang loudly,
delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa, so that this entire place was filled with their song.

Śrīdhara: "Dancing" means they are dancing. "Sweet-voiced" (*rakta-kaṇṭhyaḥ*) means their throats are colored by various melodies. "Delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa" means by his contact. Vaṃśīdhara: "Touch" (*abhimarśa*) refers to a specific kind of contact that awakens the arousal of desire. Alternatively, it refers to pride (*māna*).
Those for whom honor was performed by Kṛṣṇa; "covered," because it was witnessed by the gods; those [honored] by means of song, that is, by their singing;

those who love pleasure, meaning they are devoted to amorous delight; "dancing," meaning they were performing a dance; or alternatively, those for whom honor—respect shown by Kṛṣṇa—was performed by means of dancing; those with "red throats," meaning [voices] possessing various musical scales (*rāga*).
His throat was rendered impassioned. The musical modes (*rāgas*) have been described in the *Saṅgītasāra*: "There are as many musical modes as there are species of living beings;
among them, sixteen thousand excellent ones were formerly created by the Gopīs."

Those for whom *rati*—the love whose agent is Kṛṣṇa—is their very dear [delight]; they were gladdened by the touch and other caresses of Kṛṣṇa, whereby the fatigue from dancing and so forth did not arise. By the song, that is, by the song whose agent was he, this world—the entire universe—was at that time covered, meaning it was pervaded. That...
Or, "by means of song" refers to that action which is performed through song; the meaning is that even today they are still sung by people living in the world. ||9||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: "By that song this [world] was pervaded," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: by those very songs sung by them, various musical compositions (*prabandhas*) were created by the authors of the treatises on music (*saṅgīta-śāstra*);
by those very compositions, these three worlds were pervaded. The sense is that there was no city like that before.
"Dancing" (nṛtyamānāḥ) means those for whom there is honor (*māna*)—that is, worship (*pūjā*)—performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa during the dance. ||9||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, having described the predominance of their dancing due to the intensity of their great joy, he speaks also of their singing with the word "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*). By the phrase "while dancing," even in the act of dancing, a particular excellence of skill is shown through such singing. He states the purpose of the singing and so forth with the word "delight" (*ratiḥ*).

Their beloved is that very love which has Śrī Kṛṣṇa as its agent. One should not suspect that they experience fatigue from loud singing and so forth; thus he says: "delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa"—this too is to be understood as one reason. He demonstrates the high pitch of their song: "by whose singing [the space] was covered and pervaded."

Alternatively, the meaning is that this world was pervaded by the songs of those [goddesses] through a collection of musical modes (*rāga*) conceived by themselves; consequently, the world became intent on singing in accordance with them. It is these very sixteen thousand musical modes produced by them that are distributed throughout the world.
This is well known from the treatises on music (*saṅgīta-śāstra*). As it is stated in the *Saṅgīta-sāra*: "There are as many musical modes (*rāga*) as there are species of living beings;
among them, sixteen thousand excellent ones were formerly composed by the cowherd girls."
Or else, "anyat" refers to something other than those [qualities].

Alternatively, they are those for whom there is honor—that is, the respect bestowed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa—by means of His dancing. By the term "rakta-kaṇṭhyaḥ," meaning those whose throats are moist with love, their supreme sweetness is expressed. This applies to singing loudly.

The cause is "because of delight" (ratī) and "because of Kṛṣṇa. Alternatively, it is because [the singing] was even higher than the loud chanting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. He states the reason for this with the three qualifiers beginning with "red" (raktā).
One should understand that among these, the relationship of cause and effect occurs as desired. Thus, regarding the phrase "there she shone exceedingly with them":
By this, their excellence in qualities such as singing, which is like their physical beauty, is indicated; however, it will be made explicit later on. ||9||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, due to the intensification of their great joy, having described the increase of their dancing and singing—or rather, the preeminence of the dancing—the author speaks also of the singing with the word "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*). Regarding the phrase "while dancing": even in the act of dancing, there is a particular excellence of skill due to such singing.
[The purpose] has been shown. He states the purpose of the singing and so forth: *ratiḥ* is sexual pleasure, love, or the love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

She alone is the beloved whom [they sing for]; and he says that one should not suspect them of fatigue from loud singing and the like: they are delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa, who captivates the heart and whose essence is a mass of supreme bliss.
Thus, by singing loudly, he reveals this: that [the world] was "enveloped" (āvṛtam)—meaning pervaded—either by those songs or by that song;

or else, the meaning is that by the song of that [Lord], such as the Gītā and so forth, the world was enveloped by verses composed for the people, becoming entirely permeated by that single aesthetic flavor (rasa). In this way, His majesty has been described. The rest [was sung] by them.

This has been explained. Alternatively, "māna" refers to honor through the dance; or, "māna" refers to pride, such that those who possess pride even greater than [that of] Kṛṣṇa due to the dance are "rakta-kaṇṭhyaḥ," meaning those whose throats are softened by love—this refers to singing.

Its supreme sweetness is described by its being composed of the essence of divine love (*prema-rasa*). The reason for singing loudly is stated as "Rati" and "Kṛṣṇa"; or else, it means [singing] with a voice even higher than that of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself. Thus it has been said by the venerable Parāśara:
"Kṛṣṇa sang the *rāsa* song with a very high-pitched voice;
meanwhile, they sang 'Well done, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! with a twofold intensity.
(Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.56). He states the reason for this with the three qualifying adjectives beginning with "attached" (*rakta*), etc., in their respective order.

The relationship of cause and effect is to be inferred. Although it is possible that she too might sing loudly in that same manner due to her joy from touching them, nevertheless, compared to the singing of the *rāsa*,
such [loudness] would not be achieved because of her helplessness due to love or her longing to hear their loud singing.
This is to be understood; the rest is the same. ||9||

The sequence of composition: By the songs of those [gopīs], which themselves imagined a multitude of *rāgas*, this world became filled; the meaning is that it became devoted to singing in accordance with them. It is stated in the treatises on music (*saṅgīta-śāstra*) that the sixteen thousand *rāgas* created by them were indeed distributed throughout the world. (9)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He describes the manner of singing referred to by the word "gāyantyaḥ" (singing) with the words beginning with "uccaiḥ" (loudly). Those for whom dancing (*nṛtye*) is their honor (*mānaḥ*) and worship (*pūjā*). They have red throats (*rakta-kaṇṭhāḥ*), meaning their throats are reddish due to delicacy; or, because *rakta* refers to the cluster of passion (*rāga-kadamba*) and is singular by virtue of being a genus (*jāti*), [it means] that passion resides in their throats.
They possess the capacity to transform passion according to the occasion. Their delight consists of the objects of dance and song;
their faith is in Him, and they are dear to Kṛṣṇa. "Touch" (abhimarśa) means contact, that is to say, an embrace.
The meaning is that, being delighted by observing His skill in singing, they were embraced by Him at every moment.

Being thus, the truthful ones sang aloud even as they danced: "By the song of this lute-player, this world—which was previously covered, pervaded, and rendered insignificant by the songs of Brahmā and others following the ancient traditions of music—is now surpassed;
indeed, by his song this entire universe is enveloped, and beyond this there is nothing else."
The meaning is that it might be sung by some. ||9||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described the mere flurry of dancing, he speaks of the song that is variegated with dance—beginning with "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*). "Dancing" (*nṛtyamānāḥ*) means those who are dancing; or else, it refers to those whose pride (*mānaḥ*) is fixed upon the dance.
Because their dancing is preeminent, they sang loudly. Now, one might ask: in the flurry of dancing...
Anticipating the objection that singing would be impossible, he states the reason for their loud singing: "delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa.

The touch (*abhimarśa*) of Kṛṣṇa—who is the embodiment of supreme bliss—consists of stroking with the hand and so forth; being delighted by that touch is the primary reason. By this, the removal of fatigue is also implied.

It has been said that the word "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*) connects with both [dancing and singing]. Thus, the manifestation of a particular excellence of skill in dancing and singing has been described. Alternatively, those who possess pride because their own dancing exceeds that of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are referred to by the word "loudly"; this is the dependence of that term even upon the previous singing.
Excellence. Or rather, it is "loudly" (*uccais*) because of the intention to express the superiority of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s singing.

He states the reason for the excellence of the singing: *rakta-kaṇṭhyaḥ*. This means those whose throats are colored by various melodies (*nānā-rāgaiḥ*). By this, it is indicated that [the singing] is pleasing to the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. When...

He speaks even more highly of their devotion (*rati*)—namely, that by the power of their song, even Śrī Kṛṣṇa was stunned. As for the phrase "by whose song this universe was pervaded," this is the intended meaning. Regarding the expression "delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa," [it refers to] by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

When one's own bliss is established within them through the touching of their breasts and other limbs, fullness of bliss (*pūrṇānandatva*) is thereby indicated. For this very reason, the sense is that at the time delimited by the act of amorous play (*ramaṇa*), all living beings (*jīva*) become filled with happiness. ||9||

Viśvanātha: "Dancing" means dancing; or alternatively, those for whom there is honor—that is, respect shown by Kṛṣṇa—by means of their dance. "Red-throated" means having throats colored by various musical modes (*rāga*). And the musical modes have been described in the *Saṅgītasāra*:
"There would be as many varieties of passion as there are species of living beings;
among them, sixteen thousand were formerly performed by the Gopīs.
Thus, they are those for whom love (*prīti*)—the delight produced by Kṛṣṇa—is indeed dear. [This occurs] through the touch of Kṛṣṇa.

"Joy through touch and so forth" means the absence of exhaustion from dancing and other such activities. The meaning is that at that time, this entire world was "covered," that is, pervaded, by that song—by the song which had [the gods] as its agents. Alternatively, it means by the song which had [the world] as its object. Even today, by the people inhabiting the world, that...
The meaning is that they are indeed being sung. ||9||
A certain woman, honored by Mukunda who was pleased with her, sang the notes of the Svara-jāti unmixed [with others], while he praised her, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"— o)0(o—
He raised her very firmly and bestowed upon her great honor.

Śrīdhara: Along with Mukunda, she sang the melodic scales (*svarajāti*) beginning with *ṣaḍja*; these were unmixed—that is, not confused—with those produced by Kṛṣṇa. Being delighted and honored [by Him], she raised them; having certainly made that very raising of the scale into the specific rhythm called *dhruva*, she "raised" it—meaning she performed it. ||10||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*.
*Rasikāhlādinī*:

Viśvanātha says that he asked him [this] in order to respectfully intimidate even those people who had come from many villages and cities as pilgrims; this is the underlying meaning. For this very reason, [he is called] Hṛṣīkeśa.
He caused all the people there to focus their minds one-pointedly upon the words spoken by Sudarśana.
One woman, exhausted from the *rāsa* dance, grasped with her arm the shoulder of the mace-wielder standing at her side, as her bracelets and jasmine garlands grew loose.

Śrīdhara: Thus, he describes the conduct of those women who were honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa through dancing, singing, and so forth—a conduct characterized by the playfulness of their intense love—beginning with the words "A certain woman" (kācit). She is one whose bracelets and jasmine garlands are slipping off. (11)
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:

*Krama-sandarbha*: A certain [commentary]. He is Gadābhṛt (the Mace-bearer) because he bears a mace—a staff in the form of a mace—either suitable for protecting the cowherds or appropriate for the Lord of the host of dancers. //11//
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*:
*Rasikāhlādinī* by Viśvanātha. "By whom were they brought?"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. (11)
There, having smelled Kṛṣṇa’s arm resting on one shoulder— which possessed the fragrance of a blue lotus and was anointed with sandalwood paste— he, his hair standing on end with joy, kissed it.
Śrīdhara: His arm, which possesses the fragrance of a blue lotus. ||12||

Vaṃśīdhara: In that *rāsa*, [she was] perfumed by Utpala with his garland; "with hair standing on end" refers to the emergence of *sāttvika* emotion, as stated in the passage beginning, "stiffness, perspiration, and horripilation," and so forth.
By the phrase "kissed him," her state of being agitated by desire is indicated. "Resting on the shoulder" means situated upon her own shoulder.

"Even when anointed with sandalwood paste, she possesses a fragrance like that of a blue lotus"—this is because her natural bodily scent of the blue lotus so greatly overpowers the scent of the sandalwood.
Since her actions are identical to those described in the previous chapter, she is surely Śyāmalā. (12)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Kṛṣṇa, too, out of playful fatigue, placed His arm upon the shoulder of one [gopī];
thus He says, beginning with "There," and so forth. At that moment, one [gopī] kissed Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arm resting on Her own shoulder; by that very kiss, Her fatigue vanished.

"Having the fragrance of a blue lotus" means it possesses a natural fragrance, as if anointed with sandalwood; it is not made fragrant by that [sandalwood], for it is fragrant by its very nature. Thinking, "He has placed his own arm upon my shoulder," she whose body hairs stood on end out of joy, considering her own excellence of fortune above all others. (12)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, by way of similarity to her previous actions, he describes the pastime of Śrī Śyāmalā with the words "tatra" (there). One gopī had [the Lord] resting upon her shoulder—that is, situated on her own shoulder; the meaning is that his natural fragrance was even greater than that of the blue lotus flower. Specifically...
It was thoroughly smeared with sandalwood paste in an excellent manner, such as by making decorative patterns (*bhakti-ccheda*). "Ha" indicates clearly.

The reason for the kiss is that her hair stood on end (*hṛṣṭa-roma*); the meaning is that she was rendered helpless by love. By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), even her hairs were thrilled; the sense is: what more need be said of her own joy? This...
Boldness is the consequent emotion arising from confidence. As it has been said by the learned: "Boldness is defined as fearlessness in one's performances" (Uṇādisūtra 11.21). ||12||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: One gopī [placed] upon His shoulder—that is, situated on His own shoulder—[a garland] whose fragrance was naturally superior even to that of the utpala flower, and which was specifically and thoroughly smeared with sandalwood paste in an excellent manner such as by being cut into appropriate shapes; thus, the arousal of amorous passion is indicated.
This is clear. The reason for the kiss is that her hair stands on end (*hṛṣṭaromā*); the meaning is that this occurs due to being overwhelmed by love (*prema-vaivaśya*).

By means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), her body hairs (*romāṇi*) are also "thrilled. The sequence of the composition implies the sense: "What need is there to mention her own joy? This has not been explicitly explained.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, Kṛṣṇa, being fatigued, spoke so that his arm might rest upon the shoulder of someone; "There," and so forth. There, in that rāsa festival, one fortunate woman kissed Kṛṣṇa’s arm resting on her shoulder—an arm that was naturally fragrant like a blue lotus and smeared with sandalwood paste.

Having smelled it by applying [the scent] to her nose and examining it with her sense of smell, she was in doubt: "Is this fragrant because of the sandalwood, or is it its own inherent nature? Having experienced the fragrance as being the very nature of the blue lotus—[realizing], "It is the fragrance of a blue lotus"—she kissed it with her hair standing on end; this is the meaning. Therefore, [he says] "smeared with sandalwood."
The greatness of the meaning of the script's natural state: here, Kṛṣṇa’s languor and her intense longing are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). ||12||
The Composition of Joy (317): Regarding the "sāttvika" [emotions] therein—it is clear. ||12||
*Prītisandarbha* (322): "Confidence in one's performances is called *pragalbhatā* (boldness) by the learned" (*Uṇādisūtra* 11.21).
And that [boldness] was demonstrated in the passage beginning with "there, on one shoulder," etc. (12).

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, Kṛṣṇa, being weary, spoke as follows—"There," and so on—to indicate that he might rest his arm upon the shoulder of someone: "In that rāsa festival, one fortunate woman kissed Kṛṣṇa’s arm resting upon her shoulder, which was naturally fragrant like a blue lotus and smeared with sandalwood paste."

Having smelled it by applying it with the nose and examining it, she was in doubt as to whether it was fragrant because of the sandalwood or because of its own nature. Having experienced the fragrance of the blue lotus as its very nature—meaning, having perceived the fragrance as being the essence of the object itself—she kissed it with her hair standing on end; therefore, [the phrase] "smeared with sandalwood" is used.
The greatness of the meaning of the nature of the script: here, Kṛṣṇa’s indolence and her longing are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). ||11-12||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: To describe the conduct of a certain [gopī] whose desires were fulfilled, [the author] speaks of a particular pastime of that very leader of the group, beginning with the word "there. There, in that *rāsa*-maṇḍala, a certain gopī had Kṛṣṇa’s arm upon her own shoulder because she was embraced by him with his hand. From the *utpala*...
"Even more than the blue lotus" means that its fragrance is innate;

"especially smeared with sandalwood" means it is completely anointed with sandalwood paste in various decorative patterns, by which its quality of extinguishing the heat of passion is expressed; "having smelled" refers to the act of smelling with a particular state of being (*bhāva*). Therefore...
The virtuous woman, filled with bliss and possessing a fragrance that had intensified in solitude, indeed kissed his arm.

The intended meaning is that she performed the kiss as if mimicking the very definition of joy or, alternatively, of full-blown bliss. The phrase "the scent of a blue lotus" refers specifically to her natural [fragrance].

The phrase "saurabhaṃ candanāliptam" (the fragrance [of that] which is smeared with sandalwood) indicates a specific confusion. The purpose of smelling these two is for the sake of discernment; however, it is suggested that this discernment belongs only to those who are supremely clever and endowed with extraordinary insight, and not to others. Smelling leads to the destruction of discernment and fortitude.
Or even a kiss is sufficient for nourishment. ||12||

Viśvanātha: She is surely Śyāmalā, for although sandalwood paste is applied to her shoulder—that is, upon her own shoulder—she possesses a fragrance like that of a blue lotus; because her natural bodily scent of the blue lotus so greatly overpowers the scent of the sandalwood, she is certain to be this very girl mentioned in the previous chapter due to the similarity of her actions.
To one woman who was touching her cheek against another’s cheek— her own cheek adorned with the luster of earrings swinging during the dance— he gave a piece of chewed betel.

Śrīdhara: [The Lord] was joined with her own cheek, which was thus adorned by the luster of two earrings that were displaced and trembling due to her dancing and movement, as she brought them together and applied them to her own cheek. ||13||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Here, [the Lord] himself [placed His hand] on the face of a certain friend who was dancing nearby.

Or rather, he describes their mutual affection through the principle of *kaimutika* (how much more so) by stating that out of maternal tenderness (*vātsalya*) she gave her a chewed betel leaf: "To a certain one," and so forth.
A certain dear friend gave—that is, she offered with great care—a chewed betel leaf to another dear friend.
Or, as she pressed her cheek against his own cheek, which was adorned by the luster of the earring displaced during their dance;
or rather, someone gave it to another; or perhaps Kṛṣṇa himself, out of curiosity, gave the chewed betel to someone, or gave it with great intensity, or took it back. At that time—

Regarding the phrase "on the cheeks adorned with the luster of earrings," it should be understood as referring to the two cheeks (*gaṇḍau*) of Kṛṣṇa himself; by that, his dancing (*nāṭyam*) should also be understood here. Alternatively, a certain [woman] placed her cheek upon the cheek of someone, or Kṛṣṇa took hold of a cheek; it is the touching of cheek to cheek out of affection.
He led her away. "Where there is the chewing of betel" (tāmbūla-carvita) means that because of the chewing of betel, [the lips] were swollen on the outside;
furthermore, by means of a kiss, the red dye from the chewing of betel on the lower lip became attached there—thus, preceded by a kiss.

The meaning is "the touching cheek to cheek. Otherwise, by joining cheek to cheek, the giving and taking of the chewed betel would be difficult to perform, and thus it would not be very graceful. Of what sort [is she]?
Of one who is *sandadhatī*, performing a *sandhāna*, that is, making a close contact. Or else, [she is] chewing the betel.

"Placing cheek to cheek while correctly giving" has two meanings as explained previously. Furthermore, Kṛṣṇa said, "Give me [your cheek]," and thus he performed the act of holding cheek to cheek; however, she did not accept even what was given by him. It is merely out of curiosity—thus there are eleven meanings. (13)
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha — o)0(o—
Dancing and singing, with her anklets and girdle tinkling,
one woman stood by the side of Śiva, whose lotus-hand had slipped away, and being weary, she pressed him against her breasts.
Śrīdhara: She is one whose anklets and girdle are tinkling. ||14||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: there is only one [work] of this name.

Having become utterly exhausted by the simultaneous performance of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, she herself provided a remedy for that; thus he says, beginning with "nṛtyati" (she dances). "Nṛtyatī" means "while dancing. Likewise, "gāyantī" means "while singing.
The sound of the tinkling anklets and girdle itself constitutes the instrumental music. Being exhausted, [she leaned] upon the one standing at her side who had slipped away.
Or, standing at her side, she placed a lotus-hand upon her breasts, cool as Śiva himself.
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha [says]: because of which curse... ||14||
Having obtained Acyuta, the beloved who is the exclusive favorite of Śrī,
the gopīs embraced His neck with their arms and wandered about while singing of Him.
Śrīdhara: In this way, other gopīs also sported with various amorous dalliances as they pleased; thus he says: "The gopīs... (verse 15).
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Krama-sandarbha*: [This refers to] that Gopī; or rather, it refers to Him who is the object of love even for Śrī, surpassing even the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha and others, yet was not attained by her. Him.

Having obtained their beloved lover, it was not merely a gain; rather, the meaning is that they were such that their necks were grasped by his two arms, for he could not endure even the slightest separation. [From] the *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "Then, having rested for a moment, they again began their wandering."
He said: "The gopīs," and so forth. The gopīs are the glories (śrī) of Śrī, appearing in the form of cowherd girls.

Having obtained Acyuta—the beloved, most dear, charming, and desirable one—who is the exclusive favorite, they, with their necks embraced by His arms (Acyuta’s arms), sing of Him; and by that which was performed at that very moment...

The meaning is that they sported, singing with verses describing the sweetness of the beauty of his qualities, employing skill in various melodies and so forth; "sang" implies that they also danced. ||15||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says: "O Dispeller of Disease, O Destroyer of Suffering, I bid farewell; I beg permission to go to my own world. (15)
With the beauty of faces marked by perspiration on the cheeks, adorned with ear-lotuses and hair-ornaments, accompanied by the sounds of bracelets and anklets as if they were musical instruments;
The gopīs danced together with the Lord in the rāsa assembly, their flower garlands falling from their hair as bees sang along.

Śrīdhara: While the disputants, singers, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others were being bewildered by the immersion in aesthetic rasa (*rasāveśa*), He displayed another excellence of musical instruments and the like, and described the agitation of the *rāsa* dance with the verse beginning "With ear-lotuses" (*karṇotpalaiḥ*). [The phrase] "with ear-lotuses" refers to those adorned with curls and decorated with locks of hair.

Those whose faces possessed beauty and splendor with their cheeks flushed by the heat; those whose tinkling ornaments were small bells, or rather, those whose voices were like the sound of small bells; those from whose own hair the garlands had slipped due to the sounds of bracelets, anklets, and musical instruments;
by this [description], it is shown that their hair, satisfied by the rhythmic movement of the beat, shook their heads and rained down flowers at his feet.

"They danced as if making [the forest] dance"—this is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣita*). They danced together with the Blessed One. Where? In that assembly for the *rāsa* dance, in which the bees themselves were the singers. || 16 ||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Now, they danced together with the Blessed Lord.

He said: "Karṇotpala," and so forth. The gopīs danced together with the Blessed One. The meaning is: "in the same manner as the Blessed One danced. The word *sama* has both the sense of "together" (*saha*) and the sense of "similar" (*sadṛśa*), because both meanings appear simultaneously. In that regard, dancing is first of two kinds: without song (*nirgīta*) and with song (*sagīta*).

And: *nirgīta* (without song) is dancing performed slowly with only instrumental accompaniment, accompanied by a gentle *satāla* rhythm, and characterized by the gradual movement of the face, throat, eyebrows, eyes, and so forth; *sagīta* (with song) is that which corresponds to the meaning of the song and possesses specific movements of the hands (*hastaka*) and other limbs. Here, first of all, this is *nirgīta*.

Regarding "the dance": it is where there is no interruption in the song by bees or singers. [The women possess] beauty upon their faces through the *karṇotpala* (ear-lotuses), the *ālaka* (curved locks), the *viṭaṅka* (ornamental curls), the playful movements of the locks (*alaka-vibhrama*), as well as the perspiration on their cheeks.

By means of the swaying ear-lotuses caused by the movement of the face, eyes, neck, and so forth— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary explaining the verse concerning the dancing women.]
The meaning is: with the curling tips of their locks of hair moving and the perspiration on their cheeks shimmering;

and with the sounds of bracelets and anklets themselves serving as musical instruments, even more so than other instruments, they were incessant at that time. By this, it should be understood that there were other musical instruments as well previously. At that time, however—

The meaning is that the dance was performed by means of the music of the bees' humming and the instrumental music of their bracelets. "Those whose garlands were falling from their own hair" means those whose garlands were slipping down from their own locks; thus, by virtue of the garlands slipping halfway down, [the state of] their hair [is indicated].
It is an excellence of beauty. The word "sva" (own) signifies being distinct from the Blessed One. The sense is that a garland exists upon his hair in exactly that same manner. ||16||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Viśvanātha — o)0(o)—
Thus the Lord of Ramā took delight with the beautiful women of Vraja through embraces, the touch of their hands, affectionate glances, unrestrained charms, and laughter.
Just as a child [is deluded] by the errors of his own reflected images.
Śrīdhara: Just as the gopīs sported with the Lord through various amorous dalliances, so too the Lord rejoiced with them through His own playful charms; thus he says, "In this way.
An illustration for the pleasure of one who is not overwhelmed by those charms is given: "Just as a child," and so forth.
He is like one whose play consists of the delusion [caused] by his own reflections. By this it is shown:
having transferred his own skill in all arts, as well as his fragrance, loveliness, sweetness, and so forth, onto them, he sported with them just as a child plays with his own reflections. (17)
Vaṃśīdhara: By those gopīs; "their amorous charms" refers to their *vilāsas*, and he is "unconquered" or "unoverpowered" by them. As for *vilāsa*:
it consists of the movements of walking, standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as the actions of the face, eyes, and other limbs.

"Bewitchment (*vilāsa*) is a momentary distinctiveness born from union with the beloved," so it was stated by Bharata [in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* 11.31]. By this illustration, this particular occurrence is shown. As for *lāvaṇya* (loveliness): "Like the shimmering quality within the shadow of pearls..."
That which appears as loveliness (*lāvaṇya*) in the limbs is what is called here [by that term]. As for sweetness (*mādhurya*):
that from which the mind does not depart is said to be sweetness.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of a melodious voice (*sauśvaryam*) is intended. *Tāsu* refers to those gopīs. *Saṃcārya* means having caused [the child] to enter among them.
*Tābhiḥ* refers to those gopīs. *Arbhakaḥ* means a young boy. By this as well, the fault of inconsistency (*vyabhicāra-doṣaḥ*) is refuted;
for since reflections have their existence dependent upon the original object (*bimba*), they are in reality inseparable from it.

It is indeed non-difference from Him. And thus, because the gopīs are non-different from the Lord by virtue of being His reflections, their pastimes—as well as His—are likewise inconceivable, like those of a child. In this way, He states that even Kṛṣṇa’s sexual enjoyments were fulfilled through the rāsa dances alone: "Embracing" means an embrace with each one individually.

During the dance of the pair, there is the touching or stroking with the hand; this occurs at the conclusion of the dance movement in the form of placing a rhythmic beat (tāla) with one's own right hand upon the left breast of the beloved. There is also a tender glance, a loving look directed toward her secret limbs. And there is unrestrained dalliance under the pretext of bestowing a reward.

Kissing and so forth; laughter, moreover, refers to the blossoming of the face or jesting following the attainment of those various [pleasures]. *Rameśaḥ* means that he displayed his sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) over *Ramā*, Lakṣmī, and took delight with the beauties of Vraja, but not that he caused them to take delight (*ramaya*). Just as a child is innocent, so too was he toward them.
The meaning is that, because he was subject to love (*premādhīnatva*), he maintained only the state of innocence (*maugdhyam*), and not the sovereignty (*aiśvaryam*) as [he does] with Ramā.
Now, one might ask: how could he, being alone, sport with those thousands of women? To this he says:
he whose "delusion" (*vibhramaḥ*)—that is, his playful manifestation (*vilāsaḥ*)—is such that each woman is merely his own reflection (*pratibimbam*).
"Having displayed Himself to men whose eyes were not yet satiated and who had not performed sufficient austerity, He withdrew His own form, which is the eye of the world. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.11).
Just as the word *bimba* here denotes the essential nature (*svarūpa*), so too does it mean the same here. By each one...

The meaning is that He enjoyed with His beloved in each individual form, because they constitute His very nature as His *hlādinī* (bliss-giving) potency. Since it is inappropriate for them to be mere reflections of Himself, no other interpretation is desired. ||17||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Thus" [is said]. This has been explained by them. Therein, the introduction is understood precisely through the force of the illustration. The explanation beginning with "just as a child" and ending with "he himself" follows this very [introduction]. In both cases, those things which stand in the place of reflections...

This is because there is constant mutual imitation between the Śrī-gopīs and the Śrī-Bhagavān, who occupies the position of a child. In that context, the Śrī-Bhagavān himself engages in activity for the sake of playful pastimes (vilāsa) like a child; thus, his own initiation [into play], his instigation of others, and the specific varieties of his pastimes are found therein. From that...
The example given for sexual union applies only to one who is not overwhelmed by her charms; thus, this appears to be incidental.

As for what was explained as "that which has been shown by him" and so forth, therein it is understood that those very [charms] are the manifestors of his qualities, just as a child [perceives objects] only through the medium of a reflection.

Just as one experiences the sweetness of one's own mouth through another and not by oneself, so too it is understood that the Śrī Bhagavān does so only through the medium of His beloved consort; for without the emergence of their love-filled state, He does not emerge.

Or rather: although He is the Lord and Master of Ramā, He took delight with the beautiful women of Vraja alone. Indeed, by the word "with her" (tayā), it is intended that their excellence of love, virtue, and beauty is even greater than His. Or again: He is indeed the Lord and Master of Ramā, but not her lover; yet He took delight with the beautiful women of Vraja nonetheless.
This is exactly what was intended. And since that pleasure too is indeed unique, he says with aesthetic relish (sacamatkāram):
"In this way. Therein, "embracing" (pariṣvaṅga) is their clasping; "touching with the hands" (karābhimarśa) is the stroking of their hands;
"affectionate glances" (snigdhekṣaṇa) is the gazing with passion upon their faces and other features; and "unrestrained playfulness" (uddāmavilāsa) [is the rest].

The touching of her breasts and so forth, as well as laughter— a smile manifested through the intensity of emotion (bhāva)— by these [acts], he demonstrates through an illustration both the mutual equality and the attachment between him and them, due to their shared quality of being the supreme object of service. "Just as"— for example, a certain child...

Just as one who, by the very nature of his youth, is utterly addicted to play and possesses a charming grace that causes him to mistake his own reflection for another, and thus delights with those reflected forms as if they were his equals;
so too does he, by the nature of being under the sway of love, become absorbed in play consisting of that [object of love].
Because they are His own manifestations by virtue of being His own essential potencies (*svarūpa-śakti*), He sported with them as if they were reflections.

For this very reason, with the intention of expressing their similarity to Him, he previously did not call them "cowherd women" (*gopa-vadhvaḥ*) but rather "Kṛṣṇa’s wives" (*kṛṣṇa-vadhvaḥ*). And so it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*:
He who, being the self of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very powers (kalās) which are manifested from the essence of bliss and consciousness as His own inherent nature.
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.37).
And here, just as a child performs such actions as moving his face and so forth,
even the reflected images of him perform exactly the same, because he himself is eager for play.

Thus, it should be understood that Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs performed [these acts] because of their mutual attachment. By this, the transformation of affection (sneha-vikāra) manifested through the word "snigdha" is shown to exist in Him as well, just as it did in them;
and that [transformation] is described by Śrī Parāśara as being of the nature of sattva (sāttvika).

"Having come into contact with the cheeks of the gopīs, Hari’s two arms attained the density of rain clouds through the water of perspiration, serving as grain for the emergence of horripilation. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.55) ||17||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Embracing is the clasping of the gopīs; the touching of their hands is the grasping of their hands, or else it is the touching of them with one's own hand, such as the touching of their breasts and so forth; affectionate glancing is the passionate gazing at their faces and other features; and unrestrained dalliance is...
The loosening of the waist-knot and so forth; and laughter is a smile manifested through the intensification of emotion.

Although he is the Lord and Master of Ramā, he took delight only with the beautiful women of Vraja, and not with her. Alternatively, by the phrase "the Lord (īśa) of Ramā," his status as her master implies that she is unfit for such passion; rather, [he delighted] with the beautiful women of Vraja.

Their very fitness for that [union] is intended here. Showing that very [fitness] through specific qualities such as skill in emotion (*bhāva*) even compared to Lakṣmī, he states with an illustration the mutual equality between the Blessed Lord and them, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*).
Just as there is no dissimilarity whatsoever between a child and his reflection, so it is with them.

The meaning is: "together with Kṛṣṇa. Just as a child intent on play performs such actions as moving his hands and so forth, even his shadow performs the same; for just as the shadow would act, he too imitates it in that very same way because of his childhood. In this manner, just as the Blessed Lord played, they too [did the same].
They rejoiced in that very same way; the meaning is that as they rejoiced, he too rejoiced in the same manner.

By this, the splendor of the Blessed Lord’s own love (*bhagavad-rati*) is also indicated; for such [joy] would not be possible if there were any disparity. This is the general direction. Furthermore, a transformation of love (*prema-vikāra*) on his part is intended to be just like theirs, and this has been stated by Śrī Parāśara:

"Having come into contact with the cheeks of the gopīs, Hari’s two arms attained the density of rain clouds through the water of perspiration, serving as a field for the sprouting of horripilation. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.55) ||17||
The rest has been explained by them.

Or rather, just as a child—who possesses a playful delusion through his reflection—delights while being solely intent upon that [reflection] and knowing nothing else, so too does this [Lord]. Or else, thus...

In the manner described, He enjoyed with those very beauties of Vraja through embraces and other such acts, and they likewise performed similar embraces and so forth; this he expresses by way of an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
The rest is the same. Thus, His pleasure was derived solely from their embraces and other such acts, and He himself—
Therefore, by his imitating them, he has demonstrated that their greatness exceeds even his own. ||17||

The sequence of the composition: Although he is the Lord and Master of Ramā, he took delight only with the beautiful women of Vraja, and not with her. Or rather, he is indeed the Lord and Master of Ramā, but not merely her lover;
yet he did indeed take delight with the beautiful women of Vraja. ||17||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He clarifies that the word *samam* (together) signifies similarity in the phrase "they danced together"—namely, "in this manner" (*evam*) and so forth. In this way (*evam*), by means of these [actions] such as embracing and the rest, the Lord of Rāma (*remeśaḥ*) took delight; with whom? Together with the beauties of Vraja (*vraja-sundarībhiḥ*). By their association (*sāhityena*), they too took delight.
[They] have arrived. Therefore, regarding the embrace, there is agency belonging to both him and them;
for in that embrace, they embrace him, and while they are embracing, he embraces them—and such is the manner [of action] in cases such as the touching of hands and so forth. In that regard:
The illustration: "just as a child," meaning like a child. What kind of child?

One who has various delusions regarding his own reflections, that is, his own shadows. The intended meaning is this: just as the child himself moves, he becomes variously deluded when the reflection moves in accordance with him.

“Who is this who is like me? He acts exactly as I do,” or rather, “He acts just as I act”—thus deluded, he becomes paralyzed with pride. Likewise, this [individual] also becomes paralyzed by intense bliss (*sāndrānanda-stabdha*), and they too become pure.

The meaning is as follows: Alternatively, he is one whose play (*vilāsa*) consists of the delusion (*bhrama*) regarding his own reflection; thus, he sports with his own shadow just as a child does. Or rather, being accompanied by the beautiful women of Vraja in the delusion of reflections, he took delight like a child, remaining motionless as if he were a mere infant.

The meaning is this: through their proximity (*sāhitya*), His own reflection was fixed in them and their reflections were fixed in Him due to their translucent nature (*svaccha-bhāva*). He was thus characterized by *vibhrama*—that is, a specific delusion (*viśiṣṭa-bhrama*)—in that regard. Previously, they too had likewise [experienced] Kṛṣṇa’s reflection fixed in themselves; now, beholding Him, [they wondered], "What, have I become manifold? (*kim ahaṃ nānā bhūtvā*)?
The delusion arises: "Is Kṛṣṇa clinging to each of their bodies individually? Or are these reflections of me? When Kṛṣṇa is clinging to their reflections as well, a similar delusion occurs for them;

thus, through the similarity between the two children, their state of being subject to delusion is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). [This occurs] when the third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*saha-artha*).

Because [the property] is connected through the relation of the qualified and its qualification (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*). For example, in the case of "Devadatta is fat and possesses cows because of his son," both [the fatness and the possession of cows] belong to Devadatta alone. ||17||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, in order to speak of the conclusion of all the pastimes, he declares the preeminence of the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-vilāsa already introduced with the words "evam" (thus). He describes the excellence of their good fortune as surpassing even that of Lakṣmī. "Evam" means in the manner previously described; "pariṣvaṅgam" means an embrace.

Then there is the touching with the hands, such as the contact with the breasts and other parts; the affectionate gaze, which reveals inner emotion (*bhāva*), consisting of the looking at various limbs; and unrestrained, intensely powerful *vilāsa*. As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*:
A gait as deep as that of a bull, a steady gaze,

and speech accompanied by a smile— this is called *vilāsa* (graceful charm). Furthermore, in the case of a fourfold glance, when the look is imbued with emotion (*bhāva*), it is characterized by these smiles.

Or rather, [this refers to] the embracing and so forth of the beauties of Vraja. Therein, "embracing" means an embrace preceded by praise such as "Well done! Well done! as a mark of favor during a particular dance;
immediately following that is the touching of the hands, which is the pressing [of her hands] with one's own two hands through a special display of skill.

A "glistening glance" (*snigdhekṣaṇa*) is a look that relishes specific emotional states (*bhāva*), such as the dancing of the eyebrows and so forth. "Unbridled" (*uddāma*) means unrestrained grace (*vilāsa*). As it is said in the *Rasārṇava*:
"At the moment of attaining the beloved, [there occurs] the activity of the eyebrows, eyes, and face..."
"That which is a momentary particularity is called *vilāsa*.

[Rasārṇavasudhākara 1.201] Laughter caused by embracing and so forth— by means of these [actions], even the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu), disregarding his status as the husband of Śrī, took delight with the beauties of Vraja because he perceived such feelings within Ramā.

He explains this by means of the analogy of equanimity (*sāmarasya*), saying: "Just as a child," and so forth. A child, acting spontaneously without any deliberate purpose, performs actions such as the movement of hands and face;
when he sees such an action in his own reflection, he then engages in play with it. It is just like that.

For as much as the artisan (*arbhaka*) makes, to that same extent does his reflection (*pratibimba*) also make. Indeed, in every respect, there is a lack of similarity [if the reflection were independent]; first there is the making of the original (*bimba*), and afterwards the making of the reflection occurs.
And just as there is a single nature between the original and its reflection by way of their properties, but not otherwise—

And its own nature is perceived as distinct from its own nature; for this very reason, a child does not recognize the self reflected in a mirror, but rather [perceives] it as a second [self], and through the sight of that reflection, there arises an increase in enthusiasm and an attachment to play. It is the same here as well.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is like the original object (bimba), enjoyed with them—who are like reflections—through His own acts of embracing and other such means that serve as excitants (uddīpana) for them.
This is the meaning: first there was the arising of amorous play in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and subsequently, in accordance with that, it arose within them.

Regarding the phrase "the arising of their grace" (*vilāsodaya*): it has been explained by the teachers that the Lord took His own skill in the arts (*kalā-kauśala*) and, having infused it into them, sported with them. The intended meaning of this is that their grace arises from the arising of Kṛṣṇa’s grace; it does not mean that the skill in the arts and so forth originates within them.

Thus, otherwise there would be the occurrence of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*). As for the illustration of the child, it refers to the similarity of their actions, not to falsity; otherwise, the perception of the gopīs would be considered qualified by a limiting condition (*sopādhika*). In reality, however, just as Śrī Kṛṣṇa is a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*), so too they are of the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Because they are of a different nature, due to the slackening of Rama’s passion, Rama cannot arise from them.

Alternatively, although the Lord of Rama (Rameśa) is endowed with skill in all arts, knowing that the pleasure of illicit love (*aupapatya-sukha*) is superior, He took delight with the beauties of Vraja. Of what sort was He? One who sports with His own reflection.
He whose charm and grace (vibhrama) are possessed of a mass of loveliness due to His own reflection— which is like a mirror— being reflected in the cheeks of the gopīs;
or rather, he whose manifold delusions arise from the multiplicity of reflections seen in their cheeks.
The delusion of one who perceives: "How can I, who am single, possess a manifold form? arises because he fails to discern his own true nature, being overwhelmed by their charms;
or else, it arises because the reflection of those women in himself is mirrored in his hands, fingers, nails, and so forth.

He whose agitation was such that he watched with intense longing, wondering, "How have these dancing girls come here?"— just as he had delighted in embraces and other pastimes with the beauties of Vraja,
so too did he delight in embraces and other pastimes with their reflections. Just like a child...
He sports together with his own reflection through questioning, laughter, touching hands, and so forth;
or rather, he is one whose delusion has vanished regarding the peerless forms of the gopīs,
because he has ascertained that the beauty in the very nature of the gopīs is incomparable— even the beauty, grace, and other qualities found in Ramā [Lakṣmī].
And in the world, He enjoyed with the beautiful women of Vraja as if they were but a faint reflection.

This is the intended meaning: while Ramā (Lakṣmī) enters the worlds of the lords of gods, the lords of Daityas, and so forth, through Her own portions, these [women of Vraja] have no entry elsewhere; because of their non-duality, they remain only in My Vraja. Therefore...

Thus, it is indicated that there is no delusion [on their part] regarding the thought, "I should cultivate an excess of love for these [gopīs]," because He Himself is eternally dear to Vraja. And so it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*:
"By those who are permeated by the essence of the blissful, spiritual nectar..."

"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who, having become the soul of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very potencies which are His own essential nature. [Brahma-saṃhitā 5.37] Thus it is said.

Viśvanātha: Thus, he states that the limbs of Kṛṣṇa’s sexual union are also accomplished by means of the very limbs of the *rāsa* dance: "Embracing" (*pariṣvaṅga*) is the act of hugging with each individual woman during the paired dancing;
"touching" (*abhimarśa*) is the contact made with the hand, and that occurs with his own right hand at the conclusion of the movement of the dance.

Rameśa [delights] by placing his palm upon the left breast of his beloved, by gazing with affectionate eyes at her secret limbs, by intense amorous play such as kissing and so forth under the pretext of bestowing rewards,
and by laughter, which is either a radiant smile or a jest following the attainment of various [desired objects].

The meaning is that while manifesting His sovereignty over Ramā (Lakṣmī), He took delight with the beautiful women of Vraja, but not with Ramā herself; and just as a child is innocent, so too, because He was under the sway of love for them, He maintained only that innocence,
and not the sovereignty He possesses over Ramā.

Now, one might ask: how did He enjoy with those thousands of women? To this He says: He whose *vibhrama*—meaning His playful manifestation (*vilāsa*)—is such that it appears as His very own reflection (*pratisvarūpa*).
This was shown to men who had not performed sufficient austerities and whose eyes remained unsatiated.
"Just as he who, taking his own form which is the eye of the world, vanished" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.11)—

here, just as the word *bimba* denotes one's essential nature (*svarūpa*), so too here the meaning is that He sported with each beloved in His respective essential form. This is because they are His *hlādinī* power.

Because it constitutes their very nature, and because it is improper for them to be mere reflections of themselves, no other interpretation is accepted. (o)0(o)— those whose senses are agitated by the touch of his limbs, the woman.

O best of the Kurus, the women of Vraja, with their flower-garlands and ornaments disarrayed, were not able to bind up their hair, their fine silk garments, or the cloth-bands around their breasts without further assistance.

Śrīdhara: He says "tadaṅga... to explain that they became overwhelmed by the Lord's playful charms. Their senses were overwhelmed and rendered helpless by the intense joy arising from contact with His body; thus, they were unable to easily restore their loosened hair and other ornaments as they had been before.
They became incapable; those whose garlands and ornaments had fallen away. ||18||

Vaṃśīdhara: Those gopīs; of that Kṛṣṇa; by the contact of his limbs—that is, through physical touch—with that joy; "loosened" means slackened. By addressing him as "O best of the Kurus," he shows that one becomes submissive to Kṛṣṇa through devotion; therefore, you too, because of being born from the pure Kuru lineage, should cultivate devotion toward Kṛṣṇa.

He urges them forward by saying, "Do [this]," so that they may become dependent [on Him]. Alternatively, the intention is: "Because you are born of a pure lineage, I speak this secret pastime to you. Thereupon, he says "tadaṅga" (thereby) to show that they became overwhelmed with bliss through the Lord's amorous sports; "prakṛṣṭā mūtiḥ" means supreme bliss.
With their senses agitated by her, they were not capable—indeed, not able—to bear up against her bodice and her breast-band. ||18||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And thus, the cessation of the *rāsa*-dance occurred precisely because they were overwhelmed by extreme bliss; this he states with the words "tadaṅga... etc. Their senses became agitated by the joy (*mud*) and delight (*harṣa*) which reached its peak through the successive contact with His limbs. He describes the characteristic of their agitated senses with the words "keśān" etc.
By the word "etcetera": *dukūla* is the lower garment, a linen cloth; *kucapaṭṭikā* is that which serves as a bodice;
and *uttarīya* is the upper garment. ||18||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: And then, he says "tadaṅga... to express that supreme bliss was born within them. "Aṅga-saṅga" refers to the contact with her limbs—the meeting through embracing and so forth.
He describes the state of their agitated senses with the words beginning with "keśān" (the hair), etc., [and mentions] the *dukūla* (fine silk garment).
Her lower garment was of fine silk (*kauśeya*), as were her breast-band, upper cloth, or bodice—or perhaps she wore only two of these.

The meaning is that, due to the particular intensity of their love, it was entirely fitting for those women of Vraja to be in such a state. Thus, their abundance of bliss is established; for this very reason, the prefix *pra-* [in "pramadā"] is used.

This was said with the intention that you have understood this as well; or else, considering that because the gopīs have attained their supreme goal, even he possesses a state of being similar to theirs, and thus deeming him the supreme fortune of the Kuru lineage, he addresses him as "O upholder of the Kurus. (18)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, while they were sporting, he describes their renewed immersion in love with the words beginning "by contact with His limbs" (*tad-aṅga-saṅgena*). By that supreme joy (*mud*) which arose from contact with His limbs...

The meaning is that their senses were agitated and they were unable—not capable—to restrain their falling hair, silk garments, and so forth. Here, the possession by love is the primary element (aṅgin), while fatigue is the subordinate element (aṅga). ||18||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described the pinnacle of aesthetic relish (*rasa*), [the author] says "tadaṅga... to explain that, once [that state] was attained, He—seeing no further growth beyond this point—induced a slight relaxation in those [emotions] in order to bring about further development. By that [means], namely through the touch of all his limbs via the embrace of her body and so forth...

The sense is that their senses became agitated by that supreme bliss which has reached its ultimate limit; thus, all of them became devoid of any further duty to perform. Regarding the words "the hair"—he mentions this as a sign of agitation—their braided hair (*kabarān*), their fine silk garments (*dukūlam*), and the upper cloths they were wearing.

The meaning is that the women of Vraja became unable— not capable— to lift up the bodice over the breasts so as to recover it entirely as before— that is, to hold it and restore it to its proper place— due to their lack of familiarity with such specialized skill.

What is intended is the absence of self-control. He states the cause of their exhaustion when the senses are agitated: "those whose garlands and ornaments have become disheveled and fallen from their places.
Alternatively, it means those who bear, as it were, slightly (*ā*), garlands that have become disheveled and broken, leaving only the threads remaining.

"O best of the Kurus, perceive the King as devoid of external activity through the bliss of exhaustion from the *rāsa*-dance"—this is the intended meaning of what was stated regarding the "delusion of one's own reflection," namely:
first there is action in the original object (*bimba*), and subsequently in the reflection (*pratibimba*) as well; thus it is with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

The activity pertaining to play follows accordingly among the queens of Vraja. Now, when Kṛṣṇa is overcome by their amorous charms, there is a cessation of his own activity; at that time, however, there is a cessation of activity on their part as well.
Just as when the original object (the *bimba*) is devoid of activity, its reflection (*pratibimba*) is likewise necessarily devoid of activity.
Nevertheless, it is reasonable to infer that she has become one whose garlands and ornaments have fallen away. ||18||

Viśvanātha: And then, he says "tadaṅga... [and so forth], to express that they became overwhelmed with bliss by the pastimes of the Blessed One. Their senses were agitated by that supreme joy (*pramud*), which is bliss (*ānanda*). They were not able—that is, not capable—of bearing, that is, supporting, their bodice (*kucapaṭṭikā*) or their jacket (*kañculikā*). ||18||
Seeing Kṛṣṇa’s playful sport, the women of the sky-dwellers were bewildered;
afflicted by desire, they were struck with longing, and Śaśin, along with his retinue, was filled with wonder.
Śrīdhara: Not only were those [gopīs] whose senses were agitated, but even the goddesses [were so];

thus he says, "The sporting of Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, he says, "And the Moon. By this it is indicated that all those who had previously gone along with the Moon became bewildered when they forgot their departure upon seeing him.
The planets remained right there, and so they sported at their pleasure during those exceedingly long nights. || 19 ||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:

*Krama-sandarbha*. The reading "kāmārditā" in the plural form alone is the one accepted by the commentary; however, since the phrase "devyo 'pi" (even the goddesses) acknowledges that it is precisely they who are afflicted by desire (*kāmārdita*). Furthermore, [the word] "śaśāṅka... [is used].
And because it is accepted that the word *ca* and so forth constitute separate sentences. ||19||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Thus, he says "Kṛṣṇa-vikrīḍitam" and so forth, stating that even the wives of the gods were enchanted when Kṛṣṇa sported. "Khecarāḥ" refers to the gods; their wives are the "khecara-striyaḥ. Here, the word *kha* signifies heaven (*svarga*). They know *kham* to mean both heaven and the sky. Which of these celestial women were not tormented?

Rather, all [the planets] indeed [were so]. But Śaśāṅka, moreover, together with his attendants and the host of constellations, became struck with wonder; the meaning is that he was covered by astonishment. Śaśāṅka’s being covered by wonder implies a cessation of motion, and by that, the nights [passed].
Length is manifested. ||19||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Having thus described, in brief, the pastimes performed on the conclusion of one day by way of general illustration (*śṛṅga-grāhika-nyāya*), [the author] will now describe other such pastimes as well, which are endless; therein, while elucidating the delusion of the goddesses who have husbands, he describes [the state] of [Śiva] along with his attendants.

He describes the delusion of even Candra: "Kṛṣṇa" refers to Kṛṣṇa, the embodiment of supreme bliss or the embodiment of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment). Having seen His playful pastimes (*vikrīḍita*) in the form of the *rāsa*-dance, the sky-dwellers—the gods and others—some as singers, some as instrumentalists, and some [as dancers], [were filled with wonder].

The showerers of flowers, some of the members of the assembly—all these were always authorized to witness the divine play (līlā). However, because they had arrived where women predominated, they too were deluded by their infatuation; thus he says: "The sky-dwellers—the gods and others—and their wives, were infatuated. Hereafter...
These very points will be stated in the following pair of verses: "The women traveling in the celestial chariot" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.35.3).
