He states the reason for this: "Afflicted by desire"—tormented by worldly passion directed toward Kṛṣṇa—if there is delusion even among the men, such as the gods and Gandharvas, then what need is there to mention the delusion of the women?

It must be said: for even those men, having moved forward, stood there motionless, forgetting their own unfitness and their bodies and so forth. Furthermore, Śaśāṅka—the Moon—along with his Gaṇas, accompanied by the host of luminaries, was struck with wonder. Thus it has been explained by the Teachers: by Śaśāṅka...

The literal meaning is as follows: when her own movement had been forgotten, the movement of the other hosts of luminaries situated above her was brought to a halt; consequently, they sported at will during exceedingly long nights. This very point intended by [the author] himself was stated at the beginning: "The Blessed One also [passed] those nights..."

Thus, the cessation of divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya-nirodha*) has been described. And at the conclusion, it should be understood in the same way from the cessation of sovereignty; for there occurs the cessation even of Time (*kāla*), which consists of His activities. This was stated in the *Devakī-stuti*:
"O friend of the unmanifest, they say that this Time is Your activity, by which the universe is set in motion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3.26).
Therefore, when the obstruction of the stellar sphere in the form of the Śiśumāra, which rests upon That [Time], occurs...
The cessation of the hosts of luminaries that serve as its support occurred spontaneously; and thus, when the nights became exceedingly long, he took his pleasure as he desired.
Now, upon the cessation of [his] sovereignty, there might indeed be a cessation of the wheel of luminaries dependent on time, such as the moon.

If it is asked how there is the cessation of those who possess separate courses of existence, he says in response: when [the mind] was restrained within the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the cessation of the moon also occurred, because his [the moon's] mind is an effect.
For the Vedic revelation states, "The moon was born from the mind. Furthermore, regarding the goddesses who have descended into the discus...

Intending to convey that when the cessation [of the stars] occurred through the playful power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who presides over them, the cessation of the host of stars—which are their constituent parts—also occurred, it was said: "He, along with his attendants, became forgotten.
Consequently, they took delight during the exceedingly long nights without any constraint. ||19||

Viśvanātha: "Afflicted by desire" means tormented by the longing directed toward Kṛṣṇa. According to the reading *kāmārdita*, even the moon, upon beholding Kṛṣṇa, attained a feminine state and was likewise afflicted by the longing for Kṛṣṇa. [This occurred] through the power of Yogamāyā alone, regarding the limbs and graceful movements of the beauties of Vraja.
The reversal of views regarding the person has already been explained previously. ||19||
Having made himself as many-fold as there were cowherd women,
the Blessed One, though delighting in his own self, sported with them in play.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having done what": this is the intended meaning— "O Kātyāyanī, O Great Māyā, O Great Yoginī, O Sovereign Lady!
O Goddess, make the son of Nanda-gopa my husband; salutations to you! [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.4]

Thus, because each of them had made such a request, and because the Blessed One had likewise promised, saying, "O gopīs, having attained perfection through me, you shall enjoy these nights," he multiplied himself into that many forms and took his pleasure with them. *Yāvatīḥ* means as many as there were. 20.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī: Now, after resting following the Rāsa dance, he describes a particular pastime performed [by the Lord].
Having said this, [the Lord spoke] with two verses. "The self as the light of the self" is the meaning.

And although He is in the middle state according to the principle that "He is neither within nor without," that is because of the all-pervasive nature (*vibhutva*) of His glorious form (*śrī-vigraha*).
"How wonderful! Indeed, by means of a single body, simultaneously and separately..."

"In each house, one man married sixteen thousand women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.69.2); thus, this manifestation was according to His will. This apparent redundancy occurs because they were unified during the time of rest.
"Gopa-yoṣitaḥ" means women of the gopa caste; consequently, some were married and others were not.

And it should be understood that they are "maidens" (kanyā) as well; for in the twenty-first and twenty-second chapters, there is a separate description of the love previously felt by both the married women and the maidens. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement in the *Śrī-Harivaṃśa*: "The young women and the cowherd girls, having gathered together at night... (*Ha.vaṃ.* 2.22.18). And this has been written according to their actual nature.
This is clear from the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* and other such works. He "played" (*rarāma*) by means of "playful sport" (*līlayā*), which is the dalliance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
The repetition of the word "Bhagavān" is intended to manifest the entirety of the essence of His divine sweetness (*bhagavattā-sāra-mādhurya-sarvasva*). Of that very [divinity]...

Because it consists of the specific play of the ripening of the essence of divine love (*prema-rasa*); likewise, because by that very [love], which attracts the minds of the world, a particular expansion of love is spontaneously manifested; and this will become clear further on. Furthermore, it has been explained in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta* with the words "even though he is one who delights in the Self" (*ātmārāmo 'pi*), the meaning of which has already been stated. And that delighting in Him is as follows:
Separately, each in their own nearby groves and such, in that very place. ||20||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Regarding that very point, he states the supreme fruit with two verses beginning with "kṛtvā. Even by the specific power of anyone, the reality of manifoldness is indeed established; "gopa-veṣitāḥ" means those who were dressed as cowherd girls. Consequently, some were married women and some were maidens. Or else:

The women of the cowherds were their wives. Thus, it should be understood that some were indeed their wives, while others— though having performed the vow of Kātyāyanī and being solely devoted to the Blessed One, and though they had not yet married— were somehow proclaimed as wives by all due to the Blessed One’s illusory power (māyā) and the like, because of the thought [of marriage].

And this is made perfectly clear in the *Lalita-mādhava* and other works written by Śrī Rūpa. He "rejoiced" (*rarāma*)—that is, he took delight—through "play" (*līlayā*), which means through the sport of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) or through various amorous gestures (*saurata-ceṣṭā*). By using the term "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*), the sense is that this very act reveals the entire essence of His blessedness (*bhagavattā*). Of that very [act]...

Nevertheless, because it consists of the particular manifestations of the ripening of the essence of divine love (*prema-rasa*), and because that very [essence], which attracts the minds of the world, spontaneously expands a specific form of love, such is the direction [of the argument]; this will become clear further on.
And it has indeed been explained in the *Śrī-Bhāgavatāmṛta*. The phrase "even though he is one who delights in the Self" (*ātmārāmo’pi*) refers precisely to the meaning already stated.

And that dalliance took place separately in nearby groves and such right there, or perhaps in the very place of the *rāsa*-dance itself; in this way, as before, both His majesty (*aiśvarya*) and sweetness (*mādhurya*) are to be understood.
As for the sequence of the composition: "the Self as the manifestation of the Self" is the meaning. (20)

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, manifesting His splendor—which corresponds to the individual age, disposition, physical proportions, and artistic skill of each of them—the Lord says "He sported" (*reme*), beginning with the words "Having done... (*kṛtvā*). The Blessed One possesses inconceivable supreme sovereignty; He is one who delights in the Self through His own selves.
It is so called because He sports together with devotees who are almost like Himself; or else, although already full of His own attainment and independent,
by way of divine play or curiosity, He manifests Himself in as many, of whatever age, companions, intentions,
forms and varieties, and as much skill in arts as there may be.
The meaning is that she ceased after having manifested her own nature; the meaning is that she became such as they were in their various forms and so forth. ||20||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, fulfilling his own promise, Śrī Kṛṣṇa concludes the manifestation of His many forms according to their intention. With the words "having made," he refers to as many Vraja women as there were; in Vraja, the gopīs are of five kinds: one is eternally perfected (*nitya-siddhā*), and [others are] perfected through practice (*upāsanā-siddhā*).

The goddesses, the Upaniṣads, and the sages dwelling in Daṇḍaka made themselves as many as that according to their respective intentions; this is because the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa possesses inconceivable power and is complete. Thus it has been said here by the Ācāryas: "In the case of bondage, there is completeness through the filling of two finger-breadths."

He shows another point: furthermore, the non-repetition of the middle word and the use of the singular number are intended from the perspective of the gopīs' vision; as for the plural number, its meaning has already been stated, and he will explain it further ahead.
"How wonderful it is that this one man, with a single body, simultaneously married sixteen thousand women individually in their respective homes! Thus,
although he was one who delights in the Self, he disregarded his state of self-contentment and took delight in playful dalliance with them.
It is said that for a woman, play is effortless labor. If one asks, "How can there be honor for those who belong to a single herd?
he says in response: "The Blessed Lord. This means He shines with sovereignty that manifests His power;
therefore, the entire nourishment of those many women is provided through the sweet nectar [of His love].

Viśvanātha states that everything requested individually by those devoted to the worship of Kātyāyanī—namely, "Make me your wife; salutations to you"—was promised by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself and was all accomplished. Consequently, there also occurred secret amorous play with each of them individually in the groves.

Thus he says, "having made. As many as there were—meaning however many in number—the cowherd women (*gopa-yoṣitaḥ*), cowherd brides (*gopa-vadhvaḥ*), and cowherd maidens (*gopa-kanyāḥ*), to that same extent he manifested himself, assuming that same number of self-manifestations;
this is explained by the phrase "even though he delights in the Self" (*ātmārāmo’pi*). ||20||
O dear one, when they were exhausted from excessive exertion, he, full of compassion, lovingly wiped their faces with his most peaceful hand.
Śrīdhara says: He expresses his great compassion with the words, "Of them" (tāsām). ||21||

Vaṃśīdhara: He wiped—that is, he thoroughly cleansed—the faces, that is, the mouths, of those gopīs. "Aṅga" is a term of address. [From this point onward, Viśvanātha’s commentary is extracted in its entirety. By means of his most peaceful touch, which generates bliss... ||21||
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Rati" is the mutual passion between a husband and wife; "vihāra" is sport consisting of that [passion], characterized by various clever gestures. Even with the reading "ativihāreṇa," the meaning is the same. By that, for those who are fatigued...
He wiped them thoroughly with a hand that was peaceful and composed of supreme bliss;

he made them radiant by removing drops of sweat, arranging their locks of hair, and so forth. For while compassion—the state of being unable to endure the suffering of others—is present, it is not common to all; yet for those women, those [actions] were indeed [compassionate].

By the word "prāmṛjat" (he wiped), supreme distinction is shown. For love (*prema*) is a softness born in the heart through the contemplation of excellence and when the objects of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "mine-ness" (*mamata*) are unified;
even among these, that which consists of such a state is supremely distinguished, being itself compassion and so forth.

He includes [this] within [the previous]. By the phrase "with the most peaceful," it is stated that even by the mere touch, there is the production of supreme bliss by its very nature, and therein purification; and therein also with love, and therein again by "the most peaceful," supreme satisfaction is expressed. The word "O dear one" (aṅga) is an address of affection. ||21||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Rati" means sexual union; that itself is the "vihāra" (pastime). Thus, freedom from inhibition therein is indicated. Alternatively, "vihāra" in the context of "rati" refers to various clever gestures;
by that [vihāra], Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the crest-jewel of the clever or the supremely delighted—is [pleased] with the most peaceful [state].

With his hand, which was of the nature of supreme bliss, he thoroughly wiped [him], making him radiant by removing drops of perspiration, arranging his locks of hair, and so forth; for he was compassionate and merciful. And it was not merely out of compassion toward others, but rather—

He says "by love" (*premṇā*) because [the Lord] is supremely dear. By this, a particular kind of compassion (*kāruṇya*) is intended. By "most peaceful" (*śantamena*), it is meant that by its very nature, even a mere touch produces supreme bliss; and therein is the cleansing (*pramārjana*). Furthermore, by saying "by love" in that context, supreme satisfaction is expressed. Alternatively, [it means] "by love incarnate" (*mūrta*).

Thus, the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) arises immediately from those various acts of love, because they cause the entire universe to weep. The word "O dear one" (*aṅga*) is an address of affection. In this way, by wiping the faces of all [the gopīs] simultaneously with a single hand, there is both majesty and a worldly quality, as before.
It should be understood as a manifestation of the essence of the sweetness of the Blessed One; so it is elsewhere as well. ||21||
The *krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: While thus sporting, seeing their exhaustion, he himself performed the diversion of removing it; this is what he says with the words beginning "of them" (*tāsām*), etc. With that which is most peaceful and very cool...
By merely wiping his face with his hand, his fatigue was dispelled; the meaning is that he caused his energy to increase once again. ||21||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, it is shown that their honoring was performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone. Śrī Śuka speaks of his own experience with the words "tāsām" (of them). They were exhausted by excessive wandering, by the impetuosity of the *rāsa*-dance, or by their intense absorption in amorous play within the forest bowers (*nikuñja*) and other places; thus, they were unable to increase [their merit].

And as if they were his own limbs, he used his hand— singular in number because the unity of the whole body was intended— to refresh the faces of all five of them with a most peaceful, supremely bliss-inducing, and sweet essence;
he wiped away the droplets of perspiration.

The meaning of the prefix *pra-* is that even in cases where [the emotions] are clear yet distinct, the sweet flavor (*madhura-rasa*) is renewed once more by means of such things as the hanging down of the cheeks (*gaṇḍa-maṇḍala*). Since it is compassionate (*karuṇa*), therefore the compassionate flavor (*karuṇa-rasa*) is indeed included within the sweet flavor. By the use of the singular number, the identity of their essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) alone is intended. [This is expressed] by the word "through love" (*premṇā*).

In these [verses], it is indicated that, due to the intensity of their love, the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa by them is the supreme goal of human life (*parama-puruṣārtha*). By the address "O dear one" (*aṅga*), it is made known that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is dependent upon them.
Thus, the simultaneous wiping of the faces and so forth of all of them is performed by the hands of a single person.
The intended meaning is that by demonstrating lightness, he manifests inconceivable power. ||21||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the reading "tāsāṃ rati-vihāreṇa" or "tāsām ativihāreṇa," the meaning of "śrāntānām" (of those who were weary) is that, perceiving their exhaustion from amorous play, he became compassionate and desisted from further dalliance. "With the most peaceful" means with that which consists of bliss. "He wiped away" is an elliptical expression [for wiping away their sweat].
He also performed the fanning, the anointing, the decoration of the limbs, and the offering of betel. (21)
The cowherd girls, with their shimmering golden earrings and the luster of their locks of hair—
Bearing pride through their smiles and glances well-placed with the splendor of their virtues,
they sang of the meritorious deeds of Ṛṣabha, rejoicing at the touch of his fingernails.

Śrīdhara: Then he describes the conduct of the gopīs who were exceedingly joyful—with the words "The gopīs... By means of the splendor (*tviṣā*) of their shimmering golden earrings and locks of hair upon their cheeks, and by that well-composed (*sudhitena*), nectar-like (*amṛtāyitena*) glance accompanied by smiles, [they beheld] the Bull among men, their husband Kṛṣṇa.
Maintaining their pride, they performed acts of worship and sang of his deeds— those women who experienced great joy from the touch of his sprout-like hands and nails.
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Thus, when fatigue has been dispelled, they once again become possessed of enthusiasm for that very [path].
He says "they sang" and so forth: "the gopīs," etc. The gopīs sang of the pastimes performed by Ṛṣabha. Of what nature were they?

Meritorious, meaning they generate merit. He will describe those very pastimes with the words beginning, "The sporting with the women of Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.40). The meaning is that these belong to Ṛṣabha, who is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme.

Doing what? Bearing honor—that is, carrying out respect or performing it—with a sidelong glance accompanied by a smile that is pervaded by nectar (sudhā) and beautified by the splendor of their cheeks, which is produced by the shimmering luster of their golden earrings and their locks of hair. In the first case [of the interpretation]:...
The two words ending in the instrumental case, beginning with "sphurat-puraṭa-kuṇḍala," should be understood as qualifying Kṛṣṇa;
in the second verse, they qualify those very [gopīs]. Furthermore, of what nature were they? Those whose supreme joy was aroused by the touch of his sprout-like fingers. (22)
Rasikāhlādinī: Viśvanātha: —o)0(o—
Accompanied by them, he dispelled his fatigue with the touch of her limbs— she whose garland was crushed by their contact and who was stained with the saffron from her breasts.
Followed by Gandharva maidens,
he entered the waters like a weary lordly elephant with its female mates after breaking through a dam.

Śrīdhara: Now he describes the water-play with the words "by them" (*tābhiḥ*). By the friction and rubbing against their limbs, the garland was crushed; therefore, it was colored by the saffron from their breasts. From the fragrant filaments associated with that garland, those who were like Gandharvas—lords of the Gandharvas—sang.
That Kṛṣṇa, whose abode was pursued and followed by them, entered the water;
he had broken the embankment, torn down the ramparts, and himself transgressed the boundaries of both worldly convention and the Vedas. ||23||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ*: Now, furthermore, when fatigue arises, for its removal—

He speaks of the eagerness for water-sports: "Accompanied by them," and so forth. "Accompanied by them" means joined with them in the water—that is, in the waters of the Kālindī; for this will be stated later in the passage beginning, "In the grove of Kṛṣṇa" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.25). To do what? To dispel, that is, to remove, fatigue. Of what kind [of water]?
Of the Yamunā? [The meaning is: those whose withered garlands were rubbed by contact with her limbs;

at the time of entering, the withered garlands were removed by him and placed upon her by them. She was colored by the saffron from the breasts of the cowherd girls—that is, by the saffron from their breasts applied to herself (the Yamunā).

The sense is that first their breast-saffron adhered to Kṛṣṇa, and afterwards she too was colored by what fell from His body. Here, the word *sva* refers to Kṛṣṇa, because the word *sva* is connected with the agent through the active suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) in the verb *ādiśat*. Alternatively, [it may refer to] "of himself" (*svasya*).

"Stained by the saffron from the breasts of the cowherd women"—here, the word "self" (*sva*) refers to Kṛṣṇa. The sense is that she entered there after having adorned the Yamunā with both garlands and body-unguents. She is "Gandharvapā" because she protects the Gandharvas; she has their very nature.

Those who were not weary, accompanied by them, having reached their vicinity and running with haste, were joined by those [weary ones] due to the joy of singing and seeking refuge, and because they did not accept the cessation of that [activity]. And those [weary ones] likewise [joined] out of curiosity; thus it is an expression of emotion (*bhāvokti*) regarding what was appropriate. Like whom? Like one who is exhausted [being joined] by exhausted female elephants.

Like a lordly elephant who has broken a dam; in the case of the elephant, one that has breached the embankment, and in the other sense, one who has transgressed the boundaries of the science of love (*kāmatantra*). As it is said: "When the circle of passion (*raticakra*) has begun, there is neither scripture nor prescribed order. Alternatively, he is simply one who has overstepped the boundaries of both the world and the Vedas. (23)
*Rasikāhlādinī*:

Viśvanātha. And then he describes the water-sport, which is like the concluding purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*) for the Rāsa festival—[describing Kṛṣṇa] "joined with them. To "apohitum" means to cast away or remove. With which ones? Those who...

Those [garlands] which were colored by the saffron from their own breasts through the agency of amorous play, and which were rubbed and crushed by the contact of their limbs; in the reading "sa-kucā," "sa" refers to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*, "gandharva" may mean a species of deer, a singer, or a celestial being.

Pursued by those foremost singers who were like Gandharvas, he entered the waters of the Yamunā with his bridge broken and his defenses shattered; in the dark fortnight, he has transgressed the boundaries of the world. —o)0(o—
O dear one, being sprinkled with water by young women here and there as they looked upon him with love and laughed,
he was praised by the celestial beings in their chariots who showered flowers.
Delighting in himself, he sports here with the grace of a lordly elephant.
Śrīdhara: Though his delight is in the Self and he is one who rejoices in the Self, here in this circle of gopīs, as it were in water... || 24 ||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā;
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: *Krama-sandarbhaḥ* has not been commented upon.
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbhaḥ* describes the manner of sporting in the water, beginning with the words "He, in the water... (*so'mbhasy alam*, etc.).
"Enough, indeed! Though being sprinkled on all sides by young women, he was drenched only by love, and not by those various waters.

Even while being sprinkled here and there from every direction, he did not suffer the humiliation caused by such sprinkling; this is the meaning. For this very reason, [he was showered] by those raining flowers..."

Addressed with cries of "Victory! Victory! by the inhabitants of the celestial mansions (vaimānika), and praised by those laughing excessively—that is, laughing most heartily—he took his pleasure; the meaning is that he himself also sprinkled them. He whose delight was in them.
The phrase "with the grace of a lordly elephant" provides the analogy for the sprinkling with water from the long trunk. Thus, he took pleasure himself.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: either there is love for oneself, or because they take refuge in such a sprinkling of water, there arises an even greater love for oneself alone; this is the intended meaning. ||24||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha notes that there are variant readings such as *premeṇekṣitaḥ* and *premeṇokṣitaḥ*. He is one for whom his own wealth consists solely of passion (*rati*) and play (*krīḍā*). (24)
And then, in the grove of Kṛṣṇa, where the slopes of the quarters were filled with breezes scented by the flowers of water and land;
He moved about surrounded by throngs of women like a rutting elephant accompanied by herds of female elephants.
Śrīdhara: Having shown the sports on land and in water, he now shows the forest sports, beginning with the words "Then... (*tataś ca*).

[The place] was one where the borders and limits of the quarters were graced by a breeze carrying the fragrance of flowers from both water and land in the grove of the Yamunā; or alternatively, it was one where the quarters themselves served as the banks and the dry land.
In the grove, he was surrounded by swarms of bees and groups of young women. ||25||
Vaṃśīdhara: Then, after the water and land sports; "water-blooms" refers to lotuses (*kumuda*) and the like; "land-blooms" refers to *saugandhika*, *kunda*, and so forth; "enjoyed" means perfumed.
He states "or rather" (*yad vā*) because, at the end of the word *taṭa* (bank), it is more logical to resort to the primary meaning through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *taṭa* is neuter when it means a field; however, in the sense of a riverbank, *taṭī* is used in all three genders. In the context of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), [the term] refers to one who sheds intoxication—that is, who removes the pride of the wicked. He is a "dvirada" (elephant) because he effects the non-recording (*ada*) of both merit and demerit;
the meaning is that he is one for whom the recording of merit and demerit is performed by Citragupta. By what means? By his trunk (*kara*).
With atoms within the range of his hand, using fine-pointed pens; or, as if surrounded by singing women who are like bees. "Then" means after the water-sport.
By the word "ca" (and), it is implied that this occurs after the wiping of his limbs and the putting on of garments and ornaments brought at that moment by the forest deities.

And he went to that forest grove on the banks of the Yamunā, which contained more than a thousand bowers, for the sake of the pastimes of sleeping there; what kind of place was it? It was one whose horizons were graced by breezes carrying the fragrance of flowers growing in Janasthala.
He is surrounded by swarms of bees and groups of young women; he is one from whom the flow, the trickling, and the oozing of intoxications has ceased.
*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Not explained.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is that after the water-sports (*jala-krīḍā*), following the removal of the previous costume (*pūrva-nepathya*), because the forest attire (*vanya-nepathya*) is then more pleasing, it is due to the desire for specific sports characterized by an abundance of that [attire]. *Tv*.
Now, the letter *ca* begins a new section: she wandered here and there, sporting in various ways such as gathering flowers and hiding within groves;
she was surrounded by swarms of bees because they came along with her during the flower-gathering.

Because their limbs were washed during the water-sport and because of their naturally sweet fragrance which was exceedingly manifest, they were repeatedly called "intoxication-droppers" (*madacyut*); this served as the reason for being surrounded by swarms of bees, as well as for their status as the best of elephants and their devotion to their own mates. (25)

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Then, after the water-sports" means that because the flower garlands and other items have withered due to the water-sports, [she goes] for the purpose of gathering flowers and so forth. Furthermore, the particle *ca* (and) indicates a change in the subject matter (*bhinnopakrama*). "Water-born flowers" refers to lotuses and the like; "land-born flowers" refers to...

Jātī, kunda, and other such flowers; through association with their respective fragrances, the wind acquires coolness and sweetness. By the word "juṣṭā" (frequented), its gentleness is also to be understood. He wandered here and there, sporting in various ways, such as gathering flowers and hiding within the bowers.
She wandered about. She was surrounded by swarms of bees because she had come accompanied by them while gathering flowers.
Or perhaps, because during water-sports the cosmetic unguents had washed away, her natural, sweet fragrance was revealed.
Or perhaps, because they are by nature excitants of emotion (*bhāvoddīpana*), she always accepted them. Or perhaps—
Because they are constantly drawn by the fragrance of the lotus garland and other ornaments upon His glorious face, they are mentioned repeatedly.

The term "exuding rut" (*mada-cyut*) serves as the reason for their being surrounded by swarms of bees; likewise, it indicates their status as excellent elephants and their state of being intoxicated with passion. Furthermore, through their association with Him, the same qualities are implied for the female elephants as well.

This illustration applies everywhere. Generally, because the lordly elephant is intoxicated by passion and is likewise always surrounded by his herd, their intoxication with love is expressed; for this very reason, they are called *pramadā*. ||25||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, at the conclusion of the water-sport, all the women and he himself were provided with garments, ornaments, and unguents by Yogamāyā, each according to their respective rank.

He says "then, moreover," and so forth, to explain that she extended her play of drinking honey after having dressed herself. "Leaving the sandy bank in the grove of Kṛṣṇā" means having gone into the middle of the grove; otherwise, those traveling by celestial chariot would have seen her. [She was adorned] with water-born flowers such as white lotuses and various kinds of large blossoms.

The wind carrying fragrance is the "fragrant breeze" (*gandha-pavana*); the quarters and the slopes [of the mountain] graced by that are the "quarters-and-slopes" (*dik-taṭā*). By the phrase "surrounded by a multitude of female bees," a quiet, secret dalliance is indicated, because at that time even the male bees were not present. Through the simile "like an elephant shedding rut," his state of intoxication is shown.
And by that [indication], the drinking of honey is suggested. ||25||
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha: Then, after the water-sport—and by the word "and" (*ca*), after the wiping of the limbs and the putting on of garments and ornaments brought by the forest deities—immediately thereafter.

And for the sake of the pastime of sleeping, He went to Kṛṣṇa’s grove on the banks of the Yamunā, which was endowed with more than a thousand forest bowers; what kind of place was it? It was one whose horizons were graced by breezes carrying the fragrance of flowers growing both in the water and on the land.
He is surrounded by swarms of bees and groups of young women; he is one from whom the flow, the trickling, and the emission of intoxications has fallen away.
Thus, that Satyakāma, accompanied by his devoted group of women, passed nights illuminated by the rays of the moon.
Having internalized within himself the essence of amorous pleasure, he cultivated all the aesthetic sentiments that form the basis of autumnal poetic narratives.

Śrīdhara concludes the description of the *rāsa*-pastime with the words "Thus" (*evam*). That Kṛṣṇa, whose resolve is ever true, spent all the nights in this manner while remaining right there among the multitude of passionate women.
These [nights] were the locus of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) described in the autumnal poetic narratives—that is, the flavors found in the poems composed during the autumn season.
The nights were the support for those [passions]. Alternatively, "niśāḥ" is in the accusative case denoting continuous connection (*atyanta-saṃyoga*).
Thus, he cultivated those stories well-known in poetry which are the locus of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) in autumn;
even so, his seminal essence (*saurataś carama-dhātuḥ*), though confined within himself, did not fail [to be emitted].
The statement regarding the conquest of desire. ||26-27||

Vaṃśīdhara concludes with the word "evam" (thus). The conclusion of the rāsa-play is its awakening. "Niśāḥ" refers to those nights in which there was "niśam," meaning extreme bliss (*śam*). The name is significant because there was not even a moment's cessation from amorous delight. "Anurata-strī-gaṇaḥ" means the group of women who were devoted to Him, or the group of women who were made to sport according to His desire.
By this, the lack of attachment to women on the part of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is illuminated. The *rasas* (flavors) consist of forms such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the comic (*hāsya*).

Since the nights are insentient, they cannot serve as the substratum for these *rasas*; therefore, he says "or rather" (*yad vā*). Here, the "final constituent" (*carama-dhātu*) refers to semen. The constituents (*dhātus*) are chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.

Thus, in this enumeration of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) by Śārṅgadhara, semen is stated to be the last. Furthermore, even according to the order of their production, semen is indeed the last. As it is said in the *Saṃhitā*:
"From rasa comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat is produced."
"From fat comes bone, from that marrow, and from that the production of semen.
Thus, "from rasa" means from the essence of food and so forth. To practice sexual union while restraining the vital energy (*vīrya*)—this indeed is the conquest of desire.
"Even in the company of a woman, he whose semen does not fall through the will of another is a blessed man in this world; he is called a conqueror of desire"—thus it is stated in the Saṃhitā. (26)

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Thus, regarding the phrase "niśā siṣeve śaśāṅkāṃśu" (she served the moonbeams at night), the word *niśā* is used in the plural; it does not denote each individual night. Since it is not possible for all nights to have possessed the moon previously, the plural form *niśāḥ* refers collectively to many nights taken as one. Therefore, by that very [usage]...

Regarding the word *śaśāṅka*: the host of the moon (*śaśāṅka*) was struck with wonder; thus, by virtue of the aforementioned wonder, there was a state of motionlessness. Through that, the secret is the abundance of the time-form known as night. [The rays] are resplendent with praises of the portions of such a moon.

There is a compound with an indeclinable, like *uccairmukha* and so forth. By this very [rule], it was previously explained as "the night" (*rātriḥ*). In the same way, why? Because he is one whose desires are true and whose volitions are true;
in this very manner, he previously formed a volition, having internalized within himself the state of bliss (*saurata*).

The meaning is that he restrained the pleasure of sexual union because love itself is the true essence of sexual union (*surata*). Alternatively, the single compound *avaruddha-saurata* means "one by whom the sexual act (*saurata*)—that is, vulgar carnal practice (*grāmya-dharma*)—has been restrained within himself. For that Lord and for those Goddesses, such vulgar carnal practice is unbecoming.

The authors of the *Rasa* treatises maintain that "nothing other than impropriety (*anaucitya*) is a cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor" (*Dhvanyāloka* 3.14). However, in the case of such a couple,
mutual lip-sipping, kissing, embracing, and so forth, constitute *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) precisely because they are free from obstruction.

In what manner were the nights? They were "the locus of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of autumnal poetic narratives" (*śarat-kāvya-kathā-rasāśrayāḥ*); that is, they served as the basis for the aesthetic flavor of those poetic narratives concerning poets—such as descriptions of the six seasons and so forth, as well as moonrises, festivals of wine-drinking, and the like—which occur during the autumn season of the year. (26)

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, concluding the *rāsa*-pastime performed by these two on the full moon day of autumn, and teaching its method for other occasions as well, [the author] indicates other pastimes too with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Thus" means in the manner of the *rāsa* previously described, during the autumn season.

The meaning is that he attended to, or served with supreme reverence, all the nights illuminated by the moonbeams of every coming autumn; otherwise, since other seasons would also occur, there would have been lunar,
dark, and secret nights involving his entry into various houses and his trysts with her.
The sense is that [this occurs] sometimes by means of lying in forest bowers and so forth, and sometimes by means of the *rāsa* dance.

To indicate the distinction of the latter group, he qualifies them as "foremost" (*apūrva*): those nights which are the locus of the infinite pastimes performed by the Blessed Lord, in which the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) of poetic narratives that arise in autumn are found.

Regarding the word *vyāpya* (pervading): in the context of the subject (*pakṣe*), he cultivated all those autumnal poetic narratives that can be described by poets from all lands and times; however, the meaning is that he cultivated only those whose basis is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), i.e., those for which aesthetic flavor itself is the foundation, and not even those which have been composed by some as being devoid of flavor.

And this is an illustration of others as well; or rather, even those nights associated with spring and other seasons that were graced by the rays of the moon, He enjoyed in the manner of the *rāsa* dance. Likewise, there are infinite poetic narratives concerning the six seasons, beginning with autumn, which are to be understood as before.
He enjoyed them all, yet only as the substrates of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Being of what nature did he enjoy them? To this he says: "In his own self"—that is, within his mind—he had "confined" or established on all sides the "erotic states," namely the internal conditions such as *bhāva* and *hāva* related to sexual union (*surata*), by which he was characterized.
"Being present"—the implication is that he was therefore unable to abandon them. Here, by the mention of the substantive, all states such as emotion (*bhāva*) and so forth are understood.
Thus, through amorous conversations, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī...
"Delighting in his own self, he took delight with Ramā, imitating the ways of the world of men" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.58).

Here, the word *saṃlāpa* (conversation) is indeed employed for the purpose of specifying this particular distinction. The reason for his state of having subjugated the power of *surata* (sexual passion) within himself is that he was surrounded by a multitude of devoted women (*anuraktā-balā-gaṇa*). Constantly...

The group of women is devoted to him; such is the nature of that [king]. Because those women possess affection (*anurāga*) and love (*preman*), it is *anurāga* alone that is the cause there, and not *kāma* (lust) as it is for lustful people—this is the meaning.
He is one whose desire is true (*satya-kāma*), meaning his longing is free from deviation. Thus...
Thus it was said by Śrī Parāśara and Vaiśampāyana:
"In this way, Kṛṣṇa, adorned by the circles of gopīs, rejoiced happily during the autumnal nights under the moon. (Hari-vamśa 2.20.35) Thus it is said.

In the commentary, however, it should be understood that by the words "even thus" (*evam api*) and so forth, an alternative explanation of the term *saurata*—though not commonly known—was provided in order to demonstrate the mere absence of subjection to passion (*smara-pāravaśya*). ||26||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Having thus described the rāsa-play performed on that night, and while gathering other pastimes not yet mentioned therein, he concludes by observing that even though it lasted for many nights, it was of such a nature—as stated by the word "thus" (*evam*), meaning in the manner already described. On that night, it was like this.

The supreme play (*parā krīḍā*) is also indicated; the sense is that it cannot be described because of its extreme vastness. Likewise, by the use of the plural "nights" (*niśāḥ*) and the word "all" (*sarvāḥ*), it is understood that the complete *rāsa*-play occurred throughout the entirety of Her youth during every single night; this was also stated by Śrī Parāśara.
This has already been stated: "He too [was in] the stage of youth" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.13.60). And regarding that:

"Childhood lasts until the end of the fifth year; paugaṇḍa extends up to the tenth; kaiśora lasts until the sixteenth, and after that, one enters youth" (Bhagavad-gītā-ṭīkā by Śrīdhara Svāmī 2.1.309).

From such statements as these, it should be understood that her constant play took place here in Gokula from the eleventh year until the fifteenth year. Furthermore, as stated by Śrī Uddhava in the Third Canto of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*: "There, for eleven years, He whose radiance is hidden dwelt with Balarāma" (*Bhā.Pu.* 3.2.26). And that...

Because during the stages of childhood (*kaumāra*) and boyhood (*paugaṇḍa*), which are unsuitable times [for such pastimes], the *rāsa*-play does not arise, there is no manifestation of His specific divinity; therefore, this is with the intention that His sovereignty is concealed. For this very reason, He is described as "having hidden radiance" (*gūḍhārcis*). For this same reason, at the site of Rāṅga, the Śrī Bhagavān Himself spoke thus to His parents:
It will be stated: "O dear one, [this is not from us, but from you two]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.45.3), and so forth;

and because the playful boldness (*prāgalbhya-līlā*) of the Lord, which will be described upon His entry into Madhupurī, arises [only in youth]. Otherwise, according to such passages as "with smiles and glances" (10.45.27), some would maintain that [these qualities exist] even in the Lord's youth.
The view that He is considered to be engaged in pastimes at Gokula is not entirely consistent;

for even in His adolescence, due to His extraordinary cleverness, bold and playful pastimes are possible. Otherwise, there would be no basis for Akrūra’s perception expressed as "the two youths, dark and white" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.38.29), nor for the description of them as "two youths."

There might be a contradiction with the statement of the city women, "They have not yet reached their youth" (BhāgP 10.44.8); this is the general direction. Furthermore, by the word "thus" (*evam*), it is indicated that the sporting of that night was exactly like the sporting of other nights; and consequently, previously at the commencement of the *rāsa*-sport, of the Śrī-Bhagavān and of them...

The mutual dialogue and the exchange of questions and answers in the midst [of their conversation] proceed as if eternally new, because they are not subject to the limitations of analytical investigation, being instead completely immersed in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of supreme love.
Thus, everything may indeed occur again and again. This has already been written previously.

"Śaśāṅka" means the full moon; for by its very fullness, the mark resembling a hare rises perfectly. By its rays, they were especially resplendent, illuminated as if by day. Thus, during those nights for the sake of the glorious Lord’s rāsa-dance, [the quarters shone].
It should be understood that He rises with His full orb, just like the moon on the night of the full moon. As the venerable Vaiśampāyana has said:
"In this way, Kṛṣṇa was adorned by the circles of gopīs."

"He rejoiced happily on moonlit autumn nights" (*śāradīṣu sa-candrāsu niśāsu mumude sukhī*). In this context, the term "autumnal" (*śāradīṣu*) is illustrative; alternatively, it should be understood as "like autumnal" (*śāradīṣv iva*). Or else, it is like the exchange of sons performed by Śrī Vasudeva in the midst of the city of Mathurā.
"The distinction [of the worlds] is to be postulated based on the established division of the kalpas.
Now, one might ask: "How could that play be accomplished during such a night, which is indeed eternal, by means of such modes of action and so forth?
To this, he says: "He whose desires are true" (satya-kāma).
One might object: "Even so, because of pride and the like, or because of dependence on husbands and others, I consider those women to be always difficult even for him to attain.

To this he replies: "In whom there is a connection with the multitude of weak women—the gopīs who are entirely dependent on him—characterized by being 'anu-rata,' meaning constantly delighted and devoted, through every means, whether by extensive effort or by total disregard [for all else]."
Alternatively, one might ask: since they are not independent due to their husbands and others, how could there be a constant attainment [of the Lord]?
To this he says: "Because of being devoted" (*anuraktā*). The meaning is that, setting aside everything else, they are always delighted in Him alone.
Or rather, because of their devotion, through a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), at any time, in any place, and by anyone whatsoever—[they attain Him].
The sense is that [the goal] will indeed be accomplished by this means. And since there is no possibility of failure in that regard, he says:
"He is a connoisseur of the rasa of rāsa, the great deluder.
Nor could there ever be satiety therein for any reason; thus he says: "It is true, however—"
Overpowered by love; he by whom the *saurata*—the totality of sexual union, or the heightening of playful dalliance—has been restrained and mastered, because he has descended for that very purpose.
And since that [union] resides within himself alone, it means that he did not merely delight them himself with indifference, but rather [delighted] within his own self.

"Thus, he has attained the state of erotic union (*saurata*). However, the meaning is that by directly accepting [the experience] within himself and through his attachment to it, he himself also experienced it. Alternatively, "with the self as the instrumental cause" means that, disregarding such things as delighting in the Self (*ātmārāmatā*), even he was supremely awakened by that [experience].

It was not only the *rāsa*-pastime of the aforementioned kind that was performed, but also various forms of diverse amorous play (*vicitrā rati*) with them; thus he says, "In autumn" (*śaradi*). This refers to the intensity of desire (*kāma*) in autumn and the beauty of the riverbanks and so forth. Alternatively, the term *hāyana* (year) is used here as a synonym for autumn.

Thus, according to the statement of Amara: "In whatever season, month, or day within the year, whatever stories are described in poetic works, he pursued them; that is to say, he devotedly practiced their themes. These [themes] are to be understood as being of the nature described in such works as the *Śrī-Gītagovinda* and the *Vidagdhamādhava-nāṭaka*.
The rest has been explained by them. Alternatively, by the phrase "thus she served," the *rāsa*-pastimes during the nights have been described.
Now, he indicates that at other times, even during the days, there were similar other pastimes as well—by the words "all.
She attended to all the autumnal poetic narratives (*kāvyakathā*). In this context, by the word "poetry" (*kāvya*), supreme variety is intended.

Their [classification] has been indicated; they are well known from works such as the *Gītagovinda*, and likewise should be understood as the types found in the sections on giving (*dānakhaṇḍa*) shown by Śrī Caṇḍīdāsa and others. This is the general direction [of the matter]. The rest is the same. ||26||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
The *Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha* concludes with the words "Thus," etc.: Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose desires and resolves are true, pervaded the night illuminated by the rays of the moon.

The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of the aforementioned types. "Autumnal poetic narratives" (*śarat-kāvya-kathāḥ*) refers to those poetic narratives occurring in the autumn season,
which arise from the six seasons and consist of stories that form part of the poetry, such as forest excursions, water sports, drinking wine, amorous festivals, and so forth.

The meaning is "those [pastimes]. Because such pastimes are extremely secret and because listeners lack the qualification [to hear them], they were concluded by the Lord through a symbolic code (saṅketa) by Śrī Śukācārya. In that regard, by the analogy of an elephant from which rut has flowed, the drinking of honey is [described] as the erotic pleasure contained within oneself.

By this, the festival of rasa is indicated. *Avarodha* means that which is confined (*avaruddha*). *Sauratam* is simply *suratam* (sexual union). One whose confinement within oneself is *sauratam* has thus described the limits of sexual pleasure (*rata-maryādā*) by means of a conventional sign (*saṅketa*); such is the general direction [of the meaning].
And that is the sense of "contrary rasa" (*viparīta-rasa*). They are the supports of rasa, meaning they are the supports of the erotic rasa (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). ||26||

Prīti-sandarbha 300: Thus, in the manner previously described, Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra— wherein the multitude of women are constantly and passionately devoted— has restrained and firmly established within His own heart (ātman) the erotic sentiment (saurata).

Being thus endowed with the *bhāvas*, *hāvas*, and other expressions related to sexual union (*surata*), and for that very reason possessing true desire— a particular form of love free from deviation— he cultivated all those poetic narratives based on aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that exist in connection with the autumn season.

Alternatively, the word "autumn" (*śarat*) here refers to the entire year. Consequently, it should be explained that the state of being illuminated by the moon's rays is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
This is likewise seen in the playful jests of Śrī Rukmiṇī, such as in the passage: "with amorous conversations" (*saurata-saṃlāpaiḥ*, Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.58).

The word *saurata* is used in that sense. (Prīti-sandarbha 300) Rasikāhlādinī: Thus, by extending [the description] to the pastimes performed on a single night as being of one form, he concludes with the words "evam" (thus). Just as the pastimes were performed on the first night of the autumn season, so too [were they performed on other nights].

"In this same manner, in all [the nights]"—he says "in this way" (evam) by means of this method—that the moon (śaśāṅka), with its rays, attended to (*siṣeve*) all the nights, shining and radiant; the meaning is that he sported in them without interruption. Thus, the play performed during a single night has been shown in brief.
The sense is: who is able to describe that which has been described over many nights?
Parāśara also said:
"Madhusūdana, honoring his youth, [remained there]..."
"The immeasurable-souled one, having destroyed his enemies, took delight with them during the nights.
Thus, Kṛṣṇa, adorned by the circles of cowherd women,
rejoiced happily during the autumnal nights illuminated by the rays of the moon.

Thus, because of the fullness of the moon, all nights are indeed full. Although all seasons reside in Vṛndāvana, nevertheless, in that particular region as their locus, there are those aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) found in the poetic narratives of the autumn season— those narratives which are like the domain of Indra himself.

The *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments are their substrata; or rather, she cultivated the entire narrative of autumnal poetry which has rasa as its substratum. In accordance with that, she sported within those [works], as is well known in the *Gītagovinda* and others.

[Objection: But what would be gained by sporting with one who is indifferent? [Reply: If that were so, there would always be incapacity for sport during the nights and a state of detachment; therefore, he says "one whose desires are true" (*satya-kāma*). Alternatively, those whose desire or longing (*abhilāṣa*) is to be awakened (*bodhya*) as true are "those whose desires are true. Or else, in truth...

Those for whom there is desire for the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; because the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is real, the desire directed toward it is also real. Indeed, He is "one whose desires are true" (satya-kāma) precisely because of His essential identity with them. Now, one might object that the pastimes could be occasional due to the gopīs' dependence on husbands and others at certain times; therefore, he says:

"Anuratabalāgaṇaḥ": one in whom a group of women (*abalā-gaṇa*) is devoted (*anurata*), having disregarded obstacles such as husbands; or rather, one by whom a group of women is followed (*anusṛta*) and devoted (*anurata*) to experiencing amorous sports (*vilāsa*) continuously. By this, their constant association is indicated.
Because of the desire for truth, there is constant delight in those [states], and not merely occasional; for delight is not possible without desire. Thus it has been said:
"No action whatsoever is seen here or anywhere in this world for one who is without desire."

"Whatever a living being does, all that is the activity of desire. When even an ordinary creature acts with desire, how much more so must it be for one who is supremely passionate? Thus it is said in the *Gītagovinda*: "O friend, love is incarnate."

Regarding the word "iva": even for them, the fruit of their desire is solely the attainment of the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not the enjoyment of sense objects. This has been stated by His own mouth: "For those whose minds are absorbed in Me, desire does not lead to further desires."

"Roasted and boiled grains are generally not fit for seed" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.22.26). Now, one might object that constant dalliance would lead to a loss of relish; therefore, he says: "In whom sexual pleasure is contained within the Self," because his desires are fulfilled by Truth, and because his mind is immersed in the amorous pastimes of the Queen of Vraja.

And: he is one by whom the emission of the final element (carama-dhātu) related to sexual union (surata) has been withheld within his very own self. This indeed is the nature of ordinary desire (*prākṛta-kāma*):
that having caused the falling of the final element at the end of sexual union, it produces a sense of distaste. [This is] non-ordinary desire (*aprākṛta-kāma*).

Rather, increasing his fresh passion at every moment and arresting the discharge of the vital fluids (*dhātu*), he generates ever-increasing pleasure; for otherwise, at the conclusion of sexual union, there would be the undesirable consequence of a loss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhaṅga*). Or rather, "contained within himself" means held in his own mind—that skill in the arts conducive to sexual union (*saurata*).
"By skill alone, there is no falling of the vital elements (dhātus).

Or rather, he states his own purpose: he is one by whom eroticism—the adornment of sexual union—is restrained within himself for the sake of his own pleasure, with "self" as the cause; therefore, it is true, being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.

The meaning is: one whose desire or longing is directed toward the circle of gopīs. Precisely because His desires are true, the groups of women—being devoted, following Him, and having attained dependence upon Him—honor Him as their husband;
thus, because the object of His desire is real, His desire is true. This is because ordinary, material desire is incapable of entering into Him.

As for the statement regarding the conquest of desire, it is a logical argument of speech: if there were entry into ordinary desire, then its conquest might be possible; however, that is not the case.
Or rather, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose desires are ever-fulfilled, [manifests] as the locus of rasa for His own pleasure, with Himself as the instrumental cause.

When he devoted himself to poetry and storytelling, even the autumn season attended upon him as he enjoyed himself; for me, every night was uninterrupted and graced by the full moon's rays. Thus, it is well known that during the autumn season, [the season] itself acts as an attendant and serves as a source of effortless delight. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Concluding the *rāsa*-dance performed on the night of the autumnal full moon, he describes how he continued to engage with them in various, diverse, and countless similar pastimes during other nights as well.
Thus, by the power of Yogamāyā, all those nights were illuminated by the rays of the moon.
"He served" means that he tasted the bliss of the nights of Vṛndāvana through his own amorous pastimes.

By using the root *sivu* (to sew/to enjoy) as the agent, it is illuminated that those nights, which are conducive to play, are to be enjoyed with the highest respect; how much more so, then, the amorous delights found therein. [He partook of] the food of great grace (*mahā-prasāda*).
It is like the expression "the devotee serves.
He says that the amorous pastimes should not be understood as being ordinary: "one whose desires are true" (*satya-kāma*).
This means he is one for whom the amorous pastimes are true, having the nature of real, substantial entities. Furthermore, he is "one whose host of women are devoted to him" (*anuraktābalā-gaṇaḥ*).

He states that he caused both himself and those gopīs to attain the state of being the agents of amorous play (*ramaṇa*): *anu tad-ramaṇānantaram*, meaning "after that amorous play," [he was] where even the groups of women (*abalā-gaṇāḥ*) were the ones who took pleasure (*ratāḥ*), i.e., the agents of amorous play.
By the word *abalā*, the absence of their sovereign power (*prabhaviṣṇutva*) in that situation is suggested.

And at that time, the Blessed One’s mind was focused solely on the continuous flow of those amorous sports day and night; thus he says: "having confined the amorous states within himself. Within himself—that is, within his own mind—he had confined, meaning he had restrained and established, the amorous states (*sauratāḥ*) related to sexual union, such as *bhāva*, *hāva*, *bibboka*, *kilakiñcita*, and so forth.
He is one by whom longing, joy, and other emotions, as well as paralysis, perspiration, change of color, and so forth, along with looking, touching, and embracing, [are aroused].
Thus, through amorous conversations, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, [was pleased].
"Delighting in his own self, he sported with Rāmā, imitating the ways of the world of men" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.58).

In this instance, the term "conversation" (*saṃlāpa*) is employed specifically because a particular distinction is intended to be expressed. However, in the present case, it should be understood that all of them are included without such distinction.
She spent all twelve months of the year in such nights as these: what were they like?

They were "resorts for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of poetic narratives concerning the autumn. This is because the lexicon states, "The word *hāyana* is not feminine; *śarat* [is feminine]; *samāḥ* [is feminine].
Thus, during the autumn—which is the very middle of the year—there are aesthetic flavors of poetic narratives concerning the seasons and so forth.

The foundations for these [descriptions] arise from those very nights of the year that take place in Śrī Vṛndāvana and serve as the locus for Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes; relying upon these, excellent poets— both ancient and modern,
such as Vyāsa, Parāśara, Jayadeva, Līlāśuka, Govardhanācārya, Śrī Rūpa, and others— [have composed their works].

The meaning is that even after describing stories and sentiments—predominantly the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*)—in their own respective poetic works, they would not reach the end [of the subject]. Therefore, the intention is that since it is impossible for me as well to describe it in its entirety, only this general direction has been shown. ||26||

Sarasvatī-Ṭhākura (CC 2.14.158): Thus, by the state described, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—whose desires are true and whose resolves are eternally true—is "anurata-abalā-gaṇaḥ," meaning He is one in whom the multitude of women are *anurata* (attached) and *ākṛṣṭa* (drawn); that is to say, He is situated amidst a multitude of passionate women. Within Himself...

Thus, one by whom "sauratāḥ"—that is, sexual activities (*surata-vyāpārāḥ*)—have been mastered is "avaruddha-saurataḥ"; such a person is "ātmārāmaḥ," meaning he is a non-worldly god of love (*aprākṛta-kāmadeva*). [The phrase] "śarat-kāvya-kathā-rasāśrayāḥ" means those which are the locus (*āśraya*) of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) described in autumnal poetic narratives (*kāvya-kathā*); or alternatively, [it may mean...]

They are the substrata for those aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) appropriate to autumnal poetic narratives; or rather, in the construction "autumnal poetic narratives are the substrata of the *rasas*," they are those stories well-known in literature during the autumn season which serve as the substrata for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). They are illuminated by the rays of the moon—the moon's...
He spent all the nights, which were radiant and beautiful with rays and beams, engaged in the sport of the rāsa dance. ||26||
The King said:
"For the establishment of dharma and for the pacification of its opposite,"
For the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, has indeed descended with a portion of his being.
Śrīdhara and Vaṃśīdhara:
"The Lord has indeed descended," and so forth— this is the question of Parīkṣit, [contained in] the *Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*.

That from which a collection of parts (*kalā-kalāpa*) is divided or apportioned is called a *aṃśa* (a partial incarnation); thus, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the one whose portions are complete (*paripūrṇa-bhāga*), for He has descended as the Supreme beyond the supreme. [He is accompanied] by His partial incarnation (*aṃśa*), Baladeva. (27)
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*,
and *Krama-sandarbha*: for certain individuals among those very people who were present there but did not understand the true nature of those [works].
Having reflected upon their doubt, and for the sake of their very welfare, he raises that same doubt under the pretext of his own uncertainty and asks: "For the purpose of establishing... (27).

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, one should not feel astonishment at this, for as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.29.16, "O King, you need not be amazed at the Blessed One, the Unborn, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga," the King, although his objection had been refuted by these words, asks again with the three verses beginning with "saṃsthāpanāya" (for the sake of re-establishment), in order to dispel the doubts of the listeners.

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, by first describing how the King of Cedi attained perfection through the narration of the excellence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds, Śrī Śuka has brought satisfaction to the King's mind; now, however, even though he is already filled with supreme bliss by hearing of the *rāsa*-līlā...

As they sat in the assembly hall— men of many tongues devoted to fallacious logic— they experienced supreme bliss upon hearing of the amorous pastimes of the beauties of Vraja; yet, by the contraction of their eyes,
they suspected in their own minds that Śrī Kṛṣṇa was equal to a mere living soul (jīva), their faces turning away from the truth.

Perceiving his intention, and seeing that [the others] were unable to question the Lord of Sages, the King— who was skilled in reading gestures— raised a doubt and challenged him for the sake of establishing the Dharma (*dharmasaṃsthāpanāya*). "For the establishment of the Dharma" means for the establishment of the Dharma which had been uprooted by those who rely on mere reasoning (*haituka*), by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

The purpose of this work is to demonstrate its authority by means of the words of learned yogis and to provide firm establishment through their conduct; furthermore, it is for the pacification and total eradication of that unrighteousness (adharma) which has been promoted by others who are excessively extroverted, proponents of worldly ends, and devoted to fallacious reasoning.

The meaning is: "for the sake of uprooting [the afflictions] along with their latent impressions (*savāsanā*). The Blessed One, although possessing the sixfold sovereignty (*ṣaḍ-aiśvarya*) manifested [within himself], descended together with his partial manifestation (*aṃśa*), Baladeva; or else, he descended together with his partial manifestations of knowledge, power, sovereignty, and so forth.
For he is the Lord of the World (*jagadīśvara*), the controller of the worlds—of all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary and moving.

They transgress the boundaries of dharma; for all of them, punishment must be administered because, by overstepping dharma, they bring about the destruction of the world. This protection of dharma and the removal of unrighteousness is, in general, the duty of an avatāra; as it is said in the Gītā:
"For whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and an uprising of adharma, then I manifest Myself" (Gītā 4.6).
Thus, the question arises as to what constitutes the specific task of the Incarnate Śrī Kṛṣṇa; for Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Supreme Lord.

Although it has already been stated that [He acts] "Himself," there is nevertheless an objection raised in order to determine the specific nature [of His action], since the protection of Dharma and so forth could be accomplished by other incarnations in a general sense. He Himself determines the specific task: namely, the protection of the particular Dharma of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the one who is to descend.
The meaning is that there are two purposes: the setting forth [of dharma] and the removal of specific forms of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

This is for the sake of establishing the dharma spoken from the Blessed One’s own mouth as "dharma is that which produces devotion to Me," and for the sake of suppressing other [practices] devoid of utility for devotion, and for preventing their dissemination among those who lack devotion.
Because it is heard that qualities contrary to devotion are to be abandoned, it is said here:
"Those who perceive the same purpose even in heaven, liberation, and hell.
Alternatively, the Lord, endowed with all powers, has descended here in Gokula with His plenary portion, while remaining elsewhere in part.

The meaning is that He is the controller and Lord of the worlds, the cosmic eggs. Having caused those who are excessively extroverted to hear— those who perceive Śrī Kṛṣṇa as equal to other living beings— the King,
though himself satisfied by hearing of the rāsa-līlā and free from doubt, speaks again in order to establish them in fallacious reasoning.

The underlying meaning is that she asks this in order to attribute unrighteousness (*adharma*) to the Blessed One and thereby establish the sovereignty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the mouth of the Lord of Sages. He alone is the protector of the world by means of establishing righteousness (*dharma*) and by means of removing unrighteousness. (27)

Viśvanātha: Now, Parīkṣit, having observed the doubt that had arisen in the hearts of those seated in the assembly—such as the performers of ritual action (*karmis*) and the knowers of reality (*jñānis*), who possessed various latent tendencies (*vāsanās*)—asks [the following] for the purpose of destroying that doubt, beginning with the words "for the sake of establishing... [and so on]. As for that which is other, namely unrighteousness (*adharma*)...

Lord Viṣṇu becomes the Lord of the Universe by His partial expansion; that Blessed One has descended as Savya. Alternatively, it is said that together with Baladeva, He performed unrighteousness—which is adverse and contrary—merely as a matter of His own spontaneous play. In that case, having accepted the curse of Brahmā, He experienced its fruit.
And just as one might at times accept [the existence of] God, so too, having accepted sin, one must necessarily accept its fruit; this is the objection—this is the first question. ||27-28||
O Brahmin, how could he, who was the speaker, the creator, and the protector of the bridges of Dharma, have committed such an act contrary to righteousness as the violation of another's wife?

Śrīdhara: "Pratīpam" means contrary or adverse dharma; he "practiced" (ācarat) means he performed it. And this was not merely an unrighteous act like eating *kalañja* and so forth, but rather a great act of audacity;
thus he says: "the violation of another's wife. (28)
Vaṃśīdhara:
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: How could one act in opposition? What indeed [is that]?
To this he says: "Coveting the wives of others" (28).
The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī,
the Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī,
and the Krama-sandarbha have not been commented upon.

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: "The opposite" means contrary. What is that? To this he says: "the violation of another's wife," meaning sexual union with another's woman according to the external sense; but in reality, however, the "wife" (*dārāḥ*) refers to the powers of one's own bliss (*svānanda-śaktayaḥ*), who are higher than the highest, for they "tear asunder" (*dārayanti*) ignorance. (28)

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Regarding "the bridges of dharma"—dharma itself constitutes the bridges; these are the boundaries capable of protecting the world. He is not merely their speaker or instructor, but also their performer. As it is said in the *Gītā*: "These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action" (*Gītā* 3.24).

He is protected on all sides by the refutation of the fallacious arguments of heretics and by the destruction of those who forcibly tear down the bridge of Dharma. Thus, as a protector of Dharma in many ways, he is not opposed [to it].
Nevertheless, the example is given: "Who indeed would accept that authority of Ṛṣabha?"

It is said that such conduct would surely bring about what is undesirable for the world; thus, it is called "contrary" (*pratīpa*). When there is an expectation as to what that is, he says: "the violation of another's wife. This means that which is a great act of recklessness (*mahāsāhasa*).
The status of Dharma as a speaker is seen directly: "For women, the supreme duty is the devoted service of their husband."

Having said, "Indeed, by means of guilelessness," and having spoken of service to her husband, she accomplished her pleasure; therefore, a contradiction arose between her speech and her action. Since she forgot what was to be said and protected her pleasure on all sides, how is this "contrary" (*pratīpa*)?
He acts? [This is] because he asks out of ignorance of the intention, for there is nothing whatsoever contrary in that regard.

That the Lord possesses the quality of performing contradictory attributes and so forth—just as it is heard that both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) reside in the Lord—it is said thus: in the case of the Lord, one thing is his conduct and another is his actual practice.

There is nothing contradictory here; nevertheless, the sense is that we inquire into the contrary nature of the perceptions and actions of the Lord, who is intent upon maintaining the world-order. ||28||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— The Lord of the Yadus, whose desires were fulfilled, indeed performed that which is loathsome.
With what intention did you say this? O observer of noble vows, dispel this doubt of ours.

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that this [act] is not unrighteous for one whose desires are fulfilled, then, since there is an absence of desire, he asks with what intention he performed the censurable act—“one whose desires are fulfilled” (āpta-kāma). || 29 ||

Vaṃśīdhara explains: "Of one whose desires are fulfilled" (*āptakāmasya*). If that is so—that he has fulfilled his desires—then, since it is improper for one whose desires are fulfilled to engage in censurable conduct, what is the intention?
The meaning is: "What is his purpose? or "What is his underlying motive? regarding this state of having fulfilled one's desires.
"Of censurable conduct"—this is said in view of the local society there, as they are many [in number]. "O you of good vows":
although he is established in celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the intention behind the address is "speak," by virtue of my grace. ||29||
Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā: not explained.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The meaning is that even though he is known as "the Lord of the Yadus" (*yadupati*) because he has descended into the lineage of the pious Yadus, he ought not to act in such a manner. The word *vai* indicates well-known fact. The word *etam* (this) means that there is no other doubt regarding this matter whatsoever. The plural form *naḥ* (of us) is used with the intention of referring to the entire group of those who were in doubt.
Regarding the word "doubt" (*saṃśaya*): for him, who is the crest-jewel of the authoritative ones (*āpta*), there is certainly no suspicion of fault;
however, because we lack firm conviction in that matter due to its contradiction with the scriptures, our minds would waver—this is the meaning.
"O Suvrata! means "O you who are devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*)"; thus [he addresses] those such as yourself.

That, however, is contrary to established conduct and is indeed loathsome. Alternatively, the sense is that by being "devoted to good conduct" (*sadācāra-niṣṭhā*), you would otherwise be violating the good conduct approved by people like yourself.
In the case of *śleṣa* (punning), [the meaning is] his own lordship over the Yadus who are related to the Pāṇḍavas.

By the phrase "he approaches" (*abhipraiti*), the absence of fault is implied. Alternatively, the meaning is that because he is the Lord of the Yadus, who are His devotees, He is worthy of transgressing dharma out of affection for His devotees (*bhakta-vātsalya*). What contemptible act did He commit?
On the contrary, He did nothing of the sort; rather, He performed only what is approved by the assembly of devotees. Why?
He is one by whom his own desire has been attained through the *rāsa*-dance and other pastimes, and whose heart's wish is the expansion of his own devotional love (*prema-bhakti*).

This is because he propagates that devotional love which is most difficult for all to achieve, and rather than engaging in censurable conduct, he instead brings satisfaction to the assembly of the virtuous; such is the meaning. Nevertheless, [we still have] our doubt.

Regarding the word "prāyaḥ" (mostly): this is because there is no doubt among certain individuals who know the true essence of the scriptures, who are devoted to devotion, and who are immersed in the nectar of the True Reality, concerning His rāsa-dance and other pastimes which consist of the aesthetic flavor of premonitive devotion (*prema-bhakti-rasa*).

Alternatively, by the phrase "mostly at this time of fasting," the unworthiness of doubt is expressed; therefore, its immediate severance is intended. The word "our" (*naḥ*) includes even adversaries by virtue of their being one's own [through spiritual kinship].
This is for the purpose of making them aware of their status as supreme adversaries through innate humility and so forth, or perhaps through verbal skill.

Therefore, the intention is that I am asking this solely for the benefit of those of poor intellect present here, and not out of my own doubt. Thus, "towards them" (*abhi*) means so that there may be fearlessness; that is, without causing them fear, please sever the chain of their doubts. O you of noble vows! (*suvrata*)—O [Lord]! [This is the meaning.]
"Exclusively devoted to devotion. ||29||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "The Lord of the Yadus"—if he had committed such an improper act, he would not even be the lord of the Yadus, who are supremely righteous. "This one"—the meaning is that there is no doubt whatsoever about this. The plural number in "na" (they do not) refers to the group [of Yadus] in view of the doubt.

"Doubt" refers to mental wavering caused by both the fact that this was practiced by one wearing a crown and its contradiction with the scriptures. "O Suvrata!"—meaning "O you who are steadfast in celibacy and other vows"—implies that the conduct of those like you is contradictory and therefore indeed contemptible. Alternatively, "O you who are steadfast in good conduct" may be interpreted otherwise [as a sarcastic address].
The sense is that he has violated the traditional conduct (sadācāra) accepted by you and others.

In the context of the pun (śleṣa), the meaning is that as the Lord of the Yadus—the devotees—he might, out of compassion for his devotees, occasionally be worthy of transgressing dharma; however, what contemptible thing did he actually do? On the contrary, nothing at all.
The meaning is that He acted exactly in accordance with the consensus of the circle of devotees. Why?
Because He is one by whom His own desire for the expansion of devotional love through the *rāsa*-dance and other pastimes has been attained and fulfilled;
rather than censuring those who engage in such practices, He does so by promoting devotional love, which is the most excellent of all goals to be accomplished.

The meaning is: "precisely because of satisfying the assembly of the virtuous. Nevertheless, [the phrase] "our doubt" is intended to refer to the group of those present who were still hesitating, expressed by the gesture of moving the hands with palms joined;
and this was done with humility, as is generally the case there, for the sake of certain individuals who knew the true essence of the scriptural meaning and were devoted to faith.

Because those who are consecrated by the six flavors (sad-rasa) possess no internal doubt regarding His rāsa-dance and other pastimes—which consist of the essence of the rasa of divine love—the sense is this: I ask for the sake of the benefit of certain people here who are inattentive, and not out of my own doubt. Therefore, [grant] fearlessness (*abhaya*)... as follows.
The meaning is: "Without fear of them, you should sever their chain of doubt.
