O observer of good vows! O you who are solely devoted to devotion! ||29||

The sequence of the argument: For one whose desires are fulfilled, there would be no inclination toward what is loathsome; therefore, the meaning is: with what intention did he perform that which is loathsome? ||29||

*Bṛhatkramasandarbha*: "Vai" indeed means "disgusting"; "vigata-jugupsitam" means that which has departed from being disgusting, i.e., "vijugupsitam. That very thing is "vaijugupsitam," with the suffix *aṇ* used in the sense of the base word itself. ||29||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, one might ask: "Could this [Lord] not indeed be one whose desires are already fulfilled? For we observe His engagement in what is loathsome. If this is argued, the answer is no; for when a desire has been attained, no one would perceive such engagement as blameworthy. Indeed, He is one whose desires are fulfilled because He is the Lord of Ramā.

And because he bestows all perfections (*sarva-siddhi*). He is called "Yadupati" because he was born in the Yadu lineage, which is the supreme abode of Dharma. Furthermore, he is the protector of those born of a noble lineage through his instruction in Dharma.
What was his intention? With what purpose did he [perform] that which is loathsome and censured?
He has certainly acted [thus], because the meanings are mutually contradictory.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between being one whose desires are fulfilled and being an agent of censurable acts is impossible. If it is argued that there is nothing inconsistent because the Lord is the substratum of contradictory attributes;

Nevertheless, one might doubt that this purpose should be stated, thinking, "This is not for the benefit of the world because it lacks a complete purpose. Anticipating this, [the author] addresses everyone collectively and requests: "Obeisance! O Suvrata—one whose resolve (saṅkalpa) is excellent—please sever our doubt regarding this matter for all of us."

Nothing else should be spoken except for the pastimes (līlā) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; if this were improper, then your faith would not have been as previously stated. Furthermore, if this were unrighteous (adharma), there would be no delight in your narration. It is merely a certain diversion for the world.

Therefore, the underlying intention must be stated. As for the actual meaning: he is the Lord of the Yadus (Yadupati), by whom the desires were obtained through association with the gopīs. This is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O beautiful lady, these Yādavas are indeed eternally my own qualities."
O Goddess, they are always dear to me and possess qualities equal to my own.

Thus, the eternality of the pastimes in Dvārakā has been described; and by the statement, "Mathurā is where Lord Hari is eternally present," the eternality of the pastimes in Mathurā has also been indicated. Even there, His dependence upon His own [devotees] is indicated. For generally, what is loathsome? Indeed, nothing, since—abhi...

He acted in such a way that it was free from fear. Therefore, I have no doubt; I ask this out of deference to certain proponents of logical reasoning. "Cut through my doubt"—that is, my uncertainty. ||29||

Viśvanātha: If it is argued that this [act] is not unrighteousness (*adharma*) on the part of the Supreme Lord, he asks with what intention He performed this censurable act—by saying "one whose desires are fulfilled" (*āpta-kāma*). The sense is that one should not offer the reply that He did this for the sake of fulfilling His own desire. In this incarnation...
If it is argued that such a loathsome act must indeed be performed, he says in response: "The Lord of the Yadus.
The implication is: how could He be the lord of the Yadus, who are supremely righteous? [He replies] "No," meaning:
"I have no doubt at all in this matter. Even though His desires were already fulfilled...
The underlying sense is that even though He delights in Himself (ātmārāma), it is entirely fitting for Him to engage in longing amorous play with those gopīs, whose very nature is the bliss of love;

this is because He has already realized the essential secret of the Siddhānta. Furthermore, O Suvratā, since even you, who are devoted to virtuous conduct, have been seen to be so intensely absorbed in this very pastime, these [gopīs]... [are indeed such].
The meaning is that they have doubts. ||29||
Śrī Śuka said:
Transgression of dharma and reckless behavior are observed even among the lords.
It is no fault for those who are more powerful, just as it is not a fault for fire to consume everything.

Śrīdhara: In order to refute [the objection] regarding the Supreme Lord by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic, he states the conduct of great beings in general: "Transgression of dharma... and so forth. And rashness is observed in the case of Prajāpati, Indra, Soma, Viśvāmitra, and others; yet that does not constitute a fault for those luminous beings.
It comes to be. ||30||
Vaṃśīdhara: "To avoid" means to prevent or ward off. "In general" means by way of commonality.

"Of the lords" refers to those possessing the supernatural powers of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*). "Sāhasa" (rashness) is conduct contrary to the scriptures. [Examples include] the approaching of Prajāpati Brahmā’s daughter, Indra’s approaching Ahalyā, and Soma’s...

The approach to the wife of one's guru and to Tārā; Viśvāmitra’s engagement in eating forbidden meat; the effort of the seven ṛṣis, beginning with Ādya, to eat a corpse; Ajīgarta’s sale of his son; and Parāśara’s union with the daughter of a slave—all these are to be accepted as heroic acts (*sāhasa*) performed by those such as Prajāpati and the others.

The phrase "of those possessing greater splendor" (*tejīyasām*) is a qualifying term containing a reason: because rashness has been burnt away by the splendor arising from the power of asceticism (*tapas*) and other virtues, it does not lead to fault or sin. Regarding the word *tejas*, Yādava states: "Splendor (*tejas*) is found in strength, power, light, flame, semen, butter, and fire. In this context, there is a relevant illustrative example:

He says: "Of fire. For the meaning is that fire does not incur the fault of killing a Brahmin or similar offenses by burning the impure bodies of cows, Brahmins, and so forth, because of its inherent brilliance. ||30||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjuṣā*: It establishes the conclusion that for God—who is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise—even the transgression of the laws He Himself has established serves to nourish His divinity rather than contradict it; for [the verse says]: "The transgression of dharma... regarding the Lords.
This applies even to Prajāpati, Indra, and the others, let alone to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all lords.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "of fire, which consumes everything. (30)

The Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī comments: He sets aside [the objection] out of his innate compassion or out of regard for affection toward his disciple, by means of seven verses beginning with "Dharma... The meaning is: those who possess the capacity for both knowledge and devotion regarding the Lords, and who are free from dependence on ritual action and the like due to their worship of the Blessed Lord.
Transgression of *dharma* (*dharma-vyatikrama*) is the violation of specific rules, such as Brahmā and others’ desire for their own daughters.

*Sāhasa* is fearlessness, as seen in Indra and others. Just as fire consumes, devours, or burns everything, so too, despite burning everything, there is no fault of killing or the like in that [divine being], just as there is none in fire.

It would not be so; that is the meaning of "tadvat" (like that). The rest has been explained by them. Alternatively, *sāhasa* (rashness) is simply the transgression of *dharma*. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *tu* (but/rather). For the sake of distinguishing [this] from those who lack mastery (*anīśvara*), the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* [states]: "either out of innate compassion or out of regard for affection for his disciples."

Having first refuted the fallacious appearance of their [the opponents'] arguments, he refutes their own established doctrine as demonstrated through wordplay (*śleṣa*) by means of seven verses beginning with "dharma. The meaning is: "of the lords" (*īśvarāṇām*), that is, those who are devoid of dependence on karma and so forth; "their transgression of dharma" refers to what is observed, such as in the case of Brahmā and others.

Likewise, the audacity and fearlessness observed in [the case of] Kāma’s desire for his daughter, as well as that seen in Bṛhaspati’s approach to Utathya’s wife and so forth—all those acts, due to the superior power (*tejas*) of those individuals, do not constitute a fault or a transgression (*pratyavāya*).
In this regard, there is an illustration: just as the capacity to consume everything on the part of the all-consuming fire does not constitute a fault.
The meaning is that it is not like that for the sake of impurity. ||30||

The sequence of composition: Transgression of dharma is seen, such as the desire for [their own] daughters by Brahmā and others; likewise, audacity and fearlessness are seen, such as Bṛhaspati’s approach to the wife of Utathya. All that is not non-[dharma] on the part of those who are possessed of great splendor.
This leads to transgression; the meaning is that just as fire consumes everything, its capacity for consuming all things does not result in impurity. ||30||
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "transgression of dharma" (*dharma-vyatikrama*), and so forth.

For the lords (*īśvara*), a transgression of dharma is indeed unseen; it is never observed anywhere. Likewise, there is no rashness—that is, nothing done impulsively. The lords never practice unrighteousness (*adharma*); nevertheless, if...

When this is observed, then for those who possess splendor—the capacity to act, to refrain from acting, or to act otherwise—any transgression of dharma on the part of those endowed with such splendor does not constitute a fault; rather, it results only in merit. However, one must seek a specific cause for what is performed by them, for that [action] is not prompted by passion (rāga). Therefore, this is a transgression of dharma [only in appearance].

Thus it appears, yet in reality there is no transgression of the Dharma. Here is an illustration: "of fire," and so forth. Just as for fire—that is, for the flame—the term *sarvabhujaḥ* (all-consuming) is used in the plural form with the *kvip* suffix; its state of consuming everything is not acquired through passion, but rather is innate.

In the same way, this too must be accepted by him: "This is the sport (*līlā*) of the Lord, not a transgression of Dharma, because it is impossible for the Lord to act otherwise. Therefore, the meaning of the text is that these women do not possess the status of another's wives, nor does this constitute a transgression of Dharma for Him. This will become clear further on.
The plural number in the word "īśvarāṇām" (of the lords) intends to convey that [the Lord] is the Lord of all. ||30||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Thus, Śrī Śuka refutes by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhi-vāda*) the objection raised as to how [the Lord] could have acted in a manner contrary to other incarnations;
having acknowledged that which was objected to based on the intention of the causal theorist (*hetuvādī*), who argued that there was a transgression of dharma (*dharma-vyatikrama*).

He addresses this with the following verse, as if to dispel doubt: Even among the lords—who are free from dependence on bodies and the like—transgression of dharma and overstepping of boundaries are observed. For example, Brahmā conceived a desire for his own daughter, and Soma took the wife of Bṛhaspati;
likewise, others who are equal to the lords and who act by transgressing boundaries through the power of their knowledge and devotion [are seen].

Transgressing the laws of the present is seen as an act of audacity, and fearlessness in doing what is not currently possible is also seen [as such], because it is performed impulsively without deliberation.
If this were so, one might ask: "To whom would the fruit of sin (pratyavāya) not accrue? To this, he says: "Of those who are more powerful... (*tejīyasām*).
For those who possess splendor, it does not lead to fault by way of producing unrighteousness (*adharma*).
Even a cause that produces fault does not become a fault for those capable of burning away the defects of action;
regarding this, he states an illustration: "Just as there is no fault in fire, which consumes everything, even while it burns all things."
The fire, while consuming everything, does not partake in its defects. ||30||

Viśvanātha: [To answer] the first question—that even for lords (*īśvara*), the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*) performed might not accrue, much less for the Supreme Lord—He says "dharma" and so forth in six verses.
Even for lords such as Rudra and others, a transgression of dharma, that is, unrighteousness, is observed; as is recklessness (*sāhasa*).

The meaning is that it is caused by rashness. It leads neither to fault nor to transgression. The meaning is that just as everything consumed by fire does not result in fault, nor does it become impure, so it is in this case. ||30||
One who lacks self-mastery should never practice this even in thought;
for by practicing it out of delusion, one perishes, just as Rudra did when he consumed the ocean-born poison.

Śrīdhara: Anticipating the objection that, according to the principle "Whatever a superior person does, others should likewise do" (Gītā 3.21), anyone else might also act accordingly, he says: "Not this," etc. "Non-sovereign" means dependent on the body and so forth; just as one other than Rudra, while practicing or consuming poison, [is not sovereign]. ||31||

Vaṃśīdhara: He objects to that with the words "In that case" (*tahiṃ*). [The opponent says: "Another [who acts thus] is more feeble. This is a rash act. Even in thought (*manasā*), how much less so by deed (*kāyena*)? "He perishes" means he is cut down along with his very roots. This occurs through delusion (*mauḍhyāt*), that is, ignorance (*ajñānāt*), or from the excess of anger and the like. Regarding the reading *naśyasy āśv ācaran*: *vaṃśīdharaḥ*: tatrākṣipati—tarhīti | anyaḥ atejīyān | etat sāhasam | jātu manasāpi kim uta kāyena | vinaśyati samūlaṃ chinno bhavati | mauḍhyāt ajñānāt krodhādy-udrekato vā | naśyasy āśv ācaran iti pāṭhas tu ||
This is because of the statement in the *Vijayadhvaja* commentary. Therein, "immediately" means at the very moment following the drinking, and not after a delay.

Anticipating the objection that "another might also do the same according to the maxim 'Whatever the best person practices... (*Gītā* 3.21), he says: "one who is non-sovereign," meaning one who is inferior, such as anyone other than Rudra, when practicing or consuming poison.
It perishes immediately; however, Rudra, on the contrary, shines even more by virtue of his blue throat—this is the intended meaning. ||31||
The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā states: "But one who acts thus while not being the Lord is certainly afflicted," and so he says, "Not this.
Here is the illustration: just as Rudra conquers poison, whereas one who is not Rudra—one distinct from Rudra—is destroyed even while drinking the Kālakūṭa poison. ||31||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Then, what is the status of others in that regard? To this he says: "Not this.
One should not properly perform this conduct of the Lord, which consists of the transgression of dharma and so forth. The emphasis lies on the prohibition of "properly";
the meaning is that one should not perform it even in a single part. *Jātu* means at any time whatsoever. In that context...

And it is destroyed not even by the mind, much less by speech or action—certainly so—in its specific manner, such as causing suffering in both worlds along with its very roots. The meaning is that this occurs due to the delusion of the lords, who fail to recognize their own sovereignty and their own incapacity. Thus, in the act of devouring, delusion alone is the cause.

It has been said: otherwise, there would be no inclination to consume it. By the phrase "sea-born kālakūṭa," what is intended is immediate destruction due to its extreme sharpness. However, Īśvara would certainly not perish;
on the contrary, he shines through the manifestation of his particular sovereignty and so forth, just as he does by virtue of having a blue throat and other such marks.
The sense is that he is Śiva. ||31||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: One should not properly practice this rash conduct of the Lord. The word "properly" (*samyak*) has the intended meaning of prohibition. Never (*jātu*), at any time whatsoever, should one do so even in thought, much less by speech or action. For (*hi*)—whether indicating a reason or a certainty—it is especially so from its very root.

It would perish by way of causing suffering in both worlds and so forth; that is to say, out of delusion (*mauḍhya*), [the gods] did not recognize the sovereignty of the lords and their own incapacity. Thus, in the case of eating [it], delusion alone is stated to be the cause; otherwise, there would be no inclination toward eating. "Born from the ocean" means *kālakūṭa*.

The intended meaning is that destruction occurs immediately due to extreme sharpness; however, Īśvara would certainly not be destroyed, but rather shines even more through the manifestation of His particular sovereignty and so forth, just as Śrī Mahādeva does through His blue throat and other attributes—this is the sense. ||31||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, one might object: "In that case, even one who is not the Supreme Lord (an-īśvara) could act according to his own will from this perspective. Anticipating this, he says: "Not this," and so forth. No one other than Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even if they were not the Supreme Lord, would ever—at any time—even in thought—perform such a rash act. As for performing it... [who could do so?]

What is the obstruction? To this he says: "He perishes," and so forth. Acting out of delusion, he perishes and is quickly destroyed. But if the Lord acts, it results in the manifestation of His supreme sovereignty and the revelation of the welfare of all the world; thus he says: "Just as," and so forth. Just as the poison Kālakūṭa...

While manifesting his own sovereignty and acting for the benefit of all, [the Lord] in reality committed the consumption of poison, which is a transgression of dharma and an act of rashness; yet this was not obtained through passion on his part, but rather for the sake of the welfare of others. Moreover, that poison was not something intended for another's enjoyment.

Even in the present context, this does not constitute a transgression of dharma nor an act of rashness, because those [women] are not intended for the enjoyment of others. Furthermore, his embracing of them is for the sake of their ultimate welfare;
as he will say later: "sporting," and so forth. In the reading *abdhijaṃ viṣam* ("poison born of the ocean"), it means practicing—that is, consuming—it.
The root *car* is also used in the sense of eating. ||31||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: [Objection: "But if, by the analogy of fire, there is an absence of fault, then how does the world attain its highest good (*śreya*)? For it has been said: 'Indeed, by practicing that which has been established, one becomes fit for the welfare of the world.
To this, he says: 'Not so'—this [practice], being of the nature of a transgression of dharma, is not right."

"One should perform [actions] properly, with extreme disregard for prohibitions. In this regard, one must resolve that "not even in thought, much less in speech or action"—for one is oneself not the Lord, being dependent on the body and so forth; due to delusion, there is the error of imagining similarity to the Lord, and because one lacks the capacity like the Lord, there is the notion of possessing such capacity in the Lord.

By practicing [forbidden things] excessively, one perishes from the very root. For example, anyone other than Rudra who consumes the ocean-born poison known as Kālakūṭa would die instantly; yet Rudra, even while consuming it, does not perish, but rather shines forth due to his benefit to the world. Thus, in the absence of such power, [one perishes].

Those who practice [in this way] should be known as fools; for this very reason, one should never, even out of curiosity, perform an act done by a lord. Now, how can the same single action produce an inauspicious result, or how can it produce an auspicious result?
To this he says: "Because of the very difference among the various qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*), everything is consistent.
He states that Rudra [consumed] the poison born from the ocean; thus, he explains how even by swallowing the *kālakūṭa* poison, benefit for the world was achieved. ||31||

Viśvanātha: Anticipating the objection that, according to the principle stated in the *Gītā* (3.21), "Whatever a superior person does, others will also do," someone else might likewise act, he says, "This is not so. An inferior being, a *jīva* who is not the Lord—just as one other than Rudra perishes immediately upon consuming poison—whereas Rudra, having consumed it...
On the contrary, the sense is that he shone all the more by virtue of his blue throat. ||31||
The word of the lords is true, and their conduct is likewise in some instances;
a wise person should practice that which is consistent with their own words.
Śrīdhara: How, then, is the authority of right conduct established? To this he says: "Of the lords.

Their word is true; therefore, one should indeed practice what they have spoken. However, [mere] conduct is only sometimes true. Therefore, whatever is consistent with their own words—that is, whatever is joined with and not contradicted by their speech—that very thing [is authoritative].
One should act in this manner. ||32||
Vaṃśīdhara again objects: "How so? [This refers to] the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*), that which is practiced by the good.

Therefore, regarding this objection, he provides the resolution: "Of the lords" (*īśvarāṇām*). It is true that it grants what is desired as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); therefore, because of its truthfulness, it is said to be "spoken by the Lord. [This applies to] speech.

If this were indeed the case, one might ask: what is the status of the injunction, "The wise man, though unattached, should act with a desire to maintain the world"? To this he says: "But [such conduct] is practiced in some cases.
The phrase "in some cases" is used for the purpose of avoiding laughter and the like; it refers to that which is for the purpose of demonstrating the Vedic path.

That practice is indeed the truth. Therefore, because of their very existence, the Lord is grasped by His own word through His own speech; likewise, whatever conduct is appropriate and non-contradictory according to the speech—the utterance in the form of the Veda—of those Lords, that is the conduct of the Lords.
The meaning is that one should indeed do so.

Alternatively, whatever be the word of those lords—meaning their own speech—that is appropriate and not contrary to the Vedas, the wise man should practice and accept it; however, that which is contrary to the Vedas he should not.

The sense is that because the Lord is dependent upon His devotees, He may occasionally act otherwise [than what is prescribed]; therefore, such actions should not be accepted as authoritative. For this very reason, Devala, Bodhāyana, and Kauśika have said:
"Whatever deeds have been performed by the gods and likewise by the sages..."
One should not perform those actions, nor should one speak ill of them even after hearing of them.
Thus it has been said: "If that which is always to be performed conforms to the sacred tradition (āmnāya), then, should it contradict the Veda, it must be abandoned in accordance with the Smṛti."
In the same way, one should abandon a worldly statement if it contradicts traditional scripture (smṛti). A man who abandons the words of a panegyrist would be liable for penance;
however, a worldly statement must be abandoned if it is something spoken by the Lord.
Whatever may be contrary to the Veda, a man does not become a sinner on that account.

Thus, as it has been described in various ways in the *Nirṇayasudhākara* and other works, we shall now conclude. Furthermore, since there is a scriptural injunction stating, "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable, one should not attempt to apply logic to them," and because even the Lords possess an inconceivable nature, logic is entirely ineffective in that regard; therefore, regarding the Lord, logic is [set aside] by scripture.
It is prohibited. ||32||
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: not explained.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By the word "svakīyena" (by his own), the phrase "yuktaṃ sva-śabdena" (joined with the word 'his own') excludes speech that is inconsistent with proper conduct and spoken like one intoxicated by being overwhelmed with love. "Buddhimān" means "having reflected upon each [matter]"; otherwise, the implication is that he would be utterly lacking in intelligence.

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "The word of command is true" means it should be accepted as authoritative because it is not contradicted by one's own words; by the word "one's own," their [the Vaiṣṇavas'] own investigation is indicated, thereby manifesting the superior strength of the command. "The wise one" means that one should investigate each of those points accordingly. Otherwise—
The meaning is that he is indeed devoid of intelligence. ||32||
The sequence of composition: Speech is the command; truth is the authority. ||32||

*Bṛhatkramasandarbha*: Furthermore, since the speech and conduct of the lords (*īśvara*) such as Brahmā and others are indeed true, would even a non-lord (*anīśvara*) perform such conduct? To this he says: "Of the lords," and so forth.
Of the independent lords, Brahmā and the rest, only their word is true, and not their conduct; nowhere at all.

The conduct of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of lords, is indeed true because His pastimes are characterized by truth. A wise person should perform only that which is intended by those lords and by the Lord of lords, provided it is consistent with His own words and established by the Vedas; however, one should not perform everything He intends merely on the basis of its being "true," for [His intentions may be] based on His word.
But one should perform everything indeed, because it is the word of the Lord. ||32||
*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, if it is asked how the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*) possesses authority, he says in response:

"Of the lords" (*īśvarāṇām*). This refers to the lords who have attained power through devotion and knowledge; as it is said in the *Gītā*: [18.66] "Whatever a great soul does, that very thing other people do. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are masters of their own selves. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from selfish motives. Moreover, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are endowed with compassion. And finally, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment. Therefore, the conduct of the virtuous is indeed authoritative. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from delusion. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from fear. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these five reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from pride. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from envy. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these seven reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from hypocrisy. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from ostentation. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these nine reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from greed. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from anger. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these eleven reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from passion. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from hatred. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these thirteen reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from delusion. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from egoism. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these fifteen reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from possessiveness. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to worldly objects. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these seventeen reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to sense-objects. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the fruits of action. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these nineteen reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the body. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the mind. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these twenty-one reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to speech. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the intellect. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these twenty-three reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the ego. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the subtle elements. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these twenty-five reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the gross elements. And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the senses. Thus, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative on account of these twenty-seven reasons. Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the objects of the senses.
And the conduct of the virtuous is authoritative because it is performed by those who are free from attachment to the mind-born sons (the
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. (Gītā 14.2) For those who have thus obtained the grace of the Lord, their very command is the truth.
If it is argued that [the existence of God] is established because certain specific activities are observed, then that would indeed be true;

however, in the case of God, qualities such as merit and demerit, knowledge and ignorance, power and lack of power, and detachment and non-detachment are not observed. Likewise, for those characterized by the qualities of God, there are no mutual causes for what is desired or undesired.
It was said with a specific intention: "One should practice whatever they say is the truth as their established conduct.

One should not practice their arbitrary conduct, for they speak otherwise. Having reflected that the words regarding the meaning of the method are not true for those who are superior, the wise person [should act] according to what is appropriate for his own station.
One should practice [in this way]; otherwise, it would become a cause for the undesirable—this is the meaning. ||32||
Viśvanātha: How, then, is the authority of the conduct of the virtuous established? To this he says: "Of the lords," and so forth.
It is true that it is beneficial for the virtuous; in some cases, the meaning is "provided one is a son of Daśaratha. Therefore, he states that this is the settled rule:
"The wise person should practice only that which is consistent with his own word and is non-contradictory. Thus ends the section on the conduct of the virtuous.

In that regard, too, it must be considered: even though there was the Blessed One’s word, "Let this sinful man be bound, for he is an assassin and a kinsman," Arjuna did not carry out the execution of Aśvatthāman. Thus, [the rule] is not universal. //32//
O Lord, for those who are free from egoism, there is no personal interest here achieved through the practice of wholesome deeds, nor is there any misfortune resulting from their opposite.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, why do they also act with such audacity? To this he says: "By virtue of their merit," etc.
The meaning is that their only task is the mere exhaustion of their *prārabdha* (commenced) karma, and nothing else. ||33||

Vaṃśīdhara further objects to the [notion of] Lords with the words "nanu" (but surely). "Te'pi" means even those Lords. In that context, "īśvara-sāhase" refers to the audacity of those Lords. The meaning of the word "īśvara" has already been stated. The sense is that the wise are merely awaiting the exhaustion of their past impressions (*prārabdha*), and do not perform any action out of attachment to karma.

The intention [is as follows]. The meaning of the verse is this: for those who are free from egoism (*nirahaṅkārin*), there is no purpose or motive (*artha*)—such as the happiness of heaven and so forth—for the practice or performance of virtuous acts such as austerity, charity, and sacrifice; nor is there any misfortune (*anartha*) characterized by hell and so forth, resulting from the opposite, such as attachment to another's wife, drinking liquor, and the like.
Thus, this is a qualification containing a reason; the meaning is "because of being devoid of egoism" (*nirahaṅkāritvāt*).
Egoism is attachment to actions, and that alone is the cause of bondage. The intention is that because they are unattached to those [actions], there is no bondage. ||33||

*Caitanyamata-mañjūṣā*: How does the Lord exercise His sovereignty? Truly, because that which is independent cannot be constrained, He shows that this is merely His divine play (*līlā*) by saying, "By the performance of virtuous deeds by these," and so forth. "These" refers to the Lords, Rudra and the others.
The meaning is: "by means of virtuous practices. Conversely, through contrary or opposing conduct, there is misfortune;

yet neither of these two exists for those who are free from egoism—those devoid of the sense of "I" in the thought "I am doing this," for the very sense of "I" is the cause of being stained. The address "O Lord" is an invocation accompanied by lamentation.
Even though these many greatnesses have been heard, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is still advanced there, exclaiming: "Oh, what extraordinary power! ||33||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By the performance of their virtuous and meritorious conduct, there is welfare for these lords; by the word "ca" (and), it is implied that this is so even in the hereafter. "Artha" means the fruit [of action]. "By the opposite," meaning by sin; the word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction. There is not even misfortune. Why? Because they are free from egoism (*nirahaṅkāriṇām*).

The meaning is that for those distinct from the egoists (*ahaṅkārin*), there is an absence of action because of the absence of ego; thus, they are unstained by karma. "O Lord" (*prabho*) means "O you who are capable of understanding!"—the sense being that this is indeed perfectly understood by you.
Alternatively, he addresses him as "O Lord" (*he īśvara*) with the intention of referring to his status as the Supreme Lord. ||33||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: By the word "ca" (and), it is implied that this applies even in the next world; the word "vā" (or) is used for conjunction. There is not even any lack of purpose. Why? Because for those who are free from ego—meaning those distinct from those possessed of ego—there is no tainting by actions due to the absence of ego; this is the meaning. O Lord, O capable one! This has been understood by you.
The meaning is that he indeed understands correctly. Alternatively, he addresses him with the intention of [recognizing] his lordship: "O Lord! ||33||

The sequence of composition: [this applies] to those who are free from egoism and not possessed [by divine power]. Nevertheless, the meaning is that even so, each respective action occurs solely by the force of *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma). ||33||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, for Rudra and others who are merely lords (*īśvara*), there is neither benefit nor harm in performing auspicious or inauspicious acts due to their sovereignty, because they are devoid of egoism (*nirahaṅkāratvāt*).
But what about this Lord of Lords? To this he says with two verses beginning with "By the performance of virtuous deeds," and so forth. Of these...

For the lords, such as Rudra and others, there exists neither the attainment of desired goals nor the occurrence of undesirable misfortunes in this world through the performance of wholesome deeds or unwholesome deeds respectively; the reason for this is that they are free from egoism. //33//

*Rasikāhlādinī*: If it is asked, "Why do they not act for themselves in the same way that they describe it to others? the author replies with the word *kuśala*. For these lords, there is no personal interest whatsoever in performing virtuous deeds in this world, because they are spontaneously full of bliss.
Even by the practice of unwholesome deeds, no harm exists [for such a person], because for those who are free from egoism,
it is the one possessed of egoism who is subject to the Vedic injunctions and prohibitions that communicate what is to be done and what is to be avoided, and not anyone else;
the sense is that just as there is the attainment of the desired state through prescribed action, so too there is the absence of the undesired state through prohibited action.
The meaning is that one need not fear being tainted by actions for those who are devoid of the conceit of being the agent of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Or rather, the address "O Lord" is used to indicate that [the Lord] is capable of understanding within His own mind; or else, it is an address as "O Lord" intended to make known that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is distinct from all other forms of yoga. ||33||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
How much less so for all beings— animals, mortals, and gods—
the connection with wholesome and unwholesome [karma] belonging to the ruler and those subject to his rule?

Śrīdhara says: He states the subject at hand with the words "What need is there to say more" (*kim uta*). The meaning is: what further need is there to state that no connection with the wholesome or unwholesome exists? ||34||

Vaṃśīdhara: "The subject at hand is the topic under discussion. The meaning is that for the Lord—the controller and regulator—of all those to be ruled, namely animals, birds, humans, and gods (i.e., beasts, fowl, men, and deities), there is no connection with the auspicious or inauspicious, which is to say, no taint of the fruits of merit or demerit. If...

The meaning is this: for those whose egoism has departed through the knowledge obtained by the side-glance of His compassion, there is no connection with the fruits of wholesome or unwholesome actions;
how then could that [connection] belong to the Blessed Lord, the Controller of all? He states the relevant point: "How much more so... (34).

The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā states: "All that which has been said applies only to those who possess the general quality of lordship (*īśvaratva-sāmānyavat*), let alone to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of lords. He says this with the words beginning "kim uta" (let alone).

[He is the] Lord (*īśituḥ*) of all beings (*akhila-sattvānām*), from Brahmā down to the individual souls (*svanv-antānām*), who are subject to His rule (*īśitavyānām*) and pervaded by Him (*vyāpyānām*).

This is the established conclusion: that for Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the all-pervading Lord of all lords, the cause of all causes—there is neither benefit nor harm resulting from the performance of virtuous or non-virtuous deeds. ||34||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Ah! If even for them [the liberated souls] there is an absence of misfortune merely through the state of being devoid of egoism, then how could there be even a suspicion of misfortune for the Supreme Lord who has descended for the welfare of all living beings? This is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*).
To confirm this, he says: "How much more so... [The phrase] "of all beings" (*akhila-sattvānām*) means of all living creatures;

"animals and so forth" refers to those who are, respectively, of tamasic, rājasic, and sāttvic nature. "Of those to be ruled" (*īśitavyānām*) means that they are by their very nature subject to control. By this, it is implied that even the liberated (*muktānām*) are dependent upon Him. [This applies to] both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Merit and demerit: through these two, there is *anvaya*, meaning connection. This is because He is the controller of all, having no other controller, and because of His supreme independence. The sense is that this indeed constitutes what is called "supreme lordship" (*parameśvaratva*). The rest has been explained by them [the commentators]. Alternatively, regarding those who are to be ruled—His devotees—
And how much more so? ||34||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: "Aho! If even for them the absence of misfortune occurs merely through the state of being free from egoism (*nirahaṅkāritā*), then how could there even be a suspicion of misfortune for the Supreme Lord who has descended for their benefit? Thus, strengthening the point by means of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), he says: "What..."?
"Uteti" [means]: Among all sentient beings, those such as animals and so forth are, respectively, tāmasa, rājasa, and sāttvika.

By the phrase "of those to be ruled," meaning those who are by their very nature subject to control, it is indicated that even the liberated (muktas) are dependent upon Him. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *tu* (but/rather). [This refers to] those to be ruled by means of the wholesome and unwholesome—namely, merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*).
The connection with the preceding clause is as follows: "Is that [connection] not indeed even more so present?
This is because there is no other controller due to His being the controller of all. The sense is that this alone is what is called "supreme lordship" (*parameśvaratva*).
According to Amara, *balavat* means "well," *kim uta* means "how much more so," and *suvati* means "exceedingly" or "intensely. (34)

The sequence of the composition: The connection or association of those who are subject to His rule with merit and demerit—namely, virtue and vice—that [association] does not exist for the Lord; how much more so, then, is it utterly absent?
This is the connection with what precedes. According to Amara, *balavat* means "well," *suṣṭhu* means "excellent," *kim uta* means "how much more so," and *svati* means "extremely" or "intensely."

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: What more, then, can be said of this Lord of all lords? He says: "What more, indeed?"—that is, what further need is there to say? Regarding this Ruler, the Lord of all lords, the entire arrangement of the auspicious and inauspicious—the connection between good and evil among those subject to His rule and among His pastimes—is such that every one of His pastimes is of an auspicious nature.
The meaning is as follows: the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that [the Lord is so called] because his conduct is the auspiciousness of all auspicious things.

However, this is not a path for removing the fault of one who is devoted to cowherd women by transgressing *dharma*; rather, this is indeed a transgression of *dharma*. For the cowherd women possess the power of their own bliss (*svānanda-śakti*), and thus their physical union with him is an integral part of that [bliss].
It is indeed spontaneous. ||34||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, if the state of *niṣṭhā* (steadfastness) were to arise merely through the absence of egoism accompanied by knowledge, then what room is there for even the slightest suspicion of harm in the case of one whose very nature is *līlā* (divine play), who has descended for the sake of the welfare of the worlds perceived by Him, and whose egoism is accompanied by divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)?
He states this by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument with the words "how much more" (*kim uta*).

It has been stated that, by the command of the Lord, the attendants (*pārṣadas*) possess the authority to govern all beings— whether insects, animals, mortals, or celestial dwellers— who are characterized as *tāmasa*, *rājasa*, or *sāttvika*, and who are subject to his rule, governed by him, and appointed to their respective offices.

"He is not subject to the sequence of the wholesome and the unwholesome. Thus it has been stated; even in the case of Ajāmila, when he was associated with the unwholesome, the decision was made by the attendants themselves. Since the Supreme Lord is not subject to the control of another, the meaning is that one should not even suspect a connection with merit or demerit—that is, a sequence of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Viśvanātha states the subject at hand: "What more [need be said]? (34).
Those who are satisfied by serving the pollen of his lotus feet,
having shaken off all bonds of karma through the power of yoga;
Even sages move about freely only when they are not bound; for one whose body has been seized by His will, how could there be bondage at all?

Śrīdhara explains this very point: "Those who are satisfied by the service of the dust of whose lotus feet; or alternatively, those for whom there is service to the dust of whose lotus feet—and they are also satisfied—this is the meaning of 'devotees' (bhaktāḥ). Likewise, the wise (jñāninaḥ) are not bound, meaning they have not fallen into bondage."

Vaṃśīdhara: This very point is the *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"). He clarifies or makes manifest [this] by stating that there is no mention of satisfaction in service to the Lord being greater than [service to] animals or dead matter—as seen in such expressions as "May the touch of Your feet be mine day and night. Because this [literal sense] lacks internal consistency (*asvārasya*), he states another meaning, beginning with "Or rather" (*yad vā*). And those...

"Satiated by the nectar of service to Hari, they have attained the sense of 'enough' regarding other objects"—this is the meaning. "We are not satiated with the streams of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories, which bring even small pleasures," according to such statements;
this is the meaning. "Sages" (*munayaḥ*) refers to those whose nature is reflection and who possess knowledge. And likewise, like devotees.

Bondage consists of attachment toward sons and others, taking the form of affection or being produced by past karma; it may also arise from one's own persistence or from the personal desire of devotees. The meaning is that since Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who has assumed a physical form—lacks attachment and other causes of bondage, even the suspicion of bondage does not arise. ||35||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: However, he says that this is not adultery on His part—namely, "because" (*yat*).

Since [the word] "gopīs" is to be supplied after "yā," they have assumed bodies by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; in reality, however, they are the energies of Śrī Kṛṣṇa's own bliss (*svānanda-śakti*). Of these...

The state of being a cowherd girl is merely a dramatic performance for Him; therefore, how could there be bondage? The meaning is that they do not become causes of bondage. What do those [cowherd girls] do when they have assumed their forms?
To this he says: of the dust of whose lotus-feet—that which clings to the lotus-feet—...
They were satiated by the service of the saffron pollen from their own breasts; "niṣeva" means service, and "niṣeva" (as a noun) denotes a constant state of devotion.
Their bonds of all karma were shaken off by the power of that "yoga"—the union with the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—and thus they became such as they were described.
Alternatively, "those whose entire bonds of karma have been shaken off by the power of yoga" is an epithet of the sages;
they move about at will, being fearless from any quarter, self-luminous, or independent, certainly not as the wives of cowherds. Just as the sages are yogis, for even they are not bound or fettered.
That is to say, by means of *prārabdha*-karma; but these [women] are not like that, and therefore they do not become the wives of others. ||35||

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Regarding the word *parāga*, a particular form of devotion is shown through service characterized by extreme humility (*atinamratva*). The prefix *ni-* in the phrase *nitarāṃ seveta* (one should serve constantly) is intended to express that their attachment to service is innate. Alternatively, *parāga* may be intended to mean "distant service," and by the prefix *ni-*...

It has been stated that [the path] requires only a very slight degree of service; nevertheless, they are arrogant because of its greatness, possessed of pride such as fearlessness and the like. For this very reason, they roam at will, disregarding scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, performing actions solely according to their own whims, since they are neither bound nor overwhelmed by them.

In that regard, "due to non-attachment. If the reading is *tṛptāḥ*, the meaning is: "satisfied with that [state], content elsewhere, and having no dependence on anything else. Furthermore, by the power or influence of yoga—whether understood as the eight-limbed path (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or knowledge—the bond consisting of karmas accumulated over infinite millions of births has been specifically shaken off and severed.

Those by whom that form of bondage or the bond itself [is assumed] are even sages (*munayaḥ*). By the word "even" (*api*), the inferiority of the sages compared to the devotees is indicated. With this very intention of [showing their] excellence, they are called "haughty" (*dṛptāḥ*).
Of him by whom the body was assumed—that is, manifested—by his own will, independently; [this refers to one who acts] through supreme will.
"By whom [the forms] were assumed"—meaning the Fish, Tortoise, and other incarnations—thus his supreme sovereignty is stated by virtue of being an *avatāra*.
Therefore, how could there be bondage? Rather, the meaning is that it could not possibly exist in any way.
The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].

Alternatively, "yoga" refers to *bhakti-yoga*; the meaning is that even sages [possess this], let alone those who are devoted from the very beginning. Or rather, what need is there to say? Devotees are also practitioners of yoga (*yogins*). What need is there to say? Practitioners of yoga are also those intent on ritual action (*karma-paras*); thus, they should be understood as being of three kinds. In this regard, among the sages, for the most part...
Through the state of a householder, there is devotion to ritual action (*karma*); nevertheless, their independent conduct arises precisely from their state of being a knower (*jñānin*).

Consequently, knowers themselves are of two kinds: some are devoted to yoga (*yoga-parāḥ*), and some are devoted to action (*karma-parāḥ*). Thus, among these, there is a progressive decrease [in excellence] as one goes further down the list. Everything else is the same. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "also" (*apy-arthe*). What [is the point]?
It must be stated that this applies to them [the men] and to those [the women] as well; and for the sake of dispelling doubt regarding all of them, the word "eva" (only/itself) is used there. ||35||
*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He clarifies that very point by means of another *kaimutya* (argument a fortiori) with the words "yat" (that which).

Because of the correlative connection between "yat" and "tad," and because [the phrase] "by the power of yoga" and so forth is included within that [context], "yat" has the sense of "yasya" (of whom).
The *sul* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*). That [person] whose [mind is fixed] upon the pollen of the two lotus-feet...

The meaning is that they are satisfied by the intense service of the atoms of His splendor through the practice of meditation, having no thought of anything else and being full of love for Him; and those who, by the power of that very yoga—
by the light of the means known as *bhakti-yoga*— have shaken off all bonds of karma, they too [are liberated].

The sages move about at their own will and according to their own desire; they perform both what is prescribed and what is forbidden, yet they are not bound therein. Therefore, how could there be bondage for him?
Rather, the meaning is that there is no bondage at all. Having shown this very point by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument:
He demonstrates his lack of bondage even through the distinction of being a possessor of attributes (viśeṣaṇa) by saying "by will" (icchayā).

This means by mere will, and not due to subjection to karma as is the case with the individual soul (jīva); for he is one by whom a body has been brought even into the phenomenal world (prapañca) through its connection with devotion to Him. Therefore, [this refers] to the grace bestowed upon a particular devotee.

The sequence of verses suggests the thought that, due to his contempt for Durvāsas, he might even transgress some boundary; thus it is said, "by the power of yoga," referring even to those possessed of knowledge. ||35||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Even if He, by virtue of His power to act, not to act, or to act otherwise, possesses activities that transcend both the world and the Vedas, [the author], being possessed by the majesty of the Lord, asks "What does He have to do with that? and speaks as follows, beginning with "Whose lotus feet... and so forth.
Even those whose every bond has been shaken off by the power of yoga,

being satisfied by serving the pollen of His lotus feet, wander at will; being pure, they move about beyond both worldly and Vedic conventions, neither bound nor fettered by auspicious or inauspicious karmas.

Being bound—of what nature are these sages? They have "assumed bodies" (ātta-vapuṣaḥ), meaning they have taken on physical forms out of a desire for the bliss of worship, due to their indifference toward liberation. For it is said that even those who are liberated assume a form by way of divine play (līlayā) and worship the Lord. Is their bondage for the sake of that very Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose service [they seek]? That service to whose feet...
It is that which cuts the bonds; for one who acts according to his own will, how could there be bondage? ||35||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: He clarifies this very point through an argument *a fortiori* (*kaimutya*): "Those who are satisfied by even the mere service—that is, worship characterized by the word 'ni' [in *niṣevā*], which implies a separation [from the dust]—and who perceive this world as something to be abandoned; for 'service,' 'worship,' and 'devotion' (*bhakti*) are synonyms.

The pollen of whose lotus feet—even the worship of that [pollen] consisting of service performed with the prefix *ni-* (implying a distance)—is sufficient for satisfaction; those who possess such a perception of renunciation toward this world are the ones described. "Service" (*sevā*), "worship" (*bhajana*), and "devotion" (*bhakti*) are synonymous terms.

Those who are supremely devoted—meaning the devotees characterized by the hearing and chanting [of the Lord's names]—move about freely due to their being filled with the bliss of devotion and their firm conviction in Him; they perform actions according to their own will, without regard for scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, yet they do not act in ways contrary to devotion, as was the case with Nārada and others. Thus it has been said:
In the *Pādme*: "For Vaiṣṇavas, there exists neither the bondage of karma nor rebirth. This is also stated in the *Ekādaśī-khaṇḍa*:
"Of the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, men, ancestors..."
O King,
he who has with his whole being gone for refuge to Mukunda, the worthy refuge, abandoning all other duties, is neither a servant nor a debtor.

For this very reason, they do not wander about unrestrained, bound by the burden of actions performed according to their own whims, being subject to no one's control. Of what nature are they? Yoga here refers to *bhakti-yoga*; by its power—that is, by its extraordinary majesty of potency—they are "shaken off," meaning they are thoroughly cleansed of all impurities.

Right here, Hari, the Supreme Lord, severs the millions of seeds of all karmic accumulations and prārabdha-karma for His beloved devotee who has abandoned all other inclinations and takes refuge at the base of His own feet.
"Whatever improper action has arisen in any way, He who is seated within the heart shakes it all away" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.42).
Alternatively, even the sages such as Sanaka and others wander according to their own will; yet "artha" (purpose) here is not the primary sense.

It is performed. Of what kind? Those for whom the entire bond of karma has been shaken off—that is, destroyed—by the power of yoga, whether it be the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*) or the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*). As it has been said: "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes" (Gītā 4.37). The word "of that" (*tasya*) refers to that which elsewhere possesses absolute sovereignty.

Or rather, other forms are assumed by His will for the sake of being constrained [by devotees]; or else, it refers to those forms such as the Fish (Matsya) and others which are assumed by Him according to the desire of His devotees. As it is said:
"O You of wide renown, whatever form they conceive in their minds, that very form You assume out of Your grace for the sake of the virtuous" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8.9).

If the independence of the incarnations such as Matsya and others is preceded by such sovereignty, then how could there be bondage for Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the source of incarnations whose glory is unrestrained and who represents the ultimate limit— by means of his various high and low deeds? This is a statement of the supreme *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so") intended for the common folk.

The word "only" (*eva*) is used for the purpose of removing doubt. The thought is: if, by the mere touch of his lotus feet, there is generally an absence of the bondage of karma for devotees, then how could there be any fear for those who are his beloveds and whose very life-sustenance is Śrī Kṛṣṇa? ||35||
Viśvanātha: He states that even his devotees are not bound by merit and demerit with the words "yat...

(That which...). *Niṣeva* means constant service. Through the power of that *bhakti-yoga*, the bondage of karma of all those who perceive their own [true] nature is shaken off; how much more so for himself? By whom [are they shaken off]? By those [devotees].

The sages (*munayaḥ*), whose nature is contemplation, though they are devotees, are not bound—that is, they do not incur bondage. But as for him, he has assumed or taken possession of bodies—the bodies of other men's wives—by his own unrestrained will alone. //35//
He who moves within all embodied beings— the gopīs, their husbands, and everyone else— is the Supreme Overseer; he assumes a body here for the sake of divine play.

Śrīdhara: Having previously resolved the objection by accepting that the gopīs were the wives of others, he now states that for the Blessed One, who is the inner controller of all, there is no such thing as "serving the wives of others"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with *gopīnām*.

He who moves within as the presiding overseer and witness of the intellect and so forth, he alone, through his divine play (*krīḍana*), assumes a body; [it is not that he acts out of worldly passion].
[This is] because [he] would be equal to us and others, whereby there would be a fault. ||36||

Vaṃśīdhara: In reality, the gopīs do not possess the status of being another's wives, because they were married according to the Gāndharva rite. Nevertheless, following the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied even by what is accepted through persistence," that objection was addressed by accepting and acknowledging it—[as stated in] the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*: "Obeisances to the lotus feet... [BhP 10.47.58].

This has been answered by [the verses beginning with] 10.33.34. He says "Now" (idānīm) to show that, upon investigation of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), the Blessed One's act of going to another's wife does not truly occur. "None" (na kācit) means not even anything at all. He who is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is Kṛṣṇa himself.
By means of play (krīḍana), that is, as a pastime (līlā), he is here in this world; "possessing a body" (deha-bhāk) means one who has manifested a physical form.
[From here onwards, it is according to the commentary of Viśvanātha. ||36||

The Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā clarifies this very point for the sake of restraining those who are extroverted with two verses beginning with "gopīnām": "He who possesses a body for play (krīḍana-deha-bhāk) assumes the bodies of the gopīs as his playthings; thus he is the presiding witness (adhyakṣa), manifest (pratyakṣa) indeed as the inner controller (antaryāmī). Therefore, his transcendence (paratva)..."
The meaning is "of that [person]," so it is said. ||36||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Thus, even while accepting that the gopīs were the wives of others, the fault has been removed. In that case, however, their status as unchaste women (*kulaṭā*) and their status as mistresses (*jāra*) does not disappear; indeed, such a name does not ultimately result in anything other than reproach. Unable to tolerate this, [the author] establishes their status as the wives of others.

Thus he refutes [the objection]. "Of the cowherd women" (*gopīnām*)—this has been explained by them [the commentators] as meaning that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the witness of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. Therefore, since there is no one else superior (*para*) to Him, who indeed could be another's wife (*para-dārāḥ*)?
This is the intended sense.
[Objection: But is it not heard that He is formless? Therefore, because He possesses form, is He not exactly like us and others?

[Reply: No; regarding this, he says: "He Himself" (*sa eva*). This word *eva* is drawn from the phrase *caiva*. And here, the word *ca* does not exist in some versions. [The phrase] "by means of sport" (*krīḍanena*) means by His own will at His pleasure, and not...

The meaning is that, by virtue of being subject to the power of karma, He becomes the cause and the impeller within the appropriate body and in the appropriate place. Because there is no dependence on any form in His state as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin), He is described there as being "formless" (nirākāra), but not so in reality.

The sense is that some [hold this view] because of the second-person usage in the statement: "They see the Person, the size of a thumb, dwelling within the space of the heart of their own bodies" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.2.8);
however, it is not as with the individual souls such as ourselves, who are mutually dependent on non-self and subject to karma.

The meaning is as follows: there is a reading "eṣa krīḍana-deha-bhāg" (he is the one who possesses a body for play), and another reading "krīḍaneneha deha-bhāg" (possessing a body here through play). Alternatively, he who moves within all beings, such as the gopīs, in the form of the Supreme Self, bestowing their respective qualifications, is indeed the Adhyakṣa—the presiding controller. [What then of] the gopīs?

For those women who manifested such specific states of being characterized by *mamatā* (possessive attachment), as expressed in passages beginning with "He acted... (*bhā.pu.* 10.21.9), "O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā... (*bhā.pu.* 10.22.4), and "Ah! In Madhupurī... (*bhā.pu.* 10.47.21), their presiding witness was indeed the form of their husband.
This is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: "In what way does He play in the form of the Supreme Self, and in what way does He play in this [human] form?
To that, he says: This very Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is manifest externally, is the means for such play.
It occupies the body and constantly supports it, but it is not the innermost Supreme Self (paramātman) residing within.
Even in the alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*), the phrase "here [it is] only in the form manifest externally," and so forth, should be applied.

Thus, in the subsequent [section] as well, this is for the purpose of avoiding the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the status of being one's own wife (*svadāratva*) in the case of the doctrine of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*).

Something else has been brought forward and explained; nevertheless, according to Rukmiṇī’s words beginning with, "Their bodies are filled with feces and urine, their skin, beards, nails, body hair, and head hair... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.45), [it is understood].

The activity of Him, whose body is the supreme light consisting of the manifestation of pure being, reveals only its loathsomeness, and does not inspire delight such that one would become intent upon it merely by hearing of those pastimes—according to the principle of *bhā.pu. 10.33.37*. Therefore:

It is taught that for some women who have entered the inner apartments and whose bodies are not yet perfected, there is the casting off of those very bodies. Nor should it be thought otherwise because such activity is observed even among maidservants and the like; for it is said: "From the touch of Mukunda, she immediately became the most excellent of women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.42.8).

By such statements as these, it is understood that—just like the accounts of the touchstone, the philosopher's stone, and the magnet, or like the eternal body (dhruva-deha)—having attained the state of being supreme women characterized by bodies suitable for Him, the capacity for His pastimes arose within them. Furthermore, one should not consider even these [other celestial maidens] to possess such a nature, as they were shaken off by them [the gopīs]. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa)

In passages such as this (10.32.10), on the contrary, it is stated that He shone even more intensely because of them. Furthermore, from statements such as "He is not a limb of Śrī" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.58), their worthiness and supremacy are established over Śrī herself, over the celestial women, and indeed over all other women.

It is obtained. Since it was stated with emphasis, "How could there be another?", therefore, because their distinctness is understood, a different explanation must be made precisely on the basis of that distinctness. For instance, [there is a distinction] between the gopīs and those specific [others], as well as between their husbands and those who are currently their husbands.

He who moves within and conquers all perceived beings, as well as all embodied ones such as cowherds and cattle— according to the vision expressed in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.90.48, "He who dwells within the abode of living beings," and according to the manner of *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.14.32, "Oh, what fortune!
Oh, what fortune!"— he who stands among the cows, he who [leads] the cows...

"He protects" (pālayati)—according to the *Tāpanī* Śruti, He eternally sports with pastimes appropriate for that [state]. That Śrī Kṛṣṇa, though manifest as the presiding lord (*adhyakṣa*) of worldly beings, moves about and performs only those pastimes appropriate for each [condition]. This is the cause for His sporting in both ways. This is so.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa is by nature playful and is characterized by manifesting the form of Śrī Gopāla. Alternatively, even while being perceptible to the world, He sports by engaging with those very bodies—the gopīs and others—which are His own playful forms and the instruments of His pastimes. This is also the case in another reading.

"Characterized by play" means bodies that have that very form. Thus, because they dwell with Him eternally in that same manner, they possess the state of being His eternal beloveds. Consequently, their identity as bodies resembling His is not explicitly shown.
In this regard, within the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*), doubt is expressed by one who describes the supreme relationship [between them and Him].

Furthermore, out of the intensity of his blissful absorption, Śrī Śukadeva himself clearly stated their nature as being that very form, saying "the beloveds of Adhokṣaja" (*adhokṣaja-priyāḥ*) and "the beloveds of the Blessed One" (*bhagavat-priyāḥ*), and [referring to them as] "the wives of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇa-vadhvaḥ*) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.7]. And in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*, Durvāsas said to them directly: "He who dwells among the cows... [Goṭā Upaniṣad].

In such passages as [2.23], by describing the supreme relationship with the words "for He becomes your Master," that very point is established by the method of *kaimutya* (the principle of the obvious) regarding the unmanifest pastimes, which are free from doubt.
Furthermore, in the *Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣara-paṭala*, Lord Brahmā states in his own *Saṃhitā*:
He who, being the self of all, dwells in Goloka itself by means of those very digits (kalās) which are manifested from the essence of bliss and consciousness as His own inherent nature.
"I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person" (Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa 5.48).

Here, although they have attained the status of being His own essential nature (*nija-rūpa*) by virtue of being His portions (*kalā*), this is stated as "by way of their own essential nature" (*nija-rūpatayā*) in order to dispel any doubt regarding their being "belonging to others" (*parakīyatva*) within the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*). And this very point is present in both the introduction and the conclusion concerning them.
By the mention of Lakṣmī-hood and Supreme Personhood (parama-puruṣatva) in that [verse], it is determined in the very same way;

for instance, in the passage beginning with "in the palaces amidst clusters of wish-fulfilling gems" (Brahma Purāṇa 5.29), the opening is: "[the Lord] being served with the flurry of hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs."
"The beloveds of Śrī, and the Supreme Person is their beloved; they are wish-fulfilling trees"—this is the concluding summary.
This applies both there and elsewhere. They are directly designated by the term "gopīs."

Likewise, the venerable mantras, headed by the eighteen-syllabled one, remain speaking in that very manner. And so it is stated in the *Gautamīya Tantra* within the commentaries on those respective mantras:
"The venerable feet of the divine sages (*devarṣi*), who were the seers of those respective mantras and who hold them as primary, [proclaim] the name of the Blessed Lord."
Even disregarding conventional usage for the sake of engaging those with external perspectives,

they explain the two-fold nature of the Lord of All through the distinction between the splendor of *māyā* and the essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), in order to inspire the devotion of those internal devotees who have entered into meditation upon Him and His beloved consort.

Out of a preference for that very state of being the husband of Śrī Gopālī, they have established that the form of Śrī Gopāla culminates ultimately in that [state] as the superior position; and therein, by means of the word "eva" (only/alone), they have refuted His well-known status as a paramour in the manifest pastimes. As it is said:
One should know that "gopī" is primordial nature (prakṛti) and "jana" is the aggregate of the principles (tattvas).
The Lord is the support of these two by virtue of pervasion and causality;
He is described as the supreme light of intense bliss, existing as the Beloved.
Alternatively, the gopīs are *prakṛti* and the people are the circle of her portions;
the beloved of these two is declared to be the Lord known as Kṛṣṇa, the Sovereign.
Therefore, by means of the Vedas, He is celebrated as the Lord of cause and effect.
"Or rather, he is the very husband of the gopīs who have attained perfection through many births;
he is called the son of Nanda, the increaser of the joy of the three worlds.
Regarding this, [the Lord said]: "Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna."

As in [Gītā 4.5], this very passage clarifies that they have indeed been brought down through a lineage established since beginningless time by means of the Śrutis, Purāṇas, Tantras, and so forth; therefore, in reality, they do not even possess the status of another's wife, let alone be unfit.
The state of being. ||36||
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: The connection of this [verse] is with the word "sa" (he). He alone has become manifest as "this" [person].

He is the "overseer" (*adhyakṣa*) either by virtue of being a portion of Him or by being impelled by Him; for the investigation of reality culminates in His very state of being the enjoyer. Or rather, even in the case of the Māyāvādins, regarding His nature as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).

According to the Advaita interpretation, since there is no status as another's wife (*para-dāratva*), the pursuit of another's wife does not exist; thus, [the objection] is refuted. For this very reason, it is said "of all" (*sarveṣām*) in order to establish His nature as the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*).
This [Lord], the lover of the Gopīs, acts "by way of play" (*krīḍanena*); the meaning is "by means of sport" (*līlayā*). Alternatively, it means "for the sake of play" (*krīḍanena hetunā*).
The meaning is "for the sake of sport. "Possessing a body" means manifesting His own glorious form. The rest has been explained by them [the commentators].
Alternatively, the meaning is that He is the "Supervisor," the presiding controller of all minds and the impeller of all the senses.
For this very reason, he moves within; thus, by acting as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) through the instigation of all actions,
just as there may be no staining of him by their virtues or faults, so too,
for others who act in all works with the vision of the inner controller, there may likewise be no staining by them.

The sense is that it may be so here as well. In that regard, among the gopīs and others, due to the varying degrees of the manifestation of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), their [bondage] is understood to decrease progressively; thus, the absence of the previously mentioned bondage through supreme sovereignty is indicated as the cause. And this is especially so for the sake of the *rāsa*-dance pastimes.
The meaning is that he who possesses a body has manifested a form as a beautiful young cowherd (gopa-kiśora) suitable for that [pastime].

The essential principle of the established doctrine is that for one who has descended for the purpose of expanding the mellows of divine love (prema-rasa), conduct corresponding to that [purpose] alone is appropriate. ||36||

*Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* (171): Thus, the manifest pastimes (*prakaṭa-līlā*) have been shown according to their intrinsic nature. Now, he describes the two types of unmanifest pastimes (*aprakaṭa-līlā*) through specific meanings, beginning with the words "of the gopīs": [He manifests] within, that is, in such a way as to remain internal and unmanifest, for the gopīs and their husbands.

He who, assuming a body for play among those who consider Him their Lord, moves about and sports as their sovereign by virtue of His status as the crown prince of Gokula— even while manifesting His divine pastimes—
He likewise assumes a body for play for all embodied beings dwelling within the universe, and for them...

Even while acting as their supervisor (*adhyakṣa*) by virtue of being their protector (*pālaka*), he moves among them. Therefore, because they have been accepted from time immemorial as his playmates (*krīḍā-śālin*), there is in reality no fault of adultery (*para-dāra-tā-doṣa*) in union with those who are of the nature of his own powers (*tac-chakti-rūpā*). Consequently, he possesses the status of their husband (*tat-patitva*). Indeed, they did not feel resentment.

According to the direction to be explained in passages such as *kṛṣṇāya* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.37], for them and for her, this was merely a matter of perception and not physical; and that production of such a perception was for the purpose of nourishing their longing—thus has the ultimate limit of the established doctrine of that section been shown. ||36||

The structural arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): Although it is explained here according to the commentary that for the gopīs there are no such things as "the Supreme Lord’s wife" (*para-dārā*), this explanation does not contradict their unworthiness [to be approached]. ||36||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Furthermore, the cowherd women are like dolls for His play, being no different from His play-body; His worship of them is not merely an external pastime, for His state as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmitā*) is indeed His external pastime. Thus he says, beginning with "Of the gopīs," etc. He is this very one.

The description of His essential nature is as follows: Śrī Kṛṣṇa possesses a body for pastimes, and the goddesses of Vraja possess bodies for pastimes; He enjoys them. The suffix *kvip* is used here in the sense of habitual action. He is the presiding lord (*adhyakṣaḥ*), meaning directly perceptible (*pratyakṣa*).
He moves within all embodied beings—the gopīs, their husbands, and everyone else—in the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) and the master of the gopīs; He is the master of all those who merely appear as masters, as well as of all embodied beings.
However, His status as the inner controller is not common to all the gopīs, because His very nature is one of blissful form (*ānanda-vigraha*).
