By this it is shown that His sporting with the women of Vraja is indeed a pastime of His own essential nature (*svarūpa-vihāra*), and not [a mere concession].
The meaning is that it is a transgression of the Dharma. ||36||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Previously, having accepted that the gopīs were the wives of others, the objection regarding the verse beginning with "yat-pāda-paṅkaja" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.34] was resolved; now, however, there is no such thing as "another" (para) by whom the status of being another's wife could apply to the gopīs—this is the response given to certain individuals seated in the assembly.
Seeing the lack of joy on the faces of those turned outward, He, as their inner controller,

reveals His primary lordship over all living beings— both female and male— and declares His supreme sovereignty by being untouched by the attributes of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "Within [the hearts] of the gopīs and their husbands..."

He always moves within the hearts of the gopīs, manifesting there in His own essential form; He moves within all their husbands and within all embodied beings by means of His power. The word "eva" (indeed) serves as a constant restatement. As it has been said by the Blessed One’s own mouth: "The saintly are My heart; I am the heart of the saintly. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa)

[This is according to Pāṇini 9.4.68. Here, there is a statement of its own form (*svarūpa*), whereas elsewhere it is by means of its attribute (*dharma*). For this very reason, the *adhyakṣa* is the witness (*sākṣin*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. By this, its status as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is stated.
Now, if it is thus the witness of the intellect and so forth, then would there not be a perception [of it] as being formless (*nirākāra*)? No.

He said: "By means of play—that is, for the sake of pastimes such as the *rāsa* dance—he assumes a body. For play is an activity that depends upon a circle of dear associates (*priya-varga*). Just as, despite being eternally connected through His nature as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) and despite initiating all activities, He remains untainted by the respective merits and defects [of those activities], so too [is He here]."

The sense is that the form consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss remains untainted by high and low actions. Or rather, he who moves within is the presiding witness; for the sake of sport, like an actor, he assumes a human body through his divine play.

Now, if He is the Supreme Self, how could He have had contact with a despised Sairandhrī? To this he will provide the answer: "By the touch of Mukunda, she immediately became the most excellent of women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.42.8). The divine form possesses a single nature both externally and internally; it is not worldly.

And it has been said: "For such a capacity cannot belong to anyone else," meaning that even upon contact with a *sairindhrī* [outcaste woman], there is freedom from defilement; yet, one should not infer that these [women] possess a resemblance to a *sairindhrī*.
This is not the favor of Śrī, whose limbs are ever devoted to Him;
how much less so that of the celestial nymphs, who possess the fragrance and luster of lotuses?
For during His Rāsa festival, their necks were grasped by His staff-like arms— [whereas others were not].
"He who arose for those beloved women of Vraja who had received His blessing" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.60).

Otherwise, Uddhava’s prayer for the dust of their feet would not be appropriate. Therefore, the gopīs cannot be considered the wives of others, nor can Śrī Kṛṣṇa be considered a paramour by comparison with other embodied beings.

Because it is the primary master of all embodied beings by virtue of being the initiator of all actions and the enjoyer of the fruits of all actions— and because this is the final conclusion reached through the systematic synthesis of all scriptures, and because the principle that "the fruit of a scripture belongs to its performer" applies— there is nothing whatsoever inconsistent [in this view]. ||36||
Viśvanātha: However, from that particular perspective, there are none who are "other" than the Blessed Lord, the inner controller of all;

thus he says, "Of the gopīs... The sense is: what fault is there in embracing externally him who moves within? The term *adhyakṣaḥ* means the witness of the intellect and so forth. Regarding the sight of his secret and external limbs...

"What is the fault?"—this is the sense. Here, in the circle of Vraja, for the sake of sporting, he attends to the bodies—the bodies of the gopīs—by wiping away the sweat caused by the fatigue of amorous play and so forth. (36)
Having assumed a human body for the sake of favoring his devotees,
he engages in such pastimes that upon hearing of them, one may become intent upon him.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "If this is so, why would one whose desires are fulfilled engage in what is censured? To this he says:

"For the sake of grace" (*anugrahāya*). The meaning is: in order to make even those who are extremely extroverted—whose minds are drawn away by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*)—devoted to Him alone. ||37||

Vaṃśīdhara: Here he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). If this is so, then even for one who is free from desire, although he may assume a body by his own will, [the following applies] regarding the contemptible... [the Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā states]: such pastimes are performed solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon the devotees.

He engages in amorous pastimes with the gopīs, and by hearing of them, His devotees experience supreme bliss. Indeed, the devotees who possess the latent desire for rasa are delighted by this very pastime because of its social nature; having heard of it, they do not merely occupy a human body as ordinary humans do.
But one who possesses discernment and similar qualities becomes intent upon that; and this will be stated later:
"And this sport of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.40), and so forth. ||37||

*Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: Now, one might ask: how can there be any inclination toward play for one whose desires are already fulfilled? And how much less so toward that which is censured by the world from the perspective of outsiders? To this, he says: "Anu" (following). It is for the sake of favoring His devotees—for the amusement of My devotees—that I perform various activities.

From the words of the Blessed Lord in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Having assumed a human form, though He Himself is the support of all by virtue of His nature as Brahman, He has made [Himself] a support. Thus, the state of being the supreme support of that whose essential nature is the Supreme Brahman is demonstrated. This is stated in the tenth [book]:

"The tenth objective is that which consists of the non-distinction between the support and the supported" (*Bhāvārtha-dīpikā* 10.1.1). And likewise, the *Bhagavad-upaniṣad* states: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (*Gītā* 14.27).
Even if the reading were *āsthitaḥ*, the meaning remains the same: that He has been made the object of reverence.
It is not tenable to explain that he has now assumed a human body by his own will, because in that other world,
the Supreme Brahman in the form of a person named Kṛṣṇa was experienced by the venerable cowherds as their presiding deity. Thus...

It is intended that such play is for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees. Even though His desires are already fulfilled, the act of bestowing grace upon devotees is appropriate because it is the very nature of one whose essence is pure (*viśuddha-sattva*). This is observed elsewhere as well, in whatever state of being one is conditioned; for example, in the life of Śrī Jaḍabharata, who was a benefactor to Rahūgaṇa, or as follows:

"In me, who am favored by you. In this context, by the word *bhakta* (devotee), all the goddesses of Vraja, all the people of Vraja belonging to the three periods of time, and other Vaiṣṇavas are included.

[The distinction is made] by means of the goddesses of Vraja through their *pūrvarāga* (premonition of love) and so forth, the people of Vraja through their births and so forth, and others through [their respective spiritual states].
Because through seeing, hearing, and so forth regarding each of those [pastimes], there arises a manifestation of their unprecedented nature; for this very reason,

by association with such devotees, He engages in those same kinds of play that captivate the hearts of all, hearing which even a person other than the devotees would become intent upon them— how much more so [the devotees themselves]?
The meaning is: "having heard this Rāsa-līlā. And it will be said: "And this sport of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.40), and so forth.
Or rather, every living being who has taken recourse to a human body should become devoted to that [Lord] in the mortal world.

Because she is the primary means of worship through the descent of the Śrī Bhagavān, and because for human beings alone the hearing and other practices thereof are easily accomplished; and regarding the reading "of all beings" (bhūtānām),
it refers to all people, including those attached to sense objects, by virtue of their connection with the devotees who are the cause of His own descents.

This means [it is for] those seeking liberation and those already liberated. Thus, supreme compassion alone is stated to be the cause. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the grace toward all occurs solely through the connection of devotion (*bhajana*). Other matters were [discussed] by them. In that context, the phrase "even those who are extroverted" intends to express that [devotion] extends even to them.
Because it consists of the ultimate pinnacle of supreme love, even Śrī Śuka was impelled toward an excessive description of it.
Regarding the phrase "of the gopīs," it has been explained in another sense as follows:
"But even so, let Him sport in that manner eternally and secretly; what need is there for those belonging to the mundane world?"

By what means was He revealed? To this he replies: For the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees situated within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), He took recourse in a human body—a mortal form that is a portion of the cosmic body (*virāḍ-deha*)—and thus became manifest therein.
This is the meaning. As the scripture states: "He whose body is the earth," and so forth. Even there...
Because of the use of the word "body" (*śarīra*) for that [state], and because it is indicated by the word "human" (*mānuṣa*) as belonging to that world;
the rest is the same.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "he may become intent upon that," since there is a plurality of beings who are devotees, they [are not meant here].

[If it were not so,] they would follow [the Lord] through transformation and so forth by virtue of being agents; furthermore, in another interpretation, difficulties such as supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*) and the like would arise. However, the term "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is obtained from the context itself even in those various interpretations.
Therefore, He engages in such sports that even upon hearing of them, [one is moved], and He Himself [participates].
"He should be intent upon that. The meaning is simply this: whenever he hears [it], at those very times he becomes absorbed in it.

*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*: He elaborates on this very point with the words "for the sake of grace" (*anugrahāya*). Alternatively, being manifest (*adhyakṣaḥ* = *pratyakṣaḥ*), for the purpose of sport—that is, for the sake of His own play—those who have descended as bodies [are meant].

He is so called because He enjoys and delights those very people—the gopīs or the inhabitants of Vraja. Therefore, since they serve as the instruments for His play as He moves within and without them, the sense is that no fault whatsoever can accrue to Him through His pastimes; this is the general direction of the argument. Enough with excessive elaboration. [This applies] to the devotees.

"For the sake of favor"—meaning, "I perform various activities for the amusement of My devotees," according to such words of the Śrīmad-Bhagavat; having assumed a human form, He manifested [Himself]. Or rather, the sentence concludes with "He manifested. Thus, for the sake of favoring His devotees.

That is intended to mean "His play. In this context, by the word *bhakta* (devotee), all the gopīs and the people of Vraja, as well as others connected with the three periods of time and other Vaiṣṇavas, are included.
Alternatively, although the gopīs alone are mentioned as the primary devotees, by the inclusion of the primary ones, others are also implied.

The favoring of all is indeed desired. For this very reason, He "enjoys" (bhajate) His play; the meaning is that He brings it about with delight. By way of wordplay (*śleṣa*), it may also mean that He "follows" or "manifests" [His play]. Thus, the eternally established nature of His plays is indicated. And by that, every fault is naturally dispelled.
The meaning is that they are of such an indescribable nature as to attract all hearts. By means of a pun (*śleṣa*), the sense is:
if even by hearing of the pastimes similar to the *rāsa* dance one may become intent upon them, how much more so by witnessing the *rāsa* pastime itself?
By the word "that" (*tat*), it may refer to the Blessed Lord, the devotees, the pastimes, or indeed every person.
Alternatively, every living being who has assumed a human body should be intent upon that [the Lord]. In the mortal world,

because the Blessed Lord descends as an incarnation and because worship through the appropriate means of devotional yoga is most accessible for humans, happiness belongs to humans alone, as they achieve the perfection of hearing and other such practices.

Alternatively, the verse should be explained by introducing the word *api* (even): "Even though he has resorted to a human body—how much more so in the case of sages, gods, and others. From this, the intended meaning is that this [manifestation] is solely for the sake of favoring his devotees.
Regarding the reading *bhūtānām*, it refers to all people whatsoever: those attached to sense objects, those seeking liberation, and those who are liberated.
"And for His devotees"—this is the meaning. Thus, supreme compassion has been described.

In this way, by the verse beginning with "How could He [be the destroyer] of the bridges of dharma" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.27), the answer to one question is provided: namely, how He could have acted in a manner contrary to dharma.

By such statements as *dharma-vyatikramaḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.29) and others, as well as by *tathā āpta-kāmaḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.28), one must discern that for the Perfect One there can be no desire; therefore, the phrase "for the sake of favoring the second" (*anugrahāya*) is to be understood as the reason. ||37||
Regarding the sequence of composition: if those [mantras] were indeed arranged by others, such an arrangement would be inconsistent;
for if there were malice toward them on the part of many, then [statements such as] "that which is a friend, supreme bliss," and so forth, would be contradicted. ||37||

*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*: Now, one might ask: "In that case, why did he manifest such a secret pastime on earth? To this he replies with the words beginning "for the sake of grace" (*anugrahāya*). For the sake of gracing his devotees, he engages in such pastimes, hearing which anyone who has taken up a human body may become devoted to them.

One should become devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Devotees are indeed diverse, owing to the diversity of aesthetic flavor (rasa). Therefore, He performs pastimes consisting of various rasas, according to the differences in the inclinations and modes of worship of each individual. Thus, the pastimes exist solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon the devotees. By hearing of them, some person who possesses a human body [attains the goal].
The meaning is "he is liberated. ||37||

*Rasikāhlādinī*: Now, one might ask: "How can there even be play for one whose desires are fulfilled, since there is no purpose? For even a fool does not engage in action without aiming at some purpose. To this, he says: "For the sake of grace" (*anugrahāya*).
He has assumed a human form solely for the purpose of showing grace to His devotees. As it has been said:
At the beginning of the tenth book (*daśama-skandha*), in the tenth chapter, the tenth objective is stated as "the union of the supported and the support" (*āśritāśraya-vigraha*).
This has been said in the Upaniṣad:
"Some say creation is for the sake of enjoyment; others say it is for the sake of sport."
"This is indeed the very nature of the Lord; for one whose desires are fulfilled, what longing could there be?

Thus, it is solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees that He engages in such pastimes that imitate human beings and imitate all states of mind—or rather, He performs other pastimes similar to the *rāsa*-pastime. As for play (*krīḍā*):...
It is dependent upon His own circle of dear ones; or rather, for the sake of bestowing grace upon all the devotees of Vraja;

or rather, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the devotee-gopīs, He engages in such pastimes that are beyond the reach of words; or rather, [it is for] the grace toward the devotees which resides within Himself.

The meaning is that she has attained for his sake such things as side-glances, falling [at his feet], and embraces. She indulges in those aforementioned pastimes, such as the stretching out of arms and so forth, hearing which every person would become devoted to them.

Or rather, for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees, such as the gopīs and others, He assumed a human body of a similar nature, a human form; for it would not have been possible to transmit bliss to them through a body of a different species. Such indeed is the pastime consisting of concealment (nirodha), which is His divine sovereignty.
Having set aside His own bliss with the gopīs, He moved on; thus, according to the reading "bhūtānām," for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who are liberated or seeking liberation,
He engages in other pastimes similar to the rāsa dance so as to make even them devoted to Him— pastimes which, upon hearing, one becomes intent upon and devoted to the service of the gopīs.
The meaning is that without the grace of the gopīs, even hearing of their secret pastimes is difficult to attain.
This was said by Uddhava: "O, may I become one who enjoys the dust of the feet of these women" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.60).
Or rather, having heard this, even another living being who has assumed a human body...
One should be intent upon that. ||36||

Viśvanātha: He provides the answer to the second question—“What was the intention behind his contemptuous act?”—with the words “for the sake of grace” (*anugrahāya*). For the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, he engages in such pastimes; hearing which, the individual soul (*jīva*) who has assumed a human body becomes intent upon that [grace].
It is understood that one should possess faith directed toward that [divine play],

for this play— which consists of sweet nectar (*madhura-rasa*)— possesses a certain inconceivable power, like that of jewels, mantras, and great medicinal herbs, which distinguishes it from other forms of play. In the same way, [this power exists] only for one who possesses a human body.
It is intended that eligibility for devotion to Him is the primary [qualification]. ||36||
Indeed, deluded by his illusory power, the inhabitants of Vraja felt no resentment toward Kṛṣṇa,
for they each imagined their own wives to be standing right by their own sides.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely others who follow different practices also say that their own conduct is exactly like this; to that he replies with the words "without envy. The sense is that those who act in such a manner while lacking such sovereignty (aiśvarya) should be known as sinful. || 38 ||
Vaṃśīdhara:
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā:
Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī.
*Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī*:
*Krama-sandarbha*;
*Bṛhat-krama-sandarbha*.
*Rasikāhlādinī*:
Viśvanātha says:
[This is for] those who, free from envy, practice the discipline of such a woman as imagined through *māyā*.
"There shall never again be union with the husbands of the queens of Vraja" (Uṇī.
3.32). Therefore: "Because of the inconceivable power of the Lord, of His beloveds, of the abode, and of the sacred law (samaya), what indeed is not possible here? (La.Bhā. 1.5.515).
When the night had turned to dawn, the cowherd women, beloved of the Blessed One and approved by Vāsudeva,
returned to their own homes against their will.
Śrīdhara: When the Brahma-muhūrta of the Brahman-night has arrived, that is, when it has come. ||38||
